title: dxsrc’s Global RSS Feed Is Now a Paid Feature
description:
TL;DR: Access to dxsrc’s main feed—which features some exclusive content—now requires becoming a dxsrc supporter.

Over the years, dxsrc has become one of the leading sources of frontend development news and tools. dxsrc’s growing archives provide unique access to the history of the wider field of web development.

Providing this service for free is not sustainable, however. Book sales pay for some of the work, but so far, few people acknowledge dxsrc’s value by supporting the project on Open Collective.

Starting today, the global RSS feed (with the 250 newest articles and videos) is a paid feature.

You can secure access by a monthly or yearly contribution.

If you don’t like to support dxsrc, you can still follow dxsrc’s individual topic feeds as well as dxsrc’s social media accounts on Mastodon and Bluesky. These are less convenient and reliable but still workable options to stay up-to-date.

Also, if you want to support dxsrc in a different manner and so that the main feed may be made free again, consider buying dxsrc’s books or contributing to the project on Open Collective. You’re not alone: We do the same for the projects we use and like. Thank you.

title: October 23, 2026
description:
API Gateway

Deprecated

Negative backend deadlines are deprecated

A negative backend deadline in an OpenAPI 2.0 x-google-backend extension or a gRPC BackendRule uses the default deadline, the same as 0. Negative values there are deprecated and will be rejected in a future release; until then, creating an API config with one returns a warning in the operation metadata. OpenAPI 3.x backends already reject a negative deadline. To use the default, omit the field or set it to 0.

For more information, see OpenAPI 2.0 extensions and OpenAPI 3.x extensions.

Cloud Database Migration Service

Security

On Saturday, October 17, 2026, Google received a report from a security researcher regarding the compromise of private keys associated with eight eMudhra subordinate Certification Authority (CA) certificates, including those cross-signed by AAA Certificate Services. Consequently, these CA certificates are no longer trusted and are being revoked.

To continue connecting to a source database after its CA certificate is updated, upload the new CA certificate to the Database Migration Service source connection profile:

  • Update the connection profile using gcloud database-migration connection-profiles update or the connectionProfiles.patch API method.
  • Modify the connection profile in the Google Cloud console:
    • MySQL connection profiles
    • PostgreSQL to Cloud SQL connection profiles
    • PostgreSQL to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL connection profiles
    • Oracle to Cloud SQL connection profiles
    • Oracle to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL connection profiles
    • SQL Server to Cloud SQL connection profiles
    • SQL Server to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL connection profiles

For more information, see security bulletin GCP-2026-071.

Fixed

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Security

In response to GCP-2026-071, Google is updating Cloud SQL's managed components. No manual updates to the certificate store are required for Cloud SQL-managed instances. The fix is shipping in a new maintenance version that will be applied during scheduled maintenance. You can also apply the fix by performing self-service maintenance. An announcement will be published when the self-service maintenance fix is available.

What should I do?

  • If you use the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy, then upgrade the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy to 2.26.3 or later and the Cloud SQL Proxy Operator to 1.8.4 or later. If you run the standalone proxy binary, then also update the host's certificate authority (CA) certificates.

  • If you use a Cloud SQL Language Connector, then update the language runtime and operating system CA certificates used with the Cloud SQL Language Connector (for example, Go 1.26.10 or 1.27.3 or later, certifi 2026.10.19 or later).

  • If you're using the gcloud CLI to install the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy, then update the gcloud CLI to 590.0.1.

title: October 30, 2026
description:
Agent Registry

Feature

Agent Registry supports cross-project management boundaries (Preview), letting you centrally discover, search, and govern AI agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and tools across multiple Google Cloud projects from a central management project. For more information, see Cross-project boundaries and Configure a management boundary for multiple projects.

AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Fixed

For AlloyDB clusters compatible with PostgreSQL 18 or later, an instance restart is no longer required when you enable or edit Advanced Query Insights settings, including changing the query length or enabling active query analysis. For clusters compatible with PostgreSQL 17 or earlier, saving changes still requires an instance restart.

For more information, see Use Advanced Query Insights and Monitor active queries.

Apigee hybrid

Announcement

v1.16.13

On October 30, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, v1.16.13.

  • For information about upgrading, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid to v1.16.13.
  • For information about new installations, see The big picture.
Note: Do not use Apigee hybrid v1.16.12 due to a potential regression in apigee-connect-agent (see known issue 578314600). Use v1.16.13 instead.
Note: This is a patch release. The container images used in patch releases are integrated with the Apigee hybrid Helm charts. Upgrading to a patch by using the Helm chart automatically updates the images. You don't typically need to make manual image changes. For information about container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Feature

New ApigeeValkey custom resource

Apigee hybrid v1.16.13 adds the ApigeeValkey custom resource definition (CRD), the apigee-valkey Helm chart, and the valkey configuration properties. ApigeeValkey is the replacement for the ApigeeRedis resource.

In version 1.16.13, the runtime continues to use ApigeeRedis. When you upgrade, install the new CRD with the other CRDs. Leave the new ao.args.valkeyBackend property set to its default value, false. You don't need to install the apigee-valkey chart or change your configuration.

For the supported upgrade sequence, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid. For more information about the resource, see Kubernetes resources.

Bug ID Description
578314600 Fixed an issue where apigee-connect-agent ignored HTTPS_PROXY and failed to establish a tether in clusters that require an HTTP forward proxy for egress; the agent now uses HTTP/2 keepalive pings on the control-plane connection while honoring HTTPS_PROXY (including proxy credentials).
576707253 Removed the compromised emSign roots and the cross-signing Comodo AAA Services root from the system and Java (cacerts) trust stores across containers.
573622417 Fixed an issue where apigee-ingressgateway forwarded the x-envoy-decorator-operation header to upstream runtime and target backends.
492041991 Fixed an issue where VerifyAPIKey and VerifyAccessToken set the apiproduct.operation.llmTokenQuota.* flow variables from unmatched LLM operations; they are now set only from the LLM operations that matched the request.

Backup and DR

Feature

Note: These fixes and updates are available starting with Backup and DR release 11.0.17.508. These fixes aren't rolled out to the 11.0.16 release. To receive these updates, upgrade the backup/recovery appliance to version 11.0.17.

The following feature is available for the Backup and DR agent:

  • Expanded Linux Changed Block Tracking (CBT) support across kernel updates for Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) 8, RHEL 9, and RHEL 10 distributions. For more information, see Backup and DR supported operating systems and kernels.

Security

Note: These fixes and updates are available starting with Backup and DR release 11.0.17.508. These fixes aren't rolled out to the 11.0.16 release. To receive these updates, upgrade the backup/recovery appliance to version 11.0.17.

The following security updates are available for the backup/recovery appliance:

  • Addressed multiple input sanitization vulnerabilities, including SQL injection and OS command injection, across appliance backend services and management workflows.
  • Strengthened TLS, certificate truststore, and SSH host key validation across appliance and cluster communications.
  • Remediated authorization and validation vulnerabilities in policy option management and host lookup workflows.
  • Addressed memory safety and access control vulnerabilities in appliance storage management services.

The following security updates are available for the Backup and DR agent:

  • Strengthened local device access controls for Linux Changed Block Tracking (CBT) components to prevent unprivileged local access.
  • Improved temporary file creation, path verification, and file permission handling across Linux and Windows Backup and DR agents to mitigate symlink race conditions and local privilege escalation vulnerabilities.
  • Hardened Oracle and IBM Db2 database integration scripts on protected hosts to improve credential and directory permission handling during recovery and migration workflows.
  • Addressed memory handling vulnerabilities and refined system logging rules in Linux Backup and DR agent components.

The following library updates are available for the backup/recovery appliance:

  • Upgraded the Java runtime environment and third-party application libraries on the appliance to remediate reported security vulnerabilities.
  • Updated base operating system and database packages across backup/recovery appliance and management server images to mitigate reported vulnerabilities.

Feature

You can now back up Cloud SQL instances to a backup vault that's located in a different region to the instance. This approach enhances data resilience and helps meet strict compliance and disaster recovery requirements by storing backups in a separate geographic location.

Feature

You can now edit existing backup plans for Cloud SQL instances to update settings such as backup rules and maximum custom on-demand retention periods. To learn more, see Back up Cloud SQL instances to a backup vault.

Fixed

Note: The following fixes and updates are available starting with Backup and DR release 11.0.17.507. These fixes aren't rolled out to the 11.0.16 release. To receive the following updates, upgrade your backup/recovery appliance to version 11.0.17.

The following issues are resolved for the backup/recovery appliance:

  • Application discovery and management API requests can time out when multiple discovery operations run concurrently.
  • Hostnames containing special characters prevented active jobs from being accurately detected during Backup and DR agent upgrade pre-checks.
  • Excessive informational log messages in appliance service logs when replication optimization was turned off.
  • Appliance image packaging issue by including required system libraries for fresh appliance deployments.

The following issue is resolved for the Backup and DR agent:

  • Scheduling conflict where concurrent database log backups and full database backups, such as SAP Sybase IQ and SAP MaxDB backups, can interrupt an in-progress backup job.

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Announcement

Starting November 1, 2026, at 02:00 a.m. local time, unpatched Cloud SQL for MySQL instances that evaluate certain local Canadian time zones (across Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, and Northwest Territories) will lag by one hour because the instances still follow the autumn fall back schedule. Stored timestamp data isn't modified.

What should I do?

Before November 1, 2026, do one of the following fixes:

  • Apply self-service maintenance (Recommended): If your applications rely on database functions to calculate, schedule, or display times in these Canadian time zones (such as Calgary, Edmonton, Vancouver, or Winnipeg), then update your instances to the latest maintenance release using the Google Cloud console or the gcloud CLI.

    Updated time zone rules that reflect permanent standard daylight offsets across Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, and Northwest Territories are supported in Cloud SQL for MySQL maintenance release *.R20260726.00_36 or later.

    For more information, see Perform self-service maintenance.

  • Database configuration stopgap: If your organization can't restart instances before November 1, 2026, then you can set the time zone for your database session without causing downtime for your instance. Set the default_time_zone flag for the database session to your target fixed numeric offset (for example, '-06:00' for Alberta, '-07:00' for British Columbia, or '-05:00' for Manitoba).

    For more information about configuring database flags, see Configure database flags.

Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL

Announcement

Starting November 1, 2026, at 02:00 a.m. local time, unpatched Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instances that evaluate certain local Canadian time zones (across Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, and Northwest Territories) will lag by one hour because the instances still follow the autumn fall back schedule. Stored timestamp data isn't modified.

What should I do?

Before November 1, 2026, do one of the following fixes:

  • Apply self-service maintenance (Recommended): If your applications rely on database functions to calculate, schedule, or display times in these Canadian time zones (such as Calgary, Edmonton, Vancouver, or Winnipeg), then update your instances to the latest maintenance release using the Google Cloud console or the gcloud CLI.

    Updated time zone rules that reflect permanent standard daylight offsets across Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, and Northwest Territories are supported in Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL maintenance release *.R20260712.01_44 or later.

    For more information, see Perform self-service maintenance.

  • Database configuration stopgap: If your organization can't restart instances before November 1, 2026, then you can set your database session time zone without downtime to an anchor zone.

    ALTER DATABASE database_name SET timezone TO 'anchor_zone';

    Replace the following:

    • database_name: the name of your database.

    • anchor_zone: the anchor zone to use as the time zone for your database. Specify an anchor zone that operates on a permanent offset.

      For example, 'America/Regina' for Alberta and Northwest Territories (UTC-6), 'America/Whitehorse' for British Columbia (UTC-7), or 'America/Coral_Harbour' for Manitoba (UTC-5).

Cloud SQL for SQL Server

Announcement

Starting November 1, 2026, at 02:00 a.m. local time, Cloud SQL for SQL Server instances that evaluate certain local Canadian time zones (across Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, and Northwest Territories) will lag by one hour because the instances still follow the autumn fall back schedule. Stored timestamp data isn't modified.

What should I do?

For SQL Server, Microsoft has published guidance, recommending updating each applicable instance's time zone to the Windows time zone with the matching fixed offset.

Update each instance's time zone to the Windows time zone with the matching fixed offset:

Jurisdiction Current time zone Recommended time zone Fixed offset
British Columbia Pacific Standard Time Yukon Standard Time UTC-07:00
Alberta / Inuvik, NWT Mountain Standard Time Canada Central Standard Time UTC-06:00
Manitoba Central Standard Time Eastern Standard Time (Mexico) UTC-05:00

You can make the change in the Google Cloud console (Edit instance > Flags and parameters > Time zone) or with gcloud:

gcloud sql instances patch INSTANCE_NAME \
  --project=PROJECT_ID \
  --time-zone="Yukon Standard Time"

Computer use tool is available in General Availability

The Computer use tool is available in General Availability (GA). This release introduces comprehensive Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) safety governance, enabling developers to selectively configure or override specific confirmation policies (such as financial transactions or data modification) while allowing administrators to mandate organization-wide guardrails using the configurableComputerUseToolSafetyPolicies constraint.

Feature

Inference request metadata logging (GA)

Inference request metadata logging is generally available. Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform can write one Cloud Logging entry for every inference request your project serves. Each entry records the model, region, consumption option, token counts, Provisioned Throughput usage, latency and error code. Entries record metadata only and never contain prompts or responses. Logging is supported for Gemini models that use generateContent and streamGenerateContent, and for Claude models that use rawPredict and streamRawPredict.

You can turn on logging in the Google Cloud console, from the Provisioned Throughput page, or with the REST API. Turning on logging in the console also turns on detailed metrics, which chart Provisioned Throughput traffic at one-second resolution. With logging on, the model observability dashboard adds 1-second resolution options to its charts for pay-as-you-go traffic. To attribute usage to a team, application or tenant, add request headers with the x-goog-agent-platform-observability-label- prefix, and query the entries with SQL in Observability Analytics.

For more information, see Log inference request metadata.

Looker

Announcement

On November 1, 2026, several Canadian provinces and territories—Manitoba, Alberta, British Columbia, and parts of the Northwest Territories—transition to permanent daylight saving time (DST) or remain on their summer UTC offsets year-round. On unpatched Looker instances, these changes affect scheduled content delivery fire times and table calculations that use now() with the affected Canadian time zones (America/Winnipeg, Canada/Central, America/Rainy_River, America/Edmonton, Canada/Mountain, America/Vancouver, Canada/Pacific, and America/Inuvik). Patched Looker builds update the scheduler (Ruby) and browser (JavaScript) time zone data, while server-evaluated now() table calculations on the JVM still use the bundled JDK time zone database (tzdb 2026b). To learn how to upgrade to a patched Looker build or configure an alternative schedule delivery time zone, see 2026 Canadian time zone changes.

Issue

Starting October 24, 2026, Managed Airflow (Gen 3) and Managed Airflow (Gen 2) environments running Python 3.11 with google-api-core package versions 2.28.0 to 2.43.0 (including versions 2.30.3 to 2.43.0, which weren't previously affected) might experience degraded performance because of a Python 3.11 deprecation check that scans installed package metadata on every new Python subprocess import. You might observe increased DAG parsing times, longer task execution times, higher CPU usage on Airflow DAG processors and workers, and frequent FutureWarning log entries from google/api_core/_python_version_support.py about Python 3.11 support ending on 2027-10-24.

For the list of affected builds and available workarounds (installing google-api-core>=2.43.1 on compatible Airflow 3 builds or applying a sitecustomize.py runtime patch), see the known issue for Managed Airflow (Gen 3) or Managed Airflow (Gen 2).

For more information, see Secure SAP applications with Google SecOps.

Feature

Spanner supports equality and ordering comparisons on JSONB and JSON values. You can use these values in GROUP_BY and ORDER BY clauses without first converting them to another data type.

In GoogleSQL, you can also convert other data types to JSON using CAST(expression AS JSON) and compare JSON values directly with non-JSON values. Spanner can implicitly coerces the non-JSON value to JSON for comparison.

Additionally, you can use search indexes to accelerate equality comparisons such as = or IN on JSONB and JSON columns and subpaths.

For more information, see JSON comparison and sorting , JSON comparison coercion , CAST AS JSON , JSON search indexes , and Working with JSONB.

Feature

Spanner Graph supports the following enhancements:

  • You can write simplified queries on schemaless dynamic properties without explicit conversions to SQL data types. This lets you group and sort dynamic properties, and compare them directly with literal values or other dynamic properties. For more information, see Filter, compare, and sort by dynamic properties and JSON comparison and sorting.

For mutual TLS (mTLS) on Application Load Balancers, frontend mTLS validation relaxations are generally available.

The ALLOW_VALIDATION_RELAXATIONS client validation mode on the Client Authentication (ServerTlsPolicy) resource allows you to configure specific X.509 certificate validation exceptions to standard client certificate validation rules. This simplifies migrations of legacy workloads while maintaining an active security posture.

This mode supports the following client certificate validation relaxation parameters:

Breaking

Permissions to grant access by using Unified Access Policies (UAPs) are included in the following roles:

  • Owner (roles/owner)
  • Admin (roles/admin)
  • Security Admin (roles/iam.securityAdmin)
  • Organization Administrator (roles/resourcemanager.organizationAdmin)
  • Folder IAM Admin (roles/resourcemanager.folderIamAdmin)
  • Project IAM Admin (roles/resourcemanager.projectIamAdmin)

If users have these roles and aren't denied permission to modify UAPs or bind them to resources, then they can grant any permission by using UAPs. Granting access in this way is not limited by custom organization policies that limit role granting.

If you want to prevent these users from granting access by using UAPs, do one of the following:

  • Enforce the iam.managed.disableAccessPolicyBinding organization policy constraint in your organization.

Announcement

Released Edge Microgateway 3.3.12.

Edge Microgateway 3.3.12 includes the following component versions:

Component Version
microgateway 3.3.12
plugins 3.3.9
edgeauth 3.2.2

To upgrade, install version 3.3.12 of the edgemicro npm package or pull the gcr.io/apigee-microgateway/edgemicro:3.3.12 Docker image. For the npm upgrade steps, see Upgrading Edge Microgateway. For earlier Edge Microgateway releases, see Edge Microgateway release notes.

Breaking

Removed support for Node.js 20 from Edge Microgateway. Use Node.js 22, 24, or 26 instead.

Edge Microgateway 3.3.12 supports only Node.js 22, 24, and 26. Support for Node.js 26 is new in this release. Before you upgrade an npm installation of Edge Microgateway to 3.3.12, upgrade the Node.js runtime on each host to version 22, 24, or 26. The 3.3.12 Docker image is built on Node.js 24, so Docker deployments need no action for this change. For supported versions, see Supported software and supported versions.

Breaking

Removed the npm and npx command-line tools from the Edge Microgateway Docker image. Install custom plugin dependencies before you add the plugins to the container.

Starting with version 3.3.12, the Edge Microgateway Docker image doesn't include npm or npx, and commands that run either tool inside the container fail. The change doesn't affect how Edge Microgateway runs. If your custom plugins have npm dependencies, run npm install in each plugin directory before you add the plugins to the container, so that each plugin's node_modules directory is included. For the steps, see Adding a custom plugin. This change doesn't affect npm installations of Edge Microgateway.

Bigtable

Feature

Bigtable offers conversational analytics, which lets you query your operational data using natural language. This feature uses the Conversational Analytics API and is in Preview. For more information, see Conversational analytics for Bigtable overview.

Feature

The QueryData tool lets you query the data in your database using conversational language and build data agents. This feature is available in Preview. For more information, see QueryData tool overview.

Cloud Run

Feature

Cloud Run ephemeral disk is in General Availability (GA). Ephemeral disk allows you to mount a volume that persists only for the duration of your service, job, or worker pool instance.

Cloud SQL for SQL Server

Feature

Cloud SQL for SQL Server now supports read pool autoscaling (GA), which helps you more easily manage your application's workload needs.

This feature automates read pool scale in and scale out operations based on one or both of the following conditions:

  • Allowed CPU usage of the read pool
  • Allowed number of client connections to the read pool

Change

Cloud SQL for SQL Server supports additional metrics within the system insights dashboard (GA) related to engine memory, performance, and replication.

For a detailed list of metrics and their descriptions, see Cloud SQL for SQL Server default metrics and Cloud SQL metrics.

Cloud Storage

Feature

You can pause hard deletions for a bucket when you need more time to restore soft-deleted objects before they're permanently deleted. For more information, see Pause permanent (hard) deletions of soft-deleted objects.

Cloud Workstations

Feature

The Cloud Workstations base editor (Code OSS for Cloud Workstations) includes the Antigravity extension by default.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Switch between teams in the mobile app

You can switch between multiple teams in the Gemini Enterprise mobile app without logging out and rescanning the QR code. (Teams were previously called instances.)

When you open a team for the first time, the mobile app saves it to your teams list. Additionally, you can rename teams in the list and you can remove teams from your list.

This feature is generally available (GA). For more information, see Teams in Use the mobile app.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Provisioned Throughput support for supervised fine-tuned models (GA)

Provisioned Throughput support for supervised fine-tuned models is generally available. Burndown rates for fine-tuned model inference can include a premium that's directly proportional to the model's fine-tuned inference pricing premium.

Feature

AlphaGenome gRPC and unified HTTP serving support

AlphaGenome (alphagenome-004) now supports unified HTTP/2 gRPC streaming and chunked binary protobuf HTTP streaming on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform:

  • Streams compressed binary tensor chunks directly over gRPC on shared endpoints (PredictionService.StreamDirectRawPredict on port 8081) and chunked binary protobuf payloads (proto_b64) over HTTP on dedicated endpoints (streamRawPredict on port 8080) across all seven DnaModelService methods (predict_sequence, predict_interval, predict_variant, score_variant, score_interval, score_ism_variants, and output_metadata) and 11 genomic modalities, reducing latency for 1 MB track predictions.
  • Supports concurrent multi-variant evaluation for in silico saturation mutagenesis (score_ism_variants) without HTTP gateway timeouts.
  • Supports model fold selection (ALL_FOLDS, FOLD_0, FOLD_1, FOLD_2, and FOLD_3) across both gRPC and HTTP clients through the unified alphagenome_cloud_sdk Python SDK.
  • Retains alphagenome-003 in Model Garden for backward compatibility with existing legacy HTTP deployments.

For more information, see the AlphaGenome documentation.

Announcement

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for VMware 1.35.700-gke.124 is now available for download. To upgrade, see Upgrade clusters. Google Distributed Cloud 1.35.700-gke.124 runs on Kubernetes v1.35.8-gke.100.

If you use a third-party storage vendor, check the listing of our previously-qualified storage partners.

After a release, it takes approximately 7 to 14 days for the version to become available for use with GKE On-Prem API clients: the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, and Terraform.

Feature

The following changes were added in 1.35.700-gke.124:

  • Updated system components and container base images to remove the distrusted eMudhra (emSign) and AAA Certificate Services root CAs and reject compromised eMudhra intermediate CAs.
  • Upgraded Container-Optimized OS (COS) to milestone 121 (cos-121-18867-652-7), which removes the distrusted eMudhra (emSign) and AAA Certificate Services root CAs.
  • Updated the Ubuntu 24.04 node and admin workstation base image to ubuntu-gke-op-2404-1-34-v20261024 to remove the distrusted eMudhra (emSign) root CAs (USN-8944-1).

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.35.700-gke.124:

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Fixed an issue where audit-proxy retried audit log exports indefinitely on permanent errors, generating excessive audit logging traffic.
  • Fixed an issue where the Kubernetes preflight health check scanned all namespaces in the admin cluster instead of the target cluster's namespace, causing cluster upgrades to fail if an unrelated cluster had stale reconciling resources.

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for bare metal

Announcement

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for bare metal 1.35.700-gke.124 is now available for download. To upgrade, see Upgrade clusters. Google Distributed Cloud for bare metal 1.35.700-gke.124 runs on Kubernetes v1.35.8-gke.100.

After a release, it takes approximately 7 to 14 days for the version to become available for installations or upgrades with the GKE On-Prem API clients: the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, and Terraform.

If you use a third-party storage vendor, check the listing of our previously-qualified storage partners.

Feature

The following changes were added in 1.35.700-gke.124:

  • Updated system components and container base images to remove the distrusted eMudhra (emSign) and AAA Certificate Services root CAs and reject compromised eMudhra intermediate CAs.

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.35.700-gke.124:

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Fixed an issue where removing a node from a cluster left behind its local PersistentVolume resources instead of garbage collecting them. This fix applies to Google Distributed Cloud for bare metal local PersistentVolume resources created after upgrading to 1.35.700-gke.124; existing orphaned PersistentVolume resources must be deleted manually.
  • Fixed an issue where resetting or removing a control plane node could remove the wrong etcd or etcd-events member if another control plane node's IP address shared the same prefix (for example, 10.201.0.2 and 10.201.0.26), causing the affected node to become NotReady and stalling cluster upgrades.
  • Improved containerd resilience against state corruption if a node reboots while unpacking container images.
  • Fixed an issue where the periodic configuration drift health check failed with a version not supported error while a cluster upgrade or rollback was in progress.
  • Fixed an issue where audit-proxy retried audit log exports indefinitely on permanent errors, generating excessive audit logging traffic.
  • Fixed an issue where the Kubernetes preflight health check scanned all namespaces in the admin cluster instead of the target cluster's namespace, causing cluster upgrades to fail if an unrelated cluster had stale reconciling resources.

Google SecOps

Announcement

[Spotlight Feature] Consolidated Settings and Navigation

The Consolidated Settings and Navigation feature is now in public preview. It replaces the separate SIEM Settings and SOAR Settings menus with a single Settings menu, grouped into Administration, Access Management, Investigation, Detection and Data Management, and also updates the left navigation menu. Each settings page is shown only to users with the correct permissions. Cloud IAM, Viewer and Editor users can now view certain SOAR settings pages in read-only mode. The Google SecOps documentation has been updated to reflect the new navigational changes.

For more information, see Navigate the Google SecOps platform.

This feature is being rolled out in waves starting Monday, November 9 and continuing through Thursday, November 12.

Knowledge Catalog

Feature

Data products in Knowledge Catalog let you request access to an access group for a Google Group or on behalf of another user, in addition to yourself or a service account. Both the requester and the requested user or Google Group receive email notifications when an access request is submitted, approved, or rejected. This feature is generally available.

For more information, see Request access to data products and Manage data product access requests.

Announcement

The latest versions in the Looker (Google Cloud core) release channels are beginning deployment as follows:

  • Latest version in the Regular channel: Looker 26.20

The latest version in the Rapid and No Channel channels remains Looker 26.22.

Apigee Edge for Public Cloud

Announcement

Scheduled maintenance of Management/Control Plane for the Apigee Edge for Public Cloud on November 6, 2026.

Scheduled maintenance of Management/Control Plane for the Apigee Edge for Public Cloud production will take place on Friday, November 6, 2026, from 9:00 PM PT to 10:00 PM PT (Saturday, November 7, 2026, from 5:00 AM UTC to 6:00 AM UTC). This maintenance follows the monthly maintenance window schedule documented in the Apigee Edge release notes archive.

During the scheduled maintenance window, the following services will be temporarily unavailable, and attempts to access them will return a 4xx status code:

  • Management Services UI
  • Management Services APIs
  • Monetization Management APIs
  • New proxy deployments
  • DevPortal Service
  • Microgateway Services
  • Edge Query (Analytics Stats APIs)

Runtime API calls to deployed API proxies are unaffected. While access to analytics queries may be temporarily unavailable during the maintenance window, all analytics and metrics data from this period will be available once maintenance ends.

Apigee hybrid

Announcement

v1.14.10

On November 5, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, v1.14.10.

  • For information about upgrading, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid to v1.14.10.
  • For information about new installations, see The big picture.
Note: This is a patch release. The container images used in patch releases are integrated with the Apigee hybrid Helm charts. Upgrading to a patch by using the Helm chart automatically updates the images. You don't typically need to make manual image changes. For information about container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Fixed

Fixed in this release

Bug ID Description
578314600 Fixed an issue where apigee-connect-agent ignored HTTPS_PROXY and failed to establish a tether in clusters that require an HTTP forward proxy for egress; the agent now uses HTTP/2 keepalive pings on the control-plane connection while honoring HTTPS_PROXY (including proxy credentials).
576707253 Removed the compromised emSign roots and the cross-signing Comodo AAA Services root from the system and Java (cacerts) trust stores across containers.

571378258 The apigee-redis container now uses the Valkey engine (version 8.1.10). The RESP2 wire protocol and redis-server and redis-cli binary names are unchanged.
554114419 Fixed an issue where an AssignMessage, HTTPModifier, or RaiseFault policy that creates a new request (createNew="true") in an HTTP/2 flow could not set the :path and :authority pseudo-headers and failed with an invalid-header error.
524115876 Fixed an intermittent HTTP 400 error in the OASValidation policy's strict parameter validation that rejected valid requests under load.
449228485 Fixed an issue where podDisruptionBudget overrides configured in the Helm charts were dropped by the Kubernetes API server.
432315283 Fixed an issue where changes to a multi-certificate truststore's trust anchors required a Message Processor restart when features.truststore.multi_cert_bundle.enabled was toggled at runtime; the outbound SSLContext now rebuilds automatically.

Feature

You can combine tables vertically in Data Studio blends by using the Union merge operator, which appends rows across up to five tables and removes duplicate rows. For more information, see How blends work in Data Studio and Create, edit, and manage blends.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Prepaid credits for Pay-as-you-go subscriptions and usage above quota

Prepaid credits are generally available (GA) for self-serve (online) Cloud Billing accounts. You can buy credits to pay for usage without an invoiced billing account. Your billing account's credit balance covers usage in the Pay-as-you-go edition and pay-as-you-go usage above quota in the Gemini Enterprise app, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, and AI developer tools, such as Google Antigravity. Pay-as-you-go subscriptions have no license fee because you pay for what you use at pay-as-you-go rates. Cloud Billing still bills your account directly for seat-based license fees in editions such as Standard and Plus.

  • Buy credits and configure auto-reload: Buy prepaid credits, track your balance and transactions, and configure auto-reload with an optional monthly auto-charge limit. Usage is blocked if your credit balance reaches zero or a project reaches its monthly spend limit. Because credits are deducted after usage occurs, your balance might briefly drop below zero if usage occurs before the deduction runs.
  • Use AI developer tools on self-serve accounts: With an upgraded paid self-serve billing account and an active non-trial Gemini Enterprise subscription, you can enable AI developer tools and pay with prepaid credits for Pay-as-you-go edition usage or pay-as-you-go usage above quota. Eligible editions include Standard, Plus, eligible Standard Emerging Market, and Pay-as-you-go. Free-trial subscriptions, free-tier billing accounts, and reseller-managed subaccounts aren't eligible.
  • Monitor costs and invoices: View 30-day costs across the Gemini Enterprise app, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, and AI developer tools, and view and download prepayment and monthly consumption invoices.

For more information, see:

  • Manage prepaid credits
  • Configure pay-as-you-go usage above quota
  • Quotas and pricing for the Pay-as-you-go edition
  • AI developer tools overview
  • View costs

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash (gemini-omni-1.2-flash) is available in General Availability (GA). Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is an omni-modal foundation model that processes text, image, and video inputs to generate text and high-definition video with synchronized audio through the Interactions API.

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash introduces the following capabilities:

  • Standalone video upscaling: Upscale previously generated videos from 360p to 720p or 1080p, and from 720p to 1080p or 4K using task: "upscale". See Upscale videos.

  • Extended video generation and editing duration: Generate or edit videos up to 15 seconds in length across text-to-video, image-to-video, reference-to-video, and video editing tasks (up to 10 seconds for first-and-last-frame interpolation and video extension).

  • Reference-guided video editing and extension: Supply up to 2 reference images along with an input video when editing or extending videos. See Edit videos and Extend videos.

  • Deterministic generation and billing labels: Specify seed for reproducible video outputs and attach custom labels to Interactions API requests.

  • Standard PayGo and Provisioned Throughput: Available with Standard Pay-as-you-go (PayGo) and Provisioned Throughput (685 tokens per second per GSU).

Feature

Interactions API long decodes for Gemini 4 Argon

Long decodes up to 1,048,576 tokens (minus input tokens) on the Interactions API (v1beta1) are available in General Availability (GA) for Gemini 4 Argon (gemini-4-argon and gemini-4-argon-cyber-permissive). You can extend single-turn outputs beyond the per-segment limit (65,536 streaming or 32,768 non-streaming tokens) using automatic continuation in the Google Gen AI SDK (google-genai >= 2.34.0 for Python, @google/genai >= 2.32.0 for JavaScript/TypeScript, Go >= 1.77.0, and Java >= 1.80.0), server-managed background execution (background=true), or custom stored (store=true) and stateless (store=false) continuation_token loops.

For code samples, continuation options, and implementation rules, see Long decodes in the developer's guide to Gemini 4 Argon.

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Verification tool-turn guardrails: Added exploratory tool-turn limits to cm verify sessions to prevent unbounded command execution loops.
  • Release notes link in update prompts: Added a direct link to DevSite release notes when CodeMender prompts to update to a newer CLI version.
  • Agent IAM diagnostic guidance: Added actionable roles/aiplatform.agentsUser IAM binding commands to CLI setup and error messages for service account and CI/CD environments.
  • Bug fixes:

    • Improved compatibility across shell environments.
    • Improved the sign-in flow during interactive activation.
    • Improved error reporting when the service is temporarily unavailable.
    • Includes security and stability improvements.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Managed Service for Apache Airflow

Security

Updated: 2026-11-20

Managed Airflow service released new Managed Airflow versions addressing CVE-2026-114938 vulnerability.

Users who want to eliminate scanner notifications about JVMs being vulnerable to CVE-2026-114938 in their Managed Airflow Gen 2 environments are requested to upgrade to the latest Gen 2 version: composer-2.18.2-airflow-2.11.1.

Users of early Managed Airflow (Gen 2) versions (composer-2.5.3-* or earlier) are requested to upgrade to the latest Gen 2 version, or migrate to Gen 3 versions:

  • Gen 2 version: composer-2.18.2-airflow-2.11.1
  • Gen 3 versions: 3.3.1-build.10, 3.2.2-build.14, and 2.11.1-build.27

As temporary mitigation solution that doesn't require upgrading, you can set the following environment variable in the environment:

  • Variable name: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
  • Variable value: -XX:+IgnoreUnrecognizedVMOptions -XX:UseAVX=2

If the JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS variable is already set, append the -XX flags to the existing value.

Additionally, for all Managed Airflow Gen 3 and Gen 2 environments starting from version composer-2.5.4-*, running any of the following operations sets this environment variable automatically, if it's not set already:

  • Upgrading the environment to any other supported version (preferrably to the latest Managed Airflow version).

  • Managed Airflow (Gen 2):

    • Enabling or disabling saving task logs to the environment's bucket.

  • Managed Airflow (Gen 3):

    • Adding, removing or updating any environment variable.
    • Adding or removing custom PyPI packages, or changing their constraints.
    • Adding, removing or changing Airflow configuration option overrides.
    • Loading an environment snapshot.

Published on: 2026-11-19

Managed Airflow service is preparing a fix for the CVE-2026-114938 vulnerability. This fix will be published in an upcoming Managed Airflow version, and will be backported to past Managed Airflow versions released between 2024 and 2026.

After the fix is deployed to production, Managed Airflow will provide instructions detailing the steps customers must take to prevent potential exploitation of CVE-2026-114938.

In the meantime, all customers are requested to configure the following environment variable in their Managed Airflow environments, which effectively blocks exploitation of CVE-2026-114938:

JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=-XX:+IgnoreUnrecognizedVMOptions -XX:UseAVX=2

title: Vercel Connect adds webhook triggers for more providers
description:
Vercel Connect now supports webhook triggers for Resend, X, Twilio, Notion, and Telegram.

Connect receives webhook events, such as Telegram bot messages or emails received by your Resend domain, and forwards them to an endpoint in your Vercel project. It verifies incoming requests and handles provider heartbeats and verification challenges for you.

To get started:

  1. Open Vercel Connect in the dashboard. Enable triggers when creating a connector for your provider or in an existing connector’s settings. Connect registers webhooks automatically for Resend and Telegram.

  2. For Twilio, Notion, and X, use the webhook URL from Connect and follow its instructions to complete setup in the provider’s settings.

  3. Add a trigger destination to choose the project and endpoint that should receive events.

You can turn triggers on or off later in the connector’s settings.

In the connector’s Observability tab, select Live to watch incoming trigger events.

These connectors join existing trigger support for Slack, Discord, Microsoft Teams, GitHub, and Linear.

Learn more in the Connect triggers documentation.

title: Node.js 26 LTS is now Generally Available on Vercel
description:
Node.js 26 LTS is now Generally Available for builds and Vercel Functions.

This release includes:

  • HTTP/2 by default for built-in fetch (Undici 8) lets multiple requests share a connection with servers that support it. This can reduce latency when your functions call APIs or databases over HTTP.

  • Temporal API offers an alternative to Date with immutable values and built-in time zone and calendar support.

  • V8 version 14.6, the updated JavaScript engine, adds features such as Map.prototype.getOrInsert() to retrieve an existing value or insert a default when a key is missing.

Using Node.js 26

Node.js 26 is the default for all new projects.

  • Automatic upgrades: If engines.node in your existing project’s package.json allows 26, such as >=20, your Node.js builds on Vercel will use 26 on the next deployment.

  • Manual upgrades: Set engines.node to 26.x in your project's package.json and redeploy.

  • Prebuilt deployments: Use Vercel CLI version 65.8.0 or later to deploy Node.js 26 Functions.

  • HTTP/1.1 in Functions: To keep HTTP/1.1, set the VERCEL_FETCH_DISABLE_H2 environment variable to 1 and redeploy.

Minor and patch updates to Node.js 26 roll out automatically for builds and Vercel Functions.

Read the Node.js version documentation to learn more.

title: Vercel Flags starts 7x faster and no longer extends function duration
description:
On Vercel, the Vercel Flags SDK now initializes faster on cold starts, and usage reporting no longer keeps functions running after the response.

Faster cold starts

Two changes speed up SDK initialization on cold starts:

  • The SDK loads and parses the flags datafile bundled with your deployment as soon as the client is created, so it’s ready before your code evaluates its first flag.

  • Every function invocation now includes the current datafile revision, so the SDK can check whether the bundled datafile is up to date without a network request.

In internal testing, eliminating the network wait reduced p75 cold-start SDK initialization time from over 70 ms to 10 ms, roughly 7x faster.

After initialization, flag reads are effectively instant. Across cold and warm invocations, p99 flag-read latency is under 1 ms.

Usage reporting no longer extends function duration

The SDK previously used waitUntil for usage reporting, keeping functions running after the response was sent. It now passes usage events to the Vercel runtime, so reporting no longer adds to function duration.

Update @flags-sdk/vercel to version 1.5.3 or later and redeploy your application:

Learn more in the Flags SDK documentation.

title: Simplifying runtime caching on Vercel
description:
Today, we’re bringing Data Cache into Runtime Cache, giving developers one product for data caching across frameworks and APIs. If you use Next.js fetch caching or unstable_cache, you won’t need to change your code. Pro and Enterprise projects will get larger storage allocations.

Runtime Cache lets your code reuse fetched or computed data across requests without operating a separate caching service. Over the past year, we’ve improved read performance during traffic bursts, increased storage budgets, and made cache usage easier to investigate.

Why we built Runtime Cache

Data Cache was originally launched as Vercel’s data caching service for the Next.js App Router, used by fetch caching and unstable_cache. Unlike CDN caching, which stores complete HTTP responses, Data Cache stores data your application uses to generate those responses. A product page, for example, can reuse cached catalog data while rendering a personalized response for each visitor.

We wanted developers to have access to that service without depending on Next.js. Last year, we introduced Runtime Cache with a direct API: getCache from @vercel/functions. Applications can use it for feature flag lookups in Routing Middleware, caching CMS content during builds, and data caching in SvelteKit and Nuxt apps.

Frameworks can expose this service through their own APIs, too. On Vercel, Next.js itself uses the Runtime Cache API for 'use cache: remote', which caches function and component outputs.

How Runtime Cache works

The infrastructure behind Runtime Cache is a distributed caching service shared by many teams. A Go API handles requests, backed by Redis fleets in every Vercel region. Every hour, the service handles more than 440 million reads and moves more than 18 TB of data.

Each region has its own cache. A cache hit takes one round trip to the cache service in the region where your code runs. Vercel handles authentication with short-lived credentials, so you don’t need to manage API keys.

On a cache miss, your app or framework fetches or computes the value and writes it to that region’s cache. The service doesn’t check other regions for a cached copy.

Each cached entry stores its tags and write time. When the service reads an entry, it checks a separate tag store in the same region for those tags’ invalidation timestamps. If any tag was invalidated after the entry was written, the entry is stale.

For example, an application can tag all its cached product data with catalog. When the catalog changes, invalidating that tag writes a single timestamp, even if a million entries share the tag. The service doesn’t need to find and delete those entries individually.

The invalidation immediately updates the tag store in the region receiving the request. Vercel’s shared tag infrastructure, also used by the CDN, distributes the timestamp through the global push pipeline, typically reaching other regions within a few hundred milliseconds.

Your app or framework chooses what to cache and handles misses. Runtime Cache handles regional storage, authentication, and distributing tag invalidations across regions.

What we’ve shipped

Faster reads during traffic bursts

Checking whether an entry is still fresh adds a dependency to every cache hit. During traffic bursts, a slow shard in the tag store could delay reads even when the cached value was already available.

We added circuit breakers that let reads temporarily check freshness using tag timestamps cached in memory, so they can proceed without waiting for the slow shard to respond. During this fallback, a read can briefly treat recently invalidated data as fresh.

We enabled the breakers in every region in August. During the heaviest bursts in our largest region, p99 cache-service read latency fell to about one fifth of its previous level at comparable traffic. On-call alerts for this failure mode stopped.

More storage and fewer evictions

We raised Runtime Cache storage budgets for Pro projects in June and Enterprise projects in October, giving applications more room for data they reuse. This reduces the need to evict cached entries to make room for new data. Among Enterprise projects with frequent evictions, cache miss rates roughly halved within a day.

More visibility into cache behavior

We’ve added deployment markers, revalidation causes, and write utilization to the Runtime Cache view in Observability. These help you compare changes in cache behavior with releases, see why entries are refreshed, and identify data that gets written to the cache but rarely read.

Bringing Data Cache into Runtime Cache

We’re simplifying caching on Vercel by consolidating on Runtime Cache. Until now, Next.js fetch caching and unstable_cache have used Data Cache, while getCache and 'use cache: remote' have used Runtime Cache. The migration brings all four APIs under Runtime Cache, so you and coding agents have one set of storage budgets and usage tools to work with.

If you use fetch caching or unstable_cache, nothing changes in your code. On Pro, each project and environment gets its own storage allocation, with 8x the space of Data Cache’s previous team-wide pool. Enterprise projects get 10x their previous Data Cache storage.

Previously unbilled Data Cache reads and writes will follow Runtime Cache pricing. New teams use Runtime Cache automatically, and existing teams will receive their migration and billing details in advance.

See the changelog for the rollout, pricing, and early opt-in details. Before migrating, review your cache usage and follow the optimization guide to reduce unnecessary reads and writes.

title: Introducing Geist Serif
description:
Geist started as a monospace typeface for developers, built for the editors and terminals where they spend their day doing their work. From there it grew into Geist Sans for product interfaces, and then into Geist Pixel, which was inspired by the grids of early computer screens.

Today, we're adding a new member to the family: Geist Serif.

Geist Serif is a high-contrast display serif built on the same foundations as Geist Sans, Geist Mono, and Geist Pixel. It has fine, saw-toothed serifs and sharp hairlines, and it was drawn to communicate messages powerfully both in the physical world and on the high-density screens on modern devices.

Same system, new voice

At Vercel, Geist Sans runs the product. For headlines, though, we wanted a second voice, one that belongs to the same system, instead of a stranger picked from a drop-down menu.

A lot of tech brands have moved away from clean sans-serifs to get some personality back, and many of them borrow from vintage computer ads. Geist Serif takes a different path: toward fashion, editorial design, and magazine headlines. It's our homage to the artists behind Rolling Stone and Harper's Bazaar.

From the beginning, each Geist family has read from a chapter of type history: the Swiss design movement, early terminal and DOS computing, and now editorial print.

Display first

Geist Serif began as a set of sketches by Evil Rabbit, which Andrés Briganti then expanded. The first letters already showed an expressive serif, in the spirit of typefaces like Victor Serif and Stanley.

When Mark Davis took over the drawings, we made the first release a display face for headlines, posters, and other large sizes, while work on the full family continued. Print has always struggled to hold fine hairlines and sharp serifs, but today's displays can handle a high level of detail. We wanted the new face to take full advantage of modern screens, so we thinned every downstroke by 50% and tightened the sidebearings to push the contrast as far as it would go.

Each serif has a wedge on one side and a curve on the other, so the proportions are classical and look beautiful in print, but the construction is new and optimized for digital devices.

From the first prototype to today

The first prototype of Geist Serif was shared on April 1, 2026. Here's the same word, Geist, in that prototype, compared with the display drawing shipping today.

Geist grew teeth

The goal was to honor our original intent and keep the serif closely tied to the sans, even when the letters sit on top of each other. Geist Serif’s stems match Geist Sans, and the two share widths and postures.

The saw-toothed serifs and high contrast give Geist an editorial voice. One phrase kept coming up as each character was drawn: “Geist grew teeth.”

Four families, one x-height

Geist Serif uses the same cap height and x-height as Geist Sans, so you can drop it into any Geist layout without moving a line. Mix Sans, Mono, Pixel, and Serif in the same sentence and every word looks the same size.

Metric

Geist Sans

Geist Serif

UPM

1000

1000

Cap height

710

710

x-height

530

530

Ascender

710

750

Descender

-150

-200

Four variants, one axis

Like Geist Pixel, Geist Serif has a variable axis that swaps the shape of every dot in the font, including those on i and j and in punctuation. The axis is called Element Shape (ELSH), and it gives you four variants: Regular with round dots (the default), Square, Triangle (a nod to the Vercel logo), and Heart.

Each variant also ships as its own static file. If you use the variable font, pick a variant with font-variation-settings:

Crafted by hand

In July the font had 227 glyphs. It now has 894 and covers 352 Latin-script languages, and we worked through more than 52,000 kerning pairs to get the spacing right. Some of the details are tiny. The eye of the g, for example, is tilted exactly 7°.

Specs at a glance

Geist Serif ships with:

  • 1 weight (Regular)

  • 4 variants (Regular, Square, Triangle, Heart)

  • 894 glyphs

  • 5 stylistic sets (ss01 to ss05)

  • 352 supported languages

Getting started

Geist Serif ships in the same package as the rest of the family:

Exports and CSS variables:

  • GeistSerif (variable, all shapes): --font-geist-serif

  • GeistSerifRegular: --font-geist-serif-regular

  • GeistSerifSquare: --font-geist-serif-square

  • GeistSerifTriangle: --font-geist-serif-triangle

  • GeistSerifHeart: --font-geist-serif-heart

Each one has its own entry point, so you only ship the font file you use. For example, in layout.tsx with GeistSerifRegular:

You can also download the font files, test every stylistic set, and inspect each glyph at vercel.com/font.

What’s next

Regular is the first style we’re releasing, and the rest of the family is already in progress. We’re testing future versions while building this one, so this release is just the start.

Weights from Thin to Black

The variable font will range from Thin (100) to Black (900). In this week’s proofs, the g in Black is the letter we can’t stop looking at.

Toward a text face

To explore a text version, we built a foundry tool that measures strokes, including where they meet, and thickens the display outlines. It edits the outlines directly, so we can set real words and see which strokes need more weight.

Italics, built rule by rule

We’re also developing an italic generated entirely in Python. We slanted existing italics back upright and compared them with their romans. With the angle removed, the remaining differences show up clearly, and we turned them into rules we can test and revise. This italic won’t be the final version, but breaking glyphs in code helps us find the limits faster.

More scripts and Google Fonts

Cyrillic support is planned to match Geist Sans and Geist Mono, and Geist Serif will come to Google Fonts after launch.

One family

With Geist Sans, Geist Mono, Geist Pixel, and now Geist Serif, the family runs from UI text and code to expressive display type, and all four feel at home together.

Download Geist Serif and start building.

Thank you to everyone who made Geist Serif possible.

None of this would have been possible without an incredible group of people behind the scenes.

Huge thanks to Andrés Briganti for starting this journey with me and drawing the first version that everything else grew from, and to Mark Davis for carrying it across the finish line with obsessive craft, from the expanded glyph set and variable axis to every last kerning pair. Thanks also to Patrick McDonald and Marijana Pavlinić for the poster designs, to Luis Gutierrez Rico for the motion and incredible magic, to Christopher Kindl for shipping the package and rebuilding the landing page down to the smallest details, and to Zahra Jabini for the coordination and technical support that brought it all together. This was a true team effort, and I’m grateful to have built it with all of you.

title: Blocking malicious npm packages before and during installation
description:
Vercel now checks for blocked npm packages before and during dependency installation in builds, helping prevent malicious install scripts from running.

The checks use a blocklist of specific package versions selected for blocking because of malware or security vulnerabilities, with new rules typically reaching new builds within minutes.

  • Before installation, Vercel checks supported lockfiles, including when dependencies are restored from the build cache.

  • During installation, Vercel blocks affected public npm downloads.

Existing checks of installed dependencies and function outputs continue before deployment.

These protections apply automatically to new builds on all plans, with no configuration required.

If a blocked dependency is detected, Vercel fails the deployment, identifies the package and version in the error, and attempts to invalidate the affected build cache. Update the dependency to a safe version and update the lockfile, then redeploy.

title: Vercel MCP now supports Client ID Metadata Documents
description:
Any MCP client can now ask to connect to Vercel MCP. You still log in and approve each connection, but the client no longer has to be reviewed by Vercel first. Previously, Vercel reviewed and allowlisted each client and its redirect URIs by hand, and anything not on the list was rejected.

To connect, a client publishes a Client ID Metadata Document (CIMD), a JSON file on its own domain that describes it, and uses that file's HTTPS URL as its OAuth client_id. This follows the MCP authorization spec, which now recommends CIMD over Dynamic Client Registration.

Because Vercel hasn't reviewed these clients, the consent screen shows where each one comes from: its name, its logo, and the hostname that serves its metadata document, for example "Claude Code by claude.ai". CIMD clients don't get the Vercel verified badge, so the hostname is what you're trusting when you approve.

Apps already registered with Vercel are unchanged.

Read the Vercel MCP documentation to connect your client.

title: Introducing Vercel Schedules
description:
Cron jobs are useful for work that needs to happen regularly. You can use them to do things such as back up your database on a schedule, or keep data in sync between two systems.

You define them once in code and then can update them by editing their config and redeploying. But today, agents interact with users as work evolves, and schedules need to be updated in real time.

We built Vercel Schedules to allow agents and applications to create, change, or cancel one-time and recurring schedules through code, without redeploying.

What are Vercel Schedules?

Schedules builds on the static approach used by Vercel Cron Jobs, but are designed to let users and agents decide when work should happen while your application is still running. A schedule tells Vercel when to trigger a task and where to send it. Your application provides the code that carries out the work.

You can use schedules for both static and dynamic jobs:

  • Static schedules keep the timing in vercel.json or Build Output API configuration and sync when you deploy. You can use them to call private functions or HTTP paths, or send messages to Queue topics.

  • Dynamic schedules let your app create and manage schedules through the JS SDK, CLI, or API as it runs. They support one-time and recurring work through Queue topics.

You can also test scheduled work on Preview deployments and in custom environments before running it in Production.

How Schedules works

Take this example: A user could ask an agent with web access, “Tomorrow morning, summarize the top five stories on Hacker News.” The traditional solution would be storing the request and its schedule time in a database, then using a cron job to check for work that is due.

With Schedules, an agent can create a schedule that records the request and when to run it, without a separate database and polling job. The example below defines an AI SDK tool that gives an agent this capability.

When the task is due, Vercel uses Queues to deliver the saved request to your app. Your app provides code to read that request, check the user’s current permissions, and start the agent. The agent fetches the top five Hacker News posts with a web tool, then returns a summary for your app to save for the user.

If you already build agents with fx’s JavaScript library, libfx or Pi’s agent library, you can add a similar scheduling tool. The eve agent framework uses Vercel Schedules to provide dynamic scheduling tools for production agents hosted on Vercel.

Run recurring application jobs

You can schedule recurring work with Vercel Schedules. Schedules can be created dynamically via the JS SDK, API, and CLI, or set up in your project’s configuration.

For example, to create a job that cleans up expired records every day, you could define a schedule that invokes a private function in your chosen time zone:

Vercel calls this cleanup code directly, without exposing it at a public URL. It checks that each call comes from the scheduling service, so you don’t have to add that check yourself.

If your app already uses the Nitro 3 server framework, its experimental integration lets you run the recurring jobs in your existing scheduledTasks configuration as private functions.

You can also try the agent task and cleanup locally with vercel dev, then test them on a Preview branch or in a custom environment before production. Use Run Schedule in your project’s Schedules tab to try either task without waiting, and see when past runs happened.

Get started

Vercel Schedules is now in Public Beta, and you can use it for the recurring tasks your application already runs. When a user or agent chooses when work should happen, your code can create and manage a schedule for that task.

To get started, check out the Vercel Schedules skill and read the documentation.
