title: Decision-1.1 now available on AI Gateway
description:
Decision-1.1 from Microsoft AI is now available on AI Gateway. It is more accurate, better calibrated, and faster than Decision-1.

The decision model returns structured answers instead of free-form text for tasks such as routing support requests, choosing which model should handle a request, selecting the next step in a workflow, or grading AI responses.

  • Boolean: the probability that a condition is true

  • Choice: a selected category and probabilities for each option

  • Score: a numerical rating on a scale you define

Multiple questions can share the same input in one request. Better calibration means the model's probabilities track how often it is right, so your application can set thresholds for when to act, flag a case for review, or escalate.

Decision-1.1 accepts the same request format as Decision-1. To switch, change the model ID to microsoft/decision-1.1.

Call it through the AI SDK, the OpenAI-compatible Decisions API, or the AI CLI. The examples below require ai 7.0.128 or later for TypeScript, or the OpenAI Python SDK 3.26.0 or later for Python.

Decision requests appear in request logs, count toward budgets, and support decision fallbacks.

Try Decision-1.1 in the model playground, or see the decision models documentation for request formats and question types.

Read more

title: Introducing eve 1.0
description:
Today we're announcing eve 1.0, the open-source framework for building production-ready agents.

Since the public preview in June, we've worked with early adopters to prepare eve for 1.0, shipping 230+ releases and merging thousands of pull requests. With this release, eve is now generally available.

We've made eve faster, expanded integrations, and improved observability. Security controls let you decide which actions need approval and what data gets collected. We've also made it easier for coding agents to build with, measuring that experience with a rigorous evaluation suite.

With eve handling your harness and infrastructure, you and your agent can focus on building instead.

Build production agents on a harness you own

The harness in eve is the loop that calls models, runs tools, and delegates work to subagents. You choose the model, add or replace tools, edit instructions, and decide which actions need approval. The open-source Workflow SDK saves progress as the agent runs, so it can pick up from its last completed step after a crash. Multiplayer sessions and agent-to-agent calls are built in.

For managed hosting, deploy your eve agent to Vercel. Vercel Workflows handles durable execution, and Vercel Sandbox runs agent-generated code in isolation.

Build software factories that turn requests into tested pull requests, company brains that answer questions from your business data, or customer-facing agents in your product.

Thousands of businesses already run eve in production for internal and customer-facing agents. Rillet built a software factory on eve that takes in customer requests, converts them into specs, tests the changes, and opens PRs for human review. Rillet tripled its shipping rate in three months. Clay built monty, a data agent that answers employees’ questions in Slack. Just over two months in, 30–40% of the company used it every week.

Lindy's agent framework roundup names eve “Best for durable backend agents”.

Collaborate in multiplayer agent sessions

Multiplayer lets several people work with an agent in one shared session. eve keeps track of who said what and directs approvals and sign-ins to the right person. You can set up memory for each user or the whole team.

In the native Slack channel, each thread is one shared session. Approvals appear as buttons that only the right person can answer, and a live task card shows progress and timing. You can follow up in the thread without mentioning the agent again, cancel the current turn, or reset the session from Slack.

Ambient mode lets an agent listen in channels you choose, even without being mentioned. Guided by goals you set per channel, it decides when to speak up, help, or take on a task, and when to stay quiet. To limit model costs, a small decision model screens every message first, and only the ones that might be for the agent start a turn.

Slack is one of several native channels, alongside Microsoft Teams, Discord, Telegram, GitHub, Linear, Twilio, Web Chat, and iMessage. The Chat SDK channel adds support for any Chat SDK platform adapter, including WhatsApp, Messenger, Google Chat, and email. Each channel is one file, and the same agent can work across all of them. See the integrations directory for the full list.

Build agent UIs with Next.js and other frameworks

eve 1.0 expands our native integrations for Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, TanStack Start, and Vite. The framework integrations build your agent alongside your app and set up its routes. On Vercel, you can deploy the agent and your site as one project, or host them separately.

The client libraries let you work with tool calls, approval requests, and questions in a consistent way across frameworks. Use that session data to build custom UIs: stream replies into agent chats, embed an agent in a page, or show the agent's tool calls in your own components.

Use eve add channel/web to scaffold a chat app with AI Elements components, or add eve's React, Vue, or Svelte bindings to an existing UI.

Build multi-tenant agents

One support-agent deployment can connect to each customer's ticketing system with their own credentials and apply that customer's approval rules.

Your application authenticates the user and identifies which tenant they belong to. You can then set memory, connection credentials, and approval policy for that tenant and user.

Before each model call in the main agent loop, dynamic definitions load the agent's capabilities from the session and external data. In 1.0, they cover models, connections, and subagents as well as tools, skills, and instructions.

Give agents memory across sessions

We added native memory so agents can carry context from one session to the next. You choose the memory's scope and can use the built-in file memory, a memory provider, or one you build yourself.

Built-in fileMemory keeps data in memory in eve dev and in a private Vercel Blob store you configure on Vercel.

Other providers include claude-mem, Hindsight, Kybernesis Arcana, Memanto, memco, Supermemory, and Upstash AgentKit.

Trace agents with OpenTelemetry

We rebuilt eve’s tracing around OpenTelemetry, so you can follow an agent’s work in the tracing tools you already use. eve dev records traces locally by default. If you host eve yourself, you can export them to an OpenTelemetry backend, including one you run yourself.

Tracing integrations include Raindrop, with more options in the integrations directory. Add one with eve add instrumentation/<name>, or use the instrumentation APIs to build your own integration.

Traces now show when an agent is waiting for a person, including tool approvals, questions, budget prompts, and sign-ins. They record model selections and approval decisions alongside model usage and cost, and follow calls into MCP servers and remote agents.

You choose what eve collects for tracing. Content you exclude from collection stays out of every destination. You can filter out spans or redact inputs and outputs per destination. Private conversations in production send only metadata by default, without prompts or tool results. The OpenTelemetry guide explains these controls.

On Vercel, Agent Runs uses the same traces to show sessions, model calls, tool execution, subagent activity, and approval decisions in the dashboard. When eve deploy creates a new Vercel project, it sets up trace sampling automatically. See the Agent Runs guide for setup and configuration.

Lower agent turn latency

At the start of September, our hosted stress test on Vercel Workflows took a median of 3.036s per turn. In 1.0, the same 100-turn workload took 414ms. The test sends messages one at a time, with one immediate mock-model response and no tool calls per turn. We measure from sending a message until the turn finishes, capturing eve and Workflow overhead without the time a model takes to generate a response.

Hosted stress run

Median turn latency

p95

September 1, beta baseline

3.036s

3.692s

November 15, 1.0.0

414ms

633ms

We worked with the Workflow team on spec 9, which gives each run a single orchestrator so background steps no longer replay the workflow. The team also moved event and stream writes to WebSockets and cut redundant history reads. eve agents get these improvements through Workflow SDK.

eve also caches the information it needs to route messages to each session and can move idle sessions to a newer deployment between turns. Web UIs can prewarm a session before the first message arrives, so the first reply starts sooner.

Lower workflow costs for long agent sessions

For a 50-turn Evo Docs session, the estimated Vercel Workflows cost drops from 5.4¢ to 1.3¢, about 76% lower. That assumes roughly two model steps per turn and 30-day retention. eve now uses Workflow SDK 5.5 and saves only the conversation data that changed between turns. We've also cut repeated work in workflow steps, checkpoints, and sandbox setup:

  • Workflow steps save changes and refer back to data already stored, instead of repeatedly copying a growing conversation into each step. Steps that don't need history no longer receive it.

  • Checkpoints store references to image files returned by tools, so they don't have to copy the image bytes each time.

  • Sandboxes from prepared snapshots skip repeated setup. Stop a sandbox and keep its files for reuse. Cleanup starts when the session ends.

The storage changes are part of the open-source Workflow SDK, so agents you host yourself on other Workflow backends also store less duplicate session data. The cost estimate above uses Vercel Workflows pricing.

On Vercel, workflow steps run on Fluid compute. They need extra storage writes for inputs above the payload size limit, so sending less session data helps keep turn times consistent as sessions grow. Images and files can still require those writes.

For model calls, tool and skill listings can stay out of the initial prompt until they're needed. Connection tools run through eve__search and eve__tool, so each search no longer has to expand the model's tool list. We also changed how eve marks parts of a prompt for provider caching, so more content can be reused between calls.

During an earlier migration to eve, an engineer at Evisions reported:

Share agent capabilities with extensions

Since the preview, we've added extensions so teams can share tools, skills, instructions, connections, channels, schedules, hooks, and subagents without copying files between agents. You can use extensions from the extensions directory or create your own with npx eve@latest extension init <name>.

For example, agent-browser adds browser automation, Mux Video adds tools for video assets and clips, and Link adds wallet and purchase tools.

eve builds workspace extensions from source and reloads changes during development. You can update shared capabilities in one package and try the changes in your agents as you work.

Build coding agents with eve’s shared tools

The 1.0 code extension builds on eve’s default file tools, adding coding instructions and skills that follow your repository’s AGENTS.md. It's included in the eve package, so there's nothing extra to install. Give it a repository in its sandbox and your agent can investigate code, edit files, and run the project's checks. It uses the same harness and extension system as your other agents, so you can replace or disable tools, override skills, and add your own instructions.

See the benchmark results for comparisons with other coding harnesses using the same tasks and model.

Add the coding extension to your agent:

The companion eve/extensions/git adds GitHub and pull request workflows, using credentials and authorization you configure. On Vercel, the optional remote self-modification extension lets your agent propose changes to its own source in a draft pull request. You review the changes, merge them, and deploy.

Build with the same public APIs eve uses

We built eve's subagents, sleep, and question tools on the same workflow system you can use through defineWorkflowTool. Your tools can return a result, start a background task, or keep accepting messages as a resumable task. They can wait for a person, webhook, or timer without keeping compute running, and their runs survive restarts. You don't need a separate background-job system to coordinate that work.

Once you've defined a reviewer subagent, this tool returns a receipt immediately. The task body waits for the reviewer's result, which is delivered to the model in a later message:

Upgrade to eve 1.0

If you already have an eve agent, the 1.0 upgrade guide walks through the changes to extension builds, agent APIs, session events, clients, and saved history. Follow it before deploying your upgrade.

eve follows semantic versioning, so breaking changes to stable APIs only happen in major releases. Experimental and internal APIs, including experimental fields, can change between major releases.

To work through the upgrade with your coding agent, copy this prompt:

Create your first eve agent

Start in the terminal to build locally, use the browser builder to create and deploy an agent, or choose a template for your use case.

Start in the terminal

Create a new agent from the CLI with Node.js 24 or newer:

In an interactive terminal, this installs dependencies and opens the eve terminal UI. If your selected team has AI Gateway access, you can start chatting without creating a Vercel project or copying an API key. eve can use your existing Vercel CLI credentials to call models through AI Gateway locally. Use /login to sign in to other connections.

In eve dev, you can ask the agent to add a tool, change its instructions, or write a skill. With self-modification, it edits its own source and reloads the change for the next turn.

Start in the browser

From the Vercel dashboard, the agent builder scaffolds an agent, creates its Git repo, and deploys it. Go to Add New → Agent, pick a model, and add web chat or Slack along the way.

title: Pull-request-only preset now available for preview builds
description:
A new Ignored Build Step preset lets you skip preview builds for branches without an open pull request. Production deployments and previews for branches with open pull requests continue to build.

On GitHub and GitLab projects, skipped preview deployments are canceled before consuming any Build CPU Minutes.

To enable this, open your project’s Deployments > Configuration. Under Ignored Build Step, select Only build previews for pull requests from the Behavior menu and click Save.

Learn more in the Ignored Build Step documentation.

title: Vercel Blob now supports TTLs for automatic deletion
description:
Vercel Blob can now delete blobs automatically. Pass ttlDays when you write a blob and it is deleted that many days after upload, from 1 to 730 days. The TTL counts from the blob's upload date.

Use TTLs for blobs you would otherwise delete yourself, such as session transcripts, exports, and temporary uploads.

ttlDays works on put(), copy(), putImage(), multipart uploads, and presigned upload URLs. Every write result and head() response now includes expiresAt, so you know when a blob is due for deletion.

setTtl() changes or removes the TTL of blobs you already have, one URL or up to 1,000 at a time, without re-uploading them.

In Vercel CLI 65.16.0 and later, pass --ttl-days to vercel blob put, put-image, copy or presign, and use vercel blob set-ttl on existing blobs.

Setting a TTL costs one Advanced Operation per started 60 days, on top of the write. A 7-day TTL costs one, and the 730-day maximum costs 13. Clearing a TTL and the deletions themselves are free. You can track TTL operations in the Blob section of the Observability tab.

npm install @vercel/blob@2.9.0

Learn more in the Vercel Blob documentation.

Read more

description:

On Pro, Standard builds cost $0.014 per build minute, and your monthly usage credit applies to build usage. Enterprise rates follow your contract. Standard builds remain billable after switching from Elastic to Standard for teams covered by this change.

Select a build machine in team settings or project settings, or read more about managing your builds.

title: Single-second static deployments now support more assets
description:
Instant deployments let you deploy eligible static sites to Vercel in about a second, without a build step. They now support CSS, images, fonts, and other assets alongside HTML and Markdown.

Deploy a landing page with its stylesheet and images, or a report created by your coding agent, through the Vercel CLI or REST API. With the CLI, run:

Newly supported file types include:

  • Styles and data: CSS, JSON, XML, plain text, and web manifests

  • Images: SVG, PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, AVIF, and ICO

  • Fonts: WOFF, WOFF2, TTF, OTF, and EOT

  • Documents and media: PDF, MP4, WebM, MP3, WAV, and OGG

Instant deployments support up to 100 files totaling 25 MB or less. Vercel detects eligible deployments automatically, with no configuration required.

Deployments that exceed these limits, include JavaScript or other unsupported files, or are triggered by Git still build as before. description:
GPT-Live 1.1 from OpenAI is now available on AI Gateway.

GPT-Live 1.1 is a full-duplex voice model, so it listens while it speaks and a caller can pause, interrupt, or add detail mid-reply. Compared with the previous GPT-Live model, it transcribes speech more accurately and keeps a more consistent accent and voice across languages. It uses the same Live endpoint and client delegation, so an existing GPT-Live integration only needs the new model ID.

Simple example without delegation

Run openai/gpt-live-1.1 by itself:

Delegate work and keep talking

Turn on client delegation, and use the session instructions to tell GPT-Live 1.1 when to ask for help. It asks by sending delegation-created. Answer with any text model on AI Gateway and return the result on the commentary channel for GPT-Live to speak. This example uses openai/gpt-6.2-sol and builds on the session above:

Your application controls delegated work and its permissions, confirmations, and cancellation. Delegated model requests are billed separately through AI Gateway, and voice-session usage continues while they run. These snippets omit the WebSocket connection, event parsing, transcript assembly, audio streaming, and shutdown. See the GPT-Live guide for connection setup, audio streaming, and complete examples.

title: Priority Projects now in public beta
description:
Priority Projects are now in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams. This optional upgrade for individual Vercel projects adds bot and traffic-source signals, Page Integrity for monitoring and controlling client-side scripts and connections, and additional Firewall controls and alerts.

Bot signals

Bot protection is free on all plans. You can enable it to challenge non-browser traffic while allowing verified bots. Priority adds more detailed bot signals: categories, verification status, and names where available. Use these signals in:

  • Firewall rules: Match on bot_name, bot_category, bot_status, and bot_protection in the dashboard or with vercel firewall rules add.

  • Application code: Read x-vercel-bot-category, x-vercel-bot-name, and x-vercel-verified-bot from request headers in Routing Middleware and Vercel Functions. See the header reference for verified and claimed bot names.

  • Logs and Observability: Logs show the Firewall action on all plans. Priority adds the matched rule and bot details where available. In Firewall Observability, Priority adds botCategory for unverified traffic. Log Drains also include bot classifications.

Traffic Sources

Priority adds Traffic Sources labels for requests from Tor exit nodes, VPNs, open or anonymizing proxies, and residential proxies. It also labels traffic flagged by abuse blocklists.

Use these labels in custom Firewall rules, analyze them in Firewall Observability, or read them from the x-vercel-waf-source request header in your application. A request can have multiple labels.

Use the Traffic Sources managed ruleset to log, challenge, or block traffic by source category. Review matching traffic before enabling blocking, since these categories can also include legitimate users.

To enable the Traffic Sources managed ruleset from the CLI, run vercel firewall managed-rulesets enable traffic-sources. This stages the change; review it with vercel firewall diff, then apply it with vercel firewall publish.

Page Integrity

Priority Projects get access to Page Integrity to monitor client-side scripts and connections, receive alerts when new scripts or connections are detected, and block unapproved resources.

Page Integrity maintains a resource inventory and uses Content Security Policy (CSP) for discovery and enforcement, without adding client-side JavaScript.

It operates in three stages:

  • Detect: Discover scripts using report-only CSP headers on sampled requests.

  • Review: Approve or reject scripts and record business justifications.

  • Block: Enforce a CSP that blocks scripts outside the approved inventory.

Page Integrity must be enabled separately. Configure monitoring and review resources in the dashboard; the CLI can also show its resource inventory:

Firewall controls and alerts

Anomaly alerts

DDoS alerts are available on all plans. Priority adds anomaly alerts for bot traffic and requests matching system or custom Firewall rules. Use these alerts to investigate potential attacks and unusual traffic patterns.

Configure notifications in your team’s Settings > Alerts, with delivery options including email, Slack, and webhooks.

View recent alerts with vercel alerts --since 24h. To manage alert configuration from the CLI, see vercel monitors.

OWASP Core Ruleset

On Pro, Priority lets you enable the OWASP Core Ruleset to protect against common web application attacks. Enterprise projects can already enable it without Priority.

Add it as a team default from Security > Rules, or enable it for a linked project via the CLI with vercel firewall managed-rulesets enable owasp --yes followed by vercel firewall publish. OWASP inspection is billed separately per inspected request and GB of inspected payload.

Response-based rate limiting

Priority adds response conditions to the rate-limit rules available on all plans. Count requests toward a limit only when their responses match specified HTTP status codes or response headers. For example, count 401 responses from failed login attempts or 404 responses for missing pages, rather than every matching request.

Higher Firewall limits

Priority increases the following per-project limits (shown as standard → with Priority):

Get started

Priority costs $200 per project per month. Enable it from your project’s Firewall or Settings page, or with the CLI.

For the CLI, update to the latest version with vercel upgrade, then enable Priority for the project you want to upgrade:

Page Integrity usage is billed separately. Its standard rate is $2 per 1,000 monitored page views, with each view covering up to 100 scripts.

Learn more in the Priority Projects documentation.

title: Agents can now find Vercel CLI commands by describing the task
description:
Coding agents can now use vercel help search to find Vercel CLI commands by describing a task in plain language.

The search returns a list of matching commands. Add --with-help to include the help page for the first result in the same call. For example, vercel help search "roll back production" --with-help returns the options and examples for vercel rollback.

Search also supports:

  • API endpoints: When a Vercel API endpoint matches the task, search returns a vercel api command with the request path and placeholders for every required input. The agent can fill in the values without guessing the path.

  • JSON output: Use --json to return search results as JSON. Combine it with --with-help to include usage instructions, options, and examples for the first result.

Search recognizes common wording, such as “show” instead of “list,” and handles minor spelling mistakes.

The CLI also includes a skill that tells coding agents to start with vercel help search when looking for a command. Vercel doesn't log your search text.

Update to the latest Vercel CLI with vercel upgrade.

title: Vercel completes ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification
description:
Vercel has completed its ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification, meeting the international standard for AI management systems.

This certification gives our customers confidence to ship fast with agents on Vercel, demonstrating how Vercel designs, builds, operates, and governs our AI products.

Our AI management system covers Vercel’s underlying infrastructure and core AI products, including AI Gateway, Vercel Agent, v0, AI-based open source software and frameworks, as well as the people and processes behind them.

Vercel’s certificate is available here, and additional audit documentation is available through our Trust Center.

What is ISO 42001?

ISO/IEC 42001:2023 is the international standard for AI management systems and applies to any organization that develops, provides, or uses AI.

An AI management system is the set of policies, roles, processes, and controls through which an organization consistently governs AI activities. The standard includes requirements for leadership accountability, AI risk assessment, lifecycle management, data governance, transparency, and continual improvement.

The requirement that makes ISO 42001 distinct from security standards is the AI system impact assessment. Security frameworks cover how an organization protects information, but ISO 42001 covers how it builds and uses AI, including the assessment of how an AI system impacts the people it touches, and the benefits and harms that would result when that system materially changes.

To obtain the certification, we underwent a two-stage audit performed by an independent, accredited certification body, which evaluated whether our AI management system is designed correctly and operates effectively. The certificate is valid for three years, with annual surveillance audits in between.

“Enterprises want agents in production, but no one should have to choose between moving fast with AI and governing it well,” said Talha Tariq, CTO for Security. “We built our AI governance to run as continuously as we ship, and ISO 42001 is the independent check that it works.”

What this means for customers

AI moved into the critical path of how software gets built faster than the governance around it did. Teams are shipping agents, assistants, and model-backed features on Vercel every day, and the questions that follow are no longer hypothetical:

  • Who is accountable when a model behaves unexpectedly?

  • What data reached a model?

  • How is the system monitored once it’s live?

  • Who decided the system was ready?

We pursued ISO 42001 because we are committed to providing enterprise-grade AI products. This certification attests that we run deliberate, auditable AI systems.

How we govern AI at Vercel

There are three primary ways AI is governed at Vercel.

Impact assessments

Vercel conducts AI system impact assessments which cover foreseeable benefits, harms, failures, and misuse. We reassess these risks and benefits when the system materially changes.

Evaluations before release

We maintain evals for our AI systems covering performance, safety, and security, with human review for material changes.

Clear data commitments

Where it is not the default option based on pricing plan, we provide customers the ability to set their data handling preferences ranging from zero data retention (ZDR) to training opt-out. Our AI policy is available at v0.app/policy.

Ship fast, with confidence

We are committed to helping teams ship fast with confidence in the way AI is built and governed at Vercel. ISO 42001 is proof of that commitment, giving our customers:

  • Confidence in agentic infrastructure: Vercel’s AI systems have been audited, which means customers using our AI products start from a reviewed foundation instead of an unexamined one.

  • Governance can ship at the speed of the product: Agents now drive the development and deployment of applications. Governance and oversight that occurs quarterly can’t govern software that changes hourly, so we built a system that reviews AI as continuously as we ship it.

  • Simplified and accelerated assurance: Customers and partners can rely on this certification, alongside our other compliance attestations, to meet AI governance diligence requirements for faster third-party vendor onboarding.

  • Clear lines of responsibility: ISO 42001 requires that responsibilities be allocated across the AI supply chain. Our documentation outlines what Vercel is accountable for and what remains yours, the same shared-responsibility model we use for security.

  • Discipline that holds over time: Annual surveillance audits mean this isn’t a one-time claim. As our AI products change, the system that governs them stays under independent review.

AI is changing what people build on Vercel, and we intend for the governance around it to keep pace. We’ll continue to expand the scope of our certifications as our products grow.

Read more

title: Vercel Functions now support request bodies up to 20MiB
description:
Vercel Functions now accept inbound request bodies up to 20MiB, up from 4.5MB, in Public Beta.

To turn this on, set the VERCEL_SUPPORT_LARGE_REQUEST_BODY=1 environment variable. The opt-in applies to the whole project in the environment where you set it, so you can test the larger limit on preview before enabling it in production. It requires the project's functions to use the performance memory setting of 4GB. It applies to functions on the Node.js, Python, and Bun runtimes, and to Routing Middleware. Functions and Routing Middleware on the Edge runtime keep the 4.5MB cap and return 413 on oversize bodies, so moving them onto the larger limit means switching to the Node.js runtime with runtime: 'nodejs', or proxy.ts in Next.js.

When a project opts in, Routing Middleware receives request headers and metadata but no request body, enforced at the project level. Middleware still runs and still sees every other request header, so body-dependent middleware behavior is the one thing that becomes unavailable. This avoids sending the body twice, to both middleware and the target function, which would raise cost and time to first byte.

When handling larger request bodies, read the body promptly and avoid holding it in memory to prevent backpressure and memory issues.

Learn more in the Vercel Functions limitations documentation.

Read more

title: Catch missing feature flags before they reach production
description:
Vercel Flags can now block a deployment from reaching production if you’ve declared a flag in code but haven’t created it in your project. Without that definition, your app can silently fall back to the flag’s default value, even if that turns on a feature you meant to keep off.

The Flag Definitions Present Deployment Check runs when a deployment is ready. If any flags are missing, the check fails and lists them in the results, where you can create each one before redeploying.

The check reads your Flags SDK discovery endpoint and requires FLAGS_SECRET to be set in your project’s environment.

To turn on blocking, teams on all plans can enable the check in their project’s Build and Deployment settings and mark it as required. See the Deployment Checks documentation for setup details.

Read more

title: RTB'yi teklif veren tarafından okumak: OpenRTB isteği, zaman bütçesi, win notice ve CRM'e uzanan ölçüm
description:
Programatik reklamı çoğu ekip bir panel üzerinden yönetir: bütçe girilir, hedef kitle seçilir, kampanya açılır. Panelin arkasında ise her gösterim için milisaniyeler içinde kurulan ve kapanan bir açık artırma vardır. Bu açık artırmanın dili OpenRTB'dir. Kendi bidder'ınızı hiç yazmayacak olsanız bile bu protokolü okuyabilmek; bir DSP raporundaki tuhaf bir kalemi, kaybolan gösterimleri ya da CRM'e hiç ulaşmayan tıklamaları açıklamanın en kısa yoludur.

Ben Koray Yalçın; lead yönetimi, CRM ve pazarlama otomasyonu altyapıları kuruyorum, ağırlıklı olarak gayrimenkul projelerinde reklamdan satış ofisine uzanan veri hattında çalışıyorum. Kavramın kısa tanımı için sözlükteki Real-Time Bidding (RTB) nedir sayfasına bakabilirsiniz. Bu yazıda tanımın ötesine geçip geliştirici tarafına bakacağım: bir teklif isteğinin anatomisi, zaman bütçesi içinde karar vermek, teklif vermemeyi doğru yapmak, kazanma bildirimini (win notice) güvenilir biçimde işlemek ve gösterimden CRM'deki satış fırsatına kadar ölçüm zincirini kopartmamak.

Daha önce header bidding üzerine yazdığımda yayıncı tarafındaki tarayıcı açık artırmasını anlatmıştım. Bu yazı aynı pazarın diğer ucundan, teklif veren taraftan bakıyor.

1. Bir açık artırmanın kısa yolculuğu

Kullanıcı bir sayfayı açtığında yayıncının reklam alanı bir SSP'ye (supply-side platform) bilgi gönderir. SSP ya da ad exchange bu bilgiyi bir teklif isteğine (bid request) çevirir ve aynı anda birden çok DSP'ye (demand-side platform) yollar. Her DSP kendi kampanyalarına bakar, bu gösterimin kendisi için ne kadar değerli olduğuna karar verir ve ya bir teklif (bid response) döner ya da teklif vermez. Exchange gelen teklifleri karşılaştırır, kazananı seçer, kazanana bildirim gönderir ve reklam kreatifi sayfaya yüklenir.

Bu zincirin tamamı kullanıcı sayfayı beklerken olur. Sözlükte de belirttiğim gibi bir RTB ihalesi tipik olarak yaklaşık 100 milisaniye içinde tamamlanır. Bu süre ağ gecikmesini de içerdiği için bidder'ın kendi karar süresi bunun yalnızca bir parçasıdır. Mimarinin bütün tasarım kararları bu kısıttan doğar.

2. Teklif isteğinin anatomisi

OpenRTB 2.x sürümlerinde bir teklif isteği JSON nesnesidir. Ayrıntılar exchange'e göre değişse de iskelet aynıdır. Aşağıdaki örnek, alanları göstermek için sadeleştirilmiş bir istektir; gerçek bir exchange'den alınmış veri değildir:

{
  "id": "auc-7f3a",
  "tmax": 120,
  "at": 1,
  "cur": ["EUR"],
  "imp": [{
    "id": "1",
    "tagid": "sidebar-300x250",
    "banner": { "format": [{ "w": 300, "h": 250 }] },
    "bidfloor": 0.80,
    "bidfloorcur": "EUR"
  }],
  "site": {
    "domain": "ornek-haber.com",
    "page": "https://ornek-haber.com/ekonomi/konut",
    "cat": ["IAB21"]
  },
  "device": { "ua": "...", "geo": { "country": "CYP" }, "devicetype": 2 },
  "user": { "buyeruid": "dsp-uid-91c2", "consent": "..." },
  "regs": { "gdpr": 1 },
  "bcat": ["IAB25"],
  "badv": ["rakip-marka.com"]
}

Bir geliştirici olarak dikkat etmem gereken alanlar şunlardır:

  • id ve imp[].id: Açık artırmanın ve gösterim alanının kimliği. Bütün loglar bu iki değer üzerinden birleştirilir.
  • tmax: Exchange'in yanıt için tanıdığı süre (milisaniye). Bu süreyi aşan yanıt, ne kadar yüksek olursa olsun değerlendirilmez.
  • at: Açık artırma tipi. 1 birinci fiyat, 2 ikinci fiyat anlamına gelir. Teklif stratejisi buna göre değişir.
  • bidfloor ve bidfloorcur: Yayıncının taban fiyatı ve para birimi. Taban fiyatın altındaki teklif boşa giden işlemdir.
  • bcat ve badv: Yayıncının engellediği kategoriler ve reklamveren alan adları. Bunlara uymayan teklif reddedilir.
  • user.buyeruid: DSP'nin kendi kullanıcı kimliğinin eşleştirilmiş hali. Birinci taraf segmentlerle eşleşme buradan yapılır.
  • regs ve user.consent: Gizlilik sinyalleri. Avrupa'daki trafikte rıza dizesi olmadan kişiselleştirilmiş teklif vermek, hukuki bir risk olduğu kadar teknik olarak da reddedilme sebebidir.

Bu listeyi bir sözleşme gibi ele almak gerekir: istek doğrulayıcısı ilk satırda çalışmalı, eksik ya da tutarsız istekler karar katmanına hiç ulaşmamalıdır.

3. Zaman bütçesi: sıcak yolda veritabanı yok

100 milisaniyelik bir dünyada en sık yapılan hata, karar anında bir veritabanına ya da harici bir API'ye gitmektir. Kampanya ayarları, segment üyelikleri ve bütçe durumu sıcak yoldan (hot path) önce, belleğe yüklenmiş olmalıdır. Ben bidder'ı iki katmana ayırıyorum:

  • Kontrol katmanı: Kampanyaları, hedeflemeleri, segmentleri ve bütçe limitlerini veritabanından okur, derler ve birkaç saniyede bir belleğe yeni bir anlık görüntü olarak yayınlar.
  • Karar katmanı: Yalnızca bellekteki anlık görüntüyü okur. Ağ çağrısı yapmaz, kilit beklemez, log yazımını kuyruğa bırakır.

Karar katmanının iskeleti Python ile şöyle görünebilir:

import time

SAFETY_MS = 15  # ağ dönüşü için ayrılan pay (örnek değer)

def handle_bid_request(req: dict, snapshot) -> tuple[int, dict | None]:
    started = time.monotonic()
    deadline_ms = max(0, req.get("tmax", 100) - SAFETY_MS)

    problem = validate(req)
    if problem:
        log_async("invalid", req.get("id"), problem)
        return 204, None

    bids = []
    for imp in req["imp"]:
        if elapsed_ms(started) > deadline_ms:
            log_async("timeout_guard", req["id"], imp["id"])
            break
        decision = decide(imp, req, snapshot)
        if decision:
            bids.append(decision)

    if not bids:
        return 204, None
    return 200, build_response(req, bids)

def elapsed_ms(started: float) -> float:
    return (time.monotonic() - started) * 1000

Buradaki SAFETY_MS değeri bir örnektir; gerçek değer exchange ile aranızdaki ağ gecikmesi ölçülerek belirlenir. Önemli olan, bidder'ın kendi saatine bakması ve süre dolmak üzereyken kararı yarıda kesip teklif vermemeyi seçebilmesidir. Geç verilmiş bir teklif, hiç verilmemiş bir tekliften daha kötüdür: kaynak harcar ve exchange tarafında yanıt kalitenizi düşürür.

4. Karar fonksiyonu: önce elemek, sonra fiyatlamak

Karar fonksiyonunu, ucuz kontrollerden pahalı olanlara doğru sıralanmış bir eleme hattı olarak kuruyorum:

def decide(imp: dict, req: dict, snap) -> dict | None:
    for c in snap.campaigns_for_size(imp_size(imp)):
        if not c.active_now():
            continue
        if req.get("site", {}).get("domain") in c.blocked_domains:
            continue
        if c.adomain in req.get("badv", []):
            continue
        if set(c.categories) & set(req.get("bcat", [])):
            continue
        if c.requires_consent and not has_valid_consent(req):
            continue
        if not snap.pacer.can_spend(c.id):
            continue

        segment_hit = snap.segments.contains(c.segment_id, buyer_uid(req))
        price = c.price_for(segment_hit, auction_type=req.get("at", 1))
        floor = to_bid_currency(imp.get("bidfloor", 0), imp.get("bidfloorcur", "USD"))
        if price < floor:
            continue

        return {"imp": imp, "campaign": c, "price": round(price, 4)}
    return None

Bu sırada birkaç ilke var. Birincisi, kampanyalar reklam boyutuna göre önceden indekslenmiştir; her istekte bütün kampanyaları taramayız. İkincisi, hukuki ve marka güvenliği kontrolleri fiyatlamadan önce gelir; çünkü bu kontrollerden geçemeyen bir kampanya için fiyat hesaplamanın anlamı yoktur. Üçüncüsü, taban fiyat karşılaştırması para birimi dönüştürüldükten sonra yapılır. İstekteki taban fiyat EUR, kampanyanın bütçesi GBP olabilir; bu dönüşümü atlamak sessiz ve pahalı bir hatadır.

Segment eşleşmesi de bellekte tutulur. Gayrimenkul tarafında tipik bir örnek: CRM'de "son 30 günde fiyat listesi isteyip randevu almamış" kişilerden oluşan bir birinci taraf segmenti, kontrol katmanı tarafından eşleştirilmiş kullanıcı kimliklerine çevrilir ve karar katmanına bir küme olarak yüklenir. Karar anında yalnızca "bu kimlik kümede mi" sorusu sorulur.

5. Teklif vermemek de bir yanıttır

OpenRTB'de teklif vermemenin standart yolu HTTP 204 dönmektir; yanıt gövdesinde nbr (no-bid reason) alanıyla sebep bildirmek de mümkündür. Bidder'ın büyük çoğunlukla teklif vermediğini unutmamak gerekir. Bu yüzden teklif vermeme yolu, teklif verme yolu kadar özenle tasarlanmalıdır:

  • Hızlı olmalıdır; elenen bir istek için gereksiz iş yapılmamalıdır.
  • Sebebi kaydedilmelidir; ama her isteği tek tek loglamak yerine sebep kodu bazında sayaçlar tutmak yeterlidir.
  • Sebepler kontrol edilebilir bir listeden gelmelidir: invalid, no_campaign, brand_safety, no_consent, pacing, below_floor, timeout_guard gibi.

Bu sayaçlar, "kampanya neden harcamıyor?" sorusunun cevabıdır. Panel yalnızca "düşük teslimat" der; sayaçlar ise teklif isteklerinin büyük kısmının rıza sinyali eksikliğinden mi, taban fiyattan mı, yoksa bütçe pacing'inden mi elendiğini gösterir.

6. Teklif yanıtı ve kazanma bildirimi

Teklif yanıtı da bir JSON nesnesidir. Kazanma durumunda exchange'in çağıracağı adresler yanıtın içinde gelir:

def build_response(req: dict, bids: list[dict]) -> dict:
    return {
        "id": req["id"],
        "cur": "EUR",
        "seatbid": [{
            "seat": "koray-dsp",
            "bid": [{
                "id": f'{req["id"]}-{b["imp"]["id"]}',
                "impid": b["imp"]["id"],
                "price": b["price"],
                "adomain": [b["campaign"].adomain],
                "crid": b["campaign"].creative_id,
                "adm": b["campaign"].markup,
                "nurl": WIN_URL + "?auc=${AUCTION_ID}&imp=" + b["imp"]["id"] + "&p=${AUCTION_PRICE}",
                "burl": BILL_URL + "?auc=${AUCTION_ID}&imp=" + b["imp"]["id"] + "&p=${AUCTION_PRICE}",
                "lurl": LOSS_URL + "?auc=${AUCTION_ID}&r=${AUCTION_LOSS}",
            } for b in bids]
        }]
    }

${AUCTION_PRICE} gibi makroları exchange, bildirimi gönderirken gerçek değerlerle doldurur. Burada iki ayrımı net yapmak gerekir. nurl kazanma bildirimidir; burl ise faturalanabilir olayın, yani gösterimin gerçekleştiğinin bildirimidir. Bütçe düşümünü hangisine bağladığınız, exchange ile yaptığınız anlaşmaya göre belirlenir ve bu karar dokümante edilmelidir. Bazı exchange'ler fiyatı şifreli gönderir; bu durumda çözme işlemi bildirim alıcısında yapılır.

Bildirim alıcısını yazarken uyguladığım kurallar:

  • Idempotent olmalı: Aynı bildirim ağ tekrarları yüzünden birden fazla gelebilir. auc + imp birleşik anahtarıyla tek kayıt tutulur, ikinci gelen yok sayılır.
  • Hızlı yanıt vermeli: Alıcı bildirimi kuyruğa yazar ve hemen döner; bütçe düşümü ve raporlama arka planda yapılır.
  • Mutabakat yapılabilmeli: Kendi kayıtlarınızdaki kazanma ve gösterim sayıları, exchange'in raporuyla periyodik olarak karşılaştırılmalıdır. 
CREATE TABLE rtb_event (
  auction_id   text        NOT NULL,
  imp_id       text        NOT NULL,
  event_type   text        NOT NULL CHECK (event_type IN ('bid','win','bill','loss')),
  campaign_id  text,
  price        numeric(12,6),
  currency     text,
  received_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (auction_id, imp_id, event_type)
);

-- Günlük mutabakat: verdiğimiz teklif, kazandığımız ve faturalanan
SELECT campaign_id,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE event_type = 'bid')  AS bids,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE event_type = 'win')  AS wins,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE event_type = 'bill') AS billed,
       sum(price) FILTER (WHERE event_type = 'bill') AS spend
FROM rtb_event
WHERE received_at >= date_trunc('day', now() - interval '1 day')
  AND received_at <  date_trunc('day', now())
GROUP BY campaign_id;

wins ile billed arasındaki fark, kazanılmış ama sayfada gösterilememiş açık artırmaları gösterir. Bu fark beklenenden büyükse, kreatifin yüklenme süresinden yayıncının sayfa yapısına kadar bakılacak bir sorun vardır.

7. Bütçe pacing'i: kilitsiz ama sınırlı

Bütçenin gün içinde dengeli harcanması, bidder'ın birden fazla sunucuda paralel çalıştığı düşünüldüğünde zor bir problemdir. Her teklifte merkezi bir sayaca gidip kilit beklemek zaman bütçesini yer. Benim kullandığım yaklaşım, merkezi bütçeyi küçük paylara bölüp her sunucuya kısa süreli bir harcama kotası vermektir. Sunucu kendi kotası içinde yerel olarak karar verir; kota bittiğinde kontrol katmanından yenisini ister. Gerçek harcama burl bildirimleriyle merkezde toplandığı için, kota ile gerçek arasında oluşan küçük sapmalar bir sonraki dağıtımda düzeltilir. Bu yapıda bütçe aşımının üst sınırı, dağıtılan açık kotaların toplamı kadardır ve bu sınır bilinçli olarak seçilir.

8. Gösterimden CRM'e: ölçüm zincirini kopartmamak

Benim işimde bir RTB kampanyasının başarısı tıklama oranıyla değil, CRM'de oluşan nitelikli randevularla ölçülür. Bu yüzden açık artırma kimliğini zincirin sonuna kadar taşımak gerekir:

  1. Kreatifin tıklama adresine kampanya, kreatif ve açık artırma kimliği eklenir (UTM parametreleri ve kendi auc parametreniz).
  2. Açılış sayfası bu parametreleri birinci taraf çerezine ya da oturuma yazar.
  3. Form gönderildiğinde lead kaydı bu kimliklerle birlikte CRM'e düşer.
  4. CRM'deki aşama değişiklikleri (randevu, rezervasyon, sözleşme) aynı kimlikle rtb_event verisine bağlanabilir.

Bu sayede "hangi yayıncı alanından gelen gösterimler randevuya dönüşüyor?" sorusu SQL ile cevaplanabilir hale gelir. Sonuçları kontrol katmanına geri besleyerek fiyatlamayı randevu olasılığına göre ayarlamak mümkündür; ancak bunu yaparken her değişikliği sürümlemek ve bir kontrol grubuyla ölçmek gerekir. Aksi halde fiyatlama değişikliğinin etkisini sezonsal dalgalanmalardan ayıramazsınız.

9. Sık yapılan hatalar

  • tmax'ı yok saymak: Bidder'ın kendi saati olmadığında yoğun anlarda bütün yanıtlar geç kalır.
  • Para birimini karıştırmak: Taban fiyatla teklifin farklı para birimlerinde karşılaştırılması.
  • Bildirimleri çift saymak: Idempotency anahtarı olmayan bir alıcı, harcamayı olduğundan yüksek gösterir.
  • Rıza sinyalini sonradan düşünmek: Rıza kontrolü karar hattına sonradan eklenirse bazı yollar kontrolsüz kalır.
  • Teklif vermeme sebebini kaydetmemek: Teslimat sorunları tahminle çözülmeye çalışılır.
  • Ölçümü tıklamada bitirmek: CRM bağlantısı olmayan bir RTB kampanyası, satış ekibine hiçbir şey söylemez.

SSS

Kendi bidder'ımı yazmam gerekir mi?
Çoğu reklamveren için hayır. Hazır bir DSP kullanmak genellikle daha mantıklıdır. Ama protokolü bilmek, DSP raporlarını okurken, exchange ile sorun çözerken ve CRM entegrasyonunu tasarlarken doğrudan fayda sağlar.

Birinci fiyat ile ikinci fiyat açık artırma arasındaki fark teklif stratejisini nasıl etkiler?
İkinci fiyatta kazanan, ikinci en yüksek teklife yakın bir bedel öder; bu yüzden gerçek değerinizi teklif etmek mantıklıdır. Birinci fiyatta teklif ettiğiniz tutarı ödersiniz; bu nedenle teklifi gösterimin size değerinin altında tutmak (bid shading) yaygın bir yaklaşımdır. İstekteki at alanı hangisinin geçerli olduğunu söyler.

Win notice ile billing notice arasında hangisine güvenmeliyim?
Bütçe ve faturalama için hangi olayın esas alınacağı exchange ile yapılan anlaşmada belirlenir. Teknik olarak ikisini de ayrı olay tipleri olarak kaydetmek ve aralarındaki farkı izlemek en güvenli yoldur.

Rıza sinyali olmayan trafikte teklif verebilir miyim?
Bu, faaliyet gösterdiğiniz bölgenin mevzuatına ve kampanyanın kişisel veri kullanıp kullanmadığına bağlıdır. Hukuki değerlendirme için uzman görüşü alınmalıdır; teknik tarafta yapılması gereken, rıza kontrolünü karar hattının zorunlu ve atlanamaz bir adımı yapmaktır. Bu yazı hukuki görüş değildir.

Gayrimenkul gibi uzun satış döngüsü olan bir sektörde RTB'yi nasıl ölçmeliyim?
Tıklama ve form metriklerinin yanında, açık artırma kimliğini CRM'e kadar taşıyıp randevu ve rezervasyon aşamalarına bağlamak gerekir. Döngü uzun olduğu için sonuçları kohort bazında ve yeterli olgunlaşma süresi tanıyarak değerlendirmek daha sağlıklıdır.

RTB, dışarıdan bakıldığında bir panelde seçilen birkaç ayardan ibaret görünür; içeride ise zaman bütçesine sıkışmış, gizlilik ve marka güvenliği kurallarına uyması gereken, her bildirimi doğru sayması beklenen bir dağıtık sistemdir. İsteği sözleşme gibi doğrulamak, sıcak yolu bellekte tutmak, teklif vermeme sebeplerini saymak, bildirimleri idempotent işlemek ve açık artırma kimliğini CRM'e kadar taşımak bu sistemin temel taşlarıdır. Siz programatik kampanyalarınızı CRM'deki satış aşamalarına kadar izleyebiliyor musunuz, yoksa ölçüm tıklamada mı bitiyor? Yorumlarda tartışalım.

title: Envoy Gateway vs Traefik vs NGINX: High-Throughput Kubernetes Ingress & Dynamic Configuration
description:
Envoy Gateway vs Traefik vs NGINX: High-Throughput Kubernetes Ingress & Dynamic Configuration

Executive Summary & Decision Matrix

All three proxies saturate a 25 Gbps NIC before saturating a single modern core under TLS termination with session resumption — the differentiators at scale are configuration latency, hot-reload behavior, xDS/CRD ecosystem depth, and memory behavior under 100k+ connection churn.

Decision Matrix in One Sentence: Run Envoy Gateway if you are building a Gateway-API-native platform serving >50k RPS with gRPC, mTLS, and multi-tenant traffic policy; run Traefik if you want zero-friction dynamic discovery and edge routing for teams under ~15 engineers; run NGINX (Ingress NGINX + Plus where licensed) when you have existing NGINX operational muscle, need battle-proven L7 at extreme raw throughput, or require FIPS/advanced TCP-UDP on mature, audited binaries.

Quantified Decision Matrix

Benchmarks: c5n.4xlarge (16 vCPU, 42 GB, 25 Gbps ENA), Kubernetes 1.31, containerd, HTTP/2 gRPC and HTTP/1.1 workloads via wrk2 and fortio, TLS 1.3 with X25519, 2 KB responses, load generated from 6 dedicated c5n.9xlarge drivers. Cold caches, 30-minute soak per point, p99 reported from hdrhistogram.

Metric Envoy Gateway (v1.3) Traefik v3.3 NGINX Ingress (1.12) / NGINX Plus R34
Raw L7 RPS, HTTP/1.1, TLS terminated, 16 cores ~118,000 RPS ~96,000 RPS ~142,000 RPS
p99 latency @ 50k RPS (TLS, 2 KB) 7.8 ms 11.2 ms 5.9 ms
p99 latency, gRPC streaming @ 20k streams 9.4 ms 17.6 ms (h2 tuning req.) 12.1 ms
Config convergence (CRD apply → all pods serving) 480–900 ms (xDS delta) 1.9–4.2 s (full rebuild) 2.5–8 s (reload) / <1 s (Plus, NGINX Agent)
Memory @ 100k concurrent conns 1.9 GB RSS 2.7 GB RSS 1.1 GB RSS
Memory @ 500k concurrent conns (4 replicas) 8.4 GB total OOM-restart at ~340k/rep (tuning req.) 5.2 GB total
Connection churn (new TLS conns/s, 1 core) 21,000/s 16,500/s 26,000/s
Config model Gateway API (native, GA) + xDS Ingress + native CRDs (Middleware) Ingress annotations + CRDs (Plus/VIC)
Hot reload impact on in-flight conns None (delta xDS, drain per-conn) None (atomic swap), but full listener rebuild Graceful, but master-worker fork; worker restarts drop h2 keepalives unless --reuseport tuned
Connection pool / circuit breaking First-class (per-route thresholds, outlier ejection) Basic (rewriting retries; no outlier ejection) max_fails passive only; active health checks = Plus
Community / support SLA CNCF-adjacent (Envoy core GA since 2016); Tetrate Enterprise ~34k GitHub stars; Traefik Labs enterprise F5 commercial SLA 24/7; open-source Ingress in maintenance mode (retirement announced for March 2026)
Egress/infra cost overhead at 100k RPS (aws us-east-1, 3× c5n.4xlarge) $843/mo compute $1,104/mo (needs 4th replica for same p99) $843/mo

Where the numbers come from: RPS figures are wall-clock saturation with wrk2 (-R fixed-rate, avoids coordinated omission), TLS handshakes offloaded to openssl AES-NI paths. Traefik's h2 streaming gap is a real, measured artifact of its Go HTTP/2 stack plus its router-rebuild cost on config churn — not a synthetic gotcha. NGINX's memory density advantage is its event-driven worker model with ~11 KB/connection baseline versus Envoy's ~19 KB (Envoy trades RAM for filter flexibility; each connection carries filter-state overhead).

Ratings (as configured in frontmatter): Envoy Gateway 4.8, Traefik 4.5, NGINX 4.3 — weighted 40% raw performance, 25% operational model, 20% ecosystem, 15% upgrade safety.

Architectural Deep-Dive

Envoy Gateway

Envoy is a C++ edge/service proxy exposing a gRPC xDS control plane. Envoy Gateway (EG) is a Kubernetes-native controller translating Gateway API resources into xDS ClusterLoadAssignment/Listener protos and streaming delta xDS to data-plane pods. The critical property: xDS is eventually consistent per-resource-type, and EG implements ordered resource publication (per the xDS fallback/CSDS model), so you don't get EDS-before-CDS 503 storms that plagued early Istio deployments.

flowchart TB
    subgraph EG["Envoy Gateway"]
        GWAPI["Gateway API CRDs<br/>(GatewayClass, HTTPRoute, BackendTLSPolicy)"] --> EGCTL["Envoy Gateway Controller<br/>(Go, translates to xDS protos)"]
        EGCTL -->|"gRPC delta xDS<br/>(LDS/CDS/RDS/EDS)"| DP1["Envoy Proxy Pod 1<br/>(C++17, threaded workers)"]
        EGCTL --> DP2["Envoy Proxy Pod 2"]
    end
    subgraph TR["Traefik"]
        ING["Ingress + CRDs<br/>(MiddlewareService)"] --> TB["Traefik Pod (Go)<br/>kubedynamicconf provider"]
        TB -->|"in-process atomic router swap"| TBW["Single binary: control plane<br/>and data plane are the same process"]
    end
    subgraph NG["NGINX Ingress"]
        NI["Ingress + ConfigMaps/annotations"] --> NC["Ingress-NGINX Controller<br/>(Go)"]
        NC -->|"renders nginx.conf"| NGX["NGINX master → N workers<br/>(C, SO_REUSEPORT)"]
        NC -->|"conf validation + reload<br/>(fork/exec nginx -s reload)"| NGX
    end
    DP1 & DP2 & TBW & NGX --> BE["Backend Services"]

The single most important architectural difference is control-plane/data-plane separation. Envoy Gateway separates them (controller crash ≠ traffic outage; proxy pods are stateless and horizontally scalable). Traefik fuses both in one Go binary — elegant, fewer moving parts, but config-heavy workloads burn the same goroutine budget that serves traffic, and a config pathological case (e.g., 20,000 Ingress objects) shows GC pauses of 40–90 ms in the same process that terminates TLS. NGINX sits between: the Go controller writes config, but the data plane is forked NGINX workers with nginx -s reload semantics — new workers spin up on a new shared-memory zone, old workers finish keepalive drain. Under rapid successive reloads (config churn > 1 reload/2s) you get worker accumulation: we measured 14 live worker generations consuming 8.6 GB RSS on a 16-core box during a CI-driven GitOps loop that committed config 10×/minute. Mitigation is --reload-interval tuning or NGINX Plus's dynamic upstream API, which avoids reloads entirely for upstream membership changes.

Rate-limiting and connection-state mechanics

  • Envoy: token-bucket rate limits in the local rate-limit filter (~900k checks/s/core) or a global gRPC rate-limit service; circuit breaking via per-cluster max_connections/max_pending_requests, plus outlier detection (success-rate and consecutive-5xx ejection). Everything is config, zero custom code.
  • Traefik: rateLimit middleware (token bucket, in-memory or Redis via rateLimit + distributed store — but the Redis mode adds ~1.8 ms p50). No circuit breaker with outlier ejection; you approximate with retry middleware + health-check CRDs.
  • NGINX OSS: limit_req (leaky bucket), passive max_fails only. Active health checks, queue, and zone_sync (shared state across replicas) are Plus-gated — this is the single biggest functional cliff between OSS and $2,500+/yr/instance commercial licensing (Plus R34 list pricing: ~$3,500/yr/instance, volume tiers lower).

Low-level trade-offs

  • Syscall topology: NGINX uses one epoll loop per worker with SO_REUSEPORT sharding — best raw throughput because kernel socket hash spreads accept load without cross-worker lock contention. Envoy uses libevent with a per-worker event loop too, but layers an L7 filter chain per connection — the flexibility tax is visible in the RPS column. Traefik inherits Go's netpoller; fine, but GOMAXPROCS must be pinned via automaxprocs or it reads container CPU limits wrong and over-subscribes (a chronic source of tail latency on cgroup-limited pods).
  • TLS: all three use BoringSSL/OpenSSL with AES-NI. Envoy's BoringSSL build does ~26k full handshakes/s/core (RSA-2048) and ~71k/s with session resumption; NGINX ~29k/74k; Traefik ~23k/68k. If your traffic is 90% new handshakes (mobile, no resumption), TLS CPU dominates and the RPS ranking compresses.
  • Kernel bypass: none of the three use XDP/DPKA in their standard Kubernetes distributions. If you need >1M RPS per box, Envoy has a documented path via contributed filters and can be paired with Cilium's L7 acceleration upstream of the proxy; NGINX and Traefik have no equivalent.

Real-World Benchmarks & Hard Data

Harness 

# Load driver (each of 6 c5n.9xlarge machines):
wrk2 -t8 -c512 -d30m -R50000 --latency \
     -s pipeline.lua https://shop.example.internal/checkout

# gRPC saturation:
ghz --insecure --concurrency=2000 --n=5000000 \
    --call proto.OrderService/Submit \
    --total-histogram --rps 20000 shop.example.internal:443

# Connection churn (TLS handshake storm):
wrk -t8 -c256 -d10m --new-connection-per-request ...
# watch kernel: ss -s ; sar -n SOCK 1 ; pidstat -wt 1 | grep envoy

Results

Scenario (16 vCPU data plane, 25 Gbps) Envoy Gateway Traefik v3.3 NGINX Ingress
HTTP/1.1 2 KB, 50k RPS, p99 7.8 ms 11.2 ms 5.9 ms
HTTP/1.1 2 KB, 100k RPS, p99 12.4 ms 27.9 ms (2 replicas used) 9.1 ms
gRPC bidi streaming, 20k streams, p99 9.4 ms 17.6 ms 12.1 ms
Config convergence, 1 route change 610 ms 2.8 s 3.9 s
Config convergence, 500-route batch 1.4 s 6.1 s 11.7 s (reload storm risk)
30-min soak, 100k conns, RSS drift +2.1% (conn pool steady state) +4.8% (Go heap, no leak) +0.4%
TLS churn, 15k new conns/s, p99 setup 14.2 ms 19.8 ms 11.7 ms

Soak detail worth engineering attention: Envoy's +2.1% RSS drift stabilized at minute 11 — it's the connection-pool high-water mark, not a leak. Traefik's drift is Go runtime behavior; force GOGC=75 and set GOMEMLIMIT explicitly or Kubernetes OOM-killer will find your proxy before saturation does. NGINX is flat because its allocator doesn't fragment under this pattern — but see the worker-generation trap below.

Total Cost of Ownership

Assumptions: us-east-1, 3-year term with 40% reserved discount on compute, NGINX Plus list pricing, Traefik Labs Enterprise mid-tier, Tetrate/EG Enterprise for the Envoy tier. Managed alternatives (AWS ALB/NLB, GCP LB) priced for context.

Tier Envoy Gateway Traefik NGINX
Startup (~$100/mo): <5k RPS, 2× c5.large, self-managed $96/mo infra, $0 license, ~10 eng-hrs/mo $84/mo infra, $0 license, ~4 eng-hrs/mo (lowest ops burden) $96/mo infra, $0 (OSS), ~12 eng-hrs/mo (annotation debt)
Scale-up (~$2,500/mo): 60k RPS, 4× c5n.4xlarge, mTLS, multi-team $1,124 infra + Tetrate EG Enterprise ~$1,300 = $2,424 $1,124 infra + Traefik Enterprise (2 nodes) ~$1,500 = $2,624 $1,124 infra + NGINX Plus ×4 ($3,500/yr→$584/mo ea. w/ volume tier) = $3,460
Enterprise ($25,000/mo): 500k RPS, 3 regions, 99.99% SLA, F5/Tetrate support ~$9,400 infra + Tetrate Enterprise ~$15,000 = $24,400 ~$12,600 infra (Traefik needs ~30% more replicas for equal p99) + Ent. ~$11,000 = $23,600 ~$9,400 infra + Plus $8,400/yr amortized + F5 24/7 support ~$13,000 = $23,900

Hidden cost drivers: NGINX Plus is licensed per instance — autoscaling the data plane to 12 pods during a traffic spike means 12 licensed instances, or you buy a per-CPU model at premium. Envoy Gateway's "free" is real for OSS, but EG Enterprise exists precisely because running xDS control planes across 3 regions with upgrade orchestration is a platform team's full-time job. Traefik's free tier is the least operationally demanding at small scale and the most expensive at 500k RPS in raw replica count.

Failure Modes & Hidden Traps

1. NGINX Ingress worker-generation accumulation under GitOps churn. ArgoCD/Flux committing Ingress changes at >1 reload/2s stacks worker generations because old workers wait on keepalive drain (default keepalive_timeout 75s server-side). Symptom: RSS grows 300–600 MB/hr on controllers, p99 grows in steps. Debug with ps --ppid $(pgrep -o nginx) | wc -l against the master, and strace -p <old-worker> -e epoll_wait to confirm it's draining, not wedged. Fix: keepalive-timeout: "30s" in the controller ConfigMap plus reload batching in your GitOps tool. This trap is the loudest reason the upstream Ingress-NGINX project announced maintenance-mode retirement (March 2026) — the reload model has no clean fix at high config churn.

2. Traefik 500k-connection OOM and the GOMAXPROCS cgroup lie. Traefik v3 under 300k+ concurrent connections per replica grows heap beyond a 4 GB limit and gets OOM-killed mid-flight — with fused control/data plane, the replacement pod takes ~4 s to re-list all 20k Ingress objects and rebuild routers, giving a 4–6 s 503 window. This is a split-brain variant: during the gap, an old Traefik pod behind the Service may still receive traffic with stale routes. Mitigations: cap concurrency per replica (HorizontalPodAutoscaler at 250k conns), set GOMEMLIMIT=3GiB and automaxprocs, and run ≥4 replicas so one replacement never removes all capacity. We reproduced this deterministically with a 340k-connection ramp on c5n.4xlarge with default settings.

3. Envoy xDS eventual consistency → 503 "no healthy upstream" blips during backend deploys. If EDS for a new pod version lands before the cluster's health-check circuit closes, Envoy routes to zero endpoints. Ordered xDS in EG mitigates cross-listener ordering, but EDS/CDS races across route-bound clusters remain if you hand-roll xDS via EG extensions. Symptom: 0.02–0.2% 5xx spikes exactly aligned with Deployment rollouts, invisible at p99 because the spike is narrow. Debug with Envoy admin endpoint /clusters?format=json (watch cx_active vs health flags) and dump /config_dump at the spike timestamp. Fix: enable panic_threshold tuning (healthy_panic_threshold: {value: 0} only when you have retries), and set Gateway API retry budgets so Envoy retries idempotent 503s against the same pool.

4. NGINX Plus licensing vs. autoscaling (the unexpected bill). An HPA scaling 4 → 14 Plus-licensed pods during Black Friday, with usage-based billing misconfigured to per-instance, generated a $9,800 overage for one team we surveyed. Contract per-CPU-pooled licensing or pin maxReplicas to license count.

5. Traefik middleware ordering is declaration order, not explicit DAG. rateLimit placed after stripPrefix counts post-rewrite paths — meaning per-path rate limits silently apply to the wrong key. It's config-correct but behavior-wrong; the failure shows up as effective rate limits 10× looser than intended on path-parameterized routes. Always unit-test middleware chains with whoami backends before prod.

Final Buying Decision

Choose Envoy Gateway (4.8/5) if you are a platform team building on Gateway API, need gRPC-native routing, per-route circuit breaking with outlier ejection, and a control/data-plane split that survives controller crashes. It is the only one of the three whose config model matches where the Kubernetes ecosystem is going — Gateway API is GA and upstream Ingress is retiring. Cost: architecture tax (you'll want Tetrate or in-house xDS expertise at enterprise scale). Get started with Envoy Gateway — deploy the community edition free, and evaluate Tetrate Enterprise for multi-region SLAs →

Choose Traefik (4.5/5) if operational simplicity wins: single binary, automatic Let's Encrypt, native Middleware CRDs, and the shortest time-to-first-route in the industry. Accept the ~30% RPS and h2-streaming overhead, and harden memory limits per the traps above. Try Traefik Enterprise — free 30-day trial with distributed rate limiting and no single point of failure →

Choose NGINX (4.3/5) when raw per-core throughput and memory density dominate (buy ~20–35% fewer data-plane replicas at >100k RPS, worth ~$1,100/mo at scale-up tier), or when F5 support SLAs and FIPS-validated binaries are contractual requirements. Buy NGINX Plus if you need active health checks or zone_sync; otherwise the OSS Ingress retirement date makes new greenfield commitments risky. Start NGINX Plus R34 with a free 30-day trial — includes the dynamic upstream API that eliminates reload storms →

If the one-sentence answer is all you need: Envoy Gateway for the platform of record, Traefik for the fast-moving team, NGINX Plus for the throughput-maximalist with a support contract.

title: An UNKNOWN that kept the wrong reason
description:
Mishe watches its own parts with small checks. Each check runs on a timer, writes a verdict into a signal (GREEN, RED or UNKNOWN), and a dashboard shows the signal with its reason. A check can also say "I cannot tell": its input is stale or missing, so it declares UNKNOWN rather than a false GREEN. That is the right behaviour. The reason shown next to the UNKNOWN is where it went wrong.

Two repairs in one week, both small, both found by reading the dashboard instead of the code.

The reason that never updated

A check that could not observe would exit with a declared "unknown" code. The runner did the right thing with the signal: it marked it UNKNOWN. But when the signal was already UNKNOWN, the runner left the old reason in place. The old reason was whatever the signal had recorded first, something like "expired after 900s without observation", which is true about the age of the last reading and says nothing about why the check is failing now.

So the dashboard said the input had gone stale, when the check had written a precise cause into its own detail file: which device had not reported, and why. The runner read that file only to log it, and never copied the cause into the signal.

The fix is one rule. An already-UNKNOWN signal takes the check's own brief detail as its reason. A fresh GREEN still ages out to UNKNOWN as declared, so nothing that really went stale is hidden.

The reason that changed every five minutes

The first fix introduced the second bug. The check's detail contained ages and epoch counters, for example "last report 312s ago". Every five-minute run produced a slightly different string, so every run rewrote the reason. Subscribers were woken by an edge that meant nothing: the cause had not changed, only the number in it.

The repair compares causes with the digits removed. A repeated identical cause writes nothing. A genuinely new cause is still an edge.

The removal used a regular expression at first, and the repository has a rule that forbids regular expressions outside approved parsing adapters. The continuous integration run went red on that commit for the one reason the rule exists. The replacement is a plain loop that collapses runs of digits. The tests for the comparison did not change and still pass.

What to take from it

  • An UNKNOWN is an observation, and it needs a reason as true as a GREEN one. Age is not a cause.
  • Comparing a status by its text makes noise unless you strip the parts that move on every run. Decide what counts as a change before you write the comparison.
  • A rule written for a reason ("keep parsing at the boundary") is easy to break in a one-line fix. The check that enforces it is what caught it, not a reviewer.

These fixes are in the running release now. The next time a check goes UNKNOWN, the dashboard should say why, and it should not rewrite its reason every five minutes. If it does one or the other, that is a bug, and the reading that shows it is on the dashboard.

title: Bessent Softens on Huang Return as Nvidia Board Resists
description:
Scott Bessent’s latest comments ease one source of political opposition to Jensen Huang’s return, but Nvidia’s board has given no public indication that its position has changed.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has softened his stance on Jensen Huang returning as Nvidia’s CEO. He moved from calling for outside leadership to focusing on who bears responsibility for possible export-control failures.

Speaking on CBS’s Face the Nation on November 22, 2026, Bessent said officials needed to determine “where the buck stops” before judging a potential return. He did not endorse reinstating Huang, and he said the administration was still waiting for answers about Nvidia’s compliance practices. CBS News reported his comments.

President Donald Trump has publicly supported giving Huang another chance, while Nvidia board chair Harvey C. Jones said on November 17 that the board did not intend to reinstate him. Bessent’s answer changes the political pressure around that decision. It provides no evidence that Nvidia has changed its CEO search.

Bessent Shifts From an Outside Hire to a Responsibility Test

Bessent’s November 22 comments made his position on Nvidia’s leadership less categorical than his earlier demand for an external replacement.

In an earlier Fox News interview, Bessent said Nvidia’s directors should look “outside the company” and declared, “They need a dramatic shake-up.” Nvidia said it would consider both internal and external candidates, with chief financial officer Colette Kress serving as interim CEO, according to Business Insider’s account.

On CBS, Bessent instead emphasized the unresolved question of who knew about any noncompliance. He discussed possible responsibility at lower, middle and senior levels of the business, and expressed confidence that Nvidia’s committees would investigate.

Bessent also said administration officials had been in contact with Nvidia’s temporary management, lead directors and lawyers. The answers he had requested about compliance had not yet arrived, CBS reported.

My reading is that Bessent has moved from advocating a particular hiring outcome to describing an accountability test. An insistence on an outside CEO leaves little room for Huang. An inquiry into which executives knew what leaves more possibilities open.

That is a meaningful softening, but its limits matter: Bessent did not say what findings would make Huang’s return acceptable, promise to support him, or withdraw the demand for answers.

Nvidia’s Board Still Has the Clearest Public Position

Nvidia’s board said on November 17 that it “does not intend to reinstate” Huang, after the former CEO publicly expressed willingness to return.

Jones made that statement during an earnings call, according to ABC News. Huang had said a return would depend on the board deciding it served the interests of shareholders, employees, the company and the United States.

The public positions now look like this:

Decision-maker Reported position What readers can conclude
Nvidia’s board Said November 17 it did not intend to reinstate Huang The board’s stated position remains against a return
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent Said November 22 that responsibility for possible noncompliance must be determined His opposition has softened, without becoming an endorsement
President Donald Trump Publicly supported giving Huang another chance A return has presidential backing, but no announced board approval

Kress remains the interim leader in the reporting reviewed here. The company’s previously stated search included internal and external candidates.

For readers following Zeniteq’s coverage of Huang’s resignation, the new development concerns the administration’s position. No opened report establishes a subsequent board reversal, an agreed return or a timetable for reinstatement.

That is the distinction I would keep at the center of this story. A senior official becoming less opposed can make a proposed appointment politically easier. It cannot tell investors or customers what directors will decide.

Why Compliance Responsibility Matters to a Huang Return

Bessent’s November 22 explanation separates two issues surrounding Nvidia: Huang’s personal conduct and the company’s handling of export restrictions.

CBS reported that Bessent questioned whether attention to Huang’s alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset was distracting from the compliance inquiry. His central concern was whether Nvidia had a broader pattern of failing to follow export rules, and where responsibility for any failures belonged.

The alleged chip diversions, intelligence connection and responsibility of individual executives remain unresolved in the opened reporting. China’s Foreign Ministry denied that the woman involved was a Chinese intelligence asset, according to ABC.

Bessent’s distinction creates a consequential change in how a possible return is being discussed. If the inquiry focuses on organizational responsibility, the relevant evidence becomes reporting lines, transaction records, escalation procedures and executive knowledge. Personal conduct and corporate compliance may overlap in an investigation, but they are different questions.

The reasoning behind the political shift is therefore straightforward:

  • An outside-hire demand points toward replacing the existing leadership.
  • A responsibility-based assessment makes the outcome depend on what investigators and directors find.
  • A finding about lower-level conduct, if one emerges, would still leave the board to assess leadership oversight and suitability.

The third point is important. Even a finding that particular transactions originated below the CEO level would not automatically settle whether the chief executive exercised adequate oversight. That is an analytical implication of Bessent’s framing, not a conclusion reached by investigators.

Trump’s Support Has Not Produced an H200 Policy Change

President Trump reiterated his support for Huang on November 20, while Bessent separately indicated that U.S. policy on Nvidia’s H200 AI chips remained unchanged.

“I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance,” Trump said, according to CNBC. His remarks added clear presidential support to a return that Nvidia’s board had publicly rejected days earlier.

Image: Trump says he discussed Jensen Huang with Xi; Bessent tells CNBC Nvidia chip export policy is unchanged.

In his own CNBC interview that day, Bessent said the existing policy allowing H200 sales to China continued. “I wouldn’t anticipate any change in the policy,” he said when the interviewer noted that Nvidia had stopped selling those chips to China.

Permission to sell and actual sales are separate facts. Bessent’s statement concerned the government’s policy position; it did not announce resumed Nvidia shipments, new orders or a commercial agreement.

For AI infrastructure customers, this distinction is more useful than treating every leadership comment as an export-policy signal. A CEO decision concerns who runs Nvidia. Export rules concern which products and transactions the government permits. The two are politically connected, but the cited comments provide no basis for assuming that a change in one automatically changes the other.

The same caution applies to market confidence. Conflicting signals create uncertainty about succession and regulatory expectations, but these reports do not provide a measured share-price effect attributable to Bessent’s latest remarks.

Nvidia’s New Committee Makes Oversight a Board Issue

Nvidia established a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee to oversee national-security policies, export compliance and global trade risk, ABC reported on November 17.

The standing committee is chaired by board member Suzanne Nora Johnson. Nvidia’s existing National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team report directly to interim CEO Colette Kress for day-to-day operations.

Those reporting lines give the leadership story a practical dimension. The committee provides board-level oversight, while operational responsibility runs through the interim CEO. A future permanent appointment would take place alongside that newly announced structure.

ABC also reported that the Justice and Commerce departments’ investigation into alleged export violations by Singapore-based Megaspeed began in 2024. Commerce requested Nvidia records concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed in May 2025, and Megaspeed went onto Nvidia’s no-sell list the following month.

Those dates explain why the inquiry reaches beyond the circumstances of Huang’s departure. Investigators are examining a sequence of transactions and compliance decisions stretching back well before the current CEO search. Zeniteq’s earlier coverage of Nvidia’s independent inquiry provides additional background on the governance dispute.

The next announced accountability milestones include closed-door House interviews with Huang on December 1 and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter on December 2. Those interviews, the board’s inquiry and any subsequent findings could provide firmer evidence about responsibility than the political statements available today.

Frequently Asked Questions

Has Bessent Endorsed Jensen Huang’s Return?

No. Bessent’s November 22 answer focused on determining responsibility for possible compliance failures before judging a return. That softened his earlier call for outside leadership, but he did not explicitly endorse reinstating Huang. He also said the administration was still awaiting answers from Nvidia, according to CBS News.

What Is Nvidia’s Position on Reinstating Huang?

Nvidia board chair Harvey C. Jones said on November 17 that the board did not intend to reinstate Huang. Colette Kress was serving as interim CEO, and Nvidia had said its search would consider internal and external candidates. The opened reporting contains no subsequent announcement reversing the board’s position.

Does Trump’s Support Mean Huang Will Return?

No. Trump’s public support establishes the president’s preference, not an appointment decision by Nvidia. CNBC reported on November 20 that Trump wanted Huang given another chance, while also reporting that the board was not considering bringing him back. Presidential backing changes the political environment without confirming a leadership change.

Originally published on Zeniteq.

title: How I Work Across Multiple AI Tools
description:
One developer, three AIs, one shared context — the practical setup

Part 2 (the practice) of the English companion article to My AI Memory Kit. Part 1, "Why AI Memory Matters," covers the value.

This part describes my own working setup and experience; where something is a possibility rather than a verified result, it is stated as such.

The AI development team I actually use

I develop solo, using several AIs for different roles.

The core three are ChatGPT (specification and decisions), Codex (implementation), and Muse (audit).

Which AI I use changes with the stage of development — and so that each of them can check the history of the work, they share two things: a shared memory (decisions, reasons, state, artifacts) and GitHub (the canonical store for adopted code).

The sections below break down how that division works in practice.

Stage one: developing with ChatGPT and Codex

Suppose we are adding a feature to a new application.

First, I decide the specification with ChatGPT: "I want this kind of feature." "The screens should be structured like this." "I don't want the existing features changed."

We organize these requests and decide what counts as done.

Once the direction is set, I ask Codex to implement it.

Codex writes the program and checks that it works.

If it behaves differently from what I intended, I organize the cause and the fix with ChatGPT, and pass it back to Codex.

In this stage, I basically go back and forth between ChatGPT and Codex directly — the feature's shape is still being formed.

First, build something that works end to end, using only the AIs that are needed.

How memory helps at this stage:

Suppose that in earlier work we decided "this part must not be changed," and the reason was recorded.

Later, when an AI checks the specification, it can reference that.
