Because past reasons can be checked, the risk of repeating the same discussion, or accidentally changing something already decided, goes down.

A record does not mean mistakes never happen. But keeping the information needed for decisions has real meaning.

Stage two: the audit loop with Muse and Codex

Once the basic features are in place, the next stage is checking quality. This is where Muse comes in.

By combining this with bot operation, I aim to reduce the need to instruct every step in conversation with ChatGPT each time, and to keep ChatGPT-side token consumption down as well.

Shared memory helps here too.

Suppose Muse finds a problem in a feature. If that problem occurred before, past records of the cause and the fix can inform the investigation.

If what was fixed and which tests confirmed it are recorded, the next audit can use them too.

The AI is no longer just repeating fixes; it can proceed while referencing past failures and decisions.

How GitHub and shared memory are divided

One more important piece is GitHub — a service for managing program source code and its change history.

In my development, I use it as the canonical store for adopted code.

The two have different roles. By combining them, an AI can reference not only the current code but also the history of how it got there.

Note that each AI needs its own connection and access permissions to check GitHub.

Saving information in shared memory does not mean the latest state of GitHub becomes known automatically.

What the VPS is for

My development environment also uses a VPS — a virtual server on the internet, a place other than my own PC where applications and integration services can run.

In my case, the systems I developed and the AI integration mechanisms run on the VPS.

The important point is not to gather everything into one place.

It is to arrange things with different roles so that an AI can reference them when needed.

And the storage does not have to be a VPS: a configuration where memory is saved on your own PC and accessed by compatible AIs is equally possible. (That is the form the product introduced in Part 1 takes.)

Doesn't using multiple AIs cost more?

Using several AIs means thinking about cost: AI service fees, API fees, server running costs, and so on.

Adding more AIs does not automatically raise development efficiency; depending on how you use them, processing becomes complicated and extra cost appears.

So I switch the AIs' roles by development stage.

1. Don't add AIs for small tasks.

For a small code fix, ChatGPT and Codex are enough.

There is no need to pass every task to Muse and run the audit loop.

2. Don't re-explain decided specifications from scratch every time.

In long-term development, specifications and decision histories accumulate.

Passing all of it to an AI every time makes the input enormous — and with APIs, the number of input and output tokens can affect the price.

Searching past records and passing only what is needed helps here.

For example, when fixing a screen display, there is no need to pass the long development history of unrelated features every time.

You mainly reference the necessary specifications, the reasons for past changes, and the current state. This can keep input tokens down.

However, searching and retrieving memory also takes processing. How much the token count and cost actually decrease depends on the AI used and the work involved.

3. Don't run the audit loop without limits.

The Muse–Codex audit loop is also limited to the necessary range.

So first, the task's scope and completion conditions are decided.

The necessary fixes are made, the results checked, and when the conditions are met, we move to the next stage.

The point is not to run many AIs. It is to run the necessary AI at the necessary time.

Finally, check the finished work

When the Muse–Codex audit is done, I check the final deliverables once more.

If needed, small fixes are made with ChatGPT and Codex, the completion conditions are confirmed, and we move to the next stage of development.

What matters here is the handover to the next work.

What is finished? What is still unfinished? What will be developed next — and what was the reasoning behind that decision?

If this information is recorded, it can be referenced when the next session starts.

Even when a conversation with an AI ends, the project itself does not end. It can be resumed on another day, or handed over to another AI.

A note on what is verified: the workflow above is my own development setup, built on a shared memory I operate myself (on a VPS) together with GitHub. For the product, My AI Memory Kit, the verified AI-to-AI sharing is the case described in Part 1 — records and a file saved by Codex, retrieved by Muse through a read-only bridge (November 21, 2026). Other combinations and directions (for example, an external AI writing into the kit, or a handover completed through ChatGPT's screens) are possibilities this setup points to, not verified product behavior.

Part 1: "Why AI Memory Matters" — why shared context changes the work. https://dev.to/ahousecreate/why-ai-memory-matters-55p0

Product page (Gumroad, English edition): https://housecraft00.gumroad.com/l/my-ai-memory-kit — My AI Memory Kit, $4.99. Japanese edition: sold on note (https://note.com/noiz0560_082/n/nb4da4758eae8).

title: A router recommends. A gateway runs it. They're not the same purchase.
description:
Start with the shape of the integration, because it tells you almost everything. A model router — Not Diamond is the clean example — takes a prompt and a candidate list you author, predicts which model will answer best, and returns a recommendation. Then you call the provider, with your key. Its own setup documentation asks for a key for every provider you route between, in every environment you run. The call, the credentials, the ceilings, the log: yours.

A managed gateway inverts all of that by sitting in the request path. It executes the call. Provider credentials are managed behind one gateway key you can scope per customer, service, or agent run — mint and revoke without a deploy. Spend ceilings are enforced at org, team, user and key scope before the request goes out. Guardrails run on the way in and out. When a provider is down, fallback is a property of the path, not retry logic in every caller. And every request leaves one log row: model, variant, key, team, cost, latency, outcome.

The routing decision itself

Here's where people expect the gateway to claim a smarter router. It doesn't have one. What it has is a deterministic split: pin two candidates, assign variants by hashing a stable identifier so the same user lands on the same variant every time, and read cost against quality per variant from the same source as the bill. A cost header rides on every response — and when the cost can't be determined, the header is absent rather than zero, which matters more than it sounds.

The published case for learned routing is real — RouteLLM, Hybrid LLM, FrugalGPT — but every result in that literature is a number from an evaluation harness on a named dataset. Whether it holds on your traffic needs a stable assignment, a per-variant cost, and a quality signal you chose. That apparatus is the deterministic split. The trade, stated honestly: a trained router adapts per query and a fixed split does not; a fixed split is reproducible three weeks later and a trained router is not.

What the router genuinely does better

Our comparison says this itself, and it's right: the trained classifier, including one trained on your own traffic (we ship none and plan none). Automatic prompt optimization as a first-class feature — prompt management is a different thing. Pricing that is genuinely narrow. And no catalog constraint: since you bring the keys, a router can reach any model you can, including self-hosted ones. If your candidate set includes a model outside the gateway catalog, that's dispositive.

Reproducing a decision

The scenario that actually sends teams shopping: a customer says answers got worse sometime last month. With a recommendation layer, the choice lives in the router's session records and the call in your logs, if you logged it — and the join key had to be recorded before the incident. With the gateway, all four answers (which model, when the mix changed, what it cost, what else changed) come from the same request log. The component that made the decision should be the component that recorded it.

Switching is mechanically small; the learned policy is what doesn't carry over — it's encoded in a model you can't export into routing rules, so you re-derive it as a readable split, ideally run alongside the router for a fortnight first. And if none of the operational gaps hurt yet, keep the router. The two can also coexist: router recommends, gateway executes.

Full comparison: https://nrouter.ai/blog/product/notdiamond-alternative

title: The prompt outgrew the model
description:
On 31 July 2026 at 20:27 UTC, a run writing specification documents for a large Java codebase sent the model a prompt of 264,934 tokens. The model's window holds 262,144. The provider refused the request:

"Invalid request: Your request exceeded model token limit: 262144 (requested: 265529)"

The run ended there with an error and no answer. The run was session 81e51c61, the same session whose final answer the guard rejected the next morning at 24 of 25.

Nothing about this failure was the model's fault. The model never saw the request. I built a prompt too big for the model, and I sent the prompt anyway. Like carrying a package to a door you already know is locked.

Two things let the prompt grow. After each finished task, Merlin compacts the conversation, keeping the working state and folding the history away. The rule skipped compaction whenever there had been recent errors. After the last compaction at 20:12, the next five finished tasks all had recent errors, so all five compactions were skipped. The prompt went from 24,030 tokens to 255,706 in fourteen minutes.

The second thing let the prompt leave the building. Prompts over 49 percent of the local model's window are escalated to a larger cloud model, and 114 of the session's 117 model calls went there. Merlin checks every prompt against the window of the model about to receive the prompt, and compacts or refuses before sending. For the escalation tier, I had left the window unset on purpose. My specification recorded the reasoning: the provider owns its limits. An unset window read as zero, and a zero window switched the check off. So a request certain to fail went out, the refusal came back, and the run ended in a state no resume was able to recover.

The run had paused itself at its token budget at 19:45 local time, and five resume attempts each stopped again immediately before the sixth ran. The crash came at 23:27 local. The first hour was spent debugging why we kept exhausting the budget, and then we realized the problem: we are an RLM orchestration engine, of course the prompts are going to grow with each turn. The first thing was we doubled the budget and kicked off another run. Then we implemented context compiling and summarization to remove repeated context from the prompt.

The fixes went in overnight. The escalation tier now declares its real window, 262,144 tokens, so the check runs on every call. A failed run is now re-armed from its last checkpoint on request instead of being lost.

At 06:36 UTC the run resumed from its checkpoint. Two minutes later, before any model call, the check fired: the prompt stood at 261,331 tokens against the 262,144-token window, with 24,576 reserved for the answer. Merlin compacted the prompt to 25,648 tokens and carried on. Half an hour later the run produced the 24-of-25 answer the guard rejected.

A limit left unset is not an unlimited limit. In my code, absent meant skip the check, so one missing line in a configuration file switched off a safety rule, and nothing reported the switch. I had written "the provider owns its limits" in the spec as if the provider would also own the consequences.

The test: for every limit your system reads from configuration, find what an absent value does in the code. If absent means "skip", delete the value in a test environment and send a request one token over the real limit. See whether anything stops the request before the provider does.

Source: session 81e51c61 from my logs, and Spec 009 data model and plan, amended 1 August 2026 (commit 7d0accf92).

title: Time tracking without surveillance: a policy template for remote teams
description:
Most remote teams that try time tracking hit the same wall. The tool goes live on a Monday, a screenshot setting nobody discussed is switched on, and by Wednesday someone in Slack asks, half joking, whether they need permission for a coffee break. Trust drops, people start performing activity instead of doing work, and the data you wanted becomes useless.

The tool is rarely the real problem. The missing piece is a written policy that says what is tracked, why, who sees it, and what it will never be used for. This post gives you a template you can copy, plus the steps for rolling it out.

Why tracking feels like surveillance

It usually comes down to four things:

  1. Surprise. People learn what is collected after it has already been collected.
  2. Vague purpose. "For visibility" sounds a lot like "we don't trust you."
  3. Asymmetry. Managers see everything about a person, and that person sees nothing.
  4. No way to correct. A bad idle reading or a forgotten timer sits in the record forever.

A good policy fixes all four in writing before anything is switched on.

Five principles to build on

  • Track for a reason you can say out loud. Client billing, project estimates, payroll for hourly staff, spotting overload. If you can't name the reason, don't collect the data.
  • Collect the minimum that serves that reason. If you bill by the hour, you need time on tasks. You may not need screenshots at all.
  • Same data for both sides. Anything a manager can see about a person, that person can see too.
  • Data starts conversations, it doesn't end them. A low activity number is a question, not a verdict.
  • Give people controls. Pausing, correcting and asking for changes should be normal, not a favour.

The policy template

Copy this, replace the brackets, and cut anything that doesn't apply. Keep it to one page.

TIME TRACKING POLICY: [Company name]
Version [1.0], effective [date]. Owner: [name]

1. Why we track time
We track time to [bill clients accurately / plan project estimates /
pay hourly contractors correctly / spot people who are overloaded].
We do not track time to measure how hard anyone works.

2. What we collect
- Time spent on projects and tasks, started and stopped by you.
- [Screenshots every X minutes, blurred / not collected.]
- [Keyboard and mouse activity levels / not collected.]
- [Apps and websites used while the timer runs / not collected.]
- Idle time, which is removed from tracked time.

3. What we never collect
- Anything while your timer is off.
- [Personal devices / private messages / webcam / audio.]

4. Who can see it
- You: everything recorded about you.
- Your manager: [list].
- Clients: [only totals per task in reports / nothing].
- Nobody else.

5. How we use the data
- To invoice clients and plan future work.
- To notice workload problems early.
- As a starting point for a conversation, never as the only evidence.

6. How we will never use the data
- No ranking of people by activity level.
- No disciplinary action based on activity scores alone.
- No reviewing screenshots unless [a client dispute / you ask us to].

7. Your controls
- Stop the timer for breaks or personal tasks, any time.
- Add or correct time through a manual request; your manager
  responds within [2 working days].
- Ask what data exists about you at any time.

8. Retention
We keep screenshots for [X days] and timesheets for [X years,
or as required for invoicing and tax].

9. Changes
We will share any change to this policy [14 days] before it takes
effect and discuss it at [team meeting].

Section 6 is the one people read first, so be specific there. "We respect your privacy" means nothing. "We don't rank people by activity" is a promise someone can hold you to.

Rolling it out in four steps

1. Share a draft, not a decision. Post it in your team channel with a week for comments. Expect questions about screenshots and activity levels. Those are the ones to answer properly.

2. Run a two-week trial where the data doesn't count. Everyone tracks, nobody is evaluated. People learn the tool, you find settings that are wrong, and the first data you see isn't tied to anyone's job.

3. Match the tool settings to the policy, line by line. If the policy says screenshots are blurred, check that they are. In TimoDesk, for example, screenshots can be set anywhere from every 3 to every 60 minutes, blurred, and set to notify the member when one is taken, and idle time is removed from tracked time. Whatever tool you use, the point is the same: the software should behave exactly as the document says.

4. Review after 30 days. Ask two questions: what data did we actually use, and what did we collect but never look at? Turn off the second category.

Honest trade-offs

Screenshots. If you're an agency billing by the hour, clients sometimes want proof of work, and screenshots can settle disputes. For an internal product team, they mostly add anxiety. A middle path is blurred screenshots at a long interval, viewed only in a dispute.

Activity levels are noisy. Reading a spec, sketching on paper and taking a client call all show low keyboard and mouse activity. Writers and designers will look "less active" than someone answering email all day. Use these numbers to spot a sudden change for one person over several weeks, not to compare people.

Leaderboards. Some tools, TimoDesk included, offer performance leaderboards. They can work for a team that has explicitly agreed to them. For most teams, they reward whoever games the metric. If you won't use one, say so in section 6.

Client visibility. Sharing reports with clients builds trust, but your team should know exactly what clients see. A view-only report with totals per task is usually enough.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Switching on every feature because it's included.
  • Looking closely at trial data and then claiming "it didn't count."
  • Letting individual managers add their own checks outside the policy.
  • Writing the policy once and never revisiting it.

The test of a good policy is simple: could you read every line aloud to your team without anyone wincing? If yes, you're ready to switch the tracker on.

If you want a tool to test this policy with, TimoDesk has a 15-day free trial with every feature and no card needed: https://timodesk.com

This article was drafted with AI assistance for the TimoDesk team.

title: Is your offline AI stack truly offline?
description:
This article was originally published on the Actian blog.

In this tutorial, you'll run an egress audit against a self-hosted AI stack. You'll block outbound traffic with a deny-by-default firewall, record every hostname and packet the stack tries to reach, and apply offline settings until nothing gets out. You'll need a Linux environment with Docker Engine, Docker Compose, iptables, and tcpdump. The egress audit repo has the full setup.

The test stack was a local RAG app built with LlamaIndex, Actian VectorAI DB Community Edition for retrieval, Ollama running Llama 3.2 3B, a local Hugging Face embedding model, and Arize Phoenix for tracing. It answered queries with the network cut, and it still tried to call out 52 times.

The results at a glance

Run DNS lookups Blocked packets Query answered
Pre-staged (models cached) 68 52 Yes
Cold start (caches removed) 61 32 No
Hardened (offline settings) 2 1 Yes
Component Call type Requested destination Pre-staged packets Cold-start packets
Ollama Cloud catalog and model registry ollama.com, registry.ollama.ai 3 4
RAG app and Hugging Face libraries Model metadata checks and downloads huggingface.co 48 26
Arize Phoenix Remote documentation service arizeai-433a7140.mintlify.app 1 1
VectorAI DB Deployment-usage notification elspv.pervasive.com 0 1

Counts include retries, so they're higher than the number of unique requests. In the cold-start run, the packet capture recorded 31 attempts and the firewall log recorded one more from VectorAI DB.

Before you begin

The audit ran on Ubuntu 24.04 under WSL2, with all four application components in Docker containers. Clone the repo and open the project folder.

git clone https://github.com/actian-devs/developer-content.git
cd developer-content/blog/egress-audit

Follow the README to stage the Ollama and Hugging Face models while you still have internet access. Start the stack with the base Compose file, confirm the RAG app can answer the sample query, and then move on to the audit.

1. Block outbound traffic and start monitoring

The stack's internal network keeps running, so components can talk to each other while external connections are blocked. A logging DNS sinkhole records requested hostnames, and firewall rules in Docker's DOCKER-USER chain log and reject outbound packets.

Point Docker Compose at the base file and the audit overlay, which adds the DNS sinkhole. Run this in both terminals you use for the audit.

export COMPOSE_FILE=docker-compose.yml:docker-compose.audit.yml

Prepare the containers without starting them.

docker compose down
docker compose up --no-start

Turn on the firewall and clear the previous DNS and kernel logs so the new records match this run.

sudo ./audit/egress-deny.sh on
sudo truncate -s 0 capture/dns.log
sudo dmesg -C

The policy allows traffic between containers on br-rag and blocks external IPv4 egress. In the second terminal, start the packet capture before the services launch.

sudo tcpdump -i br-rag -nn -s 0 -w capture/prestaged.pcap 2>&1 | tee -i capture/prestaged.tcpdump.txt

Back in the first terminal, start the stack and run the test query.

docker compose up -d
docker compose run --rm app --question "How long are adult patient records kept?"

Keep the capture running for 30 more minutes to catch scheduled retries and background requests, then stop tcpdump with Ctrl+C.

sleep 1800

The DNS sinkhole configuration is in the repo's audit/dns folder.

2. Identify and classify every outbound caller

Give each container a fixed IP address so you can match network traffic to the component that sent it.

ollama:
  networks:
    rag:
      ipv4_address: 10.77.0.11

Save the DNS and kernel logs from the run.

sudo cp capture/dns.log capture/prestaged.dns.log
sudo TZ=UTC dmesg --time-format iso > capture/prestaged.kernel.log

Then group outbound activity by component and destination with the summarizer script. It reads the DNS log, packet capture, firewall log, and tcpdump statistics.

sudo ./audit/summarize.sh capture/prestaged

Classify each attempt as a setup dependency, a runtime check, or a background request. Then repeat the run with empty caches to find dependencies that would stop an offline deployment from starting.

In the cold-start run, Ollama tried to reach its registry and the embedding libraries tried to download model files from Hugging Face. Both failed under the firewall, so the query never completed.

Outbound activity Seen in the audit When it occurs Primary risk
Ollama model registry pull Yes, cold start Setup Needs external access to download unstaged model files
Ollama external service request Yes Runtime, startup May disclose information about the deployment and breaks zero egress
Hugging Face model download Yes, cold start Setup Missing files can stop the RAG app from starting
Hugging Face metadata checks Yes, pre-staged Runtime, during model loading May reveal model identifiers and usage metadata
Arize Phoenix documentation request Yes Runtime, at startup Contacts an external service, with no trace-data exposure established
VectorAI DB deployment-usage notification Yes, cold start Periodic background Nonessential to retrieval, and still breaks strict zero egress
Hosted embedding or inference API No, hypothetical Runtime, if configured Can send prompts or document content to an external provider

The highest risk comes from calls that carry prompts or document chunks. LlamaIndex falls back to OpenAI's hosted embeddings when Settings.embed_model doesn't point to a local model, so check that setting first. The Hugging Face Hub docs also note that hf_hub_download can check for newer versions of files already in the local cache.

3. Disable unnecessary external dependencies

Apply offline settings in a Docker Compose override file. These are the settings the hardened rerun used.

services:
  ollama:
    environment:
      - OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD=1

  phoenix:
    environment:
      - PHOENIX_ALLOW_EXTERNAL_RESOURCES=false
      - PHOENIX_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false

  app:
    environment:
      - HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1
  • OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD=1 turns off Ollama's cloud features.
  • HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 stops Hugging Face libraries from making HTTP requests to the Hub.
  • The two Phoenix flags restrict external resources and turn off telemetry.

Set Settings.embed_model to a local Hugging Face embedding model, and stage every model weight and embedding file before you enforce these settings. Some background requests have no setting to turn them off. For those, keep the network block in place and document the remaining attempts.

4. Re-test and keep the evidence

Repeat the pre-staged query with the offline settings and the deny-all firewall active, then compare the results with your first capture.

During a 32-minute observation window, the hardened run recorded one blocked connection, the VectorAI DB deployment-usage notification, and no attempts from Ollama, the RAG app, or Phoenix. Blocked packets fell from 52 to 1, DNS lookups fell from 68 to 2, and the app still answered the test query correctly.

Save the DNS logs, packet captures, firewall logs, and query output with the configuration for each run. That record shows an auditor the app worked without external connections and traces any attempts that remain.

Closing the gap in production

The audit tested firewall isolation, DNS logging, and application-level offline settings. A production air-gapped enclave also needs the following controls.

  • Remove external network routes and restrict DNS to approved internal services.
  • Bring model weights, container images, packages, and patches in through approved, verified, and signed physical media, and document each transfer.
  • Review every monitoring or tracing service, since they handle prompts and retrieved context.

Wrapping up

Running a model and a vector database on your own hardware doesn't remove every external dependency. With the network cut, this stack still reached for model registries, metadata checks, and background services. VectorAI DB kept retrieval working locally the whole time, and a few offline settings brought the outbound attempts down to one.

What's next

  • Run the audit against your own stack with the egress audit repo.
  • Pull VectorAI DB Community Edition for offline retrieval.
  • See five edge AI architecture patterns for disconnected environments.

title: LM Studio: what it picks when you load a model, and where to look first
description:
LM Studio: what it picks when you load a model, and where to look first

What LM Studio is

LM Studio is a desktop app that runs AI models on your own computer. You search for a model inside the app, download it, and chat with it in a window.

You can start without changing a setting, because LM Studio picks the settings for you. When it loads a model, it decides how much of the model goes on your graphics card. It also sets the context length, which is how much text the model can hold at once. It can run a small server too, so that other programs on your computer can use the model.

This guide lists the choices LM Studio makes. For each one we give the name LM Studio uses and where you can change it. Where LM Studio states the value it ships with, we give that value too.

The settings LM Studio chooses for you

Everything below comes from LM Studio's own documentation, read on 14 November 2026, when the download page offered version 0.4.28. A newer version may ship different values, so each item links its source.

  • Context Length Context length is how much text the model can hold at once. That text is your question, the conversation so far and the model's answer, counted in tokens, which are pieces of words. LM Studio sets it each time it loads a model, and you can change it in the load settings before the model loads. With a longer context the model can work on a longer document or conversation, but it needs more memory. LM Studio's documentation does not state the value a new model starts with, so we do not name one here. Source: LM Studio's page on settings for each model. memory

  • GPU offload GPU offload is how much of the model goes on the graphics card. When you do not set it, LM Studio's documentation says the app will automatically determine optimal GPU usage. You can also set it yourself, from none of the model to all of it. Source: LM Studio's page on loading a model. graphics card

  • Max Concurrent Predictions This setting caps how many requests one loaded model answers at once. It ships as 4. LM Studio's documentation says it applies to models that run on its llama.cpp engine. To see it, open the model loader and turn on "Manually choose model load parameters". Then pick a model and turn on "Show advanced settings". Source: LM Studio's page on parallel requests. sharing

  • Idle TTL Idle TTL is how long a model stays in memory with nothing to do before LM Studio unloads it. TTL is short for time to live. It matters when another program uses the model through LM Studio's server. A model that the server loads on demand ships with an idle time of 60 minutes. A model you load with the command lms load has no idle time, and stays loaded until you unload it. With a longer idle time the next request does not wait for the model to load again. The model keeps its memory for that whole time. Source: LM Studio's page on idle TTL and auto-evict. waiting

  • Auto-Evict Auto-Evict controls what the server does when another program asks it for a different model. It ships turned on. The server then loads the new model for that request. Before it does, it unloads the model it loaded for the previous request. A model you load yourself, for example with lms load, stays loaded. You turn it on or off in the Developer tab, under Server Settings. Source: LM Studio's page on idle TTL and auto-evict. sharing

  • Without the window LM Studio also has a version with no window, for a server or a rented machine. Its name is llmster. You start it with lms daemon up and its server with lms server start. The server answers on port 1234 unless you choose another. The same settings are there under other names: lms load takes --context-length, --gpu and --ttl. Sources: LM Studio's page on running without the window and its page on loading a model. where

Values that ship the same on every computer

You can leave every value as it ships and still chat with the model. LM Studio sets two of them each time it loads a model: the context length and the GPU offload.

Other values ship as one number for everyone. Two examples are 4 requests at once and 60 minutes of idle time for a model the server loads on demand. One number must suit a laptop and a workstation with several graphics cards, so LM Studio picks one that is safe on any of them.

That number is the same whatever model you load, and whether you use it alone or share it with a team.

To find out whether another value suits your computer better, you have to measure on that computer.

What we are testing

We are testing LM Studio on our own computers, first as installed and then as tuned. The results will go on this page with their full setup.

Three settings to look at first

Each item below says where to find the value LM Studio uses on your computer today.

  • Context Length Open the tab that lists the models you have downloaded, and click the gear icon beside your model. The dialog that opens lists the load settings this model starts with, context length among them. first

  • GPU offload It is in the same dialog. If you have never changed it, LM Studio is choosing it for you each time the model loads. second

  • Max Concurrent Predictions Open the model loader and turn on "Manually choose model load parameters". Then pick your model and turn on "Show advanced settings". This one matters when more than one person or program uses the model. third

Get the next guide by email

Some readers come here looking for an LM Studio alternative. Ollama is another free tool that runs models on your own computer, and we wrote a guide to Ollama too. To see how we compare the two, read how we test them.

We send each new measurement and guide by email, and we offer free tuning consultations to the list first. Sign up for the guides by email.

Get the guides

title: Extract images from a PDF vs convert pages to images: why a 10-page PDF gave 0 files
description:
Some PDF toolboxes list "extract images" and "PDF to image" side by side, and the names sound like one job with two labels. A small test on 2026-11-20 put the same files through both on one Apple-silicon Mac, each tool run once. A 10-page PDF that contains only text (137,782 bytes) came back from extraction with 0 files. Rendered at 216 DPI, the same PDF produced 10 page images, 2,881,860 bytes as WebP. Neither run failed. They are two different operations that both end in image files.

A text-only PDF has nothing to extract

pdfimages -all from poppler 26.08.0 wrote 0 files for the text-only PDF. A browser tool, ImgIng at https://imging.ai/ , reported 0 results and 0 KB for it too.

The second sample is a home-made one-page PDF with a few rectangles, a circle, a polyline and one line of text, 1,303 bytes for the whole file. Extraction gave 0 files again, and pdfimages printed nothing at all. Rendering at 216 DPI gave one 1785×2526 image: 41,388 bytes as WebP, 94,317 as JPG, 148,530 as PNG. pdftoppm -r 216 wrote a 44,563-byte PNG and a 109,413-byte JPEG, so the exact size moves with the encoder. A 1,303-byte file with no picture in it still becomes a full page of pixels.

Extraction copies objects and rendering paints the page

A PDF page is a list of drawing instructions: put these characters here in this font, stroke this path, place image object number N inside this rectangle. Text and shapes exist only as instructions, while a photo is a separate object stored in the file with its own pixel size and compression.

Extraction walks the file and copies those image objects out. When there are none, zero is the correct answer and not an error. Rendering runs every instruction against a blank canvas at the resolution you ask for and saves the canvas, so it returns one image per page, sized by page size and DPI. An A4 page at 216 DPI was 1785×2526 or 1786×2526 here, whether it held text or three shapes. Adobe's help page for Acrobat carries a note in the same direction (read on 2026-11-20): raster images can be exported, vector objects cannot. Acrobat itself was not part of this test.

File counts follow objects in one case and pages in the other

Once pictures are present the two operations still disagree. The counts below come from the browser tool.

Sample Pages Extracted files Rendered files
Home-made product catalogue, product images stored oversized on purpose 6 8 6
Three-page sheet with a text page, a chart page and a photo page 3 2 3
Creative Commons newsletter 10 32 10

The catalogue has 8 image objects drawn 19 times across its 6 pages. Extraction returned 8 files, one per object, and its 7 JPEGs were byte-identical to the data inside the PDF (same SHA-256). Rendering returned 6 files because there are 6 pages. The photo inside is Bonnie Moreland's "Lake Mountain Landscape" from Wikimedia Commons, CC0; the catalogue around it is home-made and its content is fictional. The newsletter row is Creative Commons' ccNewsletter #12 (2009), CC BY 3.0.

A scanned page is an image even when it looks like text

The reverse case exists too. One sample was a home-made two-page scan: each page was rendered as a 2481×3508 JPEG and embedded whole, with no text layer. On screen it looks like two ordinary pages. Extraction returned 2 files, and they are the full pages. Extraction reports what the file stores, not what the page looks like.

Extracted originals are not always the bigger files

Extracted originals sound like they should outweigh page renders, and on these samples that held only sometimes. Against 216 DPI WebP pages, the catalogue's extracted files were 5.83 times the size (5,410,209 bytes against 928,416), which is the deliberately oversized sample, and the three-page sheet's were 1.32 times (897,884 against 679,406). The newsletter went the other way at 0.22 times. Against PNG page renders, extraction was smaller on every sample in the comparison, between 0.04 and 0.54 times.

Pick by what you want to keep

For a photo at the resolution it was stored in, extraction can give it back unchanged; the JPEGs here came out byte-identical. For a chart, a formula or a whole slide, there may be no image object to copy, so rendering at a chosen DPI is what produces a file. A zero from extraction more likely says "this content is vector or text" than "the tool is broken". Two things stay open: JPEG 2000 and JBIG2 images were not in any sample, and Acrobat's own export was not tested.

title: I ran a 130-line SEO meta tag audit on 10 well-known sites. Here's what it flagged (and where it was wrong)
description:
AI disclosure: I wrote this article with AI assistance (Claude). The script is a trimmed-down version of an auditor we maintain, and every line of output below comes from running it on 2026-11-23. We reviewed and tested everything.

Most "SEO audit" problems that actually cost you traffic are boring: a template that ships the same <title> on 400 pages, a staging noindex that made it to production, a canonical that points at the homepage, hreflang tags that forget the page itself. None of that needs Lighthouse or a headless browser to find. It's all in the raw HTML and response headers, so one plain GET per URL is enough.

This post builds a standalone Node script (Node 18+ and cheerio, about 130 lines) that checks a list of URLs against a small rule table, runs it on 10 public sites, and then goes through the two bugs I found in my own script while doing it.

The checklist

These are the rules the script checks. The thresholds are common rules of thumb, not Google requirements, and I'll come back to that.

Check Rule (severity) Why it matters
<title> Missing: error. Under 30 or over 60 characters: warning The title is usually the clickable headline in search results. Google truncates by pixel width (roughly 600 px), and about 60 characters is a safe proxy. Very short titles waste the slot.
Meta description Missing: error. Under 70 or over 160 characters: warning Google often uses it as the snippet. It isn't a ranking factor, but it affects click-through. Long ones get cut off with "...".
rel="canonical" Missing: warning. Points to a different URL: notice Tells search engines which URL is the "real" one when the same content is reachable at several URLs (tracking params, http/https, trailing slashes). A canonical that points somewhere else is sometimes intended, and sometimes a template bug that deindexes a whole section.
noindex In <meta name="robots"> or the X-Robots-Tag header: error The classic production accident. The header version is easy to miss because it's not in the HTML at all.
<h1> count None: error. More than one: notice One clear main heading helps users and parsers. Google says several <h1>s are fine, so this is only a notice.
Open Graph og:title, og:description or og:image missing: notice Controls the preview card on LinkedIn, Slack, Facebook, Discord and so on. Not a ranking signal, but a page without og:image shares badly.
hreflang No self-referencing entry: warning. No x-default: notice Each language version must list itself as well as its alternates, or search engines may ignore the whole set. x-default covers users whose language you don't target.
Image alt <img> with no alt attribute at all: warning Accessibility first, image search second. alt="" is correct for decorative images, so the script only counts images where the attribute is missing completely.
HTTP status 400 or above: error Obvious, but bulk lists of URLs from old sitemaps are full of 404s.

The script

Save this as audit.mjs, run npm i cheerio, then node audit.mjs site1.com https://site2.com/page. Add --json for machine-readable output.

// audit.mjs: bulk on-page SEO meta audit over plain HTTP.
// Usage: node audit.mjs example.com https://other.site/page [--json]
// Needs Node 18+ and `npm i cheerio`.
import * as cheerio from 'cheerio';

const UA = 'Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; MetaAuditScript/1.0)';
const RULES = { titleMin: 30, titleMax: 60, descMin: 70, descMax: 160 };
const txt = (s) => (s || '').replace(/\s+/g, ' ').trim();

async function get(url, timeoutMs = 15000) {
  const ctrl = new AbortController();
  const timer = setTimeout(() => ctrl.abort(), timeoutMs);
  const t0 = Date.now();
  try {
    const res = await fetch(url, {
      redirect: 'follow',
      signal: ctrl.signal,
      headers: { 'user-agent': UA, accept: 'text/html,*/*;q=0.8', 'accept-language': 'en-US,en;q=0.8' },
    });
    const body = (await res.text()).slice(0, 5_000_000);
    return { status: res.status, finalUrl: res.url, headers: res.headers, body, ms: Date.now() - t0 };
  } finally {
    clearTimeout(timer);
  }
}

// Small robots.txt check for the "User-agent: *" group. Supports * and $ wildcards;
// the longest matching rule wins, Allow wins ties (as in RFC 9309).
const ruleToRegex = (v) => new RegExp('^' + v.replace(/[.+?^{}()|[\]\\]/g, '\\$&').replace(/\*/g, '.*').replace(/\\?\$$/, '$'));
async function robotsAllows(url) {
  const u = new URL(url);
  const path = u.pathname + u.search;
  try {
    const r = await get(`${u.origin}/robots.txt`, 8000);
    if (r.status !== 200) return true;
    let inStar = false, lastWasAgent = false, best = null;
    for (const line of r.body.split(/\r?\n/)) {
      const [k, ...rest] = line.replace(/#.*/, '').split(':');
      const key = k.trim().toLowerCase(), val = rest.join(':').trim();
      if (key === 'user-agent') {
        inStar = (lastWasAgent && inStar) || val === '*'; // consecutive UA lines share one group
        lastWasAgent = true;
        continue;
      }
      if (key) lastWasAgent = false;
      if (inStar && (key === 'allow' || key === 'disallow') && val && ruleToRegex(val).test(path)) {
        const allow = key === 'allow';
        if (!best || val.length > best.len || (val.length === best.len && allow)) best = { allow, len: val.length };
      }
    }
    return !best || best.allow;
  } catch { return true; }
}

function audit({ status, finalUrl, headers, body }) {
  const $ = cheerio.load(body);
  const issues = [];
  const add = (sev, code, msg) => issues.push({ sev, code, msg });

  const title = txt($('head title').first().text());
  const desc = txt($('meta[name="description" i]').attr('content'));
  const canonical = $('link[rel="canonical" i]').attr('href');
  const robots = (txt($('meta[name="robots" i]').attr('content')) + ' ' + (headers.get('x-robots-tag') || '')).toLowerCase();
  const h1 = $('h1').map((_, e) => txt($(e).text())).get();
  // The OG spec says property="og:*"; some sites use name="og:*". Read both, flag the second.
  const og = {};
  let ogByName = 0;
  $('meta[property^="og:"], meta[name^="og:"]').each((_, e) => {
    const key = ($(e).attr('property') || $(e).attr('name')).slice(3);
    if (!$(e).attr('property')) ogByName++;
    og[key] ??= $(e).attr('content');
  });
  const hreflang = $('link[rel="alternate" i][hreflang]').map((_, e) => ({ lang: $(e).attr('hreflang'), href: $(e).attr('href') })).get();
  const imgs = $('img');
  const noAlt = imgs.filter((_, e) => $(e).attr('alt') === undefined).length; // alt="" is valid for decorative images

  if (status >= 400) add('error', 'http-error', `HTTP ${status}`);
  if (!title) add('error', 'missing-title', 'no <title>');
  else if (title.length < RULES.titleMin || title.length > RULES.titleMax) add('warn', 'title-length', `title is ${title.length} chars`);
  if (!desc) add('error', 'missing-description', 'no meta description');
  else if (desc.length < RULES.descMin || desc.length > RULES.descMax) add('warn', 'description-length', `description is ${desc.length} chars`);
  if (!canonical) add('warn', 'missing-canonical', 'no rel=canonical');
  else {
    const abs = new URL(canonical, finalUrl).href;
    if (abs !== finalUrl) add('notice', 'canonical-elsewhere', `canonical -> ${abs}`);
  }
  if (robots.includes('noindex')) add('error', 'noindex', 'page is noindex');
  if (h1.length === 0) add('error', 'no-h1', 'no <h1>');
  else if (h1.length > 1) add('notice', 'multiple-h1', `${h1.length} <h1> tags`);
  const ogMissing = ['title', 'description', 'image'].filter((k) => !og[k]);
  if (ogMissing.length) add('notice', 'open-graph', `og:${ogMissing.join(', og:')} missing`);
  if (ogByName) add('notice', 'og-name-attr', `${ogByName} og: tags use name= instead of property=`);
  if (hreflang.length) {
    const self = hreflang.some((h) => { try { return new URL(h.href, finalUrl).href === finalUrl; } catch { return false; } });
    if (!self) add('warn', 'hreflang-no-self', `${hreflang.length} hreflang links, none points to this URL`);
    if (!hreflang.some((h) => h.lang === 'x-default')) add('notice', 'hreflang-no-x-default', 'no x-default');
  }
  if (noAlt) add('warn', 'img-alt', `${noAlt} of ${imgs.length} <img> without alt`);

  return { finalUrl, status, title, titleLen: title.length, descLen: desc.length, h1: h1.length, hreflang: hreflang.length, images: imgs.length, issues };
}

const args = process.argv.slice(2);
const asJson = args.includes('--json');
const urls = args.filter((a) => !a.startsWith('--')).map((a) => (/^https?:\/\//.test(a) ? a : `https://${a}`));
const out = [];
const t0 = Date.now();

for (const url of urls) { // sequential on purpose: one request at a time
  if (!(await robotsAllows(url))) { out.push({ url, skipped: 'disallowed by robots.txt' }); continue; }
  try {
    const page = await get(url);
    out.push({ url, ms: page.ms, ...audit(page) });
  } catch (err) {
    out.push({ url, error: err.name === 'AbortError' ? 'timeout' : err.message });
  }
  await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 500)); // be polite between sites
}

if (asJson) console.log(JSON.stringify(out, null, 2));
else {
  for (const r of out) {
    if (r.skipped || r.error) { console.log(`${r.url}\n  SKIPPED: ${r.skipped || r.error}\n`); continue; }
    console.log(`${r.url} -> ${r.finalUrl} (${r.status}, ${r.ms} ms)`);
    console.log(`  title ${r.titleLen} ch | description ${r.descLen} ch | h1 x${r.h1} | hreflang ${r.hreflang} | img ${r.images}`);
    for (const i of r.issues) console.log(`  ${i.sev.padEnd(6)} ${i.code.padEnd(22)} ${i.msg}`);
    if (!r.issues.length) console.log('  no issues');
    console.log('');
  }
  console.log(`${out.length} URLs in ${((Date.now() - t0) / 1000).toFixed(1)} s`);
}

A few deliberate choices:

  • Sequential, with a 500 ms pause. For an audit you don't need speed, and hammering a site with parallel requests is the quickest way to get a 429 or a block page instead of real HTML.
  • robots.txt is checked before every URL. It's a small parser: only the User-agent: * group, with * and $ wildcards and "longest match wins". More on why that matters below.
  • Cheerio, not regex, for the HTML. In the tech-stack post I used regex because I only needed attribute values. Here I need things like "the <title> inside <head>, not an SVG <title>", which regex gets wrong easily.
  • X-Robots-Tag is merged with the meta robots tag, because a noindex in a header is invisible if you only look at the HTML.

A real run on 10 sites

I picked a mix of docs sites, a CMS, a government site, a news site, a payments company and one client-side app. This is the unedited output from 2026-11-23:

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/ -> https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/ (200, 74 ms)
  title 12 ch | description 145 ch | h1 x1 | hreflang 0 | img 1
  warn   title-length           title is 12 chars
  notice og-name-attr           10 og: tags use name= instead of property=

https://wordpress.org -> https://wordpress.org/ (200, 407 ms)
  title 55 ch | description 90 ch | h1 x1 | hreflang 157 | img 16
  no issues

https://nextjs.org -> https://nextjs.org/ (200, 165 ms)
  title 39 ch | description 64 ch | h1 x1 | hreflang 0 | img 17
  warn   description-length     description is 64 chars

https://www.python.org -> https://www.python.org/ (200, 73 ms)
  title 21 ch | description 52 ch | h1 x5 | hreflang 0 | img 1
  warn   title-length           title is 21 chars
  warn   description-length     description is 52 chars
  warn   missing-canonical      no rel=canonical
  notice multiple-h1            5 <h1> tags

https://www.gov.uk -> https://www.gov.uk/ (200, 73 ms)
  title 17 ch | description 68 ch | h1 x1 | hreflang 0 | img 4
  warn   title-length           title is 17 chars
  warn   description-length     description is 68 chars

https://stripe.com -> https://stripe.com/en-es (200, 1009 ms)
  title 54 ch | description 148 ch | h1 x2 | hreflang 89 | img 31
  notice multiple-h1            2 <h1> tags

https://www.wikipedia.org -> https://www.wikipedia.org/ (200, 181 ms)
  title 9 ch | description 130 ch | h1 x1 | hreflang 0 | img 7
  warn   title-length           title is 9 chars
  warn   missing-canonical      no rel=canonical

https://web.dev -> https://web.dev/ (200, 13906 ms)
  title 7 ch | description 66 ch | h1 x0 | hreflang 44 | img 10
  warn   title-length           title is 7 chars
  warn   description-length     description is 66 chars
  error  no-h1                  no <h1>

https://app.netlify.com -> https://app.netlify.com/ (200, 333 ms)
  title 7 ch | description 102 ch | h1 x0 | hreflang 0 | img 0
  warn   title-length           title is 7 chars
  warn   missing-canonical      no rel=canonical
  error  no-h1                  no <h1>

https://www.bbc.com/news -> https://www.bbc.com/news (200, 157 ms)
  title 93 ch | description 249 ch | h1 x1 | hreflang 2 | img 44
  warn   title-length           title is 93 chars
  warn   description-length     description is 249 chars
  notice open-graph             og:image missing
  notice hreflang-no-x-default  no x-default
  warn   img-alt                22 of 44 <img> without alt

10 URLs in 26.9 s

Before I read anything into this: a warning here means "doesn't match my rule table", not "this site has bad SEO". These are some of the best-known sites on the web, and most of them rank fine. What the output is good for is spotting patterns across many URLs of your own site.

With that in mind:

  • wordpress.org passed every check, including 157 hreflang links with a self-reference and an x-default. That's what a well-maintained template looks like.
  • Short homepage titles are everywhere: Wikipedia (9 characters), Netlify (7), web.dev (7), MDN Web Docs (12), Welcome to Python.org (21). For a brand homepage that people search for by name, a short title is a reasonable choice. On a product or article page it would be a real problem. If you run this on your own site, you'll probably want different thresholds for the homepage and for content pages.
  • python.org has five <h1> tags: "Functions Defined", "All the Flow You'd Expect", "Compound Data Types" and so on, one per slide in the homepage code carousel. It also has no canonical link. Neither is likely to hurt a site with python.org's authority, but on a smaller site both are worth fixing.
  • BBC News has a 93-character title and a 249-character description. Google will truncate both. It has og:title and og:description but no og:image in the server HTML.
  • stripe.com redirected me to /en-es, because I ran this from Spain. The page is fine (89 hreflang links, self-reference included), but it's a reminder that what you audit depends on where you run the script from. More below.
  • web.dev and app.netlify.com have no <h1> in the raw HTML. For app.netlify.com that's expected: it's a client-side app, and the 7-character title Netlify is the whole server-rendered page as far as SEO tags go. I didn't check web.dev's rendered DOM, so all I can say is that the server response has no <h1>.
  • No site was noindex, which is good news for them but means the live run didn't exercise that rule. I tested it separately against a local server that sends X-Robots-Tag: noindex, a canonical to another path, an hreflang set without a self-reference and one <img> without alt. Every rule fired as expected.

Where my script was wrong

Bug 1: my robots.txt parser blocked three sites

My first version matched robots rules by prefix and simply cut each rule at the first *. The first run started like this:

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/
  SKIPPED: disallowed by robots.txt

gov.uk and web.dev were skipped the same way. MDN's robots.txt has Disallow: /*/files/. Cut at the *, that becomes Disallow: /, which blocks the entire site. web.dev's Disallow: /*?*authuser= had the same problem.

The fix is to turn each rule into a real pattern (* becomes "anything", a trailing $ anchors the end) and pick the longest matching rule, with Allow winning ties. That's what RFC 9309 specifies, and it's what the version above does. The lesson: a robots parser that fails "closed" looks responsible but silently drops data. Test it against a few real robots.txt files.

Bug 2: MDN "had no Open Graph tags"

The first run reported og:title, og:description, og:image missing for MDN. MDN has all of them. It writes them as <meta name="og:title"> instead of <meta property="og:title">. The Open Graph spec uses property, but in practice many consumers accept both. The script now reads both and adds a separate notice when it sees the name= form. That's more honest than calling them missing.

Images "without alt" that aren't really images

BBC News shows 22 of 44 <img> without alt. Looking at the HTML, at least some of those are grey placeholder images with aria-label="image unavailable" and a hide-when-no-script class: lazy-loading stand-ins that JavaScript replaces. A raw-HTML audit counts them anyway. The count is still useful as a trend, but check a few by hand before you file a ticket.

Honest limits

  • JavaScript-rendered pages. If the title, meta tags or content are set by client-side JavaScript (many SPAs, React apps without SSR), plain HTTP sees the empty shell. That's what app.netlify.com looks like above. Google does render JavaScript, but later and not always fully, so tags that only exist after rendering are a risk in themselves. If you need to audit the rendered DOM, you need a headless browser, and you pay for it in time and memory.
  • robots.txt. The script respects User-agent: * rules and skips disallowed URLs. That's the right default, but it means some URLs in your list will come back as "skipped". The parser also ignores agent-specific groups and crawl-delay.
  • Rate limiting and bot protection. Big sites may answer a script with 429, 403 or a challenge page. The script reports what it gets, so a Cloudflare challenge page would show up as "missing description, no h1". If a site blocks you, record it and move on. Don't try to get around it.
  • Geo and language. Redirects like Stripe's /en-es mean the URL you audit isn't necessarily the one a US user or Googlebot sees. The accept-language header and your IP both matter.
  • One page, one moment. No crawling, no duplicate-title detection across pages, no Core Web Vitals, no structured data validation. Duplicate titles and descriptions across a site are one of the most useful checks in practice, and they need a crawl plus a map of title to URLs.
  • Thresholds are judgment calls. 30 to 60 and 70 to 160 characters are proxies for pixel width. Treat the warnings as a list to review, not a score to optimize.

Scaling it up

For a few dozen URLs, the script is enough. For a whole site you'll want:

  • A crawler that follows internal links (or reads the sitemap) up to a page limit and depth, with include/exclude patterns.
  • Site-level checks after the crawl: duplicate titles and descriptions, canonical chains, hreflang reciprocity between pages.
  • Limited concurrency (a few requests in parallel), a per-host delay, and retries with backoff on 429/5xx that honor Retry-After.
  • JSON or CSV output, one row per URL with the issue codes, so you can sort by "noindex" or filter for "title-length" in a spreadsheet.

If you'd rather not build the crawler

We run the bigger version of this as an Apify actor: SEO Audit & Meta Tag Checker. It crawls a site (or takes a list of URLs), checks everything above plus viewport, lang, thin content, structured data and duplicate titles/descriptions across pages, and outputs one row per page with a score and issue codes. Full disclosure: it's ours. It's free to use until December 6, 2026, and after that it's pay per use, about $3 per 1,000 pages audited. Failed pages aren't charged. It has the same limits described above, including no JavaScript rendering.

For a handful of URLs, though, the script above is all you need. Copy it, adjust the thresholds for your pages, and run it before your next deploy.

title: I Built Uphoto – A Free Online Passport & Visa Photo Maker
description:
Have you ever needed a passport or visa photo but didn't want to visit a photo studio?

That's one of the problems I wanted to solve with Uphoto.

Uphoto is a free online tool that helps people create passport, visa, and ID photos using their own pictures.

What can you do with Uphoto?

  • Create country-specific passport and visa photos.
  • Remove photo backgrounds using AI.
  • Change background colors.
  • Crop and resize photos.
  • Download high-quality JPG and PDF files.
  • Prepare photos with print-friendly dimensions.

Why I built it

My goal was to make passport photo creation easier, faster, and more accessible. People shouldn't need complicated software just to prepare a passport or visa photo.

Uphoto is designed to work online without requiring users to install software or create an account.

I'd love your feedback!

What feature would you like to see added to Uphoto? Are there any improvements that would make the tool more useful?

Website: https://uphotos.pages.dev/

Thanks for checking out my project!

title: OpenAI Wants to Cap AI Power Using Perplexity
description:
1. The Unseen Ceiling: Why OpenAI’s Chief Scientist Wants a Speed Limit on Model Smarts

  • Hook: Picture an F1 race where teams suddenly ask for an engine governor because the cars are becoming too fast to control.
  • Introduce Jakub Pachocki’s proposal (reported by Reuters and Bloomberg) to cap AI capability across the industry based on 'perplexity'—a core metric measuring how well a model predicts the next word.
  • Thesis: Instead of regulating compute or hardware, OpenAI is advocating for a functional red line tied directly to model intelligence.

Picture a Formula 1 grand prix where every team simultaneously pulls into the pit lane, walks into the stewards' room, and asks for a mandatory engine governor. The cars, they warn, are becoming too fast to control—outstripping human reflexes and the physical limits of the track.

That is essentially what is happening at the forefront of artificial intelligence. In a proposal detailed by Bloomberg and Reuters, OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki is urging the industry to enact an explicit, shared speed limit on model performance across competing labs.

Pachocki’s framework centers on a metric deeply familiar to AI researchers: perplexity. In machine learning, perplexity measures how uncertain a model is when predicting the next word in a sequence. High perplexity means the system is guessing blindly; low perplexity means it understands patterns and context with high confidence. Under the proposed standard, once a model’s training run breaches a specific threshold of low perplexity, developers would be required to pause training and run rigorous evaluation protocols before proceeding.

The initiative marks a sharp departure from standard policy debates in Washington and Brussels. Lawmakers have spent months trying to restrict AI development by placing chokepoints on physical infrastructure—tracking shipments of advanced semiconductors or setting thresholds based on total computing power used in training.

OpenAI's position turns that logic upside down. Instead of regulating compute or hardware, OpenAI is advocating for a functional red line tied directly to model intelligence.

It is a significant shift in regulatory strategy. Regulating raw computing power is like limiting the size of a factory floor—it is an indirect proxy that quickly becomes outdated as algorithms get better at doing more with less. Measuring perplexity targets the actual capability of the software. If a system reaches an unprecedented level of predictive accuracy, the theoretical speed limit kicks in, regardless of how many chips or megawatt-hours were required to build it.

2. Demystifying 'Perplexity': The Metric Turning Into a Safety Switch

  • Plain-English explanation of perplexity: It measures a model's 'surprise' when seeing new data. Lower perplexity equals higher accuracy, better reasoning, and greater unpredictability.
  • Why traditional hardware caps (like restricting GPU clusters) are failing as algorithmic efficiency surges.
  • Cite Seeking Alpha on how tying safety brakes to perplexity forces companies to pause training when a model crosses a specific 'smartness' threshold, regardless of how many chips were used to build it.

To understand why scientists are pushing for a brake based on perplexity, you first have to strip away the mathematical jargon. At its core, perplexity measures a language model's "surprise" when it encounters new information.

Imagine reading a sentence like "The cat sat on the..." Your brain instantly fills in "mat" or "couch." If the next word is "quantum reactor," your surprise is high. A high perplexity score means the AI is equally bewildered, constantly guessing among endless possibilities. But when perplexity plunges, the model stops guessing. It anticipates human thought, complex logic, and code structures with sharp precision.

Lower perplexity directly correlates with better reasoning and higher accuracy. The catch? It also marks the threshold where model behavior becomes far more capable—and potentially unpredictable.

Until recently, regulators tried to manage AI risk by counting hardware. They restricted the size of GPU clusters or capped the total electrical power a company could draw during training. That strategy is rapidly crumbling. AI researchers are discovering smarter training algorithms every month. An efficiency breakthrough can allow a modest setup of a few hundred chips to achieve the same low perplexity that required ten thousand GPUs just a year ago. Controlling AI capability by counting chips is like trying to enforce a highway speed limit by restricting the size of a car's gas tank—engineers simply build a more efficient engine.

This surge in efficiency is driving the call for a hardware-agnostic benchmark. As detailed by Seeking Alpha, tying safety brakes directly to perplexity forces tech companies to pause training the moment a model crosses a specific intelligence threshold, regardless of how many chips were used to build it.

Consider how this works in practice. A team might be training a new model on a modest hardware setup. Halfway through the training run, an algorithmic tweak causes the model's perplexity score on organic chemistry and network security data to plummet past a regulatory red line. Under old rules based purely on chip count, the training run would proceed unnoticed. Under a perplexity tripwire, the system triggers an automatic pause. Engineers must verify the model's safety profile before turning the GPUs back on.

By pivoting from physical hardware to mathematical surprise, the metric transforms from a standard benchmark into an enforceable safety switch.

3. Self-Regulation or Gatekeeping? The Strategic Split in AI's Frontier

  • Analyze the tension: Is this a genuine effort to prevent systemic existential risk, or a clever moat built by an industry leader to slow down agile open-source competitors?
  • How a perplexity ceiling reshapes the AI race: Open-source models would hit regulatory walls much earlier, while giants like OpenAI can pivot to specialized, post-training alignment within the allowed limit.
  • The compliance nightmare: Who sets the global baseline for perplexity, and how do you audit a metric that shifts depending on the test dataset?

When an OpenAI scientist proposed industry-wide AI limits tied to model intelligence metrics, the reaction was instant and deeply divided. On paper, capping how accurately a system predicts text—measured by perplexity—looks like a pragmatic safety brake against runaway capabilities. In practice, it exposes a growing rift across the industry: is this a genuine attempt to manage systemic risk, or a clever tactic to build a regulatory moat around early market leaders?

If lawmakers adopt a ceiling on base-model perplexity, open-source developers will hit that wall first. Open-source projects depend on raw, unconstrained pre-training scale so the broader developer community can adapt and fine-tune the models later. A hard limit on pre-training intelligence forces open-source creators to stop building before their models reach competitive baseline performance.

Incumbents operate under a completely different business logic. A company with massive resources can simply stop pre-training at the mandated perplexity threshold and pivot to specialized post-training. They can funnel compute into proprietary reinforcement learning, targeted chain-of-thought fine-tuning, and specialized system prompts. The base model remains strictly compliant with the legal perplexity limit, yet the finished product retains immense real-world utility.

Then comes the compliance nightmare. Perplexity is not a static hardware metric like FLOPS or clock speed; it is a relative measurement tied to the dataset used to evaluate the model.

Consider a concrete example. Test a model on standard Wikipedia text, and its perplexity might look high, staying well within legal safety limits. Evaluate that same model on a specialized dataset of software vulnerabilities or synthetic chemistry papers, and its perplexity could plummet, showing high predictive precision in high-risk domains.

Who decides which reference datasets set the global baseline? If international auditors rely on moving evaluation suites, small labs and independent developers will spend more time chasing compliance paperwork than writing code, while industry giants leverage their compliance teams to navigate the red tape.

4. The Enforcement Trap: What Happens When AI Intelligence Escapes the Metric?

  • The core paradox: Perplexity measures text prediction, not real-world agency, persuasion, or dangerous task execution.
  • Open tension: If we fixate on capping perplexity, we risk creating a false sense of security—stopping models from getting 'smarter' on paper while missing emerging capabilities in autonomous action.
  • Concluding thought: A metric-based speed limit buys humanity time, but it forces us to answer an uncomfortable question: Are we trying to make AI safe, or are we just trying to stop it from surprising us?

Perplexity measures a narrow slice of what language models do: statistical text prediction. Lower perplexity simply means a model is less surprised by the next word in a sequence. It does not measure real-world agency, political persuasion, or the execution of dangerous multi-step tasks.

This gap exposes the central paradox of the proposal. As OpenAI's chief scientist urges industry limits tied to performance metrics, researchers warn that a model's ability to act in the real world does not scale linearly with its next-token accuracy. A system can score moderately on standard evaluation benchmarks while remaining capable of executing complex social engineering or automated cyberattacks when paired with external tools and agentic workflows.

Fixating on a single statistical cap creates a dangerous illusion of control. If regulators freeze perplexity thresholds to keep models from growing too powerful, labs will naturally pivot. Developers can optimize post-training techniques, expand context windows, or construct multi-agent reasoning loops that dramatically raise a system's operational capability without ever altering its baseline perplexity score. The system looks tame on paper, but its practical agency continues to expand.

That leaves safety framework designers in an uncomfortable position. A metric-based speed limit buys humanity time, but it targets the thermometer rather than the fever.

By treating raw statistical compression as a proxy for physical-world threat, policy proposals risk fighting yesterday's battles while missing the rapid evolution of autonomous execution. The debate forces an uncomfortable question that regulatory bodies have yet to answer: Are we genuinely trying to make AI safe, or are we just attempting to stop it from surprising us?

Sources

  • OpenAI scientist proposes industry AI limits tied to model intelligence metric - Reuters
  • OpenAI Chief Scientist Urges Industry Limits on AI Development - Bloomberg.com
  • OpenAI calls for industry-wide AI brake tied to perplexity - Seeking Alpha

title: Stale responses in Redux Toolkit: the requestId guard you probably need
description:
A todo list shows the right results for a moment, then flips back to the old ones. There's no error in the console, and every test passes.

I ran into this while fixing an issue in an open source React + Redux Toolkit app. Two fetchTodos requests were in flight at the same time, the older one answered last, and the reducer wrote its result over the newer one. Here is the bug, two variants of it that are easy to miss, the fix, and how to test it without fake timers.

The bug

This is the slice most of us write for a list:

export const fetchTodos = createAsyncThunk(
  'todos/fetchAll',
  (filters: TodoFilters) => todosApi.getAll(filters),
);

// in the slice
builder
  .addCase(fetchTodos.pending, (state) => {
    state.status = 'loading';
  })
  .addCase(fetchTodos.fulfilled, (state, action) => {
    state.status = 'idle';
    state.items = action.payload.data;
    state.total = action.payload.meta.total;
  })
  .addCase(fetchTodos.rejected, (state) => {
    state.status = 'error';
  });

Nothing here links a response to the request the UI is waiting for. Whichever response resolves last wins, not whichever request started last.

That happens more often than you'd think:

  • The user types in a search box: a, then ab. The a query is slower (more results) and returns after ab.
  • They click through pages quickly.
  • You refetch on window focus while a filter change is still loading.
  • The first request hits a cold cache or a slow network; the second one doesn't.

The result is a list that doesn't match the filter on screen. It's hard to reproduce because it depends on timing.

Two variants people miss

A stale error. The old request fails after the new one has already succeeded. The data on screen is correct, but status is now 'error', so the UI shows an error banner over good data.

A response that arrives after logout. A fetch starts, the user logs out, and the slice resets to its initial state:

.addCase(logout, () => initialState)

Then the response arrives, fulfilled runs, and the reset state is filled with the previous user's list. If the next person signs in on the same tab, they can see it. Of the three, this is the one I'd fix first.

The fix: action.meta.requestId

createAsyncThunk gives every dispatch a unique requestId. It's on action.meta for pending, fulfilled and rejected, so all three actions of one dispatch share it.

Store the id when a request starts, and ignore any result whose id doesn't match:

builder
  .addCase(logout, () => initialState)
  .addCase(fetchTodos.pending, (state, action) => {
    state._fetchTodosRequestId = action.meta.requestId;
    state.status = 'loading';
  })
  .addCase(fetchTodos.fulfilled, (state, action) => {
    // an older request answering late (or one started before logout)
    // must not overwrite the list
    if (action.meta.requestId !== state._fetchTodosRequestId) return;

    state.status = 'idle';
    state.items = action.payload.data;
    state.total = action.payload.meta.total;
  })
  .addCase(fetchTodos.rejected, (state, action) => {
    if (action.meta.requestId !== state._fetchTodosRequestId) return;

    state.status = 'error';
  });

All three cases are handled:

  • Reverse order: the second pending overwrites the stored id, so the first response no longer matches.
  • Stale error: same check in rejected.
  • Logout: initialState has no stored id, so a response from before the reset can't match.

I named the field with a leading underscore and typed it as optional. It's bookkeeping, not UI state, and no component should read it.

Testing it without timers

You don't need fake timers or setTimeout in the mock. Return a promise you resolve yourself, then resolve the requests in the order you want:

it('keeps the latest request when two resolve in reverse order', async () => {
  let resolveFirst: (value: TodosResponse) => void = () => undefined;
  vi.mocked(todosApi.getAll)
    .mockReturnValueOnce(
      new Promise((resolve) => {
        resolveFirst = resolve;
      }),
    )
    .mockResolvedValueOnce({ data: [todoB], meta: { total: 1 /* ... */ } });
  const store = makeTodosStore();

  const first = store.dispatch(fetchTodos({ ...filters, query: 'a' }));
  await store.dispatch(fetchTodos({ ...filters, query: 'ab' }));
  resolveFirst({ data: [todoA, todoB], meta: { total: 2 /* ... */ } });
  await first;

  expect(store.getState().todos.items).toEqual([todoB]);
  expect(store.getState().todos.status).toBe('idle');
});

The other two tests follow the same pattern:

  • Stale error: call reject on the first promise after the second request succeeds, and check that status is still 'idle'.
  • Logout: dispatch logout() between starting the fetch and resolving it, and check that items is still empty.

To check the tests themselves, I put the reducer back to the version without the guard. All three new tests failed and the rest of the suite still passed. That's how I know they test the race and not something else.

Alternatives, and when to pick them

Approach Stops the stale write Cancels the request Cost
requestId guard in the reducer yes no a few lines
promise.abort() on the previous dispatch yes: it ends right away as rejected with meta.aborted, and its fulfilled never runs only if the thunk passes thunkAPI.signal to fetch you have to keep the handle and remember to call it
condition option skips starting a new fetch — wrong here: the newer request has new filters
RTK Query yes yes moving the endpoint over

If you can move the endpoint to RTK Query, do that. It caches each argument separately, so a slow a response can't replace the ab results. Abort and the guard work well together. Abort saves the network call, and the guard still protects you anywhere someone forgot to abort.

Limits

  • The guard is in the reducer only. The stale rejected action still reaches middleware, so a global "show an error toast on any rejected action" listener will still fire. If you have one, apply the same check there or skip rejected actions whose request is no longer current.
  • I used one id per thunk type. If two parts of the screen use the same thunk for different lists at the same time, they will cancel each other's results. Then you need one id per list, keyed by something in action.meta.arg.

The rule I keep now

If a reducer writes the result of an async call, it should first check whether this is still the request the UI is waiting for. With createAsyncThunk that check is a single line.

How do you handle this in your apps: abort, a request id, or RTK Query everywhere?

title: Apple Developing General-Purpose Computer-Use AI Agents
description:
Apple is actively recruiting for a team focused on building proactive, general-purpose computer-use AI agents. According to recent job postings, the company is looking to integrate these agents into the existing Siri, UI frameworks, and Apple Foundation Models infrastructure.

Technical Scope

The project aims to create agents capable of performing multi-step tasks across diverse environments, including:

  • Cross-App Orchestration: Moving fluidly between browsers, document editors, and terminals.
  • Code Execution: Writing, debugging, and executing code in real-time.
  • API Interaction: Calling external services and coordinating specialized sub-agents.
  • UI Interaction: Interacting with UI frameworks to execute commands as a human user would.

Design Principles

Safety, privacy, and security are explicitly stated as central design pillars. Unlike standard LLM implementations, these agents are intended to be proactive, meaning they can initiate tasks without direct user prompting, provided they are within the scope of the user's intent.

Developer Implications

For developers, this signals a shift toward more autonomous system-level interactions. As Apple integrates these capabilities into its platforms, we can expect new APIs or frameworks that allow third-party apps to expose their functionality more effectively to agentic workflows. Developers should focus on ensuring their app's UI elements are properly annotated for accessibility and automation, as these will likely be the primary hooks for future agentic interactions.

This move aligns Apple with competitors like Meta and OpenAI, but with the expected emphasis on on-device processing and privacy-preserving architecture.

Source: https://www.macrumors.com/2026/11/19/apple-ai-agent-development/

title: Desktop AI Workbench Architecture in 2026: 4 Models Compared for Multi-Agent Engineering
description:
Engineering teams adopting desktop AI agents in 2026 are converging on four distinct architectures rather than one feature list: multi-model desktop workbenches like Ghast Workbench (18,452 registered accounts and 9,655 compute top-ups through October 31, 2026 across 13 model families on 0G Compute), single-vendor clients like Claude Desktop and OpenAI Codex, MIT-licensed open-source clients like Hermes Desktop, and self-hosted gateways like OpenClaw.

The full live architecture comparison and verification notes are published at ghast.trapezohe.ai/ai-workbench-comparison.

Why parallel prompts break down in real repositories

Running three agents in separate terminal tabs generates more code, not better code. When each session holds its own prompt history and no shared definition of done, three failure modes show up within an hour:

  • Context drift across handoffs: the agent writing a patch does not inherit the constraints agreed on during planning.
