  • Unverified completion claims: an agent summarizes that a fix is ready without running the exact test command or showing the diff.
  • Same-family blind spots: asking the same model that wrote a patch to review that patch rarely catches subtle assumptions.

This is why desktop AI workspaces have shifted from single-thread chat windows to structured local workbenches with explicit file scope, model portability, and human acceptance gates.

Four desktop AI workbench architectures compared

Every setup below was checked against public documentation and pricing on November 22, 2026.

1. Multi-model desktop AI workbench (Ghast Workbench)

  • Platforms: macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel) and Windows x64.
  • Architecture: Native desktop app combining Chat, scoped local Coding, editable Persistent Memory, and Agent Team (named task owners, Roundtable discussions, independent review loops, and human acceptance checks).
  • Model routing: 13 supported model families through 0G Compute (including OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, Qwen, Grok, and Llama), plus optional client-side encrypted backups to 0G Storage.
  • Local agent interoperability: Existing Codex and Claude Code installations on your machine can join an Agent Team workflow as teammates while keeping their own local sessions.
  • Pricing: Free desktop download ($0); pay-as-you-go model and connected-service usage.
  • Trade-offs: Closed-source desktop client; not built to run as a 24/7 headless chat-bot daemon when your laptop is closed. (Note: Ghast Protocol for verifiable paid AI services is a separate layer currently in development.)

2. Single-vendor desktop clients (Claude Desktop with Cowork, OpenAI Codex)

  • Platforms: macOS and Windows (plus web, mobile, CLI, and IDE integrations depending on vendor).
  • Architecture: Deep OS-level sandboxes (Apple Virtualization on macOS 13+, Hyper-V on Windows 10/11 for Claude Cowork; dedicated parallel repo threads and diff views for OpenAI Codex).
  • Model routing: Locked to one vendor (Anthropic Claude or OpenAI models only).
  • Pricing: Bundled into monthly plans ($8 to $500/month across ChatGPT tiers; $20/month Claude Pro or $100 to $200/month Claude Max for heavy Cowork usage) or vendor API billing.
  • Trade-offs: Zero API-key friction inside one ecosystem, but no cross-family model switching and heavy multi-step runs can hit subscription quotas quickly.

3. Open-source desktop and CLI agents (Hermes Desktop by Nous Research)

  • Platforms: macOS, Windows, Linux, and CLI.
  • Architecture: MIT-licensed client with automatic workspace snapshots (/rollback) before edits, reusable agentskills.io skill files, and optional bridges to Telegram, Discord, Slack, and Microsoft Teams.
  • Model routing: 200+ models via BYOK API keys, OpenRouter, or local inference endpoints.
  • Pricing: Free open-source software (MIT); direct provider API billing.
  • Trade-offs: You manage your own provider keys and router billing; built more around single-agent delegation and self-improving skills than structured multi-owner Roundtable reviews.

4. Self-hosted agent gateways (OpenClaw)

  • Platforms: macOS, Windows, and Linux (local machine or VPS).
  • Architecture: MIT-licensed Node.js daemon connecting local shells, browsers, and markdown memory to WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack, Discord, and cron schedules.
  • Model routing: BYOK across configured cloud or local LLM APIs.
  • Pricing: Free open-source software (MIT); BYOK API bills ($50 to $500+/month on heavy frontier-model loops) plus optional VPS hosting ($23 to $70+/month).
  • Trade-offs: Maximum control over 24/7 headless automation, but higher maintenance load, wider local shell exposure, and real risk of runaway token spend from background loops.

A reliable writer-reviewer pattern for local repositories

Whether you coordinate agents inside Ghast Workbench or script handoffs between local CLI tools, keeping multi-agent edits predictable comes down to bounding every task with an explicit owner, allowed file scope, verification command, and independent reviewer before a human accepts the change.

Here is a minimal task contract pattern that prevents agents from stepping on each other:

task_id: fix-webhook-signature-check
owner: local-codex-session
reviewer: claude-family-model
scope:
  read:
    - src/webhooks/
    - tests/webhooks/
  write:
    - src/webhooks/verify.ts
    - tests/webhooks/verify.test.ts
verification:
  command: "npm test -- tests/webhooks/verify.test.ts"
  require_passing_output: true
acceptance_gate:
  require_independent_review: true
  require_human_signoff: true
  block_on_unrequested_file_changes: true

In practice, run the workflow in four strict steps:

  1. Assign one scoped file change: The owner edits only files listed under scope.write and runs the exact verification command locally.
  2. Pass the diff to a different model family: The reviewer inspects the diff against the original task objective and flags missing edge cases, unrequested edits, or untested branches.
  3. Send revisions back to the owner: Keep all review feedback attached to the same task thread so context survives the handoff.
  4. Verify before human acceptance: Inspect the final diff and rerun the test command locally before accepting the work item.

For two end-to-end walkthroughs verified on Ghast Workbench release 0.1.33, see the scoped Python bug-fix workflow and the Agent Team review and revision loop in the official docs.

When to pick a different architecture

No single desktop AI workbench fits every engineering constraint:

  • Pick Hermes Desktop or OpenClaw if MIT open-source code, Linux desktop support, or 24/7 unattended chat-app triggers are hard requirements.
  • Pick Claude Desktop or OpenAI Codex if your company standardizes on one vendor subscription and you do not need cross-provider model routing.
  • Pick Ghast Workbench if you work on macOS or Windows and want multi-model Chat, scoped local Coding, editable Persistent Memory, and structured Agent Team review alongside your existing local Codex or Claude Code sessions.

Read the full architecture matrix at ghast.trapezohe.ai/ai-workbench-comparison or the tool-by-tool 2026 review at ghast.trapezohe.ai/best-desktop-ai-agent-workspace.

title: Stop Guessing: How to Choose the Right AI Model
description:
Choosing an AI model for your application sounds simple: find a powerful model, connect its API, and start building.

But things get complicated when your application starts handling real users.

A model that produces excellent answers might be too slow for your API. A cheaper model might fail at structured extraction. A locally hosted model might improve data control but struggle with your available hardware.

The best AI model isn't necessarily the most powerful one. It's the model that meets your application's requirements with the right balance of quality, latency, cost, privacy, and operational complexity.

In this guide, we'll explore five practical techniques for selecting and evaluating AI models, with Python examples you can adapt to your own projects.

1. Choose a Model Based on the Actual Task

Before comparing providers or model benchmarks, define what your application needs the model to do.

Different tasks require different capabilities.

Application task Model tendency
Simple classification Fast, low-cost model
Text summarization General-purpose model
Complex code analysis Reasoning-oriented model
Large document analysis Long-context model or RAG
Private, offline inference Self-hosted open-weight model

Consider a support-ticket classification system. It needs to categorize incoming tickets into:

  • Network
  • Hardware
  • Software
  • Security

Using an expensive reasoning model for every ticket may be unnecessary. A smaller model or conventional machine-learning classifier could be sufficient.

Start by documenting your requirements:

requirements = {
    "task": "support_ticket_classification",
    "input_type": "text",
    "output_type": "single_label",
    "allowed_labels": [
        "Network",
        "Hardware",
        "Software",
        "Security"
    ],
    "max_latency_ms": 2000,
    "monthly_budget_usd": 50,
    "privacy": "no_training_on_customer_data"
}

Practical takeaway: Select the model category after defining the task, expected output, workload, and constraintsnot before.

2. Benchmark Model Quality Instead of Trusting Rankings

Popular benchmarks can help you discover candidate models, but they don't guarantee performance on your application.

A model might perform well on general reasoning benchmarks while consistently returning invalid JSON in your application.

Build a representative evaluation dataset containing real-world examples.

For example:

test_cases = [
    {
        "input": "VPN connection fails after an update.",
        "expected": "Network"
    },
    {
        "input": "The desktop computer does not power on.",
        "expected": "Hardware"
    },
    {
        "input": "The application crashes during startup.",
        "expected": "Software"
    },
    {
        "input": "Suspicious login activity detected.",
        "expected": "Security"
    }
]

Evaluate every candidate using the same inputs, instructions, output requirements, and evaluation rules.

For classification, useful metrics include:

  • Accuracy: Overall percentage of correct predictions.
  • Precision: How many predicted positives were correct.
  • Recall: How many actual positives were identified.
  • F1-score: Balance between precision and recall. 
from sklearn.metrics import (
    accuracy_score,
    classification_report
)

actual = ["Network", "Hardware", "Software", "Security"]
predicted = ["Network", "Hardware", "Software", "Security"]

print("Accuracy:", accuracy_score(actual, predicted))
print(classification_report(actual, predicted))

For extraction, measure field-level accuracy and schema validity. For code generation, measure test-pass rates. For summarization, use a defined review rubric and human evaluation.

Practical takeaway: A model's performance on your representative dataset is more useful than its popularity or a generic leaderboard position.

3. Measure Latency, Context, and Throughput

A model can produce accurate results and still create a poor user experience.

Three important performance dimensions are:

Latency: How long does a request take?

Context length: How much input and conversation history can the model process?

Throughput: How many requests or tokens can the system handle over time?

For interactive applications, measure total response time and time to first token (TTFT). Streaming can make an application feel more responsive even when total generation time remains similar.

Here's a simple Python example for measuring request latency with a local Ollama model:

import time
import httpx

def benchmark_model(prompt: str) -> None:
    started = time.perf_counter()

    response = httpx.post(
        "http://localhost:11434/api/generate",
        json={
            "model": "llama3.2:1b",
            "prompt": prompt,
            "stream": False
        },
        timeout=120
    )

    response.raise_for_status()

    elapsed = (time.perf_counter() - started) * 1000

    print(f"Latency: {elapsed:.2f} ms")
    print(response.json().get("response", ""))


benchmark_model("Explain Python decorators.")

Run multiple tests with representative prompts and compare median and p95 latency rather than trusting one measurement.

Context capacity also matters. A large context window doesn't automatically mean better results: unnecessary input can increase cost, latency, and noise. Use retrieval when providing an entire document collection is inefficient.

Practical takeaway: Measure performance under realistic input sizes and expected concurrency before choosing a model for production.

4. Calculate Cost Before Scaling

A model that works well in a prototype may become expensive when request volume increases.

Hosted model APIs commonly charge separately for input and output tokens. Pricing can also vary with cached inputs, batch processing, and other provider-specific features.

A basic cost formula is:

Request Cost =
    (Input Tokens × Input Price per Million / 1,000,000)
  + (Output Tokens × Output Price per Million / 1,000,000)

Monthly Cost =
    Request Cost × Monthly Requests

You can implement the calculation in Python:

def estimate_cost(
    input_tokens: int,
    output_tokens: int,
    input_price: float,
    output_price: float
) -> float:

    input_cost = (
        input_tokens * input_price / 1_000_000
    )

    output_cost = (
        output_tokens * output_price / 1_000_000
    )

    return input_cost + output_cost


cost = estimate_cost(
    input_tokens=2000,
    output_tokens=500,
    input_price=0.15,
    output_price=0.60
)

print(f"Estimated cost: ${cost:.6f}")

The prices above are illustrative inputs, not a current pricing recommendation. Check the provider's official pricing page before using actual rates.

Also consider retries, caching, concurrency, tool calls, and operational expenses.

Practical takeaway: Estimate cost per request and monthly cost using realistic token usage before committing to a provider.

5. Compare Hosted and Local Models, Including Privacy

Your deployment environment can be just as important as model capability.

There are two common approaches.

Hosted models Self-hosted open-weight models
Provider manages inference infrastructure You manage infrastructure
Usually easier to integrate Requires runtime and hardware setup
Commonly billed per token/request Hardware and operational costs
Provider policies govern data handling Greater potential data control
Provider handles much of the scaling You manage scaling and maintenance

For local experimentation, Ollama provides a straightforward way to run open-weight models.

Install a small model:

ollama pull llama3.2:1b

Test it:

ollama run llama3.2:1b

Or call its local API:

curl http://localhost:11434/api/generate -d "{\"model\":\"llama3.2:1b\",\"prompt\":\"Explain model selection\",\"stream\":false}"

Local inference can be useful for experimentation, offline workflows, and applications requiring greater control over data processing. However, performance depends on hardware, model size, quantization, context length, and concurrent requests.

Remember that open-weight does not automatically mean unrestricted commercial use. Review the exact model license.

For hosted providers, examine data retention, training-use policies, regional processing, rate limits, pricing, and commercial terms.

Never expose an unauthenticated local inference endpoint directly to the public internet.

Practical takeaway: Choose hosted, local, or hybrid deployment based on privacy requirements, infrastructure, budget, and operational capacity.

Bonus: Build a Model Selection Scorecard

You can combine your evaluation results into a weighted decision matrix.

For example:

Criterion Example weight
Task quality 35%
Latency 20%
Cost efficiency 20%
Context capacity 10%
Throughput 5%
Privacy and governance 5%
Deployment simplicity 5%

Calculate the weighted score:

weights = {
    "quality": 0.35,
    "latency": 0.20,
    "cost": 0.20,
    "context": 0.10,
    "throughput": 0.05,
    "privacy": 0.05,
    "deployment": 0.05
}

scores = {
    "quality": 4,
    "latency": 5,
    "cost": 4,
    "context": 4,
    "throughput": 4,
    "privacy": 3,
    "deployment": 5
}

total = sum(
    weights[key] * scores[key]
    for key in weights
)

print(f"Weighted score: {total:.2f}/5")

These weights are illustrative. Adjust them to reflect your application's priorities.

A scorecard makes trade-offs visible and helps explain why a particular model was selected.

Final Thoughts

AI model selection is an engineering decision, not a popularity contest.

Before integrating a model into your application:

  1. Define the task and acceptance criteria.
  2. Shortlist models with the required capabilities.
  3. Evaluate quality using representative test data.
  4. Measure latency, context usage, and throughput.
  5. Estimate costs and review privacy and licensing requirements.
  6. Document the trade-offs behind your final choice.

The objective isn't to find one model that wins every benchmark. It's to build an AI system that performs reliably within your actual technical and business constraints.

Build Smarter AI Applications with DevSpireHub

Found this useful?

  • Bookmark this article so you can revisit the model-selection checklist.
  • Comment below: Do you prefer hosted APIs, local models, or a hybrid architecture?
  • Follow DevSpireHub for practical AI engineering tutorials, Python projects, open-source tools, and developer resources.

title: AI Can Extrapolate Your Sales Data in Ten Seconds. That Is Not a Forecast.
description:
Drop three years of monthly sales into a chat window, ask "forecast next year," and you get a smooth upward curve in ten seconds.

Would you sign a purchasing budget against it?

Two follow-up questions usually end the conversation:

  1. If a new regulation lands next March, will that curve tell you in advance? No.
  2. Can you explain how the curve was produced? Usually not — which means when it drifts, you can only say "it was wrong" after the fact.

If you can't answer those, the missing piece isn't a better model. It's the boundary around what you're asking for.

Extrapolation is arithmetic. Forecasting is judgment.

Most of what people call "AI forecasting" at work is actually extrapolation: extending a past trend forward on the assumption that the past pattern keeps holding.

Forecasting requires answering a second question: will the pattern change?

  • Extrapolation → arithmetic. AI is excellent at it and finishes in milliseconds.
  • Forecasting → judgment. AI has no meeting notes from next March and doesn't know your industry is about to switch standards.

So the division of labor is clean: let AI do the arithmetic, and write down the judgment yourself. What you write down is called an assumption — and an assumption is not a disclaimer. It's a sentence that can be proven false by facts.

The 28% that turned out to be 9%

A restaurant supply chain team ran this in late 2023: extrapolate 2024 flour purchasing volume from store count growth. AI returned +28%. The year actually came in at +9%.

The post-mortem found nothing wrong with the arithmetic. AI used new store openings as the driver. Real purchasing volume was pinned by declining per-store usage at existing locations. Two variables moving in opposite directions, and the model only saw one.

That's not a math error. Nobody wrote "per-store usage stays flat" down as an assumption, so nobody tested it.

Three tests before you let AI extrapolate anything

Miss one, and the honest move is to admit this round shouldn't be extrapolated.

1. The history must cover at least two complete cycles.
Monthly data: 36 months minimum. Quarterly: 12 quarters minimum. Two cycles, not two data points — with a single peak-and-trough you cannot separate seasonality from coincidence.

A school uniform wholesaler had only one autumn peak (2023) and AI projected 2024 autumn would double. It had learned a one-off back-to-school bulk order as if it were a pattern.

2. Definitions must not have changed over the timeline.
This is the most commonly missed failure. Finance teams hit it constantly: in 2022 a category was reclassified from admin expense to sales expense, the two tables got stitched together, and the trend line shows a fake inflection exactly at the merger month.

Before feeding anything to a model, mark the months where the definition changed — or cut the series and restart from the change point.

3. Outliers must be removed or explicitly flagged.
A few months of 2022 offline retail data are a cliff for anyone who looks. That's an event, not a trend. Feed those points into a linear fit and both slope and intercept get dragged.

All three satisfied → extrapolation is worth doing.
Two of three → downgrade the output to a "reference range," not a target.
None → refuse. Eight months of sales history produces a confidence interval so wide it has no decision value. Use year-over-year comparison plus human judgment instead.

Write the assumption so it can be proven wrong

The test is brutal: after writing the sentence, can you state what would make it false next year? If not, it's filler.

A usable assumption has three parts: variable, range, time window.

Bad: "Assume the market continues to grow steadily."

Good: "Assume East China monthly active customers stay within 2,800 ± 300 from Q1 to Q2 2026, with no single month below 2,400."

An HR version:

"Assume voluntary attrition stays between 1.8% and 2.5% per month through H1 2026, with no single month above 4% caused by organizational restructuring."

Why does that work? Next July you open the attrition report and immediately know whether the assumption held. If it held, the extrapolated hiring demand is usable as a reference. If it didn't, the model is void and you start over — no arguing about whose fault it was.

Practical note: put all assumptions in a table next to the result, not in an appendix. Three columns:

Assumption What it looks like if wrong Who watches it
East China MAU within 2,800 ± 300 Two consecutive months below 2,400 → re-run with new baseline Regional ops lead
No definitional change in cost categories A reclassification memo appears → split series at the change month Finance controller
No new regulation affecting lead times Policy draft published → move to scenario mode Compliance

That third column matters most. An assumption nobody watches is an assumption that doesn't exist.

What the confidence interval actually tells you

Here's where tools diverge, and it's worth being precise.

Spreadsheet route. Run a regression on the history (36 monthly points is a comfortable size), take slope and intercept, project forward, and use the built-in forecast sheet if your version has it — it draws the band for you. If your version doesn't, compute the interval yourself from the residuals.

The critical caveat: that band is derived from historical residuals. It says "if past volatility continues, the future probably lands here." It knows nothing about next year's policy change. Read it as a statistical volatility band, never as a business risk band.

Chat-model route. Good for fast multi-variable exploration, bad for the final number. A prompt that keeps it honest:

You are a data analyst. Here is 36 months of monthly sales (attached). Do only the following:
1. Fit a linear trend and report slope, intercept, R².
2. Project the next 4 quarters.
3. For each projected quarter, give a prediction interval and state the method used.
4. List every assumption your projection depends on, one sentence each.
5. Do NOT adjust for seasonality, policy, or "market conditions." If you think an adjustment is needed, say so instead of applying it.
6. Flag any month in the history that looks like an outlier, and say which ones you excluded and why.

Point 5 is the one people skip. Without it, the model silently applies its own judgment and you lose the ability to separate arithmetic from opinion.

Keep policy and shocks outside the model

The rule I use: anything that hasn't happened yet does not belong inside the extrapolation. New regulation, a competitor entering, a subsidy expiring — these are scenario switches, not data points.

Run the base extrapolation on clean history. Then, separately, write down: "If regulation X lands in March, base volume drops by roughly Y% for Z months, based on [comparable past event]." Now you have two artifacts — a baseline you can defend and a scenario you can update — instead of one curve pretending to know the future.

The uncomfortable summary

Extrapolation is cheap. Assumption-writing is the work.

  • Two full cycles, stable definitions, labeled outliers → otherwise don't extrapolate.
  • Every assumption gets a variable, a range, and a time window — and an owner.
  • The confidence interval is a volatility band, not a risk assessment.
  • Anything that hasn't happened yet goes outside the model, as a scenario.

The value isn't a more accurate number. It's that when the number turns out wrong, you can point at the assumption that broke — and fix the process instead of blaming the tool.

I wrote a longer Chinese version of this walkthrough — including the three prompt templates I actually use, the small-sample refusal rule, and a full failure-case teardown — here: 历史数据外推的边界：三件事AI算不准

If you've had an extrapolation blow up in a budget meeting, I'd genuinely like to hear which assumption failed.

title: Still green or over-despilled? Test the edge hue, not its chroma
description:
The last post ended on a limitation I flagged upfront: every metric in it needed something a real pipeline doesn't have. Spill fraction needs the source background G. Edge color deviation needs a clean foreground F. I had both because I built them, which is fine for an explanation and useless as a regression gate.

A reader, AI Flip Room, suggested a fix in the comments:

To catch removing too much, I'd add a check that the edge color stays inside the range of the nearby opaque colors, so a magenta or gray pushed too far gets flagged even when spill reads as improved.

That's the right instinct. No F, no G, just the image. So I implemented it and ran it against the same seven variants. It works on the obvious cases and it collapses on the only case that matters. This post is what I found, and the test I ended up shipping instead.

The setup, in one paragraph

Same ground truth as the last post: a white ceramic mug, 1200×800, an Apple Vision matte (VNGenerateForegroundInstanceMaskRequest), a clean foreground F extrapolated from the eroded opaque core, and a known source background G at RGB (46, 204, 113). Seven variants share one alpha matte — 9,959 partial-band pixels, 11,961 inner-ring pixels — and differ only in the RGB stored under that alpha. F and G exist only to construct the variants. No metric below is allowed to look at them.

That constraint isn't academic for me. I work on PicViva, an editor for seller product photos, and the matting runs there go out over shop inventory: a cutout arrives as a PNG with an alpha channel and nothing else — no original, no clean foreground, no record of what background was removed. So a metric I can't compute from the file alone is a metric that never runs. The code below is plain numpy, scipy and scikit-image, imports nothing from our stack, and works the same on anyone's output; this isn't a product comparison.

Variant What it simulates
A clean correct straight RGB, no spill
B raw blend edge kept the green-screen color
C half despill half the green removed
D over-despill pushed too far, toward magenta
E alpha only clean RGB, alpha grown 2 px
F thresholded alpha binarized, spilled RGB left on opaque pixels
G colour chaos every edge pixel drifts a different way

Test 1: the local envelope

For each partial-alpha pixel, take the opaque pixels within 8 px, compute a per-channel 5th–95th percentile range, and ask whether the edge pixel falls inside it.

def env_ok(stored, y, x, opaque, r=8):
    m = opaque[y-r:y+r+1, x-r:x+r+1]
    if m.sum() < 20:
        return None
    patch = stored[y-r:y+r+1, x-r:x+r+1][m]
    lo = np.percentile(patch, 5,  axis=0)
    hi = np.percentile(patch, 95, axis=0)
    v  = stored[y, x]
    over = np.maximum(lo - v, v - hi)      # > 0 means outside
    return float(over.max())               # signed excursion
Variant Edge px Outside the envelope Mean excursion
A clean 9,959 0.3% 0.9
B raw blend 9,959 94.6% 78.0
C half despill 9,959 91.4% 39.5
D over-despill 9,959 91.5% 39.7
G colour chaos 9,959 98.4% 106.1
E alpha grown 0 n/a n/a
F thresholded 0 n/a n/a

Read the C and D rows together. 91.4% versus 91.5% of pixels outside. Mean excursion 39.5 versus 39.7 levels. The test cannot tell "still green" from "over-despilled", and those two are opposite bugs. If I gate on it, I ship D — a magenta-rimmed cutout — while reporting that the edge is contaminated. The diagnosis is right, the remedy is the wrong direction.

That's not a tuning problem. I moved the percentile band, the radius, the opaque threshold; the two rows track each other within a point at every setting, because they are constructed to. C = 0.5·S + 0.5·F and D = F + 0.5·(F − S) are equally far from F, in opposite directions.

Why the envelope fails

The envelope answers one question: is this colour plausible for this object? For C and D the answer is identically no, because both moved the same distance off the body's colours. Plausibility is a magnitude, and the two failure modes differ only in sign.

The same thing kills a second reference-free idea I tried: estimate the local background from nearby clear pixels, project the edge deviation onto (G_est − F_loc), and check that it scales with 1 − alpha. Two problems, both fatal:

  • Transparent pixels often don't carry a usable background colour. Only 1,963 of 9,959 band pixels had one (19.7%). This export writes foreground colour under alpha = 0.
  • The direction of the deviation was never compared to anything. Coherence — how consistent the edge deviation direction is across the boundary — came out 0.914 for C and 0.921 for D. Both are "coherent"; coherent in opposite directions. R² against 1 − alpha was 0.010 and 0.001, i.e. no linear relationship either way.

Two independent reference-free checks, same blind spot. That's a signal about the class of test, not about my implementation: anything that only looks at the edge band relative to nearby body colours measures distance, not direction.

You don't ship straight alpha

Here's the swing that fixed it, and it came from asking what actually reaches the buyer. A PNG with straight alpha is an intermediate. What renders is your pixels composited onto the shop's background — white, in practically every marketplace.

So measure there. Composite the stored RGB onto the target background using the alpha you already have, convert to CIE Lab, and read two numbers: chroma C* = hypot(a, b) and hue h = atan2(b, a).

Now the reference question changes. I don't need a clean F at every edge pixel. I need the product's own body — opaque pixels, uncontaminated by definition — as a single color reference. That's available on any real cutout. It's the difference between "what should this pixel have been" (unknowable) and "what colour is this object" (readable from 90% of the image).

TARGET = np.array([255.0, 255.0, 255.0])   # the background you ship on
ALPHA_T, CORE_ERODE = 250, 6

def chroma_hue(stored, alpha, mask):
    a = alpha[mask][:, None] / 255.0
    comp = stored[mask] * a + TARGET * (1 - a)      # what the buyer sees
    lab = color.rgb2lab(comp[None, ...] / 255.0)[0]
    C = np.hypot(lab[:, 1], lab[:, 2])
    h = np.degrees(np.arctan2(lab[:, 2], lab[:, 1])) % 360.0

    w = C + 1e-9                                     # chroma-weighted circular mean
    hs = np.radians(h)
    mean_h = np.degrees(np.arctan2((w * np.sin(hs)).sum(),
                                   (w * np.cos(hs)).sum())) % 360.0
    return {"C_mean": float(C.mean()), "hue": float(mean_h)}

The body reference from the same function, restricted to the fully opaque core:

opaque body        C* 2.20   hue 112.1°  (yellow-green)

Results

Δhue is the edge band's circular-mean hue minus the body's, wrapped to ±180°.

Variant Body hue Edge hue Δhue Edge C* Verdict
A clean 112.1 109.1 −3.0 1.53 no colour cast
B raw blend 112.1 154.6 +42.5 11.39 background colour still present
C half despill 112.1 150.1 +38.0 6.32 background colour still present
D over-despill 112.1 357.9 −114.2 5.03 pushed past neutral
G colour chaos 112.1 150.5 +38.4 21.93 background colour still present
E alpha grown 112.1 108.7 −3.4 3.22 no colour cast
F thresholded 112.1 143.2 +31.1 9.12 background colour still present

Seven variants, seven correct verdicts. C and D — the pair nothing else could separate — land 152° apart in hue.

The C-vs-D case, for the record

Chroma alone is the trap, and D is why. C sits at C* 6.32, D at 5.03. If "lower chroma is better" is your gate, D passes and C fails — exactly backwards. D has less colour left because the despill didn't stop at neutral; it crossed over into magenta, which reads as low chroma on a white background while being visibly wrong.

The hue is unambiguous: +38° means the edge is rotated toward the green background. −114° means it went past the body's 112° and out the other side. One number, one sign, two different bugs.

So the decision rule needs the hue first, chroma second:

d = (edge_hue - body_hue + 180) % 360 - 180

if abs(d) <= 10:   verdict = "no colour cast"
elif d > 10:       verdict = "background colour still present"
elif d < -90:      verdict = "pushed past neutral (over-despill)"
else:              verdict = "cast on the far side of the body"

Report C* alongside as visibility, not as the gate. Below C* ≈ 2 the hue angle is noise-dominated — a near-grey pixel has no meaningful angle — which is why the mean is chroma-weighted. A and E sit at C* 1.53 and 3.22: both are close enough to neutral that their Δhue is a weak signal on its own, and their low chroma is what makes the "clean" verdict safe rather than the −3° itself.

One more reading of the table: E is clean and still wrong. Alpha grown by 2 px, perfect colour, Δhue −3.4. This test says the colour is fine, which is true, and says nothing about the 2 px of white halo. That's the same division of labour as before — colour metrics don't see geometry. Use the edge-geometry metrics for that.

And F: 31.1° of residual green in pixels labelled fully opaque. That's the inner-ring spill from the last post (0.085) rediscovered by a completely different method. Two independent measurements agreeing on the same hidden defect is the only kind of validation I trust in this space.

Why ±10°, and what it costs

The neutral band isn't a round number I liked. It's calibrated: I re-ran the clean variant across 18 parameter combinations (core erosion 3–10 px, clear threshold 3/5/10) and measured Δhue for A every time.

Δhue(A clean)  min −4.9°   max −1.8°   spread 3.1°
body hue       111.5° .. 112.4°

The clean variant is never exactly 0°. Its band samples the rim, where the object itself is shaded and slightly darker than the body interior, so there's a systematic −3° bias. ±10° is roughly three times the observed spread — wide enough not to fire on a clean cutout, narrow enough that the smallest real cast here (+31.1°) is caught with room.

Two costs, stated plainly:

  • The threshold is per-material. A glossy metal object has a wider intrinsic hue spread at its rim than matte ceramic. Calibrate on one known-good cutout of that material before you gate on it; the constants are not portable.
  • It needs a known target background. White is right for marketplaces. If you ship on several, run the test on each, or use the lowest-chroma one, where a cast is most visible.

Where the test breaks

Saturated products. If the product body is genuinely green, the body hue is the background hue and a green fringe looks consistent. The test measures "is the edge the same colour as the body", not "is the body the colour it should be". For white, grey, black, metal and skin — most of e-commerce — the body chroma is low and any hue deviation stands out. For a green bottle it won't. Mitigation: build the body reference per region rather than globally, and compare each edge pixel to its own local body patch, which is where the reader's envelope idea comes back in — as a reference, not as a pass/fail test.

Chroma near zero. Hue is undefined at the origin. A perfectly desaturated edge can produce any Δhue, so gate on C* too, in the direction of "don't trust the hue below 2".

Multi-coloured products. A single global body hue is meaningless on a printed t-shirt. Same fix: per-region reference.

It reports direction, not amount. Δhue tells you which way the edge is wrong and roughly how badly. It does not give you "this pixel is 25% background", which is what spill fraction gave on a known G. If you have G, keep using spill fraction — it's strictly more informative. This test is for when you don't.

Lab is not ΔE. A 30° hue rotation at C* 9 and at C* 40 are not equally visible. I report chroma next to hue for that reason, but I haven't built a perceptual model, and I wouldn't claim the band is perceptually uniform.

Reproducing

The whole metric is about thirty lines of numpy on top of three dependencies (numpy, scipy, scikit-image). The variants come from a Vision matte on one Unsplash photo; the metrics never touch F or G.

To run it on your own pipeline: drop an RGBA cutout in as variant A, set TARGET to the background you ship on, and print the table. Then look at your real pipeline's output the same way. If your despill is a fixed fraction, the sign tells you where you stand — a hue between your body and the background means you didn't finish, a hue past the body means you overshot. Those have different fixes, and now they have different numbers.

The thing I still don't have: a reference-free check that catches both a cast and a 2 px alpha error with one number. My guess is it doesn't exist, because they live in different channels and the composite hides the second one. Happy to be shown otherwise.

When your despill overshoots, do you catch it before or after the image reaches the listing?
