title: I built a Modbus simulator that Claude drives over MCP: test SCADA without a PLC
description:
Disclosure: I work on fieldpuppet, the open-source simulator in this post. It is maintained by the team behind PLCGateway.

Here is a prompt I can now type into Claude:

Set up 50 energy meters starting at port 6000. Make meter 12 stop answering for 30 seconds, then tell me which registers my SCADA read from it.

A few seconds later there are 50 Modbus TCP devices listening on my laptop, one of them goes silent on schedule, and I get a report of what my software polled. No PLC, no meter, no cabinet.

This post explains why I built it, how the MCP part works, and how to use it without any AI at all.

The problem: the hardware is never on your desk

If you write software that talks Modbus TCP (a SCADA screen, a gateway, a historian, a data collector), you know this situation. The code is ready, but the PLC is in a cabinet at the customer site, the energy meter has not shipped yet, and nobody will let you unplug a pump just to see how your software handles a timeout.

A register table that returns fixed numbers does not help much. Real testing needs:

  • Many devices at once, because polling 1 device and polling 200 behave very differently.
  • Values that move, so trends, alarms and scaling can be checked.
  • Faults on demand: slow answers, no answer, exception replies, dropped connections. These break software in the field and are the hardest to reproduce with real equipment.
  • A record of what your software asked for, so you can see whether it polls the registers you think it does.

Why MCP fits this job

Setting up test devices is boring, repetitive work: copy a register list from a manual, pick ports, write a fault timeline. It is exactly the kind of work an assistant does well if it has the right tools.

fieldpuppet is a single Rust executable of about 2 MB with an MCP server built in. It exposes 22 tools, such as create_device, set_signal, apply_scenario, inject_fault and get_traffic_log. Every tool carries read-only and destructive hints, so the client knows which calls change state.

For Claude Code it is one line:

claude mcp add fieldpuppet -- /full/path/to/fieldpuppet mcp

For Claude Desktop, each release has an .mcpb bundle you can install from the Extensions settings. Any MCP client that can start a local server over stdio works.

Things I ask it most often:

  • "Here is the register list from a device manual. Build a simulated device that matches it."
  • "Make the tank level rise from 20 % to 95 % over two minutes, then switch the high level alarm on."
  • "Pump 2 should answer with a device busy exception for the next 30 seconds."
  • "Which registers has my SCADA been reading from the drive in the last minute?"

A read-only web dashboard on http://127.0.0.1:5080 shows every device, its live values and a feed of everything the assistant changed, so you are never guessing what it did.

It works without AI too

Describe the devices in YAML:

devices:
  - id: pump-1
    template: pump
    port: 5020

  - id: dosing-skid
    port: 5021
    points:
      - name: chlorine_ppm
        table: input
        address: 0
        scale: 0.01
        unit: ppm
        value: 0.8
        signal: { type: random_walk, min: 0.5, max: 1.2, step: 0.02 }

Run it:

fieldpuppet run water-station.yaml

Point your own software at 127.0.0.1, port 5020 or 5021, unit id 1. The chlorine value drifts between 0.5 and 1.2 ppm like a real sensor would. Addresses are zero-based protocol addresses, so holding register 40001 is address 0.

Test the bad days, not only the good ones

Four fault types are available, each with an optional time limit:

  • delay: correct answers, but late
  • no_response: your client sees a timeout
  • exception: a Modbus exception such as device busy
  • disconnect: the connection closes on every request

This is how you find out whether your software reconnects, whether one dead device stalls the polling of the other 49, and whether stale values are marked as stale.

Limits

  • Modbus TCP only. No serial RTU or ASCII yet.
  • Devices do not model process behaviour. A pump does not stop because its run coil was cleared; a scenario or the assistant has to change the values.
  • Simulation only. It answers requests sent to it and never connects to real equipment.

Try it

The code is on GitHub under MIT / Apache 2.0: CybriantOps/fieldpuppet. It is a new project, so bug reports and feature requests are very welcome.

Which fault case has caused you the most trouble in the field?

title: What Does a Browser Agent Actually Cost?
description:
My n8n workflow said the run cost $0.0065.

The full bill was $0.0161, two and a half times that.

Not because anyone hid anything. A browser agent runs on three meters, and most tools only show you one of them: the model. The browser and, above all, the proxy traffic are billed separately, and on the wrong page they're most of the bill.

If you're:

  • pricing a product that runs browser agents for customers,
  • moving a scraper or a workflow to an agent and want to know the monthly cost,
  • or staring at a usage dashboard that doesn't match what your code reported,

This breakdown is for you.

I ran 15 sessions on Browser Use Cloud on November 18, 2026: three tasks, four models, proxy on and off. Then I read the full cost of every session from the API. All numbers below come from those runs.

TL;DR

  • Range: the same kind of work cost from $0.0024 to $0.164 per run, almost a 70× spread
  • Proxy: on a heavy page (21 MB) the residential proxy was up to 94% of the bill. Turning it off cut that run from $0.109 to $0.0098, with the same answer
  • Model: BU 4.0, the new default, cost 7.5 to 15.5 times more in model fees than gpt-6-luna on the same tasks, with the same answers
  • Browser time: a rounding error, $0.001 to $0.0013 per session
  • Gotcha: read the cost after the browser closes. Right after the run, every session showed a $0.08 browser line that later settled to about $0.001

The three meters

Every Browser Use session is billed on three lines. These are the prices on the pricing page and in the docs, read on November 18, 2026:

Meter Price What drives it
Model (LLM) Per million tokens, from $0.12 in / $0.60 out (gpt-6-luna) to $1.80 / $9.00 (BU 4.0) and up Number of steps and how much of the page the agent reads
Proxy traffic $5 per GB through the managed residential proxy, $0.20 per GB direct (proxy off) How heavy the pages are
Browser time $0.06 per hour, billed by the minute, 1-minute minimum How long the browser stays open

New accounts get a $1 credit, and credits are bought from $5. Since November 16, 2026, new projects default to BU 4.0. Older projects defaulted to gpt-6-luna, about 15 times cheaper per token.

The trap: "totalCostUsd" means two different things

When a run finishes, Browser Use returns a totalCostUsd. In my n8n tutorial I quoted that number. It's real, but the billing docs are explicit: a run's totalCostUsd is its LLM and web-search charge only.

The full bill lives on the session:

curl https://api.browser-use.com/api/v4/sessions/SESSION_ID/cost \
  -H "X-Browser-Use-API-Key: YOUR_API_KEY"

{
  "numRuns": 1,
  "llmCostUsd": "0.012437",
  "browserCostUsd": "0.001667",
  "proxyCostUsd": "0.013567",
  "proxyUsedMb": "2.778537",
  "totalCostUsd": "0.027671"
}

That's a real session from my n8n workflow. The run reported $0.0124. The session cost $0.0277. Across the five runs from that tutorial, the session total was 2.2 to 3.9 times what the run reported, and proxy traffic was 49% to 69% of it.

Same field name, two scopes. If you budget from the run's number, you'll undercount.

The test

Three tasks, chosen to stress different meters:

  • A, light page: the top 5 stories on Hacker News, a small HTML page.
  • B, heavy page: the top 5 on a Product Hunt daily leaderboard, a JavaScript-heavy page that showed me a Cloudflare check when I opened it in an ordinary automated browser.
  • C, multi-step: on the browser-use GitHub repo, find the latest release and the open issue count. Two pages, about 21 MB of traffic per session.

Each task ran on four models with the default US residential proxy: bu-4.0 (the new default), bu-4.0-mini, bu-ultrafast and gpt-6-luna. Then each task ran once more on gpt-6-luna with the proxy off (proxyCountryCode: null). Every run had a maxCostUsd cap of $0.30. None hit it.

For every session I read the cost endpoint twice: 20 seconds after the run finished, and again about four minutes later, after the browser had stopped.

Here's part of the test as it shows up in the Browser Use dashboard. The us US tag marks the sessions that went through the residential proxy:

The results

Final costs, read after the browser stopped:

Task Model Proxy Steps Model fee Proxy (MB) Browser Total
A light bu-ultrafast on 2 $0.0014 $0.0000 (0.02) $0.0010 $0.0024
A light gpt-6-luna off 3 $0.0024 $0.0000 (0.02) $0.0010 $0.0034
A light gpt-6-luna on 3 $0.0024 $0.0002 (0.03) $0.0013 $0.0039
A light bu-4.0-mini on 3 $0.0040 $0.0002 (0.03) $0.0013 $0.0055
A light bu-4.0 on 4 $0.0371 $0.0002 (0.03) $0.0013 $0.0386
B heavy bu-ultrafast on 13 $0.0054 $0.0013 (6.78) $0.0013 $0.0081 ⚠️
B heavy gpt-6-luna off 11 $0.0074 $0.0009 (4.84) $0.0013 $0.0096
B heavy bu-4.0-mini on 5 $0.0071 $0.0083 (1.69) $0.0013 $0.0167
B heavy gpt-6-luna on 11 $0.0080 $0.0087 (1.79) $0.0013 $0.0181
B heavy bu-4.0 on 5 $0.0602 $0.0090 (1.84) $0.0013 $0.0705
C multi-step bu-ultrafast on 5 $0.0020 $0.0041 (20.99) $0.0010 $0.0071
C multi-step gpt-6-luna off 8 $0.0043 $0.0042 (21.46) $0.0013 $0.0098
C multi-step gpt-6-luna on 7 $0.0047 $0.1033 (21.15) $0.0013 $0.1093
C multi-step bu-4.0-mini on 7 $0.0075 $0.1036 (21.22) $0.0010 $0.1121
C multi-step bu-4.0 on 6 $0.0569 $0.1064 (21.79) $0.0010 $0.1643

⚠️ = wrong answer (see below). The whole test cost $0.58.

Every other configuration returned the same data for its task: the same five Hacker News stories, the same five Product Hunt products with the same vote counts (Creatify Max 425, RankSpot 435, TheBold 421, Appxiom 287, EkLine 268), and the same release (1.0.6) and issue count (172) on GitHub.

What actually moves the bill

1. Proxy traffic, on heavy pages

The GitHub task moved about 21 MB per session. Through the residential proxy, at $5 per GB, that's $0.10, between 65% and 94% of the bill depending on the model.

With the proxy off, the same 21 MB was billed at the direct rate, $0.20 per GB: $0.004. The session dropped from $0.1093 to $0.0098, 11 times cheaper, and returned the same answer.

On the light Hacker News page the proxy barely registered (0.03 MB). On Product Hunt, turning it off cut the run from $0.0181 to $0.0096, and the agent still read the right numbers.

The dashboard shows the same pattern over a month. Across all my Browser Use sessions in the last 30 days, proxy data was 94% of the browser-side spend and browser time 6%:

The footer on that screen lists browser time at $0.02 per hour. My sessions were billed $0.001 per minute, which is the $0.06 per hour on the pricing page.

The proxy exists for a reason: sites that block data-center traffic, and pages that change by country. Browser Use turns a US residential proxy on by default, and for many sites you need it. But it's a choice per task, not a tax you have to pay on every run. Test the site without it first.

2. The model

On the same three tasks, BU 4.0 spent $0.037, $0.060 and $0.057 in model fees. gpt-6-luna spent $0.0024, $0.0080 and $0.0047. That's 7.5 to 15.5 times more, for the same answers on these tasks. Against bu-4.0-mini the gap was 7.6 to 9.3 times.

The usage dashboard adds it up. BU 4.0 only ran in this test's three sessions: $0.154 in model fees. BU Mini's three sessions, on the same tasks: $0.019.

That matters because BU 4.0 is now the default for new projects. If you never set model, you're on the expensive end. Browser Use describes BU 4.0 as its best balance and BU 4.0 Pro as the most capable, but simple extractions like these didn't need either. Pick the model per task, and set it explicitly.

3. The cheapest model isn't always right

bu-ultrafast was the cheapest on all three tasks, at $0.0024, $0.0081 and $0.0071. On Hacker News and GitHub its answers matched the others.

On Product Hunt it got the vote counts wrong: 143, 121, 75, 45 and 125, where every other model read 425, 435, 421, 287 and 268. It also took 13 steps, more than any other model on that page. A cheap run that returns wrong data isn't cheap. Validate the output before you trust a model on a new site.

A detail I can't fully explain: the bu-ultrafast sessions billed their traffic at the direct rate (about $0.20 per GB) even with the default proxy setting. Its GitHub run moved 20.99 MB and paid $0.0041 for it.

4. Browser time barely matters

Every session in this test billed 1 to 1.33 minutes of browser time: $0.0010 to $0.0013. At $0.06 per hour, browser time only shows up on your bill if you keep browsers open for a long time, for example with a long keepAlive waiting for follow-ups.

Read the cost after the browser stops

This one caught me off guard.

Twenty seconds after each run finished, the session cost endpoint showed browserCostUsd: "0.080000" on all 15 sessions. Four minutes later, after the browser had stopped, it had settled to $0.0010 to $0.0013. The proxy line moved too: on the GitHub run with gpt-6-luna it grew from 17.56 MB ($0.0857) to 21.15 MB ($0.1033) between the two reads.

The docs warn that browser and proxy costs keep changing until the browser stops, and that LLM charges can settle up to about 90 seconds after a run. In practice: if you log costs per run, read them a few minutes after the session ends, not in the same step that receives the result.

A simple cost calculator

Per run:

cost ≈ model fees + (proxy MB ÷ 1,024 × proxy rate) + (browser minutes × $0.001)

with a proxy rate of $5 per GB through the residential proxy, or $0.20 per GB with it off.

The same formula in Python, using my measured averages as defaults:

def run_cost(llm_usd, proxy_mb, proxy_on=True, browser_minutes=1.0):
    rate = 5.00 if proxy_on else 0.20          # USD per GB
    return llm_usd + proxy_mb / 1024 * rate + browser_minutes * 0.06 / 60

# GitHub task, gpt-6-luna: measured llm $0.0047, 21.15 MB
print(round(run_cost(0.0047, 21.15, proxy_on=True), 4))   # 0.109
print(round(run_cost(0.0047, 21.15, proxy_on=False), 4))  # 0.0098

Scale it to a month, using the measured totals:

Workload Per run Per month
Daily Product Hunt digest, gpt-6-luna, proxy on $0.0181 $0.54
Same, proxy off $0.0096 $0.29
1,000 GitHub-style checks a day, BU 4.0, proxy on $0.1643 about $4,900
Same, gpt-6-luna, proxy off $0.0098 about $295

Same work, same answers in my tests, about a 17× difference at scale. Two settings decide most of it: the model and the proxy.

How to keep the bill down

  • Set model explicitly. Don't inherit the default. Start with a cheaper model and move up only for tasks that need it.
  • Try the task with the proxy off (proxyCountryCode: null). If the site loads and the data is right, keep it off for that site.
  • Set maxCostUsd on every run. It's a hard cap per run, and a loop that goes wrong stops there.
  • Validate the output, especially with the cheapest models. A wrong answer costs more than the run.
  • Stop browsers you don't need. Closing your CDP connection doesn't stop a cloud browser. PATCH /api/v4/browsers/{id} with {"action": "stop"} does.
  • Budget from the session cost, read after the browser stops, not from the run's totalCostUsd.

FAQ

How much does a browser agent cost per task?

In my tests on Browser Use Cloud, between $0.0024 and $0.164 per run, all-in. Simple pages with a cheap model cost well under a cent. Heavy pages through a residential proxy with the BU 4.0 model cost more than ten cents.

What is the most expensive part of a browser agent?

It depends on the page. On light pages it's the model. On heavy pages it's the residential proxy: on a 21 MB GitHub task the proxy was up to 94% of the bill. Browser time was never more than $0.0013 per session.

How much does Browser Use charge for browsers and proxies?

$0.06 per browser hour, billed by the minute with a 1-minute minimum, plus $5 per GB through the managed residential proxy or $0.20 per GB with the proxy off. Model fees are per million tokens and depend on the model.

Why doesn't the run's totalCostUsd match my bill?

Because a run's totalCostUsd only covers model and search charges. Browser time and proxy traffic are billed to the session. Read GET /api/v4/sessions/{id}/cost for the full amount, after the browser has stopped.

Can I turn off the proxy to save money?

Yes. Set proxyCountryCode to null in the run's browserSettings. Traffic is then billed at $0.20 per GB instead of $5. It worked on all three sites I tested, but some sites block traffic that doesn't come from a residential IP, so test each site.

Is the cheapest model good enough?

Sometimes. bu-ultrafast was the cheapest on every task and right on two of three, but it read the wrong vote counts on Product Hunt. Check a model's answers on your own pages before you switch to it.

Key takeaways

  • A browser agent's cost is model + proxy + browser. Most tools only show you the model.
  • On heavy pages, the residential proxy is the bill. Turning it off, where the site allows it, cut a run 11×.
  • The default model is the expensive one. Choosing the model per task cut model fees 7.5 to 15.5×, with the same answers here.

From here

If you want to build something with these numbers, my n8n browser agent tutorial runs a daily workflow for about two cents a run, and the Browser Use review covers the stealth tests behind the proxy.

A browser agent isn't expensive or cheap.

Two settings decide which one yours is.

Looking for technical content for your company? I can help — LinkedIn · kevinmenesesgonzalez@gmail.com

title: We copied the new jar to every server before restarting any of them and the ones still waiting started throwing ZipException
description:
Our pricing service is a Java application on ten virtual machines. The deploy script used to work through them one at a time: drain the server from the load balancer, copy the new jar over the old one with scp, restart, wait for readiness, put it back. With two minutes of draining per server, a release took about twenty five minutes, and most of that was waiting.

In October we made it faster. The script now copied the jar to all ten servers in parallel first, and then did the drain and restart sequence. The copy took forty seconds. The first release with the new script went out on a Tuesday afternoon, and within a minute of the copy the servers that had not yet been restarted were logging java.util.zip.ZipException: invalid LOC header (bad signature) and NoClassDefFoundError for classes that were plainly in the jar. Quote requests that touched them failed with 500s.

The JVM keeps its jar open for as long as it runs. It reads the jar's directory once, when it opens the file, and fetches each class from the file when it first needs it, at the offset that directory gave. scp writes into the existing file, so the open file now had the new jar's bytes under the old jar's directory. Every class the running JVM had already loaded was fine. Every class it had not needed yet, the currency fallback path, an error handler, was read from the wrong place. Under the old script the window between copy and restart on any one server was seconds. We had stretched it to twenty minutes.

We stopped the deploy, restarted the waiting servers, and every error stopped with the restart.

The script still copies in parallel, but never onto the running jar. Each release is uploaded to its own file named with its version, and the unit file points at that path through a symlink that is switched on each server only as part of its own restart, so a running JVM never sees its file change. The previous jar stays on disk, which made rollback a symlink and a restart. A smoke test after each restart now calls the endpoints that exercise the rarely used code paths, not just the health check.

The jar a JVM runs from is not a file it has finished reading. We had changed it underneath nine processes that were still using it.

– Sergey Shinder

title: Does This Bama Bound Clip Already Have Letterboxing or a Black Border Inside the 9:16 Frame? (ffmpeg + Python, Tested)
description:
The file you download from bamabound.app is already 9:16. That does not, by itself, tell you whether the picture fills the 720×1280 frame or whether a near-black letterbox, a pillarbox, or a thin dark border is already sitting inside that frame. Those are different problems. Letterboxing a vertical clip onto a landscape television adds bars around a 9:16 picture. I am measuring bars that may already be in the picture.

I build the studio. I did not invent a customer file for this. I ran the same detector on four labeled synthetic controls and on the official imported field preview the homepage plays. That preview is labeled "Imported field preview" — an external reference of the sign clip, not a billed generation from this studio. I re-checked the pricing page today (23 November 2026, 15:24 Asia/Shanghai). A single 480p Field banner run is $7.98 (798 credits); 720p is $9.98 (998); 1080p is $16.98 (1923); 4k is $24.98 (3921); tax is added at checkout. Every command I quote exited 0.

The method, and why these thresholds

I decode each clip to 8-bit RGB with ffmpeg 7.1.5 and compute Rec.709 luma, 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B, in Python (numpy + Pillow; no OpenCV). A row counts as a bar row if at least 98% of its pixels have luma ≤ 16. The top band is the run of such rows starting at y = 0; the bottom, left and right bands are the same walk from the other three edges, with columns used for the sides.

I chose 16 because 8-bit limited-range video codes black as 16, so the range 0–16 is "near-black" whether the file is tagged full or limited. Today's official preview has color_range and color_space unspecified, so I did not want a threshold of 0 that would miss a legal-black bar. I chose 98% so a dark object in one corner does not become a "bar," while a true letterbox — a nearly solid black strip across the width — still counts. A 90% check on the official file did not invent a band either; I am reporting the 98% numbers as the method.

The official imported file (src/ref.mp4, SHA-256 prefix 9dcb91af) is 720×1280, H.264 High, yuv420p, progressive, 24 fps, 193 frames. The video stream lasts 8.041667 seconds; the container and the AAC LC 32 kHz stereo soundtrack last 8.096 seconds. I re-probed those figures today with ffprobe 7.1.5.

Four synthetic controls, with known bar heights

I built four 720×1280, 24 fps, 24-frame clips with Pillow and muxed them with ffmpeg. They are synthetic fixtures, not studio output. A yellow square walks across a green field (mean luma well above 16) so the picture is not a still.

On clean_fullframe.mp4, with no bars, the detector reported top, bottom, left and right all equal to 0 pixels on every frame. The maximum near-black fraction on any edge was 0.0. The first row's mean luma sat between 124.646200 and 133.260644. The clean control does not trip the method.

On letterbox_80.mp4 I painted 80-pixel black bars at the top and bottom, leaving a 720×1120 content box. The detector reported top = 80 and bottom = 80 on every frame, left = 0 and right = 0. The top and bottom edges had a near-black fraction of 1.0 and a mean luma of 0.0. The left and right edges showed a near-black fraction of 0.125, which is exactly the 160 black pixels of the two 80-pixel bars in a 1280-pixel column — below the 98% row rule, so they are not counted as pillarbox. That is the behaviour I want.

On pillarbox_40.mp4 I painted 40-pixel black bars on the left and right. The detector reported left = 40 and right = 40 on every frame, and top = bottom = 0. The side edges had a near-black fraction of 1.0. The top edge's near-black fraction was 0.111111, which is 80/720, the two 40-pixel side bars sitting in the top row, again under 98%.

On border_8.mp4 I painted an 8-pixel black border on all four sides. After the libx264 ultrafast / CRF 18 encode, the top row's mean luma was no longer a hard 0.0 — it ranged from 0.001604 to 0.066347 — but it was still far below 16, and the 98% rule still counted all eight rows. A thin dark border survives this method. I am not going to pretend the re-encode left the black at mathematical zero.

The official imported preview has no bars under this method

I ran the same walk on all 193 frames of the official imported preview. Top, bottom, left and right were 0 pixels on every frame. Under this method, the official 9:16 file does not contain a letterbox, a pillarbox, or a thin near-black border inside the frame.

That is not the same as saying the picture has no dark pixels. Every frame has a minimum luma of 0.0 somewhere. The left edge's near-black fraction ranged from 0.028125 to 0.075781 (median 0.051562); the maximum is on the last frame, index 192, where 0.075781 of the left-most column is ≤ 16. The right edge's maximum was 0.032031. The top and bottom edges had a near-black fraction of 0.0 on every frame. The first row is a bright field or sky: its mean luma ranged from 118.395467 to 132.562111 (median 122.113952). Frame 0 was 132.562111 at the top and 82.615865 at the bottom; frame 96 (the midpoint) was 120.688886 at the top and 153.363722 at the bottom. Those are picture edges, not bars.

0.075781 is a long way from 0.98. If I had dropped the coverage rule and treated "any dark pixel on the edge" as a border, I would have invented a bar that is not there. The 98% rule is doing the work.

Why I did not use ffmpeg blackdetect for this

blackdetect is a good tool for a different question: does a stretch of the timeline go black. It does not tell you whether the black is a 80-pixel letterbox at the top of a 9:16 frame, a fade to black in the middle of the field, or a single dark costume against a dark tree. I wanted a height and a width, in pixels, for each edge, on each frame. A row walk gives me that, and it gives me the near-black fraction on the first line when the run is 0, which is the number that shows how close the official file comes to being called a bar.

I also did not threshold on the mean luma of a whole row alone. A row that is half black and half green can have a mean under 16 if the green is dark enough, or a mean over 16 if it is not. The 98% coverage rule is about the shape of a bar: almost every pixel on that line is near-black. The official left edge, at its darkest, is 0.075781 of a column. The mean luma of that same left column on frame 192 is 85.182435. Both numbers say "some dark pixels, not a pillarbox."

A closer look at three official frames

Frame 0, the first picture, already shows the pattern. Top band 0, bottom 0, left 0, right 0. The top row's mean luma is 132.562111; the bottom row's is 82.615865. The left-edge near-black fraction is 0.039062; the right is 0.005469. There is at least one pixel with luma 0.0 in the frame (ymin is 0.0), and the mean luma of the whole frame is 92.432974. Dark pixels exist. They are not organized as a bar.

Frame 96 sits at 4.000 seconds (96/24). Top, bottom, left and right are still 0. The top row is 120.688886; the bottom row, unusually bright for a "footer," is 153.363722. The left-edge near-black fraction is 0.040625; the right is 0.0. Mean luma of the frame is 93.692654.

Frame 192, the last picture, is the left-edge maximum for the whole clip: 0.075781 of that column is ≤ 16, and the left-column mean luma is 85.182435. The top row is 122.565509; the bottom is 76.553142, the darkest bottom row of these three but still nowhere near 16, and the bottom-edge near-black fraction is still 0.0. Right-edge near-black fraction is 0.0. Bands are still 0, 0, 0, 0.

I am quoting those three frames so the 0-pixel consensus is not a single summary statistic hanging in the air. The last frame, which has the most dark pixels on the left edge, still fails the 98% rule by a wide margin.

If the detector ever reports a non-zero band

On today's official file it did not. On the fixtures it did, and the arithmetic is simple enough to keep next to the script. A top band of 80 pixels on a 1280-tall frame is a crop of crop=720:1120:0:80 if you want the content box only. A 40-pixel pillarbox is crop=640:1280:40:0. An 8-pixel border is crop=704:1264:8:8. Those commands are a post-download edit. They do not change what the studio generates, and I did not run them on the official file because there was nothing to crop under this method.

If you do crop, you are changing the pixel dimensions. A platform that wants a strict 9:16 file will need a scale back to 720×1280, or a pad, and either of those can put bars back if you are not careful. That is a different job, and I did not run it on a file that measured 0.

What this does not claim

It does not claim that a paid generation from this studio is free of letterboxing. I measured the official imported preview, not a customer file. Paid clips follow the same 9:16 preset in the FAQ ("about eight seconds, in a vertical 9:16 frame"), and I am not substituting a file I do not have.

It does not claim that a dark costume, a dark tree, or a later crop cannot put near-black pixels on an edge. It claims that, on this official file, those pixels do not form a 98% near-black run at luma ≤ 16.

It does not tell you how to display a 9:16 clip on a 16:9 television. That adds bars outside this frame. Today's question is whether bars are already inside it.

It also does not turn a 0-pixel result into a delivery specification. If you need to check a file you actually downloaded, run the same script on that file. The numbers above are only from commands that exited 0.

What I would actually use

For a post-download QA pass on a Bama Bound clip, I would run this walk before I posted or before I added my own overlay. If the method reports 0 on all four edges, the 720×1280 frame is filled under these thresholds, and any black bars you see later were added by a player or a crop. If it reports a non-zero band that matches a known height — 80, 40, 8, or something else — you can decide whether to crop or leave it.

The official imported preview, today, is the first case: 193 frames, 0-pixel bands, a left-edge near-black fraction that never rose above 0.075781, and a first row whose mean luma stayed above 118. On the synthetic side, the same script recovered 80, 40 and 8 pixels exactly, and reported 0 on the clean control.

None of this changes what the studio will generate. The preset is still a 9:16 clip of about eight seconds, you still cannot type a new duration, and a 480p run is still $7.98 before tax unless the pricing page has moved since this afternoon. The work happens after the download, on a copy of the file.

The scripts I used, make_letterbox_fixtures.py and letterbox_check.py, build the four controls, decode every frame, apply the luma-16 / 98% walk, and write the per-edge runs and near-black fractions. I only report figures from a run that finished with exit 0.

title: Our carrier moved its labels to URL safe base64 and Python decoded some of them without an error into something that was not a PDF
description:
Our label service asks a parcel carrier's API for a label and gets back JSON with the PDF inside it as a base64 string. A Python worker decodes it with base64.b64decode and sends the bytes to the depot print server.

In October the carrier moved its label endpoint to a new API version. One line in the changelog said labels were now encoded with the URL and filename safe alphabet. That alphabet uses a minus sign and an underscore where standard base64 uses a plus sign and a slash.

The next morning most label requests failed with binascii.Error: Incorrect padding, which was loud and quickly traced. What worried us more were the ones that did not fail. About a fifth of the labels decoded without any error, were sent to the printers and came out as blank pages or half a label.

b64decode does not validate by default. The documentation says that with validate left false, characters outside the base64 alphabet are discarded before the padding is checked. Every minus and every underscore in the carrier's string was silently dropped. If the number dropped left a length the decoder could accept, it decoded the rest, and from the first dropped character onwards every byte was shifted and wrong. The first bytes, including the %PDF header, often came through intact, so the file looked like a PDF to anything that only glanced at it.

The worker now maps the minus and underscore back to plus and slash, adds the padding the new version leaves off, and calls b64decode with validate=True, so any character outside the alphabet is an error and not a deletion. Every other decode of data from outside got the same flag. After decoding, the worker checks that the bytes start with %PDF- and that the document opens with a PDF library before it reaches a printer, and a label that fails goes back to the queue with the reason. The carrier's sandbox for the new version is now in our contract tests, and the changelog feed goes to the integration channel.

The decoder had a choice between failing and guessing. Its default was to guess, and a guessed label looks like a label until somebody tries to scan it.

– Sergey Shinder

title: I Built a Python CLI to Tackle Oracle Cloud's "Out of Host Capacity" Problem
description:
I Built a Python CLI to Tackle Oracle Cloud Ampere A1's "Out of Host Capacity" Problem

Getting an Oracle Cloud Ampere A1 instance can be frustrating.

You may have your OCI account configured, your network ready, your quotas checked, and your VM configuration prepared — but capacity availability can still get in the way.

I wanted a simpler way to handle this workflow.

So I started building a Python automation tool for Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). What began as a personal automation script gradually evolved into a cross-platform CLI with interactive configuration, installation scripts, monitoring capabilities, safety checks, and support for AI coding agents.

!OCI Always Free A1 VM Automation

Today, I'm sharing it with the developer community.

GitHub: https://github.com/mudassir-93/OCI-Always-Free-VM

The Problem I Wanted to Solve

Working with OCI A1 instances involves more than just clicking the Create Instance button.

Before attempting to launch an instance, there are several things worth checking:

Is A1 capacity currently available in my region and availability domain?
Are my OCPU and memory quotas sufficient?
Is my existing VCN and subnet configuration valid?
Is the selected image appropriate?
Am I staying within my intended compute and storage budget?
How can I monitor capacity without repeatedly doing the same manual checks?

I didn't want to build another cloud dashboard or a complicated infrastructure platform.

I wanted a lightweight tool that could automate repetitive checks and provide a manageable workflow from the terminal.

What I Built
OCI Always Free A1 VM Automation

A Python-based CLI designed to help OCI users inspect their environment, check A1 capacity, validate configuration, and optionally request one VM through an explicitly guarded workflow.

The project supports Windows and Linux.

What It Can Do

  1. A1 Capacity Monitoring

Check OCI A1 availability and monitor capacity using configurable retry and backoff behavior.

  1. Quota and Configuration Checks

Validate important settings such as:

Home region and availability domain.
Existing VCN and public subnet.
Compute and storage limits.
A1 instance configuration.
Image and SSH public-key settings.
Existing instances and resource usage.

  1. Interactive Terminal Interface

Instead of remembering every command, users can open the application and navigate through an interactive terminal menu.

  1. Guided Configuration

The configuration editor allows users to work through settings in organized groups, validate values, review changes, and save safely.

  1. Windows and Linux Installers

The project includes PowerShell and shell installers that create an isolated Python environment and initialize a safe starter configuration.

  1. AI Coding-Agent Support

The repository includes instructions and project memory for tools such as:

Claude Code
OpenAI Codex
Gemini CLI
GitHub Copilot
Other agentic development environments

The idea is to make it easier to understand, maintain, and extend the project with AI assistance.

Some Implementation Decisions I Found Interesting

This project was also a useful exercise in making an existing automation tool more reusable.

A few decisions shaped the architecture.

Keeping the Existing Engine

Rather than rewriting the original automation logic, I introduced a new oci-platform CLI layer around the existing Python engine.

This allowed me to preserve existing functionality while improving how users interact with it.

Handling Windows and Linux Differences

One portability issue came from using the POSIX-only fcntl module for process locking.

That approach wasn't suitable for Windows.

I replaced the unconditional platform-specific import with a cross-platform locking implementation.

It was a good reminder that cross-platform support needs to be considered at the application level, not just in the installer.

Making Configuration Safer

I didn't want setup to accidentally arm VM creation or overwrite an existing installation.

The installers refuse to overwrite an existing target directory, and the configuration workflow keeps VM creation disabled.

These are deliberate design decisions, not just documentation warnings.

Safety Is a Core Part of the Design

Because this application interacts with cloud infrastructure, I wanted the default behavior to be read-only.

VM creation requires three independent safeguards:

mode.creation_enabled=true in the local configuration.
The exact confirmation phrase LAUNCH_ONE_ALWAYS_FREE_INSTANCE.
The CLI flag --enable-create.

An actual launch also requires the operator's explicit authorization.

The application is designed around an existing network rather than automatically creating or modifying networking resources.

It does not upgrade OCI accounts, terminate existing instances, or promise guaranteed capacity or zero billing.

A capacity check is not a reservation, and Always Free eligibility must always be verified against your own OCI account and current Oracle terms.

Development and Testing

I wanted to validate more than just whether the Python code worked on my own machine.

The repository now has GitHub Actions workflows covering:

Python 3.11 and 3.12.
Windows and Ubuntu.
Application compilation and unit tests.
CLI startup and packaging.
Installer safety checks.
A fresh Linux installer integration test.

The Linux integration test checks installation in a clean temporary directory, verifies the installed commit, confirms the starter configuration keeps creation disabled, and checks that existing directories are preserved.

I also encountered an environment-related problem while trying to run a Linux installation test in an isolated Debian container: DNS resolution for raw.githubusercontent.com failed.

Instead of marking that attempt as successful, I added hosted Ubuntu integration coverage to the CI workflow.

The latest main commit passed all six CI jobs.

I also tested a fresh Windows installation and the interactive CLI on a second PC; that result was reported by the operator.

There is still work to do around live OCI validation, so I am not claiming that every real-world tenancy or capacity scenario has been verified.

Getting Started

You need:

Git
Python 3.11 or newer
Windows (PowerShell)

Download the installer:

powershell
Invoke-WebRequest "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mudassir-93/OCI-Always-Free-VM/main/install.ps1" -OutFile install.ps1

Review the installer:

powershell
Get-Content .\install.ps1

Run the installer:

powershell
.\install.ps1

Linux

Download the installer:

bash
curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mudassir-93/OCI-Always-Free-VM/main/install.sh

Review the installer:

bash
less install.sh

Run the installer:

bash
bash install.sh

Launch the Interactive CLI

Windows:

powershell
$cli = "$HOME\oci-automation-platform.venv\Scripts\oci-platform.exe"
& $cli

Linux:

bash
CLI="$HOME/oci-automation-platform/.venv/bin/oci-platform"
"$CLI"

Start with local configuration and diagnostics before connecting to your OCI environment.

The installer creates a starter configuration with VM creation disabled. Follow the detailed instructions in the repository before running live OCI checks.

What's Next?

The initial V1 code-delivery milestone is complete, but I see this as the beginning of community testing rather than the end of development.

Some areas I'd like to improve through feedback:

More real-world OCI A1 edge-case testing.
Better diagnostics and operator feedback.
Additional installation and configuration testing across environments.
Improvements to monitoring and retry behavior.
More useful workflows for AI-assisted maintenance.

I also want to keep the project lightweight rather than turn it into a large platform with unnecessary services.

I'd Love Your Feedback

I'm especially interested in hearing from developers who use Oracle Cloud, Python automation, or cross-platform CLI tools.

A few questions:

Would you find a tool like this useful for managing OCI A1 capacity?
What edge cases should I test before a wider release?
Is the interactive terminal experience a good approach, or would you prefer a different workflow?
What would you improve in the current architecture?

Feedback, bug reports, and contributions are welcome.

Explore the Project

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/mudassir-93/OCI-Always-Free-VM

Thanks for reading!

title: The Riemann Hypothesis proof was accepted after a check, not after the announcement
description:
On 20 November 2026, Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, posted that he believed he had, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. The checkable artifact was not a short paper. It was a Lean library of 17 million lines of code.

The announcement did not settle the claim. The check did.

On 21 November, the Lean and Mathlib communities issued a joint statement, endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative. They said they have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct. Scott Aaronson, who had written about the announcement the day before, updated his post the same day: the proof had been verified independently, and he judged that degree of checking to be higher than a typical human paper accepted to a math journal.

What they actually checked

The community did not ask whether the library was large, or whether it compiled on one machine, or whether the author was confident. It applied four criteria, which the statement says were all satisfied.

  1. The statement being proved is the standard one. In this case, Mathlib's RiemannHypothesis, already vetted by experts in Lean and number theory.
  2. The library compiles. Dozens of people reproduced the same raw proof export, with no build failures.
  3. The theorem proved in the library is exactly that standard statement. Two independent comparison tools confirmed the match, against a file that imports only Mathlib.
  4. Independent proof checkers accept the export. Those included Lean's official kernel and checkers that come with a formal argument that they cannot accept a false proof. The checks ran on an inert export, out of reach of code in the Lean sources.

That is a narrow, boring, and unusually clear bar: prove this exact statement, and show that independent checkers agree you did.

A second announcement, the same day

The same day, a separate, human-written draft also appeared. Ravi Vakil posted a hurried announcement of Alessandro Masullo's proposed proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, a manuscript Science reported had been under review for months, with a plan to spend another year polishing it before a public release. The AI announcement forced an earlier posting of an unfinished draft.

On 22 November, Vakil updated the post: several people had reported problems in the proposed proof, identified with the assistance of different AI models. He was clear that all issues need to be resolved to the community's satisfaction before the proof would be accepted, and that he made no claim as to the correctness of the strategy.

Two announcements in one day. Only one has, so far, been accepted after an independent check against a standard statement. That is the news that matters for anyone who has to decide when a large change is actually done.

What this is not

This is not an argument that a PHP migration is a 166-year-old problem in number theory. It is not an argument that a commercial checker is a proof kernel, or that 858 matching fixtures are a formal proof. They are not.

It is an argument about sequence. A 17-million-line library was an announcement. Acceptance waited until someone else could check a precise statement, with tools that were not the author's, and say what had been checked.

A compiled Java 21 service, a green staging deploy, or a walkthrough that "looked right" is also an announcement. It tells you the new system exists and that some paths were tried. It does not tell you that the new system behaves like the old one on the journeys that matter: the same HTTP responses, the same database writes, the same outgoing calls.

If you are moving a PHP monolith, use the same sequence

AI will write more of the migration, not less. That makes the check more important, not less, because a large generated artifact is easy to announce and hard to read line by line. Science reported that mathematicians expect it could take years to distil Alpöge's library into something humans can study. You do not have years at cutover. You need a check you can run, and you need to know what that check misses.

That is what we built MigrateForge for. We convert plain PHP and CodeIgniter 3 applications to Java 21 / Spring Boot (Laravel is next) and replay recorded user journeys against both systems: HTTP responses, DB writes and outgoing API calls. Cutover stays blocked until they match. The PHP app itself must first replay its own recording at 99.5% or better. Your code stays on your machines.

We also test the checker. Benchmarks so far (not client projects): four verified waves on WA Blast Pro and InvoicePlane, 858 fixtures, 100% parity. On one wave the first pass reached 82%, and needed 9.7 hand fixes per 1,000 lines. Lost writes and missing escaping are always caught; NULLs and .00 amount differences can be missed. A self-test of injected faults was caught at 57.14% and 35.89% in two runs. That is why we publish the miss rate next to the parity number, and why we do not treat the checker as complete coverage on its own.

If you run plain PHP or CodeIgniter 3, start with the free migration report. It covers size, risks, an indicative wave plan and a price range. No source code is needed.

https://migrateforge.com

CTOs: before you cut over a rewrite, or an AI-generated migration, what independent check do you require — and what has that check been shown to miss?

MigrateForge

title: What a Browser Timer Should Do When the Tab Is Frozen, Cached, or Discarded
description:
Most timer bugs people talk about are about drift or throttling. This post is about a different failure: the page stops running entirely, then comes back later, or never comes back at all. Browsers do this on purpose to save memory, battery, and CPU, and there are a few events you can use to survive it.

The states that matter

Chrome's Page Lifecycle documentation describes a page moving through these states: active, passive, hidden, frozen, terminated, and discarded. Three of them matter for anything that tracks time:

  • Hidden. The user switched tabs, minimized the window, or moved to another app on mobile. MDN's visibilitychange reference says the move to hidden "is the last event that's reliably observable by the page," and recommends treating it as the likely end of the session.
  • Frozen. Chrome's guide says that in this state "the browser suspends execution of freezable tasks," which means "JavaScript timers and fetch callbacks don't run." The same thing happens to a page held in the back/forward cache. The web.dev article on bfcache explains that browsers "pause any pending timers or unresolved promises" for cached pages.
  • Discarded. The browser unloads the page to free memory. According to the Chrome guide, "No tasks, event callbacks, or JavaScript of any kind can run in this state," and the discard itself fires no event. The tab title and favicon often stay visible, so to the user it looks like your page is still open.

The freeze and discard behavior comes from the WICG Page Lifecycle draft, a Draft Community Group Report dated 9 June 2022. It is not a W3C standard, and the freeze, resume, and document.wasDiscarded APIs are Chromium features. Treat them as extras. Everything below still works without them.

What breaks

Picture a countdown whose state lives only in memory: a setTimeout for the end, plus a variable holding the time remaining.

  1. Frozen or cached: the pending timeout is paused. When the page resumes, the callback can fire late, and an in-memory "remaining" value is stale by however long the page sat frozen.
  2. Discarded: memory is gone. When the user comes back to the tab, the browser reloads the page from scratch. Without saved state, the countdown starts over or is simply lost.
  3. Closed on mobile: Chrome's guide notes that when users close the tab or the browser app on mobile, beforeunload, pagehide, and unload may not fire. Saving state in those handlers alone loses data.

A four-step pattern

1. Save at hidden, not at unload

Write the minimum you need to rebuild the timer, which is the end time as a wall-clock timestamp plus a status, every time the page becomes hidden. Chrome's guide recommends persisting view state to sessionStorage "that you'd want restored if the page were discarded and reloaded later."

const KEY = 'countdown-state';

function saveState(state) {
  // state: { endsAt: number (epoch ms), status: 'running' | 'paused' | 'done' }
  sessionStorage.setItem(KEY, JSON.stringify(state));
}

function persistIfHidden() {
  const hidden = document.visibilityState === 'hidden';
  if (hidden && currentState) saveState(currentState);
}

document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', persistIfHidden);

Save on every Start, Pause, and Reset as well, so a crash between visibility changes doesn't lose the latest action.

2. Rebuild on load, and note whether it was a discard 

function restoreState() {
  const raw = sessionStorage.getItem(KEY);
  if (!raw) return null;
  const state = JSON.parse(raw);
  if (state.status === 'running' && Date.now() >= state.endsAt) {
    state.status = 'done'; // it finished while the page wasn't running
  }
  return state;
}

let currentState = restoreState();

if ('wasDiscarded' in document && document.wasDiscarded) {
  // Chromium only: the tab was discarded while hidden and has just reloaded.
  // Useful for telling the user, not required for correctness.
}

MDN notes that sessionStorage is partitioned by origin and by tab and "survives over page reloads and restores," so two tabs running the same page keep separate countdowns.

3. Recompute on bfcache restore

A page restored from the back/forward cache does not run its load code again. web.dev says pageshow fires on the initial load "and any time the page is restored from bfcache," with event.persisted set to true for the restore case.

window.addEventListener('pageshow', (event) => {
  if (event.persisted && currentState) {
    rescheduleFrom(currentState); // recompute remaining from endsAt, reset the timeout
  }
});

rescheduleFrom stands in for your own code. It should clear any old timeout, compute endsAt - Date.now(), and either schedule a fresh timeout or go straight to the finished state.

4. Optionally handle freeze and resume

In Chromium you can listen for freeze and resume on document. Chrome's guide recommends stopping timers and closing connections on freeze. Since step 1 already saved state at hidden, which comes before frozen, the main job here is clearing stale timeouts on freeze and calling rescheduleFrom again on resume.

What this pattern can't do

None of these events let code run while a page is frozen or discarded. If a countdown ends during that time, the page can't play a sound or update the screen at that moment. All it can do is notice afterward, once the page runs again, that the end time has passed, and show that clearly. For an alert that must go off on schedule while the tab sleeps, you need something outside the page's own event loop, and that's a separate topic.

So a timer page can promise to remember when it ends and to report correctly when you come back. It can't promise to wake itself up.

Sources

  • Chrome for Developers, Page Lifecycle API: https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/page-lifecycle-api
  • web.dev, "Back/forward cache" article
  • MDN Web Docs, visibilitychange event, pageshow event, pagehide event, and Window: sessionStorage references
  • WICG, Page Lifecycle, Draft Community Group Report, 9 June 2022

    ramp_to(IDLE, at=next_beat_boundary)
    armed = false
    on satellite_session_completed_or_canceled_or_exited_or_message_sent_or_received():
        # satellite messaging UI gone �‰  motor envelope restored
        await user_resume(); await next_named_beat(); arm()

on homekit_or_home_doorbell_live_view_or_camera_feed_or_intercom_opened():
    ramp_to(IDLE, at=next_beat_boundary)
    armed = false
    on live_view_opened_or_dismissed_or_talked_through_or_door_notification_ignored():
        # Home live-view or Intercom UI cleared �‰  motor authority
        await user_resume(); await next_named_beat(); arm()

on continuity_camera_or_iphone_as_webcam_or_desk_view_opened():
    ramp_to(IDLE, at=next_beat_boundary)
    armed = false
    on continuity_camera_or_desk_view_started_or_ended_or_sheet_dismissed():
        # camera-handoff UI gone �‰  previous intensity restored
        await user_resume(); await next_named_beat(); arm()

The satellite-SOS rule is easy to mix up with an Emergency SOS countdown, Crash Detection, or a Medical ID emergency call, a cellular "No Service" or "SOS only" coverage sheet, a Wireless Emergency Alert, a regular iMessage or RCS thread, and Find My Play Sound or Lost Mode. Emergency SOS and Medical ID are emergency-call flows on the usual radios. "SOS only" on a coverage sheet is a cellular no-service state, not a satellite messaging session. A WEA is a carrier or government broadcast you receive. A message thread is regular messaging. Find My is a locate-or-lock flow. Emergency SOS via satellite and Messages via satellite are satellite connection or satellite-text surfaces. Completing or canceling that session clears that surface; it must not restore motor authority.

The Home doorbell / camera-live-view rule sits next to �ü” but is not �ü” a Sound Recognition banner that classified a doorbell or siren on-device, an ordinary incoming voice or video call, an iMessage or RCS thread, a Notification Center pull-down, a Live Activity or Dynamic Island, or opening a generic push notification. Sound Recognition is an on-device microphone classification alert. A phone call is the ordinary incoming-call interrupt. A message thread is regular messaging. Notification Center is a system shade. A Live Activity is a compact live status. A generic push is just a notification open. A Home doorbell live view or Home Intercom sheet is a Home / HomeKit live camera or two-way-talk surface. Dismissing the live view or ending the Intercom only clears that Home UI; it must not restore motor authority.

The Continuity Camera / Desk View rule is a system camera-handoff that claims this phone as a webcam, not Handoff or Continuity moving a task to another device, not local screen recording or casting this screen, not an external display, Sidecar, or Stage Manager desktop, not an in-app Photos or Camera picker, not a Visual Intelligence, Writing Tools, or Camera Control overlay, and not CarPlay or Android Auto. Handoff moves a task. Screen recording or casting captures or mirrors this screen. Sidecar and Stage Manager are desktop-display modes. A picker is an in-app sheet. Visual Intelligence and Camera Control are on-device camera overlays. CarPlay is vehicle projection. Ending Continuity Camera or Desk View only clears that camera-handoff UI; it must not restore motor authority.

Buyers can test all three without code: start Emergency SOS via satellite or Messages via satellite mid-session and see whether completing, canceling, or exiting the satellite session restarts intensity; open a Home doorbell live view or Intercom then dismiss it or talk through it; and start Continuity Camera or Desk View then end the webcam handoff. The acceptance question is the same in each case: clearing the satellite-messaging, Home live-view, or Continuity Camera UI must not put motor authority back on. These map to questions like "how do AI stories control physical devices" and "Lovense alternative with AI stories."

This is the model CRAVE AI uses for story-controlled play on official devices: AI story-controlled vibrator. Principle write-up: narrative-to-device sync. Devices: AI sex toys.

title: We Moved Our Estimating Files Into SharePoint and Four Thousand Workbooks Became Too Long for Excel to Open
description:
Last March we finished moving our file shares into SharePoint. The largest was our estimators' share, about three hundred and eighty thousand files, organised the way estimators think: customer, then site, then job, then revision, with descriptive names at every level. It used to be mapped on every estimator's laptop as drive S.

The migration tool checked every file against SharePoint's limits, which allow a full path of up to four hundred characters, and reported none over it. Everything arrived. Estimators synced the library to their laptops and carried on working in their usual folders.

On the first Monday the service desk received eleven calls from estimators who could not open take off workbooks they had used the week before. Excel said the file name was not valid. Opening the same files in a browser worked.

Excel will not open a file whose full path is longer than two hundred and eighteen characters, a limit it has had for many years. On drive S, a typical path began with S, a colon and the word Estimating. After the move, the synced copy of the same file lived under C, Users, the estimator's full name, our company's full registered name, and the site and library names joined by a dash. That added between sixty and ninety characters in front of every file before the first customer folder. About four thousand one hundred workbooks that had been comfortably under the limit were now over it. The deepest belonged to our largest customers, whose jobs had the most revisions, so the files that failed were the ones that mattered most.

We could not shorten the company name or the estimators' names. We could shorten everything after them. The site and library were renamed to Est and Jobs. Jobs closed more than two years ago moved to an archive library that nobody syncs. New jobs use the job number for the folder name, with the description inside the file rather than in the path. A weekly report now lists any file whose synced path would be over two hundred characters on the longest user name we have, and sends it to the estimator who owns the job, who has always been better at choosing a shorter name than we are.

A migration keeps the files and changes their address. Every limit that counts characters in the address has to be checked against the place people will open the file from, not the place it is stored.

– Serguey Shinder

title: Your Database Uses Transactions and Nobody on the Team Knows Which Isolation Level
description:
A report shows a strange total. The sum at the top does not match the rows underneath, but only now and then, and only while orders are being placed. Someone says it might be the isolation level. Nobody in the room is sure what that is, or what yours is set to.

It is worth an afternoon to find out.

When two transactions run at the same time, the database has to decide how much each one can see of the other's unfinished or newly finished work. The SQL standard, from 1992, describes four levels, from loosest to strictest: read uncommitted, read committed, repeatable read and serializable.

The levels are defined by which odd effects they allow. A dirty read is seeing another transaction's change before it has been committed. A non-repeatable read is reading the same row twice in one transaction and getting different values, because someone committed in between. A phantom is running the same query twice and finding new rows the second time.

Your report is probably a case of the second or third. Under read committed, each statement sees the data as it was when that statement started. So a total calculated in one query and rows fetched in another can come from slightly different moments.

The defaults differ between databases, which surprises many people. PostgreSQL, SQL Server and Oracle use read committed by default. MySQL with its usual InnoDB engine uses repeatable read. PostgreSQL also accepts read uncommitted but treats it as read committed. Code that behaves one way on one database can behave differently on another.

You can check yours. In PostgreSQL, run SHOW transaction_isolation. In MySQL 8, run SELECT @@transaction_isolation.

Stricter is not automatically better. Under serializable, the database may refuse to commit a transaction that would have clashed with another, and your code has to be ready to retry it. That is the price of the stronger guarantee.

If you want to go further, read A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels, a 1995 paper by Berenson and colleagues, which showed the standard's definitions were looser than they looked. Then try it yourself. Open two database sessions side by side, start a transaction in each, and watch what one can see of the other. Ten minutes of that teaches more than any diagram.

– Asael Shinder

title: Architecture reality check: monolith vs microservices
description:
90 percent of companies building microservices do not need microservices.

They adopted them because Google and Netflix did.

Here's the quiet reality nobody admits on tech blogs.

The setup nobody questions

Your product has 2,000 daily active users. Yet you are running:

  • 35 microservices
  • A tangled Kubernetes cluster
  • Distributed tracing tools just to find a single bug
  • A $12,000 monthly cloud bill

Instead of an in-memory function call taking 2 milliseconds, every user action triggers 15 network hops across internal services.

Network failures happen. Latency multiplies. Development slows to a crawl.

The cost comparison

Monolith Microservices
Latency ~5ms ~500ms
Network hops 1 47
Cloud bill ~$100/mo ~$15,000/mo

These numbers won't match every company, but the shape of the trade-off is consistent: every hop you add between a request and a response is a hop that can fail, get slow, or need its own monitoring.

It's not just a hot take — look at who's done this

Amazon's Prime Video team consolidated one of their distributed microservices tools (their audio/video quality-monitoring service) back into a monolith, cutting that specific service's infrastructure costs by 90 percent. They didn't abandon microservices company-wide — they still run them elsewhere — but it proved the default architecture isn't automatically the right one.

Shopify runs one of the biggest e-commerce platforms in the world on a modular monolith, not a microservices mesh.

Stack Overflow answered millions of developer queries for years on a small handful of on-prem servers.

None of these are small, unserious companies. They chose simplicity because the data told them to, not because it's trendy.

What microservices actually solve

Microservices solve an organizational scaling problem: when you have thousands of engineers across dozens of teams who can't coordinate deploys and releases without stepping on each other, splitting services lets teams move independently.

They do not solve bad software architecture. A messy monolith split into 35 messy services is still a mess — just with network calls between the messy parts now.

What to do instead

Start with a clean, modular monolith. Keep clear boundaries inside it (separate modules, separate concerns, no tangled imports across domains) so a future split is possible.

Only split into services when team boundaries force you to — when two teams genuinely can't ship independently while sharing one codebase — not because of resume-driven development.

The question worth asking

Are the microservices in your company actually helping, or just inflating your AWS bill?

If you're not sure, that's usually the answer.

title: A New Species Is One Line In The Register
description:
A new species does not need a new cage welded by hand. It needs one line in the register - and writing that line turned up blank pages nobody had noticed.

👋 Hi, I'm Anton - a software engineer. These days I work on a platform: contracts, generated code, data paths and the tooling around them. Running notes live on my GitHub: github.com/brilliant-almazov.

The dictionary section of the manifest and the closed-set package behind it are built into the shared library and its generator; five services use the package. The two findings below were found and fixed in the same pass.

This is part 7 of the series on what a shared platform does for every service, told as a zoo. Maybe you already do it better, maybe you'd do it another way - this is how it is going, and where it stops.

In real life

A new species arrives at the zoo: a lizard nobody has kept before. Nora reaches for the welding torch - "A new lizard! Weld a cage?" Pip stops her: "Put the torch down, Nora."

Because a new species in a well-run zoo is not a new cage. It is one line in the register: name, what it eats, how warm it likes it. The cage follows from the line.

Writing the line is where the story turns funny. Pickle opens the register to add the lizard and finds two columns that were never filled in for anybody - "since when?" asks Nora, and nobody knows. And Miso reports that the checker at the gate, the one who checks that the register matches the cages, had been saying no to everyone. Pip finishes the joke: "Even to the right answers."

A closed set of codes is a species

Our services have many small closed sets: statuses, kinds, types of things, each code with a title, sometimes with a parent code or a group. Every one of them needs the same handful of operations: parse a code, check it is valid, get its title, ask whether one code descends from another, ask whether a code belongs to a group.

Before, a new set meant a new piece of Go in the service - a cage welded by hand. Now the shared library has one package for closed sets, and the service manifest has a dictionary section. A new kind is a manifest entry; the printed package of the service holds only the table of codes; parsing, checks and walking the tree live in the library.

As a form - the names are illustrative:

dictionary:
  - name: <kind>
    values:
      - { code: <a>, title: <A> }
      - { code: <b>, title: <B>, parent: <a> }

The library's changelog puts it as plainly as the comic: a new kind of dictionary is a line of the manifest, without a line of Go.

Five gates on five lookups

A lookup that runs on every request is a place where small costs pile up. The closed-set package has allocation ceilings on its five lookups - parse, valid, title, descends, in group - the same kind of gate that the library uses elsewhere: a test fails if a lookup starts allocating more than its ceiling.

Lookup Question it answers Gate
parse is this string a code of the set? allocation ceiling
valid is this code allowed? allocation ceiling
title what do people call it? allocation ceiling
descends is this code under that one? allocation ceiling
in group does this code belong to the group? allocation ceiling

On the reading side, a handler uses the set through the same five questions. In the shape of the code, with names shortened:

// in a handler - a form
code, ok := kinds.Parse(raw)            // is this a code of the set?
if !ok || !kinds.Valid(code) {
    return refuse(reasonUnknownKind)    // a refusal with a reason, not a panic
}
if kinds.Descends(code, parent) && kinds.InGroup(code, group) {
    title := kinds.Title(code)          // what people call it
    // ...
}

None of those five functions is written in the service. The service wrote the table; the questions came with the library.

The blank pages

Writing the dictionary section through the generator was the first time anyone read the old manifest fields closely enough to print from them. Two findings came out of it, both in the library's changelog.

The manifest had fields for a migration's enum type and its values. They were declared - you could write them, and nothing complained - but the generator never printed them. A field that is accepted and ignored is worse than a missing field: it tells the author the job is done.

And the drift check in a service made from the template - the check that compares the manifest with what is printed - always refused. Every run, every service. A check that always says no gets ignored, and an ignored check is no check at all.

What went wrong

Both findings are the same failure in two costumes: something declared looked done. Fields accepted by the manifest looked like they worked, because nothing rejected them. A drift check existed, so drift looked guarded - except it rejected everything, so everyone learned to ignore it. Neither was found by looking for it. Both were found because a new, small feature had to walk through the same code honestly.

The lesson I keep from it: every declaration needs a reader that proves it is used. A field that is declared must be printed, or rejected. A check must be seen to pass on a correct input before its "no" means anything.

What I do not claim

  • Not that every closed set in every service has moved to the manifest. Five services use the package.
  • Not how long the two blank fields were blank. The changelog records the find, not the start.
  • Not measured numbers for the gates here. They are ceilings that fail a test when crossed.
  • Not the exact manifest format. The form above shows the shape.

What of this is method

  • A new kind is data, not code. One line in the manifest; the library does the rest.
  • Declared is not done. A field is printed or rejected; a check is seen to pass before its "no" counts.
  • Small features walk old code honestly. That is where blank pages are found.

Zoo keeping, built in - Part 7. Next: No Night Watchman For Partitions.

If your closed sets live in code, how many cages did you weld last year? If your manifests accept fields, how do you know each one is read? If you have a check that always fails, who still looks at it? What blank page is waiting in your register?

title: Your Mentee Has Joined a Team Whose Code Has No Tests and Wants to Fix It All
description:
Your mentee is three weeks into a new job and full of energy. The main service has almost no tests. Deployments are done carefully, on a Thursday, with someone watching the logs. They have already drafted a plan to add tests everywhere, introduce a new framework and make test coverage a required check. They want your opinion before they present it to the team on Monday.

Admire the energy first, out loud. Then help them slow down, because a plan like this, from someone three weeks in, usually lands as criticism of everyone who built the system.

Start with curiosity. Ask what they know about why there are no tests. Often the reasons are ordinary. The code was written in a hurry by two people for a deadline, or it is hard to test because everything talks to the database directly. Those reasons matter, because they tell you where to begin.

Then give them a better first move. In his 2004 book Working Effectively with Legacy Code, Michael Feathers defines legacy code simply as code without tests, and describes a technique called characterization tests. Instead of writing tests for what the code should do, you write tests that record what it actually does today, odd behaviour included. They do not judge the code. They protect it, so the next change cannot quietly alter something people rely on.

Suggest they pick the next piece of code they genuinely need to change for a ticket, and add a few characterization tests around that one spot before touching it. Then make the change. Then mention in the pull request what the tests caught or confirmed. One real example does more than any proposal.

Help them notice the team's feelings too. The people who kept this system running without tests have skills your mentee does not have yet, such as knowing which parts are dangerous. Encourage them to ask those people which area worries them most, and start there.

And suggest they save the big plan. If, after a couple of months, the small tests keep paying off, the team may well ask for a wider approach. At that point your mentee will be the obvious person to lead it, because they will have shown it working instead of describing it.

– Asael Shinder

title: اختبار كود API المولّد بالذكاء الاصطناعي: دقّقه كما يتحقق Lean من البراهين
description:
اختبر واجهات API المكتوبة بالذكاء الاصطناعي كما يتحقق Lean من البراهين

يكون اختبار الشيفرة البرمجية لواجهات API المولّدة بالذكاء الاصطناعي أفضل ما يكون عندما تحاكي الطريقة التي يتحقق بها علماء الرياضيات اليوم من البراهين المكتوبة بالذكاء الاصطناعي: ثبّت العبارة قبل أن يبدأ الذكاء الاصطناعي، ودعه يكتب ما يشاء، ولا تقبل النتيجة إلا إذا اجتازها مدقّق صغير مستقل. وبالنسبة إلى API، فإن العبارة هي مواصفة OpenAPI الخاصة بك، والمدقّق هو مجموعة من اختبارات العقد التي يستطيع وكيل البرمجة تشغيلها لكنه لا يستطيع تعديلها.

جرّب Apidog اليوم

يرشدك هذا الدليل إلى الأجزاء التي تُبقيها موثوقة، والخطوات التي تحوّل المواصفة إلى بوابة دمج، وأوامر Apidog CLI التي يشغّلها وكيلك للتحقق من عمله بنفسه.

ماذا يعني اختبار الشيفرة البرمجية لواجهات API المولّدة بالذكاء الاصطناعي؟

اختبار الشيفرة البرمجية لواجهات API المولّدة بالذكاء الاصطناعي يعني التحقق من نقطة نهاية كتبها وكيل برمجة مقابل عقد لم يكتبه الوكيل. فأنت تقارن الاستجابات الفعلية من نسخة قيد التشغيل برموز الحالة والحقول والأنواع في مواصفة API لديك. ويجوز للوكيل إصلاح شيفرته حتى تنجح الفحوص، لكنه لا يغيّر المواصفة أو الفحوص أبدًا.

هذه القاعدة الأخيرة هي الفكرة كلها. فالاختبارات التي يكتبها الوكيل لشيفرته الخاصة تؤكد افتراضاته هو: إذا أخطأ في قراءة المتطلب، فستخطئ اختباراته في قراءته أيضًا، وسيصبح كل شيء أخضر.

لماذا يُعد برهان Lean النموذج المناسب؟

في 20 نوفمبر 2026، قال ليفنت ألبوغي، أحد أعضاء الطاقم التقني في Anthropic، إنه أثبت فرضية ريمان بالعمل مع Claude. وكما ذكر موقع phys.org، فقد أطلق الحجة على شكل شيفرة Lean فقط، وقال إن الطريقة تغطي أيضًا فرضية ريمان المعممة الأوسع، وهي النسخة المتعلقة بدوال L لديريكليه.

لا يستطيع أحد قراءة النتيجة سطرًا بسطر. قال كيفن بازارد من إمبريال كوليدج لندن لـ Al Jazeera إنها «17 مليون سطر من شيفرة Lean». ويتوقع علماء الرياضيات أن يحتاج فهمها إلى أسابيع من العمل، كما قدّم باحث ما بعد الدكتوراه في جامعة ستانفورد برهانًا منافسًا بشكل مستقل. ومع ذلك حظي الادعاء باهتمام جاد من اليوم الأول لسبب واحد: يتحقق Lean من كل خطوة بما يسميه القائمون عليه «نواة موثوقة دنيا»، ويُدرج الجدول الزمني الخاص بـ Lean FRO النتيجة بوصفها برهانًا متحققًا منه بـ Lean.

أنت تواجه نسخة أصغر من هذا كل أسبوع. يكتب وكيلك 400 سطر من شيفرة المعالجات والمُسلسِلات في دقائق، ولا يمكنك مراجعة كل ذلك بعناية. لذا لا تثق بالمؤلف. ثق بالمدقّق.

اربط مدقّق البرهان بواجهة API الخاصة بك

يقسّم Lean العمل إلى جزء غير موثوق يمكن أن يكون بذكاء وتعقيد وأخطاء كما يشاء، وجزء صغير موثوق يقول نعم أو لا. وتحتاج سير عمل API لديك إلى التقسيم نفسه.

Lean سير عمل API لديك من يملكه
بيان المبرهنة مواصفة OpenAPI لنقطة النهاية أنت، وتُجمّد قبل أن يبدأ الوكيل
البرهان (التكتيكات، والمصطلحات) المعالج والنماذج والترحيلات وكيل البرمجة
النواة اختبارات العقد المولّدة من المواصفة أداة مشتركة، للقراءة فقط بالنسبة إلى الوكيل
#print axioms قائمة الفحوص المتخطّاة أو المعطّلة تُطبع في كل تشغيل
مقبول / مرفوض تقرير النجاح/الفشل في CI بوابة الدمج

لا يهم الخطأ إلا إذا تجاوز الجزء الموثوق. فاسم حقل خاطئ في المعالج يُرفض. أما اسم حقل خاطئ في المواصفة فلا يُرفض، ولهذا يكتب شخص ما المواصفة ويجمّدها.

كيف تتحقق من نقطة نهاية كتبها الذكاء الاصطناعي قبل الدمج؟

  1. جمّد المواصفة أولًا. اكتب تعريف OpenAPI أو حدّثه لنقطة النهاية، بما في ذلك كل رمز استجابة يهمك (200، 400، 404، 409). ثم ادمجه قبل أن توجد أي شيفرة. هذه هي عبارة مبرهنتك.
  2. سلّم الوكيل المواصفة، لا وصفًا لها. «نفّذ POST /objects كما هو محدد في المواصفة» يترك مجالًا أقل للتخمين من «أضف نقطة نهاية تنشئ كائنات».
  3. ولّد الفحوص من المواصفة. يجب أن تأتي اختبارات العقد من مستند OpenAPI، لا من الشيفرة التي كتبها الوكيل للتو. فتحقّق المخطط من استجابة 200 يفشل بمجرد أن تُسقط الشيفرة حقلًا مطلوبًا أو تُرجع سلسلة نصية حيث تنص المواصفة على عدد صحيح.
  4. شغّلها مقابل نسخة حقيقية. شغّل الخدمة، ووجّه الاختبارات إليها، وسجّل التقرير. فالنسخة الوهمية التي تشارك الوكيل افتراضاته لا تثبت شيئًا.
  5. اعتبر أي فشل رفضًا. مهمة الوكيل أن يغيّر شيفرته حتى تنجح الفحوص. وليس من حقه تخفيف تحقّق أو تعديل المواصفة لتطابق ما بناه.
  6. احكم الدمج في CI. يُدرج التشغيل نفسه في خط أنابيبك مع تقرير JUnit، بحيث يمنع فحص أحمر طلب السحب سواء قرأ أحد الفرق أم لا.

الخطوة الخامسة هي حيث تزلّ الفرق. فالطريق الأسرع للوكيل إلى اللون الأخضر غالبًا هو تغيير الاختبار: النسخة الخاصة بـ API من برهان يتخطى الخطوة الصعبة.

ما الذي تكشفه اختبارات العقد ولا تكشفه اختبارات الوكيل نفسها؟

الوكيل الذي يكتب الشيفرة واختباراتها الوحدوية يختبر ما بناه، لا ما طلبته منه. وتكشف اختبارات العقد المدفوعة بالمواصفة ما يلي:

  • حقول مطلوبة مفقودة. تنص المواصفة على أن id وname وdata مطلوبة؛ لكن المعالج يُرجع id وname فقط.
  • انحراف الأنواع. يعود السعر كـ "19.99" (سلسلة نصية) بدلًا من 19.99.
  • رموز حالة خاطئة. يُرجع إنشاء مورد رمز 500 عند التكرار بدلًا من 409 الذي تعد به المواصفة.
  • أشكال أخطاء غير موثّقة. تأتي أخطاء التحقق على شكل صفحة HTML الافتراضية لإطار العمل بدلًا من كائن خطأ JSON الخاص بك.
  • حقول إضافية صامتة. يتسرّب حقل داخلي مثل password_hash أو tenant_id إلى الاستجابة لأن الوكيل سلسل صف قاعدة البيانات بأكمله.

لا يحتاج أي من هذه إلى اختبار ذكي، بل إلى اختبار تأتي توقعاته من مكان آخر غير الشيفرة. لإلقاء مدخلات حالات حدّية مولّدة على المواصفة نفسها، راجع مقارنتنا بين Apidog وSchemathesis.

امنع الاختصارات: نسخة API من sorry

لدى Lean مخرج تهربي يُسمى sorry: فهو يتخطى خطوة، ويضع Lean علامة على كل تعريف يستخدمه. ويجد الوكلاء المخارج التهربية نفسها في مجموعات الاختبار:

الاختصار كيف يبدو في الفرق (diff) كيف تمنعه
اختبار متخطّى skip، only، حالة معلّقة أفشل CI إذا زاد عدد الفحوص المتخطّاة
تحقّق مخفّف يتحول toEqual إلى toBeDefined، وتُزال مراجعة المخطط أبقِ اختبارات العقد خارج المستودع الذي يعدّله الوكيل
مواصفة معدّلة ينتقل حقل مطلوب إلى اختياري في طلب السحب نفسه تحتاج تغييرات المواصفة إلى طلب سحب منفصل يراجعه إنسان
تبعية وهمية يستدعي الاختبار بديلًا يُرجع مثال المواصفة شغّل مجموعة اختبارات العقد مقابل نسخة حقيقية فقط
