The first select! arm borrows the pinned future as &mut work. If shutdown wins, the second arm can continue polling that same future from where it left off. The current chunk has a chance to finish its transaction, and the import can record what committed before it stops.

The Quit handler puts a five-second bound on this. It signals the root token, closes the tracker, and waits for the workers to drain. If the deadline expires, it logs a warning and stops waiting. For a user trying to find out whether a particular file made it into the library, that warning alone tells them very little. The answer comes from the batch record.

What happened to the ten files?

One of the import registry tests starts with ten requested files. It records three imports, two skips, and one failure, then stops the batch. Six files have an outcome. Four are still unprocessed.

That last category earns its place in the UI. If the dialog counted the four untouched files as failures, the user would have five files to troubleshoot, even though the importer encountered an error on only one. And because the database-writing pass updates its result counts after the corresponding transaction commits, the three imported files are already part of the library. The current filename in a progress event makes a much weaker claim. It tells the UI what the worker is looking at.

Cancellation also has to survive the worker’s ordinary completion code. In the test, the worker sends a final update with stage: "complete". The registry sees that the token was cancelled and carries forward the last meaningful stage and its counters. The final snapshot can now say the batch stopped during import with six of ten files accounted for.

When the last progress event goes missing

The backend records each progress snapshot before sending its event. While the webview is following an import, it also asks Rust for the current snapshot every five seconds, with at most one query in flight. A missed completion event costs the dialog an extra wait until a successful query. If a query fails, the dialog can keep waiting. Silence alone can’t tell it whether a worker is stuck or busy.

The guard in the registration snippet covers a different failure. If the worker future drops while the batch is still active, the guard marks it done and records Import worker stopped before reporting a result. The next status query can surface that error. Both the guard and the snapshot live in the Rust process, so recovering across a hard process kill would require durable job state and a restart policy.

There’s a test for the uneventful case that I’d keep alongside the cancellation tests. An import finishes with four files imported and one skipped. The test reads the terminal snapshot, then calls stop on the finished batch. The token stays live and the result still says four imported, one skipped. By then the task manager can be finished with the future. Someone looking at the dialog still needs those numbers.

title: PGConf.Asia 2026 recap
description:
Just back from PGConf.Asia 2026 in Hong Kong.

Meeting people I had only known from the pgsql-hackers mailing list, in the same room, was a strange feeling. A good one. I came home motivated.

I watched people with so much technical passion for Postgres give talks, ask questions, and talk with each other. I've only just started contributing myself, but being in that room as one of them was genuinely moving.

Thanks to PgUS for the travel grant that got me there.

There were so many genuinely useful talks. Here are the ones that helped me the most personally:

If you want a sense of which features make it into Postgres core and which stay in contrib, an extension, or a fork, start with Bruce Momjian's "What's Missing in Postgres?"
https://momjian.us/main/writings/pgsql/missing.pdf

Shinya Kato's "Vacuum Observability" walks through real vacuum troubleshooting cases.
https://pgconf.asia/EN/2026/proposals/?id=c73d384d-2677-49f9-84ce-720c826e72ee

Nikhil Chawla on putting Postgres data on F2FS instead of a traditional file system like XFS, turning scattered small writes into large sequential ones.
https://pgconf.asia/EN/2026/proposals/?id=f119f3bf-8438-4717-9271-15a6a4d7b1af

Haritabh Gupta's "Multigres Under the Hood" shows how Multigres decides, statement by statement, whether to share, pin, or reject, so pooling never silently breaks session features.
https://pgconf.asia/EN/2026/proposals/?id=f8340529-b68d-45ca-b56d-ace4fa32e7b3

title: The Afternoon Clerk Broke My Cloudflare App (and What It Taught Me About vinext vs OpenNext)
description:
I had a perfectly normal Next.js app, and I wanted it running on Cloudflare Workers. That's it. That was the whole plan.

Then I found out there are two ways to do it in 2026, and because I can't leave well enough alone, I tried both.

Road one is vinext, a Vite-native framework that's compatible with Next. Road two is OpenNext (specifically @opennextjs/cloudflare), which takes Next's own server output and tucks it inside a Worker.

Spoiler: both work. And both are "free" as far as the platform bill goes. But "free" is doing a lot of heavy lifting in that sentence, because what you actually pay with is:

  1. Config you have to write and keep alive
  2. Compatibility gaps you have to patch yourself
  3. Build time and Worker size
  4. The upgrade treadmill you quietly sign up for

I found all four the hard way. Here's the story, with real code from a production-ish app: Next 16, Clerk for auth, Prisma on Neon, server actions, and next/image.

The short version (for the skimmers)

  • The platform bill is the same. Both run on Workers, so requests, CPU time, subrequests and egress cost the same (Workers pricing).
  • The real bill is your time. On vinext, Clerk needed three separate workarounds. On OpenNext, it needed none.
  • vinext gives you faster builds, a smaller Worker, and a dev loop that runs in workerd.
  • OpenNext gives you real Next.js, but only on the Next versions it supports.
  • If you're staying on Cloudflare for the long haul, I'd take OpenNext. The cheapest adapter is the one whose problems someone else already fixed.

The app (boring on purpose)

The app is unremarkable in the best way: the App Router, "use server" actions, revalidate, next/image, Clerk for login, and Prisma over Neon. There's no framework-specific code anywhere: no vinext imports and no @opennextjs imports in app/.

That's the good news. The app code is portable. Everything I'm about to complain about (or praise) lives in the adapter.

vinext OpenNext Cloudflare
What runs A Next-compatible reimplementation on Vite/RSC Your real next build output
Config files vite.config.ts + cloudflare.config.ts + wrangler.jsonc next.config.ts + open-next.config.ts + wrangler.jsonc
Dev server vite dev (edge-accurate) next dev (Node) + wrangler bindings
Next version Loose Pinned (`next >=15.5.29 <16 \

Step 1: The config pile

First up: what do you actually have to write before anything runs?

The vinext way

You wire up the Cloudflare Vite plugin next to vinext, then describe your Worker in a TypeScript config.
{% raw %}

// vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import vinext from "vinext";
import { cloudflare } from "@cloudflare/vite-plugin";
import { imagesOptimizer } from "@vinext/cloudflare/images/images-optimizer";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    vinext({ images: { optimizer: imagesOptimizer() } }),
    cloudflare({ viteEnvironment: { name: "rsc", childEnvironments: ["ssr"] } }),
  ],
});

// cloudflare.config.ts
import { bindings, defineConfig, defineWorker } from "cf/config";

export default defineConfig({
  worker: defineWorker({
    name: "my-app",
    entrypoint: "vinext/server/fetch-handler",
    compatibilityDate: "2026-11-20",
    env: {
      DATABASE_URL: bindings.secret(),
      CLERK_SECRET_KEY: bindings.secret(),
      NEXT_PUBLIC_CLERK_PUBLISHABLE_KEY: bindings.text("pk_test_..."),
    },
  }),
});

The bindings get typed from that config (.cloudflare/types/index.d.ts), and your app reads them as plain process.env:

const connectionString = `${process.env.DATABASE_URL}`; // just works

The OpenNext way

Here the config lives in your Next config plus a wrangler file. You also pick a cache, like an R2-backed incremental cache, and turn on nodejs_compat.

// next.config.ts
import type { NextConfig } from "next";
import { initOpenNextCloudflareForDev } from "@opennextjs/cloudflare";

initOpenNextCloudflareForDev(); // makes bindings available in `next dev`

const nextConfig: NextConfig = { /* your normal Next config */ };
export default nextConfig;

// open-next.config.ts
import { defineCloudflareConfig } from "@opennextjs/cloudflare";
import r2IncrementalCache from "@opennextjs/cloudflare/overrides/incremental-cache/r2-incremental-cache";

export default defineCloudflareConfig({ incrementalCache: r2IncrementalCache });

// wrangler.jsonc
{
  "main": ".opennextjs/cloudflare-worker.js",
  "compatibility_date": "2026-11-20",
  "compatibility_flags": ["nodejs_compat"],
  "assets": { "directory": ".opennextjs/assets" },
  "vars": { "NEXT_PUBLIC_CLERK_PUBLISHABLE_KEY": "pk_test_..." }
}

Bindings come from wrangler, and your app reads them through the Cloudflare context:

import { getCloudflareContext } from "@opennextjs/cloudflare";

const { env } = getCloudflareContext();
const connectionString = env.DATABASE_URL;

My take: it's about the same amount of config either way. vinext puts it in TypeScript with generated types and process.env everywhere. OpenNext keeps it all in wrangler.jsonc as one source of truth, but you end up calling getCloudflareContext() in your data layer.

Step 2: Where does your code run while you're building it?

This is where the two feel totally different.

vinext's vite dev runs your app inside workerd, so your local dev loop is the real deployment runtime. I loved that. The require gotchas, the missing Node APIs and the Workers quirks all show up right at localhost, instead of waiting for you in a preview deploy.

OpenNext's dev server is plain next dev in Node, with initOpenNextCloudflareForDev() slipping the bindings in. It's fast, it's familiar, and everything just works. But now your app is running on a different runtime than production, and the differences show up later, at opennextjs-cloudflare preview time.

You'll make this trade over and over:

  • vinext: painful at dev time, predictable at deploy time.
  • OpenNext: smooth at dev time, surprises at deploy time.

Step 3: The Clerk saga (where my afternoon went)

Okay, grab a coffee. This is the part where the money goes.

My very first vite dev boot put this in the browser console:

@clerk/nextjs: SignedOut can only be used within the <ClerkProvider /> component.

Great, except ClerkProvider was sitting right there in app/layout.tsx. The error was lying to me. What was really happening: Vite's dependency optimizer had split Clerk's React context into two separate module instances.

SignedOut$1              (…/.vite/deps/@clerk_nextjs.js)
ClerkContextProvider     (…/@clerk/clerk-react/dist/index.mjs)

Vite actually tried to warn me, right above the error: client component dependency is inconsistently optimized. It's recommended to add the dependency to optimizeDeps.exclude.

Workaround #1: keep Clerk away from the optimizer 

// vite.config.ts (vinext)
environments: {
  client: {
    optimizeDeps: { exclude: ["@clerk/nextjs", "@clerk/clerk-react", "@clerk/shared"] },
  },
},

Workaround #2: turn off Clerk's keyless check

That fixed it, and then the next error showed up. Clerk's dev-only "keyless" check fires a Next server action on mount, and vinext's browser router answered with:

Browser router state is not initialized

The fix is one env var:

NEXT_PUBLIC_CLERK_KEYLESS_DISABLED=1

Workaround #3: the require() boss fight

And then came the real one:

[vinext] Server render error: ReferenceError: require is not defined
    at currentUser (node_modules/@clerk/nextjs/dist/esm/app-router/server/currentUser.js:5)
    at Home (app/page.tsx:29:22)

Here's what's going on. The ESM build of @clerk/nextjs contains literal require() calls: require("server-only") inside auth() and currentUser(), and require("next/navigation") inside its routing hooks. Next's Node server has a require global, so it works there. workerd doesn't have one, and vinext deliberately skips rewriting require() inside node_modules ESM.

This one has no config knob. It needs an actual plugin:

// vite.config.ts (vinext) — the tax
import { defineConfig, type Plugin } from "vite";

function clerkRequireShim(): Plugin {
  const markers = /require\(\s*["'](?:server-only|client-only)["']\s*\)\s*;?/g;
  const navigation = /require\(\s*["']next\/navigation["']\s*\)/g;
  return {
    name: "clerk-edgesafe-require",
    enforce: "pre",
    transform(code, id) {
      if (!/[\\/]@clerk[\\/]/.test(id)) return;
      let out = code.replace(markers, "");
      if (navigation.test(out)) {
        navigation.lastIndex = 0;
        out = `import * as __vinext_next_navigation from "next/navigation";\n` +
              out.replace(navigation, "__vinext_next_navigation");
      }
      return out === code ? undefined : { code: out, map: null };
    },
  };
}

It works. I checked it on /, /sign-in, /sign-up, server actions and Prisma queries. But look at what I'd just bought myself:

  • Three workarounds for one library
  • One of them a source transform that will quietly rot the day Clerk changes its build output
  • A debugging session that ate a couple of hours of profiler and stack-trace digging

On OpenNext, none of this exists. It runs your real next build output on Next's own server, so require is provided, contexts get bundled once, and server actions are Next's own. The equivalent cost? Zero lines.

That's the real headline of this whole story: the adapter you don't have to write is the cheapest one.

Step 4: How big is the thing, and how fast does it wake up?

Both adapters land on the same Workers runtime, so request and CPU billing is identical. The difference is the package you ship.

  • OpenNext bundles Next's server and its runtime into the Worker. Expect a multi-megabyte bundle and slower cold starts, plus a real next build in CI.
  • vinext produces a Vite/RSC bundle, which is smaller and builds much faster (seconds, not a minute-plus).

Don't take my word for it. Measure it on your own app:

# OpenNext: build, then look at the Worker size
npx opennextjs-cloudflare build
npx wrangler deploy --dry-run --outdir=.worker-out

# vinext: build, then the same check
npx vite build
npx wrangler deploy --dry-run --outdir=.worker-out

Think of bundle size as a cold-start tax. For a content site with steady traffic, who cares. For a low-traffic app where every request is a cold start, your users will feel it.

Step 5: Okay, but what does it actually cost?

Straight answer: the platform bill is the same. Both are Workers. Requests, CPU time, subrequests and egress are all priced the same way, and neither adapter adds a per-request fee.

So where does the cost land?

Cost line vinext OpenNext
Platform (Workers) Identical Identical
CI build time Low (Vite) Higher (next build + transform)
Cold starts Lower (smaller bundle) Higher
Your engineering time Higher: you patch compat gaps Lower: Next semantics are Next
Upgrade risk Tracks Next loosely Pinned to supported Next versions
Ongoing maintenance Your workaround code Adapter upgrades

If your time is worth $100/hour and my Clerk adventure took two hours, vinext "cost" $200 up front. And every future library with a require() in its ESM build costs more.

Step 6: The upgrade treadmill

This is the one nobody talks about. @opennextjs/cloudflare@1.20.x declares:

"peerDependencies": { "next": ">=15.5.29 <16 || >=16.4.5" }

If you're on next@16.0.8, you have to upgrade to >=16.4.5 before OpenNext will even install cleanly. That's a four-minor-version jump on a React 19 app, which is a real risk, not a checkbox.

vinext doesn't pin you like that. Which is exactly why the require() gap lands on your desk instead of the adapter's.

So the trade is honest:

  • OpenNext: you upgrade Next on the adapter's schedule, and the adapter fixes compatibility for you.
  • vinext: you upgrade Next whenever you want, and you fix compatibility yourself.

The scorecard

vinext OpenNext
App code changes None None
Adapter config ~40 lines TS ~30 lines JSON/TS
Library compat Patch it yourself (Clerk: 3 fixes) Handled
Dev loop accuracy workerd, matches prod Node, diverges
Build speed Fast Slower
Worker size Smaller Larger
Next version freedom High Constrained
Long-term maintenance Yours Adapter's

So what would I actually do?

  1. Shipping Next on Cloudflare for the long haul? Take OpenNext. Pay the Next upgrade once, stop writing workarounds, and let the adapter own compatibility. It's the supported path, and my Clerk afternoon is the proof of why that matters.
  2. Want the Vite dev loop, or stuck on a Next version OpenNext doesn't support yet? vinext is fine. Just budget for one workaround per "Next-ecosystem library with a weird build output" you adopt, and keep those patches in one file so you can delete them later.
  3. Either way, try it in a branch. Run bunx wrangler deploy --dry-run --outdir=.worker-out on both builds, then check /, a server action and a Prisma query under opennextjs-cloudflare preview. That's one afternoon, and it'll answer the question for your app better than any benchmark post.

The takeaway

The adapter with fewer files isn't the cheaper one. The cheapest adapter is the one whose compatibility gaps someone else already fixed.

Want the opposite conclusion? If you need next/font, ISR and image optimization to behave exactly like Next, OpenNext is the only option that gives you Next's own implementation.

The config snippets come from a real Next 16 / Clerk / Prisma-Neon app. The vinext workarounds are accurate at the time of writing, so check them against your Clerk version before copying.

Btw, I'm Sajal, a Full-Stack JavaScript Developer specializing in React and Next.js.

I help businesses increase conversions and revenue through performance-driven website optimization, focusing on performance, SEO, and user experience.

Looking to get more out of your website? Let's connect.

title: How to Stop Background Jobs from Quietly Failing in Production
description:
Most background job failures don't trigger loud, immediate alerts. They happen quietly. A job fails to process a webhook at 11 PM, the exception gets swallowed inside a broad try/catch block, no dead-letter queue catches it, and background tasks silently stop while user actions keep piling up.

Over time, a few recurring anti-patterns cause these silent failures in production:

  • Fire-and-forget background jobs executing without structured retry mechanisms.
  • Swallowing exceptions to prevent the worker process from crashing.
  • Non-idempotent job handlers that risk charging customers twice or sending duplicate emails if retried.
  • Zero visibility into worker failures until an end user reports an issue.

Building reliable background job pipelines requires intentional architecture. You can eliminate silent failures by following a step-by-step approach to retries, isolation, and failure visibility.

1. Ensure Handlers Are Idempotent

Before adding retries to any background job, your processing logic must be idempotent. If a worker crashes midway through processing and retries the job, executing the function a second time with the exact same payload must produce the exact same result without duplicate side effects.

Achieve idempotency by creating unique deduplication keys (such as an order_id or event_id) and enforcing database upserts or atomic status checks before running side-effect code.

2. Checkpoint Completed Steps

Instead of treating a complex task as a single monolithic block of code, divide multi-step workflows into smaller checkpoints. If Step 1 (charging a card) succeeds, but Step 2 (generating a PDF invoice) fails, a subsequent retry should pick up at Step 2 rather than re-running Step 1.

Here is a Python pattern illustrating step checkpointing and idempotency checks using Redis to store execution state:

import logging
import redis

db = redis.Redis(host="localhost", port=6379, db=0)
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def process_order_job(job_id: str, payload: dict):
    job_status_key = f"job_status:{job_id}"

    # 1. Idempotency Check: Skip if job already succeeded
    if db.get(job_status_key) == b"COMPLETED":
        logger.info(f"Job {job_id} already processed. Skipping execution.")
        return

    try:
        # 2. Step Checkpoint: Charge Payment
        if not db.sismember(f"job_checkpoints:{job_id}", "payment_charged"):
            charge_customer(payload["customer_id"], payload["amount"])
            db.sadd(f"job_checkpoints:{job_id}", "payment_charged")

        # 3. Step Checkpoint: Send Email Receipt
        if not db.sismember(f"job_checkpoints:{job_id}", "email_sent"):
            send_receipt_email(payload["email"], payload["amount"])
            db.sadd(f"job_checkpoints:{job_id}", "email_sent")

        # 4. Mark job as fully completed
        db.set(job_status_key, "COMPLETED")
        logger.info(f"Job {job_id} completed successfully.")

    except Exception as exc:
        logger.error(f"Job {job_id} failed during execution: {str(exc)}", exc_info=True)
        # Re-raise to let the queue orchestrator handle retry backoff
        raise exc

3. Configure Retries with Exponential Backoff

Retrying a failed job immediately in a tight loop often worsens the underlying issue, such as network congestion or database lock contention. Always configure task queues (such as Celery, BullMQ, or Sidekiq) to use exponential backoff with random jitter.

This spreads out retry attempts across increasing intervals (e.g., 5 seconds, 30 seconds, 5 minutes) and prevents a "thundering herd" scenario against downstream dependencies.

# Example Celery task configuration using exponential backoff and jitter
@app.task(
    bind=True,
    autoretry_for=(TransientNetworkError, DatabaseTimeoutError),
    retry_kwargs={'max_retries': 5},
    retry_backoff=True,       # Enables exponential backoff
    retry_backoff_max=600,   # Caps delay to 10 minutes
    retry_jitter=True        # Adds randomness to prevent simultaneous retries
)
def sync_user_data_task(self, user_id: str):
    perform_data_sync(user_id)

4. Route Poison Pills to Dead Letter Queues

Never catch exceptions without re-raising them or routing failing jobs to a dedicated Dead Letter Queue (DLQ).

When a job exhausts all configured retry attempts, move the payload to a DLQ alongside error stack traces, execution metadata, and retry counts. Tie automated alerting (such as Slack alerts or Sentry events) directly to your DLQ metric. If the DLQ length increases, your team should know instantly, with enough context to inspect and replay the message manually once the bug is resolved.

Summary

Reliable system architecture isn't about ensuring background jobs never fail. It is about making sure that when failures occur, they are isolated, fully visible, and safe to recover without manual database cleanups.

About me

Tanmay builds AI agents and automation for businesses and is open to freelance projects. Feel free to connect on LinkedIn to discuss backend engineering, system architecture, or automation pipelines.

title: react-pdf was squeezing my letters: how I patched its line breaker and justifier
description:
I build Folium, a free resume builder. The live preview and the PDF you download come from the same renderer, @react-pdf/renderer (4.9, with @react-pdf/textkit 7.0.1), so whatever the layout engine does, people see it twice.

A user told me their resume "didn't look well arranged". They were right, and the cause was not in my templates. It was in how textkit breaks and justifies lines. This post is what I measured, the three changes I made, and how I keep them from silently disappearing on the next npm install.

What was wrong

I rendered 30 templates with 5 kinds of content each (sample data, a realistic resume, the same one justified, and both again with a bigger font) and measured every line with PyMuPDF. Three problems showed up:

  1. Letters squeezed in left-aligned text. About 1 line in 8 had its letters compressed, by up to 2%. Not justified text: plain left-aligned paragraphs.
  2. Letters stretched in justified text. On lines with few words, the gaps were filled by spreading the letters apart, up to +24% on the worst lines.
  3. Huge gaps in narrow columns. Sidebars set to justify, with no hyphenation, ended up with rivers of white space.

Cause 1: the line breaker lets left-aligned lines overflow

textkit uses a Knuth-Plass style line breaker. Each space is a piece of "glue" that can stretch and shrink. The defaults:

const opts = { width: 3, stretch: 6, shrink: 9 };
// per space: shrink = (width * opts.width) / opts.shrink  -> a third of the space

That shrink is applied whatever the alignment, so the breaker happily accepts a left-aligned line that is a bit wider than the box, counting on squeezing the spaces later. Then, when each line is aligned:

const shouldJustify = align === 'justify' || lineWidth > line.box.width;

A line that overflows gets sent to the justifier even if it is left-aligned. The justifier can only take a little out of each space, so it takes the rest out of the letters.

Fix: only justified text is allowed to count on shrinking spaces. A left-aligned line can never be wider than its box, so it never reaches the justifier.

const shrink = align === 'justify' ? (width * opts.width) / opts.shrink : 0;

Cause 2: the justifier moves letters, not just spaces

The justifier distributes the extra (or missing) width with priority factors. Spaces go first, but once each space has moved beyond a small limit, letters start absorbing the difference (EXPAND_CHAR_FACTOR is 37/256 per side). That is where the +24% came from.

Fix: letters get a factor of 0, spaces get a very large one, so all of the adjustment always fits in the spaces:

const EXPAND_WHITESPACE_FACTOR = { before: 50, after: 50, priority: WHITESPACE_PRIORITY, unconstrained: false };
const EXPAND_CHAR_FACTOR       = { before: 0,  after: 0,  priority: LETTER_PRIORITY,     unconstrained: false };
const SHRINK_WHITESPACE_FACTOR = { before: -50, after: -50, priority: WHITESPACE_PRIORITY, unconstrained: false };
const SHRINK_CHAR_FACTOR       = { before: 0,  after: 0,  priority: LETTER_PRIORITY,     unconstrained: false };

Why not just mark spaces as unconstrained? I tried. The unconstrained path in getDistances only adds the "before" side of a space when the glyph before it is also unconstrained, so half of the adjustment gets lost and justified lines come out short. Large constrained factors avoid that path entirely.

Cause 3: narrow columns should not be justified

Without hyphenation, a column of about 20 to 25 characters per line cannot be justified nicely. No factor fixes that. So below 25 em, justified text is laid out like its last line (usually left-aligned):

const FOLIUM_NARROW_EM = 25;
const folNarrowJustify = (attributes, width) => {
  if (!attributes || attributes.align !== 'justify' || !(width > 0)) return attributes;
  if (width >= (attributes.fontSize || 12) * FOLIUM_NARROW_EM) return attributes;
  return Object.assign({}, attributes, { align: attributes.alignLastLine || 'left' });
};

It is applied in two places: when breaking lines (so the breaker treats the paragraph as not justified) and when aligning each line.

Patching node_modules without losing the patch

These are changes inside node_modules/@react-pdf/textkit/lib/textkit.js, applied by a postinstall script. Each patch is a find/replace on an exact fragment of the library. The rule I follow: if neither the original fragment nor the patched one is found, the script fails. A library update must make me look at the patch again; it must never drop it silently. That way the build, the Cloudflare workers, the tests and my scripts all see the same textkit.

Tests that fail without the patch

The test lays out a real paragraph with textkit at 30 widths (18 to 44 em at 10 pt), left and justified, with hyphenation turned off like in the templates, and checks four things:

  • every letter keeps its natural advance (difference under 0.001 pt), in every width and alignment;
  • left-aligned lines never exceed the box;
  • in a wide column, justified lines fill the box using the spaces;
  • under 25 em, justified text breaks into exactly the same lines as left-aligned text.

Three of the four fail on unpatched textkit, which is how I know the patch is still doing something.

Result

Across 150 PDFs (30 templates times 5 cases), no document changed its number of pages, and no line has squeezed or stretched letters anymore. Justified resumes look justified in the main column and calm in the sidebars.

If you use react-pdf with justified text or long paragraphs, it is worth measuring a few of your PDFs: open them with PyMuPDF, compare each glyph's advance with the font's natural width, and see how many lines were "fixed" by moving letters. I was surprised by how many.

title: Building Responsive Layouts with Tailwind CSS Grid (and the auto-fill Trick I Wish I Knew Sooner)
description:
I have a confession: for the first couple of years I wrote CSS professionally, I avoided Grid completely. Flexbox was my hammer, and every layout was a nail. Nested flex containers, negative margin hacks, flex-basis: 33.333%. I made it all work, sort of. Then I opened the TechHub dashboard I was building on an actual tablet and watched my carefully nested flexbox layout fold into something that looked like a ransom note.

That was the project that finally forced me to learn CSS Grid properly, through Tailwind's utilities. This post is more or less everything I wish someone had told me before I started.

Why Grid, and why through Tailwind

Flexbox is one-dimensional. It's brilliant for a navbar, a button group, or centering an icon next to text. But the moment you're arranging content in two dimensions, rows and columns that need to stay in sync, flexbox makes you fight for it.

Grid thinks in two dimensions natively. And Tailwind's grid utilities map almost one-to-one onto the CSS spec, so nothing you learn here is wasted. grid-cols-3 is just grid-template-columns: repeat(3, minmax(0, 1fr)) under the hood, so you can always drop back to raw CSS when you outgrow the utilities.

The core utilities you'll actually use 

<div class="grid grid-cols-1 md:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-3 gap-6">
  <article class="rounded-xl border p-6">...</article>
  <article class="rounded-xl border p-6">...</article>
  <article class="rounded-xl border p-6">...</article>
</div>

This is the pattern behind maybe 70% of the layouts on TechHub: one column on mobile, two on tablet, three on desktop, with gap-6 doing the spacing work that used to need margin gymnastics.

The important mental shift: the gap belongs to the container, not the children. No more last:mr-0 hacks, no more space utilities breaking the moment items wrap.

Mobile first, always

Every Tailwind breakpoint prefix is min-width. grid-cols-1 md:grid-cols-2 means one column by default, two from 768px up. Write the phone layout as the unprefixed default and add columns as space appears.

The card grid (and where it broke)

TechHub has a projects page: a grid of cards with a thumbnail, title, tags and stats. My first version:

<div class="grid grid-cols-1 sm:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-4 gap-4">

It looked great on my monitor. Then someone on a 1280px laptop said the cards looked squished. Four columns at lg gave each card barely 280px. The fix I settled on:

<div class="grid grid-cols-[repeat(auto-fill,minmax(280px,1fr))] gap-4">

auto-fill with minmax tells the browser: fit as many 280px-minimum columns as you can, then stretch them to fill what's left. No breakpoints at all.

One gotcha: auto-fit collapses empty tracks, so with only two cards on a wide screen they stretch enormously. auto-fill keeps the empty tracks, so cards stay a sane size. I got this backwards the first time and spent a while wondering why two lonely cards were each the width of a small country.

Spanning: the dashboard shell

The brief: a stats row, a big chart, a sidebar of recent activity, and a full-width table. With flexbox this would have been three nested containers. With Grid it's one:

<div class="grid grid-cols-1 lg:grid-cols-3 gap-6">
  <!-- stats row: full width, its own inner grid -->
  <div class="lg:col-span-3 grid grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-4 gap-4">
    <StatCard /> <StatCard /> <StatCard /> <StatCard />
  </div>

  <!-- chart takes 2/3, activity feed takes 1/3 -->
  <section class="lg:col-span-2">...chart...</section>
  <aside>...recent activity...</aside>

  <!-- table spans everything -->
  <section class="lg:col-span-3">...table...</section>
</div>

On mobile everything stacks in source order. At lg the spans kick in and it becomes the dashboard. One container, and the source order still makes sense for screen readers.

What I'd actually do

  • Start with one column and add breakpoints only when the design actually breaks in the browser, not when you think it might.
  • Use auto-fill + minmax for card grids, breakpoint columns for page shells. Content-driven sizing and design-driven sizing are different problems.
  • Don't abandon flexbox. Grid for the page, flex for the components inside it.
  • Go easy on arbitrary values. gap-[13px] in a code review usually means the design hasn't been thought through.
  • Resize the browser slowly across the whole range. The bugs live between the breakpoints. My squished-card bug shipped because I only ever checked 375, 768 and 1440.

If you're flexboxing everything and quietly dreading two-dimensional layouts, pick one page and rebuild it with Grid. It'll feel awkward for about an hour, and then you'll wonder why you waited so long.

Originally published on the TechInnoLab blog. We're a small remote studio building web apps and SaaS dashboards for UK and EU businesses.

title: The Stopped Flag Stops Nothing That Already Started
description:
After the reject, the workers keep looping. That is the hole in yesterday's pre-fill piece, and sunnatulla_dev found it before I did. In his run, tasks 6 to 9 started at 301 to 421 milliseconds, after the call had already rejected at 272, and a second later every slot read ok. So the array calls them skipped, they ran, and anyone who retries them runs them twice. His fix is one line: set stopped = true in the catch, and let the workers check while (!stopped && ...) before picking up the next task.

I ran his version on the same shape. Ten tasks, three workers, task 4 throwing after 150 milliseconds. Same delays as yesterday, both arms twice, and both repeats came back identical. The flag works. It also leaves two tasks double-running, and those two are the interesting part.

Here is the shape, with the flag in:

async function mapWithConcurrency(tasks, limit) {
  const results = tasks.map(() => ({ status: "skipped" }));
  let next = 0, stopped = false;
  async function worker() {
    while (!stopped && next < tasks.length) {
      const i = next++;
      try {
        results[i] = await tasks[i]();
      } catch (err) {
        results[i] = { status: "failed", error: err.message };
        stopped = true;
        throw err;
      }
    }
  }
  await Promise.all(Array.from({ length: limit }, () => worker()));
  return results;
}

The reject lands at the same moment in both arms, 275 to 277 milliseconds across the four runs. The flag costs nothing on wall time, because it does not stop anything that is already running. It only stops new pickups, and there is nothing to pick up until a worker finishes a task.

No flag Stopped flag
Reject wall time 277 ms 277 ms
Tasks started after the reject 5 (tasks 5–9, at 302–743 ms) 0
Slots reading "skipped" at the reject 7 7
Slots reading "skipped" 1.2 s later 0 5
Tasks double-run by retrying the "skipped" slots 7 2

Read the no-flag row first, because it is worse than it sounds. At the reject, seven slots read skipped. A second later, none of them do. Tasks 5 to 9 started after the call had already failed and finished fine, and tasks 2 and 3 were still running when the reject landed and finished fine too. The array drifts under the caller. A retry built from the reject-time snapshot runs all seven again. Seven tasks doing real work twice, because the label was written before the work happened and nobody updated it after.

The flag arm fixes five of the seven. Tasks 5 to 9 never start. A second later they still read skipped, and this time the label is true: nothing ran there, nothing will, and a retry runs each of them exactly once. That is the whole win, and it is a real one. Five phantom runs gone, for one line and zero measurable cost.

But look at the last row. Two double-runs survive the flag, and they are tasks 2 and 3, the pair that was mid-flight when task 4 threw. The flag cannot reach them. They are inside an await when stopped flips to true, and the loop condition is only checked after the await resolves. They finish, they write ok into their slots, and the caller that read "skipped" at reject time retries them anyway. In my run they finished 24 and 44 milliseconds after the reject. The window is small. The double-run is not.

This is the part the one-line fix cannot close. The flag answers the question "has a worker picked this up yet" at the moment of the reject, and for the two in-flight tasks the honest answer at that moment is "yes, and it is not done". The array says skipped because nothing has written anything else yet. There are only two ways to tell the truth about those two slots. One is to mark a task "running" when the worker picks it up, so the caller can see the difference between untouched and in-flight and decide what a retry means for each. The other is to wait before retrying: let the stragglers land, read the array again, and retry only what still reads skipped after everything has settled. The first costs a line. The second costs a delay, and the delay is the honest price of a retry you can trust.

So sunnatulla_dev is right, and the flag is worth adding, and it is not the whole fix. Add it. It turns seven double-runs into two, for free. Then mark the in-flight tasks, or wait for them, because the two that survive are the ones doing real work when the batch falls over, and they are the ones a blind retry will run twice. A stopped flag stops the queue. It stops nothing that already started.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

title: I made my first npm library: scrollbars that don't shove your layout around 🙏
description:
Hey everyone 👋

You know when a list gets one item longer, a scrollbar pops in, and everything jumps a few pixels to the left? Buttons move, text re-wraps, centered stuff is suddenly off-center.

That annoyed me enough that I made a little library for it. It's my first one ever.

One line, that's it 

import { MrScroll } from "plz-mr-scroll/react";

<MrScroll />

Put it at the root of your app. You don't add anything to your components.

Not using React? installMrScroll() from plz-mr-scroll does the same thing.

What it actually does

It finds every scroll area on the page and gives the scrollbar a spot that doesn't move your content:

  1. The area has enough right padding → it shrinks that padding by the scrollbar width
  2. The content is centered → it balances both sides so the center stays put
  3. The padding is on the parent → it floats the scrollbar just outside the area
  4. No room anywhere → it floats the scrollbar over the edge of the content

No reserved gutter, and it's still the native scrollbar — not a custom-drawn one.

Try it

  • 👉 Live demo: https://justicehwan.github.io/plz-mr-scroll/
  • GitHub: https://github.com/justicehwan/plz-mr-scroll
  • npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/plz-mr-scroll

Please tell me what's wrong with it 🥲

Since it's my first library, I honestly have no idea what I got wrong. If you have a minute, please try the demo and tell me what's broken, confusing, or just dumb.

P.S. I'm Korean and English isn't my first language, so sorry if anything here reads a bit off.

Thanks for reading!

title: Who Plays Whom? Designing the Casting Step for a Multi-Person AI Body Swap
description:
Most AI video demos show one person in the frame. Real short videos often have two or three: a duo dance, a trio routine, a skit with a friend in the background.

I build Memevibe, an AI body swap for short clips. You drop a clip and a photo, and the person in the clip is replaced with the person in the photo, while the scene, camera and sound stay as filmed.

With one person in the clip there is nothing to design. With three, there is a question the product has to answer before anything renders: which photo replaces which person? This post is about that step.

Why it is not a face swap problem

A face swap tool can get away with "pick a face in the frame". Body swap replaces the whole person: face, hair, build and outfit all come from the photo. If the mapping is wrong, the user does not get a slightly off result. They get their friend's body dancing in the wrong position for the entire clip, and they have paid for it.

There is no preview before a render, because the render is the expensive part. So the mapping has to be right the first time, and the user has to be confident that it is.

Step 1: turn the clip into a cast list

After upload, the clip is read and every person in it becomes a card. Each card has three things:

  • a number that matches a marker on the frame
  • a position, such as left, centre or right
  • a short plain-language description, for example "brown hair tied back, white tank top, grey sweatpants"

The description matters more than I expected. Position alone breaks down as soon as people move, and in a dance they swap places constantly. A number alone means nothing. "The one in the pink sweatshirt" is how a person actually identifies someone in a video.

A simplified sketch of the shape (illustrative, not the production code):

type PersonSlot = {
  id: number;                 // matches the marker shown on the frame
  position: "left" | "centre" | "right";
  description: string;        // hair, top, bottoms
  photo?: UploadedPhoto;      // undefined = keep as filmed
};

type Cast = {
  clipId: string;
  slots: PersonSlot[];
};

Step 2: empty is a valid answer

The key decision is in that optional photo field. A slot without a photo is not an error. It means "keep this person as filmed".

This makes three use cases fall out of one model:

  • replace only the lead and leave the others
  • replace two out of three
  • recast the whole group, one photo each

The only rule is that at least one slot needs a photo before the render button is enabled.

function canStart(cast: Cast): boolean {
  return cast.slots.some((slot) => slot.photo !== undefined);
}

I considered requiring a photo for every person. It would have been simpler to explain and it would have killed the most common case, which is one user who wants to be the lead in a group clip.

Step 3: say what will not work before the user pays

Some clips cannot be swapped well, and the casting step is the last cheap moment to say so.

  • A person whose face never shows cannot be swapped. Back views and heavy motion blur give the model nothing to anchor a likeness to.
  • When several people are being replaced, the higher tier keeps everyone steadier than the standard one. The interface says this on the cast list, next to the tier choice, not in a help page.
  • Clips over 15 seconds only run on the top tier. The tier selector reflects that instead of letting the user pick something that will fail.

The pattern is the same each time: a constraint of the model becomes a visible state in the UI at the point where the user can still change their mind.

Step 4: the price follows the choices

Tier, resolution and clip length decide the cost, and the number of credits is written on the start button. Change the tier and the button changes.

I wrote about the billing side in an earlier post, so I will only repeat the principle: the user should never have to do arithmetic to know what a click will cost.

Step 5: the render is a background job

A render usually takes 3 to 6 minutes. That is too long to hold someone on a spinner, so the job is detached from the page:

  • the user can leave, and the result shows up in a "My videos" list
  • an email can be sent when it is done
  • the original audio of the clip is put back under the generated video, so the output is ready to post
  • if the render fails or the model's safety check stops it, the credits go back to the balance automatically

That last point shapes the casting step too. Because a failed render costs the user nothing, the UI can warn about risky clips without blocking them outright.

Consent is part of the cast list

Body swap puts a real person into a video they did not film. Two rules are enforced at this step:

  • the user confirms that each photo is of themselves or of someone who agreed to appear
  • photos of celebrities and public figures are not accepted

On the data side, photos and clips are passed to the video model through links that expire within an hour, are not used for training, and are deleted after 30 days.

It would be easy to treat these as legal boilerplate. I think of them as part of the same design problem: the casting step is where a person's likeness gets assigned, so it is where the rules about likeness belong.

What I would do differently

Likeness is still not guaranteed. The photo is the usual cause when a result looks off, and I surface photo advice too late in the flow. A check at upload time, before the user gets to casting, would save renders.

I would also like the description on each card to be editable, for the cases where the reading of the clip gets a detail wrong and the user loses confidence in the mapping.

If you have built a flow where users map inputs to detected people or objects, I am curious how you handled identification. Numbers, thumbnails, descriptions, or something else?

title: React.lazy() and Suspense in react.
description:
In React, when we build a large application, it may contain many components and pages. Loading all the JavaScript code at once can increase the initial loading time of the application.

To solve this problem, React provides two important features:

  • React.lazy() – Loads a component's code only when it is needed.
  • Suspense – Displays a fallback UI while the component is loading.

Together, these features help us implement code splitting and improve the loading experience of a React application.

What is React.lazy()?

React.lazy() is a React function that allows us to load a component dynamically instead of loading it immediately.

This technique is called lazy loading.

In simple words, React.lazy() loads a component's code only when React needs to render that component.

Syntax:

import { lazy } from "react";

const MyComponent = lazy(() => {
    return import("./MyComponent");
});

What is Suspense in React?

Suspense is a React component that allows us to display a fallback UI while its child component is not ready to render.

In simple words, Suspense shows a temporary loading screen until the required component is ready.

Syntax:

import { Suspense } from "react";

<Suspense fallback={<h2>Loading...</h2>}>
    <MyComponent />
</Suspense>

title: Your lake is slow per table, not per row
description:
Flock's data team wrote up how they moved about 480 dbt models off AWS Glue and onto DuckDB, and cut their core build from 97 minutes to 25. The numbers are good. The line that stuck with me is the diagnosis: "Build time grew with the number of models, not the size of the data."

I hit the same wall from the query side, on a Trino lake over Iceberg. Different engine, different job, same wrong assumption. I thought a lake was slow because of the data. It was slow because of the tables.


Measured on my own lake: the same query through each catalog, a few runs each after a warm-up.

The cost you pay per object

In Flock's old setup, dbt sent every model to a hosted Spark session, one statement at a time, and checked for the answer once a second. A model of a dozen rows cost about 35 seconds. About 1 second of that was its actual SQL. Multiply that by 150-odd models in their core project and a build takes over an hour, however little data moves.

On my lake, Trino asked a remote catalog where each table lived, in every query, with no memory between queries. The catalog sat in one region and the engine in another, so each lookup cost about half a second. A question that touched 25 tables waited about 13 seconds before it read a single row.

Neither problem shows up when you test with one table. Both get worse every time someone adds a model or joins one more table.

Count round trips, not rows

The check is the same in both cases: find out how much time passes before any data is touched.

Flock's version was a 12-row model taking 35 seconds. In Trino, the query log tells you directly. Analysis is the step before any data is read:

SELECT query_id, analysis_time_ms, planning_time_ms,
       date_diff('millisecond', created, "end") AS total_ms
FROM system.runtime.queries
ORDER BY created DESC
LIMIT 5;

If analysis is a big slice of the total, and it grows with the number of tables in the query, the time is going to lookups, not data. A bigger cluster won't fix that.

Stop paying the per-object cost at run time

Flock kept their tables and their catalog. In their words, "the only thing that moved is where the SQL runs." DuckDB runs inside the dbt process itself, so there is no session to wait for and no round trip per statement. A small model now finishes in seconds.

I kept the engine and moved the lookup. I gave Trino a local address book: an Iceberg catalog in Postgres that holds each table's current metadata pointer. Analysis on the 25-table question went from about 13 seconds to 0.8. On a small question it went from 1.5 seconds to 0.17.

Two different fixes, one rule: if something is paid per table or per model, get it out of the path every query takes.

"Identical" is the hard part

The speedup is the easy half. Proving nothing changed is the real work.

Flock's list of quiet differences between Spark and DuckDB is the best part of their post. Arrays start at 1 instead of 0. concat skips NULLs instead of returning NULL. round() can land a penny out. Ascending sorts put NULLs last. Casting to an integer rounds instead of truncating. All of it is SQL that runs on both engines and quietly gives different answers. They compared every table between the old and new builds, in both directions, before anything was promoted.

My change was smaller, a pointer instead of an engine, but I held it to the same bar: the answers before and after had to be byte-for-byte identical. They were. If they hadn't been, the speedup wouldn't have counted.

The bill you take on

Neither fix is free.

Flock now owns their containers and their out-of-memory errors. About 15 of their 480 models needed a bigger container, and their table maintenance spend roughly doubled, because DuckDB writes merges as delete files that need compacting more often.

I now own a refresh job. Every time new data lands, the address book has to point at each table's newest metadata file, or Trino serves the previous version of the table: consistent, but stale. That is one remote call per table per refresh, instead of one per table per query. A good trade for a lake that is read far more than it is written, but still a job someone has to run. The full story of making that lake fast has the rest of the trade-offs.

Moving work out of the hot path doesn't delete it. It moves it somewhere you control.

Next time a lake feels slow, don't start with the row counts. Count the tables.

title: Code vs Config? You're Already Orchestrating
description:
Most workflows don't start out as workflows.

They start as one function that calls two services. Then someone adds a retry. Then an undo step for when payment fails. A few months later, that function decides what runs, in what order, and what happens when something breaks.

That's orchestration. It just doesn't look like it, because it's sitting inside your code.

The debate misses the point

Teams love to argue about whether workflows belong in code or in config. But once your code calls other services and has to manage the order and the failures, you're already orchestrating. So the real question isn't code or config. It's where the plan lives.

Keep the blocks small

Let each function do one thing: reserve stock, charge a card, create a label. Wire them together somewhere else. The code stays cleaner, easier to test and easier to maintain.

What about choreography?

Services reacting to each other's events is nicely decoupled. The catch is visibility. When nobody holds the whole plan, a failure means chasing events across services to find out what happened.

So, code or config?

Neither wins. It's your code that gets orchestrated either way. Keep that code simple, and keep the plan in one place you can see.

Where does the plan live in your system? Tell us in the comments.

title: AI just made your old PHP monolith a faster target
description:
Cloudflare's CEO Matthew Prince is warning of up to two years of widespread technology disruption, because AI is finding and exploiting decades-old software flaws fast. One example in the coverage: an AI-found Ghostscript flaw ("Upload2Shell") that has since been patched.

That changes the maths on legacy code.

End-of-life runtimes don't get patches

When a flaw is found in a supported runtime, a patch follows. When your PHP runtime is past end of life, no patch is coming. If AI is shrinking the time between "flaw exists" and "flaw is exploited", an unpatched runtime is exposed for longer and found faster.

A rushed migration is a risk too

The obvious answer is "migrate". But a migration done in a hurry swaps a known risk for an unknown one: the new system quietly behaving differently from the old one.

The fix is to prove the new system behaves exactly like the old one before cutover.

How we verify it at MigrateForge

We replay recorded user journeys against both the PHP app and the Java 21 / Spring Boot version and compare three things:

  • HTTP responses
  • Database writes
  • Outgoing API calls

Cutover stays blocked until they match.

Benchmarks so far (not client projects): 4 waves, 858 fixtures, 100% parity, 0 write-effect diffs.

Before release, verification caught a delete that would also have wiped a client's invoices and payments, and a page missing its login check. Neither would have shown up as a failed HTTP status.

Free migration report: migrateforge.com

Your turn

What PHP version is your oldest production app still on, and what's stopping the upgrade?

title: PageSift 1.7 "Resolve": Stop Trusting Retrieved Text — Verify the Conclusion
description:
PageSift is a Rust web-content engine for LLM pipelines (305 stars, Apache-2.0). Version 1.6 made retrieved text auditable: every passage stored with provenance, version lineage, and an observation timestamp. Version 1.7, released today, adds the layer that was still missing — checking the conclusions you draw from that text.

The problem: nobody verifies the answer

A retrieval pipeline hands text to a model. The model states conclusions: "the price is $42 a year", "it ships in March", "this tool causes fewer support tickets". Those sentences go into answers, reports, and databases. Nobody checks them.

And they rot. The price changes next month. Two sources disagree and the pipeline keeps whichever it read last. A press release gets copied by five sites and starts to look like five independent confirmations. A study that found a correlation gets quoted as proof of causation. Last year's price gets repeated as today's.

Scraping got the text back. Context (1.6) made the text traceable. The conclusion drawn from it was still taken on faith. Resolve is the layer that checks it.

One scenario, end to end

Say you monitor a product's price. The vendor's page says Widget Pro costs $42 per year. A reseller lists the same product at $45 per year. Your pipeline produces the sentence "Widget Pro costs $42 per year" and you ask Resolve to check it against the stored evidence.

The verdict is conflicted. Resolve tracks support and refutation as separate facts instead of averaging them into a score: one independent source supports the sentence, another independent source refutes it, and the record says exactly that, with citations to both.

Two weeks later the vendor raises the price to $50. The stored conclusion is not left standing. When the underlying evidence changes, Resolve re-checks only the conclusions that depend on the changed passages — and this one flips to refuted, with its full revision history preserved. A conclusion in Resolve is not a one-time judgment. It is a maintained object that stays answerable to its evidence.

The four ideas

1. A conclusion is a stored, versioned record. Each checked answer becomes a ConclusionRecord with one of nine states — supported, supported with qualifiers, refuted, conflicted, insufficient, temporal mismatch, causally unidentifiable, needs human review, observation degraded. Two of those states deserve emphasis: insufficient ("the evidence does not settle this") and causally unidentifiable ("the evidence shows correlation, not causation"). The system is allowed to say it cannot tell, and it does.

2. Checking is deterministic, in seven layers. The checker anchors every claim to its subject, so one product's price can never "confirm" another's. It keeps two time axes apart: when a page was observed versus the period the fact is valid for — a 2024 price cannot confirm a claim about today. It normalizes quantities, currencies, and billing periods, so $42 per month does not confirm $42 per year. It guards negation and dropped qualifiers ("does not include shipping" refutes "includes shipping"; an omitted "unless" downgrades a claim to qualified instead of supported). It refuses causal language on correlational evidence. It collapses copied sources that share one origin, so a syndicated reprint counts once, not five times. And it verifies that every citation actually reaches the passage it claims to support.

3. It argues against itself. After a check, Resolve runs a counter-search: it actively looks for errata, exceptions, and contradicting records that would overturn the conclusion, and attaches an audit of what it searched. The audit states its own limit in plain terms — in an open world, finding no counter-evidence is not proof. Absence of evidence is recorded as absence, never converted into confidence.

4. Conclusions are maintained, not just made. When sources change, an incremental reconciliation finds the affected conclusions and re-verifies only those, cutting off early when a change is a pure relocation or a reconfirmation. In the release evaluation this ran 4.47× faster than full re-verification — which is what makes it practical to re-check every stored conclusion every time its evidence moves, instead of auditing samples once in a while.

What the evaluation says

The release ships an adversarial evaluation set of 64 cases built to fool a checker: mirror copies, stale prices, billing-period swaps, negation traps, causal overreach. A keyword-overlap baseline — "the words appear in the source, so the claim is supported" — produced a false-support rate of 0.8333. It blessed five out of six wrong answers. Resolve's false-support rate on the same set was 0.0000, with supported precision and recall both at 1.0. In the mirror test, naive source counting gave false support at a rate of 1.0; after origin collapse, 0.

The core check runs at 9,448 checks per second (p50 96µs) on the benchmark machine. That number matters for one reason: verification this cheap does not have to be a nightly audit. It can run on every answer, at the moment the answer is produced.

One honest limitation, from the same evaluation: in deterministic mode, Resolve abstains on heavily metaphorical paraphrases — 3 out of 3 cases came back insufficient, with zero false supports. It would rather say "cannot tell" than guess at what a metaphor means. An optional hybrid mode lets a configured LLM judge those leftovers, but only with verbatim quote grounding, and it can never override a deterministic refutation.

When to use it, when not to

Use Resolve when a conclusion has to stay true: price and spec monitoring, answer auditing for RAG and agent systems, research claims you keep citing, any pipeline where a wrong sentence costs more than the check does.

Do not use it for one-shot scraping. If you fetch a page once and throw the text away, a plain fetch is cheaper and Resolve has nothing to maintain. Its value is entirely in conclusions that live over time and must answer for themselves when the evidence moves.

Surfaces

One implementation, every surface: CLI (pagesift resolve check / reconcile / revalidate / history / graph), HTTP (/v2/resolve*), MCP (pagesift_resolve, 12 tools total), Python and Node SDKs, and a C ABI. Conclusions checked through one surface can be read and maintained through any other.

cargo install pagesift        # or PyPI / npm: pagesift
pagesift resolve check --store ./data --source-id pricing \
  --answer "Widget Pro costs $42 per year." --persist
  • GitHub: https://github.com/YOLOW92/pagesift
  • Release notes: https://github.com/YOLOW92/pagesift/releases/tag/v1.7.0

Where this goes next is a direction, not a promise: from checking conclusions toward computing over evidence. Details when it ships.

title: Oracle AI Database 26ai(23.26.4):BAR_CHART - A New Way to Visualize Data
description:
Oracle introduces the BAR_CHART SQL function to make query results easier to read and understand. This function converts numeric or Boolean values into visual bars using characters.

How Does BAR_CHART Work?

The function uses a value to determine the length of a bar. You can also customize its scale, width, and display character.
The general syntax is:
BAR_CHART(value, maximum, minimum, width, symbol)
The function accepts five arguments:
value: The numeric or Boolean value to display as a bar. 
maximum: The upper limit of the scale. Default: 100 for numeric values and 1 for Boolean values.
minimum: The lower limit of the scale. Default: 0.
width: The maximum bar length in characters. Default: 10 for numeric values and 1 for Boolean values.
symbol: The character used to draw the bar. 

Only the first argument is required.

Displaying Tablespace Utilization

One practical use of this function is monitoring tablespace utilization.
For example:

SQL> SELECT tablespace_name,
       ROUND(used_percent, 2) AS used_percent,
       BAR_CHART(used_percent) AS utilization,
       CASE
         WHEN used_percent >= 95 THEN 'CRITICAL'
         WHEN used_percent >= 85 THEN 'WARNING'
         ELSE 'NORMAL'
       END AS status
FROM   dba_tablespace_usage_metrics
ORDER BY used_percent DESC;

TABLESPACE_NAME       USED_PERCENT UTILIZATION    STATUS
__________________ _______________ ______________ ___________
TBS2                         99.06 █████████▉     CRITICAL
TBS1                         93.01 █████████▎     WARNING
TBS3                         20.48 ██             NORMAL
SYSTEM                       16.01 █▋             NORMAL
SYSAUX                        6.97 ▊              NORMAL
UNDOTBS1                         0                NORMAL
TEMP                             0                NORMAL

7 rows selected.

In this example, BAR_CHART displays tablespace utilization as a visual bar. A tablespace with higher usage gets a longer bar, making it easier to identify tablespaces that are running out of space.
Customizing the Bar
You can customize the appearance of the bar by specifying its width and symbol.
For example:

SQL> SELECT tablespace_name,
  2         ROUND(used_percent, 2) AS used_percent,
  3         BAR_CHART(used_percent, 100, 0, 20, '#') AS utilization,
  4         CASE
  5           WHEN used_percent >= 95 THEN 'CRITICAL'
  6           WHEN used_percent >= 85 THEN 'WARNING'
  7           ELSE 'NORMAL'
  8         END AS status
  9  FROM   dba_tablespace_usage_metrics
 10* ORDER BY used_percent DESC;

TABLESPACE_NAME       USED_PERCENT UTILIZATION             STATUS
__________________ _______________ _______________________ ___________
TBS2                         99.06 ####################    CRITICAL
TBS1                         93.01 ###################     WARNING
TBS3                         20.48 ####                    NORMAL
SYSTEM                       16.01 ###                     NORMAL
SYSAUX                        6.97 #                       NORMAL
UNDOTBS1                         0                         NORMAL
TEMP                             0                         NORMAL

7 rows selected.


Here:
100 defines the maximum value.
0 defines the minimum value.
20 sets the bar width to 20 characters.
'#' specifies the character used to draw the bar.

You can also use a CASE expression to select different symbols based on a condition:

SELECT tablespace_name,
       ROUND(used_percent, 2) AS used_percent,
       BAR_CHART(
           used_percent,
           100,
           0,
           30,
           CASE
             WHEN used_percent >= 95 THEN '!'
             WHEN used_percent >= 85 THEN '+'
             ELSE '#'
           END
       ) AS utilization
FROM   dba_tablespace_usage_metrics
ORDER BY used_percent DESC;


This allows you to represent different utilization levels with different characters.

Combining Multiple Bars

Another useful capability is combining multiple BAR_CHART results using the concatenation operator (||).

SQL> SELECT tablespace_name,
  2         ROUND(used_percent, 2) AS used_percent,
  3         BAR_CHART(used_percent, 70, 0, 10, '=') ||
  4         BAR_CHART(used_percent, 85, 70, 10, '+') ||
  5         BAR_CHART(used_percent, 100, 85, 10, '#')
  6         AS utilization
  7  FROM   dba_tablespace_usage_metrics
  8* ORDER BY used_percent DESC;

TABLESPACE_NAME       USED_PERCENT UTILIZATION
__________________ _______________ _________________________________
TBS2                         99.06 ==========++++++++++#########
TBS1                         93.01 ==========++++++++++#####
TBS3                         20.48 ===
SYSTEM                       16.01 ==
SYSAUX                        6.97 =
UNDOTBS1                         0
TEMP                             0

7 rows selected.


This example creates a bar with three different sections, each representing a specific range of tablespace utilization. The first section represents values from 0 to 70, the second from 70 to 85, and the third from 85 to 100.

Treat this as a one-day snapshot from one board's filters; counts move daily. The pattern is still clear: about four in five IdentityIQ posts were tagged on-site, and only 3 of 82 said the employer would sponsor a visa. If you are outside the US, plan around that.

Titles we saw (October to November 2026)

  • SailPoint IdentityIQ Consultant
  • IAM Integration Engineer (SailPoint IdentityIQ, Java)
  • Senior SailPoint Developer (IdentityIQ, BeanShell, Java, REST APIs)
  • Cybersecurity IAM Engineer / SailPoint IdentityIQ and ISC Developer, Yale University
  • ICAM SailPoint IdentityIQ Engineer, GDIT
  • Lead Spec, SailPoint IdentityIQ Developer, Energy Transfer (Houston)
  • SailPoint SME, Robert Half
  • SailPoint Developer, Accenture (Arlington, VA)

"ICAM" (identity, credential and access management) is the term US federal programmes use, so ICAM in a title often signals government or contractor work. The Yale title, and the TCS role in the pay table below, also name Identity Security Cloud (ISC), SailPoint's SaaS product, so expect some posts to want both.

Advertised pay

Role and employer Location Posted Advertised pay
ICAM SailPoint IdentityIQ Engineer, GDIT Remote (US) 19 Nov 2026 $170,000 to $230,000 a year
Sailpoint with ISC, TCS Morristown, NJ 17 Nov 2026 $100,000 to $130,000 a year
ICAM Software Engineer (SailPoint / Radiant Logic), GDIT Fort Meade, MD 10 Nov 2026 $162,037 to $219,227 a year
SailPoint Developer, Accenture Arlington, VA 2 Oct 2026 $102,100 to $194,900 a year

Contract SailPoint roles in the same searches (Mindlance, Robert Half, IntePros, Cloud Destinations, Kaizen IT) advertised about $60 to $80 an hour. Sources: the employers' own posts on Indeed and other US job boards, read 22 November 2026. These are advertised ranges, and the TCS role is an ISC post we kept because it shows how often the two products appear together.

We left out salary-aggregator averages. Some blocked our reader, and the others we could only see as search snippets, so we could not check them.

The skills that kept repeating

Across the posts, the same six items came up again and again: BeanShell rules, Java, REST APIs, connector-based application onboarding, integrations with Workday, ServiceNow and Active Directory, and access certifications. We did not tally exact counts per skill for the US posts, so read this as "repeated across many posts", not as percentages. Here is what each one means in practice.

1. BeanShell rules

IdentityIQ is a Java application, and most of its customisation hooks are rules: small BeanShell scripts that IIQ calls at fixed points. The rule types you meet first are usually Correlation (match an account to an identity), Customization and BuildMap (shape data during aggregation), and Before or After Provisioning (adjust a request before or after it goes to a target system).

A typical correlation rule looks like this. It is illustrative and assumes your identities have an employeeId attribute:

// Correlation rule: link an aggregated account to an identity by employee ID.
// IdentityIQ passes the incoming account in as a ResourceObject named "account".
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

Map result = new HashMap();
String empId = (String) account.getAttribute("employeeID");

if (empId != null && empId.trim().length() > 0) {
    result.put("identityAttributeName", "employeeId");
    result.put("identityAttributeValue", empId.trim());
}
return result;

When a post says "BeanShell", it usually means writing and debugging rules like this across many applications without breaking aggregation.

2. Java

BeanShell is loosely typed Java, so the Java requirement starts there. Beyond rules, US posts often expect you to read IdentityIQ's object model (Identity, Link, Application, ProvisioningPlan), write custom classes or plugins when a rule gets too large, and troubleshoot from logs and stack traces. "Senior Developer" titles lean on this most.

3. REST APIs

REST shows up in two directions. Outbound, IdentityIQ talks to target applications through a web services connector: you configure endpoints, authentication and response mapping so aggregation and provisioning work against a SaaS app's API. Inbound, other systems call IdentityIQ's own REST interfaces, for example to submit access requests or read identity data. Comfort with HTTP, JSON, OAuth tokens and a tool like Postman covers most of what these posts mean.

4. Connector-based application onboarding

"Onboard applications" is the daily work in many IIQ roles. For each application you define the connector (JDBC, delimited file, LDAP, Active Directory, web services and others), the account and group schema, aggregation tasks, correlation, and provisioning policies. On a large programme you repeat this for dozens of applications, so a clean, repeatable process matters as much as knowing the screens.

5. Workday, ServiceNow and Active Directory

These three form the common US pattern:

  • Workday is usually the authoritative HR source. Hires, transfers and terminations in Workday drive joiner, mover and leaver events in IdentityIQ.
  • ServiceNow is usually the front door or the ticketing layer. Users request access in ServiceNow, or IdentityIQ opens ServiceNow tickets for systems it cannot provision directly.
  • Active Directory is usually the first and most important target, provisioned through IdentityIQ's AD integration (the IQService component on Windows).

Being able to explain one joiner flow end to end, from a Workday hire through an identity refresh to an AD account and a ServiceNow ticket, covers a lot of what these posts imply.

6. Access certifications

Certifications are IdentityIQ's access reviews: managers or application owners confirm or revoke what people can access, and revocations flow back as provisioning requests. In practice that means configuring review campaigns, making sure revoked access is actually removed, and producing evidence that auditors can follow. This is where identity governance meets compliance.

What this means if you are preparing

  • Lead with Java and BeanShell. They appear in the job titles themselves, not only in the skill lists.
  • Learn one integration pattern properly rather than ten superficially. Workday to IdentityIQ to Active Directory is the safest choice for the US market.
  • Be ready to talk about scale: how many applications you onboarded, how long aggregation took, how you handled certification campaigns.
  • Check work authorisation before you apply. With 3 of 82 posts marked as sponsoring, it decides more applications than any skill list.

We teach a live online IdentityIQ course from Hyderabad. For learners in North America we keep a section with US and Canadian class times and the same dated job-post table: IdentityIQ training for learners in the USA and Canada. We do not place learners in US jobs or help with visas, and SailPoint's own exams are booked and paid separately with SailPoint.

Method: US job posts and one job-board search read on 22 November 2026. Pay figures are what each employer advertised in the post. Counts and posts change daily.

Written by IAM Careers, a Hyderabad-based live online IAM training provider.
