title: package.json files: what npm publish actually includes
description:
"files" in package.json is an allowlist — but it has sharp edges. Everything below was checked with npm pack --dry-run --json on npm 10.9.9.

Originally published on ReleaseShield.

1. It's an allowlist, with a few exceptions

When "files" is present, only the paths it matches go in the tarball. npm adds a few on its own and drops a few on its own:

  • Always in: package.json, README*, LICENSE*/LICENCE*, the file in "main", and every file in "bin".
  • Always out: .git, node_modules (unless bundled), .npmrc, package-lock.json, .DS_Store, npm-debug.log.

"files": [] ships package.json plus whatever matches the always-in list. Not CHANGELOG, not src/.

2. "dist" means everything in dist, dotfiles included

This is the one that bites. A directory entry pulls in the whole tree, and dotfiles aren't special. Real result from a test package with "files": ["dist"]:

$ ls -A dist
.env  a.js  a.js.map  sub/

$ npm pack --dry-run --json | jq -r '.[0].files[].path'
LICENSE
README.md
cli.js            # from "bin"
dist/.env         # <- shipped
dist/a.js
dist/a.js.map     # <- shipped
dist/sub/b.js
dist/sub/b.js.map
index.js          # from "main"
package.json

Build tools that copy .env into the output folder, write *.map next to every file, or leave a stats.json/meta.json behind all end up published. The allowlist only protects you from files outside dist/.

3. Negate inside the array 

"files": [
  "dist",
  "!dist/**/*.map",
  "!dist/**/.env*"
]

Order matters. Put negations after the entry they trim: ["!dist/**/*.map", "dist"] ships every map. In the test above, the first negation dropped the maps. .env and .env.local stayed until the second one was added.

4. Which ignore files still count

  • Root .npmignore / .gitignore: ignored for anything "files" includes. Putting dist/a.js in a root .npmignore did nothing.
  • Nested ignore files inside an included directory: still applied. A dist/.npmignore or dist/.gitignore listing a file kept it out.

So you can trim from inside dist/, but most build tools wipe that folder on every build, ignore file included. Negations in package.json survive a clean build. Use those.

5. Patterns, briefly

  • "dist" and "dist/" behave the same: whole tree.
  • "dist/*.js" is one level only. Use "dist/**/*.js" for nested output.
  • A typo matches nothing and npm doesn't warn. You find out when a user gets Cannot find module.

6. Check it on every publish 

# what would ship, nothing published
npm pack --dry-run --json | jq -r '.[0].files[].path'

# fail the publish on the usual suspects

Add this to package.json:

"scripts": {
  "prepublishOnly": "npm pack --dry-run --json | jq -r '.[0].files[].path' | (! grep -E '(^|/)\\.env|\\.map$|\\.pem$|id_rsa|coverage/')"
}

That catches filenames. It won't catch an API key a bundler inlined into dist/index.js from process.env at build time. ReleaseShield unpacks the tarball and runs secret patterns over the contents of every file that would ship — free, no login, and the same scan runs in CI via the CLI or the GitHub Action.

title: Next.js 16.4: Cache Components, ensureStatic and a Security Patch You Shouldn't Skip
description:
Next.js 16.4 landed on October 6, 2026, and it's the release where the Next.js team finally says it out loud: Cache Components is now the recommended model for every Next.js app. New projects created with create-next-app get it turned on by default, and it's set to become the default in Next.js 17.

If you skipped the last few 16.x releases or you're still on the old implicit caching behaviour, this is the version worth paying attention to. Below I go through what changed, which features I think matter most for real projects, and how to upgrade safely, including the security patch you should not skip.

Next.js 16.4 at a glance

  • Cache Components recommended for all apps and enabled by default in new projects
  • ensureStatic to guarantee a route stays static
  • navigation() and prefetch() to control what loads during a prefetch
  • next upgrade --agent for agent-driven upgrades
  • Turbopack improvements: 20–25% smaller disk cache, lazy server HMR, a shared runtime chunk and smaller production bundles
  • React 19.3 with stable View Transitions and Fragment Refs
  • Experimental: faster Rust React Compiler, disk cache garbage collection, lazy dynamic imports, worker threads

What are Cache Components, quickly?

Cache Components replace the implicit caching from earlier App Router versions with something explicit. You mark a component or function with 'use cache' and choose how long it lives with cacheLife(). Think of it as a Cache-Control header, but per component.

import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache';

async function Projects({ userId }) {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife('hours');
  const projects = await db.query.projects.findMany({
    where: eq(projectsTable.userId, userId),
  });
  return projects.map((p) => <p key={p.id}>{p.name}</p>);
}

One page can now mix a statically prerendered part, a cached part and a request-time part in the same response. To use the full model in an existing app, turn on two flags:

// next.config.ts
import type { NextConfig } from 'next';

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  cacheComponents: true,
  partialPrefetching: true,
};

export default nextConfig;

ensureStatic: keep your static pages static

This is the feature I like most in this release. The flexibility of Cache Components has one risk: a single dynamic component, like a user avatar that reads cookies, can quietly turn a fully static page into one that renders on every request. That costs server time and money.

ensureStatic makes the build fail if that happens:

// app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx
export const ensureStatic = 'navigation';

export default function Page() {
  return (
    <>
      <UserAvatar /> {/* dynamic: this now fails the build */}
      <Content />
    </>
  );
}

There are three levels:

  • 'navigation': the strictest. Navigations to the route never render at request time.
  • 'prefetch': links with explicit prefetching only fetch static content.
  • 'shell': only static content is fetched when the route is first discovered.

You can also export it from a layout, which applies the rule to every page under it. For blogs, marketing sites and e-commerce catalogue pages this is a cheap safety net.

navigation() and prefetch(): control what loads early

<Link prefetch> removes loading states, but it can also load far more data than anyone will look at. Think of an inbox: prefetching every visible message link would pull whole threads the user never opens.

16.4 adds two functions from next/cache:

  • await navigation() excludes content from a prefetch and waits for a real navigation.
  • await prefetch() excludes content from the route shell until an explicit prefetch happens. 
import { navigation } from 'next/cache';

async function Thread({ id }) {
  await navigation(); // skipped during prefetch
  const thread = await getThread(id);
  return thread.map((m) => <div key={m.id}>{m.body}</div>);
}

Wrap that component in <Suspense> and the prefetch only carries what's above it. The rest loads when the user actually clicks.

Agent-driven upgrades with next upgrade --agent 

npx next@canary upgrade --agent=latest

The command checks your installed version, picks a target, and hands your coding agent the migration guides, codemods and verification steps. There's also an experimental.agentUpgrade config that reminds you during next dev or next build when an upgrade is available. The default policy is 'security'.

Turbopack gains (no config needed)

  • Disk cache is 20–25% smaller thanks to Zstandard compression
  • Lazy server HMR: editing a shared server module only recompiles what the current request needs
  • A shared runtime chunk across routes for smaller downloads and better cache hits
  • Smaller production bundles from shorter CSS Module class names and export name mangling

Upgrade to 16.4.1, not 16.4.0

On October 14, 2026, Next.js shipped an out-of-band security update. 16.4.1 fixes two critical RCE issues (one in 'use cache' functions, one in the Image Optimization API via sharp) and a DoS in App Router apps using Server Actions. On the 15.x line, the patched version is 15.5.28.

How I'd upgrade

  1. Commit your work and create a branch.
  2. npm install next@16.4.1
  3. Run next build and fix any warnings.
  4. Turn on cacheComponents and partialPrefetching one section at a time, not all at once.
  5. Add ensureStatic to layouts that should never render dynamically, like your blog or docs.
  6. Test on staging, check Core Web Vitals and server usage, then deploy.

For new projects, start on 16.4.1 with Cache Components on. For existing App Router apps, take the version bump now for the security fixes and move to Cache Components route by route.

This post was originally published on the TechInnoLab blog. We're a small remote studio building Next.js and Laravel web apps for UK and EU businesses.

title: What's New in React 19: A Guide to the Latest Updates
description:
What's New in React 19

React 19 introduces several key features and improvements, including stable Server Components, automatic memoization via the React Compiler, and streamlined form handling.

New Features and Improvements

  • React Compiler: Automatically optimizes and memoizes components during build time, removing the need to manually write useMemo and useCallback hooks.
  • Stable Server Components & Actions: Allows components to run on the server and interact with databases directly, reducing the amount of JavaScript sent to the user's browser.
  • Simplified Form Handling: Built-in action props on forms and new hooks (useActionState, useOptimistic, and useFormStatus) eliminate repetitive boilerplate for loading states and submissions.

Pros of Using React

React offers several benefits, including:

  • Reusable Component Architecture: Lets you break complex user interfaces into small, independent pieces that are easy to maintain and scale.
  • Massive Ecosystem & Community: Gives you immediate access to thousands of third-party libraries, tools, and full-stack frameworks like Next.js.
  • Strong Performance: Features like the Virtual DOM, concurrent rendering, and server-side execution keep dynamic interfaces fast and responsive.
  • Cross-Platform Potential: Knowledge of React transfers directly to mobile app development using React Native.

Cons of Using React

However, React also has some drawbacks to consider:

  • Not a Complete Framework: React focuses strictly on the UI layer, meaning you must choose and wire up external tools for routing, global state, and authentication.
  • Steep Learning Curve: Beginners often struggle with JSX syntax, complex hook lifecycles, and deciding between client and server boundaries.
  • Rapid Pace of Change: Frequent updates and architectural shifts require developers to constantly relearn best practices.
  • Configuration Overhead: Setting up a large-scale production app from scratch takes significant boilerplate unless you adopt an opinionated meta-framework.

If you're evaluating React for a specific project, consider the following factors:

  • Project type (e.g., static website, interactive dashboard, full-stack app)
  • Your team's experience level with JavaScript/TypeScript

Conclusion

React 19 offers a powerful set of tools for building scalable and performant web applications. While it may require some learning and setup, the benefits of using React far outweigh the drawbacks. With its reusable component architecture, massive ecosystem, and strong performance, React is an excellent choice for many web development projects.

title: How We Built a 100% Browser-Local Image-to-Cross-Stitch Chart Maker (Canvas Quantization + DMC Palette Matching)
description:
A photo can look fine as a thumbnail and still make a maddening cross-stitch chart. A shadow that reads as one shape on screen might turn into several almost identical thread colors. A lone stitch in an otherwise blank area means another start and stop. We built Thread & Grid around the decisions a stitcher can make before either of those problems reaches the fabric. The browser samples the image onto a stitch grid, reduces the palette, and draws a symbol chart with suggested floss codes. The photo and chart stay in the tab during conversion.

Sample onto the grid you can actually stitch

The file picker accepts JPEG, PNG, and WebP. We decode the selected file through a browser object URL and revoke that URL when loading finishes. The app checks both file size and decoded dimensions because a compressed image can take much more memory once decoded. It also rejects unusually tall output grids before building the chart.

The user sets the chart width in stitches. We calculate the height from the image's aspect ratio, round it to a whole stitch, and apply a minimum height. We then draw the image onto a white Canvas sized to that grid and read the RGBA buffer with getImageData. Each sampled pixel now stands for one potential stitch. Compositing onto white makes transparent regions predictable, especially with the option to leave near-white cells blank.

Choose a palette the chart can carry

We round each RGB channel to the nearest multiple of 32 and clamp it to 255. The rounded triples become histogram buckets. We keep the most frequent buckets up to the requested color limit, then assign each eligible cell to the closest retained color using squared RGB distance. When the near-white option is enabled, those cells are excluded from the histogram and left blank in the chart.

This frequency-based approach gives the stitcher a direct way to trade tonal detail for a smaller legend. It has a predictable weakness. A tiny red detail may disappear when a blue background occupies most of the grid. Cropping around the subject can give a small feature more room in the sample. Raising the color limit may also help, although it adds more symbols for the stitcher to track.

Match each chart color to a DMC floss code

For each retained color, we search the bundled DMC palette using a weighted RGB distance. Green carries more weight, and the weights for red and blue vary with the mean red value of the pair. We include the closest entry's code and name in the legend alongside the symbol and stitch count. Keeping this step at the palette level means we look up a suggestion once per chart color.

The chart swatch still shows the quantized color, so the floss suggestion is an approximation. Two nearby swatches can also suggest the same floss code. Review the legend next to real floss, especially when two shades form an outline or a visible boundary. Screen color, thread sheen, and room lighting can all change how much contrast you see.

Make the output readable at the hoop

The chart uses symbols inside each filled cell and heavier lines every ten stitches. The generator counts filled cells with no filled neighbor above, below, left, or right. This catches isolated islands in the occupied area. A single contrasting stitch surrounded by filled cells can slip through that check. A lower color limit can still help simplify those busy patches, and the preview lets you see what detail you give up.

After reviewing the grid and legend, you can download a PNG or print the chart. The print layout splits tall charts into row ranges. Changing a setting invalidates the preview so that the next export uses a freshly generated grid.

One practical check before printing is to look at the symbols with the color turned down or in a grayscale print preview. If neighboring colors are hard to tell apart, the symbols still give you a way to distinguish them. The heavier grid lines help you find your place again after a break.

Turn stitch counts into a fabric plan

The cross-stitch-grid-math companion is a small, dependency-free JavaScript module for planning grid dimensions, fabric cuts, and per-color floss estimates. For example, a 140 × 105 chart on 14-count Aida measures 10 × 7.5 inches. Allow three inches on every edge and the fabric cut becomes 16 × 13.5 inches. Floss estimates are worth checking with a swatch when a design has many starts, stops, or long carries.

The browser builds the chart and its export locally. The page still loads site assets and can send aggregate usage events, such as a pattern generation event with the selected mode. That event carries no image, chart, or filename. Keeping the chart workload in the browser also makes it easy to try the same crop at two color limits and compare the legends before buying supplies.

title: Which IT Services Help an E-Learning Platform Scale for Thousands of Students?
description:
Picture launch week for a new online course. Registrations are pouring in, the first live session starts in ten minutes, and two thousand students click "join" at the same moment. The video stutters, the login page times out, and the support inbox fills up before the instructor has said hello.
That scenario is far more common than most e-learning founders like to admit. A platform that feels perfect with 200 students can fall apart at 5,000, and the reasons are rarely about the course content. They come down to the IT underneath. Here are the services that make the difference when a learning platform has to grow.

Cloud hosting that can stretch

The first question is where your platform actually runs. A single server in a back office, or a fixed hosting plan, has a ceiling. Once enough students arrive, it slows down or falls over.

Cloud infrastructure removes that ceiling. Resources can grow when demand rises, for example during enrolment week or exam season, and shrink again when things quieten down. You pay for what you use instead of buying hardware for your busiest day and letting it sit idle the rest of the year.

If you're still running on older systems, a cloud migration is usually the first big step. Done in stages, it lets you move across without switching off the platform your students depend on.

Load balancing and performance tuning

Scaling isn't only about adding more power. It's also about spreading the work sensibly. Load balancing shares incoming traffic across several servers so that no single one is overwhelmed. Caching keeps frequently used content ready so it doesn't have to be rebuilt for every student.

For video-heavy courses this matters a lot. Streaming lessons, downloadable resources and live classes all place different demands on the system, and tuning each of them keeps the experience smooth.

Reliable databases and storage

Every login, quiz attempt, assignment upload and grade is a piece of data. As student numbers grow, so does the pressure on your database. Slow queries are one of the most common hidden causes of a sluggish platform.
Good database design, regular optimisation and scalable storage for videos and documents keep things responsive. Backups matter here too. Losing a semester's worth of student progress is not something a platform recovers from easily, so tested backup and recovery plans are part of the foundation.

Security and data protection

An e-learning platform holds personal details, payment information and, often, data about young learners. That makes it an attractive target and a serious responsibility.

The basics worth having in place:

  • Multi-factor authentication for staff and instructors
  • Encryption for data in storage and in transit
  • Regular security patches and updates
  • Firewall and threat monitoring
  • Clear access rules, so staff only see what they need

Security also protects your reputation. Parents, schools and corporate clients will ask how you look after student data, and a solid answer wins trust.

Monitoring and ongoing support

This is the service people forget until something breaks. Monitoring watches your platform around the clock: server load, response times, error rates, storage space. A good setup warns you when something is heading in the wrong direction, ideally before students notice.

Support is the other half. When a live class is about to start and something goes wrong, you need someone who can respond quickly. Regular maintenance, bug fixes and updates keep the platform healthy as it grows, and they stop small problems from piling into big outages.

Systems integration

Most learning platforms don't work alone. They connect to payment gateways, video conferencing tools, email systems, CRM software, certificate generators and analytics dashboards. Each connection is a potential weak point.

Proper integration means data flows between systems without manual copying, so enrolments, payments and reports stay accurate even when volumes jump. It also saves your team from spending evenings fixing spreadsheets.

Automation of repetitive work

When you have thousands of students, small manual tasks become big time sinks. Sending welcome emails, issuing certificates, resetting passwords, enrolling students into the right courses, generating progress reports. All of these can be automated.

Automation lets a small team look after a large student base without burning out, and it reduces human errors that frustrate learners.

Help desk for students and staff

Thousands of students will generate questions. Some are simple, like a forgotten password, and others need real troubleshooting. A structured help desk with clear response targets keeps those queries from piling up and keeps your instructors free to teach.

Planning and expert guidance

Scaling is easier when someone helps you see what's coming. Capacity planning, regular reviews and a technology roadmap let you prepare for growth before it arrives, instead of reacting once the platform is already struggling.

How to put this together

You don't need all of this on day one. A sensible order for most platforms looks like this:

  1. Move to scalable cloud hosting
  2. Secure student data and set up tested backups
  3. Add monitoring and reliable support
  4. Integrate your key tools
  5. Automate the repetitive tasks
  6. Review capacity regularly and plan ahead

The order can shift depending on where your biggest risk sits today, but the principle holds: get the foundation solid first, then build on it.

Where a technology partner helps

Most education businesses are good at teaching, not at running infrastructure, and that's perfectly fine. Bringing in an IT partner means you can focus on courses and students while someone else handles the plumbing.

Spark Business Technology's digital transformation services cover areas such as cloud migration, modernising older systems, process automation and systems integration, all of which map neatly onto the needs above. And once the platform is live and growing, their support and maintenance service handles the ongoing monitoring, fixes and updates that keep things running smoothly during busy periods.

Whoever you choose, ask them how they would handle a sudden surge in students. A confident, specific answer is a very good sign.

Final thoughts

Scaling an e-learning platform isn't just about adding servers. It's about building a foundation that stays fast, secure and supported as thousands of students depend on it every day. Get the infrastructure, security, monitoring and automation right, and your team can spend its time on what actually matters: helping people learn.

Have you hit a scaling problem on a learning platform? Tell me what broke first in the comments.

title: Video Streaming APIs Explained: How Players, Content Libraries, and Backend Services Communicate
description:
When you tap play on a streaming app, a surprising amount of communication happens before the first frame appears. The app needs to know who you are, what you are allowed to watch, where the video is stored, and how to play it. None of that happens by magic. It happens through APIs.

A well-designed video streaming API acts as a communication layer between a player, a content library, an authentication service, and a payment system. It allows these components to work together without needing to know how each other operates internally.

If you are building or integrating a streaming product, understanding how these APIs work is just as important as understanding video encoding and delivery.

This article explains how these systems communicate, what each component requests, and where API integrations commonly run into problems.

What Is a Video Streaming API?

An API (application programming interface) is a defined way for one piece of software to communicate with another. A video streaming API provides the endpoints and rules through which clients, such as web players, mobile apps, and smart TV applications, request information and actions from a streaming platform.

Think of it as a menu in a restaurant. The player does not enter the kitchen directly. It selects an option from the menu, such as requesting details about a particular title, and the backend returns a predictable response.

In practice, a streaming platform may expose several groups of API operations:

  • Browsing and searching content
  • Retrieving playback information
  • Managing user accounts and sessions
  • Handling subscriptions and purchases
  • Collecting viewing activity and analytics

Teams planning an OTT platform setup usually need to decide which services they will develop themselves and which they will integrate with existing providers. The API layer connects these decisions.

How Video Streaming APIs Work Behind the Scenes

Most streaming APIs follow a request-response pattern. A client sends an HTTP request, the server processes it, and a response is returned, usually in JSON format.

Consider a simplified example of opening a title page:

  1. The application sends a request containing the user's access token and the content ID.
  2. The backend validates the token and identifies the user.
  3. The backend retrieves the title's metadata from the content store.
  4. The response returns information such as the title, artwork references, and available actions.

Playback involves another request. When the viewer presses play, the player requests playback information separately. The response typically includes the location of a video manifest or stream URL, along with session details or license information when protected content is involved.

The important concept is separation. Browsing information and playback information are often handled by different services. This is why a single screen in a streaming application can trigger several API calls.

This is the foundation of a video streaming backend: multiple focused services communicating through a consistent interface.

The Role of APIs in Video Content Management

Behind the viewer-facing endpoints is another group of APIs used by the platform's internal team. These APIs manage the content library.

A content management API commonly supports:

  • Creating and updating video titles
  • Attaching video files and other media assets
  • Organizing content into categories and collections
  • Publishing and unpublishing titles
  • Managing search and filtering operations
  • Scheduling content availability

Editors and automation tools also use these endpoints, so permissions need to be clearly defined. For example, an editor might be allowed to update a title description, while only an administrator can remove a title from the library.

A thoughtful content strategy becomes easier to manage when the content management API supports scheduling, collections, and bulk updates. The editorial plan can then be connected directly to platform operations instead of relying entirely on manual work.

One practical principle is to keep the editorial API separate from the viewer-facing API. They serve different users, have different permission requirements, and handle different traffic patterns.

How Video Players Communicate With Backend Services

A video player API can refer to the controls exposed by the player itself, such as play, pause, and seek. However, player-to-backend communication is equally important because it connects the playback experience with the services running the platform.

A typical playback sequence includes the following steps:

  • Playback request: The player asks the backend for permission and information to play a particular title.
  • Stream location: The response provides a URL for the stream manifest, which the player uses to request the media.
  • Session handling: The platform may create a playback session to track active streams, enforce device limits, or support playback continuation.
  • Progress reporting: The player periodically sends viewing events, such as the current playback position, so the application can provide a continue-watching feature.

Here is a simplified, hypothetical example of what a playback response might look like. The endpoint and field names are illustrative; individual platforms define their own API structures.

GET /v1/titles/12345/playback
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>

200 OK
{
  "title_id": "12345",
  "stream_url": "https://example.com/streams/12345/manifest",
  "session_id": "abc-987",
  "expires_in": 300
}

Notice that the response does not contain the actual video. It provides the information the player needs to locate and request the media. Keeping this boundary clear helps the API remain efficient.

Handling Error Responses

Players need meaningful error responses so they can react appropriately.

Some common HTTP status codes include:

  • 401: The user needs to authenticate again.
  • 403: The user is signed in but does not have permission to access the requested content.
  • 404: The requested content or resource does not exist.
  • 429: The client has sent too many requests.

Mapping these responses to specific application messages is much more useful than displaying a generic error. Consistent API responses make this possible.

Authentication and API Security

Every serious streaming API needs to answer two questions:

  1. Who is making the request?
  2. What is that user or application allowed to do?

These questions relate to authentication and authorization.

Authentication establishes identity. After signing in, users typically receive an access token that the application sends with subsequent requests. Access tokens are often short-lived, while refresh tokens can be used to obtain new access tokens without requiring the user to sign in repeatedly.

Authorization determines what an authenticated user can access. Someone with a basic subscription, for example, might be able to browse the entire content library but play only selected titles. The backend should check these permissions during every relevant playback request rather than relying on the client application to enforce them.

API keys serve a different purpose. They generally identify an application or integration rather than an individual user. They can be useful for server-to-server communication and third-party integrations. However, private API keys should never be placed in client-side code because they can be extracted from browsers and applications.

A few security practices are important across the entire API:

  • Always use HTTPS to protect data in transit.
  • Keep access tokens short-lived.
  • Validate incoming data on the server.
  • Apply rate limiting to prevent excessive requests.
  • Store private credentials securely.
  • Check permissions before providing access to protected resources.

Rate limiting protects service availability as well as security. It is better to include it in the initial API design than to introduce it after a performance or security incident.

REST APIs and Other Integration Approaches

A REST API for video streaming represents resources such as titles, users, and playlists through standard HTTP endpoints.

Common HTTP methods include:

  • GET for retrieving information
  • POST for creating resources or initiating operations
  • PUT or PATCH for updating information
  • DELETE for removing resources

REST is widely used because it is relatively easy to understand, works with different programming languages, and supports standard development tools.

Although other integration approaches are available, REST is a common starting point for video API integration, particularly when building public-facing or partner-facing services.

Webhooks for Event-Driven Updates

Not every system needs to repeatedly ask another system whether something has changed. Webhooks provide another approach by allowing one service to notify another when an event occurs.

For example, a billing service might send a notification when a subscription is renewed or a payment fails. The streaming backend can then update the user's access without continuously checking the billing service.

Webhooks help keep services loosely connected. However, the receiving system must verify that incoming events are genuine, usually through a signature. It should also handle duplicate event deliveries safely so that the same update is not processed multiple times.

Connecting APIs With OTT Platform Features

The value of an API-first design becomes clearer when different parts of a streaming product need to work together.

Good OTT platform development typically involves several services communicating through defined interfaces:

  • User accounts: Registration, login, profiles, and device management.
  • Subscription management: Plan status, renewals, and access permissions.
  • Content discovery: Catalog browsing, search, and recommendations.
  • Payments: Integration with payment providers and subscription services.
  • Analytics: Playback events sent to an analytics system for reporting.

Consider payment integration. Whether a platform charges through subscriptions, individual purchases, or advertising, the choice of OTT monetization models affects what the backend needs to support.

A subscription-based model requires entitlement checks connected to plan status. A pay-per-view model needs purchase records and time-limited access. An advertising-supported model may require additional integrations for ad requests and playback events.

Designing the API around user entitlements, rather than placing business rules directly inside the client application, makes the platform easier to maintain and adapt.

Common Challenges in Video Streaming API Integration

Even carefully planned integrations can encounter problems. Some challenges appear repeatedly across streaming projects.

API latency

Slow API responses can delay the start of playback. Avoid making too many sequential requests on the critical path, and cache information that does not change frequently.

Authentication failures

Expired tokens are a normal part of application behavior. Clients should handle token refresh smoothly and retry an appropriate request before showing an error to the viewer.

Rate limits

External services may restrict how many requests an application can make within a given period. Respect rate-limit headers, use backoff strategies when requests are throttled, and avoid unnecessary API calls.

Inconsistent responses

Different response formats across endpoints can make client-side development more complicated. Consistent field names, date formats, status codes, and error structures reduce the number of special cases developers need to handle.

Scalability and reliability

Streaming traffic can change quickly. A popular release or live event may increase API requests within minutes. Stateless services, sensible caching, request timeouts, and careful monitoring help the system handle sudden demand without failing completely.

Some teams reduce the amount of infrastructure they need to build by starting with a white-label OTT platform that already provides connected services and APIs. They can then extend the platform through integrations instead of developing every component independently. Whether this approach is suitable depends on the level of customization and control the product requires.

Best Practices for Building Reliable Video Streaming APIs

A few development practices can make streaming APIs easier to maintain as a platform grows.

Keep responses consistent. Use predictable structures for successful responses and errors. Clear status codes and readable messages make integration easier.

Document every endpoint. Provide request examples, response formats, authentication requirements, and error descriptions. Good documentation reduces the time developers spend troubleshooting integrations.

Handle errors deliberately. Return appropriate HTTP status codes and provide actionable information without exposing internal system details.

Version your API. API requirements change over time. Versioning allows existing applications to continue working while newer applications adopt updated endpoints. This is particularly important for mobile and smart TV applications, where users may not install updates immediately.

Secure by default. Enforce authorization on the server, protect private credentials, and review the permissions associated with each token.

Monitor continuously. Track response times, error rates, failed authentication attempts, and request volumes for individual endpoints. Problems in a video streaming backend may first appear as changes in these metrics, long before viewers report an issue.

Conclusion: Why Video Streaming APIs Matter

A modern streaming product is made up of multiple services that need to communicate reliably. The video streaming API connects these services by carrying requests from players, retrieving information from content libraries, and enforcing the rules that determine who can watch specific content.

When designing or integrating these systems, start with clear boundaries between browsing, playback, and content management. Keep authorization on the server, return predictable errors, and plan for API versioning and monitoring from the beginning.

With these foundations in place, adding subscriptions, payment services, analytics, and other platform features becomes a process of connecting well-defined interfaces rather than untangling a complicated system.

title: Micro Frontends Are an Organizational Tool Wearing a Technical Costume
description:
A practical guide to what they are, when they're worth it, how to build them, and how to avoid turning your frontend into a distributed mess

Picture a Thursday afternoon at a growing company.

The Checkout team has fixed a bug that's costing real money: some customers can't apply discount codes. The fix is three lines long. It was reviewed in ten minutes. It's ready.

And it will reach customers… in eleven days.

Because the frontend is one application, it ships as one unit. The release goes out every two weeks, after the Search team finishes their redesign, after the Account team's flaky tests are stable again, and after someone figures out why upgrading a date library broke the admin dashboard. Eight teams, one repository, one build that takes twenty-five minutes, and one release that everyone waits for.

Nobody wrote bad code. The problem is that the architecture forces independent teams to move together.

This is the problem micro frontends were invented to solve. In this article, we'll look at what they really are (spoiler: they're more about people than about frameworks), the different ways to build them, a hands-on example, the costs that rarely make it into conference talks, a checklist to decide if you need them, and a step-by-step playbook to migrate without a risky rewrite.

The real problem isn't your code

In the late 1960s, programmer Melvin Conway observed that organizations tend to design systems that mirror their own communication structure. This became known as Conway's Law, and it explains the frontend monolith perfectly.

Most companies already organize their backend around teams: the Payments team owns the payment services, the Search team owns search. But many still run a single frontend that every team edits. The org chart says "eight independent teams"; the codebase says "one big team that must coordinate everything." That mismatch is where the friction comes from.

You probably have a frontend monolith problem (not just a big codebase) if several of these sound familiar:

  • Releases are a negotiation. Shipping requires coordinating with teams whose work has nothing to do with yours.
  • Merge conflicts are a daily ritual, especially in shared files like routes, global state, or config.
  • Ownership is unclear. When something breaks, the first question is "whose code is this?"
  • Builds and test suites are painfully slow, because every change rebuilds and retests everything.
  • Upgrades are frozen. Moving to a new framework version means every team must stop and migrate at the same time, so nobody does.
  • One team's bug can block everyone's release.

Notice that none of these are about bad code. They're about coupling between teams. A clean codebase owned by eight teams can still suffer from every item on that list.

That's why the most useful way to think about micro frontends is this:

Micro frontends are an organizational tool that happens to require some technical work.

If you keep that framing in mind, most decisions in this article become much easier.

Micro frontends in one paragraph

A micro frontend architecture splits a web application into several smaller frontend applications, each owned by one team and focused on one business area, such as the product catalog, checkout, or user account. Each one is built, tested, and deployed independently. A thin app shell (also called the host or container) loads them and composes them into what users experience as a single product.

If microservices split the backend by business capability, micro frontends extend the same idea all the way to the screen. Ideally, one team owns a slice of the product end to end: its database, its APIs, and its user interface.

Five principles that make it work

1. Split by business domain, not by technical layer. "Checkout" is a good micro frontend. "All the forms" is not. Domain boundaries keep teams independent; technical boundaries force them to coordinate on every feature.

2. Independent deployment is non-negotiable. If releasing one micro frontend still requires rebuilding or redeploying the others, you have the complexity of micro frontends without their main benefit.

3. Share as little as possible. Every shared library, global store, or shared database table is a coordination point. Share deliberately: a design system, a few core libraries, and well-defined contracts.

4. Treat boundaries like public APIs. The props, events, and URLs that micro frontends use to talk to each other are contracts. Document them, version them, and avoid breaking them.

5. Prefer the platform. Browser features such as URLs, custom events, and Web Components make better integration points than clever custom frameworks, because every team and every technology already understands them.

A quick analogy

Think of a shopping mall. The mall provides the building, the corridors, the signage, and the security: that's the shell. Each shop is run by its own owner, designs its own interior, and can renovate without closing the mall: those are the micro frontends. Shoppers experience one mall, but behind the scenes, each shop operates independently. And just like in a mall, if every shop chose its own signage style, fonts, and opening hours, the experience would fall apart, which is why shared standards matter.

Five ways to stitch a frontend together

There's no single "micro frontend framework". Every approach answers one question differently: where and when do the pieces come together? At build time, on the server, at the edge, or in the browser.

1. Build-time integration (npm packages)

Each team publishes its part as a package, and the shell installs them as dependencies.

It's simple and produces one optimized bundle, but it quietly breaks principle 2: every change still requires the shell to update a version, rebuild, and redeploy. You get a nicely organized monolith, not micro frontends.

Use it for: shared component libraries and design systems, not for team-owned features.

2. Route-based splitting (separate apps per URL)

Each team runs its own complete app on its own part of the URL space, for example /shop and /account, behind a reverse proxy or a framework feature such as Next.js Multi-Zones.

This is the simplest true micro frontend setup: no shared runtime, no tricky integration, completely independent deployments. The trade-off is a full page load when users move between sections, and no mixing of teams' work on the same page.

Use it for: large sites with clearly separate sections. Honestly, it's underrated; start here if it fits.

3. Server-side and edge composition

The server (or a CDN edge) assembles the page from HTML fragments produced by different teams, using techniques such as Server-Side Includes, Edge-Side Includes, or composition libraries.

You get fast first loads and good SEO, which is why content-heavy and e-commerce sites like it. Rich client-side interactivity and shared state across fragments are harder.

Use it for: content and commerce pages where performance and SEO matter most.

4. iframes

Each micro frontend runs in its own iframe. Isolation is perfect, since no styles or scripts can leak, and any technology works.

But the user experience suffers: awkward sizing and scrolling, deep links that don't work naturally, slower loading, and weaker accessibility and SEO.

Use it for: embedding legacy or third-party tools you don't control. Rarely for your main product.

5. Runtime integration in the browser

The shell loads micro frontends as JavaScript while the app runs. This is the most popular family, with three main tools:

  • Module Federation: apps load code from each other at runtime and share libraries like React, so they're downloaded once. Best when teams use the same framework.
  • Web Components: each micro frontend becomes a custom HTML element (<cart-widget>) that any framework can use. Best for framework-agnostic widgets.
  • single-spa: an orchestrator that mounts and unmounts whole applications based on the URL, built for running several frameworks on one page. Best for multi-framework setups and migrations.

These tools combine well: a common setup uses single-spa (or a custom shell) for routing, Module Federation for sharing dependencies, and Web Components for a few cross-framework widgets.

Choosing quickly

  • Separate sections, few shared pages? Route-based splitting.
  • SEO and first-load speed are critical? Server-side or edge composition.
  • One framework, several teams on the same pages? Module Federation.
  • Several frameworks, or migrating from a legacy one? single-spa, often with Module Federation.
  • A few self-contained widgets reused everywhere? Web Components.

Let's build the most common runtime setup.

Hands-on: a store built with Module Federation

Module Federation lets one JavaScript application load code from another application while running, as if it were a normal import. It arrived in webpack 5 and is now available for Rspack and, via plugins, Vite. Each app is built and deployed separately; shared libraries such as React are loaded only once.

We'll build two apps:

  • catalog (a remote), owned by the Catalog team, exposes a ProductList component.
  • shell (the host) loads ProductList at runtime and owns the page layout and cart count.

Step 1: The catalog exposes a component 

// catalog/webpack.config.js
const { ModuleFederationPlugin } = require("webpack").container;
const HtmlWebpackPlugin = require("html-webpack-plugin");

module.exports = {
  entry: "./src/index.js",
  devServer: { port: 3001 },
  output: { publicPath: "auto" },
  module: {
    rules: [{ test: /\.jsx?$/, loader: "babel-loader", exclude: /node_modules/ }],
  },
  resolve: { extensions: [".js", ".jsx"] },
  plugins: [
    new ModuleFederationPlugin({
      name: "catalog",
      filename: "remoteEntry.js",                 // the entry point other apps load
      exposes: { "./ProductList": "./src/ProductList" },
      shared: {
        react: { singleton: true, requiredVersion: "^18.2.0" },
        "react-dom": { singleton: true, requiredVersion: "^18.2.0" },
      },
    }),
    new HtmlWebpackPlugin({ template: "./public/index.html" }),
  ],
};

// catalog/src/ProductList.jsx
export default function ProductList({ onAddToCart }) {
  const products = [
    { id: 1, name: "Running Shoes", price: 2499 },
    { id: 2, name: "Water Bottle", price: 399 },
  ];

  return (
    <ul>
      {products.map((p) => (
        <li key={p.id}>
          {p.name} – ₹{p.price}{" "}
          <button onClick={() => onAddToCart(p)}>Add to cart</button>
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

singleton: true tells both apps to use one shared copy of React. Without it, users would download React twice, and hooks can break when two React copies are mixed.

Step 2: The shell declares the remote 

// shell/webpack.config.js (same as above, plus:)
new ModuleFederationPlugin({
  name: "shell",
  remotes: {
    catalog: "catalog@http://localhost:3001/remoteEntry.js",
  },
  shared: {
    react: { singleton: true, requiredVersion: "^18.2.0" },
    "react-dom": { singleton: true, requiredVersion: "^18.2.0" },
  },
}),

Step 3: Load it like a lazy component 

// shell/src/App.jsx
import React, { Suspense, useState } from "react";
import { RemoteBoundary } from "./RemoteBoundary";

const ProductList = React.lazy(() => import("catalog/ProductList"));

export default function App() {
  const [cart, setCart] = useState([]);

  return (
    <>
      <header>My Store · Cart ({cart.length})</header>
      <RemoteBoundary fallback={<p>Products are unavailable right now.</p>}>
        <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading products…</p>}>
          <ProductList onAddToCart={(p) => setCart((c) => [...c, p])} />
        </Suspense>
      </RemoteBoundary>
    </>
  );
}

Step 4: Never let one team take down the page

If the catalog's server is down or its code throws, an error boundary keeps the rest of the page working:

// shell/src/RemoteBoundary.jsx
import React from "react";

export class RemoteBoundary extends React.Component {
  state = { failed: false };

  static getDerivedStateFromError() {
    return { failed: true };
  }

  componentDidCatch(error) {
    console.error("Remote failed to load", error);   // send to your error tracker
  }

  render() {
    return this.state.failed ? this.props.fallback : this.props.children;
  }
}

Step 5: The "bootstrap" detail that trips everyone up

Shared libraries are negotiated asynchronously when the app starts, so each app's entry file must begin with a dynamic import. Skip this and you'll see an error like "Shared module is not available for eager consumption."

// shell/src/index.js  (same pattern in catalog/src/index.js)
import("./bootstrap");

// shell/src/bootstrap.jsx
import { createRoot } from "react-dom/client";
import App from "./App";

createRoot(document.getElementById("root")).render(<App />);

Step 6: Make remote URLs configurable

Hard-coding localhost:3001 in the shell means rebuilding the shell to point at a new version, which defeats independent deployment. In production, load remote locations from a manifest that each team updates when it deploys. The Module Federation runtime (version 2.0, in the @module-federation/enhanced package) supports registering remotes at runtime:

// shell/src/remotes.js
import { init, loadRemote } from "@module-federation/enhanced/runtime";

export async function setupRemotes() {
  const manifest = await fetch("/mfe-manifest.json").then((r) => r.json());
  // e.g. { "catalog": "https://cdn.example.com/catalog/2.3.1/remoteEntry.js" }

  init({
    name: "shell",
    remotes: Object.entries(manifest).map(([name, entry]) => ({ name, entry })),
  });
}

export const loadProductList = () => loadRemote("catalog/ProductList");

Now a release is simply "update the manifest", and a rollback is "point it back to the previous version". (Check the exact runtime API for the version you install, since this tooling evolves quickly.)

What we achieved

The Catalog team can change ProductList, deploy it to their own URL, and update the manifest. The next time users load the page, they get the new version, without the shell being rebuilt or redeployed. That's the whole point.

Mixing frameworks: Web Components and single-spa

Module Federation shines when everyone uses the same framework. But real companies are messy: the Checkout team loves Vue, the legacy admin panel is Angular, and the main site is React. Two tools handle this well.

Web Components: the universal adapter

A Web Component is a custom HTML element. Because it's a browser standard, any framework can render it, which makes it a neutral contract between teams. Its Shadow DOM also keeps each widget's CSS from leaking out (or in).

Vue can turn a component into a custom element in one line. Files ending in .ce.vue get their styles placed inside the Shadow DOM automatically:

<!-- checkout/src/CartWidget.ce.vue -->
<script setup>
import { ref, onMounted, onUnmounted } from "vue";

const emit = defineEmits(["checkout"]);
const count = ref(0);
const onAdd = () => count.value++;

onMounted(() => window.addEventListener("cart:add", onAdd));
onUnmounted(() => window.removeEventListener("cart:add", onAdd));
</script>

<template>
  <button class="cart" @click="emit('checkout', { count })">🛒 {{ count }}</button>
</template>

<style>
.cart { padding: 6px 12px; border-radius: 999px; }
</style>

// checkout/src/main.js
import { defineCustomElement } from "vue";
import CartWidget from "./CartWidget.ce.vue";

customElements.define("cart-widget", defineCustomElement(CartWidget));

The Checkout team builds this into one script and deploys it to their own URL. The React shell simply uses the element:

// shell/src/Header.jsx
import { useEffect, useRef } from "react";

export function Header() {
  const cart = useRef(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    const onCheckout = (e) => console.log("Checkout clicked", e.detail);
    const el = cart.current;
    el.addEventListener("checkout", onCheckout);
    return () => el.removeEventListener("checkout", onCheckout);
  }, []);

  return (
    <header>
      My Store <cart-widget ref={cart}></cart-widget>
    </header>
  );
}

(Load the widget's script once, with a <script type="module"> tag in the shell's HTML.) Any other team can now update the cart without knowing Vue exists:

window.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("cart:add", { detail: { productId: 1 } }));

Good to know: pass simple values as attributes and objects as properties set through a ref; components report back with CustomEvents. React 19 improved support for custom element properties and events, but the ref pattern works in every version.

single-spa: many apps, one page

single-spa treats each micro frontend as an application with three lifecycle functions, bootstrap, mount, and unmount, and a small root config decides which applications are active for the current URL. It's built for running several frameworks side by side, which makes it a favorite for gradual migrations.

The root config registers applications and where they live:

// root-config.js
import { registerApplication, start } from "single-spa";

registerApplication({
  name: "@acme/navbar",
  app: () => System.import("@acme/navbar"),
  activeWhen: ["/"],                    // visible on every page
});

registerApplication({
  name: "@acme/orders",
  app: () => System.import("@acme/orders"),
  activeWhen: ["/orders"],
  customProps: { apiBaseUrl: "https://api.example.com" },
});

start();

The URLs come from an import map in the page, so deploying a new version means changing one line, with no rebuilds:

<script type="systemjs-importmap">
  {
    "imports": {
      "@acme/navbar": "https://cdn.example.com/navbar/1.4.0/navbar.js",
      "@acme/orders": "https://cdn.example.com/orders/3.0.2/orders.js"
    }
  }
</script>

Each application exports its lifecycles, using a small helper for its framework. A React app:

// navbar/src/acme-navbar.js
import React from "react";
import ReactDOMClient from "react-dom/client";
import singleSpaReact from "single-spa-react";
import Navbar from "./Navbar";

export const { bootstrap, mount, unmount } = singleSpaReact({
  React,
  ReactDOMClient,
  rootComponent: Navbar,
  errorBoundary: () => <nav>Menu unavailable</nav>,
});

A Vue app on the same page:

// orders/src/acme-orders.js
import { createApp, h } from "vue";
import singleSpaVue from "single-spa-vue";
import App from "./App.vue";

export const { bootstrap, mount, unmount } = singleSpaVue({
  createApp,
  appOptions: {
    render() {
      return h(App, { apiBaseUrl: this.apiBaseUrl });   // from customProps
    },
  },
});

Angular joins the same way with single-spa-angular, and the create-single-spa CLI generates all of this with the right build settings. The price is a steeper learning curve and more setup than Module Federation alone; many teams combine the two.

Making it feel like one product

Getting several apps onto one page is the easy part. Making them feel like one coherent product, while keeping teams independent, is where most of the real work happens.

Communication: as loose as possible

The golden rule: micro frontends should know as little about each other as possible. In order of preference:

  • The URL. /orders?status=pending is shareable, bookmarkable, survives refreshes, and every framework understands it. Use it for anything that represents "where the user is".
  • Browser events for notifications ("an item was added to the cart"), using the platform's own CustomEvent.
  • Props from the shell for things the shell owns, such as the logged-in user or configuration.
  • A tiny shared store for the handful of values many parts need (user, cart count). Keep it small.

What to avoid: one global state library shared by every micro frontend. It quietly re-couples every team to the same state shape and release schedule.

A small, documented event helper keeps things consistent:

// @acme/events (a tiny package owned by the platform team)
export const emit = (name, detail) =>
  window.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent(name, { detail }));

export const on = (name, handler) => {
  const listener = (e) => handler(e.detail);
  window.addEventListener(name, listener);
  return () => window.removeEventListener(name, listener);   // unsubscribe
};

// usage
emit("cart:item-added", { productId: 42, quantity: 1 });
const stop = on("cart:item-added", ({ productId }) => refreshBadge(productId));

Treat event names and payloads as a public API: document them, version them, and never change their shape silently.

Routing: one owner at the top

The shell owns top-level routes (/products/* goes to the Catalog team, /orders/* to Orders), and each micro frontend owns the routes inside its area. One router at the top, nested routers inside, and no two apps fighting over browser history.

Design system: your consistency insurance

The first thing users notice in a micro frontend architecture is inconsistency: three slightly different buttons, two date formats, fonts that change between pages. A shared design system (components plus design tokens for colors, spacing, and typography) is the single most effective fix. It's also the one place where a shared package is clearly worth the coupling.

Prevent CSS from leaking between teams with CSS Modules, a class prefix per team, CSS-in-JS, or the Shadow DOM. Only the shell should define global styles.

Shared dependencies: share less than you think

  • Share the big, stable ones (React, Vue, the design system) as singletons.
  • Agree on major versions, and plan upgrades as company-wide waves; a breaking framework upgrade still needs coordination.
  • Everything else stays private to each team. Each shared dependency is another meeting.

Deployment: releases become configuration

Each micro frontend gets its own pipeline that builds, tests, and uploads files to a CDN under a versioned path (/catalog/2.3.1/). The shell finds the current versions through a manifest or import map. Releasing means updating one entry, and rolling back means pointing it at the previous version, which takes seconds and needs no rebuild.

Testing: trust, but verify the seams

Each team tests its own app, but bugs love the seams between them. Add a small suite of end-to-end tests (for example, with Playwright) for the critical journeys across micro frontends, such as "search, add to cart, check out", and run it against the composed app before changing versions in production. Contract tests for events and exposed components catch breaking changes even earlier.

Observability: know whose code failed

Tag every log, error, and performance metric with the micro frontend's name and version. When something breaks at 2 a.m., "error in catalog@2.3.1" gets the right team paged immediately, instead of starting a hunt across eight codebases.

The costs nobody puts on the slide

Conference talks about micro frontends usually show the happy path: independent teams, fast releases, smiling engineers. Here's the rest of the picture.

You're building a platform now. Someone has to own the shell, the manifest, the shared event contracts, the deployment templates, the design system, and the end-to-end tests. In practice, many successful setups have a small platform team whose product is the other teams' developer experience. If nobody owns this, it decays.

Performance gets harder, not easier. A monolith's bundler can optimize everything together. With micro frontends, it's easy to ship React three times, load remotes one after another in a slow waterfall, or pay for a framework runtime just to render a small widget. None of this is unsolvable, but it needs budgets, monitoring, and discipline.

Debugging crosses boundaries. A bug might involve the shell's routing, one team's event, and another team's handler, each in a different repository with different release versions. Good observability and source maps stop being nice-to-haves.

Consistency doesn't happen by default. Independent teams naturally drift apart in look, feel, and behavior. Without a design system and shared UX guidelines, users notice that they're moving between "different apps".

Coordination doesn't disappear; it moves. You'll still coordinate on framework upgrades, shared dependency versions, and contract changes. The difference is that it happens deliberately, a few times a year, instead of every day in merge conflicts.

The distributed monolith trap. The worst outcome is micro frontends that still can't be deployed independently: they import each other's internals, share a global store, or must be released together. That gives you all the complexity of a distributed system and none of the independence.

In short, micro frontends trade code-level complexity for organizational scalability. When team coordination is your bottleneck, that's a great trade. When it isn't, it's an expensive one.

Should you do it? Five honest questions

Before writing a single line of configuration, answer these with your team.

1. Is team coordination your actual bottleneck? If releases are slow because of tests, process, or approvals, micro frontends won't fix that. If they're slow because many teams wait on each other in one codebase, they might. With only one or two frontend teams, the answer is almost always no.

2. Can you name clear business domains? Try it: "Catalog, Checkout, Account, Admin." If the boundaries are fuzzy, or every screen needs data from every area, splitting will create constant cross-team chatter. Early-stage products whose domains are still changing should wait.

3. Do teams really need to deploy independently? If a shared weekly release works fine, a well-structured monolith gives you most of the benefits with far less overhead.

4. Can you afford the platform work? Someone needs to own the shell, the deployment setup, the design system, and the integration tests. If nobody can, the architecture will slowly degrade.

5. Have you tried a modular monolith first? One repository and one deployment, but strict module boundaries, clear code ownership (for example, with a CODEOWNERS file), and build tools like Nx or Turborepo that rebuild and test only what changed. It solves many of the same problems at a fraction of the cost, and well-separated modules are easy to extract into micro frontends later if you outgrow it.

How to read your answers: if questions 1–3 are a clear yes and you can resource question 4, micro frontends are likely worth it. If you hesitated on any of the first three, invest in a modular monolith now and revisit in six months.

Situations where micro frontends typically pay off

  • Several teams (often three or more) working on the same large product.
  • Migrating away from a legacy framework without a risky "big bang" rewrite.
  • Platforms that combine tools built by different departments, or by acquired companies with their own stacks.
  • Products whose sections have very different release rhythms, like a fast-moving storefront next to a stable admin area.

A migration playbook: from monolith to micro frontends

The safest way to adopt micro frontends is the strangler fig pattern, named after a vine that gradually grows around a tree until it can stand on its own. You never stop the existing app; you replace it one piece at a time while users keep using it.

Step 1: Map your domains and owners. List the main areas of the product and which team owns each. This map is your target architecture, and the conversations it triggers ("who owns the search bar?") are valuable on their own.

Step 2: Build the thinnest possible shell. Routing, layout, authentication, and loading micro frontends, nothing else. At first, the shell simply wraps your existing monolith, so nothing changes for users.

Step 3: Set up the platform basics. A deployment template (build, test, upload to a versioned CDN path), the manifest or import map, the event conventions, error boundaries, and monitoring tagged by micro frontend name. Getting this right once saves every team from reinventing it.

Step 4: Extract one area: low risk, high value. Pick a section that is fairly self-contained, owned by one motivated team, and changes often, so independent deployment pays off quickly. Avoid starting with the most critical flow, such as checkout. Route that section's URLs to the new micro frontend while everything else still comes from the monolith.

Step 5: Measure, learn, and fix the platform. Compare deployment frequency, lead time for changes, and page performance before and after. Expect to improve the shell and templates based on what the first team runs into.

Step 6: Repeat, one domain at a time. Each extraction gets easier. Over time, the monolith shrinks until it's just another micro frontend, or disappears entirely.

A few rules that keep migrations healthy:

  • Never pause feature work for a full rewrite; extract areas as teams naturally touch them.
  • Keep the design system shared from day one, so old and new parts look the same to users.
  • Delete old code promptly once a section moves, so you don't maintain two versions.
  • Stop when it stops paying off. Not every corner of the product needs to become its own micro frontend.

Wrapping up

Let's go back to the Checkout team and their three-line fix stuck for eleven days.

With a well-built micro frontend architecture, that fix goes live the same afternoon. The team builds their micro frontend, its tests pass, the files land on the CDN, the manifest is updated, and customers can apply their discount codes again. Nobody else had to be asked. Nobody else had to wait.

That's the promise, and it's real. But it comes from organizational design backed by solid engineering, not from a particular library. Teams that succeed with micro frontends tend to share the same habits: they adopt them to solve a real coordination problem, split along business domains, keep the shell thin, invest in a design system and a small platform team, treat boundaries as contracts, and migrate gradually.

Key takeaways

  • Micro frontends solve team coupling, not code quality. If you don't have several teams blocking each other, you probably don't need them.
  • Independent deployment is the core benefit; any setup that loses it isn't worth the complexity.
  • Pick the simplest approach that works: route-based splitting is underrated; Module Federation suits same-framework teams; single-spa and Web Components handle mixed frameworks.
  • Keep micro frontends loosely coupled: URLs and events over shared global state.
  • Budget for the platform: shell, deployment, design system, end-to-end tests, and observability.
  • Migrate with the strangler fig pattern, one domain at a time.

Further reading

  • Micro Frontends, by Cam Jackson, on martinfowler.com: a foundational article on the idea and its trade-offs.
  • micro-frontends.org, by Michael Geers, and his book Micro Frontends in Action.
  • Building Micro-Frontends, by Luca Mezzalira.
  • The official documentation for Module Federation (module-federation.io) and single-spa (single-spa.js.org).

Have you split a frontend into micro frontends, or decided not to? I'd love to hear what worked, what didn't, and what you'd do differently. Share your experience in the comments.
