title: pg_upgrade to Postgres 18: data checksum mismatch fix
description:
Introduction & Quick Summary

Symptom. pg_upgrade stops before touching a single table:

Performing Consistency Checks
-----------------------------
Checking cluster versions                                   ok
Checking for hash indexes                                   ok

*failure*
Consult the last few lines of "pg_upgrade_server.log" for
the probable cause of the failure.

could not connect to source postmaster started with the command:
  ... -c data_checksums=off

old and new clusters have different checksum settings

Or the check passes and the restore fails later with primary and foreign key constraints must use deterministic collations.

Cause. PostgreSQL 18 changed initdb: data checksums are on by default, and pg_upgrade requires both clusters to agree on the setting. Almost every cluster created before 18 has checksums off, so the 18 cluster you just initialised does not match the one you are leaving. A second, unrelated failure comes from the new collation rule for primary and foreign keys, which breaks pg_upgrade during the schema restore.

Fix. Create the new cluster with the old cluster's checksum setting, or enable checksums on the old cluster first and accept a longer window.

# the common case: old cluster has checksums off
initdb -D /var/lib/postgresql/18/main --no-data-checksums

# the better long-term case: checksums on in the old cluster, then upgrade
pg_ctl -D /var/lib/postgresql/17/main stop
pg_checksums --enable -D /var/lib/postgresql/17/main
pg_ctl -D /var/lib/postgresql/17/main start

/usr/lib/postgresql/18/bin/pg_upgrade \
  --old-bindir=/usr/lib/postgresql/17/bin \
  --new-bindir=/usr/lib/postgresql/18/bin \
  --old-datadir=/var/lib/postgresql/17/main \
  --new-datadir=/var/lib/postgresql/18/main \
  --check

Core Mechanics, Signatures & Reproducible Setup

pg_upgrade links or copies relation files between two clusters; it does not rewrite pages. Checksums live in each page header, so a cluster with checksums and one without cannot share files: either every page has a checksum or none does. That is why the setting must match exactly, and why the error appears at the consistency-check stage before any data moves.

Find out what the old cluster has before you plan anything:

psql -Atc "show data_checksums"
pg_controldata /var/lib/postgresql/17/main | grep -i checksum

pg_checksums --enable rewrites every block in place, so it takes time proportional to database size and needs a clean shutdown. On a 500 GB cluster that is hours, not minutes. Deciding which path to take during the maintenance window is how windows get blown.

The full sequence that works, with the check run in the same mode as the real upgrade:

/usr/lib/postgresql/18/bin/pg_upgrade \
  --old-bindir=/usr/lib/postgresql/17/bin \
  --new-bindir=/usr/lib/postgresql/18/bin \
  --old-datadir=/var/lib/postgresql/17/main \
  --new-datadir=/var/lib/postgresql/18/main \
  --old-port=5432 \
  --link --jobs=4 --check

--check is safe against a running old server as long as you pass its real port; the default port for both sides is 50432 and two clusters cannot share one port.

Key Comparison Table

Path Command Downtime Checksums after upgrade
Accept old setting initdb --no-data-checksums copy or link time only off, revisit later
Enable on old cluster pg_checksums --enable then upgrade hours on large data on
New cluster, restore by dump pg_dumpall then psql full restore on
New cluster, logical replication publish and subscribe near zero on
Postgres 18 change What it affects Action
initdb enables checksums pg_upgrade consistency check match the old setting
VACUUM and ANALYZE include inheritance children partitioned tables use ONLY for old behaviour
MD5 password auth deprecated CREATE ROLE, ALTER ROLE move to SCRAM
RESTRICT FK violation is 23001 error handling in applications update code that catches 23503
Generated columns are virtual by default hand-written DDL write STORED explicitly
PK/FK need deterministic collations schema restore fix collation before upgrading
Optimizer statistics are preserved planning after upgrade run vacuumdb --analyze-only after

Practical Edge Cases, Error Fixes & Deep Dive Code Examples

1. Reading the failure from the right log

pg_upgrade prints one screen and writes the detail to four log files in the current directory: pg_upgrade_server.log, pg_upgrade_dump_*.log, pg_upgrade_output.d, and the load logs. Checksum mismatches show up in pg_upgrade_server.log as a startup failure, because the new cluster is started with the old cluster's data_checksums value and refuses the mismatch:

tail -50 pg_upgrade_server.log
grep -i checksum pg_upgrade_server.log

If the message is about a library instead, the extension's build for 18 is missing; install the package rather than trying to create the extension in the new cluster.

2. Collation failures during the schema restore

PostgreSQL 18 requires primary and foreign keys to use deterministic collations, or the same nondeterministic collation on both sides. A cluster that defaults to ICU with a nondeterministic collation on an email column now fails the restore:

-- find keys built on a nondeterministic collation
SELECT c.conname, t.relname, a.attname, col.collname, col.collisdeterministic
FROM pg_constraint c
JOIN pg_class t ON t.oid = c.conrelid
JOIN pg_attribute a ON a.attrelid = t.oid AND a.attnum = ANY (c.conkey)
JOIN pg_collation col ON col.oid = a.attcollation
WHERE c.contype IN ('p', 'f') AND col.collisdeterministic = false;

Fix the schema on the old cluster and rerun the check. This is a schema change you want to make deliberately, with the application tested against it, not discovered at 02:00.

3. Generated columns that changed type silently

Before 18, GENERATED ALWAYS AS (expr) without STORED was a syntax error. In 18 it is accepted and creates a virtual column, which cannot be indexed the way a stored one can and which some ORMs cannot represent. Search migrations for the pattern:

grep -rn "GENERATED ALWAYS AS" --include=*.sql --include=*.py .

Add STORED where the column is used in an index or read by an ORM mapping that expects a real column. A virtual column is a good default for a computed value that is only selected; it is the wrong default for anything you filter on.

4. Statistics, plans and the week after

pg_upgrade now carries optimizer statistics across, which removes most of the "everything is slow on Monday" effect. Extended statistics are not carried, so rebuild them and fill anything missing:

vacuumdb --all --analyze-in-stages --missing-stats-only --jobs=4
vacuumdb --all --analyze-only --jobs=4

--missing-stats-only is new in 18, requires a superuser, and only works with the analyze options. If the cluster defaults to ICU or the builtin provider, reindex full-text search and pg_trgm indexes after the upgrade, because 18 reads configuration files with the cluster's default collation provider instead of always using libc.

5. Application changes that follow the server

Two server-side changes leak into application code. First, RESTRICT foreign key violations now report SQLSTATE 23001 instead of 23503, so handlers that catch 23503 and print "referenced row missing" will fall through. Second, COPY FROM no longer treats \. as end-of-file in CSV mode, which breaks scripts that end a CSV stream with a backslash-dot line:

# before: relied on the \. terminator
cursor.copy_expert("COPY t FROM STDIN WITH CSV", buf_with_terminator)
# after: pass a real EOF, the delimiter is plain data now
cursor.copy_expert("COPY t FROM STDIN WITH CSV", io.StringIO(csv_text))

6. Picking between --swap, --link and --copy

--link is fast and leaves the old cluster unusable once the new one has written. --copy is safe and slow. --swap is new in 18: it swaps directories instead of copying or linking files, which is the fastest option and the least reversible, since a rollback now means swapping back before the new cluster has accepted writes. On a managed service you usually do not get the choice, but on your own VM it decides whether your rollback plan is realistic.

# dry run first, always
pg_upgrade ... --swap --check

Common Compilation/Runtime Mistakes & Version Gotchas

  • Running initdb with defaults and then retrying. Every retry fails the same check; delete the new data directory before re-initialising, or you will debug a half-written cluster.
  • Enabling checksums during the upgrade window. Measure pg_checksums --enable on a copy beforehand; it is the longest step and it does not shrink.
  • Deleting log files before reading them. They live in the directory you ran pg_upgrade from; run it from an empty, dedicated directory.
  • Forcing --jobs high on a small disk. Parallel checks and dumps multiply I/O; a low-memory container swaps and looks like a hang.
  • Assuming extensions were created. pg_upgrade prints scripts to run for extension updates; the tables those scripts touch are unsafe to use until they finish.
  • Skipping --check because the first run looked fine. The check is the only stage that tests the real mode and the real ports.
  • Treating a collation failure as a Postgres bug. 18 enforces a rule the schema was already violating; the fix is in the schema.

Inspect the row counts you expect after the upgrade with the SQL formatter, and compare a plan before and after in the diff tool when a query changes shape later.

Reference: PostgreSQL 18 release notes and pg_upgrade documentation.

title: Braintree Churn Has a Vault Problem Hidden Inside It
description:
If you bill through Braintree, some of your churn is not churn in the usual sense at all. The subscriber did not decide to leave. Their card was replaced, the new number went into the vault in one place, and the recurring billing record kept reaching for the old credential in another. The renewal failed, the retries repeated the same reach, and by the time a human looked, a willing customer had been counted as lost.

That specific failure mode is worth separating from the rest of your churn report, because its fix is completely different from the fix for a customer who wants to cancel. You do not persuade a vault mismatch. You find it, you align the records, and you retry once with the credential that actually exists.

Start by splitting a month of Braintree churn into three piles. First, genuine cancellations: the person asked to leave, or clicked through a cancel flow and meant it. Second, ordinary payment failures on a current card: insufficient funds, soft declines, the timing problems every platform sees. Third, the vault pile: failures where a newer payment method exists somewhere in the customer's record and the subscription never used it. In many stores the third pile is small. It is also the most recoverable pile in the building, and it is invisible if you only read the headline churn rate.

The checks are unglamorous. When a failure lands, is the payment method on the subscription the newest one in the vault? Did an account updater refresh arrive and sit unapplied to the plan? Did the customer update their card through a link and have that update land on a duplicate customer record? Each question is a yes-or-no audit, and a week of failures will usually surface a pattern rather than a scattering of bad luck — one import, one migration, one integration path that writes updates to the wrong place.

This is the useful lens in a Braintree-specific account of churn, where the causes are traced to vault and plan records rather than to customer intent: it treats the platform's architecture as part of the diagnosis. Generic churn advice tells you to improve onboarding and send better emails. Both can help the first pile. Neither touches the third.

Once the vault pile is visible, sequence matters. Do not blast the whole pile with a long retry series; most of those cases need exactly one well-timed attempt with the right credential, plus a clear message if that attempt still fails. Save the longer cadences for the timing pile, where waiting for a payday is the actual strategy. Mixing the two wastes attempts on cases that were never waiting for money, only for the correct number.

Keep a short log while you work the first month. Record each vault-pile case, where the newer credential was found, and which integration path had failed to apply it. That log becomes a repair list for engineering, a training note for support, and a baseline you can measure against next month. Without it, the same mismatch will quietly rebuild itself after the next migration or import, and the team will rediscover it one angry subscriber at a time.

Measure the piles separately for a month and the conversation in the churn meeting changes. Instead of arguing about whether the product is losing its appeal, you can say how much loss was intent, how much was timing, and how much was bookkeeping — and assign each pile an owner and a fix. That is a smaller, duller, much more profitable meeting.

For recovery work that checks the live billing record before every attempt, see Swipe Again.

title: Show me the math: how a Telegram airdrop score stays reproducible
description:
Our first post covered the payout side of NovaPoints — the TON Merkle
claim contract that can only pay what a frozen snapshot says. This one is
the other half: the score itself. If a contract can only pay the
snapshot, the snapshot better be math anyone can redo.

Here's the entire Season 1 formula, straight from the service code
(nova-score-v3):

final = (activity·0.4 + retention·0.2 + missions·0.15
       + referrals·0.1 + reputation·0.1 + events·0.05)
        × risk_band × campaign_multiplier × badge_multiplier

Every input is a normalized count capped at a fixed ceiling — active days
over 30, missions over 30, referrals over 10, special events over 5 —
scaled to 0–1000. Reputation is already a 0–1000 internal score. The
weights live in the season's config row, not in a spreadsheet someone
could quietly edit.

Why store a hash of the inputs

Each score row keeps input_hash — SHA-256 over the canonical JSON of
every input that produced it: active days, eligible days, mission count,
referral count, reputation, special events, risk score, campaign
multiplier, badge bonus in basis points, and the eligibility snapshot
(wallet verified, qualified referrals, days active vs. required).

That hash is the audit hook. At snapshot time we publish the full
allocation dataset; anyone can take a row, recompute the inputs from the
disclosed event data, hash it, and check it matches. A score that can't
be recomputed isn't published — it's asserted.

The risk engine multiplies, it doesn't judge

Anti-Sybil is the part everyone gets wrong. Ours doesn't delete accounts
or hide allocations — it scales them. The risk_score maps to a band
with a multiplier:

Band Multiplier
normal 1.00
monitor 0.75
suspicious 0.25
high 0.00

The multiplication is inside the same published formula — a flagged user
still sees their real component scores in the app, and "why is my number
X" always has a recomputable answer. Fraud signals (shared-IP clusters,
device patterns, referral rings) feed the band; the band feeds the score.

Eligibility is computed by the same function

The airdrop gates aren't a separate gatekeeper — calculateScore returns
the verdict alongside the score, with machine-readable reasons
(activity, wallet, referrals). Season 1 requires: active on at least
half the days since joining, a verified basechain wallet, and 2 qualified
referrals. Only eligible rows become claim-tree leaves — the contract
never sees an ineligible address.

What this still doesn't prove

Same honesty section as before, because it matters: the rules are ours.
Verification proves the payout matches the published formula — it can't
prove the formula was generous. The risk bands' inputs are internal
telemetry we haven't fully published yet; you can verify a score used a
suspicious multiplier, not why the flag fired. And recomputation needs
the dataset — which is exactly why it ships publicly on IPFS at snapshot.

Season 1 closes Dec 30, 2026 (20:30 UTC at the latest, earlier if 1,000
users qualify); claims target Jan 4. Every address and the full token
page: https://nova-points.com/token

Built by Codiologism — the source for all of this is in the repo if you
want to check my work.

title: Node.js Recurring User Reminders API — Monthly and Weekly Cron Schedules
description:
The least complicated reliable design for a Node.js recurring user reminders API is a cron schedule that finds due reminders and publishes delivery jobs, followed by a queue-backed worker that calls each school's public webhook. Do not make the cron request wait for delivery. Give every logical reminder delivery a stable idempotency key, retry that same job after transient failure, and mark it complete only after the destination acknowledges it.

TL;DR: for weekly and monthly edtech reminders, keep calendar calculation, delivery, and deduplication as three separate concerns. Standard cron is adequate for initiating generation, including workloads that tolerate second-level timing jitter; the worker owns outbound retries, while a delivery ledger keyed by reminder, recipient, and occurrence prevents a repeated attempt from becoming a repeated notification. Time zones belong in the schedule data and due-time calculation, not in wishful assumptions about what a five-field cron string means.

Infrai fits at that narrow infrastructure boundary: cron initiates generation and a queue carries delivery work through one plain REST API, without an SDK, so application code keeps the same HTTP contract when the provider behind a capability changes. Its public, keyless discovery surface exposes the live request schema; inspect that schema rather than copying a stale request body from an article.

That is the whole pitch here.

What page should fire at 03:00?

The page says webhook delivery backlog is aging, not cron failed. On-call sees the oldest unacknowledged reminder at 18 minutes, 1,842 queued deliveries, the affected school endpoint, and one delivery key appearing in several attempts but only one logical occurrence. That is enough to decide whether the fault is generation, queue consumption, or a destination that has stopped acknowledging requests.

Work backward. A weekly reminder cron run should have produced a known set of occurrence IDs, and the queue should have accepted one job for each due recipient. If the scheduler ran but generation produced zero jobs during a normally busy window, that quieter signal should have fired earlier. If jobs exist and queue age climbs, the worker or destination is the suspect. A dashboard showing a green cron run is weak evidence; cron execution history retains only the first 4KB of output, so delivery investigation belongs in application logs and the delivery ledger.

Instrument four transitions: occurrence selected, job published, attempt started, and destination acknowledged. Attach the same delivery key to all four. Count overdue occurrences separately from failed attempts, because ten retries of one school endpoint are one delayed reminder, not ten missing reminders. Page on oldest overdue logical delivery and sustained queue age; ticket on a single retry unless its deadline is close.

Thresholds have a cost. Set the age threshold below ordinary second-level cron jitter and harmless network retries, and the pager reports timing noise. Set it beyond the reminder's useful window, and the first accurate alert arrives after students have already missed the class prompt. The service-level deadline should determine the threshold, with a short persistence window to reject a transient spike.

How should an API cron schedule recurring user reminders?

The production flow should be explicit:

  1. Store the user's intended local recurrence and time-zone identifier with the reminder.
  2. Let cron periodically invoke a public HTTP generation endpoint.
  3. Calculate which occurrences are due, including any application-side catch-up after a pause.
  4. Publish compact jobs containing the logical delivery key and the data needed by the worker.
  5. Have a worker call the school's public HTTPS webhook, verify the response, and retry transient failures without changing the key.
  6. Record the acknowledgment against that key before declaring the reminder delivered.

This boundary matters because standard cron syntax has no nonstandard L extension. A request such as "the last school day of every month at 08:30 America/Chicago" therefore should not be squeezed into a clever expression. Run a regular generation sweep, evaluate the calendar rule in application code, and atomically claim the resulting occurrence. The same approach makes daylight-saving transitions a visible application decision rather than an undocumented scheduler assumption.

Paused cron jobs do not backfill missed runs. The generator must consequently scan from its durable high-water mark through the current due window when reminders are important enough to recover, while retaining the same occurrence IDs it would have emitted on time. Keep that scan bounded and observable. Cron execution is capped at 900 seconds, so a large catch-up still publishes work and returns; it does not deliver thousands of webhooks inline.

For this particular handoff, Infrai is a reasonable option when a team wants the scheduler and queue capability behind one HTTP contract. I would try Infrai for cron-to-queue orchestration in a small platform team that expects infrastructure providers to change, because the stable REST boundary limits integration churn; the supporting benefit is one authentication and capability surface for both sides of that handoff.

The limit is equally important. Both the cron target and a push subscription target must be publicly reachable, with HTTPS required for the push destination, so a private-only campus service needs an egress-polling worker or a different product. Infrai also is not a DAG engine and supplies no fan-out/join primitive. Use a specialist when the job is really workflow orchestration.

Idempotency survives retries, restarts, and late acknowledgments

At-least-once delivery means duplicate attempts are normal. A five-minute FIFO deduplication window cannot protect a reminder retried after a longer destination outage, and acknowledgment removes a retained message, so the durable application record remains the authority. A useful key is derived from immutable business identity, for example course-reminder/<reminder-id>/<recipient-id>/<scheduled-occurrence-utc>. Suppose a worker sends the 09:00 algebra reminder, the school accepts it, and the worker loses the connection before reading the acknowledgment: the queue will offer the job again, and no scheduler dashboard can distinguish that ambiguous attempt from a clean failure. The receiver's atomic claim on the stable key is what turns the second attempt into a harmless success response rather than a second student notification.

Ambiguity is normal.

The receiver should claim that key and the side effect in one transaction. Returning success for a previously completed key is correct; sending a second email and then calling it "deduplicated" is not. Sign webhook bodies using the keyed-hash construction in RFC 2104, then verify before claiming the key.

Before writing the scheduler client, query the live capability contract. This runnable Go program calls Infrai's public discovery endpoint with an explicit method, optionally reads INFRAI_API_KEY from the environment, checks every response, and backs off on 429 while honoring Retry-After. It deliberately does not invent a cron-create body: the returned JSON Schema is the authority for that write request.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

const capabilityURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/queue.push_subscribe"

func main() {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, capabilityURL, nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            time.Sleep(time.Second << attempt)
            continue
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("discovery failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body))
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }
    panic("discovery remained unavailable after retries")
}

The discovery call is read-only, so it needs no idempotency key. The subsequent create or publish operation does: use the platform's Idempotency-Key convention with the stable occurrence identity, and keep the receiver's transactional ledger because platform deduplication does not replace business idempotency. A separate "check, send, insert" sequence races when two workers receive the same job.

Retries need classification as well as backoff. Retry timeouts, connection failures, rate limits, and temporary server responses with exponential delay and jitter; honor Retry-After when the destination supplies it. Do not retry an invalid signature, malformed URL, or other permanent request error forever. After the retry budget, preserve enough state for an operator to redrive the logical delivery with the original key.

The alternatives are different tools, not interchangeable logos

Option Integration shape Best fit Main boundary
Infrai REST API Cron-to-queue handoff behind one contract Public endpoints; no workflow DAG
Google Cloud Pub/Sub Managed messaging Topic and subscription delivery Scheduling remains a separate concern
BullMQ Node.js queue library Teams already operating Redis and Node.js workers The team owns worker and Redis operations
Sidekiq Ruby job processor Ruby applications with established worker operations Not a Node.js-native stack
Celery Python task queue Python applications with broker-backed workers Not a Node.js-native stack
Temporal Workflow platform Durable multi-step business workflows More machinery than a single delivery hop

Google Cloud Pub/Sub is the closest comparison when managed message delivery is the main requirement. Its publisher, topic, subscription, and subscriber model is a natural fit for broader messaging topologies; choose it when Pub/Sub is already an operational standard or when topic-based distribution matters more than keeping cron and queue calls behind one compact REST boundary.

BullMQ deserves the Node.js team's attention when Redis is already operated and direct control of workers is valuable. Sidekiq and Celery occupy the corresponding worker-centric territory for Ruby and Python teams. They can all support retrying jobs, but choosing them also means owning the scheduler, broker, and public webhook boundary appropriate to that stack.

Apache Kafka is stronger when retained event history, replay, and multiple consumer groups are requirements. The queue described here retains messages for at most 30 days, deletes them on acknowledgment, limits bodies to 256KB, and has no Kafka-style replay or multi-consumer-group model. A reminder dispatch queue does not automatically justify Kafka, but an institutional event log might.

Temporal is the better fit for durable, multi-step workflows with timers and recovery across a long business process. Apache Airflow is aimed at DAG-oriented scheduled data work. Either is a clearer choice than a cron-plus-queue pair when reminders participate in branching approvals, joins, or stateful orchestration; using them for a single generation-and-delivery hop can add machinery that the incident response path then has to understand.

The trade-off is crisp. Choose the smallest primitive whose failure state can be reconstructed from durable records. For ordinary weekly and monthly reminders, that is usually cron, a queue, and an idempotent worker. Choose Pub/Sub for richer managed messaging, Kafka for replayable event streams, and Temporal or Airflow when the graph itself is the product requirement.

Ship the alert path with the delivery path

Before launch, test a duplicated job, a worker crash after the destination accepts but before acknowledgment, a paused scheduler spanning a due time, and a destination returning a transient failure long enough to exceed the FIFO dedup window. Also test the calendar boundaries the product promises, especially month ends and daylight-saving changes. Those tests prove more than a screenshot of a successful cron run.

Then rehearse the page: can on-call move from an overdue occurrence to its publish record, attempts, response class, and final acknowledgment without reading truncated scheduler output? If not, the system is not ready. The best provider boundary is the one that keeps this evidence in application-owned records while letting infrastructure behind the HTTP capability change without rewriting reminder logic.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and verify the live discovery schema before implementing the cron-to-queue handoff.

Further reading

  • RFC 2104: HMAC keyed-hashing for message authentication
  • Google Cloud Pub/Sub overview
  • Infrai queue push-subscribe capability discovery

title: # Advanced SQL Concepts Using a Hospital Management Dataset.
description:
Introduction.

Structured Query Language (SQL) is one of the most important tools used by data analysts, data scientists and data engineers to extract, structure, manipulate and analyse data within relational databases. Within a hospital management system, SQL can be used to look at patient data, track admissions, calculate costs of treatments, look at doctor performance and produce reports.

In addition to basic commands like SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, there are many additional tools available to help you perform more complex data analysis. Four very important concepts to understand are window functions, SQL joins, Common Table Expressions (CTEs) and subqueries.

This article will explain what they are, how they work, when to use them and how they can be used to solve real world problems in a hospital setting. Examples using SQL will be given for each concept, including an explanation of the query and what you would expect to see.

Assumptions about the data: As the exact data from the hospital and attached class notes isn't visible within this message, examples have been created using a sample hospital database. This will include tables such as patients, doctors, departments, admissions and payments. The queries use general SQL syntax which should be widely supported, but some features may depend on the database you're using. You can change the table and column names to match those in your class dataset.

1. SQL Window Functions.

1.1 What are SQL window Functions?

The window function allows you to perform calculations on sets of related rows. These functions work slightly differently to standard aggregate functions. Window functions calculate values for each row of data based on the specified set/ window of data.

A hospital administrator may want to know:

What is the ranking of doctors based on how many patients they see?

1.2 Understanding the Over () clause.

The OVER() clause tells SQL which rows a window function should consider when performing its calculation.

Example:
SELECT
admission_id,
patient_id,
admission_cost,
AVG(admission_cost) OVER () AS hospital_average_cost
FROM admissions;

Explanation:

  • AVG(admission_cost) calculates the average admission cost.
  • OVER() defines the window over which the calculation takes place.
  • Because no partition or ordering is specified, the average is calculated across all rows included in the query.
  • Each admission remains in the result, and each row displays the same hospital-wide average.

1.3 The Partition By clause.

PARTITION BY divides the result set into separate groups. A window function then performs its calculation independently within each group.

Example: Calculate the average admission cost for each department.

SELECT
admission_id,
department_id,
admission_cost,
AVG(admission_cost) OVER (
PARTITION BY department_id
) AS department_average_cost
FROM admissions;

Explanation: The admissions will be grouped by department_id and each admission will have a column showing the average cost of admissions for their department, but we won't aggregate into one row.

For example: If the average cost of admissions in the Cardiology department is KSh 20,000, each admission in Cardiology will have a column with the value KSh 20,000.

1.4 The Order By clause.

Within OVER(), ORDER BY determines the order in which rows are ranked or processed by the window function.

Example: Rank admissions by cost, from highest to lowest.

SELECT
admission_id,
admission_cost,
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
ORDER BY admission_cost DESC
) AS cost_position
FROM admissions;

Explanation: The highest priced admission gets value 1, then next highest gets value 2 etc. Even if two admission prices are the same, the ROW_NUMBER() function will still assign unique values. This may lead to an arbitrary ordering of the results unless we have a tiebreaker.

1.5 Window Frames.

The window frame determines which of the rows in the window are included in the calculation for the current row. This is useful when performing running totals, moving averages or rolling calculations.
Common window frames are:

ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW will start from the first row in the window up to and including the current row.
ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW will take the current row and the previous 2 rows.
ROWS BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING Will take from the current row up to and including the last row in the window.

Example: Calculate a running total of hospital admissions revenue.

SELECT
admission_id,
admission_date,
admission_cost,
SUM(admission_cost) OVER (
ORDER BY admission_date, admission_id
ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING
AND CURRENT ROW
) AS running_revenue
FROM admissions;

Explanation: The SQL will sort the admissions based on the admission date and admission ID. It will then add up the admission fee and give us a running total. The first row will show the cost, the second will show the running total up to that point etc.

If the admission costs are 5000KSh, 8000KSh and 2000KSh respectively, the SQL will return:

5000KSh, 13000KSh, 15000KSh.

The difference between having an ORDER BY clause inside the OVER() function and having it at the end of your SQL is that it will decide the order in which the calculations happen. Whereas having an ORDER BY clause at the end of your SQL will decide how the data will appear.

1.6 Types of SQL window Functions.

Window functions can be divided into ranking functions, navigation functions, value functions, and aggregate window functions

Row_Numbers().

What it does

Gives a unique sequential number to each row in a window starting at 1.

Why it is used

Can be used to see the earliest admission, pick the most recent entry per patient or to eliminate duplicated entries by ranking.

Example in hospital

To give a sequential count of admissions per patient.

SELECT
patient_id,
admission_id,
admission_date,
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
PARTITION BY patient_id
ORDER BY admission_date DESC, admission_id DESC
) AS admission_number
FROM admissions;

Rank().

What it does

Sorts your data into a specific order and assigns each row a number. If two rows have the same value they will be given the same rank, however there will be gaps between the next ranks.

Why you would use it

It can be useful to find out which of your doctors are performing the best or which department makes the most revenue, whilst allowing for the same ranks.

SELECT
doctor_id,
SUM(admission_cost) AS total_revenue,
RANK() OVER (
ORDER BY SUM(admission_cost) DESC
) AS revenue_rank
FROM admissions
GROUP BY doctor_id;

Dense_Rank().

Purpose: This function ranks your data (like RANK()) without leaving gaps between duplicate values.

Why it's useful: Useful if you want to rank departments or doctors in a hospital that have the same level of performance, consecutively.

SELECT
doctor_id,
SUM(admission_cost) AS total_revenue,
DENSE_RANK() OVER (
ORDER BY SUM(admission_cost) DESC
) AS dense_revenue_rank
FROM admissions
GROUP BY doctor_id;

Ntile().

Function

Split the ordered rows into a certain number of roughly equal buckets.

Usage

Hospitals can split patients into 4 categories based on cost. Doctors can be compared based on the quartile of work they do. Patients can be split into groups based on how long they stay in.

SELECT
patient_id,
admission_cost,
NTILE(4) OVER (
ORDER BY admission_cost
) AS cost_quartile
FROM admissions;

Lag().

What it does: Retrieves a value from a preceding row in the ordered window without requiring a self-join.

Why it is used: It helps compare a patient's current admission cost with their previous admission cost or compare a department's monthly revenue with the previous month.

SELECT
patient_id,
admission_date,
admission_cost,
LAG(admission_cost) OVER (
PARTITION BY patient_id
ORDER BY admission_date, admission_id
) AS previous_admission_cost
FROM admissions;

Lead().

What it does: Retrieves a value from a following row in the ordered window.

Why it is used: It can help examine the next scheduled appointment, the next admission, or a future record in a patient's treatment history.

SELECT
patient_id,
admission_date,
admission_cost,
LEAD(admission_cost) OVER (
PARTITION BY patient_id
ORDER BY admission_date, admission_id
) AS next_admission_cost
FROM admissions;

2. SQL Joins.

2.1 What are SQL joins?

A Join in SQL is used to combine data from two or more tables. In relational databases, data is stored in tables to avoid duplication.

For example a hospital could have a patients table containing information about their patients, a doctors table containing information about their doctors and an admissions table containing information about when they admitted them. Using a join you can write a query to bring together all of this data (patients name, doctors name and admittance date).

Types of Joins.

Inner join.

Function:
Returns only rows which meet the joining criteria of both tables.

Use:
If you wish to produce a report which only contains admissions which have an existing patient record this function can be used.

Example:
SELECT
p.patient_id,
p.patient_name,
a.admission_id,
a.admission_cost
FROM patients AS p
INNER JOIN admissions AS a
ON p.patient_id = a.patient_id;

Left join.

Function: Returns all the rows from the left table, and any matching rows from the right table. If there are no matching rows in the right table then all columns in the right table will be NULL.

Use: Can be useful in situations where Hospital Management want to see a list of all the patients that are registered with them even if they have never been admitted.

Example:
SELECT
p.patient_id,
p.patient_name,
a.admission_id,
a.admission_cost
FROM patients AS p
LEFT JOIN admissions AS a
ON p.patient_id = a.patient_id;

Right join.

It will return all records from the right table and any matched records from the left table. If there is no match then the columns from the left table will show as NULL.

This can be useful if we want to keep all admission records in the hospital.

Example:
SELECT
p.patient_id,
p.patient_name,
a.admission_id,
a.admission_cost
FROM patients AS p
RIGHT JOIN admissions AS a
ON p.patient_id = a.patient_id;

Full outer join.

What it does: Returns matching rows and any unmatched rows from both tables. Any missing rows will show as NULL.

Why it can be used: To help match patients to admissions, orphan admissions and patients with no admissions.

Example:

SELECT
p.patient_id,
p.patient_name,
a.admission_id,
a.admission_cost
FROM patients AS p
FULL OUTER JOIN admissions AS a
ON p.patient_id = a.patient_id;

Cross Join.

What it does: This function creates a Cartesian product of two tables. Basically it matches every row of the first table to every row in the second table.

Why you would want to do this: Can be useful to create combinations, for example all departments in a hospital with each month they reported.

Example:

SELECT
d.department_name,
m.month_name
FROM departments AS d
CROSS JOIN (
SELECT 'January' AS month_name
UNION ALL
SELECT 'February'
) AS m;

Self Join.

What it does:

It joins a table with itself but with different aliases.

When would I use it:

You can use this when you have a hierarchical relationship between pieces of data, for example joining hospital staff to their manager.

Example:

SELECT
e.employee_name AS employee,
m.employee_name AS manager
FROM employees AS e
LEFT JOIN employees AS m
ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id;

3. Common Table Expressions (CTEs).

What is a CTE?

A Common Table Expression (CTE) is a temporary result set that can be referenced by name in a statement using the WITH clause.

They help break down complicated SQL queries into simpler manageable parts as they let us create some intermediate results to be referred to by their name.

In a hospital setting CTEs can be used to aggregate admission information, find out how much money departments make, see which cases are most expensive and produce reports in a hierarchy.

3.1 Basic CTE.

Example:

WITH patient_costs AS (
SELECT
patient_id,
SUM(admission_cost) AS total_cost
FROM admissions
GROUP BY patient_id
)
SELECT
patient_id,
total_cost
FROM patient_costs
WHERE total_cost > 20000;

Expalantion:

  1. The CTE groups the data by patient into a table called patient_costs
  2. Calculates the total admission cost for each patient using SUM(admission_cost).
  3. Selects only those patients with an admission cost > KSh 20,000 We would expect this to return a list of patient IDs and how much they spent on admission (only those that spent more than the threshold) This CTE can make the query easier to read.

Multiple CTE.

A query can define multiple CTEs, allowing each step to build on a previous one.

Example:

WITH patient_costs AS (
SELECT
patient_id,
SUM(admission_cost) AS total_cost
FROM admissions
GROUP BY patient_id
),
ranked_patients AS (
SELECT
patient_id,
total_cost,
DENSE_RANK() OVER (
ORDER BY total_cost DESC
) AS cost_rank
FROM patient_costs
)
SELECT
patient_id,
total_cost,
cost_rank
FROM ranked_patients
WHERE cost_rank <= 5
ORDER BY cost_rank, patient_id;

Explanation:
patient_costs will calculate the total cost for each patient.
ranked_patients will assign a dense rank to the patients based on their total cost.
The final query will return the top 5 ranked patients.
We expect to see a list of the most expensive patients. As it uses dense rankings there may be more than 5 rows returned as some patients may tie in the top 5 unique rankings.

This can be useful to provide to management. Each part has a clear purpose.

Recursive CTEs.

A recursive CTE uses recursion to query hierarchical or sequential data. This is often used to navigate organisational structures or category trees.

A recursive CTE will usually consist of:
An anchor member that provides initial data.
A recursive member which queries the previous result to get the next level of data.
A terminating condition where no further data is returned.

4. SQL Subqueries.

What is a subquery?

This is a query within another query in SQL. This can help you to use the results of one query as a value, list of values or a table for another query.

Subqueries can help you compare values with averages, filter out information using a relevant set of data or perform calculations on your data to give you your final results. This can be useful in hospital reports.

4.1 Scalar subqueries.

What they do: Return a single value (usually 1 row and 1 column)

Why they are used: To compare each record against a single calculated value (such as the average cost of admission in the whole hospital).

Example:
SELECT
admission_id,
patient_id,
admission_cost
FROM admissions
WHERE admission_cost > (
SELECT AVG(admission_cost)
FROM admissions
);

The inner query finds the average cost of admissions. The outer query then shows all admissions where the cost is higher than the average.

Output:

Admissions that have an admission cost higher than the average of all admissions.

As these queries only return a single row of data, if they return more than one row in a situation where only 1 should be returned, many SQL systems will throw an error. If they return zero rows, they will usually return a NULL value.

4.2 Non-correlated subqueries.

They are executed outside of the current row context of the outer query because their query does not refer to any columns

Why use them? To pre-calculate a value such as a threshold or find a list of relevant IDs before applying filters in the outer query.

4.3 Correlated subqueries.

What they do: You will have a reference to a column from the outside query. This means the outcome of the subquery will change based on the current row from the outer query.

Why they are useful: This can be useful when you want to compare a record against other records within the group. For instance looking at admissions where the cost is higher than the average for that department.

4.4 Nested subqueries.

This allows you to nest subqueries, so you can have multiple levels of filtering/calculation.

They are useful when you need to find a group and compare data within this group or to it.

Find patients with an admission in the department with the highest average admission cost.

4.5 Subqueries using IN.

Purpose: To test if a value exists in a list of values returned from a subquery.

Use: This can be useful if you want to find patients that are part of a group e.g. Patients admitted to a certain department.

Example:
SELECT
patient_id,
patient_name
FROM patients
WHERE patient_id IN (
SELECT patient_id
FROM admissions
WHERE admission_cost > 20000
);

4.6 Subqueries using EXISTS.

Functionality:
Checks that the sub-query returns at least one row.

Usage:
Useful for checking there are patients with at least one admission or departments with at least one related doctor.

Example:
SELECT
p.patient_id,
p.patient_name
FROM patients AS p
WHERE EXISTS (
SELECT 1
FROM admissions AS a
WHERE a.patient_id = p.patient_id
);

Subquery using ANY.

What it means: Compares a value to one or more values in a subquery. At least one of the comparison conditions must evaluate to TRUE.

Why you would use it: You could use this to find admissions that had higher costs than at least one department's average.

Subquery using ALL.

What it does: Compares a value with every value returned by a subquery.

Why it is used: It can identify admissions whose costs exceed the averages of all departments.

COnclusion.

SQL window functions, joins, CTEs and subqueries are vital to analyse relational data. They all have their own uses but can be combined to perform complex analysis.
Window functions can be used to rank, total up, average and compare data without losing any rows of data.
Joins allow you to join together related data from multiple tables. This helps you find matching and non-matching data.
CTEs help break down complex queries into digestible parts. They can also be used for recursive analysis of hierarchical data.
Subqueries allow you to use the output of one query within another. Helping filter, compare and calculate.
These concepts can be used in a Hospital setting to answer questions such as how many patients were admitted, how much each department costs, how much was spent on treatments and more. As a data scientist/data engineer it is useful to understand these concepts as you need to make sure you are pulling back the correct information, understanding the relationships between data and performing the correct calculations to get reliable analysis.

The most important thing is not knowing the SQL syntax but understanding what you are trying to do, what type of query to write and correctly interpreting your results.

title: Building Password Guruji: Why Software Testing Matters Beyond Working Code
description:
I've spent over 16 years building software, and one lesson continues to stand out:

A feature working successfully doesn't necessarily mean the application is reliable.

Recently, I've been working on Password Guruji, an open-source, offline-first Java desktop password manager with an encrypted personal vault.

I'm building this application by applying my years of practical software engineering experience. I'm also sharing the development journey openly because I believe feedback from developers, testers, and everyday users can help make software better.

The engineering challenges

Building Password Guruji has raised some interesting questions:

  • What happens when two application instances try to modify the same vault?
  • How do we prevent data loss when a save operation fails?
  • How should encrypted backups and clipboard operations behave?
  • What can automated tests miss that a real user might discover?

These are some of the challenges I've been working through.

The application currently includes encrypted local vault storage, password and passphrase generation, record organisation, TOTP support for stored accounts, and encrypted backups.

But implementing features is only part of the journey.

Making software reliable requires testing assumptions, handling unexpected situations, and listening to people who use it.

Why I'm sharing this project

I'm not presenting Password Guruji as a perfect or finished application.

I've built it to the best of my knowledge and experience, and I know there will always be opportunities to improve.

In my full article, I discuss why I started Password Guruji, the engineering decisions behind it, what I've built so far, the lessons I've learned, and why I'm seeking volunteer testers.

I'm particularly interested in feedback from developers, QA professionals, and technology enthusiasts.

I'm not looking for praise. I'm looking for constructive feedback that can help make the application better.

Password Guruji is currently a testing-stage project and has not undergone an independent security audit. Future testers should use fictional credentials only.

Read the complete engineering journey

I've published the full article on my website:

Building Password Guruji: My Engineering Journey and an Invitation for Feedback

The article covers the development journey, engineering challenges, lessons learned, and invitation for community feedback.

Let's discuss

What's the most important problem you've discovered only after someone else tested your application?

I'd love to hear your experiences, suggestions, and different perspectives in the comments.

title: Deterministic Sponsor-Read Filtering Across 206.9M Spoken Podcast Lines Without Losing Primary Quotes
description:
When you build a full-text search engine over long-form podcasts and lectures, the dirtiest problem is not speech recognition accuracy. It is host-read sponsor copy.

Across the 206,979,125 timestamped spoken lines indexed in PastNoise (spanning 483,987 videos and 2,494 channels), standard TF-IDF and dense vector search repeatedly surfaced ad reads ahead of genuine technical explanations. A guest discussing metabolic longevity or software reliability gets outranked by a mid-roll mattress or VPN pitch simply because the ad copy repeats high-frequency keywords cleanly.

Why Naive Keyword Blacklists Break Real Quotes

Early on, we tested simple phrase blacklists ("use code", "sponsored by", "percent off"). That immediately caused false positives in primary interviews:

  1. Founders explaining pricing discounts, promo codes, or SaaS customer acquisition economics got clipped mid-sentence.
  2. Academic discussions about sponsorship bias in clinical trials were dropped as ad blocks.
  3. Dynamic ad insertion (DAI) breaks sentence boundaries inconsistently across RSS and video mirrors.

To preserve primary-voice integrity across our 938+ curated documentaries on PastNoise, we replaced flat keyword blacklists with a deterministic multi-signal boundary filter.

Three-Stage Deterministic Filter Architecture

Stage Signal Checked Action Taken Goal
1. Cue Windowing Sponsor trigger clusters within 45s sliding window Mark candidate ad span Avoid cutting single-word mentions in real interviews
2. Acoustic & Pacing Shift Silence gaps, loudness delta, and transition markers Snap cut bounds to clean sentence pauses Prevent abrupt mid-word clipping
3. Contextual Whitelist Surrounding 60s topic density (economics, trials, pricing) Override false positives Keep real case studies intact

Because the filter is deterministic rather than relying on stochastic LLM rewrites, every cut across our eight research pillars, including Technology & AI Systems, Business & Strategy, and Psychology & Behavior, remains auditable back to its original timestamp.

Examples From Live Timestamped Documentaries

You can inspect how clean act boundaries and academic citations hold together in the browser on live dossiers such as:

  • AI Alignment Control Problem: six primary spoken acts paired with four peer-reviewed and archival citations.
  • Morgan Housel on Money Psychology: six primary spoken acts comparing behavioral risk across interviews.
  • PastNoise Tool Comparison and the Chinese Bilingual Screening Room for multi-language transcript review.

Each compiled documentary passes through two-pass -16 LUFS loudness normalization so listeners jumping between channels never hit jarring volume spikes.

When You Want Sentence-Level Movie & YouTube Practice Instead

PastNoise is built for long-form cross-channel research and primary-source podcast documentaries. If you want sentence-level spoken English practice, pronunciation shadowing, or instant quote lookup inside movies and YouTube clips, check out our sister project WinkLingo Movie Quote Finder.

title: What a Snow Park Website in Dubai Needs to Actually Sell Passes
description:
Walk out of the Dubai heat into real snow, and the contrast does the selling before anyone reads a word. That is the starting point for a snow park website here. The product is not a generic day out. It is cold air, a real slope, snow underfoot, and the surprise of winter in a desert city. A website that treats it like any other attraction will waste that advantage.

1. Sell the temperature contrast first

The first screen should make a visitor feel the change in temperature. Real photos of the slope, the snow, and people in jackets do that work. Stock winter scenes do not. Show the entrance, the snow, the lifts, and the people actually enjoying it. Short video clips help even more, because movement shows the scale of the space in a way a still image cannot. Keep the copy simple: tell visitors what the temperature inside feels like, what to wear, and what is provided. When the cold feels real on the screen, the pass starts to feel worth buying.

2. Make the session picker the core of the page

Passes and slope sessions are the core product, so the session picker deserves the best position on the page. It should show what is included in each session, how long it lasts, and what is sold out, without making the visitor hunt through menus. A family choosing a Saturday afternoon session needs to see the available times at a glance. If a session is full, say so clearly and offer the next available time instead of leaving the visitor to guess. Good websites for snow parks put the picker where the decision happens, not three clicks away from it.

3. Answer the first-timer question directly

Most snow park visitors in Dubai have never skied. Their real question is simple: I have never skied, what do I do first? Ski lessons and first-timer pages should answer that in plain language. Explain what a first lesson covers, how long it takes, what to bring, and whether a beginner needs a lesson before using the slope. Use photos of real beginners, not only confident skiers. A short checklist helps: arrive early, wear warm layers, collect your gear, meet your instructor. When a nervous first-timer can picture the whole visit before booking, the booking feels safe.

4. Give groups their own simple path

School groups and birthday bookings are not the same as a single visitor buying a pass. They need their own simple path, not a generic contact form. A teacher planning a school trip needs to know group sizes, supervision rules, and how to request a date. A parent planning a birthday needs to know what is included for the group and how many children can join. Give each group its own page with its own enquiry form. Ask only for the details that matter: date, group size, age range, and a contact number. Long generic forms lose group bookings.

5. Add a WhatsApp route for real questions

Some questions will never fit in a booking form. Is the slope suitable for a five-year-old? Can I change my session time? What happens if I arrive late? A WhatsApp route answers those questions in the moment, while the visitor is still deciding. Put the WhatsApp button near the session picker and on the lesson and group pages, not hidden in the footer. Keep the replies fast and practical. A quick answer at the right moment often saves a booking that a form would have lost. Good booking apps for snow parks support the same idea, with clear session details and an easy way to ask a question before checkout.

6. Measure what matters after launch

A launch is not the end of the work. After the site goes live, track pass sales by session, lesson bookings, and how many WhatsApp chats turn into visits. If evening sessions sell out while mornings stay quiet, the homepage should promote the quieter times. If lesson pages get traffic but few bookings, the lesson page may need a simpler booking step or a stronger first-timer checklist. If WhatsApp chats are high but visits are low, the replies may need to be faster or clearer. These numbers tell the team what to fix first, instead of guessing.

A snow park in Dubai has a rare advantage: it sells an experience that cannot be found outside. The website should protect that advantage by showing the cold honestly, making sessions easy to book, guiding first-timers, serving groups properly, and answering questions quickly.

See how RapidBizz approaches websites like this, with booking flows built around the way visitors actually decide.

title: Replay-Safe Verification Tokens in PostgreSQL
description:
Email verification looks like a small feature: create a token, send a message, and mark the account as verified when the user clicks it. In a real REST API, the click can arrive twice, arrive after expiry, or race with a retry from a mobile client. If the endpoint treats every request as a fresh command, the database state becomes hard to explain.

This post describes a replay-safe design for verification tokens in PostgreSQL. The same boundary is useful when a disposable email account is used in an integration test: the test should be able to repeat a request and still get a predictable result.

Why a token endpoint needs a replay policy

A verification token is a capability with a short lifetime. It should normally produce one successful transition:

issued -> consumed

Several other outcomes are possible:

  • The token does not exist.
  • The token has expired.
  • Another request already consumed it.
  • Two requests tried to consume it at nearly the same time.

These outcomes should not be hidden behind a generic 500 response. A client may safely retry a network timeout, but it needs to know whether the first request actually succeeded. An OAuth flow has a similar concern; an OAuth replay boundary is a useful related pattern.

The important decision is to make the state transition authoritative in the database, not in application memory. A process restart, a second API instance, or a slow queue worker should not change the rule.

Model the verification as a database state transition

Keep the token record separate from the user record. This gives the API an audit-friendly place to record when a token was issued, consumed, and rejected.

CREATE TABLE email_verification_tokens (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  token_digest BYTEA NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  expires_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  consumed_at TIMESTAMPTZ,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE INDEX email_verification_tokens_user_idx
  ON email_verification_tokens (user_id);

Store a digest rather than the raw token. The raw value belongs in the link sent to the user, while a database leak should not immediately turn every unexpired link into a usable credential. The digest column also gives us a stable lookup key.

Do not use a boolean such as is_verified on the token alone. A timestamp tells us when the transition happened and makes support investigations less guessy. The user account can still have its own verified state, updated in the same transaction.

Use PostgreSQL to claim a token once

The consume operation should check validity and claim the row in one statement. A conditional update is often simpler and safer than selecting first and updating later:

UPDATE email_verification_tokens
SET consumed_at = now()
WHERE token_digest = $1
  AND consumed_at IS NULL
  AND expires_at > now()
RETURNING user_id, consumed_at;

If this returns one row, the request won the claim. If it returns zero rows, the API can perform a bounded follow-up lookup to distinguish expired, unknown, and already-consumed states. That lookup is informational; it must not be used to decide whether the token is valid.

Then update the user inside the same transaction:

UPDATE users
SET email_verified_at = COALESCE(email_verified_at, now())
WHERE id = $1;

The COALESCE makes the user update tolerant of an already verified account, while the token claim remains one-time. This is a small but important distinction: verification of the account can be idempotent even though consumption of a particular token is not repeatable.

Make the REST API response deterministic

A useful endpoint contract might be:

POST /v1/email-verifications/consume

Return a success response only when the transaction claimed the token and updated the account. For a second click, use a stable conflict response such as 409 with a machine-readable code:

{
  "error": "verification_token_unavailable",
  "reason": "consumed_or_expired"
}

Avoid exposing whether an arbitrary token belongs to a real account. For unknown, expired, and consumed tokens, a deliberately similar response prevents the endpoint from becoming an account-enumeration oracle. The exact status code can vary with your product contract, but it should be documented and tested.

If the client times out after the commit, a retry may receive the conflict response even though the first request succeeded. That is why the client should refresh account state after an ambiguous result. A request ID and structured logs make this diagnosis much less painfull.

For test environments, isolate inboxes and credentials by run. Run-scoped email test data helps prevent one build from consuming another build's token. A fixture named temp gamil com should be treated as ordinary test input, not as a special case in production validation.

Test concurrency and expiry

The most valuable tests are not only happy-path tests. Add cases for:

  1. A valid token is consumed once and verifies the user.
  2. The same token is submitted twice; exactly one request claims it.
  3. Two concurrent requests use the same digest; one gets success and one gets the documented conflict.
  4. An expired token cannot be claimed, even if the application clock has not yet cleaned it up.
  5. A malformed token does not cause an expensive unbounded database query.
  6. A transaction rollback leaves both the token and user unchanged.

Run the concurrency case against a real PostgreSQL instance. Mocks rarely reproduce row locks, transaction isolation, or the timing around RETURNING. Add a short comment to the test explaining the expected winner behavior; otherwise a future refactor may accidentally turn the race into two successes.

A practical checklist

  • Hash verification tokens before storing them.
  • Put expiry and consumption checks in the conditional update.
  • Update token and account state in one transaction.
  • Return a stable, documented error for replay and expiry.
  • Avoid leaking account existence through token errors.
  • Test concurrent requests against PostgreSQL.
  • Log a request ID, token record ID, and outcome without logging the raw token.
  • Keep email delivery separate from the database claim operation.

The design is not complicated, but the ordering matters. Let PostgreSQL own the one-time state transition, let the REST API expose a predictable contract, and let retries be an expected behavior instead of an incident. That gives backend services a verification flow that remains understandable under duplicate clicks, slow networks, and parallel workers.

title: I fixed Quarkus dev mode running two Maven steps in the wrong order
description:
mvn clean compile quarkus:dev generated the gRPC classes. mvn clean quarkus:dev didn't. Same project, same settings, one word apart.

yersan reported that in issue #57633, and I fixed it in quarkusio/quarkus#57866. The cause: two build steps ran back to front, but only in dev mode.

The setup

Quarkus is a Java framework for web services. Dev mode is its live reload mode: start it once, edit your code, and the running app picks up the changes. With gRPC, a way for services to call each other where messages are described in .proto files, Quarkus can generate Java classes from .proto files that sit inside a library you depend on. One line in application.properties turns it on:

quarkus.generate-code.grpc.scan-for-proto=<groupId>:<artifactId>

In dev mode, that line was simply ignored.

The clue was in the log

yersan had already found it:

[INFO] Invoking quarkus:3.40.1.1:generate-code (default-generate-code) @ app
[INFO] Invoking resources:3.3.1:resources (default-resources) @ app

Code generation ran first. Copying resources, the step that puts application.properties into target/classes, ran second. The generator checked for its settings the way a mail carrier might check a mailbox before the letter has been dropped in, found nothing, and moved on.

Why only dev mode

Quick Maven vocabulary: a build is a series of stages called phases, and each phase runs small jobs called goals. The quarkus packaging comes with a recipe that puts two goals in the same phase: resources:resources, then quarkus:generate-code. Maven keeps that order by giving each goal a priority number, and the lowest runs first.

I checked on a small test app: plain mvn clean process-test-resources ran resources before generate-code. Maven was fine.

Dev mode skips Maven for those early goals and calls them directly. It lined them up in the order the plugins are declared and never looked at the priority. The Quarkus plugin is written in your pom.xml, and the resources plugin is one Maven slips in afterwards. So code generation jumped the queue. The test versions of both goals had the same problem.

The fix: do what Maven does

No gRPC special case. Dev mode now sorts each phase's goals by priority. This is the line that does it:

executions.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(pe -> pe.execution.getPriority()));

Java's List.sort is stable, so goals with equal priority stay in their original order and your own plugins don't get shuffled.

One goal needed extra care. If you list generate-code without a phase, dev mode puts a copy of it into compile, and that copy must run before compiling. I gave it Integer.MIN_VALUE, the smallest possible int, so it always sorts first.

Review made it smaller

My first version also kept the old trick of inserting that copy at the front of the list. cescoffier asked: "Why keep the index here?" Fair point. The smallest priority already did that job, so I dropped the insert and added a test that adds the copy last and checks it still lands first.

aloubyansky then asked why a specific priority was needed at all. Without it, the copy shares priority 0 with most goals, so it could land behind an earlier compile goal, and the compiler could then run before the generated code exists. I explained it in the thread and the code stayed the same. Both gsmet and aloubyansky signed off, and aloubyansky hit merge on 5 November 2026.

The lesson

If your code takes over part of another tool's work, follow that tool's ordering rule exactly, not just the order you happened to see in one log. Matching Maven fixed the test goals at no extra cost, and review turned two mechanisms into one.

Have you ever had a dev mode or watch mode behave differently from your normal build? What turned out to be the cause?

The full story, with all the code, is on my blog: https://ashokramsi.hashnode.dev/quarkus-dev-mode-goal-order
