title: 5 MySQL EXPLAIN Signals That Tell You Exactly Why Your Query Is Slow
description:
Most slow MySQL queries announce themselves if you know where to look. You do not need a monitoring dashboard or a database consultant — you need EXPLAIN, and five signals in its output that each point at a different fix.

1. type: ALL — the full table scan

This is the loudest signal. MySQL read every row of the table no matter what your WHERE said. On a lookup table with 50 rows, nobody cares. On a table with 500,000 rows, this is your whole problem. The fix is almost always an index on the column in the WHERE clause. Run the query again after adding it and watch type move to ref.

2. key: NULL — no index was used at all

Different from signal 1 in one important way: sometimes possible_keys lists an index and key is still NULL. That means the index exists and MySQL refused it. The usual reason is the query itself — a function wrapped around the indexed column, like DATE(created_at) = '2026-11-20', or a comparison against a value of the wrong type. Rewrite the condition so the index can serve it: a date range instead of DATE(), matching types on both sides.

3. Extra: Using filesort — MySQL sorted it by hand

The index found the rows, but they came back in the wrong order, so MySQL sorted them itself — in memory if it fits, on disk if it does not. The cure is a composite index that covers the filter and the sort in one order: equality columns first, then the sort column. An index on (user_id, created_at) serves WHERE user_id = 1234 ORDER BY created_at DESC with no sort at all — MySQL reads the index backwards and stops after your LIMIT.

4. rows is huge and the result is tiny

rows is an estimate, not a count, but the ratio tells the story. If MySQL expects to examine 498,000 rows to hand you back 20, the plan is wrong even if the query eventually finishes. Compare rows with the actual result size. A ratio in the thousands means a missing index or a condition the optimizer cannot use. When the estimate itself looks suspicious, EXPLAIN ANALYZE (MySQL 8.0.18+) runs the query and reports the real numbers.

5. OFFSET grows the pain on every page

This one does not show up as a single bad column — it shows up as a query that is fast on page 1 and slow on page 1,000. LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20000 still reads and discards 20,000 rows. The fix is keyset pagination: remember the last id you showed and ask for the next rows after it with WHERE id > 20000 ORDER BY id LIMIT 20. The index does the work, and page 1,000 costs the same as page 1.

The habit

None of these signals needs a rewrite of your application. The habit is small: when a query is slow, run EXPLAIN before you change anything, read these five signals, and make the smallest change that moves one of them. I wrote up the full walkthrough — finding the slow queries in the slow query log, reading every column, and verifying each fix — here:

https://rajadevsolutions.online/blog/how-to-fix-slow-mysql-queries-with-explain

Fix the plan first. The query is usually innocent.

title: Only 19.66% of matches reach the model: auditing a coverage gate decided by source count, not difficulty
description:
Every accuracy number I have shipped carried a hidden caveat: it was computed on the subset of matches the pipeline happened to touch. Nobody reported the subset. The accuracy travelled; the denominator stayed home.

This post audits that denominator on a production football prediction system. The pool is 86,802 completed matches with an actual result from 2026-06-21 onward. The prediction table holds 49,471 rows across 3,861 models, 48,766 of them graded, at a pooled hit rate of 56.98%. That is the number everyone quotes. The number nobody quotes is 19.66%.

1. The denominator, stated plainly

Coverage: of the matches that finished with a result, how many have at least one prediction row pointing at them.

WITH pool AS (
  SELECT id FROM nami_matches
  WHERE status_id = 8
    AND match_time >= '2026-06-21'
    AND home_score_regular IS NOT NULL
), predicted AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT match_id FROM ai_predictions
)
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM pool) AS pool,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM pool p JOIN predicted x ON x.match_id = p.id) AS covered,
       round((SELECT count(*) FROM pool p JOIN predicted x ON x.match_id = p.id)::numeric
             / (SELECT count(*) FROM pool) * 100, 2) AS coverage_pct;

 pool  | covered | coverage_pct
-------+---------+--------------
 86802 |   17067 |        19.66

Four out of five finished matches never enter a model. That alone is not a bug — no system predicts everything. The problem is what the 80.34% is made of, because if the skipped matches differ systematically from the covered ones, then 56.98% is a number about a population you did not define.

The monthly split shows the first systematic difference, and it is not about football at all:

match month pool covered coverage
2026-06 1,601 39 2.44%
2026-07 11,364 77 0.68%
2026-08 19,307 10 0.05%
2026-09 19,624 3,043 15.51%
2026-10 21,414 9,036 42.20%
2026-11 13,492 4,862 36.04%

August coverage is 0.05% — ten matches out of 19,307. The service was not running that month, and its history sits in the same table as the months when it was. Every pooled statistic over the whole table is a weighted average of a pre-launch and a production period, with weights set by fixture counts. October had both the most fixtures and the highest coverage, so it dominates the headline without anyone deciding that it should.

2. The gate is a join, not a judgement

To see what separates covered from uncovered matches, the useful question is not "was this match hard?" but "did the pipeline have anything to read?" It reads quoted prices. So cross-tabulate.

WITH pool AS (
  SELECT id FROM nami_matches
  WHERE status_id = 8 AND match_time >= '2026-06-21'
    AND home_score_regular IS NOT NULL
), predicted AS (SELECT DISTINCT match_id FROM ai_predictions),
  priced AS (SELECT DISTINCT match_id FROM nami_europe_odds)
SELECT (x.match_id IS NOT NULL) AS covered,
       (q.match_id IS NOT NULL) AS has_quotes,
       count(*) AS matches
FROM pool p
LEFT JOIN predicted x ON x.match_id = p.id
LEFT JOIN priced    q ON q.match_id = p.id
GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 1, 2;

 covered | has_quotes | matches
---------+------------+---------
 f       | f          |   38044
 f       | t          |   31691
 t       | f          |     139
 t       | t          |   16928

Read the corners. Of 38,183 matches with no quote anywhere in the price table, 139 were predicted — 0.36%. Of 48,619 with at least one quote, 16,928 were predicted — 34.82%. The gate multiplies your chance of being covered 96×, and has nothing to do with the fixture.

3. It is not cherry-picking, and that is the interesting part

The natural suspicion is that the system prefers easy matches. I expected to find that. I did not.

For each match, take every source's last price in the seven days before kickoff, invert, average, normalise. The maximum of the resulting triple is a difficulty proxy: 0.40 is a near coin-flip, 0.85 a heavy favourite.

CREATE TEMP TABLE imp AS
WITH last AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (o.match_id, o.company_id)
         o.match_id, o.eu_home, o.eu_draw, o.eu_away
  FROM nami_europe_odds o JOIN pool p ON p.id = o.match_id
  WHERE o.changed_at <= p.match_time
    AND o.changed_at >  p.match_time - interval '7 days'
    AND o.eu_home > 1 AND o.eu_draw > 1 AND o.eu_away > 1
  ORDER BY o.match_id, o.company_id, o.changed_at DESC
)
SELECT match_id, count(*) AS companies,
       avg(1.0/eu_home) AS rh, avg(1.0/eu_draw) AS rd, avg(1.0/eu_away) AS ra
FROM last GROUP BY match_id;

Bucket by greatest(ph, pd, pa) and measure coverage inside each bucket:

market max probability matches covered coverage
< 0.45 17,469 5,895 33.7%
0.45–0.55 13,576 4,822 35.5%
0.55–0.65 8,694 3,175 36.5%
0.65–0.75 4,800 1,736 36.2%
≥ 0.75 3,693 1,280 34.7%

Flat. Hardest to easiest spans 2.8 points, and not monotonically — the peak is in the middle. Whatever the gate does, it is not filtering on how predictable the match looks.

Now bucket by how many sources quoted a price at all:

quote sources matches coverage
1 4,497 2.4%
2–3 3,513 8.0%
4–8 6,994 18.8%
9–20 10,664 28.0%
20+ 22,564 54.2%

Monotone, 2.4% to 54.2% — a factor of 22. Splitting both dimensions at once:

sources max prob < 0.55 max prob ≥ 0.55
1–3 4.3% (n=5,013) 5.8% (n=2,997)
4–8 17.0% (n=4,343) 21.7% (n=2,651)
9–20 27.6% (n=6,693) 28.6% (n=3,971)
20+ 52.8% (n=14,996) 56.9% (n=7,568)

Within a source band, going from a contested match to a lopsided one buys 1.03×–1.28× more coverage. Moving across bands buys 3.9×–12.3×. The gate is plumbing: it responds to how many feeds answered, not to whether the match is worth modelling.

This is good news for the 56.98%: within the priced population, coverage looks near-random with respect to difficulty, so the hit rate is not inflated by an easier subpopulation. It is also the bad news, because a random gate is still a gate. The 31,691 priced-but-uncovered matches are not a sample you can ignore — they are the population you declined to score.

4. Three hit rates from the same 16,908 matches

Here is where the denominator bites. Within the seven-day price window: 48,232 matches, 16,908 covered.

aggregation value
rows graded 48,373
hits 27,561
pooled (row-weighted) 56.98%
match-mean (per-match rate, then average) 57.32%
match-level "at least one hit" 64.95% (10,982 / 16,908)
mean prediction rows per covered match 2.86

The distribution behind that mean is the part I did not expect: 11,548 covered matches get exactly one prediction row, 1,036 get two, 455 get three, and fifteen carry more than 100 (max 358). That is 68.3% single-row. The tail makes the pooled number look like it rests on a large sample; it is a large sample of rows and a thin sample of matches.

Splitting by row count shows no accuracy premium in that tail: 57.36% for single-row matches, 58.54% for 2–3 rows, 56.68% for 4+. More models per match buys variance reduction and a bigger denominator, not accuracy.

5. What the gate costs

First, the uncovered priced population has no accuracy estimate. Those 31,691 matches are 65% of the priced pool and skew toward thin feeds — 8,010 carry three or fewer quoted sources, where coverage collapses to 2.4%–8.0%. That region of the input space is effectively unmeasured. A "56.98% accuracy" headline therefore rests heaviest on the 20+ source band: 22,564 matches, 26% of all finished fixtures.

Second, monthly drift moves more than any model comparison I have run:

month graded rows hit rate
2026-06 2,645 63.18%
2026-07 2,723 50.42%
2026-08 44 56.82%
2026-09 9,030 59.37%
2026-10 21,148 56.92%
2026-11 13,176 55.56%

A 12.8-point swing between July and June on samples of 2,645 and 2,723 rows. Shift the reporting window by one month and the headline moves further than most model-level differences anyone argues about.

6. A coverage-aware reporting contract

The fix is not to raise coverage. It is to make coverage a mandatory field on every accuracy claim. This is the gate I run before any number leaves the building.

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Claim:
    metric: str
    value: float
    pool: int         # finished matches with a result
    covered: int      # matches with >= 1 prediction row
    min_sources: int  # quoted-source floor for this slice

    def check(self) -> tuple[bool, list[str]]:
        errs = []
        cov = self.covered / self.pool if self.pool else 0.0
        if cov < 0.30:
            errs.append(f"coverage {cov:.2%} too thin to quote a point estimate")
        if self.min_sources < 9:
            errs.append("slice below 9 sources is unmeasured (coverage 2-19%)")
        return (not errs), errs

c = Claim("hit_rate", 0.5698, pool=86802, covered=17067, min_sources=0)
print(c.check())

False ['coverage 19.66% too thin to quote a point estimate',
       'slice below 9 sources is unmeasured (coverage 2-19%)']

The claim fails its own gate, which is the correct outcome. The defensible version is narrower: 56.98% on 48,373 graded rows from 16,908 matches, restricted to fixtures with a pre-kickoff quote, skewed toward the 9+ source band, blended across six months of unequal pipeline availability. That sentence is worse as marketing and better as a measurement.

One more structural fact limits every coverage report here: nami_matches.competition_id holds 1,219 distinct values, but only 3,986 of 86,802 matches (4.59%) join to nami_competitions.id. Any per-league coverage table rests on 4.59% of the pool, so I do not publish one. Fixing that key space is worth more than another model.

7. What I am not claiming

I am not claiming coverage caused the hit rate, or that raising coverage would preserve it. A gate that is random on difficulty means the covered set is not easier, which supports external validity inside the priced population — it says nothing about the 38,183 unpriced matches, where coverage is 0.36% and no estimate exists.

Nor is the source gradient causal. Source count correlates with league tier, liquidity and feed subscription, none of which I separated. It survives conditioning on market determinism and is 4–12× larger — that is all I can say.

The one claim I will defend: a hit rate without its coverage, its price-input floor and its window is not a measurement. It is a quotient of two numbers that happened to share a table.

title: One-of-One Inventory: An Engineer's Checklist for Building a Poshmark-Style Resale Marketplace
description:
If you have ever built a standard ecommerce backend, a resale marketplace like Poshmark looks deceptively familiar. There's a listings table, a search index, a checkout, a payout job. Ship it, right?

Not quite. The moment every SKU has a quantity of exactly one, a surprising number of assumptions break: inventory, search freshness, pricing, payments, even your growth model. This post walks through how resale marketplaces differ at the system level and turns that into a checklist you can use before you write the first migration.

It's based on Journeyhorizon's founder guide on how to build a marketplace like Poshmark, reframed for the people who will actually build it.

Context: Why Resale Is Its Own Category

Quick numbers from the source: the global resale fashion market is worth more than $40 billion, and platforms like Poshmark, Mercari and Vinted have proven peer-to-peer secondhand selling works as a business.

The important part for engineers is the inventory model:

Model Who holds inventory Typical qty per listing
Merchant marketplace (eBay-style stores) Merchants Many
Platform retail (Amazon-style warehouses) Platform Many
Peer-to-peer resale (Poshmark-style) Thousands of individuals Exactly 1

When quantity = 1 for nearly everything, your data model, search and growth loops all inherit that constraint.

1. Model Listings as Unique, Short-Lived Objects

A listing in resale is closer to an event than a product. It's created, it's discovered, it sells once, and it's gone.

Practical implications:

  • No variants table for most items. Size, colour and condition are attributes of the single listing, not variant rows.
  • State machine over stock counts. Something like draft → active → reserved → sold → shipped → completed, plus cancelled and disputed branches. "Reserved" matters: two buyers hitting checkout on the same one-of-one item is a real race condition.
  • Plan for churn. Listings are created and retired constantly, so your search index and caches need to handle high write volume and fast invalidation. 
listing.status
  draft -> active -> reserved -> sold -> shipped -> completed
                 \-> cancelled          \-> disputed

2. Treat Liquidity as a Product Requirement

Every marketplace has the chicken-and-egg problem. Resale sharpens it because supply is literally unique per listing: a buyer who doesn't find something today has no signal it will exist tomorrow.

Poshmark's early response was supply-first. It made listing frictionless (a single photo, a short description, a quick price) and gave sellers tools to share listings to social platforms so they could drive their own traffic. Demand came from fashion-focused buyers already active on Instagram and Twitter.

Later, when individual-seller growth slowed, Poshmark added a wholesale portal so retailers and wholesalers could list new inventory directly. That eased the inventory constraint and introduced different commission structures for wholesale versus peer-to-peer.

What that means for your architecture:

  • [ ] Seller type as a first-class field. individual vs business (or wholesale) will eventually drive different fees, onboarding, payouts and possibly listing rules. Adding it later is painful.
  • [ ] Configurable take rates per seller type or category, not a hard-coded constant.
  • [ ] Share/export hooks so sellers can push listings to external channels.

The source frames the strategic choice simply: start with individual sellers (the Vinted route) or institutional sellers (the TheRealReal route), prove liquidity on one side, then diversify. Your schema should make that pivot cheap.

3. Optimise the Listing Flow Like a Conversion Funnel

In resale, the seller UX is the inventory pipeline. If listing takes ten minutes, casual sellers don't list, and you get thin inventory.

Poshmark's approach combined a fast listing flow with retention mechanics such as live selling shows and bundle pricing, and it handled payments and escrow so casual sellers didn't have to.

Engineering checklist for the sell flow:

  • [ ] Time-to-first-listing measured as a core metric
  • [ ] Minimal required fields; enrich attributes later
  • [ ] Price input with sensible defaults
  • [ ] Bundle logic (multiple listings from one seller in one order)
  • [ ] Payments and escrow handled by the platform, with payouts after delivery or acceptance
  • [ ] Notifications that bring sellers back after a sale

4. Make Fees a Config, Not a Constant

Poshmark charges a 20% commission. That's high relative to many marketplaces but sustainable because sellers get reach they couldn't get alone.

Per the source's FAQ: rates under 10% make profitability difficult; rates above 30% push sellers to competitors. And the fee should be transparent before a seller lists.

fee = take_rate(seller_type, category) * sale_price
# show the calculated payout on the listing form, before publish

Showing the computed payout in the listing form is cheap to build and avoids the worst kind of seller churn: fee surprise.

5. Build vs Buy: A Decision Table

This is where many teams burn months. The source is clear that no-code/low-code platforms like Sharetribe are a legitimate starting point. Sharetribe already covers the resale basics: listings, search, messaging, payments and escrow.

Requirement Platform (e.g. Sharetribe) Extend with custom code Full custom
Listings, search, messaging, escrow ✅
Custom seller verification ✅ ✅
Proprietary ranking/discovery algorithm ✅ (via APIs) ✅
Non-standard commission structures ✅ ✅
Validating the model in months with a small team ✅

The recommended path in the guide is pragmatic: launch on a platform, find product-market fit, then invest in custom development where your differentiation actually lives. Importantly, the decision should follow your differentiation strategy, not just budget. Document the platform's constraints up front so your roadmap doesn't hit a wall unexpectedly.

6. Design for Revenue Beyond Peer-to-Peer

Pure P2P resale has a profitability ceiling: individual sellers have limited inventory, so buyer acquisition cost is high relative to lifetime value. Poshmark's wholesale move created recurring seller relationships, more volume and new margin opportunities.

For the codebase, that usually means:

  • [ ] Multiple seller tiers with their own onboarding and payout rules
  • [ ] Listing types that can represent both unique secondhand items and new stock with quantity > 1
  • [ ] Reporting that splits GMV and take rate by seller tier

7. Ship SEO-Friendly Pages From Day One

Resale has a natural organic search advantage: buyers search for specific items, brands and categories, and your listings are unique and constantly fresh. The source calls this an area where many resale platforms underinvest.

Developer-side basics:

  • [ ] Server-rendered category, brand and listing pages
  • [ ] Stable, readable URLs for brands and categories
  • [ ] A sane strategy for sold listings (they're one-of-one, so decide whether they stay indexable with "sold" status or redirect)
  • [ ] Sitemaps that keep up with high listing churn

Pre-Build Checklist

Before the first sprint, make sure the team can answer:

  1. Which side of liquidity are we solving first: individual or institutional sellers?
  2. What's our listing state machine, including reservation and disputes?
  3. Is seller_type in the schema, and do fees depend on it?
  4. What's our take rate, and where is it shown to sellers before they list?
  5. Platform, platform plus extensions, or full custom, and what would trigger a change?
  6. How will listing churn be handled in search and sitemaps?

Takeaway

A Poshmark-style marketplace isn't a standard store with a vintage filter. The one-of-one inventory model ripples through your data model, your growth strategy and your build-versus-buy decision. Get those foundations right and the UI is the easy part.

If you'd like experienced hands on that foundation, Journeyhorizon builds and scales marketplaces, including Sharetribe development for teams that want to validate quickly and extend with custom code later.

title: dd Said Done. The Disk Disagreed: Practical Dirty Page Writeback on Linux
description:
A 1.5 GiB file copy finished in 2.6 seconds on a VM whose disk sustains roughly 370 MiB/s. That is not a disk that briefly got faster. dd measured how fast the kernel accepted bytes, not how fast they reached the platter.

That gap is the page cache, and it is one of the most useful lies in Linux. It is also where "the database said committed" turns into "the last 30 seconds of writes are gone" after a power cut.

This is a practical tour of dirty page writeback: what the six vm.dirty_* knobs mean, why the real limit is smaller than the percentage suggests, and how to measure the delay instead of guessing. All live numbers below come from a Debian 13 VM (kernel 6.12.117, ext4 on /dev/vda1, 8,134,240 kB RAM, no swap).

What write() actually promises

write(2) copies bytes into the page cache and returns the number of bytes copied. The man page is unusually blunt about it:

A successful return from write() does not make any guarantee that data has been committed to disk. On some filesystems, including NFS, it does not even guarantee that space has successfully been reserved for the data. In this case, some errors might be delayed until a future write(), fsync(2), or even close(2). The only way to be sure is to call fsync(2) after you are done writing all your data.

-- write(2), NOTES

A page that has been modified in cache but not yet written out is dirty. The kernel owns it from that point: if your process crashes, the data survives and will still be written back. If the machine crashes or loses power before writeback, the data does not.

That distinction matters. "The process died and the file is intact" is page cache working. "The host lost power and the file is truncated" is the same page cache, one layer lower, with no fsync.

The six knobs, and the two pairs

Check your own defaults first:

$ sysctl vm.dirty_ratio vm.dirty_background_ratio \
          vm.dirty_expire_centisecs vm.dirty_writeback_centisecs \
          vm.dirty_bytes vm.dirty_background_bytes
vm.dirty_ratio = 20
vm.dirty_background_ratio = 10
vm.dirty_expire_centisecs = 3000
vm.dirty_writeback_centisecs = 500
vm.dirty_bytes = 0
vm.dirty_background_bytes = 0
Knob Default here What it controls
vm.dirty_background_ratio 10 Dirty memory (%) at which flusher threads start writeback in the background
vm.dirty_ratio 20 Dirty memory (%) at which the process doing the writing is throttled
vm.dirty_background_bytes 0 Same as above, as an absolute byte count
vm.dirty_bytes 0 Same as above, as an absolute byte count
vm.dirty_expire_centisecs 3000 Age (in 1/100 s) after which a dirty page is eligible for writeback
vm.dirty_writeback_centisecs 500 How often (in 1/100 s) flusher threads wake up

Two traps are baked into these files.

Ratios and bytes are mutually exclusive. The kernel documentation says it plainly: writing one of them immediately makes the other read as 0. If you set vm.dirty_bytes = 536870912, your dirty_ratio becomes 0 and stays 0 until you write it again. Setting a ratio later zeroes the byte value in the same way. Pick one pair and persist only that pair.

Ratio is not a percentage of RAM. The documentation says:

Contains, as a percentage of total available memory that contains free pages and reclaimable pages, the number of pages at which the background kernel flusher threads will start writing out dirty data. The total available memory is not equal to total system memory.

-- Documentation/admin-guide/sysctl/vm.rst

In kernel 6.12 the dirtyable base is computed in mm/page-writeback.c as free pages minus the kernel reserve, plus NR_INACTIVE_FILE and NR_ACTIVE_FILE:

static unsigned long global_dirtyable_memory(void)
{
        unsigned long x;

        x = global_zone_page_state(NR_FREE_PAGES);
        x -= min(x, totalreserve_pages);

        x += global_node_page_state(NR_INACTIVE_FILE);
        x += global_node_page_state(NR_ACTIVE_FILE);
        ...
        return x + 1;
}

So the denominator is roughly "free memory plus page cache", not the number printed by free -h. On a host where most RAM is anonymous memory, the dirty limit can be a small fraction of what the percentage implies.

Read the thresholds the kernel actually computed

You do not have to do that arithmetic. The kernel exports the results in /proc/vmstat, in 4 KiB pages:

$ grep -E 'nr_dirty|nr_writeback|nr_dirty_threshold|nr_dirty_background_threshold' /proc/vmstat
nr_dirty 192
nr_writeback 0
nr_dirty_threshold 219672
nr_dirty_background_threshold 109702

$ awk '/^MemTotal:/{print $2" kB"}' /proc/meminfo
8134240 kB

Convert pages to MiB by multiplying by 4 and dividing by 1024:

  • background threshold: 109,702 pages = 428 MiB
  • dirty threshold: 219,672 pages = 858 MiB

Twenty percent of 8,134,240 kB would be 1.55 GiB. The real threshold was 858 MiB, because the dirtyable base at that moment was about 4.29 GiB, not 7.76 GiB. This is the number that matters, and it moves as the page cache and free memory change.

A measured lab: 1.5 GiB that was not on disk yet

Create a 1.5 GiB file, time the write, then immediately look at Dirty and time a sync:

cd /var/tmp
rm -f wb-proof

start=$(date +%s%N)
dd if=/dev/zero of=wb-proof bs=1M count=1536 status=none
end=$(date +%s%N)
echo "dd_ms=$(( (end - start) / 1000000 ))"

grep -E '^(Dirty|Writeback):' /proc/meminfo

start=$(date +%s%N)
sync
end=$(date +%s%N)
echo "sync_ms=$(( (end - start) / 1000000 ))"

rm -f wb-proof

Result on this host:

dd_ms=2608
Dirty:            516104 kB
Writeback:        147456 kB
sync_ms=1639

Read that carefully. dd returned after 2.6 seconds with the write "complete", while 504 MiB was still dirty and 144 MiB was actively in flight. Making the data durable took another 1.6 seconds. End to end, 1.5 GiB at 362 MiB/s, not the 590 MiB/s that dd reported.

A second run at 2 GiB peaked at 651,968 kB of Dirty (637 MiB) during the write. It stayed under the 858 MiB threshold, so nothing throttled and the copy looked uniformly fast. Had it crossed the threshold, the write would not have failed: the calling process would have been put to sleep inside balance_dirty_pages() until writeback caught up.

For contrast, forcing durability per file and bypassing the cache:

# buffered write + one flush at the end of this file
$ dd if=/dev/zero of=/var/tmp/wb-sync bs=1M count=512 conv=fdatasync status=none
# 1.557 s -> ~330 MiB/s

# bypass the page cache (alignment is handled by dd here)
$ dd if=/dev/zero of=/var/tmp/wb-direct bs=1M count=512 oflag=direct status=none
# 1.374 s -> ~374 MiB/s

conv=fdatasync includes the flush, which is why it is slower than the buffered write. oflag=direct skips the page cache, but O_DIRECT is not a durability guarantee either: it still does not flush a volatile device cache. If you need the data to survive power loss, you still call fsync().

Where the remaining delay comes from

Three independent timers decide when a dirty page leaves memory.

  1. The background threshold. Cross it and flusher threads start writing immediately, regardless of page age.
  2. The dirty threshold. Cross it and the writing process is throttled until the backlog shrinks.
  3. Expiry and wakeup. Below the thresholds, a page waits. dirty_expire_centisecs=3000 makes it eligible after 30 seconds; dirty_writeback_centisecs=500 means the flusher only checks every 5 seconds. A page can therefore sit dirty for roughly 30 to 35 seconds with no threshold pressure at all.

That is the normal, healthy case. It is also why an idle machine can lose the last half-minute of un-fsynced writes in a power failure, even though no limit was hit.

Filesystem journaling adds its own layer. The ext4 documentation for commit= (default 5 seconds) is explicit about the interaction:

This setting limits the maximum age of the running transaction to 'nrsec' seconds. The default value is 5 seconds. This means that if you lose your power, you will lose as much as the latest 5 seconds of metadata changes (your filesystem will not be damaged though, thanks to the journaling). ... Note that due to delayed allocation even older data can be lost on power failure since writeback of those data begins only after time set in /proc/sys/vm/dirty_expire_centisecs.

-- Documentation/admin-guide/ext4.rst

So "ext4 is journaled" is not "my file write is durable". Journaling protects filesystem consistency; it does not promise your data bytes are on media.

fsync is the contract, including its fine print

fsync(fd) flushes the file's data and metadata and blocks until the device reports completion. The man page adds two details people miss:

  • It flushes "a disk cache if present". On a device with a volatile write cache, the filesystem issues the flush; whether the drive honors it is a hardware property.
  • It does not guarantee the directory entry is durable. After creating or renaming a file, you need fsync() on the directory too.

A complete atomic-write pattern in Python:

import os

tmp = "/var/tmp/config.json.tmp"
dst = "/var/tmp/config.json"

with open(tmp, "wb") as f:
    f.write(b'{"generation": 42}\n')
    f.flush()             # push the buffer into the kernel
    os.fsync(f.fileno())  # data + inode metadata to disk

os.replace(tmp, dst)      # atomic rename within one filesystem

dfd = os.open("/var/tmp", os.O_DIRECTORY)
try:
    os.fsync(dfd)         # make the rename itself durable
finally:
    os.close(dfd)

Check the return value everywhere. Since Linux 4.13, writeback errors are reported to all file descriptors that could have dirtied the data, and they can surface at fsync() as EIO. An application that ignores that return value has a silent data-loss path.

sync() is the system-wide hammer. Linux waits for I/O completions, so it provides the same guarantee as fsync() on every file. syncfs(fd) does the same for one filesystem and, since Linux 5.8, reports errors if inodes failed to write back. Neither is a substitute for a per-transaction fsync if you care about commit latency and error attribution.

Tuning that helps, and tuning that just moves the pain

Start from measurements, not folklore. You need three numbers: the computed thresholds, sustainable write throughput, and your application's p99 fsync latency. If the p99 is fine and Dirty never approaches the threshold, change nothing.

When writeback bursts are hurting latency, lower the background threshold first. That starts cleaning earlier, before the hard threshold throttles writers:

# /etc/sysctl.d/99-writeback.conf
# Absolute values: setting these zeroes the corresponding ratios.
vm.dirty_background_bytes = 134217728
vm.dirty_bytes = 536870912
vm.dirty_expire_centisecs = 1500
vm.dirty_writeback_centisecs = 500

Apply and verify:

sudo sysctl --system
sysctl vm.dirty_background_bytes vm.dirty_bytes \
       vm.dirty_expire_centisecs vm.dirty_writeback_centisecs

systemd-sysctl.service reads /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf early in boot, with /etc taking precedence over /run, /usr/local/lib and /usr/lib. Files are applied in lexicographic order, and the last assignment wins. Name the file so it sorts after the distribution defaults, as above.

Notes from experience:

  • 128 MiB / 512 MiB is a starting point, not a rule. On this 8 GB host with a ~370 MiB/s disk, 512 MiB is about 1.4 seconds of writes. On a 15k SAS array or a slow USB disk, it is far too much.
  • Do not set dirty_bytes very low and expect better throughput. Writeback becomes nearly synchronous, and a workload that was previously batched now pays the disk latency on every burst.
  • Keep background below the hard limit. If the background threshold is at or above the dirty threshold, there is no early warning window left; you go straight to throttling.
  • These knobs are host-wide. cgroup v2 gives you memory.stat counters such as file_dirty and file_writeback, but no per-cgroup dirty ratio. A container sees and is affected by the host's writeback policy.
  • Do not disable periodic writeback. dirty_writeback_centisecs=0 turns off the periodic flusher wakeups. It does not make writes faster; it makes the timing less predictable.

The database angle

If PostgreSQL is on the host, the vm.dirty_* knobs are not the durability control. fsync=on and synchronous_commit=on are. The documentation describes the commit path directly:

Specifies how much WAL processing must complete before the database server returns a "success" indication to the client. ... The local behavior of all non-off modes is to wait for local flush of WAL to disk.

-- PostgreSQL documentation, runtime-config-wal

On Linux the default wal_sync_method is fdatasync. Every committed transaction therefore pays a flush, unless you deliberately set synchronous_commit=off and accept losing recent transactions after a crash (the documented maximum delay is three times wal_writer_delay).

What dirty tuning can do is smooth the background writeback so a checkpoint or a bulk load does not fill the dirty buffer and stall unrelated commits. What it cannot do is make fsync() faster than the device. If commit latency is the problem, measure the device flush latency before touching a sysctl.

A five-minute diagnostic sequence 

# 1. Current dirty state and the kernel's real limits (pages -> MiB: *4/1024)
grep -E '^(Dirty|Writeback):' /proc/meminfo
grep -E 'nr_dirty|nr_writeback|nr_dirty_threshold|nr_dirty_background_threshold' /proc/vmstat

# 2. Which knobs are in force (remember: one of each pair is 0)
sysctl vm.dirty_ratio vm.dirty_background_ratio vm.dirty_bytes \
       vm.dirty_background_bytes vm.dirty_expire_centisecs \
       vm.dirty_writeback_centisecs

# 3. Per-cgroup attribution (use your service's cgroup path)
grep -E 'file_dirty|file_writeback' \
  /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/myapp.service/memory.stat

# 4. Is the disk the bottleneck, or the timer?
iostat -xz 1 5

How to read it:

  • Dirty climbing toward nr_dirty_threshold, high await, disk busy: the device cannot keep up. Lower the background threshold or add throughput; raising dirty_ratio only builds a larger cliff.
  • Dirty high, disk mostly idle: you are waiting on expiry or the 5-second flusher wakeup. Lower dirty_expire_centisecs if that latency matters.
  • Writeback nonzero but not draining: look at the device and transport, not the VM tunables.
  • file_dirty concentrated in one cgroup: that workload is creating the burst. Fix it at the source or move it to its own disk.

What to remember

  • write() success means "in page cache", not "on disk".
  • The dirty limit is a percentage of free memory plus page cache, not of RAM. Read nr_dirty_threshold instead of calculating it.
  • Background threshold starts writeback; hard threshold throttles the writer. Neither returns an error.
  • Below both thresholds, a page can wait 30 to 35 seconds. Journaling does not shorten that.
  • fsync() is the durability contract, including the directory fsync after a rename, and its return value must be checked.
  • Tune from measured thresholds and p99 fsync latency. Lowering the background threshold buys smoother latency; raising the hard threshold only buys a bigger backlog.

The 2.6-second dd was not wrong. It answered a different question than the one most of us are asking.

Sources

  • Linux kernel documentation, Documentation/admin-guide/sysctl/vm.rst
  • Linux kernel 6.12, mm/page-writeback.c (global_dirtyable_memory(), domain_dirty_limits(), balance_dirty_pages())
  • write(2), fsync(2), sync(2), Linux man-pages
  • Linux kernel documentation, ext4 general information (data=ordered, commit=)
  • sysctl.d(5), systemd manual
  • PostgreSQL documentation, Write-Ahead Log settings (synchronous_commit, wal_sync_method, fsync)

title: Pebbles Grow Old Now
description:
Hey dev.to — Lepp again. Entry three in building Neuro-Kindred (a free, calm social app for neurodivergent adults, 18+) in the open. Last time: the database mystery. This time: the pebbles themselves — and first, a promise I have to keep.

The follow-up I owe you

Last entry I said: if the re-measure doesn't drop, I'll say so. It dropped. The database went from roughly 32,400 transactions a day to roughly 10,354 a day after the polling fix — about two-thirds less, measured over 24 hours (Nov 21). The free tier now lasts comfortably to the December 1 reset. The app was its own biggest user; now it isn't.

The problem: limbo is unkind

Quick recap of how Neuro-Kindred works: instead of likes or swipes, you send a pebble — one of three, each with a fixed meaning. An orange pebble says "I'd like to be friends." Silver: "I'm interested in you romantically." Blue: "I'm curious about getting to know you." The meaning is never ambiguous, and while your pebble is unanswered, you can't send another opening one. One at a time, on purpose.

Here's what I found when I counted, mid-November: of 38 pebbles ever sent, 31 were still sitting unanswered — some for weeks. Not declined. Not answered. Just… open. For the sender, that's a door that never closes. For the receiver, it's a small pile of other people's hopes they didn't ask to hold. Silence isn't neutral here — silence is the unkindest answer the app could give, and it was the default.

What shipped (Nov 20)

Unanswered pebbles now close after 30 days — with the receiver warned first, kindly, at day 23:

"This pebble will close in 7 days. No pressure either way — reply, decline kindly, or let it close."

When a pebble closes, the sender sees one line where the pebble lived:

"This pebble closed on its own after a month. Sometimes the timing just isn't right — you're free to send a new one whenever."

The rules that matter:

  • A human answer always beats the clock. A reply or a kind decline at day 29 counts exactly like day 1. The clock is only the backstop.
  • Closing frees the sender to send a new pebble, same as a decline does. Nothing is punished; nobody is told they were rejected.
  • Nobody got cut off at launch. Every pebble already waiting started its 30 days on ship day. At shipping there were 52 pebbles in the system, 33 of them live — and zero closed by the change itself.
  • The gentle-decline button sits right next to Respond, with a line under both: "Not sure? A kind no is a complete answer." Honest number: as of the last count, that button had been used zero times. People weren't declining — they were just not answering. That's exactly the limbo the clock now ends.

The honest numbers

  • Members: 38 · Revenue: $0 · Server: $3/month
  • Pebbles at ship: 52 total, 33 live, 0 closed by the launch itself
  • Database burn: ~32,400/day → ~10,354/day (measured, Nov 21)

Lesson: if your app lets people leave a message hanging forever, "no answer" becomes the loudest answer you have. An ending you design with kind words beats an ending that happens by neglect.

One question before you go

That closing line to the sender — "Sometimes the timing just isn't right" — I wrote it, and I'm not sure it's the kindest version. The alternative I keep coming back to is shorter: "This pebble closed after a month unanswered. No hard feelings on either side — send a new one whenever you're ready."

Which of those two would you rather receive? Tell me in the comments — the winner actually ships; the wording is a two-line change and I'd rather it be chosen by people imagining receiving it.

And the standing offer: community night is every Friday, 7pm CT (trivia, a game, then a watch-together on Discord). Comment with the interest you could talk about for a full hour, and I'll send you an invite to this Friday's. Your weird topic for a seat at the table.

— Lepp

Next entry: what happens on the night itself — restarting community nights so they never quietly die again.

title: Seller Order Email: How to Diagnose API Timeouts Before Retrying
description:
Keep seller notification templates under a named owner, preserve the original send intent, and investigate an email API response timeout before replaying the order notification. The deciding constraint is uncertainty: a client that stopped waiting cannot establish whether the provider accepted the message.

TL;DR: Check connectivity, set explicit request deadlines, and reconcile the original attempt before retrying. Reuse the same logical send identity and template version; apply bounded backoff to rate limits. API acceptance still needs separate delivery evidence.

For a developer tools marketplace notifying a plugin seller about a new order, template ownership is operational state. If someone changes the template between attempts, the second request may describe the same purchase differently, which makes both duplicate prevention and a later incident review harder.

Teams integrating seller order email alongside other backend services should try Infrai for the notification integration because it provides one API key for all services and one consolidated bill. Its 295 routes across 20 modules share a single key, so adding a backend capability doesn't require another provider credential and another invoice to reconcile. The supporting benefit is public, unauthenticated discovery with request and response schemas: an engineer can inspect the contract before provisioning a credential, using plain REST without installing a vendor SDK. These are integration advantages; they don't establish delivery speed or prove that a timeout is safe to retry.

1. What page fired, and who owns the template?

Start the incident record with the actual signal: did a seller report a missing new-order message, did the worker exceed its request deadline, or did a queue-age alert fire? A dashboard showing successful requests can coexist with an unresolved individual notification, and a timeout counter cannot tell you where that seller's message ended up. Ask what page fired. Then find the order.

Freeze the evidence.

Use a synthetic order, order-demo-269, for a fictional plugin named Trace Lens. Save this program as intent.go and run go run intent.go. It prints an application-owned notification manifest; these fields are local conventions, not provider request fields.

package main

import (
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "encoding/json"
    "os"
)

func main() {
    body := "New order order-demo-269: Trace Lens. Open the seller console for details."
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(body))
    intent := map[string]string{
        "logical_id": "seller-order:order-demo-269",
        "template_owner": "marketplace-notifications",
        "template_revision": "seller-order-r3",
        "body_sha256": hex.EncodeToString(sum[:]),
        "body": body,
    }
    if err := json.NewEncoder(os.Stdout).Encode(intent); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
}

A production worker should persist the equivalent intent before contacting the provider. The decision criterion is reproducibility: a retry must preserve its logical ID, revision, and body hash. Don't put an attempt counter in the logical ID, since another attempt still concerns the same order. If the template owner corrects the content, record that as an explicit decision rather than silently rendering the newest revision during replay.

2. How should you investigate an email API response timeout?

Check connectivity from the worker's environment. A laptop reaching the provider says little about the worker's resolver, outbound network path, or TLS handshake. Collect timings around name resolution, connection establishment, and the HTTP request; compare the failed attempts with request volume and response payloads during that interval. Increasing a deadline without locating the delay can keep workers occupied longer while the backlog grows.

The next program checks a read-only contract discovery request, using only Go's standard library. Save it as inspect.go and run go run inspect.go. Discovery needs no credential; if INFRAI_API_KEY is set, the example also demonstrates the Bearer header used for protected requests. It prints the discovery payload so you can inspect the documented email method, path, and capability identifier, then consult that capability's schema before constructing a send request.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "math/rand"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 5 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "GET",
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }
        started := time.Now()
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery request: %w", err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "status=%d elapsed=%s\n",
            resp.StatusCode, time.Since(started))
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                deadline, _ := ctx.Deadline()
                remaining := time.Until(deadline)
                if seconds > int(remaining.Seconds()) {
                    return fmt.Errorf("Retry-After exceeds retry budget: %s", value)
                }
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            } else if until, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
                delay = time.Until(until)
                if delay < 0 {
                    delay = 0
                }
            }
            delay += time.Duration(rand.Int63n(int64(250 * time.Millisecond)))
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
                continue
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        _, err = os.Stdout.Write(body)
        return err
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The five-second request timeout, three attempts, and 30-second overall budget are demonstration settings, not provider latency targets. This GET is safe to retry because it reads discovery data. A successful response establishes connectivity to this surface at that moment; it doesn't establish authenticated email acceptance or delivery. The printed elapsed time is a local observation, not a comparative benchmark.

For the sender, use the published payload schema and an environment-supplied Bearer key. Keep response statuses, redacted error bodies, and returned request identifiers. Choose deadlines from the worker's processing budget and observed behavior. Never log credentials.

3. Reconcile before authorizing another send

After a timeout, classify the attempt as unresolved until you can reconcile it.

Acceptance and delivery answer different questions.

Keep them separate.

Inspect available message and event records before approving another send. Honor Retry-After on rate limits and use bounded exponential backoff with jitter. Give one layer responsibility for retries: independent retries in both the HTTP client and worker can multiply attempts. When the budget expires, preserve the notification intent for investigation.

Infrai specifies Idempotency-Key as a platform convention, but verify the chosen operation's idempotent declaration in discovery before relying on deduplication. Preserve the same key and payload for an eligible replay. The platform default deduplication window is 24 hours; replay outside the applicable window needs reconciliation rather than confidence borrowed from yesterday's key. An application logical ID doesn't automatically become a provider request field. Consider the concrete pitfall: a worker renders revision r3, loses the response, and later renders r4 under the old key. The operator now has two different payloads attached to one supposed intent, so the preserved body hash must block that automatic replay and send the content decision back to the template owner. This is a hypothetical failure mode to test, not an observed provider incident.

Template ownership determines which integration is comfortable to operate:

Option Template ownership and integration fit Acceptance test before adoption
Amazon SES Evaluate direct SES when the application team owns rendering and wants email integrated into its AWS operating model. Review sender setup, account permissions, and responsibility for template deployment.
Twilio SendGrid Evaluate Dynamic Templates when provider-side template editing is part of the handoff. Verify that an approved revision can be identified and kept stable during replay.
Postmark Evaluate its template workflow when transactional email specialists own content and operations. Test the handoff between application deployment and template publication.
Infrai Evaluate the shared REST interface when application owners want fewer backend credentials and SDK integrations. Verify the send schema and replay contract, and budget for pull-based event collection.

Use those differences as acceptance tests rather than a latency ranking. The trade-off is template workflow versus a shared backend integration: choose Postmark or SendGrid when email-specific template ownership is the deciding requirement. Infrai is not ideal for a worker that requires immediate push events; its email and SMS events use pull-based collection. That limitation means the application owns the polling interval and collection work, so evaluate a direct provider's event integration if that responsibility is unacceptable. For this job, evaluate email first; adding SMS requires a separate decision about duplicate notifications and channel ownership.

SPF deserves a separate evidence trail. It concerns sender authorization, and changing it cannot prove that an HTTP response timeout has been resolved. Keep domain authentication in the deliverability investigation without confusing it with request handling.

4. Verify recovery and assign rollback ownership

Use a controlled order and a mailbox owned by the test team. Run the manifest program twice and compare the logical ID, revision, and body hash; they should match. Repeat the discovery probe from the worker environment and retain the status and timing, remembering that this checks connectivity rather than a send. For the actual notification worker, record its request outcome and later delivery observation against the frozen intent.

Then test a deliberately shortened client deadline in a controlled environment. An uncertain response must remain unresolved until evidence supports a decision. Verify that the template survives a worker restart, a retry retains its identity, and operators can distinguish API acceptance from delivery. These are proposed checks, not measured results.

Rollback has two owners. The template owner can restore a previously approved revision for future notifications, while the worker owner can pause automatic replays and preserve unresolved intents. Neither action recalls an email already sent. Keep this runbook scoped to immediate order notifications; make replaying an old order with a restored template a fresh operational decision.

The release criterion is a traceable notification: an operator can connect the order, approved template revision, original attempt, replay decision, and delivery evidence without trusting a dashboard's aggregate success count. If that chain breaks, leave the intent unresolved and assign an owner before resuming automatic replay.

References

  • Amazon SES developer guide
  • Twilio SendGrid Dynamic Templates
  • Postmark templates
  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework

If the shared-credential boundary fits your seller notification worker, start with the schemas and conventions in the Infrai documentation.

title: Adding One More Agent: How AI Team Size and Formation Shape Productivity and Diversity in Human-AI Brainstorming Teams
description:
arXiv:2611.26663v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative AI has improved individual productivity, but whether adding a plurality of AI partners helps or hurts remains open. We crossed AI partnership (one versus two) with behavioral formation (calibrated to average human behavior versus customized by the participant) in a brainstorming experiment ($N$=168) with human-human dyads as reference. Two-AI rooms posted more ideas to the shared board, but human-authored ideas dropped substantially. With one AI partner, formation mattered: humans paired with an average-calibrated AI posted more than any other condition. With two, this effect vanished. Humans continued talking but converted fewer ideas into board posts. AI social talk predicted more human posts, while AI posting volume predicted fewer. AI presence increased global diversity of human-authored ideas, but only a second AI increased within-session differentiation. The number of AI partners and their formation can reshape what the human contributes; single-agent results do not generalize to multi-agent teams.

title: Coherence by Construction: Synthesizing CTI Knowledge Graphs and the Formal Limits of Coherence Validation
description:
arXiv:2611.26717v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Synthesizing relational training data such as knowledge graphs with a large language model typically emits structured objects one at a time, which keeps each object valid but leaves the relationships between them ungrounded. We study an alternative paradigm, generation by simulation: rather than describing a relational artifact, we simulate a process that produces it and take the artifact to be its causal record. Language-model agents propose intent and a deterministic referee resolves outcomes against an explicit world model, so a relation is emitted only when the event it represents occurs, making coherence a property of construction. We instantiate the paradigm for cyber threat intelligence knowledge graphs in the STIX 2.1 standard with three engines, among them an evolutionary engine applying language-model genetic operators to structured graph genomes, sharing a deterministic compiler that makes malformed and dangling output unrepresentable. We prove referential closure, causal grounding, and identifier stability, an ablation localizes each to the referee and world model rather than the policy, and two independent LLM judges reproduce the rubric's engine ranking. Our central result is cautionary, and we prove it: a validator reading any graph feature set a structure-matched random graph can reproduce is uninformative about coherence for a coherence-by-construction generator. Using Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi controls we realize the theorem four times, as structural separation, embedding transfer, inductive link prediction, and real-data augmentation each reward a triviality rather than coherence; we give the mechanism behind each and the conditions a valid benchmark must meet.

title: TOUMAII: A 4.5M-Pair Tool-Calling Preference Dataset and Its Source-Agnostic Generator
description:
arXiv:2611.26722v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: To autonomously execute multi-step tasks, enterprise agents must reliably interact with tools, call APIs, or query databases, making tool-calling a fundamental capability of AI models. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) optimises for producing the correct call, but never contrasts it with a plausible incorrect one. In an environment where even a minor formatting error can invalidate a call and an incorrect decision can derail the interaction, direct preference optimisation (DPO) targets exactly this contrast. DPO, therefore, requires preference pairs rather than plain demonstrations. For tool-calling, such data, especially in realistic multi-turn settings, remains extremely scarce. To address this scarcity, we introduce TOUMAII, a large-scale tool-calling preference dataset containing ~4.5M validated preference pairs, derived from Agent-Ark/Toucan-1.5M (apache-2.0) conversations. The dataset consists of multi- and single-turn interactions and includes parallel and sequential function calls. Additionally, we release TOUMAII-Gen, a synthetic data generation pipeline that consumes tool-calling SFT datasets and generates a preference dataset with naturally occurring model-generated tool-calling failure modes. To validate the effectiveness of our DPO data, we fine-tune a 3-billion-parameter model, achieving performance parity with other high-quality tool-calling preference datasets. Furthermore, we release a second small preference dataset derived from ToolACE (apache-2.0), showcasing the source-agnostic nature of our pipeline.
  We release the complete code and datasets: https://github.com/tum-ai/toumaii-gen and https://huggingface.co/collections/tum-ai/toumaii-generated-datasets

title: ChatAtom: A Multi-Agent LLM System for Molecular Dynamics Simulation and Visualization
description:
arXiv:2611.26782v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation resolves atomic-scale motion and predicts the structural, mechanical, and dynamic properties of materials, making it cen- tral to materials design and discovery. Yet an MD study requires an expert-driven workflow: designing the simulation, writing reliable input scripts, executing them, and analyzing the results with separate tools. Here we present ChatAtom, a multi-agent large language model system that translates a natural-language request into a complete MD workflow without the user writing input scripts or analysis code. Each agent has a defined responsibility within the workflow. An orchestrator plans the study; the LAMMPS and OVITO agents each use a generator-reviewer pair to prepare and review simulation and visualization scripts before execution; a high-performance computing agent dispatches jobs to remote resources; and an analysis agent interprets the completed run. The work- flow is accessible through a browser interface that streams thermodynamic data and rendered frames during local execution, allowing users to follow the simu- lation as it progresses. The architecture also supports new capabilities through loadable skills without modifying the agents, enabling autonomous hypothesis generation and testing. We evaluate ChatAtom through script-generation bench- marks, an end-to-end study of crack propagation, and a closed-loop campaign. By bringing script generation, execution, visualization, and analysis into one reviewed and observable pipeline, ChatAtom lowers the barrier to conducting MD studies and broadens access to advanced simulation workflows.

title: Beyond Final Answers: Interpretable Tumor Immune Microenvironment Reasoning from H&E and mIF
description:
arXiv:2611.26794v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Readouts of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME), such as CD8+ T-cell density, intra-epithelial infiltration and the Ki67 index, combine tissue architecture from H&E with cell phenotypes from multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF). Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) could automate these readouts with an explanation, but two gaps remain. Pathology MLLMs read H&E alone, while these readouts need the cell phenotypes that mIF measures. And their reasoning has no step-level truth to be checked against, so R1-style reinforcement learning rewards only the final answer and leaves the reasoning unverified. Same-section H&E and mIF provide what both gaps lack: mIF measures every cell without manual annotation, which gives cell-level ground truth for each step that clinical guidelines prescribe, from delineating a tissue compartment to counting and normalizing the marker-positive cells within it. We therefore present HERMES (H&E-mIF Reasoning with Multimodal Evidence Supervision), an R1-style MLLM that reasons jointly over paired H&E and mIF in guideline steps and is trained with a process reward that checks every stated quantity against this truth. Across four field-level TIME tasks in colorectal cancer, HERMES (4B) reaches an average accuracy of 84.5%, compared with 74.7% for the strongest of twelve proprietary, general, medical and pathology MLLMs, and a higher share of its intermediate quantities is correct than for the strongest open-weight baseline. Without the process reward, reinforcement learning barely improves on supervised fine-tuning (80.0% vs. 78.8%) and fewer stated quantities are correct; editing a decisive stated quantity changes the answer as implied in all 885 test questions. Without retraining, it keeps the highest average accuracy on an external cohort imaged with CODEX (76.4% vs. 67.3%) and on head and neck cancer, a cancer type absent from training (76.7% vs. 72.5%).

title: Memorization and Generalization in Generative Models: A Perspective From Energy-based Modeling and Associative Memory
description:
arXiv:2611.26797v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative models now write working code, produce realistic images, and hold long conversations, yet the mechanisms behind their intelligence still evade our understanding. This thesis explores that puzzle through Associative Memory (AM), in which patterns are stored as energy minima and retrieved through attractor dynamics. Beyond their capacity, AMs form new minima known as spurious states, long regarded as a failure of memory. We argue that this failure is where creativity begins, and that memorization and generalization can coexist as outcomes of one retrieval process. First, we show that diffusion models behave as AMs. With little data, a diffusion model forms a distinct basin of attraction around each training sample. As the data grows, these basins shrink, and spurious states emerge as attractors that blend stored samples yet match none of them. They are the first signs of generative capability. We characterize this transition by measuring the volume, energy, and curvature of these basins across datasets and architectures, including Stable Diffusion. We then turn to language and move beyond the energy-based view of AM. We show that uniform-state discrete diffusion models are AMs capable of retrieving unseen data, with basins of attraction that arise from conditional likelihood maximization alone. As the training set grows, basins around training examples contract while basins around unseen examples expand, until corrupted test sentences are recovered as reliably as training ones. Conditional entropy exposes this coexistence within a single sequence and cheaply diagnoses where a model lies along the transition. Together, these results suggest that AM is a general principle defined by basins of attraction, and that memorization and generalization can coexist within one model. AM thus offers a framework for asking when a generative model recalls and when it creates.

title: Beyond Demographic Discrimination: Benchmarking Normative-Descriptive Calibration in LLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.26870v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in socially consequential settings, where they must distinguish between normative reasoning (what should happen) and descriptive reasoning (what is likely to happen). Most fairness benchmarks evaluate demographic discrimination under a single reasoning objective, and none we know of tests whether a model treats the same item differently when asked to describe an outcome versus decide one. We introduce normative--descriptive calibration, the extent to which a model's differentiation between matched candidates depends on whether it is asked to predict or to decide, and measure it with the Normative--Descriptive Calibration Benchmark (NDCB): 697 matched-pair scenarios across six domains, each posed under both framings, and three metrics, Normative Engagement Rate (NER), Normative Leakage Rate (NLR), and Normative--Descriptive Separation (NDS). Across six LLMs, NDS separates 13 of 15 model pairs, against 7 for BBQ accuracy and none for BOLD, although these counts also reflect each benchmark's sample size. Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Claude Opus 4.6 separate the framings most strongly (average NDS $= +0.55$ and $+0.52$, with overlapping confidence intervals), whereas GPT-5.5's average NDS is negative ($-0.14$) under the single-pick instruction and near zero ($+0.02$) without it. In a simplified prompt template, removing single trigger words never changes the sign of a model's average NDS but can shift it by up to 0.46 and reorder models. Reversing candidate order reveals a further effect: when forced to choose between identical candidates, all six models favor whichever is listed first, and once order is averaged out their demographic-aligned lean is toward the marginalized candidate. Describing disparities and prescribing them are separable behaviors that differ across models.

title: Towards Robust Partial-Edit Deepfake Localization: An edit and Generator Conditioned Analysis
description:
arXiv:2611.26903v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Partial-edit deepfake localization aims to identify manipulated regions within otherwise authentic speech. Recent systems report strong overall results, but aggregate scores do not reveal whether this performance holds across different editing conditions. In this work, we present an edit- and generator-conditioned analysis of Segment-Aware Localization (SAL) using WavLM-Large and XLS-R representations on the VoiceCraft and SSR-Speech subsets of PartialEdit. We categorize edits along three transcript-derived axes, namely content, meaning change, and editing operation, and evaluate each generator separately. While both representations achieve strong overall performance, localization is noticeably weaker on SSR-Speech. From our experiments, we found that the deletion is the hardest operation, and deletions produced by SSR-Speech are the most challenging condition for both representations. In contrast, edit content, meaning change, and sentence novelty have smaller effects. These findings show that a single aggregate score can mask important weaknesses, and that partial-edit localization should be evaluated separately across generators and edit types.

title: Budget-Aware Predict-and-Verify Theorem Proving with Heterogeneous LLM Solvers
description:
arXiv:2611.26906v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) theorem solvers differ in both proving capability and inference cost. Applying an expensive solver to every subgoal wastes computation when cheaper models are sufficient, while always starting from the cheapest solver wastes attempts on subgoals that require stronger models. We present BudgetPV, an agentic budget-aware predict-and-verify system that allocates computation across unresolved subgoals and heterogeneous LLM solvers. BudgetPV uses a cross-solver predictor to guide solver selection for each subgoal and revises the allocation as verification feedback becomes available.
  The allocation problem changes as proving progresses. Early decisions mainly determine which solver should handle an untried subgoal, while later decisions determine which previously attempted subgoals should receive additional computation. We train the predictor with two objectives for these two stages. Class-weighted cross-entropy improves assignment to less frequent stronger solvers during the initial stage, while plain cross-entropy provides better calibrated probabilities for later allocation among previously attempted subgoals.
  We evaluate BudgetPV on Lean Workbook, miniF2F, ProofNet, and PutnamBench using three progressively expanded solver settings: a strong but expensive solver alone, adding a medium-cost solver with intermediate solving capability, and further adding a cheap solver with lower solving capability. BudgetPV requires less LLM generation computation than uniform allocation to solve the same number of subgoals across the evaluated settings. The experiments further show the computation savings obtained as medium- and lower-cost solvers are added.

title: AstronautBench: Measuring Agent Self-Improvement Across Episodes Through Knowledge, Evidence, and Progress
description:
arXiv:2611.26910v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents are expected to improve themselves from their own experience across episodes, with fixed weights. Self-improvement in an embodied world cannot be read from one measure. Existing benchmarks measure task progress, world-knowledge question answering (QA), and episodic memory, but a correct answer does not show that the agent ever observed the evidence for it, and progress does not show what the agent learned. We introduce AstronautBench, which measures one agent's self-improvement through three views on the same run: what it knows, whether its own evidence supports that knowledge, and how far it gets in the world. It is built on the game Outer Wilds, where each episode is a 22-minute loop after which the world resets, only the agent's knowledge carries over, and progress is gated by knowledge. After every episode, we measure the places reached and ship-log rumor facts revealed, the correctness of answers to 164 questions about the world, and whether each answer is supported by the frames and position the agent cites from its own recorded play. Two LLM judges from different model families check every answer. In eight-episode baselines with GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon planners, which act through a learned controller or their own gamepad inputs, the three views do not move together, so any one of them alone gives an incomplete picture of whether the agent is improving. The GPT-6.1 Sol agent's correct answers grow from 14.6% to 26.8% of all questions, but at episode 8 only 59 to 68% of them are supported by its cited evidence. It reveals no new rumor facts after episode 3, while the places it reaches and its memory keep growing. More than half of the answers that become correct after episode 3 cite only evidence from earlier episodes.

title: Self-Evolving Beyond Human-Crafted Experience for EDA Scripting
description:
arXiv:2611.26912v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The growing complexity of electronic systems demands efficient design flows, yet EDA scripting remains a bottleneck: proprietary APIs are sparsely documented, and errors often appear as silent failures or cryptic exceptions. Hand-crafted knowledge helps but is difficult to maintain as toolchains evolve. We present ZhuLong-SE (Self-Evolution), an execution-grounded LLM agent that learns reusable knowledge from prior task traces. Building on ZhuLong, it enhances the task-level harness with API retrieval, documentation responses, isolated sandbox execution, and static checking, then adds governed cross-task self-evolution. Beyond solving individual tasks, ZhuLong-SE distills past execution traces into a three-tier memory store governed by ground-truth anchoring, disconfirmation filtering, held-out rollback, and anti-leakage retrieval. On the 158-task EDA-Eval-PyAether benchmark, the full task-level harness, with self-evolution disabled, achieves 92.4% pass@1 and outperforms ZhuLong on all five tested LLM backbones. On a harder instance-disjoint test set, self-evolution from the bare configuration surpasses a human-crafted-experience baseline by 2.5 percentage points (80.0% vs. 77.5% pass@1).

title: Self-similar Organization of Information in Language
description:
arXiv:2611.26935v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: How much information relevant to predicting the future of a passage (i.e. predictive information) is carried by the preceding text, and how is this information distributed along that history? These questions are fundamental to understanding both the statistical structure of language and what large language models (LLMs) can learn about it. Indeed, LLMs trained to predict the next token in text must exploit this predictive information, so its organization determines how the structure of language becomes available to the model to learn. We develop a theory for the organization of predictive information based on the scaling behavior of a family of information measures, and the theory predicts that if this organization has the same form at all measured length scales -- i.e., it has a self-similar structure -- then the information measures evaluated at different lengths collapse onto a common form. We observe this scaling collapse in long text documents, showing that predictive information is present at every length scale we measure and has a self-similar structure. Self-similarity is a considerably stronger property than showing the existence of long-range dependencies, and it constrains the process generating the text. More broadly, our results give quantitative support to the empirical observation that conditioning on more distant text continues to reveal new structure in language to LLMs.

title: CodeReviewBench: An Automated Benchmark for Evaluating the Software Factory
description:
arXiv:2611.26942v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As AI agents ship more code with minimal human oversight, code review becomes the critical quality-control checkpoint -- but one without a reliable, objective verifier: review quality is nuanced and ultimately a judgment call by the PR author. Existing benchmarks are structurally misaligned with this: annotators are third-party reviewers, like the bots they evaluate, not the PR authors who actually decide what to fix. They also rely on small, static issue sets that require full re-evaluation as tools update, limiting how frequently progress can be tracked. We introduce CodeReviewBench, built on a fundamentally different signal: revealed developer preferences -- if a developer acts on a bot's suggestion, we treat it as useful; if they ignore it, we do not. This signal is mined daily from the public GitHub event stream, yielding 500K+ judged PRs across 18 tools, and refreshes continuously as tools evolve. We validate the developer preference against an independent offline benchmark: the two agree on precision rankings and independently detect the same product updates within days of vendor releases. Together, these form the benchmark.

title: Keep the Process, Change the Supplier: Runtime Governance for Tool-Using AI Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.26966v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tool-using AI agents propose actions whose authorization and external effects cannot be inferred from generated text alone. We study an execution boundary that separates agent proposals from business-controlled authority, context disclosure, and supplier selection. The Open Process Control Plane (OPCP) mediates capability calls and records uncertain outcomes when a supplier may have acted without returning an acceptable reply. We evaluate this runtime with scripted requests and synthetic suppliers: 2,400 fault episodes across four policies, 60 process-termination/restart episodes, 19,000 timed calls across 19 configurations, five targeted mutations over 43 fixtures, and 160 substitution records. No language model or autonomous agent is evaluated. OPCP and a conservative composition agree on all measured fault outcomes. Both recover after definite refusal without cross-supplier duplication; retry-all duplicates effects in every tested lost-reply-after-commit case. Persistent runtime state prevents cross-supplier replay in the restart experiments, while same-supplier duplicate prevention also requires supplier idempotency. At 128 suppliers, best-score routing has a median latency of 1.411 ms versus 0.261 ms for pinned routing. All five selected mutations are detected, and record enumeration exposes acceptance of an empty regression set. These results characterize an execution mechanism relevant to agent governance, including its costs and assumption boundaries. They do not establish improved agent task success, prompt-injection resistance, or real-vendor model portability.

title: Right Numbers, Wrong Story: When LLMs Narrate Financial Changes Beyond Their Inputs
description:
arXiv:2611.26968v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A financial report drafted by an LLM can state every number correctly but still go beyond its input, adding judgments and causes that no one supplied. We call these additions unsupported framing and find them far more often in LLM drafts than in reports written by proInput facts Revenue +3% Higher prices 10-K filings Revenue increased 3% on higher prices. 10-K writer Revenue surged 3% on higher prices, due to strong demand. LLM Fits the size? Surged: Unusual for 3% In the input? In the input? Strong demand: Not in input Higher prices: Kept fessionals, and attempts to fix them by prompting with how each word is used instead make such judgments more frequent. We therefore propose FrameCheck, a plug-in that sits beFrameCheck Revenue increased 3% on higher prices. No extra model call Judgment word Unsupported cause Supported cause tween the LLM and human review to keep each draft within its input. Specifically, FrameCheck 1) guides the draft with professional examples that report a change of similar magnitude, 2) flags judgments that professionals would not use and causes the input does not give, and 3) removes them by rule, without a model call. In experiments on 17 open LLMs and 3M drafts, FrameCheck removes almost all unsupported framing from drafts and brings the judgment rate close to that of the writers of 10-K filings, the annual reports that US firms file with regulators. Code is available at github.com/seunghan96/framecheck.

title: Run One, Get Two: Near-Free Streaming Safety Checks for Local LLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.26975v1 Announce Type: new
