title: schemagate: 91% fewer schema tokens for text-to-SQL, and only the tables the caller may read
description:
Text-to-SQL prompts usually carry the whole database schema, and pay for it on every question. schemagate sends the model only the tables a question needs, and only the ones the person asking may read.

  • 91% fewer schema tokens on real warehouses (Spider 2.0, databases with 50+ tables, median)
  • #1 on UniQL Oracle: 64.93%, ahead of Claude-4.5-Sonnet (49.61)
  • #1 on BIRD Mini-Dev Legacy: SQLite 81.0 · MySQL 72.4 · PostgreSQL 72.6
  • LiveSQLBench-Large: 34.58%, #9 among agents; the BIRD team is adding it to the board
  • In LangChain's official integrations as SchemagateRetriever (pip install langchain-schemagate); also works with LlamaIndex and MCP

What it doesn't do: it picks what the model sees; the SQL is still the model's job.

https://github.com/ashishsinha1602/schemagate

title: Inkling 2 Mini in a React chat: wiring reasoning effort through the Vercel AI SDK
description:
By the Cuelark Team. Model details come from Thinking Machines Lab's launch post and model card and from Hugging Face's release post, all checked on 23 November 2026. We didn't run the model itself. The checkpoint is about 20GB and our test box has 15GB of RAM. The code ran against a local mock of an OpenAI-compatible server, and we rendered the model's official chat template against the requests the SDK actually sent. Read this as a wiring test, not a quality review.

Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini on November 20 with open weights under Apache 2.0. It's a Mixture-of-Experts model with 26.4B total parameters and 3.4B active. Of its 24 layers, the middle 12 run three times per token, which brings it to about 5.4B effective active parameters. It takes text and images, outputs text, and supports a context window of up to 1M tokens. The checkpoint is about 20GB in mixed NVFP4 and MXFP8. The model card recommends Apple silicon with 32GB or more, a DGX Spark, or a GPU with 32GB or more of VRAM.

The launch post says it leads open-weights models under 100B total parameters on DeepSWE v1.1 (48.2%) and Vals Index v2.2 (46.5%). Those are the lab's own numbers, and we didn't check them.

For a chat app, one setting matters more than anything else: reasoning effort. Here's how to wire it from a React dropdown to the model, plus two things in the chat template worth knowing first.

Serving it

Hugging Face's post gives two commands. For local GGUF:

llama serve -hf ggml-org/Inkling-2-Mini-GGUF:IQ4_NL

And for SGLang on datacenter hardware (trimmed; the post has the full flags and notes it needs SM103):

python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini \
  --served-model-name inkling --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000

The post says Llama App, built on llama.cpp, exposes a local OpenAI-compatible API, and SGLang serves /v1/chat/completions. SGLang's example request passes "reasoning_effort": "low" in the body, so the Vercel AI SDK's generic OpenAI-compatible provider is enough.

The route 

// app/api/chat/route.ts
import { streamText, convertToModelMessages, type UIMessage } from 'ai';
import { createOpenAICompatible } from '@ai-sdk/openai-compatible';

const inkling = createOpenAICompatible({
  name: 'inkling',
  baseURL: process.env.INKLING_BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:30000/v1',
  includeUsage: true,
});

export async function POST(req: Request) {
  const { messages, effort = 'low', keepThoughts = false } = await req.json();

  // Old reasoning goes back as reasoning_content, and Inkling's template
  // puts it back into the prompt. Drop it unless you want it in context.
  const history: UIMessage[] = keepThoughts ? messages
    : messages.map((m: UIMessage) => ({ ...m, parts: m.parts.filter((p) => p.type !== 'reasoning') }));

  const result = streamText({
    model: inkling.chatModel('inkling'), // matches --served-model-name
    messages: await convertToModelMessages(history),
    reasoning: effort, // sent as reasoning_effort
    maxOutputTokens: 4096,
  });

  return result.toUIMessageStreamResponse({ sendReasoning: true });
}

On the client, useChat sends the effort with each message: sendMessage({ text: input }, { body: { effort } }). Reasoning arrives as reasoning parts, which you can render in a collapsible <details> above the answer.

What the test showed

AI SDK 7's top-level reasoning option accepts none, minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh and max. That's the same list of names Inkling's chat template uses. In our mock run, each one reached the server unchanged as reasoning_effort. provider-default leaves the field out. Streamed reasoning_content deltas showed up as a reasoning part in the UI message, and the usage chunk filled in the token counts.

Then we ran the official chat_template.jinja from the Hugging Face repo against those requests. A few things stood out:

  • Names map to numbers. none is 0, minimal 0.1, low 0.2, medium 0.7, high 0.9 and both xhigh and max 0.99. If you leave the field out, you get 0.9, so the default is close to the top. With this template, an xhigh and a max option in your UI do the same thing.
  • Numbers work in the template, but not in the SDK option. The template accepts any value from 0.0 to 0.99. The provider's reasoningEffort option only takes a string, so passing 0.35 failed before any request was sent. Passing a raw reasoning_effort: 0.35 under providerOptions.inkling got through unchanged. We didn't confirm that SGLang or llama serve accept a number there.
  • Unknown names throw. "turbo" raised Unknown reasoning_effort. Validate the dropdown value on the server.
  • Old reasoning is resent. By default the SDK sends earlier reasoning back as reasoning_content, and the template renders each one into the prompt as a thinking block. With six tiny fake thoughts, the rendered prompt grew from 1,102 to 1,681 characters. Real reasoning is much longer, so in a long chat this fills context fast. That's why the route strips it unless keepThoughts is set. We don't know whether keeping it helps answer quality.
  • Tool calls need parsed arguments. The SDK sends tool_calls[].function.arguments as a JSON string, like the OpenAI API. The raw template rejects that ("must be a parsed object, not a JSON string"). After JSON.parse, the same history rendered fine. Your server may parse it first. Test one tool round trip on yours before building an agent on it.

Honest limits

  • We didn't run the model. Everything above covers the request and the template. None of it measures speed or answer quality.
  • The lab lists its own weak spots. It isn't the strongest small model for multi-turn chat or for instructions with many constraints. It scores 50.0% on MultiChallenge and 33.4% on ComplexConstraints v1.1, both behind Qwen3.8-27B.
  • none isn't off. The model card says the minimum reasoning effort doesn't fully disable reasoning. Because the middle layers run three times, compute per token is also higher than 3.4B active parameters suggests.
  • Agent safety. The model card warns that the model may delete or overwrite files without asking. It recommends a sandbox and confirmation for destructive actions.
  • Local runtimes are new. Per the model card, support for looped models in local runtimes is new, and speed varies by runtime and hardware.

If you want to experiment, a research checkpoint, TML-d24-varloop-research, lets you change the number of loop passes. Fewer passes are faster, but answers may be a little worse.

Sources

  • Introducing Inkling 2 Mini, Thinking Machines Lab
  • Inkling 2 Mini model card
  • Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Hugging Face blog
  • thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini on Hugging Face (source of chat_template.jinja)

If you'd rather not build the reasoning toggle and message list yourself, Cuelark UI has shadcn-style AI chat components that work with this setup.

title: Cloud Storage and User Avatar Uploads: A Node.js-Based Guide to Tenant Boundaries
description:
Short answer: the easiest storage path for a Node.js avatar upload is the one that keeps the application responsible for authorization and gives the storage layer a narrow, testable job. Put each object under a tenant-scoped key, upload through a short-lived capability, keep the bucket private, and make deletion a durable workflow rather than a best-effort request.

That answer changes once the same e-commerce system must retain signed documents until an explicit deadline. Avatars are replaceable presentation data. A signed document is evidence with a lifecycle. Mixing their policies in one permissive upload path is how a convenient feature becomes a tenant-isolation incident.

I have been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries, so I treat scheduled deletion with the same suspicion as any other queue consumer: retries are normal, delivery is not exactly once, and the handler must be safe to run again. The storage API matters, but the boundary around it matters more.

The incident lesson: convenience is not an isolation policy

The bounded failure pattern is familiar. A web request accepts an upload, builds a key from an account identifier, and asks storage to save the bytes. Later, a background job finds documents past their deadline and removes them. An avatar endpoint and a document endpoint may even share the same helper because both receive a filename and a stream.

That helper hides the important differences. An avatar can usually be replaced by a newer object. A signed document needs a recorded deadline, an owner, an audit trail, and a deletion decision that survives a worker restart. If the key is the only place tenant identity exists, a typo in a prefix or an over-broad listing operation can turn an authorization rule into a naming convention. Naming conventions are not an authorization system.

The invariant I want is small enough to test: every read, write, and delete is authorized against a tenant and an object record before storage is called. The object key is derived from that record, never accepted as an authority from the browser. The storage credential used by the application cannot be treated as a user permission.

This is the tradeoff. A direct browser upload can reduce application bandwidth and make large files easier to handle, but it moves part of the protocol into a client you do not control. A server-mediated upload gives the application a stronger inspection point, at the cost of handling more bytes and keeping the request path healthy. For small avatars, that extra control is usually worth the simpler failure story. For signed documents, a short-lived upload capability can be appropriate when the server still creates the object record first and validates the completion afterward.

The advice does not apply unchanged to public image hosting, anonymous uploads, or data that has no tenant boundary. In those systems, a public delivery model may be intentional. It is a poor default for customer documents.

Which cloud storage should a Node.js-based user choose for avatars?

Ease is not the number of methods in a client library. It is the number of states an operator has to reason about at 03:00. A useful upload path has an explicit state machine: pending, accepted, available, expired, and deleted. The database is the source of that state; object storage holds bytes and metadata.

For an avatar, the record can contain the tenant ID, account ID, object key, content type accepted by policy, byte count, and a checksum or equivalent integrity value. The serving path checks the account relationship before returning a short-lived read capability. It does not turn a user-supplied key into a read URL.

For a signed document, add the retention deadline and a deletion status. Do not infer the deadline from an object timestamp. Clocks, retries, restores, and manual reprocessing make that inference hard to defend. A deadline is business data. Store it where the retention worker can query it, audit it, and test it.

The object key should be boring. For example, a generated identifier can prevent collisions without exposing an email address or a document name:

Boring is good.

package objects

import "fmt"

func Key(tenantID, objectID string) string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("tenants/%s/objects/%s", tenantID, objectID)
}

It must converge.

Keep it explicit.

The function is not a security boundary by itself. It is a consistency tool. Authorization still happens before Key is used, and the resulting key is stored with the object record so a future code path does not reconstruct it from request input.

The upload completion path deserves the same care. A client can disappear after bytes arrive, or report completion after a retry. Record an upload intent before issuing a capability, verify the resulting object against the intent, and make the completion transition idempotent. A second completion should return the already-known result, not create another document record.

Which failure modes should the design make boring?

The first is cross-tenant access. Test it directly: create two tenants, create objects with similar names, and assert that a read, overwrite, and delete for tenant A cannot affect tenant B. Test the worker too. A retention query that forgets tenant_id is more dangerous than a malformed upload because it can affect many records without a user request.

The second is duplicate delivery. A scheduler can run the same deletion task twice. A queue can redeliver it. A deployment can stop the worker after the storage delete and before the database update. The handler should therefore use a stable document ID, re-check ownership and deadline, issue a delete that is safe to repeat, and then record the outcome. If the database update loses a race, the next attempt should converge rather than resurrect the object.

Here is the shape of that decision in Go. The interfaces are deliberately generic; the useful part is the order of checks and the idempotent outcome.

package retention

import (
    "context"
    "time"
)

type Document struct {
    ID        string
    TenantID  string
    Key       string
    DeleteAt  time.Time
    DeletedAt *time.Time
}

type Repository interface {
    Find(ctx context.Context, documentID string) (Document, error)
    MarkDeleted(ctx context.Context, documentID string, at time.Time) error
}

type BlobStore interface {
    Delete(ctx context.Context, key string) error
}

func Expire(ctx context.Context, repo Repository, store BlobStore, documentID string, now time.Time) error {
    doc, err := repo.Find(ctx, documentID)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if doc.DeletedAt != nil || now.Before(doc.DeleteAt) {
        return nil
    }

    if err := store.Delete(ctx, doc.Key); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    return repo.MarkDeleted(ctx, doc.ID, now)
}

In production, the repository query and update need concurrency control appropriate to the database, and the storage delete needs a clearly defined error policy. A not-found result can be success for an idempotent delete; an authorization or transport failure cannot. The code also assumes the object record was created from a trusted tenant context. It is not a substitute for that check.

The third failure is a deadline that is technically reached but operationally invisible. Emit a count of due documents, deletion attempts, successful transitions, retryable failures, and records stuck in an intermediate state. Keep tenant identifiers out of high-cardinality metric labels; put them in structured logs only when access controls and retention rules permit it. An alert should tell an on-call engineer whether the queue is late, storage is failing, or the database is rejecting state changes.

How should avatars and signed documents share infrastructure?

Share the primitive, not the policy. A common object-store adapter can expose put, get, and delete operations. The avatar service should own image validation, replacement, and serving rules. The document service should own retention deadlines, legal holds if the domain requires them, audit records, and deletion reconciliation. Separate prefixes help operations, but separate authorization checks and records do the real work.

The same split applies to access paths. A private object with a short-lived read capability is a different contract from a public CDN URL. For avatars, caching may be useful after authorization has been evaluated, but the cache key must not accidentally collapse two tenants into one response. For documents, avoid making a long-lived URL the durable reference. Resolve access from the document record, authorize the requester, and issue the shortest practical read capability.

Node.js developers often choose storage by how quickly the first multipart example runs. That is a reasonable prototype test. It is not enough for a production choice. Compare the options against the operations your team must own: conditional writes, integrity checks, private access, lifecycle controls, auditability, retry behavior, local testing, and exit strategy. A provider with a friendly Node.js SDK can still be awkward if deletion status cannot be reconciled cleanly. A self-hosted or standards-based endpoint can be easier to test but may transfer durability and incident response to your team.

I would write the decision record around those boundaries, not around a library choice. State who can mint upload capabilities, where tenant authorization lives, how a deadline is recorded, what a repeated delete means, how orphaned bytes are found, and how a tenant can export or remove its data. That document is more durable than a library choice.

A deployment and test plan that survives retries

Start with unit tests for key derivation, tenant checks, deadline comparisons, and repeated completion. Add integration tests against the same storage protocol used in production, including a missing-object delete and a timeout after the storage operation succeeds. Then run a small end-to-end test that creates an upload intent, completes an avatar, replaces it, and verifies that the old object is eventually removed without deleting another tenant's object.

For signed documents, test the deadline as data. A document due at 2026-01-15T00:00:00Z should not be deleted by a worker whose effective time is earlier, and it should be eligible at or after that instant according to the product's stated boundary. The year in this example is a test fixture, not a retention recommendation. Use UTC in persisted timestamps and make the worker's clock injectable.

Deploy the worker with bounded concurrency and backoff. A large retry storm can be an isolation risk if it causes operators to disable checks under pressure. Prefer a dead-letter or quarantine state that preserves the document ID and failure reason without silently extending retention. Reconciliation should scan for mismatches such as a deleted database record with a remaining object, and an object record marked deleted with a recoverable storage error.

Deletion is also a compliance workflow. GDPR Article 17 describes a right to erasure, but the correct product behavior depends on the legal basis, exceptions, and other obligations that apply to the business. Treat the deadline in the record as an explicit application decision, and retain only the audit evidence needed to demonstrate what happened. Do not promise that deleting an object from one service erases every replica unless the entire data lifecycle has been mapped.

The practical choice for the original avatar question is therefore modest: choose the storage interface your Node.js team can exercise locally, secure privately, observe in production, and leave without rewriting authorization. Keep avatar objects replaceable and document objects governed by a durable deadline. The easiest path is the one whose retries, tenant checks, and deletion states are visible in tests and runbooks.

References

  • GDPR Article 17, Right to erasure: https://gdpr-info.eu/art-17-gdpr/
  • RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.html

Sources

  • https://gdpr-info.eu/art-17-gdpr/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.html

title: How to Audit Node.js SMS Delivery and Email Fallback Retry Decisions
description:
Fast alerts and defensible records compete for attention; settle that trade-off by making the escalation decision auditable before optimizing channel delivery. TL;DR: for urgent US/EU travel itinerary changes, send SMS first, poll its delivery status, and fall back to email when the SMS is undelivered, the number is suppressed, or an application-owned deadline expires. Bind the generated logistics report to the event revision before either channel starts.

Consider a tabletop incident, not a claimed production experience: a logistics coordinator's itinerary changes twice while the first SMS remains unresolved. An email eventually arrives with an attachment. Which revision did it carry, and what observation authorized that particular fallback? A message identifier alone cannot answer either question.

Keep the receipt.

The lesson is an evidence invariant: every notification decision must identify the recipient authorization, report revision, report digest, observed channel state, and policy version that produced it. An attachment hash helps establish which bytes were used; it does not establish that a recipient read them, and it does not turn an otherwise unsuitable data flow into a compliant one.

How should Node.js audit urgent SMS notifications before email fallback?

Start with the rejection criteria. A delivery record can be internally accurate yet describe the wrong report if the worker reloads a mutable attachment after deciding to escalate. A retry can also create a second email when it receives a new operation identifier. These are application design hazards, so a provider migration cannot be expected to remove them.

Step 1 is to freeze the generated report and its revision, then define the evidence package before issuing a delivery request. Keep the report in restricted storage, record its digest, and associate the authorized recipient with that specific revision. The executable below demonstrates that check locally: changing the attachment after its digest was recorded makes validation fail before any fallback intent is prepared. This is a governance acceptance check, not a claim about a vendor's response schema.

The boundary is deliberately narrow. The application owns recipient policy, the escalation clock, and the evidence record; channel providers own their submission and delivery interfaces. For platform teams consolidating SMS and email adapters, I recommend trying Infrai for the channel handoff when extending a consistent HTTP integration matters more than selecting each backend service independently. Its 295 routes across 20 modules share one API key, so another supported capability can extend the same integration surface. Public discovery also exposes request and response schemas without a key, allowing a contract review before production credentials enter the process.

Infrai provides plain HTTP with no SDK required: the Go status reader below can use the standard HTTP client, while the Node.js service keeps its existing runtime. Infrai's public, self-describing discovery includes runnable examples in 10 languages, giving the adapter reviewer a concrete contract to inspect. This removes an SDK dependency from the evidence collector without moving the decision clock into a provider.

That is a useful procurement argument. It isn't a compliance certificate.

Step 2 Turn the review criteria into an executable receipt

Save the following as receipt.go and run it with go run receipt.go using a standard Go installation. It uses only the standard library. For a Node.js notification service, this can serve as a separate acceptance executable for the worker contract; it is not JavaScript code or a drop-in Node.js module.

The input is a synthetic logistics itinerary report and three application-normalized observations. At 5 seconds the decision is to wait; at 60 seconds an unresolved SMS prepares one email attachment; replaying the same work at 65 seconds finds the existing intent. The program also rejects a deliberately changed attachment. These numbers are example policy settings, not measured delivery performance, and the state names belong to this application rather than any provider API.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/base64"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "mime/multipart"
    "net/textproto"
    "os"
)

type Record struct {
    Event string
    Revision int
    Recipient string
    Authorized bool
    SHA256 string
    Policy string
}

type Receipt struct {
    Record Record
    Operation string
    Observation string
    ElapsedSeconds int
    Decision string
}

func digest(data []byte) string {
    sum := sha256.Sum256(data)
    return fmt.Sprintf("%x", sum)
}

func validate(r Record, report []byte) error {
    if !r.Authorized || r.Recipient == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("recipient authorization required")
    }
    if r.SHA256 != digest(report) {
        return fmt.Errorf("attachment digest mismatch")
    }
    return nil
}

func decide(state string, elapsed, deadline int) (string, error) {
    switch state {
    case "delivered":
        return "stop", nil
    case "undelivered", "suppressed":
        return "prepare_email", nil
    case "unresolved":
        if elapsed >= deadline { return "prepare_email", nil }
        return "wait", nil
    default:
        return "", fmt.Errorf("unmapped observation %q", state)
    }
}

func email(r Record, report []byte) ([]byte, error) {
    var body bytes.Buffer
    w := multipart.NewWriter(&body)
    h := make(textproto.MIMEHeader)
    h.Set("Content-Type", "text/plain; charset=utf-8")
    p, err := w.CreatePart(h)
    if err != nil { return nil, err }
    if _, err = p.Write([]byte("Revised logistics itinerary report attached.\r\n")); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    h = make(textproto.MIMEHeader)
    h.Set("Content-Type", "text/csv; charset=utf-8")
    h.Set("Content-Disposition", `attachment; filename="itinerary-r8.csv"`)
    h.Set("Content-Transfer-Encoding", "base64")
    p, err = w.CreatePart(h)
    if err != nil { return nil, err }
    encoded := base64.StdEncoding.EncodeToString(report)
    for len(encoded) > 0 {
        n := len(encoded)
        if n > 76 { n = 76 }
        if _, err = fmt.Fprintf(p, "%s\r\n", encoded[:n]); err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        encoded = encoded[n:]
    }
    if err = w.Close(); err != nil { return nil, err }
    var message bytes.Buffer
    fmt.Fprint(&message, "From: dispatch@example.com\r\n")
    fmt.Fprintf(&message, "To: %s\r\n", r.Recipient)
    fmt.Fprintf(&message, "Subject: Logistics itinerary revision %d\r\n", r.Revision)
    fmt.Fprint(&message, "MIME-Version: 1.0\r\n")
    fmt.Fprintf(&message, "Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary=%q\r\n\r\n", w.Boundary())
    message.Write(body.Bytes())
    return message.Bytes(), nil
}

func main() {
    report := []byte("trip,revision,change\r\n84,8,coordinator itinerary revised\r\n")
    r := Record{"logistics-trip-84", 8, "coordinator@example.com", true,
        digest(report), "escalation-policy-3"}
    if err := validate(r, []byte("different report")); err == nil {
        log.Fatal("changed attachment was accepted")
    }
    if err := validate(r, report); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }
    identity, err := json.Marshal(struct {
        Event string
        Revision int
        Recipient string
        Channel string
    }{r.Event, r.Revision, r.Recipient, "email"})
    if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }
    operation := digest(identity)
    prepared := make(map[string]bool)
    output := json.NewEncoder(os.Stdout)
    for _, seconds := range []int{5, 60, 65} {
        decision, err := decide("unresolved", seconds, 60)
        if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }
        if decision == "prepare_email" {
            if prepared[operation] {
                decision = "existing_intent"
            } else {
                message, err := email(r, report)
                if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }
                if err = os.WriteFile("itinerary-r8.eml", message, 0600); err != nil {
                    log.Fatal(err)
                }
                prepared[operation] = true
            }
        }
        receipt := Receipt{r, operation, "unresolved", seconds, decision}
        if err = output.Encode(receipt); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }
    }
}

The output is three JSON receipts and a MIME message file containing the report attachment. No SMS or email is sent. An attachment-capable delivery adapter is still required, and its accepted request, returned message identifier, and later observations must be associated with the same operation. The example's authorization flag stands for a prior policy decision; production authorization needs its own recorded basis, not a Boolean supplied by the caller.

Notice what the operation identity excludes: the latest observation time and a fresh retry timestamp. Neither should create a new business send. It also excludes a freshly recomputed report digest, because a changed report under an unchanged event revision should fail validation rather than silently acquire permission to send again.

The in-memory map demonstrates replay within one process. Production workers need a durable uniqueness constraint on event, revision, recipient, and channel, with the evidence record and outbox intent committed together; a process-local map cannot coordinate workers or survive a restart. Persist the MIME artifact or the immutable inputs needed to rebuild it, then let a transport worker claim the outbox row. Record ambiguous submission outcomes separately from definitive rejection, and reuse the same supported idempotency key when retrying a write. A unique outbox row alone cannot guarantee a single external delivery after a crash.

Step 3 Budget the observations before accepting the SLO

An evidence review should ask whether the decision clock is achievable under backlog, not just whether a happy-path example prints the expected label. Define a decision SLO separately from delivery: for example, aim to record the escalation decision within 60 seconds, while treating actual recipient delivery as a distinct objective. A worker that wakes only every 5 seconds cannot promise an exact 60-second decision under arbitrary scheduling delay.

Capacity is arithmetic. With 1,200 unresolved SMS attempts and one observation every 5 seconds, the planned baseline is 240 polls per second before retries. That is a workload estimate, not provider capacity. Spread observation times, reserve concurrency for deadline decisions, and include request timeouts and rate-limit backoff in the budget; otherwise the polling mechanism intended to provide evidence can become the reason that evidence arrives late.

For Infrai, design around pull-based channel observations and application-owned fallback timing. Use ordinary message submission and status handling for itinerary changes, keeping OTP verification as a separate workflow. Normalize the documented response into the application's states, retain the original observation in restricted evidence storage, and leave an unsuccessful observation unresolved. Successful submission does not mean successful delivery.

For the real observation boundary, save this separate executable as observe.go, set INFRAI_API_KEY and SMS_MESSAGE_ID to your credentials and an existing submission identifier, and run go run observe.go. Run it separately from receipt.go. This read-only request has an explicit GET method and no request body; it outputs the raw status response for the evidence collector rather than guessing a delivery field. Production normalization must follow the current response schema before calling the decision function above.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func observe(ctx context.Context, key, id string) ([]byte, error) {
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 10 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "GET",
            strings.Replace("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/sms/status/{id}",
                "{id}", url.PathEscape(id), 1), nil)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")
        res, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(res.Body, (1<<20)+1))
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { return nil, readErr }
        if len(data) > 1<<20 { return nil, fmt.Errorf("response too large") }
        if res.StatusCode >= 200 && res.StatusCode < 300 { return data, nil }
        if res.StatusCode != 429 || attempt == 3 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("status request HTTP %d: %s", res.StatusCode, data)
        }
        delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
        retryAfter := res.Header.Get("Retry-After")
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            if seconds > 60 { return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry exceeds observation budget") }
            if candidate := time.Duration(seconds)*time.Second; candidate > delay {
                delay = candidate
            }
        } else if at, err := http.ParseTime(retryAfter); err == nil {
            if candidate := time.Until(at); candidate > delay { delay = candidate }
        }
        timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            timer.Stop()
            return nil, ctx.Err()
        case <-timer.C:
        }
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("observation attempts exhausted")
}

func main() {
    key, id := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"), os.Getenv("SMS_MESSAGE_ID")
    if key == "" || id == "" { log.Fatal("set INFRAI_API_KEY and SMS_MESSAGE_ID") }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 60*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    data, err := observe(ctx, key, id)
    if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }
    if _, err = os.Stdout.Write(data); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }
}

Keep observation output restricted. Don't copy recipient data into general-purpose logs.

On HTTP 429, honor Retry-After and use bounded exponential backoff rather than immediately polling again. Rescheduling an observation must not reset the business deadline. At the deadline, unresolved remains unresolved in the evidence record even if policy chooses email; rewriting it as an SMS failure would manufacture certainty that the observation never supplied. A late SMS delivery can still follow an email fallback, so the message copy and incident review must tolerate both channels reaching the coordinator.

Apply per-country allowlists and backend budget guards before sending to US/EU recipients, and rate-limit user-requested resends by event revision and recipient. Treat those as business controls. Neither a country label nor an email audit trail proves legal compliance; retention, access control, recipient authorization, and applicable obligations still need review.

Which channel responsibilities should the platform team buy?

Use the evidence package as a procurement acceptance criterion. The comparison below separates a product's role in this workflow from the work the application must retain; it makes no claim that the products offer interchangeable contracts or that a particular vendor certifies the entire logistics process.

Buy or build choice Concrete fit for this report workflow Boundary to review before adoption
Infrai A shared HTTP surface for the SMS and email handoff, with broader backend capabilities under one key Own polling and escalation policy; review the attachment contract and the evidence retained for each channel
Twilio SMS A direct SMS integration when the urgent channel warrants independent selection Pair it with an email provider and normalize the resulting evidence in the application
Amazon SES An email-focused candidate for delivering the generated attachment Evaluate the email leg separately; the SMS-first decision still needs an application owner
SendGrid Another email-focused candidate for the report delivery leg Compare its email workflow against SES for this attachment; retain the same event and revision checks
Application-owned orchestration Recipient policy, immutable report association, deadlines, and outbox uniqueness Budget storage, worker operations, retention, and the on-call responsibility for missed decisions

A specialist is the better choice when the requirement is control over a particular channel's integration rather than consolidation across backend services. An existing Twilio SMS deployment paired with SES or SendGrid can be a reasonable boundary to preserve if the team already has defensible evidence handling and operating ownership. Replacing it merely to reduce the number of integrations would need a concrete benefit, not a prettier diagram.

This advice also stops at the business requirement. If the logistics report must be emailed regardless of SMS delivery, give that email its own authorized intent; tying it to SMS fallback would incorrectly suppress a required report when SMS succeeds. If a workflow requires immediate event push, SMTP relay, or additional messaging channels, evaluate a specialist against that requirement rather than assuming the same polling design applies. Keep verification and scheduled-message lifecycle requirements in a separate acceptance review.

The release criterion is modest: reconstruct why this recipient received this report revision, then demonstrate that a retry preserves that explanation. Do that before promising a delivery SLO.

References

The independent references distinguish channel documentation from message-format and subscription standards. RFC 8058 concerns one-click unsubscribe; it is not evidence that an urgent itinerary email satisfies every compliance obligation.

  • Twilio SMS documentation
  • Amazon SES documentation
  • SendGrid Mail Send documentation
  • MIME multipart message format
  • One-click unsubscribe

Sources

For the first-party escalation contract, start with SMS first and email second if this division of responsibility fits your system.

title: Where Is My Order? Build a Client Portal That Answers It for You
description:
“Where is my order?” sounds like a simple customer-service question.

For a business handling dozens or hundreds of orders, though, answering it can become a recurring engineering and operational problem.

Someone receives the enquiry, locates the order, checks another system, asks a colleague for an update, and sends a reply. The process repeats for the next customer.

The issue isn't necessarily slow customer support. It may be that customers have no reliable way to access information the business already has.

A client portal can solve part of this problem. But building one requires more than adding authentication and displaying an order table.

The real challenge is connecting a useful customer experience to accurate operational data while enforcing the right access controls.

Here is how I would approach the problem.

  1. Identify the Customer Questions Worth Solving Before designing the interface, identify the questions customers repeatedly ask.

For an order-based business, these might include:

  • Has my order been received?
  • Is it confirmed?
  • Is it being prepared?
  • Has it been dispatched?
  • When is delivery expected?
  • Can I download the invoice?
  • Is there anything I need to do? These questions help define the portal's initial scope.

I would classify each enquiry into two categories:

Information requests: Questions that can be answered from reliable, existing data.

Intervention requests: Questions that require an employee to investigate, make a decision, or communicate additional context.

The portal should handle the first category well and provide a clear route to support for the second.

This distinction prevents a common mistake: trying to automate every customer interaction.

A delayed order, for example, might have a status that can be displayed automatically. Explaining the reason for the delay may still require human involvement.

The first engineering task is therefore not building a dashboard. It is mapping customer questions to the data and workflows that can answer them.

  1. Define a Small, Useful First Release I would start with the smallest feature set that removes the most repetitive enquiries.

A practical first release might include:

  • Secure customer authentication.
  • Customer-specific order listings.
  • Individual order details.
  • Clear order status and relevant dates.
  • Access to approved documents.
  • A support route for exceptions. The user journey should be straightforward: Login | v Customer Dashboard | v Select an Order | v View Status and Details | +------> Download Documents | +------> Contact Support

The customer should not need to understand the internal structure of the business to find an order.

I would also avoid adding features simply because they are common in other portals. Payment management, analytics, ticketing, and account administration may become useful later, but each adds implementation and maintenance complexity.

A focused first release gives the team something concrete to validate.

The important question is not whether the portal has enough features. It is whether customers can complete their most common task without contacting someone.

  1. Model Order Status as a Real Business Workflow Order status is often treated as a simple text field. In practice, it represents a business process.

Consider these stages:
RECEIVED
|
v
CONFIRMED
|
v
IN_PREPARATION
|
v
DISPATCHED
|
v
DELIVERED

This is only an example. Actual states should reflect the business's operational workflow.

I would define each state explicitly:

  • What does the state mean?
  • Which event moves an order into it?
  • Which system records that event?
  • Can the order move backwards?
  • Can it enter an exception state?
  • What should the customer see? For example, DISPATCHED should represent a recorded dispatch event, not an assumption that an order is about to leave the warehouse.

A basic application-level enum might look like this:
type OrderStatus =
| "RECEIVED"
| "CONFIRMED"
| "IN_PREPARATION"
| "DISPATCHED"
| "DELIVERED"
| "ON_HOLD"
| "CANCELLED";

The enum provides a controlled set of states, but it does not define valid transitions by itself.

I would keep transition rules in the business logic rather than allowing arbitrary status updates from the frontend.

For example, an order should not move from RECEIVED directly to DELIVERED unless the business explicitly supports that workflow.

The customer-facing label can be more readable than the internal state. IN_PREPARATION might appear as “Your order is being prepared.”

This separation allows internal workflows and customer communication to evolve without becoming tightly coupled.

  1. Design Customer Authentication and Permissions Together Authentication answers one question:

Who is this user?

Authorisation answers another:

Which records is this user allowed to access?

A client portal needs both.

This becomes especially important in B2B environments where several employees may belong to one customer organisation.

A simplified data model might contain:
Customer
├── Customer Users
└── Orders
├── Order Items
└── Documents

The application needs to enforce the relationship between the authenticated user, their customer organisation, and the requested order.

For example, an API endpoint should not simply retrieve an order using an ID supplied by the browser:
// Avoid relying on an order ID alone.
const order = await db.order.findUnique({
where: { id: requestedOrderId }
});

Instead, the lookup should also enforce the user's authorised customer scope:
const order = await db.order.findFirst({
where: {
id: requestedOrderId,
customerId: authenticatedUser.customerId
}
});

This is illustrative code; the actual implementation depends on the application's authentication and data-access architecture.

The key principle is that access checks belong on the server.

Hiding another customer's order in the interface is not access control. A user can still attempt to request its underlying API endpoint directly.

I would apply the same principle to documents, invoices, attachments, and any other customer-specific resource.

A secure portal should also account for account deactivation, password recovery, session expiration, and permission changes.

  1. Integrate With the Source of Truth This is where the project often becomes more interesting than the UI suggests.

Order information may live in an ERP, inventory system, order-management platform, CRM, or internal application. Sometimes several systems contribute different parts of the order lifecycle.

The portal needs a dependable way to retrieve and present that information.

I would begin by mapping the data flow:
Order Management / ERP
|
v
Integration Layer
|
v
Client Portal API
|
v
Customer UI

The integration approach depends on the existing systems.

An API-based integration may work well when the source system exposes suitable endpoints. Event-driven updates can be useful when status changes need to appear quickly. Scheduled synchronisation may be sufficient when near-real-time updates are not essential.

There is no universal answer.

I would pay particular attention to failure handling:

  • What happens when the source system is unavailable?
  • How are delayed updates represented?
  • What happens when an order record changes?
  • How are duplicate events handled?
  • Can the system identify stale information?
  • How are integration failures monitored? For a customer-facing portal, displaying incorrect information can be worse than temporarily displaying no update.

I would rather show a last-updated timestamp and an honest indication of a delay than present stale data as current.

The portal should not become a competing source of truth. It should be a controlled customer-facing view of the systems that own the business information.

  1. Decide When a Custom Portal Is Worth Building A custom portal is not automatically the right solution.

Before building one, I would check whether the existing business software already supports customer access or whether a smaller improvement could solve the problem.

For example, better automated notifications might address a large share of status enquiries. An existing ERP customer portal might already provide the necessary features. A small API integration could expose information without requiring a completely separate application.

A custom build becomes more interesting when the business has specific workflows, complex customer permissions, multiple disconnected systems, or requirements that existing tools cannot support well.

I would also account for ongoing ownership.

A portal needs security updates, integration monitoring, access management, backups, testing, and maintenance as business processes change.

The decision should include those responsibilities, not just the initial development effort.

The goal is not to build more software. It is to remove a recurring operational problem without creating a larger one.
Where the Engineering Effort Goes

  1. Customer questions ██████░░░░
  2. First useful features ██████░░░░
  3. Order-status workflow ███████░░░
  4. Secure access control ████████░░
  5. Data integration ██████████
  6. Build decision ███████░░░

My indicative planning emphasis: data integration and access control deserve particular attention because they determine whether customers can trust what the portal shows.
Practical Takeaway: Before You Start Building
I would want clear answers to these questions before development begins:

  • [ ] What are the most frequent customer status enquiries?
  • [ ] Which of those questions can reliable data answer?
  • [ ] Where does each piece of order information originate?
  • [ ] What order states and transitions does the business actually use?
  • [ ] Which users can access which customer records?
  • [ ] How will the portal handle stale data and integration failures?
  • [ ] Can an existing platform solve the problem already?
  • [ ] Who will maintain the portal after launch? If these questions are unanswered, I would spend more time on discovery before writing application code.

A little clarity at this stage can prevent a lot of unnecessary complexity later.
How KSoft Technologies Helps With Client Portals
At KSoft Technologies, this is part of our software engineering work: understanding operational workflows and building web applications and integrations around them. We help founders and growing companies assess, develop, and modernise systems such as customer portals, with attention to usability, data reliability, and secure access. This is our own software development service, not an independent product recommendation.
Final Thought
A client portal should do more than move an existing process onto a website.

It should make useful information easier to access, reduce avoidable communication loops, and give customers a clearer understanding of what is happening.

The best starting point is often a simple question:

What are customers repeatedly asking your team that your systems should already be able to answer?

I'm interested in how other developers approach this. When building customer-facing portals, what has been the hardest part in practice: modelling the workflow, integrating legacy systems, or getting permissions right?

I write about practical software engineering for growing businesses at KSoft Technologies.

title: Building a Luxury Indian Wedding Invitation Suite on Next.js 14 and Oracle ARM
description:
Indian weddings are among the most elaborate cultural celebrations in the world. Spanning 3 to 7 distinct ceremonies—Haldi, Mehndi, Sangeet, Pheras, and Reception—they involve hundreds of guests attending across multiple days and venues.

Yet, most modern event and wedding website builders (Zola, The Knot, Joy, Paperless Post) were designed around Western single-day ceremony paradigms. When Indian couples try using them, they immediately hit friction:

  1. RSVPs by Family Unit: In South Asian weddings, invites aren't solo or +1; they go to entire families (e.g., "Sharma Family — 4 attending").
  2. Multi-Ceremony Dietary Tracking: Tracking Veg, Non-Veg, Jain, and Vegan across Haldi, Sangeet, and Reception.
  3. WhatsApp-First Distribution: Over 90% of guests open invitations directly from WhatsApp mobile links on 3G/4G connections.
  4. Digital Shagun (Gifting): Direct, zero-commission UPI peer-to-peer gifting instead of traditional cash envelopes.

To solve this, we engineered ShadiLink—a high-performance, mobile-first luxury wedding suite built on Next.js 14 App Router, Tailwind CSS, Prisma, and self-hosted on Oracle Cloud ARM infrastructure.

Here is the architectural breakdown of how we built it.

1. Architecture Overview 

Client (Mobile / WhatsApp Webview)
              │
              ▼
    Cloudflare Edge CDN
              │
              ▼
Next.js 14 App Router (Docker Container on Oracle ARM)
  ├── Server Components (RSC) -> Dynamic HTML Streaming
  ├── tRPC Endpoints (Zod Validation)
  └── Edge Middleware (Subdomain Routing & Geo-caching)
              │
      ┌───────┴───────┐
      ▼               ▼
PostgreSQL (Prisma)  Redis (Cache & Rate Limiting)

Self-Hosting on Oracle Cloud Free Tier (ARM)

Rather than paying high monthly PaaS bills during early product validation, we architected the system on Oracle Cloud Free Tier's Ampere A1 Compute:

  • 4 OCPU (Ampere Altra ARM64)
  • 24 GB RAM
  • 200 GB NVMe Storage

This gives us tremendous headroom for zero hosting cost. We containerized the Next.js production build using multi-stage Docker builds optimized for linux/arm64.

2. Sub-Second Mobile Performance on WhatsApp Webviews

85% to 95% of our traffic arrives through WhatsApp in-app browser sessions on mid-range Android devices. If a wedding invitation takes more than 2 seconds to load, guests bounce.

We enforced a strict performance budget:

  • Sub-100KB client JavaScript per route: Heavy interactive components (photo galleries, maps, music player) are loaded with next/dynamic only when scrolled into view.
  • Fluid Typography Architecture: Instead of breakpoint jumps, all headers and typography use mathematical clamping: 
  font-size: clamp(1.75rem, 4vw + 1rem, 3.5rem);
  • Zero Heavy Raster Ornaments: Instead of bloated PNG borders, we engineered lightweight 0.75px vector SVG paths for traditional Mughal arches and jaali motifs that weigh under 2KB.
  • Lighthouse Performance Score: 96+ on Mobile with First Contentful Paint under 1.2s on 3G.

3. The Family-Unit RSVP Engine

Western RSVP systems store:
{ guestId: "123", attending: true, meal: "chicken" }

In Indian weddings, this breaks immediately. Our schema groups attendees under single households with per-ceremony granular attendance:

export interface HouseholdRSVP {
  familyName: string;
  phone: string;
  totalGuests: number;
  dietaryPreference: "VEG" | "NON_VEG" | "JAIN" | "VEGAN";
  events: {
    haldi: boolean;
    mehndi: boolean;
    sangeet: boolean;
    wedding: boolean;
    reception: boolean;
  };
  notes?: string;
}

This drastically simplified the guest experience: a single click on WhatsApp lets a head of household confirm everyone attending in less than 20 seconds.

4. Zero-Fee UPI Shagun Integration

Rather than funneling gifts through payment gateways that charge 2-3% platform cuts, ShadiLink generates native UPI intent strings (upi://pay?pa=...&pn=...&am=...&cu=INR) and dynamic on-the-fly QR codes.

When guests tap "Send Shagun" on mobile, it directly launches Google Pay, PhonePe, or Paytm on their phone and transfers 100% of the funds straight into the couple's verified bank account with zero middlemen fees.

What We Learned

  1. Domain constraints dictate UI constraints: Understanding cultural nuances (like Jain food requirements and family RSVPs) matter far more than adding generic bells and whistles.
  2. Oracle ARM is a hidden gem for indie builders: 4 ARM cores and 24GB of RAM on Oracle Free Tier provides enterprise-grade performance for free if configured properly.
  3. Mobile webview resilience is key: Always test in real WhatsApp in-app browsers, not just Chrome DevTools desktop emulation.

Check out live interactive templates at ShadiLink and let us know your feedback!

title: PHP's 19 Nov CVEs and what 8.1/8.2 teams should do
description:
On 19 November 2026, PHP shipped 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37 and 8.2.36, fixing 18 CVEs. PHP 8.6.0 was also released that day. The details are on php.net, and were also reported by BleepingComputer.

If you run PHP 8.1 or older, you got none of the fixes. Only supported versions received patches.

The worst of the 18 is a PHP-FPM request-smuggling bug rated CVSS 9.2. In some setups that reuse backend connections, it lets an attacker run code without logging in. Several session and use-after-free bugs can also lead to remote code execution. Per PHP, the critical bugs need non-default or uncommon setups.

That does not make an unpatched 8.1 or 8.2 system safe to ignore. It means you should treat this release as work to schedule, not as a reason to wait.

Who is already out of support

PHP 8.1 lost security support on 31 December 2025. PHP 7.x lost it long before. Those versions will not receive these patches, or later ones.

The next deadline is close: PHP 8.2 security support ends 31 December 2026. That's 38 days away. After that date, 8.2 joins 8.1 and 7.x: no official security fixes.

What 8.1 and 8.2 teams should do

1. Patch supported versions now. If you already run 8.3, 8.4 or 8.5, move to 8.3.37, 8.4.28 or 8.5.13. That is the immediate work, and it does not depend on any longer-term plan.

2. Inventory which applications are still on 8.1 or 8.2. A billing tool, an admin panel, or a forgotten CodeIgniter 3 app is easy to miss. You cannot plan a move you have not listed.

3. Decide, for each of those applications, whether to upgrade PHP or move off it. Those are the two options on 8.1 or 8.2. An upgrade keeps you on PHP, onto a supported version. Moving off is the point at which some teams choose another stack. Neither path is free of behavioural risk.

4. Keep behavioural proof either way. A PHP upgrade and a migration can both change how the system behaves. You need proof that the new system behaves exactly like the old one: the same HTTP responses, the same database writes, the same outgoing API calls. Without that, you are hoping the paths you clicked through are representative.

If you are moving off PHP

That proof problem is what we built MigrateForge for. We move PHP to Java 21 / Spring Boot and check it by replaying recorded user journeys against both systems: HTTP responses, DB writes and outgoing API calls. Cutover stays blocked until they match. Your code stays on your machines.

Benchmarks so far (not client projects): 4 waves, 858 fixtures, 100% parity, 0 write-effect diffs.

If you are running plain PHP or CodeIgniter 3 on 8.1 or 8.2, start with the free migration report. It covers size, risks, an indicative wave plan and a price range. No source code is needed.

https://migrateforge.com

CTOs: still running PHP 8.1 or 8.2 in production? What's blocking the move: budget, test coverage, or no proof the new system will behave the same?

#MigrateForge

title: Dynamic SQL Done Safely: sp_executesql, Parameters and QUOTENAME
description:
Originally published at SQL & Cloud Lab.

This post was drafted with AI assistance.

Dynamic SQL, building a query as a string and executing it, is sometimes the right tool: flexible search screens, choosing a sort column at run time, or maintenance scripts that loop over tables. It is also the classic route to SQL injection. The rules for doing it safely are short and strict.

The dangerous way 

-- DO NOT DO THIS
DECLARE @sql NVARCHAR(MAX) =
    N'SELECT * FROM dbo.Employee WHERE FullName = ''' + @Name + N'''';
EXEC (@sql);

If @Name contains x'; DROP TABLE dbo.Employee; --, it becomes part of the SQL and runs. Concatenating values also produces a different query text for every value, so SQL Server compiles a new plan each time and fills the plan cache.

Rule 1: pass values as parameters with sp_executesql 

DECLARE @sql NVARCHAR(MAX) =
    N'SELECT EmployeeId, FullName, DepartmentId
      FROM dbo.Employee
      WHERE FullName = @Name AND DepartmentId = @DeptId;';

EXEC sys.sp_executesql
    @sql,
    N'@Name NVARCHAR(100), @DeptId INT',
    @Name = @Name, @DeptId = @DeptId;

The values never become part of the SQL text, so they cannot change its meaning, and the query text stays the same, so its plan is reused.

Rule 2: object names go through QUOTENAME and a whitelist

Table and column names cannot be parameters. When they must vary, validate them against a list you control, then wrap them with QUOTENAME:

DECLARE @SortColumn SYSNAME = N'HireDate',
        @SortDir    NVARCHAR(4) = N'DESC';

IF @SortColumn NOT IN (N'FullName', N'HireDate', N'DepartmentId')
    THROW 50010, 'Invalid sort column.', 1;
IF @SortDir NOT IN (N'ASC', N'DESC')
    THROW 50011, 'Invalid sort direction.', 1;

DECLARE @sql NVARCHAR(MAX) =
    N'SELECT EmployeeId, FullName, HireDate, DepartmentId
      FROM dbo.Employee
      ORDER BY ' + QUOTENAME(@SortColumn) + N' ' + @SortDir + N';';

EXEC sys.sp_executesql @sql;

QUOTENAME adds square brackets and escapes any closing bracket inside the name, so even an odd name cannot break out of the identifier.

Building optional search filters

A search screen with many optional filters is the best use of dynamic SQL. Add only the conditions the user supplied, always with parameters:

DECLARE @sql NVARCHAR(MAX) = N'SELECT EmployeeId, FullName, DepartmentId, HireDate
FROM dbo.Employee
WHERE 1 = 1';

IF @Name   IS NOT NULL SET @sql += N' AND FullName LIKE @Name + N''%''';
IF @DeptId IS NOT NULL SET @sql += N' AND DepartmentId = @DeptId';
IF @From   IS NOT NULL SET @sql += N' AND HireDate >= @From';

EXEC sys.sp_executesql @sql,
    N'@Name NVARCHAR(100), @DeptId INT, @From DATE',
    @Name = @Name, @DeptId = @DeptId, @From = @From;

Each combination of filters gets its own cached plan tailored to the columns actually used, which often beats a single "catch-all" query full of (@x IS NULL OR Column = @x) conditions.

Permissions

Code inside dynamic SQL runs with the permissions of the caller, not the owner of the stored procedure. A user allowed to execute a procedure may still get "permission denied" on the tables it queries dynamically. Grant the needed permissions explicitly, or sign the procedure with a certificate, rather than giving broad rights.

Debugging tips

  • Use NVARCHAR(MAX) and N'' literals to avoid silent truncation and Unicode issues.
  • PRINT @sql; (or SELECT @sql for long strings) before executing, to see exactly what will run.
  • Test with values containing quotes, brackets and semicolons.

Quick checklist

  • Values: always parameters via sp_executesql, never concatenated.
  • Names: whitelist plus QUOTENAME.
  • Use dynamic SQL for optional filters and sorting, not by default.
  • Check permissions and test with hostile input.

Related reading:

  • How to Delete or Update Millions of Rows Safely
  • How to Fix SQL Server Deadlocks
  • Temp Tables vs Table Variables in SQL Server

More SQL Server guides on my blog, SQL & Cloud Lab.

title: Java Encapsulation and Abstraction
description:
1. Introduction

Encapsulation and Abstraction are two important principles of Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) in Java.

Encapsulation protects an object's data by controlling access through methods.

Abstraction hides implementation details and exposes only essential functionality.

Both principles help developers build secure, modular, and maintainable applications, including Java-based GenAI systems.

2. What Is It?

Encapsulation: Bundles data and methods into a class and restricts direct access to internal data using access modifiers.

Abstraction: Hides implementation details and exposes essential operations using interfaces and abstract classes.

3. Syntax / Example 

interface AIService {
    String generateResponse(String prompt);
}

class ChatbotService implements AIService {
    private String modelName = "ExampleModel";

    @Override
    public String generateResponse(String prompt) {
        return "Response to: " + prompt;
    }

    public String getModelName() {
        return modelName;
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        AIService ai = new ChatbotService();
        System.out.println(ai.generateResponse("Explain GenAI"));
    }
}

Output:

Response to: Explain GenAI

Explanation:

  1. Encapsulation: modelName is private and accessed through a getter.
  2. Abstraction: AIService defines what the service must do without exposing its implementation.

4. Practical Example

Java + GenAI Chatbot

In a chatbot application, encapsulation can protect API configuration and internal service data. Abstraction can allow the application to interact with different AI providers through a common interface without changing the chatbot's core logic.

5. Workflow and Hierarchy

Workflow

User Request → AIService Interface → ChatbotService Implementation → AI Model Integration → Response

OOP Hierarchy

Object-Oriented Programming
├── Encapsulation
│ ├── Private fields
│ └── Controlled access through methods
└── Abstraction
├── Interfaces
└── Abstract classes

6. Key Takeaways

  1. Encapsulation protects internal data and controls access.
  2. Abstraction hides implementation details.
  3. private fields support encapsulation.
  4. Interfaces and abstract classes support abstraction.
  5. Both principles improve maintainability and flexibility in Java applications.

7. Conclusion

Encapsulation and Abstraction help developers design well-structured Java applications. Encapsulation focuses on protecting data, while abstraction focuses on hiding implementation complexity. Together, they make Java + GenAI applications easier to extend, test, and maintain.

Question: Which principle would you prioritize when designing a Java-based AI service: Encapsulation or Abstraction?

#Java #OOP #Encapsulation #Abstraction #GenAI

Thanks for reading! 🚀

title: How to Unify Code, Cloud and Kubernetes Security
description:
Navigating modern cloud-native environments often feels like managing three entirely different worlds: developer code, cloud infrastructure, and Kubernetes clusters. When these domains operate in silos, security teams end up drowning in disconnected alerts while critical vulnerabilities slip through the cracks.

To build a resilient defense, engineering and security teams need a single, coherent strategy to unify code, cloud and Kubernetes security.

The Challenge of Siloed Security
Traditionally, organizations secure their tech stack using fragmented tools:

Code Security: SAST and dependency scanners find bugs in code repositories before deployment.
Cloud Security (CSPM/CWPP): Scans cloud provider configurations (AWS, Azure, GCP) to catch open S3 buckets or overly permissive IAM roles.
Kubernetes Security (KSPM): Monitors running clusters, pod configurations, network policies, and runtime behavior.
When these systems don’t talk to each other, you lose critical context. A high-severity vulnerability in your code might seem low-priority on paper, but if it runs in a Kubernetes container exposed directly to the public internet on a misconfigured cloud instance, it becomes an active crisis.

3 Steps to Unify Code, Cloud and Kubernetes Security
Connecting these layers transforms security from a reactive bottleneck into a proactive, context-aware workflow

  1. Trace Assets from Code to Cloud (and Back)
    To effectively secure your architecture, you must map every running production asset directly to its original source code. When your cloud runtime alerts you to a compromised container image, your team shouldn’t waste hours identifying who owns the code. Traceability lets you pinpoint the exact repository, commit and developer responsible in seconds.

  2. Correlate Risk with Environmental Context
    Context is everything in cloud security. To prioritize threats accurately, evaluate risks across all three layers simultaneously:

The Code: Contains a known CVE.
The Kubernetes Cluster: Runs with elevated root privileges.
The Cloud Infrastructure: Sits behind an Internet Gateway with direct public access.
By correlating these inputs, security teams can filter out low-risk noise and focus exclusively on high-priority attack paths.

  1. Shift Left and Guard Right Integration works both ways:

Shift Left: Use Kubernetes manifest checks and infrastructure-as-code (IaC) scanning directly inside developer IDEs and CI/CD pipelines to block misconfigurations before deployment.
Guard Right: Use runtime security monitoring across Kubernetes clusters and cloud resources to catch zero-day exploits and abnormal traffic in real time.
The Zero-X Cloud Approach
At Zero-X Cloud, we believe security should accelerate development, not stall it. By consolidating code scanning, cloud posture management and Kubernetes runtime protection into a unified platform, Zero-X Cloud gives your team complete visibility across your entire software lifecycle.

Eliminate tool fatigue, connect your security dots, and safeguard your infrastructure seamlessly from committing to the cloud.
