title: Angular 22: Build Reusable Components with Signal Inputs and @for | FoodieAI Part 02
description:
Angular 22: Build Reusable Components with Signal Inputs and @for

Have you ever wondered how to display 12 restaurant cards in Angular without writing the same HTML 12 times?

The answer is reusable components and data binding.

In Part 02 of my FoodieAI project series, we're learning these Angular concepts by building a food delivery homepage.

This tutorial focuses on standalone components, Signal Inputs, parent-to-child communication, and Angular's modern @for control flow.

What We're Building

FoodieAI is an educational food delivery application built with Angular 22, TypeScript, Bootstrap 5, and eventually Groq AI integration.

In Part 02, we focus on:

  • Creating a homepage and public layout
  • Building reusable Angular components
  • Understanding TypeScript interfaces
  • Passing data from a parent to a child component
  • Rendering dynamic lists using @for
  • Using interpolation and property binding
  • Building responsive restaurant cards with Bootstrap 5

Let's understand the most important part with a simple example.

1. Define a Restaurant Interface

First, define the structure of our restaurant data.

restaurant.model.ts

export interface Restaurant {
  readonly id: string;
  readonly name: string;
  readonly rating: number;
  readonly cuisine: string;
}

A TypeScript interface helps describe the expected structure of our data.

For example, the restaurant name must be a string, and the rating must be a number.

This is a simplified teaching model. The complete FoodieAI application uses a more detailed Restaurant interface.

2. Create a Reusable Restaurant Component

We can generate a new component using Angular CLI:

ng generate component features/home/restaurant-card

Now let's use Angular's modern Signal Input API.

restaurant-card.component.ts

import { Component, input } from '@angular/core';
import { Restaurant } from '../../../models/restaurant.model';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-restaurant-card',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [],
  templateUrl: './restaurant-card.component.html',
  styleUrl: './restaurant-card.component.css'
})
export class RestaurantCard {
  readonly restaurant = input.required<Restaurant>();
}

What is input.required()?

In modern Angular, Signal Inputs allow a component to receive data from its parent.

The input.required<Restaurant>() declaration means the parent must provide a Restaurant value.

Unlike a regular property, a Signal Input is read by calling it like a function:

restaurant()

This is one of the useful features of modern Angular component communication.

3. Display Restaurant Data Using Interpolation

Now open the component's HTML file.

restaurant-card.component.html

<article class="card h-100">
  <div class="card-body">

    <h3 class="h5 text-success">
      {{ restaurant().name }}
    </h3>

    <p class="text-secondary">
      {{ restaurant().cuisine }}
    </p>

    <span class="badge text-bg-success">
      ★ {{ restaurant().rating }}
    </span>

  </div>
</article>

Here, {{ }} is Angular interpolation.

It allows us to display TypeScript values in an HTML template.

The Bootstrap classes provide the basic styling without custom CSS.

4. Pass Data from Parent to Child

Next, we'll use our reusable component inside the Home component.

home.component.ts

import { Component } from '@angular/core';
import { RestaurantCard } from './restaurant-card/restaurant-card.component';
import { Restaurant } from '../../models/restaurant.model';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-home',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [RestaurantCard],
  templateUrl: './home.component.html',
  styleUrl: './home.component.css'
})
export class Home {
  readonly restaurants: Restaurant[] = [
    {
      id: '1',
      name: 'The Saffron Table',
      rating: 4.8,
      cuisine: 'Indian'
    },
    {
      id: '2',
      name: 'Basil & Brick',
      rating: 4.7,
      cuisine: 'Pizza'
    }
  ];
}

Now we have a parent component containing restaurant data and a child component responsible for displaying individual restaurants.

5. Render Multiple Cards Using @for

home.component.html

<section class="container py-4">

  <h2 class="mb-4">Restaurants</h2>

  <div class="row g-3">

    @for (restaurant of restaurants; track restaurant.id) {

      <div class="col-12 col-md-6 col-lg-4">

        <app-restaurant-card
          [restaurant]="restaurant">
        </app-restaurant-card>

      </div>

    }

  </div>

</section>

What happens here?

  1. Angular loops through the restaurants array.
  2. Each restaurant object is passed to the reusable child component.
  3. The RestaurantCard component displays that restaurant's information.
  4. The track restaurant.id expression helps Angular identify individual items efficiently.

The best part?

Whether we have 2 restaurants or 100, the same reusable component can display them without duplicating the card template.

6. Why Use Reusable Components?

Reusable components help us:

  • Reduce duplicate HTML
  • Keep application design consistent
  • Maintain code more easily
  • Separate responsibilities
  • Build scalable frontend applications

This approach is particularly useful for restaurant cards, product cards, dashboards, user profiles, and many other application features.

7. Watch the Full FoodieAI Tutorial

I've recorded a practical Hindi/Hinglish walkthrough explaining the complete FoodieAI Part 02 implementation, including the homepage, public layout, nested routing, reusable components, and data binding.

Previous Video — Part 01: Angular Project Setup

https://youtu.be/BFkGSg1Uef0

What's Next?

In the next FoodieAI tutorial, we'll move from hardcoded restaurant data to REST API integration using Angular's httpResource().

The complete series will gradually cover restaurant discovery, search, Signals, shopping cart, checkout, authentication, admin features, and Groq AI integration.

Let's Discuss!

Have you started using Angular Signal Inputs in your projects?

Do you prefer input.required() or traditional @Input()?

Share your experience in the comments!

Happy Coding!

— Testy Codeiz

Keep Practicing, Keep Coding!

title: Node.js Gaming Account Recovery: Password Reset Email and SMS Admission Rules
description:
A gaming service that emails a generated report has two different delivery problems once the recipient cannot sign in: getting the report to the player, and authorizing a password reset. Email links and SMS OTP fallback may share an integration, but ownership of recovery state must survive the channel change. A second transport cannot decide who owns the account.

Short answer: use password reset email links as the primary recovery path in Node.js, and admit SMS OTP as a separate fallback only for accounts that already support phone verification. Keep email recovery independently usable. For a US/EU rollout, treat geography and abuse controls as application policy; adding another transport does not establish compliance.

The generated report stays an email attachment in the product requirement. This article examines the recovery boundary around that workflow; it doesn't assume that a provider's attachment schema, size limits, or retention behavior have been established. Those require a separate delivery acceptance check before choosing that provider for the report itself.

How should password reset email links admit SMS OTP fallback?

Start with the account record. A request to receive a report must not become permission to change credentials, and a newly entered phone number must not become the destination for recovering an existing account merely because the SMS provider can send a code there. The application needs an explicit eligibility decision before it calls a second transport. That decision belongs beside the account and recovery state, where it can be inspected independently of the message vendor.

Keep that boundary small.

For a proposed design, store a recovery attempt identifier, its account association, the admitted channel, and the application's expiration and consumption state. These are application fields, not provider request parameters. An email delivery event is evidence about a message; the application still decides whether the recovery attempt authorizes a password change. The same distinction applies when an OTP verification result arrives.

A storage architect should ask which write commits the password change and consumes the recovery attempt. Define that transition together, then test competing submissions against it. Otherwise the email path and SMS path can each appear correct while the combined system has a replay or concurrent-consumption failure mode. This is a design requirement, not a claim about any messaging service's consistency model.

For a team already connecting report generation, storage, and outbound messaging, try Infrai for the email transport and conditional managed SMS OTP portion: its 295 routes across 20 modules use a single API key and a consistent REST API, reducing the number of separate integration contracts the team must introduce as the workflow grows. One key covers storage, email, and SMS; the team can keep one credential integration instead of adding a separate secret-loading configuration for each capability. Its public, unauthenticated discovery schemas provide a second practical benefit: developers can inspect request and response contracts before provisioning credentials. This matters before the first useful send, because the developer can review the mail contract while another team member handles account configuration, rather than making credential availability the prerequisite for understanding the adapter.

Recovery ownership stays local.

The administrative benefit is one key, one bill across services. Infrai's single-key, single-bill model gives the report worker and recovery adapter one API key for all services and one invoice to reconcile; adding SMS therefore avoids a separate credential provisioning workflow and another billing integration. For the report worker and recovery adapter, that means fewer independent secrets to configure and rotate, with a shared credential's broader access boundary as the corresponding trade-off. The broad capability surface includes storage and scheduling among 20 modules; multiple services follow a consistent interface, and breadth matters here because the report workflow extends beyond sending a message. Choose that shared surface only if those adjacent capabilities are useful to the team.

Derive fallback from account state, not message telemetry

The tempting shortcut is to send email, wait for evidence of engagement, and switch to SMS when that evidence looks weak. That mixes two questions: whether a message reached a destination and whether another destination is authorized to recover the account. Apple documents Mail Privacy Protection because mail activity is mediated by client privacy behavior; an open signal is a poor foundation for an identity decision.

Use an explicit player action to request the admitted fallback instead. In this design, a player whose account has no verified-phone recovery support remains on the email path. A player with eligible phone verification can request an SMS challenge, subject to the application's abuse and geographic policy.

The fallback is optional.

The report email doesn't depend on its existence.

Infrai supports managed SMS OTP generation and verification. Keep email recovery based on links; if the product chooses email codes instead, the application must own that code lifecycle. Event observation for email and SMS uses polling, so orchestration should allow observation lag and distinguish an unknown outcome from a confirmed failure. An immediate channel switch must not depend on a delivery observation arriving instantly.

That distinction changes the state machine.

For example, define three local outcomes for a submission attempt: accepted, rejected, and unresolved. These are proposed application states, rather than vendor response enums. An unresolved send should not silently create a fresh recovery authorization, and retrying transport should not create another business operation. Infrai specifies an Idempotency-Key convention with a default 24-hour deduplication window; inspect the selected capability's idempotency declaration before relying on it, and keep application attempt consumption separate from transport deduplication.

For SMS, build business-layer anti-fraud checks and geographic restrictions before enabling fallback. A US/EU label is insufficiently precise to decide admissible destinations, data handling, or the legal basis for processing; GDPR Article 7 describes conditions for consent where consent is the basis, rather than certifying an architecture because it uses two channels.

Inspect the contract before implementing the adapter

The smallest useful integration result is a contract the team can examine. The Python example below retrieves the public email-send discovery document; it sends no report and creates no recovery attempt, so it doesn't need a write idempotency key. Use the returned schema to design the Node.js adapter instead of guessing attachment or recipient fields. Public discovery requires no key; this example accepts an optional server-side environment key to show the Bearer header convention used for protected calls.

import json
import os
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.request
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime

headers = {"Accept": "application/json"}
key = os.environ.get("INFRAI_API_KEY")
if key:
    headers["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {key}"

for attempt in range(4):
    request = urllib.request.Request(
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/email.send",
        method="GET",
        headers=headers,
    )
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=20) as response:
            if response.status != 200:
                raise RuntimeError(f"Unexpected HTTP status: {response.status}")
            print(json.dumps(json.load(response), indent=2))
        break
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as error:
        if error.code != 429 or attempt == 3:
            detail = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {error.code}: {detail}") from error
        delay = 2 ** attempt
        retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
        if retry_after:
            try:
                delay = max(delay, float(retry_after))
            except ValueError:
                retry_at = parsedate_to_datetime(retry_after)
                delay = max(
                    delay,
                    (retry_at - datetime.now(timezone.utc)).total_seconds(),
                )
        time.sleep(delay)

This demonstrates contract inspection, not a completed password reset implementation. Public discovery removes an early credential dependency; authenticated delivery still requires a Bearer key, explicit methods, status checks, and an appropriate retry policy. The report attachment contract and sender setup must pass their own acceptance criteria before a first production send. No measured integration-time comparison is available here.

Keep provider credentials inside the server-side adapter. The account service should submit a business intent with a stable attempt identifier, while the adapter handles the chosen transport contract. This makes a provider change reviewable without letting a messaging SDK become the authority over account state.

Compare the integration contracts after fixing the recovery boundary

The useful comparison is the work each candidate leaves with the application. The table describes candidate integration plans, rather than asserting that every product supplies equivalent recovery features or that one wins a benchmark.

Candidate Role in this design Setup and credential boundary Trade-off to evaluate
Infrai Email transport plus managed SMS OTP and verification One REST API and key; inspect public schemas before configuring authenticated sends Useful when adjacent backend capabilities share the same integration; recovery policy and polling remain application responsibilities
Amazon SES Email transport candidate for the report and reset link Put the email adapter behind the team's AWS credential boundary; evaluate SMS independently A focused email choice deserves evaluation when the team wants direct ownership of an AWS mail integration rather than a broader backend surface
Twilio Verify SMS verification candidate alongside the chosen email transport Treat verification setup and credentials as a separate integration from report delivery Evaluate a verification specialist when verification is the dominant requirement; it doesn't eliminate the application's email recovery path
SendGrid Email transport candidate for report delivery and reset links Evaluate its mail API and sender setup; keep any chosen SMS verification integration separately scoped A focused mail integration may fit teams whose acceptance criteria center on email operations; adding it doesn't define recovery policy

Use each candidate's own documentation to verify exact payloads, sender requirements, geographic availability, and delivery-event behavior. The table makes no claim of feature parity. Counting SDKs alone misses the operational work: credentials need owners, delivery observations need interpretation, and the password-reset state transition still needs one authority.

A specialist or direct provider is the better choice when the team's acceptance criteria require its specific verification or mail operations and the team is prepared to own the additional adapter. Infrai fits the opposite integration pressure: several backend capabilities need to be added under a consistent contract. Its benefit is breadth with less contract sprawl, not evidence that its recovery semantics exceed those of every specialist.

Roll out email first, then admit eligible SMS attempts

Ship the independent email-link path first. Test that report delivery cannot authorize a password change, that consuming one recovery attempt prevents its reuse, and that unresolved transport outcomes don't grant new recovery rights. These checks exercise the application boundary before channel count makes it harder to inspect.

Then enable SMS for eligible accounts behind the application's geographic and abuse policy. Exercise simultaneous email and SMS submissions, delayed event observations, and transport retries. Keep the existing recovery attempt identifier through a transport retry, and reject reuse after the application's consumption transition commits.

Keep email usable.

The rollout decision is concrete: add SMS when the product already supports phone verification and the team can own fallback admission, abuse controls, and delayed observations. A generated report's attachment delivery remains a separate acceptance test; a successful password reset doesn't demonstrate that a report was attached correctly.

Sources

References for the comparison and policy boundaries:

  • Amazon SES documentation
  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • SendGrid Mail Send documentation
  • Apple Mail Privacy Protection
  • GDPR Article 7, conditions for consent

If this recovery boundary fits your system, start with the first-party email-link and SMS fallback guide.

title: How to Scrape Etsy with Node.js: Autocomplete Keyword Trees, Page-One Competition, Demand Signals, and an SEO Report (2026)
description:
"Etsy SEO tool" gets about 2,400 US searches a month, and most of the tools that rank for it are subscriptions that do three things behind the scenes: they read Etsy's search autocomplete, they look at who ranks on page one, and they guess how well those listings sell. You can build that yourself in a couple hundred lines of Node.js, and you will understand your numbers better because you know exactly where they come from.

This post builds a small keyword research pipeline with no dependencies (Node 20+, built-in fetch):

  1. suggest.mjs expands one seed ("crochet bag") into an autocomplete keyword tree
  2. serp.mjs measures page-one competition for the best terms: how many titles already contain the words, bestseller badges, small shops, ads, price bands
  3. demand.mjs opens the top listings and reads Etsy's own demand line ("57 people bought this in the last 24 hours")
  4. report.mjs joins it all into a ranked CSV and checks a listing title against the terms buyers type

Everything below ran on November 23, 2026 (Asia/Saigon morning) with Node v24.22.1. My earlier Etsy post was a Python overview of the official API and HTML. This one is only about keyword research.

Read this first: Etsy's Terms of Use prohibit scraping. Section 6.E of the Terms of Use says: "You agree not to use automated bots to access, scan, crawl, scrape, or spider any page of the Services ... without our express permission." Section 6.C adds that Etsy "may ... prohibit the use of Automated Agents for any purpose, including browsing, data collection", and that you must not circumvent its bot detection. Etsy's robots.txt also disallows /api/ and /search?*q= for all user agents. Review the terms and the legal risk for your use case and location before running anything. Where it covers your needs, use the official Etsy Open API v3 with an approved app key. It has no autocomplete endpoint, though. The scripts here made about 100 requests in total. Raw responses sit in a local cache that expires after 12 hours (delete it when you're done), and the reports keep only numbers and search terms.

Step 1: What a plain Node.js client gets

Before writing any parser, check what etsy.com sends to a script:

// probe.mjs: what a plain Node.js client gets from etsy.com today.
const UA = 'Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/131.0 Safari/537.36';
const urls = [
  'https://www.etsy.com/robots.txt',
  'https://www.etsy.com/api/v3/ajax/public/search/autosuggest?search_type=all&query=crochet+bag',
  'https://www.etsy.com/search?q=crochet+bag',
  'https://www.etsy.com/listing/4608105850/',
  'https://openapi.etsy.com/v3/application/listings/active?keywords=crochet+bag',
];
for (const url of urls) {
  const res = await fetch(url, { headers: { 'user-agent': UA, 'accept-language': 'en-US' } });
  const text = await res.text();
  console.log(res.status, String(text.length).padStart(6), new URL(url).pathname.slice(0, 40).padEnd(40), text.replace(/\s+/g, ' ').slice(0, 60));
  if (url.endsWith('robots.txt')) {
    const star = text.split(/User-agent: \*/)[1] ?? '';
    console.log('       robots.txt (*):', star.split('\n').filter((l) => /Disallow: \/(api\/|search\?)/.test(l)).join(' | '));
  }
}

$ node probe.mjs
200  55539 /robots.txt                              User-agent: Spinn3r Disallow: / User-agent: AdsBot-Google-Mo
       robots.txt (*): Disallow: /api/ | Disallow: /search?*q=
200    372 /api/v3/ajax/public/search/autosuggest   [{"query":"crochet bag pattern"},{"query":"crochet bag patte
403    793 /search                                  <html lang="en"><head><title>etsy.com</title><style>#cmsg{an
403    776 /listing/4608105850/                     <html lang="en"><head><title>etsy.com</title><style>#cmsg{an
403     80 /v3/application/listings/active          {"error":"Invalid API key: should be in the format 'keystrin

What that means:

  • Autocomplete answers plain fetch(). The JSON endpoint behind the search box returns up to 11 suggestions. But it lives under /api/, which robots.txt disallows.
  • Search and listing pages return 403 from DataDome (server: DataDome, a "Please enable JS and disable any ad blocker" page that loads a captcha from geo.captcha-delivery.com). Headless Chrome got the same block page, even for the Terms of Use page. Getting past that means fingerprint and proxy work, which section 6.C of the terms specifically forbids.
  • The official Open API rejects calls without a key in keystring:shared_secret format. With an approved app, findAllListingsActive covers keyword listing search. It doesn't give you the ranked page with ads and badges that buyers actually see, or the autocomplete.

So in the pipeline, one small client does the fetching, and everything after it is plain data work you can point at any source.

Step 2: A client with a disk cache

The scripts read Etsy through ScrapeAtlas*, which returns autocomplete (/v1/etsy/search/suggestions), one ranked search page with organic and promoted cards (/v1/etsy/search), and a listing page (/v1/etsy/listing) as JSON. Each successful call costs 1 credit, and failed ones cost nothing. Keyword research repeats itself a lot (the same listing ranks for five related terms), so the client caches every response on disk. A re-run of the report costs nothing:

// sa.mjs: tiny ScrapeAtlas client with a disk cache, so re-running a report costs 0 credits.
import { createHash } from 'node:crypto';
import { mkdir, readFile, writeFile } from 'node:fs/promises';

const KEY = process.env.SCRAPEATLAS_API_KEY;
const TTL_MS = Number(process.env.CACHE_HOURS ?? 12) * 3600_000;
export const stats = { calls: 0, cached: 0, failed: 0 };

export async function etsy(path, params = {}) {
  const url = `https://api.scrapeatlas.com/v1/etsy/${path}?${new URLSearchParams(params)}`;
  const file = `cache/${createHash('sha1').update(url).digest('hex').slice(0, 16)}.json`;
  try {
    const hit = JSON.parse(await readFile(file, 'utf8'));
    if (Date.now() - hit.savedAt < TTL_MS) { stats.cached++; return hit.body; }
  } catch {}
  if (!KEY) throw new Error('set SCRAPEATLAS_API_KEY first');
  for (let attempt = 0; ; attempt++) {
    const res = await fetch(url, { headers: { 'x-api-key': KEY }, signal: AbortSignal.timeout(90_000) });
    const body = await res.json().catch(() => ({ success: false, failure: { code: `http_${res.status}` } }));
    if (body.success) {
      stats.calls++;
      await mkdir('cache', { recursive: true });
      await writeFile(file, JSON.stringify({ savedAt: Date.now(), url, body }));
      return body;
    }
    if (res.status >= 500 && attempt < 2) { await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 2000 * 2 ** attempt)); continue; }
    stats.failed++;
    const err = new Error(`${path} ${res.status} ${body.failure?.code}: ${body.failure?.message ?? ''}`);
    err.status = res.status;
    throw err;
  }
}

// Run `limit` promises at a time; Etsy calls take 2-6 s each, so this matters.
export async function pool(items, limit, fn) {
  const out = new Array(items.length);
  let next = 0;
  await Promise.all(Array.from({ length: limit }, async () => {
    while (next < items.length) { const i = next++; out[i] = await fn(items[i], i); }
  }));
  return out;
}

// console.table without the box drawing: narrower, and pastes cleanly.
export function printTable(rows) {
  const cols = Object.keys(rows[0] ?? {});
  const w = cols.map((c) => Math.max(c.length, ...rows.map((r) => String(r[c] ?? '').length)));
  for (const r of [Object.fromEntries(cols.map((c) => [c, c])), ...rows]) {
    console.log(cols.map((c, i) => String(r[c] ?? '').padEnd(w[i])).join('  ').trimEnd());
  }
}

Etsy calls take 2 to 6 seconds each, so pool() runs 3 to 4 at a time. 27 autocomplete calls finished in 9 seconds.

Step 3: An autocomplete keyword tree

Etsy's autocomplete is the closest thing to buyer search data you can get without Etsy's seller tools. One call per prefix only gives about 11 terms. The classic trick is the "alphabet soup": query the seed, then seed a, seed b, ... seed z. A term that shows up under the bare seed and under letter prefixes is one Etsy keeps pushing:

// suggest.mjs: expand one seed into an Etsy autocomplete keyword tree.
// usage: node suggest.mjs "crochet bag" [letters]
import { writeFile, mkdir } from 'node:fs/promises';
import { etsy, pool, stats } from './sa.mjs';

const seed = (process.argv[2] ?? '').trim().toLowerCase();
const letters = process.argv[3] ?? 'abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz';
if (!seed) throw new Error('usage: node suggest.mjs "<seed>" [letters]');

// The bare seed, then "seed a", "seed b", ... Each prefix returns up to ~11 terms.
const prefixes = [seed, ...[...letters].map((c) => `${seed} ${c}`)];
const seen = new Map(); // term -> { term, hits, bestRank, prefixes: [] }

await pool(prefixes, 4, async (prefix) => {
  let res;
  try { res = await etsy('search/suggestions', { query: prefix }); }
  catch (e) { console.error('skip', JSON.stringify(prefix), e.message); return; }
  res.items.forEach(({ query }, rank) => {
    const term = query.trim().toLowerCase();
    const row = seen.get(term) ?? { term, hits: 0, bestRank: 99, prefixes: [] };
    row.hits++;
    row.bestRank = Math.min(row.bestRank, rank + 1);
    row.prefixes.push(prefix);
    seen.set(term, row);
  });
});

// A term that shows up under the bare seed AND under letter prefixes is one Etsy
// pushes hard; sort by that first, then by its best position in any list.
const rows = [...seen.values()]
  .map((r) => ({ ...r, fromSeed: r.prefixes.includes(seed) }))
  .sort((a, b) => b.fromSeed - a.fromSeed || b.hits - a.hits || a.bestRank - b.bestRank);

await mkdir('data', { recursive: true });
const out = `data/suggest-${seed.replace(/\W+/g, '-')}.json`;
await writeFile(out, JSON.stringify({ seed, fetchedAt: new Date().toISOString(), rows }, null, 1));
console.log(`${prefixes.length} prefixes -> ${rows.length} unique terms (${stats.calls} paid, ${stats.cached} cached, ${stats.failed} failed) -> ${out}`);
for (const r of rows.slice(0, 15)) {
  console.log(`${r.fromSeed ? '*' : ' '} ${String(r.hits).padStart(2)}x  best #${String(r.bestRank).padEnd(2)} ${r.term}`);
}

$ node suggest.mjs "crochet bag"
27 prefixes -> 246 unique terms (27 paid, 0 cached, 0 failed) -> data/suggest-crochet-bag.json
*  6x  best #1  crochet bag pattern
*  5x  best #3  crochet bag handmade
*  3x  best #1  crochet bag tutorial
*  2x  best #1  crochet bag charm
*  2x  best #1  crochet bag holder pattern
*  2x  best #2  crochet bag pattern pdf
*  2x  best #2  crochet bag charm pattern
*  2x  best #2  crochet bag holder
*  2x  best #6  crochet bag pattern women
*  1x  best #5  crochet bags
*  1x  best #8  crochet bags for women
   2x  best #2  crochet bag large
   1x  best #1  crochet bag accessories

* marks terms Etsy shows for the bare seed. 27 calls returned 246 unique terms, all starting with "crochet bag". Rare letters return short lists (crochet bag z: 3, x: 4, q: 5), and that's normal. One thing that surprised me: the seed itself never comes back as a suggestion, so it ends up with hits: 0 in the report. Treat it as the head term.

Step 4: Page-one competition

The search data has no result count, and the one size number you do get is useless. Every query I tried returned totalPages: 20 and 36 organic cards, including a nonsense query, zzqx crochet narwhal bag. Etsy pads results with loosely related listings. So competition has to come from what's on page one:

// serp.mjs: page-1 competition metrics for the top terms of a suggest-*.json file.
// usage: node serp.mjs data/suggest-crochet-bag.json [howMany=10]
import { readFile, writeFile } from 'node:fs/promises';
import { etsy, pool, printTable, stats } from './sa.mjs';

const [file, howMany = 10] = process.argv.slice(2);
const { seed, rows } = JSON.parse(await readFile(file, 'utf8'));
const terms = [seed, ...rows.map((r) => r.term).filter((t) => t !== seed)].slice(0, Number(howMany));

const pct = (n, d) => (d ? Math.round((100 * n) / d) : 0);
const quantile = (xs, q) => {
  const s = [...xs].sort((a, b) => a - b);
  return s.length ? s[Math.min(s.length - 1, Math.floor(q * s.length))] : null;
};
// "Preview seller" is a placeholder Etsy prints on most cards; shopId is the real key.
const shopKey = (i) => i.shopId ?? (i.seller !== 'Preview seller' ? i.seller : null) ?? i.id;
const words = (s) => s.toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z0-9 ]+/g, ' ').split(' ').filter(Boolean);
const hasPhrase = (title, term) => ` ${words(title).join(' ')} `.includes(` ${words(term).join(' ')} `);
// Etsy matches words in any order, so "Handmade Crochet Bag" ranks for "crochet bag handmade".
const hasAllWords = (title, term) => { const t = new Set(words(title)); return words(term).every((w) => t.has(w)); };

export function metrics(term, page) {
  const org = page.items;
  const prices = org.map((i) => i.price?.current).filter((p) => p != null);
  return {
    term,
    totalPages: page.totalPages,
    organic: org.length,
    ads: page.ads.length,
    exactTitlePct: pct(org.filter((i) => hasPhrase(i.title, term)).length, org.length),
    allWordsPct: pct(org.filter((i) => hasAllWords(i.title, term)).length, org.length),
    bestsellerPct: pct(org.filter((i) => i.isBestseller).length, org.length),
    under50ReviewsPct: pct(org.filter((i) => (i.rating?.count ?? 0) < 50).length, org.length),
    shops: new Set(org.map(shopKey)).size,
    p25: quantile(prices, 0.25), median: quantile(prices, 0.5), p75: quantile(prices, 0.75),
    onSalePct: pct(org.filter((i) => i.price?.original).length, org.length),
    topIds: page.listingIds.slice(0, 8),
    warnings: page.coverage?.warnings ?? [],
  };
}

const out = await pool(terms, 3, async (term) => {
  try { return metrics(term, await etsy('search', { query: term })); }
  catch (e) { console.error('skip', term, e.message); return null; }
});
const ok = out.filter(Boolean);
await writeFile(file.replace('suggest-', 'serp-'), JSON.stringify(ok, null, 1));
console.log(`${ok.length}/${terms.length} terms (${stats.calls} paid, ${stats.cached} cached, ${stats.failed} failed)`);
console.log('totalPages seen:', [...new Set(ok.map((m) => m.totalPages))], '| organic cards per page:', [...new Set(ok.map((m) => m.organic))]);
printTable(ok.map(({ topIds, warnings, totalPages, organic, ...m }) => m));

Two details in that code came from looking at the raw JSON:

  • Exact phrase vs. all words. Etsy matches words in any order. "crochet bag handmade" has 0% exact-phrase titles but 83% of the titles contain all three words ("Handmade Crochet Bag ..."). If you score on exact phrase, every long-tail term looks wide open. allWordsPct is the number that matters.
  • "Preview seller". 575 of the 696 organic cards I fetched today had the placeholder seller: "Preview seller", and the 121 with a real shop name had shopId: null. Counting unique sellers by name would tell you seven shops own page one. shopKey() uses shopId first, and then every page has 34 to 36 different shops.

Step 5: Demand signals from the top listings

The listing page carries Etsy's own urgency line, and that's as close to sales data as public pages get. demand.mjs opens the top N organic listings per term:

// demand.mjs: open the top organic listings of each term and read demand signals.
// usage: node demand.mjs data/serp-crochet-bag.json [terms=5] [listingsPerTerm=6]
import { readFile, writeFile } from 'node:fs/promises';
import { etsy, pool, printTable, stats } from './sa.mjs';

const [file, nTerms = 5, perTerm = 6] = process.argv.slice(2);
const serp = JSON.parse(await readFile(file, 'utf8')).slice(0, Number(nTerms));

// Etsy shows ONE free-text urgency line per listing: "In demand. 57 people bought
// this in the last 24 hours.", "In 20+ carts", "Low in stock, only 4 left", or none.
export function parseDemand(signal = '') {
  const num = (re) => Number(signal.match(re)?.[1]?.replace(/,/g, '') ?? 0);
  return {
    bought24h: num(/([\d,]+)\+? (?:people|person) bought this in the last 24 hours/i),
    carts: num(/In ([\d,]+)\+? carts?/i),
  };
}

const jobs = serp.flatMap((s) => s.topIds.slice(0, Number(perTerm)).map((id, pos) => ({ term: s.term, id, pos: pos + 1 })));
const rows = await pool(jobs, 4, async (j) => {
  try {
    const { listing: l } = await etsy('listing', { id: j.id });
    return {
      ...j,
      ...parseDemand(l.demandSignal ?? ''),
      signal: l.demandSignal ?? '',
      favorites: l.favorites ?? 0,
      reviews: l.reviews_count ?? 0,
      price: l.price?.current,
      titleLen: l.title.length,
      starSeller: l.isStarSeller,
    };
  } catch (e) { console.error('skip', j.id, e.message); return null; }
});
const ok = rows.filter(Boolean);
await writeFile(file.replace('serp-', 'demand-'), JSON.stringify(ok, null, 1));
console.log(`${ok.length}/${jobs.length} listings (${stats.calls} paid, ${stats.cached} cached, ${stats.failed} failed)`);
printTable(ok.map(({ id, signal, starSeller, ...r }) => r));

  • It's one line per listing, picked by Etsy. A listing that shows "In 20+ carts" may also be selling. carts and bought24h are separate columns for that reason.
  • Top results overlap a lot. The 60 crochet bag slots were only 41 different listings, and for "linen apron" one listing was #1 for all five terms. The cache turned 60 lookups into 41 paid calls. Without it you pay twice for the same page.
  • One hit skews a sum. One listing with 182 sales in 24 hours sits at #1 for both "crochet bag" and "crochet bag handmade". Look at the per-listing rows before you trust a total.
  • listedAt isn't listing age. 45 of 49 listings said "Nov 22, 2026", because Etsy shows the last renewal date. Don't use it to find "new listings that already sell".

Step 6: The report and a title check

report.mjs joins the three files. The score is a heuristic, not a search volume. A term scores well when Etsy pushes it in autocomplete, page-one listings actually sell, few top titles contain all its words, and small shops (under 50 reviews) still rank:

// report.mjs: join suggest + serp + demand into one ranked CSV, and check a title.
// usage: node report.mjs crochet-bag ["Your listing title"]
import { readFile, writeFile } from 'node:fs/promises';
import { printTable } from './sa.mjs';

const [slug, myTitle] = process.argv.slice(2);
const STOP = new Set(['for', 'with', 'and', 'the', 'set', 'of']);
const load = async (kind) => JSON.parse(await readFile(`data/${kind}-${slug}.json`, 'utf8').catch(() => '[]'));
const { seed, rows: sugg } = await load('suggest');
const serp = await load('serp');
const demand = await load('demand');

const median = (xs) => { const s = [...xs].sort((a, b) => a - b); return s.length ? s[s.length >> 1] : 0; };
const report = serp.map((s) => {
  const sg = sugg.find((r) => r.term === s.term) ?? { hits: 0, bestRank: null };
  const d = demand.filter((r) => r.term === s.term);
  const bought = d.reduce((a, r) => a + r.bought24h, 0);
  // Heuristic, not a search volume: Etsy pushes the term (hits), buyers act on page 1
  // (bought), few top titles contain all its words (gap), small shops rank (ease).
  const gap = (100 - s.allWordsPct) / 100;
  const ease = 0.5 + s.under50ReviewsPct / 200;
  const score = d.length ? Math.round(10 * Math.log1p(bought) * (1 + sg.hits / 3) * gap * ease) : null;
  return {
    term: s.term, hits: sg.hits, bestRank: sg.bestRank, exactPct: s.exactTitlePct, allWordsPct: s.allWordsPct,
    bestsellerPct: s.bestsellerPct, under50ReviewsPct: s.under50ReviewsPct, ads: s.ads,
    medianPrice: s.median, top6Bought24h: d.length ? bought : '', top6MedianFavs: d.length ? median(d.map((r) => r.favorites)) : '',
    score: score ?? '',
  };
}).sort((a, b) => (b.score || -1) - (a.score || -1));

const cols = Object.keys(report[0]);
const csv = [cols.join(','), ...report.map((r) => cols.map((c) => JSON.stringify(r[c] ?? '')).join(','))].join('\n');
await writeFile(`data/report-${slug}.csv`, csv + '\n');
printTable(report);

if (myTitle) {
  const t = myTitle.toLowerCase();
  const tw = new Set(t.split(/[^a-z0-9]+/)); // whole words: "women" must not cover "men"
  // Modifiers = words Etsy autocompletes after the seed, weighted by how often they appear.
  const mods = new Map();
  for (const r of sugg) for (const w of r.term.slice(seed.length).split(/\s+/).filter((w) => w.length > 2 && !STOP.has(w))) mods.set(w, (mods.get(w) ?? 0) + r.hits);
  const top = [...mods].sort((a, b) => b[1] - a[1]).slice(0, 12);
  console.log(`\ntitle: ${myTitle.length}/140 chars | seed "${seed}" in first 40 chars: ${t.slice(0, 40).includes(seed) ? 'yes' : 'NO'}`);
  console.log('covered :', top.filter(([w]) => tw.has(w)).map(([w, n]) => `${w}(${n})`).join(' ') || '-');
  console.log('missing :', top.filter(([w]) => !tw.has(w)).map(([w, n]) => `${w}(${n})`).join(' '));
}

How to read it: the head term "crochet bag" has the most demand (298 sales in 24 hours across the top six) and scores lowest, because 94% of page one already has both words in the title. "crochet bag pattern women" scores highest: Etsy suggests it, only 8% of top titles contain all four words, and patterns sell (23 sales in 24 hours across the top six at a $4.51 median price). The title check shows that the sample title never says "crochet bag" in its first 40 characters, and it misses every modifier buyers type most. The biggest one, "pattern", belongs to a different product (a PDF, not a bag), so don't stuff it in. Treat the "missing" list as questions to answer, not words to paste.

The same pipeline for a second seed, linen apron (letters a to h only, 5 terms, 3 listings each), cost 24 credits (9 + 5 + 10, with 5 listing lookups served from cache):
