title: Cutting Cloud Disk Bills by Two-Thirds with ZFS Compression, and What It Costs in CPU
description:
Cloud disks, such as Google Cloud's, are billed by the size you provision, so storing fewer bytes should cost less. ZFS, a file system that runs on Linux through OpenZFS, can compress data as it writes it. This article explains when that saves money, what it costs in CPU, and how ZFS decides what to compress.

Contents

  1. Disks are billed by size, and they only grow
  2. Putting numbers on the saving
  3. How ZFS organizes data
  4. Follow a write
  5. Two rules decide the real saving
  6. Follow a read
  7. Before choosing a codec
  8. Sources

Disks are billed by size, and they only grow

On Google Cloud, you pay for the disk size you ask for, not for the data you put on it so if you provision a 200 GB disk, you are billed for that entire disk space, regardless of how you use it (pricing). And a disk can only grow. You can't reduce the size of a disk; to shrink one, you replace it with a smaller one (resize docs). Hyperdisk volumes work the same way: You can't reduce the size of a Hyperdisk volume (Hyperdisk docs).

So compression saves money in two ways. A disk you already have fills more slowly, so you resize it later. And when you set up a new system or migrate an old one, you can provision a smaller disk from the start.

The price is CPU time. ZFS spends it compressing data when it writes (zio.c) and decompressing data when it reads, even when that data is already in RAM (there is an exception coming below) (arc.c).

Here is what the disk space costs. These are on-demand list prices for zonal disks (disks that live in a single zone) in us-east4, as of 2026-11-16 (pricing).

Disk type (zonal, us-east4) Price per GiB-month
pd-balanced $0.11
pd-ssd $0.187
Hyperdisk Balanced $0.08, plus IOPS and throughput above the included baseline

Regional disks cost twice as much (pricing). Committed-use discounts, which lower prices in return for a one- or three-year commitment, aren't available for these disks (CUD overview).

Putting numbers on the saving

Compression pays off most on data that is written once and rarely read again. An event store is a good example: new rows are appended at the end, old rows are seldom read, so most of the compression CPU is paid once, when the data is written.

Our generated, append-only events data set compressed 3.20× with zstd-1 and 3.01× with gzip-9, as ZFS reports it in its compressratio statistic. Our numbers come from a benchmark we ran on Google Cloud VMs with OpenZFS 2.4.1: 512 MiB per data set, stored in 128 KiB records. zstd and gzip are compression algorithms, or codecs, and the number is the level: 1 is fastest, and the top level (9 for gzip, 19 for zstd) gives the best compression ratio (zfsprops(7)).

A ratio of N× means 1/N of the bytes are left, so the saving is:

saving=1−N1​at 3.20×:1−3.21​=0.6875=68.75%

So at 3.20× you save 68.75%, not 220%.

Ratio Bytes left Saving
2× 50% 50%
3× 33.3% 66.7%
3.20× 31.25% 68.75%
4× 25% 75%

Each step up is worth less than the last: going from 3× to 4× saves only another 8.3 percentage points.

Now put numbers on it. Take 10 TiB (10,240 GiB) of history. The disk has to be bigger than the data, for two reasons:

  • Room to grow. We assume you keep 20% free.
  • Slop space. A ZFS pool (the storage ZFS builds from your disks) can't be filled to the last byte. ZFS holds back "the last 3.2% (1/2^spa_slop_shift)" of the pool (zfs(4)). In the code it is about min(32pool size​, 128 GiB) , counting a small area set aside for the intent log, where ZFS records sync writes (more on those below) (spa_misc.c). Both disks in this example are 4 TiB or more, so both hit the 128 GiB cap. Smaller pools use 3.2%.

That makes the disk roughly:

disk≈0.8data​+128 GiB

With our numbers:

                 uncompressed    zstd-1, 3.20×
data             10,240 GiB      3,200 GiB
÷ 0.8            12,800 GiB      4,000 GiB      (20% free)
+ slop              128 GiB        128 GiB
disk             12,928 GiB      4,128 GiB

At 3.20×, the disk and the monthly bill both shrink to about a third.

Over a year, that saves $11,616 on pd-balanced and $19,747 on pd-ssd.

On a disk you already have, compression delays the next resize: at a steady growth rate, a disk that would fill in one year uncompressed lasts 3.2 years.

There is one catch: a smaller disk can also be a slower one. Google warns: "Since disk performance grows linearly with the size of your disk, consider your I/O needs when choosing the size of your disk" (pricing). So a smaller Persistent Disk can have lower limits on IOPS (read and write operations per second) and throughput.

Hyperdisk Balanced works differently. It includes 3,000 IOPS and 140 MBps and bills performance above that separately (pricing).

Before counting on any of these numbers, check whether your database already compresses its own data, because compressing it twice gains little. Elasticsearch compresses stored data with LZ4 by default, or with zstd under index.codec: best_compression (Elastic docs). PostgreSQL compresses values through TOAST only when a row is wider than about 2 kB (PostgreSQL docs).

How ZFS organizes data

To see where the CPU goes, it helps to know how ZFS lays data out.

On Linux, a file system is the layer that turns a raw disk into files and directories. Many file systems, such as ext4, sit on one block device: a disk, a partition, or a volume that another tool, such as LVM, builds from several disks. ZFS manages the disks itself: you give it disks, it combines them into a pool, and you create file systems, called datasets, inside that pool.

ZFS doesn't compress whole files. It splits each file into records and compresses each record on its own.

Each record is compressed alone and stored in whole sectors.

From the top down:

  • Pool: "a collection of devices that provides physical storage" for datasets (zpool(8)).
  • Dataset: a file system or volume in the pool (zfs(8)).
  • Property: a named setting on a dataset, such as compression (zfsprops(7)).
  • Record: a file's unit of storage, which ZFS also calls a block. recordsize, 128 KiB by default, is the largest record size (zfs_prop.c, zfs.h).
  • Sector: the smallest unit ZFS writes to a disk, 2^ashift bytes. ashift=12 means 4 KiB (zpoolprops(7)). ashift is set per vdev (vdev.c). A vdev is one of the disks or disk groups (a mirror, or a RAID-Z group) that a pool is built from (zpoolconcepts(7)).

Compression is controlled by the compression property. If you set nothing, it is on, which means the lz4 codec when the pool's lz4_compress feature is enabled, as it is on current pools (zfsprops(7), zio_compress.c). If you change it later, the change "affects only newly-written data" (zfsprops(7)).

Follow a write

When an application saves data, it calls write(), a system call: a request to the Linux kernel, the core of the operating system, in this case to write bytes to a file. A successful write() doesn't promise the data is on disk yet (write(2)). For an ordinary, buffered write, ZFS keeps the data in memory and compresses it seconds later, when it flushes a batch of changes to disk.

Compression CPU is spent at transaction group sync, not at write(), even when the record ends up stored raw.

Step by step:

  1. write() copies the data into memory (zfs_vnops.c). Data waiting in memory to be written is called dirty data. If dirty data hits its limit, "new writes are halted until space frees up" (zfs(4)).
  2. ZFS writes dirty data out in batches. A batch is a transaction group (txg): changes "written to disk in the syncing state" (txg.c). Writing one out is called a txg sync. It happens "at least every" zfs_txg_timeout seconds, 5 by default (zfs(4)), and sooner when:
    • dirty data passes 20% of zfs_dirty_data_max (zfs(4)), or
    • an admin action waits on it, such as zpool sync (zpool-sync(8)) or a snapshot (txg.c).
  3. During the sync, zio_write_compress compresses each dirty record on its own (zio.c).
  4. The codec gets an output budget (Rule 1 below). If the compressed result doesn't fit, ZFS stores the record uncompressed (zio_compress.c, zio.c).

A record that doesn't fit wastes the CPU spent on it. Codecs differ in how much they waste:

  • lz4 and gzip (on Linux) stop as soon as their output overflows the budget (lz4_zfs.c, spl-zlib.c).
  • zstd-3 and higher first try a cheap lz4 pass on records of 128 KiB or more. If lz4 fails, they try zstd-1. They give up only if both fail (zfs(4), zfs_zstd.c). On compressible data, that lz4 pass is extra CPU on every write.

Two kinds of write don't wait for the next txg sync. ZFS compresses them when the application writes or syncs them:

  • Some sync writes. An application calls fsync(), or opens a file with O_SYNC, when it needs its data on disk before it carries on (fsync(2), open(2)). ZFS records sync writes in its intent log (ZIL). For some, it writes the data straight into the pool as full records and logs only a pointer to them, which compresses them right away. This happens with logbias=throughput. On pools without a separate log device, it also happens to most sync writes of 32 KiB or more (zil.c, zfs(4), dmu.c, zfs_vnops.c).
  • O_DIRECT writes aligned to recordsize. O_DIRECT is a flag that asks the kernel to minimize caching of a file's I/O (open(2)). By default, such writes bypass ZFS's RAM cache (zfsprops(7)) and go straight to the write pipeline (dmu_direct.c).

Two rules decide the real saving

Disks store data in fixed-size sectors. With ashift=12, the common setting, a sector is 2^12 bytes = 4 KiB. Think of sectors as fixed-size boxes: ZFS compresses each record on its own and stores it in whole boxes, so it can save less than the same codec would on the whole file. Two rules decide how much.

Both rules at ashift=12. A 128 KiB record saves 24 of its 32 sectors; an 8 KiB record has to halve to save anything.

Rule 1: a record must save enough. ZFS gives the codec a budget of 87.5% of the record (a 12.5% saving), rounded down to whole sectors. If the compressed record doesn't fit, it is stored uncompressed (zio.c).

budget=⌊sector size0.875×record size​⌋ sectors

Rounding down hurts small records most. At ashift=12 on ordinary vdevs (single disks, mirrors or RAID-Z groups):

Record size Must compress to at most Minimum saving
128 KiB 112 KiB 12.5%
16 KiB 12 KiB 25%
8 KiB 4 KiB 50%
4 KiB 112 bytes 97%

The last row is a special case. A 4 KiB record's budget rounds down to zero sectors, so it stays compressed only if it fits in 112 bytes inside its block pointer, the small piece of metadata that records where a block lives. That needs the embedded_data pool feature, which is on by default, and it never happens on encrypted datasets (zio.c, zpool-features(7)).

No tunable changes the 12.5%. A larger ashift means bigger sectors and coarser rounding. It is set per vdev when the vdev is created or added (vdev.c), and changing the pool's ashift property later "will not modify any existing vdev" (zpoolprops(7)).

Rule 2: what's stored is rounded up to whole sectors. A record that compresses to 7.3 sectors still takes 8 (zio.c). ZFS counts that padding in the block's size and in compressratio (zio.c), so compressratio already includes this loss.

stored=⌈sector sizecompressed size​⌉ sectors

Here are both rules applied to the 128 KiB record in the diagram, with 4 KiB (4,096-byte) sectors:

record​=131,072 bytes=32 sectors budget​=⌊0.875×32⌋=28 sectors compressed​=30,000 bytes≈7.3 sectors≤28, so it fits stored​=⌈7.3⌉=8 sectors=32,768 bytes​

The last sector carries 2,768 bytes of padding, which lowers the ratio:

30,000131,072​≈4.37× before rounding32,768131,072​=4.00× as stored

Rounding can also make different codecs land on the same ratio. gzip-9, zstd-1 and zstd-9 all reported a compressratio of 4.56× on our JSON logs. We did not inspect each record's stored size, so rounding is only a possible cause.

What the two rules mean in practice: bigger records keep more of the saving. Both rules work in whole sectors, so each one costs less than one sector per record. In a 128 KiB record (32 sectors), that is a small loss. In an 8 KiB record (2 sectors), it can be half the record.

Same data, different record sizes: small records lose part or all of the codec's saving.

Take data that compresses 2.5×, which the codec alone would shrink by 60%. In 128 KiB records it saves 59% of the disk space. In 8 KiB records it saves 50%, and in 4 KiB records nothing at all. Data that compresses only 1.5× saves nothing below 16 KiB.

That doesn't mean you should always raise recordsize. A small read decompresses the whole record, as the next section shows, so bigger records cost more CPU per read. The ZFS docs describe recordsize as "designed solely for use with database workloads that access files in fixed-size records", and suggest setting it "greater than or equal to the record size of the database" (zfsprops(7)). It can be up to 128 KiB, or up to 16 MiB with the large_blocks pool feature (zfsprops(7)), and a change "affects only files created afterward" (zfsprops(7)).

In short: data written and read in big pieces keeps more of its saving in large records; data read in small pieces is better served by a recordsize that matches the application's own record size.

Follow a read

Writes pay for compression once. Reads can pay for decompression again and again, even when the data never leaves RAM.

Like most file systems, ZFS keeps recently used data in RAM so repeated reads don't have to go to disk. Its main RAM cache is the ARC. By default, the ARC keeps blocks as they are on disk, compressed (arc.c, arc.c). That fits more data in RAM. ZFS on Linux 0.7.0 made this the default, and its release notes call the result a larger effective cache (release notes). The cost is that a block has to be decompressed before it can be used.

For a compressed record, an ARC hit decodes the whole record even when you asked for 4 KiB, unless an uncompressed copy is still in RAM.

Say an application reads 4 KiB from a file. The read takes one of three paths, from cheapest to most expensive.

Uncompressed copy: no decompression. The copy is usually in the dbuf cache, a list of recently used, uncompressed blocks. It was added with compressed ARC "to keep frequently access data uncompressed" (commit), and the read uses it directly (dbuf.c). The copy can also be another ARC buffer, which ZFS copies (arc.c).

But the dbuf cache is small. By default it targets 1/32 of the ARC's current target size, with no fixed cap (dbuf.c, dbuf.c, zfs(4)).

ARC hit, compressed: decompress the whole record. ZFS turns any byte range into whole blocks (dmu.c). Then it decompresses each block into a new full-size buffer (arc.c, arc.c). Your 4 KiB read decompresses all 128 KiB.

Disk read: the same full decompression. ZFS keeps the block compressed in the ARC, then decompresses the whole block (arc.c, arc.c).

Blocks stored raw skip decompression on every path (arc.c).

In our benchmark, on JSON and event files cached in the ARC, 96–97% of each test's 10,000 random 4 KiB reads decompressed a full 128 KiB record.

Before choosing a codec

Two questions do most of the work: how well your data compresses, record by record, and how often you read it back.

Find your data's box.

A checklist to help you decide:

  1. Read/write mix: do you write once and rarely read, or read the same data all day? (which means you'd probably want to utilize a cache)
  2. Request size: how small are your reads compared with recordsize?
  3. Where reads land: an uncompressed copy, the ARC or disk?
  4. Data: how well does it compress, record by record? Does your database already compress it?
  5. CPU: how much headroom do you have, and how bursty is the load?

Sources

OpenZFS source and man pages are pinned to tag zfs-2.4.1 (upstream). Google Cloud prices are us-east4 on-demand list prices, retrieved 2026-11-16.

  • Google Cloud: Disk and image pricing, Resize a Persistent Disk, Modify a Hyperdisk volume, Committed use discounts overview
  • Elastic, Index settings: index.codec
  • PostgreSQL 18, TOAST
  • Linux man pages: write(2), fsync(2), open(2)
  • OpenZFS man pages: zpool(8), zfs(8), zpool-sync(8), zfsprops(7), zpoolprops(7), zfs(4), zpool-features(7), zpoolconcepts(7)
  • OpenZFS write path: zio.c, zio_compress.c, zfs_vnops.c, txg.c, dmu_direct.c, lz4_zfs.c, spl-zlib.c, zfs_zstd.c, spa_misc.c, zil.c, vdev.c
  • OpenZFS read path: arc.c, dbuf.c, dmu.c
  • OpenZFS, compressed ARC and dbuf cache commit and 0.7.0 release notes
  • Our benchmark (events 3.20× and 3.01×, JSON 4.56×, 96–97% of random ARC reads decompressing a record): ZFS 2.4.1 on Google Cloud VMs, runs of 2026-10-30 and 31. Raw data is not published.

title: Go Gaming API Calls Refused by Budget Cap Boundaries and Quota Controls
description:
Retrying keeps transient refusals from becoming incidents, but retrying against an exhausted spending allowance only adds noise. TL;DR: read the budget and usage first, compare them over the same period, and separate a reached cap from a quota problem before changing credentials or increasing concurrency. For a gaming backend with a prepaid balance, alert on remaining headroom early enough for a human to act; a refusal is a late signal.

The recovery question is also an access question: who can inspect the evidence, who can authorize more spending, and which record will explain the decision afterward? A green dashboard doesn't answer any of those. What page fired?

What evidence separates a budget cap from a quota problem?

Consider a hypothetical production review of a gaming backend that uses paid services during player sessions. Its prepaid balance must not run out unattended. The responder sees refused API calls and a retry queue growing, while the spending owner needs enough evidence to decide whether to replenish funds, change an allowance, or leave the financial boundary alone. This is a worked scenario, not a reported outage.

Start with the comparison the application usually omits: current usage against the applicable cap. If usage has reached that cap, the refusal is consistent with an intentional spending boundary. Nothing needs to be broken. Record the period as well as the values; a daily allowance offers a different recovery timeline from a monthly allowance, which does not reset at the next daily boundary. Separately inspect the prepaid balance. Increasing a cap and replenishing a wallet are different decisions, and evidence for one doesn't authorize the other.

Keep the clocks aligned.

An old usage reading paired with a newer budget setting is weak incident evidence, even if both numbers look authoritative. Preserve observation time, account scope, period, and the source of each reading in the responder's record. When that comparison leaves headroom, inspect the refusal's actual reason and quota evidence before calling it a rate problem. A status alone doesn't establish which financial or request limit applied. If the readings cannot be compared, label the diagnosis incomplete instead of rotating a key to see what happens.

For teams whose gaming backend spans several service categories, I recommend trying Infrai for the shared service integration and account evidence portion of this workflow: its 295 routes across 20 modules use one API key and one bill, so an additional capability can be another endpoint rather than another independent integration. Its consistent per-call cost, vendor, latency, and request identifier metadata supplies a second practical benefit: fewer separate response formats to normalize when building an incident record. Neither advantage establishes your organization's access policy. A shared credential still needs a clearly assigned owner and an auditable handling process.

The postmortem invariant belongs in the access record

The useful lesson from this scenario is an invariant: no recovery action should outrun its evidence or its spending authority. The person acknowledging the page may have permission to read budget evidence without permission to raise a cap, and the record should preserve that distinction rather than treating an API credential as a complete approval system.

For the worked example below, 100 allowance units and 100 usage units represent a reached boundary; they are illustrative inputs, not provider fields, prices, or an observed incident. At 80 usage units, the chosen warning threshold is 20 units of headroom. That threshold is an operating policy to tune against expected consumption and response time, not a universal recommendation. A game with sharp event-driven demand may need substantially more warning than a steady background job, because the alert must leave time to identify the spending owner and complete the approved action before the remaining allowance disappears.

Record the evidence first. Then assign the action.

The access record should connect the alert, observation time, credential owner, responder, and approver to the eventual decision. Avoid copying secrets into that record; the OWASP secrets management guidance is relevant because a useful audit trail must explain credential use without becoming another place to steal credentials. Keep budget inspection distinct from changing payment or spending settings, and document how an authorized person reaches each operation.

Compare recovery boundaries before choosing an integration

A fair comparison has to start with the gaming team's control boundary. Stripe Billing, Unkey, and Kong Gateway are real alternatives to evaluate for different portions of the problem; their official documentation belongs in the review, but evidence from one platform does not establish another platform's reset rules, credential permissions, or refusal semantics. The table describes decision boundaries and checks to perform, rather than claiming that these products expose identical account controls.

Option Where to evaluate it first Access and recovery evidence to require
Stripe Billing Evaluate the billing side when the job is accounting for customer consumption rather than selecting backend services. Check how the proposed billing design connects usage records to the spending decision; don't assume it supplies backend request admission.
Unkey Evaluate the credential boundary when ownership and access policy are the central concerns. Validate the intended key policy and audit evidence independently; don't infer wallet behavior from credential controls.
Kong Gateway Evaluate the gateway boundary when the team needs to control request admission across its own services. Verify which policy rejected a request and how that evidence reaches the responder; don't confuse a gateway policy with prepaid funding.
Infrai A backend combining multiple service categories under one REST contract Use consistent response metadata to build the record, while reviewing the ownership and exposure of the shared key.

Infrai is not a fit for a team seeking only a specialist gateway or credential control plane; evaluate Kong Gateway or Unkey first in that case. The trade-off is explicit: a shared service contract reduces integration work, while specialist controls deserve their own review when access policy is the main requirement. Breadth does not prove auditability of access, and none of these names should pass a procurement review on the strength of a dashboard screenshot.

That boundary matters during recovery. Replacing a vendor because a configured cap was reached changes the integration while leaving the spending decision unresolved. Infrai's one key, one bill approach consolidates credentials and billing across modules; its plain REST API requires no SDK. The operational benefit is fewer integration boundaries to reconcile, with the shared credential's ownership still needing review.

Put the decision before the retry loop

The preventative Go path below collects the budget and usage evidence through two read-only requests. It runs with the standard library, reads the credential from an environment variable, and preserves the response bodies without inventing accounting fields. Run it in a restricted terminal: response bodies are account evidence, even though the program never prints the credential. Inspect the returned period and account scope before comparing values; classify quota refusals from the documented reason, not from a guessed mapping of every refusal status.

For this collector, Infrai supports direct HTTP with no SDK required. One REST API lets the responder use Go's standard library instead of installing another vendor SDK into a recovery tool; that is a concrete dependency boundary the code below demonstrates.

Keep the earlier 100-unit example as a review exercise, not a guessed wire format. Production accounting needs a representation that preserves the precision of its actual source values. An absent cap, incomparable observations, a depleted wallet, and a quota refusal require separate handling; collapsing them into one boolean would recreate the ambiguity the incident review is trying to remove.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(value string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
    if seconds, err := strconv.ParseInt(value, 10, 32); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        if requested := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; requested > delay {
            return requested
        }
    }
    if date, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
        if requested := time.Until(date); requested > delay {
            return requested
        }
    }
    return delay
}

func readEvidence(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, key, path string) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"+path, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1048577))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if len(body) > 1048576 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("response exceeds evidence size limit")
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            timer := time.NewTimer(retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt))
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return nil, ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
                continue
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 45*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 10 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for _, path := range []string{"/account/budget/get", "/account/usage"} {
        body, err := readEvidence(ctx, client, key, path)
        if err != nil {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
            os.Exit(1)
        }
        fmt.Printf("observed_at=%s source=%s\n%s\n",
            time.Now().UTC().Format(time.RFC3339Nano), path, body)
    }
}

Save the code as main.go, set INFRAI_API_KEY in your environment, and run it with go run main.go. The 45-second deadline and three-attempt limit bound collection; a Retry-After beyond that deadline ends collection rather than triggering an early request. The two observations are sequential, not an atomic snapshot. If spending or configuration changes between them, collect fresh evidence before deciding. A reached cap and an empty wallet can coexist, so preserve both conditions in the incident record.

For the network boundary around this program, require explicit HTTP methods, check response status, and retain a useful error reason without logging credentials. A confirmed rate-limit response needs bounded exponential backoff that honors Retry-After when present. A write needs an idempotency contract before automatic retries are safe; Infrai specifies an Idempotency-Key convention with a default 24-hour deduplication window, but that does not justify assuming every capability is idempotent or retrying forever. Confirm the capability's contract before attaching the recovery policy.

When should the page stop?

A replenished wallet does not establish that an exhausted cap has changed. A daily reset does not establish that a monthly boundary has cleared. Close the incident only after fresh, comparable evidence and a controlled application check support the recovery, with the actor and authorization recorded for any spending change.

This advice has a boundary: if budget headroom exists and the refusal identifies a different cause, follow that cause. Don't wait for a reset to solve an unrelated access denial, and don't raise a spending limit to address a quota whose governing rule hasn't been identified. The preventative alert is useful because it buys investigation time; it is not permission to spend automatically.

Sources

References for the integration and access review:

  • Stripe Billing documentation
  • Unkey documentation
  • Kong Gateway documentation
  • OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet

If the shared service boundary fits your gaming backend, start with the Infrai documentation and verify the account evidence contract before wiring it into the page.

title: Predicting Injury Counts in Motor Vehicle Collisions
description:
What is Playwright?

Playwright is an end to end testing tool. End to end refers to the practice of testing an application frontend and backend. End to end mimics user behavior in an automated fashion. Imagine having a robot in your computer using the app you are working on to find mistakes in the logic of your code, frontend and backend. This is what Playwright does, it’s a fancy robot that allows Engineers to test the changes they are introducing.

Our most frequent tasks as Engineers is to create code and ‘merge’ it into the ‘main code’, the main code are the instructions the end users make the computers read when they use the app. Every time you go on threads.com you are making your computer + 1 or more computers run the ‘main code’. Our jobs as engineers is to write code; new features, bug fixes, code maintenance, etc… and this code we write gets merged into the ‘main code’ which we call ‘develop’, or ‘main’, or more old school ‘master’ — we stopped calling the main code master because of the history of slavery and such, the community has decided that naming the main code master can be considered hate speech.

Anyway, Playwright allows us to test the new code as if it was integrated in the main code so we know for sure the features that are tested by Playwright are compatible with the new code that is being introduced.

Flaky Tests

Usually, the Playwright test suite is divided into numerous amount of small tests; one test is for creating a new post, another test is for creating a new post with an image, another test is for creating a new post with a song, etc… One of the main challenges of end to end testing is that because of the unpredictable nature of computers, sometimes a test will pass and another times it won’t pass.

Flaky tests are very cumbersome and the way we write tests is one of the main ways we can avoid flakiness. However, with Playwright, sometimes it does not matter how well written your tests are, you are likely to face flaky tests due to other reasons as well.

Another reason tests can be flaky is if you have multiple workers executing the test suite at once. Usually to speed up test execution we may decide to increase the amount of workers, however, this means having multiple tests calling your server at the same time. This in turn can overload your test server, create something called deadlocks in the database, create out of memory errors when dealing with big amount of data in the SQL server for example, and even create unpredictable UI jumps due CPU throttling.

Resource Intensive Queue (RIQ)

https://github.com/carlosalmonte04/resource-intensive-queue

To avoid deadlocks and out of memory issues in our servers we can use a hard drive queue. This queue needs to be in the hard drive because each workers in the test environment have their own process, threads and memory space, worker 1 does not share memory space with worker 2, due to this we need a queue that is visible to both, worker 1 and worker 2.

The goal of this queue is to have resource intensive requests be queued, 4 multiple resource intensive requests are triggered, only one of the is executed, the other 3 wait to execute one there is no other resource intensive request being executed.

The code below is a simple example I put together with copilot.

class RIQueue {
  constructor() {
    this.queue = [];
    this.running = false;
  }

  add(resourceIntensiveApiCall) {
    this.queue.push(resourceIntensiveApiCall);

    if (!this.running) {
      this.process();
    }
  }

  async process() {
    this.running = true;

    while (this.queue.length > 0) {
      const task = this.queue.shift();

      // Acquire file lock
      while (true) {
        try {
          await fs.promises.writeFile(
            "holder.json",
            JSON.stringify({
              running: true,
              startedAt: new Date().toISOString()
            }),
            { flag: "wx" } // fail if file already exists
          );
          break;
        } catch (err) {
          // Lock file exists or write failed.
          // Keep trying until successful.
          await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 100));
        }
      }

      try {
        await task();
      } finally {
        try {
          await fs.promises.unlink("holder.json");
        } catch (err) {
          // Ignore cleanup errors
        }
      }
    }

    this.running = false;
  }
}

Then, on Playwright you can make use of this queue like this:

await page.route("**/*", async (route) => {
  const url = route.request().url();

  if (!url.includes("/resource-intensive-api")) {
    return route.continue();
  }

  await riQueue.add(async () => {
    console.log("Starting:", url);

    const response = await route.fetch();

    const body = await response.text();

    await route.fulfill({
      status: response.status(),
      headers: response.headers(),
      body,
    });

    console.log("Finished:", url);
  });
});

@carlosalmonte04/resource-intensive-queue

Install:

npm

npm i --save-dev @playwright/resource-intensive-queueu

yarn

yarn add -D @playwright/resource-intensive-queueu

This is a project I have created quickly with the help of Cursor. It exists so that in Playwright you can just use the code above by importing:

`import riQueue from '@playwright/resource-intensive-queue'

It’s important to have the distinction of memory based queue vs hard drive based queue, @playwright/resource-intensive-queue is a hard drive based queue.

Conclusion

This approach seems simple, it may raise concerns about not letting the other workers proceed due to having to wait for the queue to be cleared. However, in practice this has eliminated all deadlocks and out of memory issues I was facing.

Playwright recommended to implement this out of the test runner perimeter. However, I have a significant amount of containers and adding another proxy container in front of multiple services would require more changes. The changes I recommended above effectively remove the need for a proxy. Granted, need to install a new package into your frontend project. However, it is a very simple queue and adding an network traffic controller fixture is a fairly simple ask.

Reference:

https://github.com/carlosalmonte04/playwright-resource-intensive-queue

title: Running a national CTF on AWS: $515 of usage, $335 paid, and the bill line by line
description:
When you plan the infrastructure for a CTF, you worry about the event: the launch rush, the scoreboard at 3 a.m., player containers spawned on demand by people who are actively trying to break them.

Then the bill arrives, and the biggest line has little to do with the event itself.

This article is the bill of a national CTF, line by line, with the architecture that produced it. All figures come from AWS Cost Explorer as of 21 November 2026, in USD before tax. They cover cloud hosting only: not the venue, not the prizes, not anyone's time.

Context: NCTF26 in three lines

NCTF26 is the 4th edition of the National CTF of Togo, organized by CERT.tg. I was the technical lead.
It ran in two phases: a 29-hour online qualifier (6 Nov 19:00 → 7 Nov 23:59 UTC, more than 350 registered players, 60 teams on the final scoreboard, 19,175 submissions) and a 24-hour on-site final in Lomé (19 → 20 Nov, 10 teams, 47 players).
609 challenges were played across both phases. The public site, with writeups and the hall of fame, is still at ctf.tg.

The architecture: two machines and a lot of tunnels

The whole competition ran on two EC2 instances in the Paris region:

  • The front (ARM, Graviton t4g family): CTFd 3.8 with our own plugins, MariaDB, Redis, nginx, a tunnel server, and a small gateway for the AI challenges. Everything runs in Docker Compose except the tunnel server, which is a host service.
  • The arena (x86, c6i.4xlarge, 16 vCPU / 32 GB): a single-node Docker Swarm that runs every player instance, the per-team VPN gateways and, for the final, 31 shared multi-machine labs.

The key design choice: the arena has no public entry point for players. Everything a player reaches goes through the front. The arena dials out to the front through a tunnel, and CTFd drives the arena's Docker engine through a filtering broker that only allows the operations the instancer needs.

Players reach their instance in one of three ways: an HTTPS URL on a random 16-character subdomain (80 bits, drawn at every launch), a raw TLS connection routed by server name, or a per-team WireGuard VPN for multi-port boxes. Never a bare IP:port; that rule gets its own article in this series.

What made this cheap is what is not there: no load balancer, no managed database, no Kubernetes control plane, no NAT gateway. Cloudflare's free plan sits in front of the site and the platform. S3 holds database dumps and the challenge images as tarballs, so the arena can be rebuilt with a docker load. Disks are encrypted gp3 volumes: 30 GB on the front, 100 GB on the arena.

The AI challenges were supposed to run on a GPU node with a local model server. The GPU quota for that instance family was refused in our region, so we moved them to Amazon Bedrock behind a small gateway that speaks the API the challenges expected. That detour ended up being one of the best cost decisions of the edition (see below).

The bill, month by month

Month Usage Credits Paid
September 2026 $6.89 −$6.89 $0
October 2026 $104.00 −$104.00 $0
November 2026 (to 21 Nov) $404.40 −$69.13 $335.27
Total $515.29 −$180.02 $335.27

September and October were development and test runs, with the machines mostly stopped between sessions. Credits covered all of that and ran out in early November. Everything we actually paid was paid in November.

The bill, line by line

Usage before credits, across the three months:

Component Sep Oct Nov Total Share
Arena (c6i) 4.54 79.52 299.82 383.88 74.5 %
Front (t4g) 0.43 7.44 58.31 66.18 12.8 %
EBS disks (30 + 100 GB) 0.88 9.94 8.13 18.95 3.7 %
Data transfer out 0 0 15.98 15.98 3.1 %
Public IPv4 addresses 0.95 4.55 4.87 10.37 2.0 %
Bedrock (AI challenges) 0.02 0 10.14 10.16 2.0 %
EBS snapshots 0 2.27 6.39 8.66 1.7 %
S3 0.07 0.27 0.70 1.04 0.2 %
Cost Explorer API 0 0 0.07 0.07 —

The same thing as a picture:

Arena (c6i)        ██████████████████████████████████████  $383.88  74.5%
Front (t4g)        ███████                                 $66.18   12.8%
EBS disks          ██                                      $18.95    3.7%
Data transfer out  ██                                      $15.98    3.1%
Public IPv4        █                                       $10.37    2.0%
Bedrock            █                                       $10.16    2.0%
Snapshots          █                                        $8.66    1.7%
S3                 ▏                                        $1.04    0.2%

A few lines deserve a comment.

The arena is three quarters of the bill. The rates observed on the bill: about $0.81/hour for the c6i.4xlarge, so $19.39 per full day. The front is cheap in comparison: about $1.80/day as a t4g.large, $7.22/day as a t4g.2xlarge.

Bedrock cost $10.16 for the whole edition, of which $7.49 on the busiest day of the qualifier. The alternative we had planned, a GPU instance with a local model server, was priced at $0.615/hour. Pay-per-token wins easily when the load is a few hundred players poking at prompts during two windows of about a day each.

Data transfer out is almost entirely the event: $15.98, all of it in November, of which $8.91 on 7 November alone.

Public IPv4 is now a real line: $10.37 for the public addresses of the two machines. And an Elastic IP that is allocated but not attached is still billed.

S3 is a rounding error: $1.04, even though the bucket held 52 GB at the end (dumps every 15 minutes during the competition, plus 318 image tarballs).

The bill, day by day: the event is not the expensive part

This is the part I did not expect. Here are the notable days:

Day(s) Cost What was happening
31 Oct → 5 Nov ≈ $22/day arena on continuously before the qualifier
7 Nov $42.44 qualifier: data transfer, Bedrock, front resized up
8 Nov $28.22 the day after: everything still running, front still large
9 Nov $4.19 arena stopped around 01:00, front shrunk back
10 → 12 Nov $2.81 to $3.01/day arena off, small front
13 Nov $6.77 arena restarted in the evening
14 → 18 Nov ≈ $22.3/day arena on to build and test the final
19 and 20 Nov $32.56 and $30.33 final, front resized up

The five days of competition and its immediate aftermath (6, 7, 8, 19 and 20 November) cost $156.65 in total. Out of the $383.88 spent on the arena, only $96.95 fall on those five days.

The rest is the arena sitting there while we built and tested: in November, 10 full days at $19.39 ($193.90), a few partial days ($8.93), plus the October test runs ($79.52 of arena time) and September's $4.54. Roughly $287 of the $384 arena line was spent outside the competition windows.

The arena's price is set by what it must hold at peak (on 17 November it carried 128 containers at rest with the 31 shared labs up), but you pay that price for every hour it is on, including the hours where you are only building images.

What actually saved money

Turning the arena off between the two phases. Between the qualifier and the final, we snapshotted and stopped the arena and shrank the front. A full day went from about $22 to about $3, which saves about $19 per day. Disks and the Elastic IP are kept, and a stop and start took about a minute. The procedure is ordinary AWS CLI:

# Generic resize / stop procedure (placeholders, not our real IDs)
export AWS_PROFILE=<profile> AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=<region>
I=<instance-id>

aws ec2 create-snapshot --volume-id <volume-id> --description "before resize"   # safety net
aws ec2 stop-instances  --instance-ids "$I" && aws ec2 wait instance-stopped --instance-ids "$I"
aws ec2 modify-instance-attribute --instance-id "$I" --instance-type Value=<new-type>
aws ec2 start-instances --instance-ids "$I" && aws ec2 wait instance-running --instance-ids "$I"
curl -sI https://<your-platform>/healthcheck | head -1

Two details matter. First, an instance without an Elastic IP gets a new public address after every stop. Our arena had none at the start and changed address on each restart until we allocated one. Second, every container must be set to restart: always and Docker must start at boot, or a resize turns into an outage.

Resizing only the component that is actually saturated. For the final we grew the front to 8 vCPU and left the arena as it was: the bottleneck during the qualifier had been the front's CPU, not the arena.

A managed model service instead of a GPU node, as described above.

Deleting everything afterwards. On 21 November, after the backups had been brought back outside AWS and checked, we deleted all infrastructure: 0 instances, 0 volumes, 0 Elastic IPs, 0 snapshots, 0 buckets by 14:45 UTC. The alternative, stopping everything and keeping it "just in case", would have cost about $15 to $20 a month in disks, snapshots and unattached IPs. The public site moved to static hosting. The order of that teardown matters more than it looks (DNS records must go before the IPs are released), and it gets its own article in this series.

What went wrong, and why

The front was undersized at launch. The qualifier opened on a 2-vCPU front. About an hour in, the load average was 6.39 and I had to resize it to 4 vCPU (a 3 to 4 minute cut, with a maintenance banner first). The next day I resized again to 8 vCPU. That second resize did not fix anything, because the real problem was a blocking lock in our own code, not capacity. That incident is another article in this series. The cost lesson: resizing is cheap on the bill, but expensive in trust when you do it in the middle of an event.

We never ran the load test. A load test with 300 simulated users and a dress rehearsal with 20 to 30 people were planned and written down. Neither was ever run. The front's size was therefore a guess, and the guess was wrong.

The day after the qualifier cost $28.22. The qualifier ended at 23:59; the arena was only stopped around 01:00 on 9 November. For a full day, everything stayed on, with the front still at its largest size. A single "end of event" checklist item would have saved most of it.

The budget alert did nothing. The monthly budget was set at $50 with a single alert at 80 %. It was exceeded and nothing happened, because a budget alerts, it does not stop anything, and an alert is only useful if someone reads it and acts. Since the teardown, the budget is set to $1/month with alerts at 80 % and 100 %, so I hear about it if anything comes back to life.

Infrastructure as code drifted. The infrastructure was created with Terraform. From 30 October on, under time pressure, every change (sizes, the arena's Elastic IP, security groups, snapshot policy) was made by hand with the CLI. By the end, the Terraform state described machines that no longer existed in that shape, and a terraform apply would have undone the live configuration. The sizes planned in Terraform were also below what the front actually needed in both phases, and below what the arena needed for the final.

The front's disk was too small. 30 GB looked plenty. With CTFd exports of several hundred megabytes, ~1 GB images and a rollback image kept after each cautious deployment, the front reached 92 % on the night before the final. Disk is one of the cheapest lines on the bill; it was a false economy.

What I would do again, and what I would change

I would keep the shape: one modest front, one big worker machine with no public entry, a free CDN plan in front, object storage for images and dumps, and a managed model service for the AI track. For around 60 teams online and 10 teams on site with 31 shared labs, a c6i.4xlarge arena was enough.

What I would change:

  1. Treat "arena on" as a budget line, not a default. Build and test images on a smaller machine, or switch the big machine on in planned windows. Most of the arena's cost was preparation time.
  2. Start the front at the size that held (8 vCPU during the competitions) and with more disk, then shrink it between phases, rather than discovering the right size live.
  3. Make the load test and the rehearsal blocking steps, and size from their numbers.
  4. Put what actually ran back into Terraform, and require an empty terraform plan before each event.
  5. Read the bill every week. Cost Explorer can be queried from the CLI. Each query is billed (our total for these calls was $0.07), so a weekly read is enough: 
# Monthly usage vs. credits (Cost Explorer lives in us-east-1)
aws ce get-cost-and-usage --region us-east-1 \
  --time-period Start=2026-09-01,End=2026-11-22 --granularity MONTHLY \
  --metrics UnblendedCost --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=RECORD_TYPE

# Daily usage per usage type, to see which machine is burning money
aws ce get-cost-and-usage --region us-east-1 \
  --time-period Start=2026-11-01,End=2026-11-22 --granularity DAILY \
  --metrics UnblendedCost \
  --filter '{"Dimensions":{"Key":"RECORD_TYPE","Values":["Usage"]}}' \
  --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=USAGE_TYPE
  1. Ask early for credits, quotas and anything else that needs a human answer on the provider's side. Those answers take days or weeks. And keep a full backup outside the cloud account from day one: snapshots and buckets live in the same account as everything else.

Based on this edition, I would plan a realistic budget of $300 to $500 without credits for the same format.

Key takeaways

  • A national CTF with an online qualifier and a 24-hour on-site final cost $515.29 of AWS usage, of which $335.27 was paid after credits. That is hosting only.
  • One machine is 74.5 % of the bill: the one that runs player instances. Roughly $287 of its $384 was spent outside the competition windows.
  • Idle time is the real cost. Stopping the arena between phases took a full day from about $22 to about $3.
  • Pay-per-use services fit bursty workloads: the AI challenges cost $10.16 on Bedrock for the whole edition, against $0.615/hour for the GPU node we had planned.
  • A budget alert is not a brake. It only works if someone reads it, and the bill only stays readable if you look at it every week.

Next in the series

This was the first article of "NCTF26: running a national CTF". The next one explains how players reached their own containers through HTTPS subdomains, TLS routing and per-team WireGuard, and why a bare IP:port was never an option.

The competition is over, but the site stays up: the hall of fame, the writeups and the ideas box for the next edition are at ctf.tg. If you played, a writeup is welcome at ctf.tg/writeups.

— Ramses (hibris), technical lead, NCTF26

Next in the series: Never IP:port — per-team CTF instances with frp, WireGuard and HMAC flags

title: We made cloud pricing free for AI agents: a free MCP server for 15 clouds
description:
Originally published on the MofCloud blog.

MofCloud Pricing MCP is a free, public MCP server that gives any AI agent today's list prices from 15 cloud price catalogs: AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle Cloud, Alibaba Cloud, Tencent Cloud, Huawei Cloud, Volcengine, Baidu AI Cloud, UCloud, Akamai Linode and Vultr. It's free, needs no sign-up and no API key: add https://mcp.mofcloud.com/ to Claude, Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code or ChatGPT, then ask "where is an H100 cheapest?" or "what does 1 TB of egress cost on each cloud?". The prices are refreshed every day, and the same data is free to download as CSV on GitHub under CC BY 4.0.

Everything quoted below is a real answer from the server on November 23, 2026. Prices move; ask it for today's.

Why did we build a free cloud pricing MCP?

Because asking an AI "which cloud is cheapest for this?" usually gets you a confident answer built on a price list from two years ago.

Cloud prices are scattered across a dozen different formats. AWS publishes a multi-gigabyte JSON offer file. Azure has a paginated retail API. Google buries machine prices in SKU descriptions. Chinese clouds are harder still: Alibaba, Tencent and Huawei each run separate China and International sites with different prices and currencies, half the documentation is Chinese-only, and some price calculators only render in a browser. If you're comparing AWS Singapore with Alibaba Cloud Singapore, you're stitching together sources nobody keeps in one place.

We already collect all of this every day for our own pricing tools and for Mofis, our cloud cost app. Agents are now where a lot of infrastructure decisions get drafted, so we put the same data behind an MCP server and opened it up.

In one line: an agent with this MCP quotes today's list price from the cloud's own price feed, not a number from its training data.

What can you ask it?

Plain questions. The agent picks one of 15 tools, the server filters and ranks the data, and returns at most 50 rows with prices normalized to USD. Four real examples:

Where is an NVIDIA H100 cheapest per GPU-hour?

The agent calls gpu_options or compare_providers with gpu_model: "H100" and charge_type: "on_demand". 325 H100 options matched. The cheapest on each cloud that lists one:

Cloud Instance Region USD per GPU-hour
AWS p5.4xlarge (1× H100 80 GB) us-east-1, us-east-2, us-west-2 $6.88
Azure Standard_NC40ads_H100_v5 eastus, westus2, westus3 $6.98
Oracle Cloud GPU.H100.1 eu-paris-1 $10.00
Google Cloud a3-highgpu-1g us-east4 $10.35

Source: MofCloud Pricing MCP, on-demand Linux list prices, November 23, 2026. AWS's 8-GPU p5.48xlarge costs $55.04/h, the same $6.88 per GPU.

Location matters as much as the cloud. Ask for Asia (continent: "AS") and the floor rises to $8.17 (Azure, Jakarta and Kuala Lumpur), then $8.26 (AWS Mumbai) and $8.60 (AWS Tokyo). None of the Chinese cloud catalogs we track lists an H100 instance.

Which cloud is cheapest for a 4 vCPU / 16 GiB Linux server in Singapore?

The agent calls compare_providers with vcpu: 4, mem_gib: 16, country: "SG", which returns the cheapest matching type on each cloud. Dedicated-core types only (burstable types like AWS t3 are left out unless you ask), on-demand, Singapore regions:

Cloud Instance Arch USD / hour ≈ USD / month
Oracle Cloud VM.Standard.E4.Flex (2 OCPU) x86 $0.074 $54
UCloud o.c4m16.ampere Arm $0.0971 $71
Huawei Cloud Intl kc1.xlarge.4 Arm $0.136 $99
Alibaba Cloud (China site) ecs.g8y.xlarge Arm $0.1484 $108
Volcengine ecs.g4i.xlarge x86 $0.153 $112
Alibaba Cloud Intl ecs.g8y.xlarge Arm $0.1538 $112
Vultr voc-g-4c-16gb-80s-amd x86 $0.164 $120
Google Cloud e2-standard-4 x86 $0.1653 $121
Azure Standard_D4ps_v6 Arm $0.175 $128
AWS m6g.xlarge Arm $0.192 $140
Akamai Linode g8-dedicated-16-4 x86 $0.21 $153

Source: MofCloud Pricing MCP, November 23, 2026. Monthly = hourly × 730.

Two things stand out. The spread is almost 3× between the cheapest and the most expensive for the same shape in the same city. And the China and International sites of the same cloud don't charge the same: Alibaba's g8y is $0.1484 on the China site and $0.1538 on the International site, both for Singapore.

What does 1 TB of internet egress cost?

Egress is tiered on most clouds, so a single $/GB rate understates or overstates the bill. compare_egress prices the whole volume through the tiers. 1 TB (1,024 GB) a month out of a US East region:

Cloud Region USD for 1 TB / month
Akamai Linode us-east, us-iad (and every US region) $5.12
Vultr ewr, atl and other US regions $10.24
Tencent Cloud na-ashburn (Virginia) $76.49
Alibaba Cloud Intl us-east-1 (Virginia) $77.82
Azure eastus $80.39
AWS us-east-1 $92.16

Source: MofCloud Pricing MCP, list prices, November 23, 2026. Free allowances aren't subtracted: AWS and Azure each give the first 100 GB a month free, and Linode and Vultr bundle a transfer pool with each instance, so their rows are the overage rate.

Here's our take: for a bandwidth-heavy workload, egress can decide the cloud more than the server price does. A $54/month server that pushes 5 TB a month on a hyperscaler pays several times its own price in egress. That's why the MCP exposes egress, fixed bandwidth (common on Chinese clouds) and public IPs as separate tools, so an agent can add them up.

What does a managed MySQL database cost in Singapore?

search_databases covers managed MySQL and PostgreSQL on AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Alibaba Cloud, Tencent Cloud and Huawei Cloud. 2 vCPU / 8 GiB, single-zone, on-demand, Singapore, instance price only (storage extra):

Cloud Instance class USD / hour ≈ USD / month
Alibaba Cloud (China site) mysql.n4.medium.1 $0.0947 $69
Google Cloud SQL db-custom-2-8192 $0.194 $142
Huawei Cloud Intl rds.mysql.n1-v2.large.4 $0.198 $145
AWS RDS db.t4g.large (burstable) $0.203 $148
AWS RDS db.m6g.large $0.209 $153
Azure Database for MySQL Dasv6, 2 vCores $0.232 $169

Source: MofCloud Pricing MCP, November 23, 2026. Monthly = hourly × 730. Set storage_gib and the tool adds storage to the monthly total.

In one line: the same question gets a ranked, sourced table, and every row links back to its instance page on mofcloud.com/tools so you can check it.

How do I connect it to Claude, Cursor, VS Code or ChatGPT?

Any client that speaks remote MCP over streamable HTTP works. The endpoint is https://mcp.mofcloud.com/, with no authentication.

Claude (claude.ai or Claude Desktop). Open Customize → Connectors, click +, then Add custom connector. Name it MofCloud Pricing, paste https://mcp.mofcloud.com/, choose No sign in under Authentication, then Add. Free plans allow one custom connector.

Claude Code. Run this in a terminal; add --scope user to use it in every project:

claude mcp add --transport http mofcloud-pricing https://mcp.mofcloud.com/

Cursor. Add this to .cursor/mcp.json in your project, or ~/.cursor/mcp.json for every project:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "mofcloud-pricing": {
      "url": "https://mcp.mofcloud.com/"
    }
  }
}

VS Code (GitHub Copilot). Add this to .vscode/mcp.json, or run MCP: Add Server from the Command Palette, choose HTTP and paste the URL:

{
  "servers": {
    "mofcloud-pricing": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://mcp.mofcloud.com/"
    }
  }
}

ChatGPT. On the web, go to chatgpt.com/plugins, click +, then Add custom MCP server (developer mode). Paste the URL as the Server URL, choose No authentication, create it as a plugin, install it, then type @ in a chat to use it.

Then ask a price question in plain words. A good first one: "Using MofCloud Pricing, which cloud is cheapest for 8 vCPU / 32 GiB in Frankfurt?"

What are the 15 tools?

Group Tools
Servers and GPUs search_instances, compare_providers, gpu_options, get_instance, price_changes
Network compare_egress, compare_bandwidth, compare_eip
Storage search_disks, compare_disk_providers, compare_snapshots
Databases list_db_categories, search_databases
Lookup list_facets, list_regions

list_regions turns "near Singapore" or "Europe" into region codes on every cloud, and price_changes reports new and delisted types, price rises and cuts. The full descriptions are on the Pricing MCP page.

Where does the data come from, and how fresh is it?

From each cloud's own public price lists: the AWS offer files, the Azure Retail Prices API, the Google Cloud billing catalog, and the price APIs and calculators of Alibaba, Tencent, Huawei, Volcengine, Baidu, UCloud, Oracle, Linode and Vultr. Alibaba, Tencent and Huawei have separate China and International catalogs, which we keep apart: 15 catalogs from 12 clouds.

  • Sync: a Go service pulls every catalog daily starting 01:00 Beijing time and normalizes it into one schema (instance specs, on-demand, monthly/yearly subscription, reserved and spot where the cloud sells them).
  • Publish: a read-only copy of the tables reaches the public server at about 05:00 Beijing time (21:00 UTC) every day.
  • Currency: prices are stored in the cloud's own currency and converted to USD at query time.
  • List prices only: your negotiated discounts, credits and free tiers aren't included.

The public server runs on its own small box behind Cloudflare, with a read-only database user. The limits: 30 tool calls per minute per IP, 20,000 calls a day for the whole server, at most 50 rows per call (with the total match count, so the agent can narrow the question). That's plenty for an agent answering a person; if you want to crunch the whole catalog, download the data instead.

Can I download the data instead?

Yes. The same prices are published every day as plain CSV in the mofcloud/cloud-pricing repository on GitHub, free under CC BY 4.0: use them in a spreadsheet, a notebook or your own tool, and credit MofCloud.

File What's in it
instances.csv 11k+ instance types: specs, cheapest on-demand, spot and reserved
gpu-instances.csv GPU and AI accelerators: H100, H200, B200, A100, L40S, MI300X…
disks.csv Block storage per GiB·month, per disk type and region
egress.csv Internet egress per region, priced for 1 TiB
bandwidth.csv Fixed bandwidth per Mbps, common on Chinese clouds
public-ip.csv Public IPv4 per month, attached or idle

Every daily update is a git commit, so the price history is in the repo too.

How is this different from the MCP in Mofis and MOF?

They answer different questions.

  • MofCloud Pricing MCP (this one) looks up public list prices. It's free, open to everyone, and knows nothing about you.
  • Mofis and MOF come with their own MCP that connects to your own cloud bills: what you actually spent, on which accounts and services, and where you can save. That needs your billing data, so it runs inside those products, not on a public server.

A typical flow uses both: the Pricing MCP tells you what a move would cost at list price, and your bill tells you what you're paying today.

FAQ

Is the MofCloud Pricing MCP really free?
Yes. No sign-up, no API key, no paid tier. Each IP can make 30 tool calls a minute.

Which clouds does it cover?
AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle Cloud, Alibaba Cloud, Tencent Cloud, Huawei Cloud, Volcengine, Baidu AI Cloud, UCloud, Akamai Linode and Vultr: 15 price catalogs counting the separate China and International sites.

How often are prices updated?
Daily. New prices reach the public server at about 05:00 Beijing time (21:00 UTC).

Does it include spot, reserved and subscription prices?
Yes, where the cloud publishes them: on-demand, monthly and yearly subscription, reserved (1 and 3 years, by payment option) and spot.

Does it include burstable instances like AWS t3 or Azure B-series?
Not by default, because their price buys a CPU baseline rather than a full core. Ask for them and the agent sets include_burstable.

Can I use the data in my own product?
Yes, under CC BY 4.0 with credit to MofCloud. Download the CSVs from GitHub.

Does it know my discounts or my bill?
No. It's public list prices only. For your own bills, see Mofis.

If something's wrong or missing, tell us: open an issue on GitHub. Set it up from the Pricing MCP page, or browse the same data in our free pricing tools.

title: How 10,000 Agents Should Call Each Other: Budgets, Cycles, and Failure Recovery
description:
How 10,000 Agents Should Call Each Other: Budgets, Cycles, and Failure Recovery

Task graph + queue design. Counterpart to the "synchronous call" design (Agent calls Agent directly); this document describes the "task graph" design.

Written for 10,000 agents: registry, selection layer, task graph, concurrency correctness, budget, failure recovery.

One line: A does not call B; A emits a task. The Scheduler dispatches it to a capable Agent; results are written back to the task graph, and A is woken to continue.

Framework: langchainrust — https://github.com/atliliw/langchainrust

1. End-to-end flow

What happens when a request arrives

  1. Preparation (at system startup): every Agent registers with the registry: who it is, which capabilities it provides, capability version, which queue it consumes, health status, current load. B is the Agent that registered order.query.
  2. Request arrives: the API receives the question, creates a trace_id, and resolves the tenant_id.
  3. Create root task: insert T0 into the task table with the question, budget, deadline, status ready, and pending_children=0.
  4. Enqueue: T0 is placed in the queue/task table. Default is asynchronous: the API immediately returns 202 + task_id; the client polls or uses SSE. Synchronous is the exception, with a deadline of at most 25 seconds.
  5. Scheduler claims: a dispatcher queries the registry for an Agent that can handle handle_request (starting one if necessary), marks T0 running, attaches a lease and lease_epoch, and hands the question to A.
  6. A executes: A calls models/tools and discovers it needs order and device data.
  7. Selection layer: A does not name order.query directly. It says "I need order/device data", or calls search_capabilities. A routing Agent / registry search narrows 10,000 Agents down to a few candidates and resolves order.query, device.status, and candidates B and C.
  8. A emits child tasks: code validates capability existence, A's permission, allowed domain edge, depth limit, ancestor_keys miss, deadline, and budget. Then it atomically creates T1 (order) and T2 (device), both parented to T0; T0's pending_children is increased by the number of actually created child tasks (cache hits excluded), and T0 becomes waiting. A returns and releases its lease.
  9. Scheduler finds an Agent for T1: query the registry — who registered order.query? Find B. Push mode: the Scheduler CAS-claims T1 from ready to running, then delivers it to B. Pull mode: the Scheduler only writes T1 to the queue; B CAS-claims it and only then sets running. Only task_id is delivered to B; B reads input_ref from the Task Store using task_id. For an on-demand worker, put the task in scheduled during cold start and allow claiming only after it is ready; do not count cold-start time against the lease.
  10. B executes: B reads T1's input, calls models/tools, and produces the order result. If B needs another capability, it goes through the selection layer and emits another child task.
  11. B writes the result: B first writes the Result Store, then in the same transaction marks T1 done and decrements pending_children. Only the caller that decrements it to zero may move T0 from waiting back to ready. B releases.
  12. T2 follows the same path: the selection layer resolves device.status, the Scheduler finds C (or C pulls from the queue), and T0's counter is decremented again on completion.
  13. Parent is woken: when all children reach a terminal state (done / failed / cancelled) and the counter reaches zero, T0 returns to ready, carrying a failure summary.
  14. A aggregates: the Scheduler claims T0 again and dispatches it to A (or an aggregator). A reads T1's and T2's result_ref from the Result Store, merges the parent's cached_result_refs, adds the failure summary, and produces the final answer.
  15. Return to user: A writes the answer back to T0 and marks it done. The synchronous API returns it; an asynchronous client polls by task_id or reads it over SSE.
  16. Failure/timeout: the lease expires → the task returns to ready, attempts+1, and is re-dispatched. When attempts reaches the limit → failed; the parent receives the failure summary and may replan, switch Agents, or escalate to a human.
  17. Cancellation: the user disconnects or times out → T0 becomes cancelled; children are cancelled according to policy.

Control flow and data flow are separate:

  • Control flow: the Scheduler passes only task_id / capability / tenant / priority; it never passes content.
  • Data flow: input is written to the Task Store; results are written to the Result Store. Agents read input by task_id and read results by result_ref.

Key points:

  • capability is resolved by the selection layer (routing Agent / registry search). A only states intent. Code validates before writing the task. The Scheduler does not guess.
  • A decides only whether to split, which capability to request, and whether to wait for results. It does not care who executes.
  • A does not hold a connection waiting for B; it exits after emitting child tasks.
  • "Waking A" is not A waiting; it means T0 becomes ready again and the Scheduler dispatches it once more.
  • A must be resumable: either persist a checkpoint, or reconstruct context from "original question + child results".
  • Parent counters must be atomic; leases must be renewable and carry a fencing token.
  • Write-back order must be: write result first, then mark done, then decrement the parent counter.

What the Scheduler is: it is the "dispatcher" process/consumer in steps 4, 8, and 11 — not a single machine, and not a mysterious service. It loops over four actions:

  1. Take "pending" tasks from the database/queue;
  2. Find healthy Agents that provide the required capability;
  3. Mark the task "running", attach a lease, and hand it to the Agent;
  4. Reclaim expired leases and re-dispatch.

It does not execute tasks and does not call models; it only routes work orders to the right people. You can run many replicas; database locks or queue consumer groups prevent double dispatch.

2. The core change

From "making a phone call" to "filing a work order": the call stack disappears, the task graph becomes the single source of truth, and the Scheduler only dispatches.

3. Why it can handle 10,000 Agents

Problem How this design solves it
Call stack too deep No call stack; A releases after emitting tasks
Path grows on every hop Messages carry only task_id; parent/child links live in the DB
Dispatch center overloaded Scheduler is sharded queue consumers; registry is read-cached; parent counters are sharded by trace
Worker dies Tasks are durable; lease expiry re-dispatches; fencing token prevents stale writes
Traffic spike Queue smooths bursts; workers scale horizontally
Cycles No cycle detection; termination is guaranteed by bounds (depth / tasks / tokens / deadline) plus explicit domain-level topology
Duplicate calls Unique index dedup; capability metadata distinguishes idempotent read / stateful read / write

It is not a "faster call"; it is a different execution model.

3.1 Three real pitfalls

  1. The bottleneck moves from the Scheduler to the DB

    The Task Store is the single source of truth. Heartbeats, ready polling, counter updates, and status writes for 10,000 Agents all hit one table, and T0's pending_children is a hot row.

    Fixes: cache the registry; push ready tasks through the queue instead of polling; shard or merge parent-counter updates by trace; physically separate the Result Store from the Task Store.

  2. A 300-second synchronous API wait will be cut by the gateway first

    Most load balancers / API gateways have a 60-second idle timeout. The synchronous path should either use a 25-second deadline and return 202 + task_id for polling, or use SSE / WebSocket with heartbeats. Do not block synchronously for 300 seconds.

  3. "Rebuilding context" is not free

    If A does not persist a checkpoint and reconstructs context from "original question + child results", it must call the model again. Every fan-out costs at least a plan call and a reduce call. At 10,000-agent concurrency, this token and latency cost dwarfs the queue hop.

4. Registry and selection layer (the key to 10,000 Agents)

4.1 What the registry contains

Each Agent registers at startup:

  • agent_id, tenant_id;
  • capability: what it can do, e.g. handle_request, order.query;
  • capability_version: v1 / v2;
  • input_schema / output_schema;
  • queue or endpoint;
  • health status, heartbeat time;
  • current load, max concurrency;
  • region / affinity labels.

4.2 How the selection layer narrows 10,000 to a few

  1. Recall: use embeddings or keywords to retrieve top-50 capabilities out of 10,000;
  2. Rule filtering: tenant, permission, region, version, health;
  3. Ranking: semantic similarity, historical success rate, load, latency;
  4. Return top-k: usually 3–10 candidates, passed to A or a routing Agent. Return read_type / max_age / capability_version with each candidate; A writes them into the task as-is, and later steps never re-query the Registry;
  5. Per-domain floor: keep at least N candidates per domain, so top-50 does not all land in 2–3 domains and leave zero after filtering.

The root handle_request task follows the same path: at large scale, use the selection layer to pick the orchestrator Agent; at small scale, an agent_id may be specified directly. When a routing Agent is used, account for it per §4.7.

4.3 Recall failure / ambiguity

  • Empty candidates → do not force a pick; return "no capability available";
  • Several candidates with similar scores → let A ask again, return candidates to the user, or escalate to a human;
  • Never "guess one" and route to the wrong domain.

4.4 Capability versions and governance

  • When order.query v1 and v2 coexist, route by schema compatibility;
  • Incompatible versions → do not dispatch;
  • Roll out new versions gradually by tenant or traffic percentage;
  • To retire a capability, drain its traffic first, then deregister it.

4.5 Health and circuit breaking

  • Registered but unavailable is normal at 10,000 scale;
  • Heartbeat expired → remove from the registry;
  • Consecutive failures → open the circuit and stop dispatching;
  • Recovery → half-open probe.

4.6 Permissions

  • Capability allowlists live on domain edges, not on individual Agents;
  • Validate at task creation: is domain(A) → target capability allowed?
  • This prevents a prompt-injected Agent from emitting arbitrary capabilities and escalating privileges.

4.7 Cost of the selection layer

If the selection layer is a routing Agent, it is itself a model call: it costs latency, tokens, and a task.
If it is only a registry search, it is cheap, but accept that rule-based recall may be inaccurate.

Budget accounting:

  • Routing Agent as a separate task → counts as 1 task + actual tokens;
  • Routing as an in-process function → tokens are charged to the caller Agent's reservation; no extra task.

  • Task Store: the single source of truth for tasks, parent/child links, status, budget, and result references;
  • Registry: capability catalog; read-heavy, must be cached;
