5.1 Push or pull

Stage Mode Why
Capability routing Push Requires instance selection, priority, affinity, gradual rollout
Execution dispatch Pull Natural backpressure; busy workers pull less; easy to scale

At large scale: push for routing, pull for execution. In pull mode, queue messages also need tenant_id / priority so consumers can rate-limit and shard.

The diagram shows pull mode; in push mode the Scheduler CAS-claims to running first, then delivers to the Agent.

6. Task table: the single source of truth

A task record should contain at least:

  • task_id: task identifier;
  • tenant_id: tenant; the unique index must include it, otherwise tenants collide;
  • trace_id: one user request;
  • parent_task_id: parent task;
  • capability + capability_version: required capability and version;
  • input_ref: where the input lives (large inputs in object storage);
  • input_hash: dedup key;
  • status: scheduled / ready / running / waiting / done / failed / cancelled / budget_exhausted / dead_letter;
  • depth: nesting depth;
  • ancestor_keys: array of (capability, input_hash) on the ancestor chain;
  • dedup_key: input_hash for reads, task_id for writes;
  • read_type_snapshot: read-type snapshot taken at task creation;
  • agent_id: who is executing;
  • attempts: attempts so far;
  • max_attempts: maximum attempts;
  • lease_until: lease expiry;
  • lease_epoch / attempt_id: fencing token; prevents stale worker writes;
  • priority: priority;
  • pending_children: number of unfinished children;
  • budget: budget;
  • deadline: deadline;
  • result_ref: where the result lives;
  • cached_result_refs: result references from cache hits that did not create a task row;
  • error: failure reason;
  • queued_at / started_at / finished_at: timestamps;
  • idempotency_key: idempotency key for side effects.

Unique index:

(tenant_id, trace_id, capability, capability_version, dedup_key)
  • Read tasks: dedup_key = input_hash, eligible for dedup;
  • Write tasks: dedup_key = task_id, unique per row; writes are never reused;
  • read_type uses the snapshot taken at task creation, not the Registry's live value.

6.1 Dedup cannot be one-size-fits-all

  • Idempotent read (e.g. order.query): reuse the result;
  • Stateful read (e.g. device.status): may reuse, but only within max_age; re-query after that;
  • Write (refund, shipment): never reuse; every write gets a new task;
  • Add read_type: idempotent | stateful | write and max_age to capability metadata.

7. Task state transitions

State Meaning
scheduled Cold start / waiting for a worker to become ready; not claimable yet
ready Pending; can be claimed by the Scheduler
running In progress, with a lease
waiting Waiting for children
done Completed; result in the Result Store
failed Terminal failure
cancelled User or upstream cancellation
budget_exhausted Budget exhausted; cannot continue
dead_letter Poison task; moved to dead-letter

Transitions:

  • Cold start complete: scheduled → ready;
  • Scheduler claims: ready → running;
  • A emits children: → waiting;
  • All children reach a terminal state (done / failed / cancelled) → waiting back to ready, with a failure summary;
  • Worker completes: → done;
  • Lease expires: running back to ready, attempts+1;
  • attempts reaches the limit: → failed;
  • Budget insufficient: → budget_exhausted;
  • Poison task fails repeatedly: → dead_letter.

"All children done" is wrong; it must be "all children terminal" — failures and cancellations must also wake the parent.

7.1 Fallback reconciler (every 30 seconds)

  • scheduled timeout → back to ready + alert;
  • waiting with pending_children=0 → set ready + alert;
  • ready with queued_at older than the queue threshold and remaining time < the capability's P99 × 1.5 → failed(deadline_unreachable) and alert deadline_unreachable_total.

8. Concurrency correctness (P0)

8.1 Parent counters must be atomic

When T1 and T2 finish at the same time, both workers can read pending_children=1, both decrement to zero, and both set T0 to ready — A is dispatched twice.

The decrement must be bound to the "mark done" CAS:

1. UPDATE tasks
   SET status='done', finished_at=now()
   WHERE task_id=:child AND status='running' AND lease_epoch=:epoch
   RETURNING parent_task_id;

2. If step 1 affected 0 rows: already handled; commit and never decrement.

3. If parent_task_id IS NULL:
   root task; commit and skip steps 4 and 5.

4. UPDATE tasks
   SET pending_children = pending_children - 1
   WHERE task_id=:parent AND pending_children > 0
   RETURNING pending_children;

   If it affects 0 rows: alert parent_decrement_noop_total; never stay silent.

5. If step 4 returns 0:
   UPDATE tasks SET status='ready'
   WHERE task_id=:parent AND status='waiting';

   If it affects 0 rows: record parent_revive_blocked_total and skip.
  • Root tasks have no parent; they must skip the decrement or every root completion will raise a false alert;
  • Only a transaction where step 1 affected 1 row may decrement;
  • The decrement must not require status='waiting', otherwise a re-dispatched parent can hang;
  • Setting ready must require status='waiting', otherwise cancelled/timed-out parents can be revived;
  • Queues are at-least-once; duplicate consumption must be blocked by the CAS;
  • If parent counters are merged/decremented in batches, do not rely on "the caller that reaches zero wakes the parent"; let the §7.1 reconciler decide. For immediate wake-up, use bucketed counters.

8.2 Leases must renew, and carry a fencing token

Expiring lease_until and re-dispatching is not enough:

  • An Agent's model call can take tens of seconds to minutes;
  • Short lease → a healthy worker is declared dead → re-dispatch → two workers run the same task;
  • Long lease → a real crash takes a long time to recover.

Add three things:

  1. Heartbeat renewal: the worker periodically extends lease_until;
  2. lease_epoch / attempt_id: monotonically increasing on every dispatch;
  3. Epoch on writes: the DB accepts only the current epoch; a revived old worker cannot write.

8.3 Write-back order

Must be:

1. Write the Result Store first
2. Then mark the child task done
3. Decrement the parent counter in the same transaction
4. Only when the counter reaches 0, set the parent task ready

Reversing the order (marking done first) → the parent wakes and reads a result that is not yet persisted.

9. Multi-tenant fair scheduling

10,000 Agents do not serve a single tenant. Staying under quota does not mean a tenant cannot saturate the system momentarily.

  • Per-tenant concurrent task limit: how many tasks a tenant may run at once;
  • Weighted fair queue: weight = plan tier, so free tenants cannot crowd out paid tenants;
  • Per-capability concurrency limit: when a capability has many instances, cap total concurrency;
  • Priority aging: low-priority tasks gain priority after waiting past a threshold, avoiding starvation;
  • Quota vs scheduling: quota is a billing limit; scheduling is momentary fairness. Both are required.

A's autonomy is covered in §1: it only decides whether to split, which capability to request, and whether to wait; it does not care who executes.

What they have in common, in plain terms:

  2. Set total turns, total tokens, and total time, and stop at the limit;

Note: not every system "only walks a pre-drawn path". LangGraph / Step Functions use explicit topology; AutoGen can call any registered tool; Anthropic's orchestrator decides at runtime which sub-agents to dispatch.
So "explicit topology" is not true for all six; only "bounded execution" is common.

"At most N times per edge" is not mainstream; most systems use "at most N turns / N tokens in total".

10.1 The 10,000-Agent solution

The problem:

With 10,000 Agents calling each other, A→B→A can loop forever; but B→A is sometimes legitimate; and you cannot write a rule for each of 10,000 Agents.

Main principles:

  • Layering / domain-level topology: split 10,000 Agents into 20 domains of 500 each; write rules only for the 20×20 domain relationships;
  • Task-based inter-Agent calls: B does not call A directly; it emits a task; the Scheduler dispatches it to A; A writes the result; B is woken;
  • Global limits: see §11.2; the tenant plan is a hard cap, and topology defaults must fit inside it;
  • Human fallback: on exhaustion, return a partial result or escalate.

Concretely for 10,000 Agents:

  1. Domains: write only 20×20 domain rules:
    • order domain → device domain: allowed;
    • device domain → order domain: allowed;
    • device domain → order-domain refund: not allowed.
  2. Task-based: while executing T1 (order.query), B discovers it needs another device D2 → writes T3: capability=device.status, input=D2, parent=T1. ancestor_keys contains only (handle_request, h0) and (order.query, h1); the target (device.status, hD2) is absent → allowed. The Scheduler dispatches it to C; C writes the result; T1's counter reaches zero and B is woken.
  3. Global budget: see §11.2; this section's domain rules do not set numbers.
  4. Legitimate re-entry: allowed by domain rules; ancestor_keys blocks only "same capability + same input", with depth ≤ 8 as a backstop. If re-entry is not needed, do not write that domain edge.
  5. Still unresolved at the limit: return a partial result, or escalate to a human.

Two cheap checks that actually prevent cycles:

  • depth: child depth = parent.depth + 1; reject above 8;
  • ancestor_keys: child ancestor_keys = parent.ancestor_keys + (parent.capability, parent.input_hash); if the target (capability, input_hash) is already present → reject. Same capability with a different input is allowed.

Only the ancestor chain is checked, not the whole graph; it is one array-membership test with negligible cost.

input_hash is computed only over normalized business input (excluding timestamps, trace_id, random ordering, temperature, and other volatile fields). Matching has two levels: exact (capability, input_hash) hit → reject; capability-only hit and the domain edge has no allow_reentrant → reject.

Note: this is one implementation of "domain rules + task-based execution + global budget"; the mainstream principles are layering, bounded execution, and human fallback. Concrete rules differ by company.

10.2 Dedup

unique(tenant_id, trace_id, capability, capability_version, dedup_key):

  • Read tasks: dedup_key = input_hash, eligible for dedup;
  • Write tasks: dedup_key = task_id, unique per row; writes are never reused;
  • Idempotent read already done → reuse;
  • Stateful read already done → check max_age; re-query when stale;
  • Write → never reuse;
  • Cache hit → do not create a task row; atomically append the hit result_ref to the parent's cached_result_refs using a DB-side array append (never an application-level read-modify-write); A aggregates by reading child result_ref ∪ cached_result_refs;
  • Currently running → wait; do not execute again;
  • failed → decide whether to retry by policy.

For the diamond A→B→D and A→C→D, D executes only once (when reuse is allowed).

11. How budgets are controlled

11.1 What the five budgets cover

Budget Covers Does not cover
depth Nesting depth; parent +1; reject above 8 Total volume
tasks Total new tasks per trace Retries and re-dispatches
tokens Actual model usage: prompt + completion + reasoning Business database reads/writes
deadline Absolute time; must finish by then Not "30 seconds per call"; it is the whole-request deadline
cost tokens × model unit price Disabled when no price table exists

11.2 Where budgets come from

When root task T0 is created, four layers apply:

  1. No topology declared: depth 8, tasks 2000, 200k tokens, 300 seconds;
  2. Tenant plan: free 48k, paid 640k; this is a hard cap;
  3. Topology default: fan-out 500k tokens (50 × 8k = 400k, leaving 100k headroom), plan 500k; it can only be allocated within the plan quota;
  4. Request override: may only lower the budget; it cannot exceed the plan cap.

Composition rule: final budget = min(plan, topology default, request override); later layers do not simply overwrite earlier ones.

Write into the T0 row:

T0: depth=0, tasks_left=2000, tokens_left=500000, deadline=now+300s, cost_left=...

11.3 How budget is divided among children

When A creates T1 and T2, each child reserves a slice:

T1: depth=1, tasks+1, reserve 8k tokens
T2: depth=1, tasks+1, reserve 8k tokens
T0: tasks_left=1998, tokens_left=474k (T0's own plan 8k and selection 2k already deducted)

Rules:

  • Each child has a per-task cap; it cannot consume the parent's entire budget;
  • Siblings split evenly or by priority, so one branch cannot starve the others;
  • Insufficient reservation → do not create the child; return budget_exhausted;
  • Reservation + deduction must be atomic: Redis Lua or a DB transaction.

11.4 When to deduct, and how many times

Moment Deduct tasks? Deduct tokens?
Create task tasks +1, depth = parent.depth + 1 Reserve
Scheduler dispatch No No (already reserved at creation)
Re-dispatch / retry of the same task (attempt+1) tasks unchanged, depth unchanged Re-reserve (whether or not it executed; full refund if it never ran; unused portion refunded if it ran)
Failure before dispatch (connect failure / startup timeout) tasks unchanged Full refund
Cache hit No No

tasks increases only when a new task is created; retries and re-dispatches only increase attempts.

Each task also needs: max_attempts=3; cumulative cost cap = max_attempts × per-task reservation; stop when exceeded. This prevents a task from failing halfway, refunding most of the reservation, and retrying forever.

11.5 Settlement on completion

Success:

Reserved 8k, actually used 3k → refund 5k
tasks is not refunded (the task was created)

Failure:

Failed after execution: tasks is not refunded; tokens settle at actual usage, unused portion refunded
Failed before dispatch (connect failure): task returns to ready, tasks unchanged; tokens fully refunded

Actual usage > reservation:

  • Enforce max_tokens / output-length limits before the call;
  • Set the reservation from the P99 output length;
  • Do not "reject after exceeding" — the call has already happened; rejection is meaningless;
  • Overdraft up to the request's total budget is allowed, but never beyond it.

11.6 What happens when budget runs out

  • tasks exhausted: stop creating tasks; let running tasks finish;
  • Reserve 10% (or a fixed 8k) at root creation as a wrap-up allowance for plan/reduce, not usable by child tasks;
  • tokens exhausted: stop calling models; return existing results;
  • deadline reached: cancel unstarted tasks; treat running tasks as timed out;
  • cost exhausted: same as tokens;
  • Finally: return partial results + what is missing, or escalate to a human.

11.7 What 10,000 Agents add

  • Tenant quotas: tokens per tenant per day/month;
  • Per-subtree budgets: each domain / branch has its own allowance;
  • Per-Agent concurrency limits: how many tasks an Agent runs at once;
  • Cost budget: multi-model cost computed from a price table;
  • Budget observability: used, remaining, and exhaustion reason per request/tenant.

11.8 A self-consistent example 

T0: depth=0, tasks_left=2000, tokens_left=500k

The following uses the paid plan + fan-out tier of 500k tokens.

T0 reserves 8k for plan:
  tokens_left=492k

Selection layer performs 2 searches (in-process, 1k each):
  tokens_left=490k

Create T1 and T2:
  T1: depth=1, tasks_left=1999, reserve 8k
  T2: depth=1, tasks_left=1998, reserve 8k
  tokens_left=474k

T1 succeeds, actual 3k:
  refund 5k
  tokens_left=479k

T2 fails, actual 1k:
  depth/tasks unchanged
  refund 7k
  tokens_left=486k

T2 retries (same task, attempt+1):
  tasks unchanged
  re-reserve 8k
  tokens_left=478k

T2 retry succeeds, actual 2k:
  refund 6k
  tokens_left=484k

A aggregates, reserves 8k for reduce:
  tokens_left=476k

  tokens_left=479k

  tokens_left=479k - 384k = 95k

11.9 Common mistakes

  • Deducting at task creation and again at dispatch;
  • Charging tasks on retries, so actual calls far exceed the budget;
  • Multiple instances reading stale values and overspending;
  • Reserving at the minimum, so the actual run immediately overshoots;
  • Looking only at tokens, not cost;
  • Not refunding unused budget, starving the parent;
  • Keeping budgets only in memory; a process crash loses everything.

One line: set the total budget at entry, reserve when creating tasks, never deduct again at dispatch, settle at actual usage, and stop when exhausted.

12. Failure, recovery, idempotency

Situation Handling
Worker crashes lease_until expires → task returns to ready, attempts+1, re-dispatched to another worker
Repeated failure attempts reaches the limit → failed → notify the parent with a failure summary
Old worker revives Writes carry lease_epoch; the DB rejects stale epochs, preventing overwrites
Duplicate side effects Side effects keyed by task_id; write results are never reused
Whole process dies Tasks are in the DB; ready tasks continue; running tasks restart from the beginning after lease expiry — they cannot "continue"
Traffic spike Queue smooths bursts; limit concurrency per capability/Agent
Poison task Move to dead-letter; alert / human

Idempotency keys need two phases: prepared / committed, with lease_epoch. A worker first claims prepared, performs the side effect, then marks committed. A new worker can take over an old prepared after a crash. But this is only an accelerator, not a correctness guarantee: write operations must bind a business optimistic lock (WHERE status='paid') or pass task_id downstream as an Idempotency-Key. Otherwise, taking over an "executed but not committed" operation can refund twice.

12.1 Partial success

50 child tasks, 47 succeed (paid plan + fan-out tier):

  • Wait for all: aggregate after every task is terminal;
  • Quorum: continue once a threshold is reached;
  • Fail fast: cancel the rest when a critical child fails;
  • Decide by topology; do not default to "wait for the slowest one".

12.2 Deadline propagation

Child deadline:

min(parent.deadline, now + per-task limit)

Before dispatch, the Scheduler checks whether the remaining time is enough to finish; if not, it does not dispatch — avoiding a 60-second task launched one second before the deadline.

Cold-start time is accounted separately and does not count against the per-task limit; during cold start the task stays in scheduled, and the lease does not start.

13. Cost and boundaries

Item Description
Extra infrastructure DB + queue + Scheduler + Registry + Result Store
Latency One extra queue hop; the bigger cost is the model call to rebuild context when A wakes
Eventual consistency Results are not immediately visible; wait for task state changes
Agent changes Must support suspend/resume, not just synchronous calls
Operations Queue backlog, leases, retries, dead-letter, DB hot rows
Cost Fan-out needs at least plan + reduce model calls; at 10,000 concurrency, token cost far exceeds queue cost

It is not a silver bullet: it trades "call-stack complexity" for "task-graph / queue / state-machine complexity".

13.1 Risks of rebuilding context

If A rebuilds context with an LLM after waking, it may emit T1/T2 again:

  • Dedup keys can block this, but only if input_hash is stable;
  • If the context includes timestamps or the message order changes, the hash changes and dedup fails;
  • Hard rules:
    • Inject the "list of existing child tasks" as deterministic input when waking;
    • Allow only one non-terminal child per (parent_task_id, capability, dedup_key); otherwise vote/debate would be blocked;
    • This rule applies only to read_type ≠ write; write-task re-entry is handled by idempotency keys + business optimistic locks, not by a task-table unique constraint;
    • Before dispatching a parent, reconcile pending_children = COUNT(*) WHERE parent_task_id=:t AND status NOT IN (terminal) and overwrite with the real value.

13.2 Cross-trace cache and capacity

  • Task dedup only covers one request; cross-request reuse goes through the Result Store cache: capability + capability_version + input_hash + TTL;
  • Partition the task table by day/tenant; archive cold done data; set a TTL on the Result Store; set a retention period for dead-letter.

14. Implementation order

  1. Task table + state machine + trace_id / tenant_id;
  2. Queue + Scheduler + leases;
  3. Instrument observability first: trace aggregation, per-hop latency, tokens, failure rate; without this you cannot tell whether the system is healthy;
  4. Registry + selection layer (recall / filtering / top-k / health / versions);
  5. Convert large topologies (fan-out / plan / vote / debate) to task emission first;
  6. Budgets, retries, idempotency, fencing, dead-letter;
  7. Keep the "synchronous call" design for small synchronous consultations; do not force a full rewrite;
  8. Scale workers, scale partitions, load-test.

Minimum metric set: parent_decrement_noop_total (must stay at 0), dedup_hit_total{read_type}, tasks_per_trace distribution, task_lease_expired_total{capability}, budget_exhausted_total{reason}, queue_depth / oldest_ready_age_seconds, cycle_reject_total{reason=depth|ancestor_key}, cached_hit_total, parent_revive_blocked_total.

Let large fan-outs use the task graph while small consultations stay synchronous; the two coexist, not either-or.

title: Why "Thread", "Load" and "Token" Break Translations: Technical Terminology for Developers
description:
Technical terms are the words and phrases that describe how a machine, product, feature or workflow operates. Their meaning is rarely defined by the word alone. It depends on the role the term plays inside a system, and that makes them easy to mistranslate even for skilled translators. Unlike scientific terms, which are judged by conceptual precision, or medical terms, judged by safety and compliance, technical terms are judged by usability: can users install, configure, operate and troubleshoot after reading the translation?

Five places it goes wrong

1. Familiar words with specialized meanings. Port, thread and driver look ordinary. A port may be a USB connection, a network endpoint or an input interface. A bridge can be a network device, a shell can be a command-line interface, and a token can be an authentication credential. Translated by everyday meaning, instructions and UI labels can sound natural and still be wrong.

2. The same term across industries. "Thread" means a sequence of instructions in software, a spiral ridge on a screw in manufacturing and a strand in textiles. "Load" can be cargo in logistics, demand on a circuit in electrical work, or processing demand on a server in software. Applying one meaning everywhere distorts specifications.

3. Product-specific names. Labels such as Smart Sync, Adaptive Queue or Safe Mode Plus may be branded features, background processes or predefined states. Without product context nobody can tell whether the name should be translated, partly localized or kept as is. The issue is missing ownership context, not dictionary meaning.

4. UI space and action. Menus, buttons and notifications need wording users grasp instantly. Apply, Reset, Sync Now and Force Stop each map to a precise system command. If translated too broadly, too long or too formally, users may misread the action or hesitate, and text expansion can hide critical options in small interfaces.

5. New technology outpaces standards. Emerging fields create terms faster than standard translations settle, so teams need to decide and document choices rather than wait.

What to do as a developer 

- Give every string a description: where it appears and what it triggers
- Mark do-not-translate items: code identifiers, placeholders, brand feature names
- Keep a shared termbase with part of speech and a short definition per term
- Show translators the real screen (screenshot or staging link)
- Run automated QA for placeholders, tags and terminology consistency

Domain references such as the ISO Online Browsing Platform and IEEE Xplore can help separate meanings across engineering fields, and QA tools such as ApSIC Xbench can check that variables and tags survive localization.

A short checklist

  1. List ambiguous terms in your product (port, thread, load, token, driver, shell) and write a one-line definition for each.
  2. Decide which product names stay in English.
  3. Review all button and menu labels for length and for the exact action they trigger.
  4. Review with a native speaker who knows the product, not just the language.

For related reading, see four UI bugs that only show up in other scripts and one product, three surfaces. Corrections and war stories are welcome in the comments.

title: Your UI Breaks in German (and Wraps Weirdly in Chinese): Designing for Text Expansion
description:
Your English UI fits perfectly. The button says "Download", the card title sits on one line, and the sidebar looks tidy.

Then someone switches the language.

German turns "Download" into "Herunterladen". A short settings label becomes a full sentence. Chinese may take less horizontal space, but it breaks lines by different rules — and if your font falls back mid-sentence, the whole paragraph suddenly changes height.

This is not a translation problem. It is a layout and font problem, and you can test for it before your users find it.

Why translated text changes size

A useful rule of thumb: expect many European languages to expand English strings by roughly 30–40%, especially for short UI labels. Short strings expand the most, because there is no room to abbreviate.

Three things change at once:

  1. Length — words get longer, or a compact English phrase needs several words in another language.
  2. Line breaking — Chinese and Japanese do not break lines at spaces the way English does, and some words in German or Finnish resist breaking at all.
  3. Font metrics — if a character is missing from your first font, the browser quietly substitutes another font for just that character. The substitute may be taller, wider, or heavier, so one line grows while its neighbours do not.

That third point is the one developers miss. The layout did not break because the translation was long. It broke because two fonts with different metrics ended up sharing one line.

Rule 1: Never give UI text a fixed height

Fixed heights are where expansion goes to die.

/* Fragile */
.button { height: 36px; overflow: hidden; }

/* Resilient */
.button {
  min-height: 36px;
  padding-block: 0.5rem;
  white-space: normal;
}

Let buttons, tabs, chips, and table headers grow vertically. A two-line button in German looks far better than a one-line button with the end of the word cut off.

The same applies to cards: design for the tallest plausible content, not the English content you happen to have today.

Rule 2: Test with pseudo-localization, not hope

You do not need finished translations to find expansion bugs. Pseudo-localization stretches your existing strings and wraps them in markers, so long text and missing characters show up immediately.

A simple version in JavaScript:

const pseudo = (str) =>
  `[${str.replace(/[aeiou]/gi, (c) => c + c)} ${"·".repeat(Math.ceil(str.length / 3))}]`;

console.log(pseudo("Download report"));
// [Doownlooaad reepoort ·····]

Run your app in this mode and click through the main flows. Anywhere text is clipped, overlaps, or pushes an icon off-screen is a bug you just found for free — before paying for a single translated word.

Rule 3: Check your font stack per language, not per page

A font stack that works for English may silently fail for another script. Before shipping a language, test three strings in your actual UI font:

  • A long, unbreakable word (German compound nouns are a good stress test)
  • A mixed string: Latin brand names inside a Chinese or Japanese sentence
  • Punctuation and numbers in the target language, not copied from English

Preview candidate fonts side by side with your own test strings — a font comparison tool makes this quick — and look specifically at line height and character width, not just whether the font "looks nice". If the fallback font is noticeably taller, your paragraphs will ripple every time the script changes.

Also set lang attributes correctly. Browsers use them to pick line-breaking rules and font fallbacks:

<p lang="de">Die Datei wurde heruntergeladen.</p>
<p lang="zh-CN">文件已下载完成。</p>

Without lang, the browser guesses — and it guesses using your page's default language, not the string's.

Rule 4: Let text wrap the way the language wants

Two CSS properties prevent most of the ugly cases:

.label {
  overflow-wrap: anywhere; /* last resort for unbreakable strings */
}

.prose:lang(zh), .prose:lang(ja) {
  line-break: strict;
  word-break: normal;
}

Use overflow-wrap: anywhere sparingly — on labels, URLs, and table cells — not on body copy, where it can split words in places readers find jarring.

And never justify CJK body text the way you justify English. Justification stretches the spaces between characters, and in a script without word spaces it produces uneven, gappy lines that are harder to read.

A 10-minute pre-launch checklist

Before adding any new language, run through this list:

  • [ ] Pseudo-localize the top 5 screens and fix every clipped label
  • [ ] Remove fixed heights from buttons, tabs, and nav items
  • [ ] Confirm your font actually covers every script you ship — no silent fallbacks mid-sentence
  • [ ] Set lang on every translated block, including mixed-language pages
  • [ ] Test one long German string, one Chinese paragraph, and one mixed-script sentence at mobile width
  • [ ] Check numbers, dates, and punctuation in the target language's own format

The takeaway

Internationalization bugs rarely look like internationalization bugs. They look like a button that wraps, a card that overflows, or a paragraph where one line is mysteriously taller than the rest.

Design for expansion, test with pseudo-localization, and treat your font stack as part of the layout system — not decoration added at the end. Your German and Chinese users will never notice. That is exactly the point.

Have a favourite pseudo-localization horror story — a label that overflowed in exactly the wrong place? I'd love to hear it in the comments.

title: What does a cloud GPU cost? The bill behind the hourly rate
description:
Cloud GPU pricing pages all show you the same thing: a number per hour. That number is real, but it is not the bill. I pulled the list prices on 2026-11-22 and worked out what a job actually costs once storage, idle time and setup are on the meter. The gap between the headline rate and the effective rate is large enough to change which card you should rent.

The short version

List prices that day ran from $0.27 per GPU-hour for a 24 GB RTX A5000 to $4.39 for an 80 GB H100. A 200 GB model library adds $20 a month of storage whether you use it or not, idle hours are billed like working hours, and setup time runs on the same meter.

For a 20-hour job, that $20 of storage turns a $0.27 rate into $1.27 per productive hour. For a 300-hour job, the same $20 is barely visible. Short jobs are where the fixed costs bite.

The five lines on the bill

  1. Compute. The hourly rate times the hours the machine is on. This is the number on the pricing page.
  2. Storage. Model weights, datasets and checkpoints that have to survive between sessions. RunPod lists network storage at $0.10/GB/month while running and $0.20/GB/month while idle, so 200 GB is $20/month running.
  3. Idle time. The meter runs while the GPU waits for you. A pod left on overnight costs exactly what a working pod costs.
  4. Egress and downloads. Moving weights or results between the provider and your machine. Some plans include a transfer allowance; marketplace hosts set their own terms.
  5. Setup and retries. Driver installs, custom nodes, a host that disappears mid-run. All of it consumes billed hours.

What the headline rate looked like

GPU and VRAM Managed Marketplace median
RTX A5000 (24 GB) $0.27/hr RunPod $0.23/hr Vast.ai
RTX 4000 Ada (20 GB) $0.76/hr DigitalOcean not listed
RTX 4090 (24 GB) $0.89/hr RunPod $0.47/hr Vast.ai
L40S (48 GB) $1.09/hr RunPod $0.68/hr Vast.ai
A100 (80 GB) $2.19/hr RunPod $0.84/hr Vast.ai
H100 (80 GB) $4.39/hr RunPod $1.73/hr Vast.ai

US list prices per GPU-hour, captured 2026-11-22, before tax. Storage and egress are extra except where the platform bundles them.

Fixed costs hurt short jobs

Storage is charged by the month, not by the hour. If you rent a 200 GB volume for a 20-hour job, the volume still costs $20. Divide that by 20 productive hours and the effective storage rate is $1/hour — nearly four times the A5000's compute rate.

The same arithmetic at three durations:

Job Compute + storage Effective rate
20 h SDXL on A5000 at $0.27/hr $5.40 + $20 = $25.40 $1.27/hr
100 h 70B INT4 on A100 at $2.19/hr $219 + $20 = $239 $2.39/hr
300 h fine-tune on H100 at $4.39/hr $1,317 + $20 = $1,337 $4.46/hr

Idle time, egress and retries are excluded here. The point is the shape: the longer the job, the smaller the fixed-cost distortion, and the closer the headline rate is to the truth.

Idle time is billed like work

An A100 left running for a day costs $52.56, whether it is training or waiting for a prompt. Ten idle hours cost $21.90. The cheapest way to waste money on a cloud GPU is to leave the pod up while you read documentation, eat dinner or sleep.

Setup runs on the same meter. A fresh marketplace host may need drivers, CUDA, ComfyUI custom nodes and a model download; two hours of setup on an A100 is $4.38. That sounds small, but it is 2% of a 100-hour job and 10% of a 20-hour job. A managed image that boots in five minutes can be worth more than a lower hourly rate.

A 100-hour A100 job, line by line

Put the lines together for a realistic small project: 100 compute hours on one A100 80 GB, 10 idle hours, 200 GB of storage for one month, and two setup hours.

Line Cost
Compute (100 h × $2.19) $219.00
Idle (10 h) $21.90
Storage (200 GB, one month) $20.00
Setup (2 h) $4.38
Total $265.28

Compute is 82.5% of the bill, but the other three lines are 17.5% — and they are the ones that vary most between providers. A marketplace host at $0.84/hr would cut compute to $84; if storage or egress is priced differently there, the total can move the other way. That is why the effective rate, not the headline, is the number to compare.

The egress question

Egress is the line most likely to be missing from a quote. DigitalOcean includes 15,000 GiB of transfer with its GPU droplets; Lambda bundles a large local SSD with its H100 and A100 instances. Marketplace hosts set their own storage and network terms. Moving a 140 GB model out of a provider is a one-off; pulling a fresh checkpoint every day is not. Ask for the egress price before you design a workflow that moves data.

Marketplace vs managed

Marketplace pricing changes the compute line, not the fixed lines. A 100-hour A100 job at the $0.84 median is $84 of compute instead of $219; add the same $20 of storage, roughly $22 of idle time and a little more setup, and the total lands around $130 — about half the managed bill.

The catch is that storage and egress terms are set by the host, and an interrupted run can consume hours you cannot recover. The marketplace wins on cost when the job is checkpointed and the deadline is soft; the managed platform wins when setup time or a missed deadline costs more than the difference.

How to cut the bill

  • Shut the pod down. The single largest saving for intermittent work. A stopped pod costs storage, not compute.
  • Right-size the card. A 24 GB A5000 at $0.27/hr runs SDXL and quantised FLUX. An 80 GB A100 at $2.19/hr does not make those jobs faster in proportion to the price.
  • Keep one volume. A persistent volume costs $20/month for 200 GB. Re-downloading the same models every session costs billed minutes; at 1 Gb/s a 20 GB model takes about 3 minutes, at 100 Mb/s about 27 minutes.
  • Quantise before you upgrade. A 4-bit model can move a job from a 48 GB card to a 24 GB card, and the price difference is usually larger than the quality difference.
  • Use the marketplace with checkpoints. A $0.47/hr RTX 4090 is half the managed rate, but only if an interrupted run can resume instead of restarting.

Common questions

Is the cheapest hourly rate always the cheapest job? No. A $0.27/hr card with a $20 volume for a 20-hour job costs $1.27 per productive hour; a $0.89/hr card with the same volume costs $1.89. Compare the effective rate.

How much does storage add? $0.10/GB/month while running and $0.20/GB/month while idle on RunPod, so 200 GB is $20/month running or $40/month idle. Other providers bundle disks or price storage differently.

Do I pay for idle time? Yes, on hourly rentals. The meter runs while the pod exists, not while it computes. Shut it down when the queue is empty and keep a persistent volume for the models.

What does a 100-hour A100 job cost? $219 of compute plus $21.90 of idle time, $20 of storage and $4.38 of setup — about $265. The headline figure is $219.

How this was built

Prices are on-demand list prices captured 2026-11-22 in USD before tax, from RunPod, Vast.ai, DigitalOcean and Lambda. Storage figures use RunPod's published running rate; idle and setup hours are illustrative and labelled as such. No throughput benchmark was run, and the effective-rate arithmetic is shown next to each figure so you can recompute it with your own numbers.

title: Part 34: The approval experience compared: what the human actually sees
description:
Part 34 · One Agent, Five Platforms

The human gate is only as good as the screen the approver sees. Part 6 put a person in front of every ERP posting and every supplier message, and the approval_id check in the process API makes that rule hard to get around. But if the approval screen shows "Approve adjustment? Yes / No" and nothing else, people will click yes without reading.

This part compares what the approver actually sees on each of the five builds. It's based on the builds in Parts 11 to 25 and vendor documentation I read on 22 November 2026. The screens in the image are mock-ups I drew, not screenshots, because no build has been run yet.

1. What an approver needs

Four things, on one screen:

  • The proposal: exactly what will change. For example, invoice 4471 from supplier 2093: accept the price variance and post an adjustment of the stated amount.
  • The evidence: the PO line, goods receipt, supplier history and price agreement the agent used, with links to the source documents.
  • The risk: the amount, how it compares to the tolerance, and anything unusual, such as a first-time supplier or a note in the invoice text that looks like an instruction (Part 10, GS30).
  • One decision: approve or reject, with a reason required on reject. The decision is tied to this exact proposal, so a changed proposal needs a new approval.

What it shouldn't contain is a chat window. The approver is deciding on a proposal, not talking to the agent.

2. The approval screen on each build

  • SAP: the ERP inbox. The approval is the supplier invoice's flexible workflow (Part 18). According to SAP Learning, approvers "display and process your tasks using the My Inbox app". They can approve, reject, claim, suspend or forward, and see the approval history. The invoice is right there, so the evidence is native. The agent's proposal and reasoning need to be added to the task.
  • Azure: a Teams card. A Logic Apps workflow posts an adaptive card and waits (Part 22). Power Automate's adaptive card overview says the card appears "in that recipient's chat and activity feeds", and the flow doesn't continue until the approver responds. A card holds a summary well, but the full evidence has to be a link out.
  • AWS: a page you build. Step Functions waits on a task token (Part 25). The approval page is yours to design: the approver signs in, sees the proposal and decides, and a small Lambda function records who decided. Full control, and full responsibility.
  • MuleSoft: your existing inbox. The Agent Fabric overview describes no approval step for agent networks, as Part 11 found. The approval goes to whatever workflow or inbox the finance team already uses, through a Mule flow.
  • Boomi: your existing inbox, too. Agentstudio's Requires Approval setting makes the agent ask before calling a tool, but that asks the person in the chat, not the finance approver (Part 15). The real approval goes to the existing inbox, as on MuleSoft.

So there are two native screens (SAP's inbox and a Teams card), one screen you build (AWS), and two builds where the screen is whatever you already have.

3. Time to decision

Approvals take hours, sometimes days, so the agent never waits in the conversation. On every build, request_approval returns "pending" straight away, and the workflow waits separately:

  • Step Functions can wait on a task token until the one-year service quota, and a heartbeat timeout stops it waiting forever.
  • Teams: the card's flow waits for a response. The Microsoft pages I read don't give a time limit for that wait, so I'd set one in the workflow.
  • SAP: the flexible workflow page I read doesn't cover deadlines or escalations.

The rule: every approval has a deadline, set in the workflow. When it passes, the case goes to a named fallback approver or back to the queue. It's never approved by default.

4. Audit trail of the decision

The approval_id from Part 6 must record who decided, when, what they saw and what they decided:

  • SAP: the task log and workflow log, viewable in My Outbox, in the same system that posts the invoice.
  • Azure: the card's response comes back to the Logic Apps workflow, which writes the approval_id with the responder's identity (Part 22).
  • AWS: you write the decision record yourself. The official approval tutorial doesn't, as Part 25 noted.
  • MuleSoft and Boomi: whatever the existing workflow records, plus the approval_id stored by the process API.

The weak point everywhere is "what they saw". Store a copy of the proposal and evidence summary with the decision, not just "approved".

5. Mobile approvals

Approvers are often away from their desks, and a slow approval costs an early-payment discount. None of the vendor pages I read today covered mobile approval, so I can't say from documentation how each screen works on a phone. Check this in a hands-on build. A screen that needs a wide table of PO lines may not work on a phone, whatever the platform.

6. What I'd standardise

Whatever the platform, the approval screen should have:

  1. A one-line summary of the proposal, in plain language.
  2. The amount, the tolerance and how far over it is.
  3. The evidence, as links to the source documents.
  4. Any risk flags, at the top.
  5. Approve and reject, with a reason required on reject.
  6. A deadline, and who it goes to next.
  7. A decision record: who, when, what was shown and what was decided.

The platform decides where the screen lives. This list decides whether the approval means anything.

What does your approver need to see before saying yes?

This series describes a reference build on a fictional company. This part is based on the documentation-only builds in Parts 11 to 25 and vendor documentation read on 22 November 2026. The approval screens are mock-ups, not screenshots; no hands-on build has been run yet. Views are my own.

title: My Bash network tool was lying to me, so I rewrote it in Rust
description:
For years I had a Bash script called netRo.sh. It was a 733-line interactive dashboard I used to check servers: CPU, memory, network, a few "security" checks. It felt useful until the day I actually read it carefully.

I sat down and wrote an audit of my own script, line by line, and it hurt. A function called update_system_info() did nothing but sleep 2 to look busy. The rootkit check always printed "skipped", forever. The unauthorized-users check flagged every account with UID under 1000, which on Linux is every system account, so it cried wolf on a clean machine. My "suspicious process" detector grepped for nmap, wireshark and tcpdump, which is to say it accused every network engineer of being a hacker. And the worst one: a "block device" feature ran iptables and then wrote the rules permanently to disk, with sudo, with no confirmation and no rollback.

No tests. No CI. No machine-readable output. Linux only. I had trusted this thing.

So I kept the idea and deleted the code. netRo 5.0 is a full rewrite in Rust, and this post is about the one rule that shaped every decision in it.

The rule: no fake data

Every result netRo prints comes from a real check. Anything a platform cannot do is reported as UNSUPPORTED, DEPENDENCY_MISSING or PERMISSION_DENIED, with a hint. This sounds obvious until you look at how many tools quietly guess. My old script guessed constantly.

The rule has teeth because of the error model. Every failure returns a structured error with a stable code (PERMISSION_DENIED, TIMEOUT, UNAUTHORIZED_SCAN, and so on), a message, and a hint, mapped to specific exit codes. A missing tool degrades one check instead of killing the whole run, which is what set -e did to the old script every time a dependency was missing.

Architecture that enforces the rule

The code is layered: a clap CLI and a ratatui TUI both sit on top of a commands layer, which calls a portable core, which talks to the OS only through provider traits.

SystemProvider, NetworkProvider, ProcessProvider, SecurityProvider, FirewallControl: adding a platform means implementing those traits, nothing in core/ changes. Linux providers parse /proc and /sys and drive ufw, firewalld, nftables and iptables. Windows providers call PowerShell and CIM. macOS uses netstat, lsof, scutil, socketfilterfw and system_profiler. I can verify the layering with one grep: there is not a single OS command string in src/core/.

The TUI is a second presentation layer over the same engine. It contains zero diagnostics of its own and never builds a command line. If the CLI and the TUI ever disagreed, that would be a bug in exactly one place.

The no-shell policy

There is no sh -c, bash -c or cmd /c anywhere in the codebase. Every external program runs with an explicit argument vector, resolved to an absolute path first so a poisoned PATH cannot swap in a different binary during a privileged call.

Windows was the interesting one. The PowerShell bridge passes fixed scripts through -EncodedCommand (UTF-16LE base64). User input is never concatenated into script text; the only user data that crosses the boundary is validated IP literals for firewall rules. Targets are validated for length, characters and a leading dash even though no shell ever re-parses them, because defense in depth is cheap.

Things that were harder than they look

DNS. I wanted real queries without depending on nslookup, so netRo has a built-in DNS client: UDP with TCP fallback, A/AAAA/CNAME/MX/TXT/NS/SOA/PTR/SRV records, RTT measurement, custom servers, reverse lookups. Parsing DNS is a rite of passage: compression pointers, loops, bounds checks. The tests include NXDOMAIN handling and pointer-loop attacks.

TLS. Port scanning is a TCP connect scan (SYN scanning is explicitly not implemented and the docs say so), but on open ports netRo grabs the service banner and probes TLS certificates with rustls to tell you what is actually listening and when its certificate expires. The TLS dependency is feature-gated so you can cross-compile without a C toolchain for the target.

Privileges. netRo never runs sudo on its own. Firewall changes check elevation first and fail with PERMISSION_DENIED plus the exact hint for your platform. There is a --dry-run that prints the exact commands and rollback without root, and applying a change requires confirmation or --yes, shows every command, and records rollback state so unblock only removes rules netRo itself created. My old script's silent iptables-save is the reason this exists.

The doctor command. One command runs every check and produces a score. The score is transparent: every deduction is listed by category with evidence, impact and a recommendation, and informational findings never lower it. A score you cannot explain is just a number that makes people anxious.

Numbers

On Linux x86_64 with the release build: startup is about 12 ms. A 10,000-port localhost scan with 512 workers takes about 370 ms. The full doctor run is about 4.7 s at 22 MB RSS. Steady-state monitoring costs about 16 ms per sample. The binary is a single static executable (thin LTO, stripped), and CI builds and tests it on Ubuntu, Windows, macOS Intel and Apple Silicon. There are 239 tests, including end-to-end CLI contract tests and snapshot-rendered TUI tests that inject hostile ANSI payloads into remote-derived strings to prove they cannot reach your terminal.

What I would tell past me

Writing the audit document was the most valuable hour of the whole project. Reading your own old code as if you were an auditor, and writing down every finding with a disposition, turns "my script is probably fine" into a concrete list you can fix one by one. The audit of the old script is still in the repo (docs/AUDIT.md), next to the engineering audit of the rewrite, because I want the receipts public.

netRo is MIT licensed: https://github.com/ALSRKAL/netRo. Linux is the primary, fully tested platform; Windows and macOS pass compile and CI runtime tests but I would genuinely love bug reports from real machines there. If you try the doctor command on something weird, I want to hear about it.

title: ISC Stormcast For Monday, November 23rd, 2026 https://isc.sans.edu/podcastdetail/10190, (Mon, Nov 23rd)
Owning the Path from Key Press to Screen
description:
Handpic is a culling app for RAW files: you page through what you shot, give stars, reject the rest, and the judgments go into metadata files saved next to the RAW files (XMP or DxO PhotoLab format). It reads only the JPEG previews embedded in the RAW files, never develops anything, and never writes to the RAW files themselves.

It started in September 2026 as a Tauri 2 app (Rust backend, TypeScript UI in WebView2). In November I rewrote the whole UI in GPUI, Zed's GPU-rendered UI framework, and deleted the Tauri app.

Developing apps make you wait every time you move to the next photo. Handpic exists partly to avoid that, so one number matters more than anything else in it: the time from pressing → to the next photo on screen.

In Tauri, getting the JPEG into the WebView, decoding it and drawing it all happened on the WebView's side, out of my reach. Moving to GPUI made the whole path from key press to screen my own code, so I could decode only what is needed, drop the copy, and draw ahead of background work. In exchange, things I never had to think about, like uploading textures to the GPU, became mine to handle too. This post goes through them one by one.

Result

Time from the key press to the photo on screen, median of three runs, in ms:

Tauri GPUI GPUI faster by
ARW 1616x1080, p50 45.20 33.63 11.57 (−26%)
ARW 1616x1080, p95 69.08 41.46 27.62 (−40%)
RAF 4416x2944, p50 130.40 61.28 69.12 (−53%)
RAF 4416x2944, p95 145.94 73.09 72.85 (−50%)

The sizes are those of the JPEG preview embedded in each RAW file. At 59 Hz, the gain is about 0.7 of a frame on ARW and about 4.1 frames on RAF.

How I measured

An app's own clock can't tell when a photo is actually on screen, so I built an external ruler, latprobe. It presses → with SendInput and records the time, then watches the screen through DXGI Desktop Duplication until a 64x64 patch in the center changes and settles. The end point is the LastPresentTime of that frame: when DWM presented it. Keyboard latency and the panel's scanout are not included, and the results move in steps of the 59 Hz display's frame, about 16.9 ms.

Absolute numbers shift by several milliseconds depending on when they are measured, so the two apps were measured back to back, alternating: per folder, one warm-up run each, then three runs of 60 presses about a second apart, with prefetching off in both and a 1600x1000 window. Runs during which CPU load went over 15% or a compiler started were thrown away and redone. The machine: Windows 11, i7-13700, RTX 4060 Ti, 32 GB, a 5120x1440 display at 59 Hz, photos on a SATA SSD, WebView2 157.

Where the time goes

Splitting each press at the moment the image finished drawing (p50 / p95, ms):

Key → drawn Drawn → screen
ARW Tauri 17.90 / 26.30 26.73 / 42.88
ARW GPUI 8.03 / 9.83 25.93 / 31.80
RAF Tauri 89.50 / 105.30 37.06 / 46.88
RAF GPUI 35.74 / 44.55 25.35 / 32.45

For Tauri, "drawn" is when the canvas drawImage call returns. With an image as large as the RAF preview, drawImage only records the draw; the actual rasterization (about 22.5 ms) runs inside the next canvas operation, so it falls on the "drawn → screen" side. For GPUI it is derived from the app's stamps (the stamp after Present, minus the vsync wait and Present itself). Each column is a median of its own, so the columns don't add up exactly to the totals above.

Nearly all of the gain is before drawing. The next three sections are what made that part shorter; the last one is about the part after drawing.

1. Decode only the pixels the screen shows

On RAF, decoding and drawing the JPEG took the most time. In Tauri, decoding with createImageBitmap took 55.2 ms at p50, and drawing onto the canvas took about another 22.5 ms. In GPUI the same RAF decode takes about 34 ms and the paint 0.71 ms: about 78 ms became about 35 ms.

GPUI decodes with mozjpeg on a background thread. The change of decoder alone did not get there: RAF decode was 47.3 ms, and on ARW it was actually slower (6.0 ms in Tauri, 9.2 ms in GPUI at p50). The rest came from fixing a problem the first on-screen measurement exposed.

GPUI, on the first paint of a new image, uploads the whole decoded texture to the GPU. A 4416x2944 preview is 52 MB. With about a second between page turns, the GPU had dropped to a low power state and PCIe to Gen1 x8, so the upload took about 33 ms and missed two DWM compositions. Present doesn't block, so the app's own clock never saw it: the frame reached the screen 14 ms after the app's stamp on ARW, whose 7 MB texture uploads in about 5 ms, and 48 ms after it on RAF.

The fix was to stop decoding pixels nobody sees. The fit view now decodes the preview at the smallest of mozjpeg's n/8 scales that still covers the canvas in device pixels: 3/8 for RAF in a 1600x1000 window, 1656x1104, about 7 MB. Layout and overlays use the source size instead of the texture's, and the 1:1 view still reads the full image. Measured before and after, back to back, on screen (p50 / p95, ms):

Before After
ARW 1616x1080 36.63 / 49.92 37.44 / 47.56
RAF 4416x2944 112.60 / 137.87 64.94 / 76.26

ARW didn't change beyond noise. On RAF, decode went from 49 to 34 ms and paint from 3.55 to 0.71 ms at p50; the remaining ~32 ms is the upload no longer stalling.

One more thing to check here: mozjpeg-sys quietly falls back to non-SIMD when NASM is missing. RAF decode went from 46 ms to 99 ms with no visible warning, so the build script now fails instead.

2. Stop copying the image across a process boundary

In the Tauri app, a page turn went like this:

  1. read — Rust reads the embedded JPEG from the RAW file
  2. ipc — the JPEG bytes are sent across the Tauri IPC into the WebView
  3. post / worker — handed to a Web Worker
  4. decode — createImageBitmap
  5. draw — drawn onto a <canvas>

Steps 2 and 3 only move bytes, yet at p50 they took 4.4 ms on a 1616x1080 ARW and 29.4 ms on a 4416x2944 RAF preview, a JPEG of 1.3–5.5 MiB. Of the RAF's 29.4 ms, 28.0 ms was the IPC copy itself. No amount of tuning inside Tauri removes that: the bytes have to get into the WebView somehow.

In GPUI there is one process. A background thread decodes the JPEG, and the decoded image goes to the UI thread as an Arc: 0.02 ms on ARW, 0.42 ms on RAF.

3. Put the page turn ahead of background work

Handpic does heavy background work while you page: a first scan pass that fills thumbnails and the index, and a second pass that runs face detection, focus and eye-sharpness models on every file.

In the Tauri app, page turns on RAF got slower while the second pass ran: from 135.33 to 153.80 ms at p50 and from 153.50 to 178.35 ms at p95, on screen. ARW barely changed. The app paused the scan's reads while a preview was being read, but the decode and the draw ran inside WebView2's own processes, and drawImage returning is not the moment the frame reaches the screen. So the pause could not cover the second half of the page turn.

In GPUI the whole path from read to paint is my code in one process, so I can order it explicitly:

  • One preview request in flight at a time, so holding → never queues stale decodes. A result for a file that is no longer current is still drawn, then the current file is requested and the files in between are skipped.
  • The preview pauses the scan before the read and releases it only after its image has been painted. While the pause is held, the second-pass workers yield at every stage boundary, so the read, the decode, the orientation and the paint get the cores.
  • The second pass runs on an eighth of the cores.

Page-turn time on screen, measured back to back (p50 / p95, ms). This was a different run from the result table, so even the values without pass 2 differ slightly.

Without pass 2 During pass 2
ARW Tauri 52.50 / 76.20 48.81 / 71.77
ARW GPUI 37.81 / 46.60 33.09 / 40.93
RAF Tauri 135.33 / 153.50 153.80 / 178.35
RAF GPUI 65.82 / 80.18 64.09 / 84.29

In GPUI, the p50 does not get slower while the second pass runs, on either ARW or RAF.

What's left: one frame after drawing

The part after drawing still takes 25.93 ms on ARW and 25.35 ms on RAF in GPUI. GPUI on Windows draws only when its vsync thread, waiting on DwmFlush, invalidates the window, so a frame that is ready waits for the next tick (7.5–10 ms at p50). It then presents just after that tick, so DWM composites it at the following one, about 15 ms later.

I tried forcing an immediate redraw from the app with a direct Win32 call. On screen, the p50 went from 33.51 to 25.10 ms on ARW and from 60.99 to 56.14 ms on RAF, but only 34–47% of presses gained a frame, and it relied on GPUI internals outside its public API. I reverted it. The right fix belongs in GPUI itself, and I haven't proposed it there yet.

Handpic is open source; see the repository for building it from source.

title: Don't Fix Accessibility After the Fact: Constraints to Put in Your First AI Website Prompt
description:
Disclosure: I am on the team behind VibUI, a paid prompt library for websites. You will see one mention of it in the last tool section. The accessibility rules here do not depend on it.

Short answer: if you want an AI-built page to pass a basic accessibility check, put the accessibility rules in the first prompt, not in a cleanup message after the layout is finished. Name the contrast target, heading order, form-label behaviour, keyboard focus, image alt rules, landmarks and a prefers-reduced-motion fallback up front. Then run a keyboard pass and an automated scan (Lighthouse or axe) before you call the page done. This applies the same way in v0, Lovable, Bolt, Cursor, Windsurf, Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Replit, GitHub Copilot, Framer AI, Google Stitch, Readdy, Aura.build and OpenAI Codex.

Why does a second "make it accessible" prompt usually fail?

Most models will happily add alt attributes and a focus ring if you ask later. They will also leave in place the decisions that caused the failures:

  • Heading levels that skip from h1 to h4 because the visual scale looked "right".
  • Buttons that are only <div>s with a click handler.
  • Form fields with placeholder text and no <label>.
  • Text on a coloured photograph that drops below a 4.5:1 contrast ratio.
  • Carousels and background motion with no pause control and no reduced-motion path.
  • Colour as the only way to show a required field or an error.

A cleanup prompt rarely rewrites the document structure. It patches symptoms. If the first prompt already forbids those patterns, the first draft is much closer to usable.

What accessibility rules should go in the first prompt?

Paste a block like this into every new-page request. Adjust the contrast figure if your legal or design team has a stricter target.

Accessibility constraints (do not skip):
- One h1 on the page. Headings follow a logical order (h2 then h3). Do not skip levels for visual size.
- Colour contrast: body text and buttons at least 4.5:1 against their background; large headings at least 3:1. Check both the default theme and any dark variant.
- Every form control has a visible <label> bound with for/id. Do not use placeholder as the only label. Errors are text, not colour alone, and are linked to the field with aria-describedby.
- All interactive elements are real buttons or links, reachable by keyboard, with a visible focus state that is not outline: none unless a clearer replacement is provided.
- Images: informative images have specific alt text from [ALT] placeholders I provide. Decorative images use alt="". Do not invent descriptions of people or places.
- Landmarks: a <header>, <main> and <footer>, plus a "Skip to main content" link as the first focusable element.
- Target size: interactive elements at least 24px by 24px, with adequate spacing.
- Motion: respect prefers-reduced-motion and provide a static fallback. No autoplaying video with sound. If a carousel exists, it does not auto-advance, and previous/next controls are keyboard accessible.
- Language: set lang on the html element. Link text describes the destination; no "click here".

The [ALT] placeholders matter. If you let the model write alt text, it will invent a scene that may not match the photo you later drop in.

What does a first prompt look like with those rules included?

Here is a compact example for a product marketing page. Swap the product details; keep the constraints.

Build a single landing page as semantic HTML and CSS (no framework unless I ask).
Product: [NAME], a [ONE-LINE JOB] for [AUDIENCE].
Primary action: [BUTTON LABEL] linking to [URL].
Visual system: off-white background #F6F4EF, ink #1A1A1A, accent #1F4E8C, 16px body / 1.6 line-height, 8px radius, system sans-serif. No dark mode in this version.
Sections in order: header with skip link and primary button; hero with [HEADLINE] and an image placeholder [ALT: ...]; three feature rows; a short pricing outline with [PLAN NAMES AND PRICES]; FAQ; footer with contact.
Copy I have not supplied must appear as [PLACEHOLDER]. Never invent customers, logos, statistics or reviews.
Include the accessibility constraints listed above.
Do not use emoji, gradient text, icon-only navigation, or a cookie pop-up.

If you are in Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot or OpenAI Codex, also name the file (app/pricing/page.tsx or pricing.html) and add "Do not edit other files." Narrow scope keeps the accessibility rules from being "forgotten" mid-edit.

Which failures should I check, and how do I prompt a fix?

Work through this table after the first draft. One failure per follow-up message.

Failure How you notice it Follow-up prompt
Skipped heading levels Outline in DevTools or an axe scan "Fix heading levels only. Keep the visual size. Do not change copy."
Contrast too low Lighthouse contrast items, or a contrast picker "Raise contrast of [element] to at least 4.5:1 against [background]. Do not change layout."
Divs used as buttons Keyboard tab skips them, or no Enter/Space handler "Replace clickable divs with button or a elements. Keep the existing styles."
Missing labels Screen reader says "edit text" with no name "Add a visible label for each input, tied with for/id. Keep placeholders as examples only."
Focus outline removed Tab through the page; you lose the caret "Restore a 2px focus ring on all interactive elements, using the accent colour at 3:1 or better."
Motion with no off switch Enable reduced motion in the OS and reload "Wrap animation in a @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) block and show a static state otherwise."
Autoplaying video The tab makes sound, or the CPU spins "Do not autoplay with sound. Poster frame first; playback is user-started and has a visible pause control."

Automated tools catch a lot. They will not catch a misleading heading, a vague link ("learn more" repeated six times), or alt text that does not match the image. Those need a human pass.

Does the same prompt work in hosted builders and in coding agents?

Yes, with a small difference in where the result lands.

  • v0, Lovable, Bolt, Replit, Framer AI, Google Stitch, Readdy, Aura.build: paste the full prompt into the first generation. After you have a preview, use the table above for follow-ups. Export or download the code so you can run Lighthouse against a real URL, not only the editor preview.
  • ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini: ask for "one HTML file with CSS included" so you can save it, open it locally, and tab through it. Preview inside the chat is not a keyboard test.
  • Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex: put the accessibility block in your rules file (.cursor/rules, CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md or .github/copilot-instructions.md) so later section-by-section edits inherit it. Still say "include the accessibility constraints" in the request, because rules files are easy to ignore when the task is large.

None of these tools is "the accessible one." The prompt and the review are what change the outcome.

How do I run a 10-minute review before shipping?

  1. Keyboard only. Unplug the idea of a mouse. Can you reach every action, see focus at all times, and operate menus and dialogs with Escape, Enter and arrows?
  2. Zoom to 200%. Text should still wrap. Nothing important should clip or overlap.
  3. Lighthouse or axe, on a deployed preview, not just localhost if your fonts load differently in production.
  4. One screen-reader sample, even a short VoiceOver or NVDA pass on the hero, the form and the footer. Listen for the skip link, the h1, and whether the primary button is announced with its label.
  5. Real content. Replace [PLACEHOLDER] and [ALT] before this review. Empty boxes hide contrast and labelling problems.

If a fix would change the brand colours, take it to the design tokens, not to a one-off override on a single button. Otherwise the next generated section will bring the old contrast back.

Where can I get section prompts that already include these constraints?

You can keep the block above in a snippet file and paste it yourself, which is what I do for one-off pages. If you generate a lot of pages and want starting points for common sections (forms, pricing, FAQs, headers) that you can adapt, that is what VibUI is for: 2,852 website prompt templates (775 full pages, 1,100 sections, 817 components and 160 animated backgrounds), and roughly 1,000 of those entries ship with source code. You pay once, and the plan does not renew by itself: $48 quarterly, $99 yearly, or $179 for lifetime access. Sixty samples are visible without paying, and a free login can copy 2 prompts, which is enough to judge the style. The accessibility review above is still required; a library does not replace a keyboard pass.

FAQ

Is WCAG 2.2 AA a realistic target for an AI-generated marketing page?
For a simple marketing or docs page, yes, if the constraints are in the first prompt and you review the result. Complex widgets (date pickers, custom selects, live filters) still need extra care and often a specialist review.

Should I ask the model to "make it WCAG compliant"?
That phrase is too vague. Models will claim compliance without checking contrast or keyboard behaviour. Spell out the rules, then measure.

Do I need a dark theme for accessibility?
No. You need sufficient contrast in the theme you actually ship. If you do offer dark mode, test both. A light theme that passes can fail when inverted carelessly.

What about cookie banners and chat widgets?
Third-party widgets are a common source of focus traps and unlabelled buttons. If you must add one, test it with the keyboard after it loads. Prefer a simple link to a policy page over a blocking pop-up on first paint.

Will this slow the build down?
The first prompt is a few extra lines. The keyboard and Lighthouse pass is about ten minutes. Reworking a finished visual design to fix structure usually takes longer.
