title: Your AI Studio Doesn't Need More Models. It Needs Fewer Decisions
description:
A lot of developers can assemble an AI demo in a weekend. The uncomfortable part comes later, when the demo has to behave like a product.

Suddenly the model is only one piece of the puzzle. People need to understand what the site is for, find the right tool without decoding model names, sign in without getting lost, trust the price they see, and get help when something goes wrong. A homepage full of impressive capabilities does not solve any of that. In fact, it often makes the experience worse.

That is the real gap in today’s AI product market. The supply of models is enormous, but the supply of calm, understandable user experiences is still surprisingly small.

The hard part is not adding tools

When builders first get access to image, video, music, and chat services, the natural instinct is to expose everything. It feels like more tools should make the product more valuable.

Users rarely see it that way. They see a wall of unfamiliar names and wonder where to begin.

A better studio starts with a sentence, not a catalog. Maybe it helps ecommerce teams make product photos. Maybe it helps independent creators turn a written idea into a short video. Maybe it gives a marketing team one place to draft copy and generate campaign visuals.

Once that sentence is clear, choosing features becomes much easier. A creator-focused workspace might need writing, images, and short video. It probably does not need every music model, developer utility, and experimental endpoint on day one.

This is less exciting than adding another model, but it is far more useful. A product becomes easier to understand when every visible feature supports the same job.

Brand the journey, not just the header

Swapping a logo is not the same as creating a branded product.

Branding shows up in the small moments: the browser icon, button colors, tool names, support contact, login screen, mobile navigation, and the domain in the address bar. If half of those pieces still look generic, users notice the seams even if they cannot explain what feels wrong.

Tool names deserve special attention. Internal model names are useful to engineers, but customers usually think in outcomes. “Product Image Maker” is clearer than a provider and version string. “Short Video Creator” is easier to scan than the name of a video model someone has never used.

Renaming the display entry does not change the underlying service, of course. It simply translates the implementation into language that matches the user’s task. That small layer of translation is one of the most important things a focused AI studio can provide.

The same rule applies to homepage copy. A long list of model names may be technically accurate, but it does not tell a visitor whether the product is meant for them. A short description of the audience and the result is usually stronger.

Login is part of the product experience

Authentication often gets treated as infrastructure that is either working or broken. From a user’s perspective, there are many shades in between.

A login flow can technically succeed while still feeling suspicious. It may send the visitor to an unexpected domain, return them to the wrong page, or make it unclear whether they are signed in. These problems are especially easy to miss when the person testing the site already has an active session.

The simplest test is also the most revealing: open a private browser window and behave like a new customer. Start on the public homepage, choose a tool, sign in, and check where you land. Then sign out and repeat the process on a phone.

Temporary redirects during authentication are not automatically a problem. What matters is whether the journey makes sense and returns the user to the right studio with the correct account state.

This is why login should be configured early, not left for the final hour before launch. If authentication changes the route, domain, or navigation behavior, you want to discover that while the rest of the product is still easy to adjust.

Pricing should feel predictable

AI services often have different cost structures, which makes pricing tempting to overengineer. The result can be a patchwork of arbitrary markups that is difficult for both the operator and the customer to understand.

A calmer approach is to begin with one site-wide pricing rule and introduce exceptions only when there is a real reason. Some services may have higher support costs or a different market price, but those should be deliberate overrides rather than the default way of working.

There is also an important distinction between a zero markup and a free service. A zero markup means the customer sees the underlying platform price without an added margin. It does not erase the usage cost.

Before opening the studio to users, check pricing from the customer side. Look at one service that follows the general rule and another with a custom rule. Follow both far enough to see the final amount. Admin settings can look correct while the storefront tells a different story.

For paid generation, a small real task is more valuable than a dozen screenshots. It proves that the displayed price, account balance, generation flow, and returned result all work together.

A custom domain belongs near the end

It is tempting to connect a polished domain as soon as the site exists. Waiting is usually safer.

First make sure the platform-provided address works. Verify the homepage, internal routes, login, tool access, and pricing there. Once that foundation is stable, the custom domain becomes a presentation layer rather than another variable in every bug investigation.

Most custom-domain setups come down to a CNAME record, but DNS is only half the story. Resolution can be correct while the HTTPS certificate is still being issued. A dashboard status is helpful, yet the final test is opening the site with https:// in a real browser and seeing no certificate warning.

Do not delete an existing DNS record just because it conflicts with the new studio hostname. It may belong to a live service. When the current use is unclear, choosing an unused subdomain is much safer than experimenting with production DNS.

Launch from the outside in

The admin dashboard is a bad place to decide whether a product is ready. It shows saved settings, not the experience those settings create.

The useful launch review happens outside the dashboard. Visit the site while logged out. Try it on desktop and mobile. Refresh an internal page directly. Complete a login. Open the support contact. Check a normal price and an overridden price. Run one inexpensive generation. Open the custom domain over HTTPS.

Mobile testing matters more than many teams expect. A site name that looks elegant on a desktop header may wrap awkwardly on a phone. A tool grid can become hard to scan. A support link may disappear below navigation. These are not cosmetic details when mobile is how a large share of users first encounters the product.

There is no need to launch with a banner, a huge catalog, or elaborate promotional copy. Empty space is better than a banner that leads nowhere. A small set of tools that work is better than a broad menu of unavailable options.

A good AI studio does not win by making the underlying technology look complicated. It wins by hiding complexity at the right moments. The model choice, routing, pricing rules, and domain configuration can remain sophisticated behind the scenes. The user should simply understand what they can make, what it will cost, and what happens after they click.

That is the difference between an AI demo and an AI product: not more capabilities, but fewer unanswered questions.

Reference

Build Your Own AI Studio from Scratch

title: Como instalar o Tencent LoopForge no Linux e executar fluxos de agentes
description:
O Tencent LoopForge organiza fluxos de agentes de programação em etapas de script, agente e aprovação humana. Cada execução pode pausar para que alguém aprove o resultado, acrescente contexto ou devolva o trabalho. A ferramenta é distribuída sob licença MIT e pode ser iniciada com um script que configura a plataforma e o MySQL em contêineres Docker. Este guia descreve a instalação da versão 0.4.0 no Ubuntu 26.04 e a configuração do serviço com HTTPS.

Prepare o servidor e instale o LoopForge

Use um servidor Linux de 64 bits com Git e sudo, e reserve pelo menos 15 GB livres para as imagens. A imagem do LoopForge ocupa 4,3 GB e a do MySQL, 1,1 GB. Para configurar HTTPS, a máquina também precisa de um domínio apontado para o servidor e das portas 80 e 443 liberadas. Mantenha a porta 8090 fechada para conexões da internet.

O LoopForge inicia dois contêineres, um para a plataforma e outro para o MySQL, e cria mais um para cada execução. O guia recomenda dimensionar a máquina conforme o trabalho dos agentes: quatro vCPUs e 8 GB de memória são uma base para agentes que usam modelos hospedados; um modelo local exige mais recursos.

O guia consulta a API do GitHub para obter a versão estável mais recente, de modo que a instalação use uma release em vez do conteúdo variável da ramificação principal. No teste descrito, a API retornou v0.4.0; o comando imprime a tag selecionada antes de usá-la:

LOOPFORGE_VERSION=$(curl -s https://api.github.com/repos/Tencent/LoopForge/releases/latest | grep -m1 '\"tag_name\"' | cut -d'\"' -f4)
echo "$LOOPFORGE_VERSION"git clone --branch "$LOOPFORGE_VERSION" https://github.com/Tencent/LoopForge.git ~/LoopForge
cd ~/LoopForge
time ./start.sh

Em uma máquina nova, o script instala Docker se necessário, cria segredos únicos para o banco de dados e as sessões, baixa as imagens e carrega o catálogo inicial. No ambiente usado pelo guia, a instalação levou 2 minutos e 8 segundos até exibir os endereços de acesso.

Antes de usar a instalação com seus repositórios, confira se o digest da imagem baixada corresponde ao publicado na página da release. Esse passo verifica se a imagem recebida coincide com a referência esperada para a versão instalada:

sudo docker image inspect ghcr.io/tencent/loopforge:0.4.0 --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}'

O teste feito durante a publicação retornou o digest abaixo. Compare esse identificador ao valor informado na página da release correspondente antes de conceder ao serviço acesso aos seus repositórios, como recomenda o guia de instalação:

ghcr.io/tencent/loopforge@sha256:87b6a3e3cba201d03f8f8d22929881f576021fc78c7c42e82f78329abbf4bda4

Crie a conta sem expor a porta

Por padrão, o serviço escuta em todas as interfaces e o instalador orienta a abrir a porta 8090. O cadastro também começa aberto, permitindo que a primeira pessoa a acessar o serviço crie a conta de administrador. Antes de restringir essas configurações, acesse a interface por um túnel SSH, sem publicar a porta. Execute o comando no computador local e substitua o endereço pelos dados do servidor:

ssh -L 8090:127.0.0.1:8090 [email protected]

Com o túnel ativo, abra http://localhost:8090 no navegador e crie a conta inicial, que terá privilégios administrativos. Use uma senha longa: embora o formulário aceite senhas de seis caracteres, a conta pode iniciar contêineres no servidor e, por isso, merece uma credencial forte.

Restrinja o acesso e configure HTTPS

No arquivo .env, desative o cadastro, limite o serviço ao endereço local e ative cookies seguros. O comando abaixo remove valores anteriores dessas configurações, grava os novos e reinicia a plataforma. Segundo o guia, essa reinicialização recria o contêiner da plataforma e preserva os dados existentes.

cd ~/LoopForge
for k in AGENTFLOW_ALLOW_SIGNUP LOOPFORGE_BIND AGENTFLOW_SECURE_COOKIES; do sed -i "/^$k=/d" .env; done
printf "%s\n" AGENTFLOW_ALLOW_SIGNUP=false LOOPFORGE_BIND=127.0.0.1 AGENTFLOW_SECURE_COOKIES=true >> .env
./start.sh

Configure o Nginx como proxy reverso para 127.0.0.1:8090. O LoopForge transmite os registros das execuções ao vivo e usa WebSockets; por isso, o proxy precisa dos cabeçalhos de atualização de conexão, de envio sem armazenamento intermediário e de um tempo de leitura longo. No arquivo, substitua o domínio de exemplo pelo domínio apontado para o servidor.

map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade {
default upgrade;
'' close;
}
server {
listen 80;
server_name loopforge.example.com;
client_max_body_size 50m;
location / {
proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8090;
proxy_http_version 1.1;
proxy_set_header Host $host;
proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;
proxy_buffering off;
proxy_read_timeout 3600s;
}
}

Instale o Nginx e o Certbot, salve a configuração do site em /etc/nginx/sites-available/loopforge e habilite-a em sites-enabled. Os comandos também removem o site padrão, testam a sintaxe do Nginx e recarregam o serviço para aplicar as mudanças:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y nginx certbot python3-certbot-nginx
sudo vim /etc/nginx/sites-available/loopforge
sudo ln -sf /etc/nginx/sites-available/loopforge /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/loopforge
sudo rm -f /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/default
sudo nginx -t
sudo systemctl reload nginx

Antes de solicitar o certificado, substitua loopforge.example.com pelo domínio real apontado para o servidor e [email protected] por um endereço de e-mail válido. O Let's Encrypt recusa endereços de exemplo do domínio example.com, então esses valores não podem ser copiados sem edição:

sudo certbot --nginx -d loopforge.example.com -m [email protected] --agree-tos --non-interactive --redirect

Depois, verifique se o cadastro foi fechado, se uma tentativa de registro é recusada e se o HTTP redireciona para HTTPS. No teste do guia, o cadastro retornou HTTP 403, o acesso por HTTP redirecionou para HTTPS e o serviço escutou apenas em 127.0.0.1:8090, como esperado após o ajuste.

Considere os riscos do Docker

O contêiner da plataforma é executado como root e recebe acesso ao socket do Docker do servidor. Esse acesso equivale, na prática, a controle root da máquina: quem controlar o LoopForge pode controlar o host, e quem executar fluxos pode rodar código em contêineres nesse mesmo servidor.

Por isso, a recomendação é dedicar uma máquina virtual ao LoopForge, sem outros serviços ou segredos. O instalador não adiciona o usuário ao grupo Docker; mantenha o uso de sudo nos comandos do Docker, pois participar desse grupo também concede privilégios equivalentes a root na máquina.

Teste as etapas de aprovação

O catálogo inicial inclui um fluxo demonstrativo que não exige chave de API: um script produz um relatório, uma etapa de aprovação humana pausa a execução e uma última etapa a conclui. A pessoa revisora pode aprovar, pedir uma nova tentativa com contexto ou devolver o resultado para retrabalho.

As tentativas ficam registradas como versões imutáveis no histórico da execução. Esse registro permite consultar qual versão de um artefato foi aprovada e qual decisão foi tomada, oferecendo uma trilha de auditoria para acompanhar mudanças nos fluxos de agentes ao longo do tempo.

O guia completo, com a sequência de instalação e os testes realizados, está disponível em ComputingForGeeks. O código do projeto e as versões publicadas podem ser consultados no repositório Tencent/LoopForge.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/instalar-tencent-loopforge-linux-agentes/

title: Aborting Mid-Token: Streaming Chat with the Vercel AI SDK and React 19
description:
Aborting Mid-Token: Streaming Chat with the Vercel AI SDK and React 19

At 3:12 a.m. the page is not a model outage. A tab never released its SSE reader after a relay blip, so Chrome sits pegged while a half-rendered assistant message freezes the thread. Quota cuts look the same from the client: the socket dies mid-token, optimistic bubbles stay wrong, and the next send stacks another fetch. I have been integrating CopilotKit/OpenBot behind an OpenAI-compatible gateway, and this is the failure mode generic streaming snippets skip.

The UI stays client-side React 19. @ai-sdk/react parses tokens; a thin fetch wrapper owns transport so the component never blocks on I/O. On the wire, https://b-lost.com/v1 is an unbuffered SSE proxy in front of self-hosted OpenBot-style agents. No extra buffer means timeouts fail fast and AbortSignal still reaches the browser.

Cancellation that actually stops the reader

streamText streams tokens, but the underlying fetch only stops if you pass an AbortSignal. Without it, a dropped link or a Stop click leaves the reader draining into state updates.

import { useState, useRef, useCallback } from 'react';
import { streamText } from '@ai-sdk/react';

interface Message {
  id: string;
  role: 'user' | 'assistant';
  content: string;
}

export function useStreamingChat() {
  const [messages, setMessages] = useState<Message[]>([]);
  const abortControllers = useRef<Map<string, AbortController>>(new Map());
  const [isStreaming, setIsStreaming] = useState(false);
  const [error, setError] = useState<Error | null>(null);

  const sendMessage = useCallback(async (content: string) => {
    const id = crypto.randomUUID();
    const abortController = new AbortController();
    abortControllers.current.set(id, abortController);

    // Optimistic UI update
    const optimisticId = `optimistic-${id}`;
    setMessages(prev => [
      ...prev,
      { id: optimisticId, role: 'user', content },
      { id: `temp-${id}`, role: 'assistant', content: '' }
    ]);
    setIsStreaming(true);
    setError(null);

    try {
      const result = await streamText({
        model: 'gpt-4o-mini', // or any compatible endpoint
        prompt: content,
        abortSignal: abortController.signal,
        experimental_telemetry: {
          isEnabled: true,
          functionId: 'chat-message'
        },
        headers: {
          'x-self-hosted': 'true' // route through OpenBot-compatible backend
        }
      });

      let assistantContent = '';
      for await (const chunk of result.textStream) {
        assistantContent += chunk;
        setMessages(prev =>
          prev.map(msg =>
            msg.id === `temp-${id}`
              ? { ...msg, content: assistantContent }
              : msg
          )
        );
      }

      // Replace optimistic with final message
      setMessages(prev =>
        prev.filter(msg => !msg.id.startsWith('temp-')).concat({
          id,
          role: 'assistant',
          content: assistantContent
        })
      );
    } catch (err) {
      if ((err as Error).name === 'AbortError') {
        console.warn('Stream aborted by user');
      } else {
        setError(err as Error);
        // Graceful degradation: show connection status toast
        setMessages(prev => [
          ...prev.filter(msg => !msg.id.startsWith('temp-')),
          {
            id: `error-${id}`,
            role: 'assistant',
            content: 'Connection dropped. Retry or check network.'
          }
        ]);
      }
    } finally {
      abortControllers.current.delete(id);
      setIsStreaming(false);
    }
  }, []);

  const abortCurrentStream = useCallback(() => {
    const controller = abortControllers.current.get('current');
    if (controller) {
      controller.abort();
      abortControllers.current.delete('current');
    }
  }, []);

  return {
    messages,
    sendMessage,
    abortCurrentStream,
    isStreaming,
    error
  };
}

Three boundaries matter. Optimistic inserts (user row plus an empty assistant row) keep the transcript from flashing blank while the first token is in flight. The signal aborts on Stop. The catch path treats AbortError as user intent and every other failure as transport: drop the temp row and surface a short recovery line instead of a blank hole. Non-abort failures belong on a retry queue with exponential backoff capped at three attempts. Partial text already painted should stay visible so the user is not staring at a wiped turn.

Pointing the SDK at an unbuffered relay

I do not maintain CopilotKit/OpenBot. I integrate it. Self-hosted OpenBot exposes an OpenAI-compatible surface; under concurrency, direct sockets are where mid-token cuts show up. The relay is the path that reproduces that behavior without adding a buffer of its own.

const config = {
  baseURL: 'https://b-lost.com/v1',
  headers: {
    'Authorization': `Bearer ${process.env.MODEL_API_KEY}`,
    'Content-Type': 'application/json'
  },
  fetch: (url, options) => {
    const controller = new AbortController();
    options.signal = controller.signal;
    return fetch(url, { ...options, signal: controller.signal });
  }
};

Override baseURL to an internal OpenBot endpoint on the same network, and keep https://b-lost.com/v1 when you need the production cut. The custom fetch above replaces options.signal with a controller nothing else can abort. That races the SDK signal and makes the hook's map theater. Forward the caller's signal. Key aborts by the same id you stored, not "current", and abort every map entry on unmount or you leak readers when the user navigates away.

The trade-off that stays ugly

Abort checks cost a few milliseconds. Against a high-latency relay they beat a 100ms poll: the main thread stops melting on 2000-token bursts, and Chrome traces show a large drop in perceived freeze versus letting the reader run out. That part is settled.

The hard part is optimistic state after tokens have already painted. Filtering temp- rows on error throws away text the user read. Keeping it means ids, the retry, and the final server message can disagree if a retry lands out of order. I would rather mark a partial assistant turn incomplete than wipe it and pretend the turn never happened. That fights both the SDK habit of replacing the row with a final message and the product desire for a clean transcript.

When you abort mid-token on a relay in front of OpenBot, do you keep the partial assistant text as the source of truth, or discard it and let the retry rewrite history?

title: Handling Uncaught Exceptions with Nested Error Boundaries in Next.js
description:
Uncaught exceptions are unexpected errors that indicate bugs or issues that should not occur during the normal flow of your application. These should be handled by throwing errors, which will then be caught by error boundaries.

Nested error boundaries
Next.js uses error boundaries to handle uncaught exceptions. Error boundaries catch errors in their child components and display a fallback UI instead of the component tree that crashed.

Create an error boundary by adding an error.js file inside a route segment and exporting a React component:

app/dashboard/error.tsx

'use client' // Error boundaries must be Client Components
import { useEffect } from 'react'
export default function ErrorPage({
  error,
  retry,
}: {
  error: unknown
  retry: () => void
}) {
  useEffect(() => {
    // Log the error to an error reporting service
    console.error(error)
  }, [error])
  return (
    <div>
      <h2>Something went wrong!</h2>
      <button
        onClick={
          // Attempt to recover by re-fetching and re-rendering the segment
          () => retry()
        }
      >
        Try again
      </button>
    </div>
  )
}

Errors will bubble up to the nearest parent error boundary. This allows for granular error handling by placing error.tsx files at different levels in the route hierarchy.

For component-level error recovery, the catchError function lets you create error boundaries that can wrap any part of your component tree:

app/custom-error-boundary.tsx

'use client'

import { catchError, type ErrorInfo } from 'next/error'

function ErrorFallback(props: { title: string }, { error, retry }: ErrorInfo) {
  const message = error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error)

  return (
    <div>
      <h2>{props.title}</h2>
      <p>{message}</p>
      <button onClick={() => retry()}>Try again</button>
    </div>
  )
}

export default catchError(ErrorFallback)

Then use the returned component as a wrapper in any layout or page:

app/some-component.tsx

'use client'

import { catchError, type ErrorInfo } from 'next/error'

function ErrorFallback(props: { title: string }, { error, retry }: ErrorInfo) {
  const message = error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error)

  return (
    <div>
      <h2>{props.title}</h2>
      <p>{message}</p>
      <button onClick={() => retry()}>Try again</button>
    </div>
  )
}

export default catchError(ErrorFallback)

Error boundaries don't catch errors inside event handlers. They're designed to catch errors during rendering to show a fallback UI instead of crashing the whole app.

In general, errors in event handlers or async code aren’t handled by error boundaries because they run after rendering.

To handle these cases, catch the error manually and store it using useState or useReducer, then update the UI to inform the user.

'use client'
import { useState } from 'react'
export function Button() {
  const [error, setError] = useState(null)
  const handleClick = () => {
    try {
      // do some work that might fail
      throw new Error('Exception')
    } catch (reason) {
      setError(reason)
    }
  }
  if (error) {
    /* render fallback UI */
  }
  return (
    <button type="button" onClick={handleClick}>
      Click me
    </button>
  )
}

Note that unhandled errors inside startTransition from useTransition, will bubble up to the nearest error boundary.

'use client'
import { useTransition } from 'react'
export function Button() {
  const [pending, startTransition] = useTransition()
  const handleClick = () =>
    startTransition(() => {
      throw new Error('Exception')
    })
  return (
    <button type="button" onClick={handleClick}>
      Click me
    </button>
  )
}

title: Configure the Kubernetes Gateway API in EKS Auto Mode
description:
Configure Kubernetes Gateway API in EKS Auto Mode

EKS Auto Mode simplifies cluster management by automatically handling node provisioning, scaling, and networking. This guide walks you through configuring the Kubernetes Gateway API (a Kubernetes API for defining traffic routing, TLS termination, etc.) on an EKS Auto Mode cluster. We’ll use the Envoy Gateway controller as the implementation.

Prerequisites

  1. AWS Account with appropriate permissions (IAM user/role with AdministratorAccess or equivalent).
  2. AWS CLI configured (aws configure).
  3. **eksctl` installed (v0.160.0+).
  4. **kubectl` installed.
  5. **Helm` installed (v3.12.0+).
  6. Basic knowledge of Kubernetes and AWS networking.

Step 1: Create an EKS Auto Mode Cluster

Use eksctl to create a cluster in Auto Mode. This automatically sets up managed node groups, VPC, and control plane.

`bash

Create a cluster in us-east-1 with Auto Mode enabled

eksctl create cluster \
--name=eks-autogw-cluster \
--region=us-east-1 \
--auto-mode-enabled \
--kubernetes-version=1.28 \
--nodegroup-name=auto-ng \
--node-type=t3.medium \
--nodes=2 \
--nodes-min=1 \
--nodes-max=3 \
--managed
`

Notes:

  • --auto-mode-enabled: Enables EKS Auto Mode (automatically manages nodes and scaling).
  • --kubernetes-version: Use v1.28+ (Gateway API requires v1.25+; v1.28 is recommended).

Wait ~10–15 minutes for the cluster to initialize.

Step 2: Update kubeconfig

Ensure kubectl connects to your new cluster:

bash
aws eks update-kubeconfig --name eks-autogw-cluster --region us-east-1
kubectl config use-context arn:aws:eks:us-east-1:<ACCOUNT_ID>:cluster/eks-autogw-cluster

Verify the cluster:
bash
kubectl cluster-info

Step 3: Install Gateway API CRDs

The Gateway API defines custom resources (e.g., Gateway, HTTPRoute). Install the CRDs first:

`bash

Apply official Gateway API CRDs (stable v1.0.0)

kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/releases/download/v1.0.0/gateway-api-crds.yaml
`

Verify CRDs:
`bash
kubectl get crd | grep gateway

Expected output: gateways.gateway.net, httproutes.gateway.net, etc.

`

Step 4: Install the Envoy Gateway Controller

We’ll use Envoy Gateway (a popular, community-maintained controller). Use Helm for installation.

4.1 Add Envoy Gateway Helm Repository

bash
helm repo add envoy-gateway https://envoy-gateway.github.io/gateway-api
helm repo update

4.2 Install Envoy Gateway

bash
helm install envoy-gateway envoy-gateway/gateway-api \
--namespace=gateway-system \
--create-namespace \
--set args="{--leader-election-namespace=gateway-system}"

Key Settings:

  • --namespace=gateway-system: Deploys resources in a dedicated namespace.
  • --set args="{--leader-election-namespace=gateway-system}": Enables high availability.

Wait for pods to be Ready:
`bash
kubectl get pods -n gateway-system

EXPECT: envoy-gateway-system envoy-gateway 1/1 Running

`

Step 5: Verify Gateway API Functionality

Deploy a simple Gateway and HTTPRoute to test end-to-end traffic routing.

5.1 Deploy a Sample Application

`bash

Deploy a test service (echo server)

kubectl create namespace test-app
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/main/examples/standard/httpbin.yaml -n test-app
`

5.2 Define a Gateway

`yaml

gateway.yaml

apiVersion: gateway.net/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
name: example-gateway
namespace: test-app
spec:
gatewayClassName: envoy-gateway
addresses:
- type: LoadBalancer
value: "example-gateway-lb"
listeners:
- hostname: "*"
port: 80
protocol: HTTP
`

Apply it:
bash
kubectl apply -f gateway.yaml -n test-app

5.3 Define an HTTPRoute

`yaml

httproute.yaml

apiVersion: gateway.net/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
name: httpbin-route
namespace: test-app
spec:
parentRefs:
- name: example-gateway
hostnames:
- ")*
rules:
- backendRefs:
- name: httpbin
port: 80
matches:
- path:
type: PathPrefix
value: "/get"
`

Apply it:
bash
kubectl apply -f httproute.yaml -n test-app

5.4 Retrieve the LoadBalancer DNS

`bash
kubectl get gateway example-gateway -n test-app -o yaml | grep 'addresses'

Output will include a DNS name like: example-gateway-lb-.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com

`

Test the endpoint:
`bash
LB_DNS=$(kubectl get gateway example-gateway -n test-app -o jsonpath='{.status.addresses[0].value}')
curl http://$LB_DNS/get

Expected: JSON response from httpbin showing a GET request

`

Step 6: (Optional) Configure TLS & Advanced Routing

Extend the configuration with:

  • TLS Certificates: Use Certificate resources (e.g., via AWS Certificate Manager).
  • Middlewares: Add authentication, rate limiting, or headers using HTTPRoute filters.
  • Multi-Cluster Meshes: Use GatewayClass to connect to other clusters.

Key EKS Auto Mode Considerations

  1. IAM Permissions:

    • Ensure the Node IAM Role has AmazonEKSWorkerNodePolicy, AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryReadOnly, and AmazonEKS_CNI_Policy.
    • The Envoy Gateway controller needs permissions to manage NLBs/ALBs. Attach the AmazonEKSLoadBalancerControllerPolicy managed policy to the IAM role used by Envoy Gateway (or use IRSA).

  2. Load Balancer Type:

    • By default, Gateway API in EKS creates Network Load Balancers (NLB). To use Application Load Balancers (ALB), deploy the AWS Load Balancer Controller and configure Gateway with serviceType: LoadBalancer and annotations.

  3. Auto Scaling:

    • EKS Auto Mode automatically scales nodes. Ensure your Gateway controller replicas are set appropriately (e.g., replicas: 2 in Envoy Gateway Helm values for HA).

Troubleshooting Tips

  • Check Controller Logs: bash kubectl logs -n gateway-system deployment/envoy-gateway -f
  • Gateway Status: bash kubectl describe gateway example-gateway -n test-app
  • HTTPRoute Status: bash kubectl describe httproute httpbin-route -n test-app
  • IAM Issues: Verify the IAM role has permissions for elasticloadbalancing:CreateLoadBalancer, ec2:Describe*, etc.

Clean Up

Delete resources to avoid costs:

`bash

Delete cluster

eksctl delete cluster --name=eks-autogw-cluster --region=us-east-1

Delete CRDs (optional)

kubectl delete -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/releases/download/v1.0.0/gateway-api-crds.yaml
`

Conclusion

You’ve successfully configured the Kubernetes Gateway API on an EKS Auto Mode cluster using Envoy Gateway. This setup provides advanced traffic management, TLS termination, and observability. Extend it further with GRPC routes, UDP routing, or policy enforcement based on your needs.

Reference: Configure Kubernetes Gateway API in EKS Auto Mode

title: A Defender for Cloud readiness checklist: what to test before you call it done
description:
My Defender for Cloud readiness notes, turned into a checklist and checked against Microsoft Learn (November 2026).
The one-page overview covered plans, roles and the first setup (Defender for Cloud in one page). This post is the part after that: the day someone asks "is it ready?" and you have to prove it.

My readiness checklist from a while ago had nine topics. When I checked it against Learn this month, two items were retired, one had changed numbers, and one feature now has two different scores with the same name. So this is the updated version, with the things I actually test.

Everything was rebuilt in my lab (rg-lab-mdc, contoso.com). Screens are redrawn, names are made up.

TL;DR

  • Know which secure score you're looking at. The Azure portal and the Defender portal now show two different models.
  • Exempt a resource with a reason and an end date. Don't just turn a recommendation off for everyone.
  • Prove alerting end to end: create sample alerts and check that they reach email, export and your SIEM. Then add suppression rules for real noise.

Table of contents

  • 1. Secure score: which one?
  • 2. Remediate, exempt or disable
  • 3. Prove that alerts arrive
  • 4. Suppress the noise, not the signal
  • 5. Email notifications: who, what, how often
  • 6. Servers: vulnerability scanning and JIT
  • 7. Items to delete from your old checklist
  • Gotchas
  • Readiness checklist
  • Sources

1. Secure score: which one?

Learn now describes two secure score models, and they don't give the same number:

Classic secure score Cloud Secure Score (risk-based)
Where Azure portal, Defender for Cloud Defender portal, Exposure Management
Based on Microsoft cloud security benchmark (MCSB) controls, points per healthy resource Risk level of open recommendations, plus asset risk factors and criticality
Good for Tracking a subscription against MCSB Deciding what to fix first

If your manager reads one portal and you read the other, you'll have a confusing meeting. Agree on one before the readiness review.

How the classic score moves, in short:

  • Each control has a max score (for example Enable MFA is 10, Secure management ports is 8). Points are split per resource. You only get the full control score when every resource passes every recommendation in the control.
  • Controls are recalculated about every eight hours. Recommendations update more often, so the numbers on the two pages can disagree for a while. Don't panic after a fix. Wait.
  • Preview recommendations don't count. Fix them anyway. They'll count later.
  • Since June 30, 2026, more than 200 AWS and GCP recommendations count too. If you have multicloud connectors and your score dropped, that's probably why.

Source: Cloud Secure Score in Microsoft Defender for Cloud

2. Remediate, exempt or disable

For every red recommendation you have three honest answers:

  1. Fix it. Many recommendations have a Fix button for several resources at once. Enforce and Deny stop new resources from making the same mistake.
  2. Exempt it. The risk is handled somewhere else, or accepted on purpose.
  3. Disable it. The recommendation doesn't apply to this whole subscription.

Exempt is the one I test most, because people get it wrong:

Category What happens to the score
Resolved through third-party service (mitigated) Resources count as healthy. The score goes up
Risk accepted (waiver) Resources are left out of the calculation. They don't count either way

What Learn says you need, and what tripped me up:

  • MCSB must be assigned on the subscription. Without it, the Exempt button can be missing.
  • Owner or Security Admin on the scope, plus permission to write Azure Policy exemptions. Rights at subscription level don't count at management group level.
  • It can take up to 24 hours to show. Exempted resources move to the Not applicable tab, and an exempted recommendation is hidden by the default filter. That's why it seems to "disappear".
  • Custom recommendations can't be exempted. Some preview recommendations can't either.
  • Create exemptions in the portal, not by calling the Azure Policy API yourself. The portal creates the exemption in every initiative that contains the recommendation. The API only does one.

My rule for the readiness review: every exemption has a reason, an owner in the description, and an expiration date. An exemption with no end date becomes the new normal.

Source: Exempt resources from recommendations

3. Prove that alerts arrive

Turning on a Defender plan doesn't prove anyone will see an alert. Test the whole path:

  1. Defender for Cloud > Security alerts > Sample alerts.
  2. Pick the subscription and the plans you enabled (Servers, Storage, Key Vault...).
  3. Create sample alerts. You need Subscription Contributor for this.

After a few minutes, the samples show up in the alert list and everywhere else alerts go: email, workflow automation, continuous export, your SIEM. That's the real test. If the sample alert is in the portal but not in Sentinel, your export or connector is broken. Better to find out now. The samples are for simulated resources, so nothing real is touched.

For a test on a real machine, Learn gives commands per resource type. The easiest one is on a Linux VM with Defender for Endpoint and real-time protection on: download the harmless EICAR test file with curl (the exact command is on the Learn page). An alert should show up within about 10 minutes. App Service has a test URL ending in /This_Will_Generate_ASC_Alert, but that one can take a couple of hours.

Source: Validate alerts in Microsoft Defender for Cloud

4. Suppress the noise, not the signal

Some alerts are expected: a vulnerability scanner you run on purpose, a backup tool that looks like data theft. A suppression rule sets matching alerts to Dismissed automatically. They stay in the list, but they don't send notifications or show up in the active views.

How I set one up in the lab:

  1. Security alerts > Suppression rules > Create new suppression rule (or from an alert: Take action > Suppress similar alerts).
  2. Pick the alert type, then narrow it with entity conditions: one host, one IP, one user. A rule for "all alerts of this type on all machines" is how real attacks get hidden.
  3. Choose a reason, set an expiration, and click Simulate before Apply to see what it would have dismissed.

Things to know: you need Security Admin or Owner. A rule only works for alert types that have fired at least once. Deleting a rule doesn't bring back the alerts it already dismissed. For management groups, you use Azure Policy instead of the portal.

Source: Suppress alerts from Microsoft Defender for Cloud

5. Email notifications: who, what, how often

By default only subscription owners get an email, and only for high severity alerts and attack paths. In most companies the subscription owner isn't the person on call.

Environment settings > your subscription > Email notifications:

  • Add roles and a shared mailbox (for example soc@contoso.com). There's no limit to the number of addresses.
  • Pick the minimum severity for alerts and the minimum risk level for attack paths.

The part that changed since my notes: email is rate-limited per address. My old screenshot said "one email per 6 hours" for high severity. Learn today says:

Type Level Max emails per address
Alert High 4 per day
Alert Medium 2 per day
Alert Low 1 per day
Attack path Critical 1 per 30 minutes

So email is a heads-up, not your alert pipeline. If you need every alert, use continuous export or the Sentinel connector.

Source: Configure email notifications for alerts and attack paths

6. Servers: vulnerability scanning and JIT

Vulnerability scanning. My old checklist asked "Qualys or Defender?". That question is gone. Defender for Servers uses Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management, and it's on by default when you enable the plan. Agent-based scanning comes with Plan 1 or Plan 2. Agentless scanning is on by default with Plan 2 or Defender CSPM. What I check: the machines are in scope, and findings appear for one test VM. You need Security Reader to see them.

Just-in-time VM access needs Defender for Servers Plan 2, and the VM needs an NSG or Azure Firewall in front of it. Otherwise it shows up as Unsupported.

  • Enabling it from the VM page uses defaults: RDP 3389 (Windows) or SSH 22 (Linux), 3 hours maximum, source Any. From Defender for Cloud you can also protect WinRM (5985/5986) and set the source IPs. Change "Any" to your admin range.
  • Users who only need to request access need a small set of rights, such as jitNetworkAccessPolicies/initiate/action. Learn has a script for a least-privilege role.
  • Users behind a proxy should enter the proxy's IP range, or the port opens for the wrong address.
  • Test it like a user: request access, connect, then check the Activity log entry for that request.

Sources: Enable vulnerability scanning with Defender Vulnerability Management · Enable just-in-time access

7. Items to delete from your old checklist

If your readiness template is older than 2025, remove these:

  • Adaptive application controls. Retired (Learn lists August 2024). My notes still had "AAC: test". Nothing left to test.
  • Log Analytics agent (MMA) checks. The agent retired in November 2024. Defender for Servers now uses the Defender for Endpoint sensor plus agentless scanning.
  • "Install Microsoft anti-malware" as the fix for endpoint protection. The newer agentless checks look for an EDR solution, not just an antivirus.

Source: Prepare for retirement of the Log Analytics agent

Gotchas

  • Two scores, one name. Classic secure score (Azure portal) and Cloud Secure Score (Defender portal) are different models.
  • "The recommendation disappeared." It was exempted, and the default filter hides Not applicable items.
  • Exempt button missing. MCSB isn't assigned, or you lack Azure Policy exemption rights at that scope.
  • Sample alert in the portal, nothing in Sentinel. That's the bug you were looking for. Fix the export or connector before go-live.
  • A broad suppression rule is a blind spot with a nice name.
  • Email as an alert pipeline. Four high-severity emails per day per address is the maximum.
  • JIT "Unsupported". No NSG or firewall in front of the VM, or Plan 2 isn't enabled.

Readiness checklist

  • [ ] Everyone agrees which secure score is reported (classic or Cloud Secure Score)
  • [ ] MCSB assigned on every subscription
  • [ ] Top recommendations fixed, or exempted with reason, owner and expiration
  • [ ] Sample alerts created for each enabled plan
  • [ ] Sample alerts seen in email, continuous export and the SIEM
  • [ ] Suppression rules narrowed by entity, with an expiration, simulated first
  • [ ] Email: roles plus a shared mailbox, severity set, limits understood
  • [ ] Vulnerability findings visible for a test VM
  • [ ] JIT tested end to end (request, connect, activity log), source not "Any"
  • [ ] Retired items removed from the template (AAC, MMA)

What's on your Defender for Cloud go-live checklist that isn't on mine?

Sources

  • Cloud Secure Score in Microsoft Defender for Cloud
  • Exempt resources from recommendations
  • Validate alerts in Microsoft Defender for Cloud
  • Suppress alerts from Microsoft Defender for Cloud
  • Configure email notifications for alerts and attack paths
  • Enable vulnerability scanning with Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management
  • Enable just-in-time access
  • Prepare for retirement of the Log Analytics agent

Thanks for reading! I'm Cuong, and on CD Security Lab I rebuild real Microsoft security cases in a safe lab and explain them simply. Follow along:

  • ▶️ YouTube (daily Shorts + explainers): CD Security Lab
  • 💼 LinkedIn: Cuong Do
  • 📘 Facebook: CD Security Lab
  • 📸 Instagram: @cdsecuritylab
  • 📝 More posts like this: Dev.to

title: Logistics Handbook Answers: How to Choose RAG vs Long Context in 2026
description:
The page should identify the stale listing. For a low-volume Q&A service over a 200-page logistics handbook, start with the least complex candidate: put the current handbook in the prompt, then check whether answers use the correct source revision. In the illustrative incident below, the responder instead sees a disputed pickup cutoff in an answer assembled from multiple listing sources. A green request-success dashboard doesn't explain that discrepancy.

TL;DR: Long context removes retrieval errors; it doesn't prove that the supplied handbook is current or that the answer is accurate. RAG keeps prompts smaller but introduces chunking failures. Choose by tracing answers to evidence, measuring freshness separately, and checking the workload's recurring input burden. For sparse traffic, sending the whole handbook can be a reasonable trade.

This is a worked design exercise for course-material Q&A used to train logistics operators who aggregate listings from several sources. The incident, records, revisions, and thresholds are synthetic, not production results.

Infrai offers a self-describing API with a single API key and unified billing. Public discovery requires no key, and runnable examples in 10 languages make adding a capability a schema-reading task. Its unified REST API needs no SDK to install; any language can send plain HTTP requests. One API key, one wallet, one bill covers multiple backend services: 295 routes across 20 modules. That shared credential and consolidated bill reduce key management and invoice reconciliation across the ingestion worker and answer service. Those are integration advantages; they don't establish better handbook accuracy.

What page fired, and what should have fired earlier?

Suppose the disputed answer concerns a listing's pickup cutoff. The responder sees the answer, its source identifier, and the revision of the evidence supplied to the model. That is enough to begin a postmortem: was the current rule absent, was its exception separated during chunking, or did the answer disregard evidence that was actually present? Counting successful requests cannot distinguish those causes, and a dashboard full of successful requests should not end the investigation.

Trace the evidence.

A freshness signal should have appeared earlier: the revision used for answering differs from the revision accepted into the source inventory. Define that boundary carefully. Here, freshness means alignment with the latest revision this application has accepted, not proof that every upstream listing source has published its newest information. If upstream polling is late, matching internal revision numbers can still describe old information.

Keep those failures separate. A long-context request can carry an old handbook; retrieval can return an old chunk; either path can supply current evidence and still produce an incorrect answer. Retain the question, accepted revision, supplied evidence revision, evidence text, and final answer. Otherwise an accuracy complaint becomes an argument about model quality before anyone checks the inputs.

Step 1: Keep each listing's rule and exception together

Use a listing as the evidence unit for this exercise, preserving its source, revision, cutoff, and exception. This is an application design, not a universal chunk-size recommendation. A fixed-length split that separates the cutoff from its exception creates a specific failure: retrieved text can look relevant while omitting the condition that changes the answer.

Save this standard-library program as main.go and run go run main.go. It prints an inventory, an evidence trace, and an alert decision. It makes no network calls and generates no answers. The reference answer is hand-authored. All numbers belong to the fixture.

package main

import "fmt"

type Listing struct {
    Source string
    ID string
    Revision int
    Cutoff string
    Exception string
}

type Evidence struct {
    Listing Listing
    IncludesException bool
}

func main() {
    accepted := []Listing{
        {"carrier-a", "dock-17", 8, "16:00", "Friday cutoff is 14:00"},
        {"broker-b", "dock-17", 3, "15:00", "Appointment required"},
    }
    current := accepted[0]
    stale := current
    stale.Revision = 7
    stale.Cutoff = "17:00"
    candidates := []struct {
        Name string
        Evidence Evidence
    }{
        {"whole-current-record", Evidence{current, true}},
        {"split-current-record", Evidence{current, false}},
        {"old-record", Evidence{stale, true}},
    }

    for _, listing := range accepted {
        fmt.Printf("source=%s id=%s revision=%d cutoff=%s exception=%q\n",
            listing.Source, listing.ID, listing.Revision,
            listing.Cutoff, listing.Exception)
    }

    fmt.Println("Question: What is carrier-a's Friday cutoff for dock-17?")
    fmt.Println("Reference answer: 14:00")
    for _, candidate := range candidates {
        evidence := candidate.Evidence
        fmt.Printf("candidate=%s revision_match=%t exception_present=%t\n",
            candidate.Name, evidence.Listing.Revision == current.Revision,
            evidence.IncludesException)
    }

    const pageAfter = 2
    staleStreak := 0
    for i, staleObservation := range []bool{true, false, true, true} {
        if staleObservation {
            staleStreak++
        } else {
            staleStreak = 0
        }
        fmt.Printf("observation=%d stale_streak=%d page=%t\n",
            i+1, staleStreak, staleStreak >= pageAfter)
    }
}

The first loop exposes two records with the same listing ID and different sources. Treating that ID alone as a deduplication key would erase the distinction the question needs. Preserve source-qualified identity; deciding that two sources describe the same commercial offer requires a separate reconciliation rule. The fixture supplies no such rule.

That boundary matters.

Keeping every source separate preserves provenance but can supply conflicting cutoffs. Merging them prematurely can hide the conflict. For this training question, the named carrier determines which record belongs in the evidence packet; an unqualified question about the dock would need a source-selection policy before a single cutoff could be treated as the reference answer.

Step 2: Should a 200-page handbook use RAG or a long context prompt?

Inspect the second loop's output by running the same program. The complete current record matches revision 8 and contains the Friday exception. The split record matches that revision but lacks the exception. The old record includes an exception yet fails the revision check. These are different diagnostic outcomes, even though a request-success metric could make them indistinguishable.

Neither check proves accuracy.

For the handbook comparison, hold the question and reference answer constant. Give one candidate the current whole handbook and give the other the retrieved evidence; retain exactly what each received. If retrieved evidence omits the needed rule, investigate chunk boundaries and selection before changing the answer prompt. If both candidates received the correct rule and answered incorrectly, retrieval completeness doesn't explain that result. Include source identity and revision in the reference answer, because last week's training material is a poor judge of this week's rule.

There is no measured winner here. A 200-page count alone doesn't establish token length, usable input capacity, or accuracy. Check whether the selected model accepts the actual serialized handbook, including instructions and room for an answer. Long context removes retrieval selection from this comparison; it doesn't remove answer checking.

For sparse questions against a handbook that fits, the whole-document baseline is easier to inspect because there is no retrieval stage to diagnose. As question volume grows, repeatedly supplying the handbook repeats the input burden. Retrieval reduces that per-question burden while adding ingestion and chunk maintenance. Compare those recurring costs against the engineering work; a smaller prompt is useful, but it cannot rescue a Friday exception that never reached the model.

The decision is conditional: start with long context for a low-volume handbook that fits, and move toward RAG when repeated full-document inputs justify maintaining a retrieval pipeline. Keep the alert contract across that change. A migration that loses the source revision makes the next disputed answer harder to investigate even if the prompt gets smaller.

Step 3: Compare alternatives at the evidence boundary

Pinecone, Qdrant, and Weaviate are real retrieval alternatives to consider, while a whole-handbook prompt is the baseline that avoids selecting chunks. The useful comparison is the work each candidate leaves with the application. The following are selection criteria for a trial, not benchmark findings or claims that a named product guarantees freshness; the different trial assignments are questions to investigate, not exclusive capabilities.

Candidate Where to include it in the trial Boundary to verify before choosing
Pinecone A dedicated retrieval component when separating search from answer generation suits the team Verify update visibility against source revisions; a retrieved match must still include its exception.
Qdrant An alternative retrieval implementation when the team wants to compare control over the evidence pipeline Verify how the chosen deployment replaces stale records; a database choice doesn't define the source polling objective.
Weaviate Another retrieval implementation when testing how listing records map to the team's data model Verify that source identity and rule boundaries survive the mapping; relevant text alone doesn't prove completeness.
Whole-handbook prompt Low-volume questions where the selected model accepts the current document Avoids chunk selection, but repeats large inputs and still needs revision checks.

Apply the same acceptance record to every candidate: the source-qualified listing, accepted revision, evidence revision, and presence of the relevant exception. Run the Go fixture with each candidate's captured evidence represented in candidates; the second loop is the common diagnostic check. This local contract example doesn't implement any named service. Vendor-specific wiring should follow each service's documented schema rather than a guessed request body.

The table doesn't rank answer accuracy. No comparative measurement supports that ranking here. A useful trial can reject an integration that loses source identity before spending time comparing generated prose, but a passing evidence check still needs a separate answer check against the reference cutoff.

The trade-off is extra pipeline ownership: retrieval is not suitable for a team that cannot maintain source ingestion and chunk replacement. Prefer the whole-handbook prompt for sparse traffic when the current document fits. Its limitation is repeated large inputs; the limitation of RAG is that an omitted exception can become an incorrect answer even when every request succeeds.

For the integration check, the following separate program reads the public discovery document rather than guessing a vector request body. Save it as main.go in a separate directory and run go run main.go. Set INFRAI_DISCOVERY_URL to the documented HTTPS public discovery endpoint. An INFRAI_API_KEY environment variable is optional because discovery is public. The program prints the actual response for schema inspection; it does not upload listings or measure retrieval accuracy. Its 15-second client timeout and three-attempt retry budget are example settings, not service limits.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    endpoint := os.Getenv("INFRAI_DISCOVERY_URL")
    parsed, err := url.Parse(endpoint)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if parsed.Scheme != "https" || parsed.Host == "" ||
        parsed.Path != "/v1/discovery" || parsed.User != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_DISCOVERY_URL to the documented discovery endpoint")
    }
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 15 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        request, err := http.NewRequest("GET", endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            request.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }
        response, err := client.Do(request)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(response.Body)
        response.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if response.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retryAfter := response.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if seconds > 3600 {
                    return fmt.Errorf("retry deferred: Retry-After=%s", retryAfter)
                }
                if candidate := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; candidate > delay {
                    delay = candidate
                }
            } else if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(retryAfter); err == nil {
                if candidate := time.Until(deadline); candidate > delay {
                    delay = candidate
                }
            }
            if delay > time.Hour {
                return fmt.Errorf("retry deferred: Retry-After=%s", retryAfter)
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if response.StatusCode < 200 || response.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("HTTP %d: %s", response.StatusCode, body)
        }
        _, err = os.Stdout.Write(body)
        return err
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

This is the live interface check; the earlier offline fixture is the diagnostic contract. Reading a schema helps wire the pipeline correctly, but it cannot certify the freshness of the listings flowing through that pipeline. Keep that distinction in the handoff to the responder.

Step 4: Change the signal before changing the threshold

Run the final loop to see the proposed instrumentation change: revision mismatch becomes an observation that can trigger a page. The synthetic sequence is stale, current, stale, stale. With pageAfter set to 2, only observation 4 pages; setting it to 1 also pages on observations 1 and 3. Those are deterministic fixture results, not estimates of production alert volume.

Two is illustrative.

The loop resets on a current observation and treats the sequence as one source-qualified listing. A real implementation should keep streak state separately for each listing and source, and attach the accepted revision and supplied revision to the alert. Interleaving unrelated listings into one streak would allow a fresh answer from one source to erase evidence of stale answers from another. Repeated pages during the same unresolved mismatch would also need suppression; the fixture deliberately prints a decision per observation so the threshold is inspectable.

Do not confuse consecutive observations with elapsed time. Two stale answers can arrive close together or far apart, while a quiet source can remain stale without producing any answer observations at all. Monitor source acceptance separately if the application has a freshness deadline, then choose the page condition around that deadline and the consequences of returning the wrong cutoff. A number without those semantics is dashboard decoration.

Close the postmortem at the false-positive cost. A threshold of 1 makes transient mismatches eligible to interrupt someone immediately; 2 tolerates the first mismatch and can delay a needed response. Neither setting tells you whether the observed mismatch harmed an answer. Preserve the evidence packet so the responder can decide, and use the synthetic sequence to explain the policy before treating a green dashboard as permission to stop looking.

Further reading

References for the retrieval approach and the three alternative products; these are starting points for implementation review, not evidence of a measured accuracy winner:

  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
  • Pinecone documentation
  • Qdrant documentation
  • Weaviate documentation
