title: When Pix lookups succeed and payments stop: rate limiting with Bucket4j and Redis
description:
Originally published on Aws Builders — Read the original article

A customer looks up a Pix key, checks the recipient’s name, and closes the app. Days later, one integration is still sending lookups at its usual rate, with healthy latency and almost no payments. When would you open an investigation?

Pix is Brazil’s instant payment system. I worked on its architecture at my institution and helped build the rate limiter for key lookups. The tricky part was deciding when a lookup should spend a token and when a later payment should return one.

What a Pix lookup costs

A Pix key lets a payer look up a recipient without typing their bank account details. The institution queries a directory operated by Brazil’s central bank, known as DICT, so the payer can check who will receive the money. Repeated reads also create an opportunity to collect personal data. [1]

A token bucket with feedback from the payment
A token bucket holds a limited number of permits. An incoming request needs a permit to proceed. Tokens refill over time, which gives a customer room for a short burst of activity.
The DICT rules also account for what happens after admission. For an individual payer’s bucket, version 8.5 of the operating manual specifies these amounts. [1]
Key found: spend one token.
Key missing: spend 20 tokens in total.
Matching payment order received by SPI, the instant payment settlement system: return one token.
Business users and participating institutions have their own parameters. An institution’s internal controls must be at least as restrictive as the DICT rules. Our local proof of concept uses a smaller, fictional penalty so the balance is easy to trace.

Why we moved the balance out of the JVM

We started with Bucket4j in memory. With a single process, I could watch the balance fall after each request. With two replicas, each could spend what it believed was the same customer’s last token. Restarting a process could also hand the customer a full bucket. [2]

What mattered in the storage decision
We considered Redis, Apache Ignite, and Hazelcast. In the practical comparison with Ignite, our engineering and infrastructure teams chose Redis for this workload. Anderson Martins Silva and I described that evaluation in an earlier account.
Contention: how long does a command take when several requests compete for the same balance?
Java integration: how much work does it take to connect the existing Bucket4j application to shared state?
Recovery: after a node fails, can the team establish how many tokens the customer still has?
In production we watched command latency, connections, memory, and replication in Grafana. During a failover exercise, I would check the customer’s balance as soon as the application reconnected. A successful connection alone tells you little about which requests will be admitted next.

Two replicas race for the last token

To reproduce the decision locally, I used spec-driven development (SDD). I wrote the acceptance criterion before generating the Java implementation and its tests. Criterion ADM-03 ties a customer-visible response to a downstream effect that we can count. [7]

The test that makes the race observable
Give one synthetic identity a single token in Redis. Freeze the test clock so no refill can occur.
Send two concurrent POST /lookups requests, one to each replica. Use the same identity with different recipient IDs and different Idempotency-Key values.
Check both responses, the directory receipts, and the final balance. One request returned HTTP 200 and read its recipient once. The other returned HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests) before reaching the directory. The balance was zero. [8]
LastTokenTest lets either replica win. The replica that returned 200 must have read exactly its own recipient. The one that returned 429 must have an empty read list.

assertThat(codes).containsExactlyInAnyOrder(200, 429);
assertThat(reads(first))
    .containsExactlyElementsOf(codes.getFirst() == 200 ? List.of("found-a") : List.of());
assertThat(reads(second))
    .containsExactlyElementsOf(codes.getLast() == 200 ? List.of("found-b") : List.of());
long remaining = balance();
assertThat(remaining).isZero();

We repeated the race with two Spring Boot containers sharing one Redis instance in Docker Compose. The directory receipt count moved from 20 to 21. Even without the test harness, we could see that exactly one additional read had occurred. [10]


Figure 1. Two replicas compete for one shared token. Only the admitted lookup reaches the directory.

What happens when a result arrives twice?

The service can reserve a token before a lookup, but it can charge for a missing key only after the directory replies. That gap matters if an event is redelivered or its consumer stops midway.

Follow one missing key from ten tokens to six
Start with 10 tokens. Reserve one before the read, leaving 9.
The directory reports a missing key. The fictional policy charges four in total, so debit three more. The balance is 6.
Redeliver the same result concurrently. The balance stays at 6, and the history contains one additional debit. [9]


Figure 2. Admission pays for the read. A conclusive miss triggers the extra charge.

A successful lookup left 9 tokens. A timeout also left 9, with an inconclusive result. A timeout tells us that a read was attempted. It tells us nothing about whether the key exists.

What survives a consumer restart
One Redis transaction commits the bucket state, the operation receipt, and the event. The consumer records completion afterward. When two confirmations arrived for the same eligible order, the balance moved from 8 to 9 just once. [9]
By this point in RedisLedger, Bucket4j has computed the new balance on a private copy. The transaction publishes that balance alongside its receipt and events. If another replica changes the watched account before EXEC, the operation retries.

try (Transaction tx = db.multi()) {
  if (snapshot != null) tx.hset(bytes(account), bytes("bucket"), snapshot);
  if (!change.fields.isEmpty()) tx.hset(account, change.fields);
  for (String event : change.events) tx.rpush("journey:events", event);
  tx.del(candidate);
  if (tx.exec() != null) return answer;
}

We injected a failure after a debit committed and before the consumer marked it complete. Further lookups for that identity returned HTTP 503 while another identity continued to work. After a restart with Redis preserved, the consumer recognized the receipt and released the identity with 8 tokens: the original 6 plus two scheduled refills. Losing Redis itself would require a separate recovery test.

Same lookup volume, different reasons to investigate

How many lookups find a key? How many lead to a payment order? We built two synthetic cases with the same 144 admitted lookups: two integrations, three ten-minute windows, and 24 lookups per integration per window. Both integrations confirmed 16 orders in the first window. [10]

Where did confirmations disappear?
After a simulated deployment, both integrations dropped to zero orders. Each logged 16 confirmation errors in each later window. I would compare confirmation traces across versions and check the shared dependency.
In the second case, Alpha had zero orders for two windows. Beta still confirmed 16 per window, and neither integration recorded confirmation errors. I would inspect Alpha’s client telemetry to see whether it ever attempted confirmation.


Figure 3. Each cell shows confirmed orders for 24 admitted lookups. Scope and persistence point to different next checks.

What to ask an investigation agent when orders disappear

Looking at those two charts, I would give an agent a narrow assignment: which trace should the on-call engineer open first, and why? Lookup volume held steady in both cases. The clue is which integration stopped confirming orders, on which version, and when.

How the agent gets its evidence
The investigator runs outside the request path. For the demo, the server creates a synthetic case, scopes it to specific integrations, versions and time windows, and makes three reads by default: lookup and order metrics, confirmation errors, and deployment history. The investigator receives those aggregates. The application retains authority over balances.
The local baseline uses deterministic rules. The optional Amazon Bedrock Converse adapter gets the same alert and facts. The model is asked to select one of two predefined hypotheses and return the source references and values that support it.[5]
Here is what BedrockAdapter actually asks the model. Along with choosing one of two hypotheses, it must cite records that an engineer can compare across windows and integrations.

String prompt =
    "Assess this synthetic alert: "
        + alert
        + ". Sources: "
        + json.writeValueAsString(facts)
        + ". Return one JSON object with hypothesis (CONFIRMATION_REGRESSION or"
        + " INTEGRATION_GAP) and evidence (map of exact source references to integer values)."
        + " Cite comparative windows and integrations.";

An evaluator looks up every cited value and checks whether the matching references, taken together, support the chosen hypothesis. The program then adds the alternative explanation, missing information and next check defined for that hypothesis. An engineer reviews the resulting report. [12]


Figure 4. The reader gathers three sources, the investigator proposes a hypothesis, and the evaluator checks its support before human review. The Bedrock path was exercised with scripted responses.

Two findings that send the on-call engineer to different places
After deployment, Alpha and Beta each recorded 16 errors and zero orders per window on v2. For example, health/alpha/v2/600/confirmationErrors is 16. A confirmation regression fits, but a downstream outage could have coincided with the rollout. The next check is dependency health and confirmation traces before and after a rollback.
In the concentrated case, metrics/alpha/v1/1200/orders is 0 while metrics/beta/v1/1200/orders is 16. Alpha recorded no confirmation errors. Did its client ever attempt confirmation? Client telemetry can distinguish an interruption from an intentional lookup-only workflow. The data leaves intent unresolved. [10]
An AI agent can also be the client making the lookups. A sequence of authorized reads can still expose personal data. The purpose of the lookup and the fields the server returns matter well beyond payments. [3]

The same question at a retail support desk

A support agent needs a delivery date. If opening the order also reveals the customer’s phone number, full address, and purchase history, a routine question exposes far more than the task requires.

What did the support ticket authorize?
Risk: genuine details about a purchase can make a social engineering message more convincing. Brazil’s federal government has documented scams that use real personal details. [6]
Control: verify on the server that the ticket, order, and agent belong together. Return the delivery date for a delivery-date question. Audit the category of data accessed without copying the phone number into the log.
Imagine two comparable shifts, each with 100 reads. One has 5 reads without a linked ticket, the other has 40. Before drawing a conclusion about either team, I would check assignment patterns and whether the integration recorded the link.

Figure 5. At the same total volume, unlinked reads rose from 5 to 40 in this fictional support example.

What we measured locally

The Java application makes the admission decision inline. Investigation runs separately on events with opaque IDs. The report deduplicates events and attributes each payment to the original lookup window.

Choose the denominator before raising an alert
Eight found keys and two missing keys give ten conclusive results. One additional timeout counts as a technical error. The missing-key fraction is 2/10, or 20%.
Eleven admitted lookups and four orders give 2.75 lookups per order. With zero orders, the report shows both counts and leaves the ratio undefined.
The default window is ten minutes, with two more minutes for the payment to arrive. A window needs at least 12 admissions to qualify for interpretation.[10]
For deterministic triage, all 16 cited values matched their sources in the deployment case, as did all 14 in the Alpha case. The scripted adapter returned 12 of 12 and 7 of 7 matching references, respectively. The evaluator recorded zero unsupported claims across the four outputs. [10]
What happens if the investigator cites the right record but gives the wrong number? Triage checks each reference and value against the case. Only matching pairs count toward support for the hypothesis.

var correct = new HashMap<String, Integer>();
evidence.forEach(
    (key, n) -> {
      if (n != null && n.equals(facts.get(key))) correct.put(key, n);
    });
boolean supported = supports(hypothesis, correct);

These counts measure citation fidelity on two synthetic cases. A live model’s usefulness on unfamiliar incidents, its latency and its cost remain open questions.

What I would measure on AWS

Amazon API Gateway: run a burst through gateway throttling and record which rejections came from the gateway and which came from the application’s per-identity rule. [4]
Amazon ElastiCache: repeat the last-token and receipt checks during a node failover. Compare the resulting balance, receipts, and directory read count.
End-to-end latency: measure lookup latency under realistic concurrency. For live Bedrock triage, separately measure response time, cost per investigation, and the fraction of claims supported by the cited evidence.

Reproduce the local result
With Java 25 and Docker running, start in the repository root. The first command runs the three test suites and the two synthetic investigations with a simulated Bedrock transport. The second starts the demo replicas on ports 8081 and 8082. [11]
sh gradlew clean build report investigate -Pmode=simulated
docker compose -f config/compose.yaml up -d --build
The recorded build passed 8 unit, 3 integration, and 4 component tests. The README walks through a lookup on one replica and POST /payment-orders on the other, including retries with the original idempotency key. [10] [11]

The question I take into architecture reviews

If lookups were still returning in a few milliseconds tomorrow, but payments stopped happening, which indicator would get your team’s attention?
Working on Pix taught me to look for that answer in the events that follow an HTTP 200.

References

[1] Banco Central do Brasil. DICT Operating Manual, v8.5, section 13 (Portuguese).
[2] Bucket4j. Java rate limiting and distributed backends.
[3] OWASP. Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows.
[4] AWS. Throttle requests to your REST APIs in API Gateway.
[5] AWS. Amazon Bedrock Runtime Converse command reference.
[6] Brazilian federal government. Advisory on impersonation using personal data (Portuguese).
[7] Proof of concept. Acceptance criteria and implementation tasks.
[8] Proof of concept. LastTokenTest, the concurrent admission test.
[9] Proof of concept. RecoveryTest, duplicate delivery and restart reconciliation.
[10] Proof of concept. Recorded test and Docker Compose results (Portuguese).
[11] Proof of concept. Run the experiments with Gradle and Docker Compose.
[12] Proof of concept. Java case reader, investigator, Converse adapter and hypothesis evaluator.

title: A Guide to Go SMS OTP for a Beginner SaaS 2FA Login Stack
description:
Payment settlement and identity verification need separate state, even when the receipt and the login challenge reach the same customer within seconds. TL;DR: for a beginner US/EU SaaS workflow, use SMS OTP with a suppression preflight and bounded status polling; keep receipt eligibility tied to settlement, and keep 2FA success tied to verification. Choose the integration by how much application code must change when the messaging supplier changes.

For a media business selling a paid publication, that distinction matters immediately: the settled order needs a receipt, while a customer opening the account may need an additional authentication challenge. A warehouse pickup code has the same tempting ambiguity between a message arriving and a person being authorized, but this example concerns media orders. Neither a receipt nor a delivery status should become an authentication credential.

Infrai is worth trying for the SMS challenge portion when a platform team wants the provider choice behind a capability contract, so changing the vendor behind that capability leaves the application's capability-facing code in place. Infrai uses a single API key for SMS and email: one key means the receipt integration and the challenge integration can share credential management while retaining separate business state. Its public discovery supplies request and response schemas plus runnable examples for reviewing that contract. This is a reason to evaluate the contract, not a promise that verification sessions or delivery semantics transfer automatically between services.

How should a beginner SaaS login stack separate SMS OTP delivery from 2FA?

Consider a bounded production design review, rather than a claimed incident: one settled magazine order, one pending login challenge, and a message that reaches a delivered state before the customer submits a code. I would reject a design that uses that delivery update to mark the challenge verified, because a transport observation and an authentication decision answer different questions, regardless of how convenient it looks to reuse one status column.

Delivery isn't verification.

The invariant is small enough to state without vendor terminology: settlement authorizes the receipt workflow; successful verification authorizes the next authentication step. A suppression result determines whether the application should attempt a message to that destination. Polling tells the application what the messaging service reports about a message. None of those observations substitutes for the others, and none establishes that a receipt was read.

This is where a beginner integration can acquire expensive coupling. A single field called status may start as an order status, become a provider message status, and eventually control account access. Replacing the supplier then means finding business decisions scattered through receipt handlers, customer support tools, and login code. Separate those meanings before the first adapter exists.

For receipt visibility, avoid using email opens as the identity signal as well; Apple's Mail Privacy Protection is another reason to examine what a transport or engagement observation can actually establish. The authentication path should consume a verification result. The receipt path should consume the settlement decision.

Buy versus build starts with the migration boundary

The useful comparison is the work each choice leaves with the application team. A managed challenge service belongs on the shortlist when custom authentication work is the dominant integration burden; a direct messaging integration belongs there when control over the messaging relationship matters more; a shared capability surface becomes interesting when the platform roadmap includes replacing suppliers without editing every business handler. These are different ownership decisions.

The table describes selection boundaries, not a feature certification or a benchmark. Each specialist still needs a review of its current regional behavior, suppression handling, and delivery evidence before a US/EU rollout. An API choice alone does not establish regional compliance. That review should include the meaning of a suppressed destination, the treatment of an expired challenge, and the point at which the application stops polling, because keeping a stable request contract does not remove differences in the business decisions that consume its responses. Make those decisions explicit before estimating the integration work; otherwise a short adapter can conceal a long operational commitment.

Budget the ownership.

Option Buy-versus-build decision Where it deserves consideration Work to budget before migration
Twilio Verify Evaluate a specialist verification integration instead of owning the entire challenge lifecycle. A team that wants verification to be the primary service boundary. Check how its challenge identifiers and verification outcomes map to application-owned state.
Vonage Verify Evaluate another specialist verification contract rather than assuming every SMS integration means the same thing. A team comparing dedicated verification services directly. Review its workflow against the required suppression and polling behavior, then estimate adapter changes.
Amazon SNS Evaluate direct messaging while treating the challenge policy as application-owned work. A team that deliberately wants the messaging boundary below its authentication logic. Budget challenge issuance, expiry, verification, abuse policy, and the receipt integration separately.
Infrai Buy OTP and verification capabilities behind a shared REST contract; retain business decisions in the application. A platform team prioritizing a replaceable messaging supplier and low initial integration effort. Validate the capability schemas and each selected vendor's behavior; keep message and challenge identifiers out of business decisions.

Try Infrai for SMS OTP in a media subscription login flow if preserving the application-facing capability contract during supplier changes is the main integration goal, and use its public schemas and examples to reduce adapter discovery work. Those are two specific benefits: fewer business call sites to revisit, and less guesswork about the request contract. Neither benefit requires moving receipt policy into the messaging service.

A specialist such as Twilio Verify or Vonage Verify is the better evaluation starting point when the verification workflow itself drives the decision. A direct Amazon SNS integration deserves consideration when the team explicitly accepts ownership of challenge behavior in exchange for choosing the lower messaging boundary. The decision should survive a support rotation, not just a successful demo.

Give polling a capacity budget and an SLO

Use suppression preflight before issuing the SMS challenge, record the resulting message reference separately from the challenge reference, and poll within a bounded application policy. Treat a blocked destination as a workflow outcome that needs a clear user response. Repeatedly retrying it is not a recovery strategy.

Start with arithmetic.

Suppose a planning exercise assumes 120 new challenges per minute and permits at most 4 status reads per challenge. That creates a budget of 480 reads per minute for one polling owner, before any retries. Two independent workers following the same schedule can double that demand. These are proposed planning inputs, not observed throughput or vendor limits; their purpose is to expose how a lightweight polling choice becomes a capacity problem when ownership is unclear.

Define a receipt SLO around the interval from settlement to the receipt workflow's recorded outcome, and an authentication SLO around the interval from challenge request to a usable verification result. A provider accepting a message does not satisfy the latter. Pick targets from the product requirement and measure them in the application; no measured latency or uptime claim is needed to decide that those clocks should be separate.

For this integration, use pull-based status and event reads in the application design. Keep country eligibility, per-destination throttling, and spend circuit breakers in the business layer. Store message metadata alongside the feature and order reference when per-feature spend attribution matters. Per-call metadata is useful input, but an application reporting requirement still needs its own accounting boundary.

There is also a migration trap in retries: a stable HTTP contract does not make a live challenge portable. Finish existing challenges with the integration that issued them, and send new challenges through the selected replacement after validating its behavior. On a write retry, preserve the logical operation's idempotency key; on rate limiting, respect Retry-After and use bounded exponential backoff. Infrai specifies an Idempotency-Key convention with a default 24-hour deduplication window, so indefinite replay is a separate application decision.

A Go status reader with a bounded retry policy

The preventative path keeps transport observations out of authentication decisions. This executable Go program reads the status of an existing SMS message through Infrai and prints the response without interpreting it as verification. Set INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_SMS_ID in the environment, using the message identifier retained by the issuing integration. The existing message is the only prerequisite beyond Go and an API key; this program does not create a challenge or send a receipt.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(header string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(header); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        candidate := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        if candidate > delay {
            delay = candidate
        }
    } else if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(header); err == nil {
        if candidate := time.Until(deadline); candidate > delay {
            delay = candidate
        }
    }
    return delay
}

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    id := os.Getenv("INFRAI_SMS_ID")
    if key == "" || id == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_SMS_ID")
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 10 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    endpoint := strings.ReplaceAll("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/sms/status/{id}", "{id}", url.PathEscape(id))
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            timer := time.NewTimer(retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt))
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
                continue
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("SMS status HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }
        fmt.Printf("%s\n", body)
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("SMS status retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

Save it as main.go and run it with go run main.go. The reader allows at most 3 HTTP attempts for this one status observation, uses a 30-second overall deadline, and respects both forms of Retry-After while increasing its backoff. If the server asks for a delay beyond that deadline, the context stops the operation rather than retrying early. That retry budget is separate from the number of status observations the workflow permits.

This is a read-only call. It does not need a write idempotency key.

Only a trusted server-side verification result should advance the authentication state, and satisfying that step must still feed the application's session and authorization policy. Add a durable receipt operation keyed to the settled order before connecting a sending adapter, so replaying settlement does not issue another logical receipt. Keep provider-specific response parsing in that adapter and preserve real error responses. Public discovery is the place to obtain exact issuance and verification schemas; a status response should remain delivery evidence.

Where this recommendation stops

Choose this approach when plain SMS is acceptable, integration effort dominates, and the team can own bounded polling and abuse policy. If voice, WhatsApp, or RCS is a requirement, evaluate a specialist against those channels before committing to the SMS contract. If an existing SMTP-based receipt system is the integration constraint, evaluate that requirement directly rather than assuming the same REST boundary fits it.

The trade-off is application ownership: this recommendation is not a fit for a team expecting the messaging contract to decide its fraud policy or to make receipt delivery an authentication factor. Prefer Twilio Verify or Vonage Verify as the specialist evaluation starting point when managed verification behavior matters more than a shared backend contract, and retain business-level abuse controls regardless of the supplier.

Keep receipt scheduling and cancellation requirements explicit during selection, and design any email-code fallback as a separate authentication flow with its own expiry and verification policy. A supplier migration is a good moment to discover policy differences in review; it is a poor moment to discover them through customers waiting for access to a paid publication.

Sources

References for evaluating the service boundaries and the meaning of delivery evidence:

  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • Vonage Verify documentation
  • Amazon SNS developer guide
  • Apple Mail Privacy Protection guide

If this boundary fits your system, start with the first-party SMS OTP, suppression, and polling guide and check its contract against your settlement and authentication policies.

title: Vector Collections Explained: Go Guardrails for Marketplace Duplicate Detection
description:
A vector collection groups records whose embeddings can be compared under one numeric contract. Its dimension must be fixed because distance functions compare coordinates position by position; a 768-value vector and a 1,536-value vector do not inhabit the same coordinate space. For marketplace duplicate detection, use one embedding model and preprocessing version per collection, validate length before accepting a write, and migrate model changes into a new collection. That preserves retrieval quality without moving contract errors onto the latency-sensitive query path.

TL;DR: dimension is part of the collection schema, not incidental metadata. Store model and preprocessing revisions with that schema, reject malformed writes, and make retries idempotent.

What does a fixed dimension actually guarantee?

An embedding is an ordered list of floating-point values. Similarity measures such as cosine similarity require equal lengths because the dot product multiplies corresponding coordinates. A fixed dimension tells the index how many values each record contributes. It does not prove that two vectors mean the same thing.

That distinction matters. Two models may both emit 768 values while assigning different meanings to the coordinates. Even one model is insufficient as a contract if one path embeds a title while another embeds title, category, attributes, and description. Record the immutable model revision, dimension, text-normalization version, distance metric, source ID, and content revision.

The invariant in my runbook is simple: every candidate compared in one search comes from the same embedding contract. Fixed length blocks invalid arithmetic; versioned provenance exposes invalid meaning.

Length is necessary. It is not sufficient.

A collection is therefore a typed index, not a bag of arrays. It owns vectors, identifiers, metadata, and indexing configuration. In retrieval-augmented generation, neighbors can become generation context. Here they become candidate marketplace listings for a later duplicate decision. Retrieval proposes. It should not silently make the final decision.

The incident lesson: validate before acknowledging the job

The production failure shape is familiar from cron and queues: a scheduled re-embedding job changes behavior, deliveries retry, and workers do not switch revisions simultaneously. Queues can deliver a message more than once, so the write path must tolerate duplicates. A loud rejection is manageable. A partly migrated corpus whose answers still look plausible is harder to detect.

Silent drift is worse.

I treat the collection boundary like an on-call boundary. Validate the declared contract before acknowledging work, and build the write key from the source revision plus embedding revision. A retry then overwrites the same artifact rather than creating another candidate. If validation fails, retain the job for repair and keep it out of the searchable set.

package vectors

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
)

type Contract struct {
    Collection, Model, Preprocessor string
    Dimension                       int
}

type Record struct {
    ID       string
    Vector   []float32
    Metadata map[string]string
}

type Store interface {
    Upsert(context.Context, string, Record) error
}

func Index(ctx context.Context, store Store, c Contract, r Record) error {
    if c.Dimension <= 0 {
        return errors.New("collection dimension must be positive")
    }
    if len(r.Vector) != c.Dimension {
        return fmt.Errorf("embedding dimension: got %d, want %d", len(r.Vector), c.Dimension)
    }
    if r.ID == "" {
        return errors.New("stable record ID is required")
    }
    if r.Metadata["model"] != c.Model || r.Metadata["preprocessor"] != c.Preprocessor {
        return errors.New("embedding contract mismatch")
    }
    return store.Upsert(ctx, c.Collection, r)
}

Do not retry a dimension mismatch forever. It is permanent until code, configuration, or data changes. Record expected and actual dimensions, revisions, job ID, and collection generation. Alert on a sustained rejection rate, while preserving each rejected item for repair.

Retrieval quality versus latency is a staged decision

Near-duplicate listings are messier than identical text. Sellers reorder words, omit attributes, translate descriptions, or reuse generic captions. Semantic retrieval can find candidates that token matching misses, but it also retrieves related products that are not duplicates. A 256 GB phone and its 128 GB sibling may be linguistically close and still be the wrong merge.

Use the vector index for candidate generation, then apply deterministic constraints and a separately evaluated decision rule. Category, region, normalized units, model number, condition, and structured attributes can filter or rerank candidates. Selective filters may save work early; weak filters may add latency without improving precision. Measure both outcomes.

Stage Purpose Quality risk Latency control
Normalize Stable embedding input Lost attributes Version and cache
Retrieve Find semantic candidates Related but distinct items Bound candidate count
Check facts Enforce listing constraints Missing fields Apply selective checks first
Decide Label or review a pair False merge Keep a review band

There is no universal similarity threshold. Build a labeled set from the marketplace's duplicate policy, including hard negatives such as adjacent sizes, capacities, bundle quantities, and refurbished versus new condition. Evaluate recall at the candidate limit because a downstream classifier cannot recover a true match retrieval omitted. Track precision separately for automatic actions; route ambiguous pairs to review.

Latency needs percentiles, not an average. Track p50, p95, and p99 with candidate recall, filtered counts, generation, and timeout rate. These are measurement buckets, not benchmark claims. A smaller candidate limit reduces downstream work but may lose duplicates. A larger one spends more latency on checks. Set it from a service objective and labeled evaluation, not a ten-record demo.

This trade-off has no free setting.

Migrating without mixing comparison spaces

A model change is a schema migration even when output dimension stays the same. Create a new collection generation, backfill it, and leave the old one serving while coverage grows. Dual-write new listing revisions if the team can operate that path safely. Otherwise record a high-water mark and catch up before cutover.

Do not query both spaces, concatenate their scores, and sort. Scores from different models are not automatically calibrated. Evaluate both generations against the same labeled queries and compare candidate recall, false-candidate burden, latency percentiles, and coverage. Promote with one atomic alias or configuration change after acceptance criteria pass. Keep rollback boring.

The scheduler needs explicit states: created, backfilling, catching up, verified, active, and retired. A lease prevents two workers from owning one partition; checkpoints bound restart work. Upserts remain idempotent. Split metrics by generation so a healthy old index cannot hide a stalled replacement.

Fixed dimension earns its keep here: different-length output fails during ingestion instead of contaminating results. Same-length semantic drift still needs generation boundaries and evaluation. Dimension alone cannot catch it.

When is a vector collection the wrong tool?

The main limitation is that semantic proximity is not identity. Exact identifiers should win when trustworthy ones exist. Use normalized manufacturer identifiers or other authoritative keys before semantic matching. Hashes and canonical fields work better for byte-identical or mechanically equivalent records. Vector retrieval helps when identity signals are missing, multilingual, or indirect, but its downside is a candidate set that still needs policy-aware verification. Automatic merging is not suitable when false positives can transfer reviews, inventory, or seller history between distinct products. In that case, keep vectors as a recall-oriented first stage and require deterministic evidence or human review before changing records.

Sometimes a slice and a loop are enough.

An index may be unnecessary when the corpus is small enough for offline comparison within the response-time requirement. It trades operational complexity for bounded online search, bringing rebuilds, backups, capacity planning, and stale-generation procedures. The operational cost is real: the team owns migrations, recovery tests, capacity alarms, and the failure mode where an apparently healthy endpoint serves an old generation. Choose brute-force offline comparison for bounded batch work, exact matching for authoritative identifiers, and a vector collection only when semantic candidate retrieval at corpus scale justifies that machinery.

The decision is not which dimension is universally best. Dimension follows the embedding contract. Select a model with representative marketplace evaluation, verify that its quality, storage, and latency fit the service objective, and lock its output length at the collection boundary. Treat later model or preprocessing changes as new indexed data with a measured migration.

Fixed dimension prevents one class of invalid comparison. Pair it with provenance, idempotent ingestion, staged decisions, and generation-based rollout. Those controls keep a scheduled embedding job from becoming a silent retrieval incident.

Sources

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-idempotent-methods
  • https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/
  • https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-constraints.html

title: Rust Axum Backend Essentials: Zero-Unwrap Error Mapping for Crash-Proof APIs
description:
Rust gives you memory safety, but calling .unwrap() inside an Axum web handler will still panic and kill the handler task on unexpected input.

Clean Error Handling With IntoResponse

Define a domain error enum using thiserror and implement IntoResponse once so handlers can cleanly use the ? operator:

use axum::{http::StatusCode, response::{IntoResponse, Response}, Json};
use serde_json::json;

enum ApiError {
    NotFound,
    Internal,
}

impl IntoResponse for ApiError {
    fn into_response(self) -> Response {
        let (status, msg) = match self {
            ApiError::NotFound => (StatusCode::NOT_FOUND, "Resource not found"),
            ApiError::Internal => (StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, "Internal error"),
        };
        (status, Json(json!({ "error": msg }))).into_response()
    }
}

title: Angular 20 end of support on 28 November 2026: planning the move to Angular 22
description:
Angular 20 end of support is on 28 November 2026. After that date the Angular team ships no more fixes for it, security fixes included. Angular 19 and every older version are already out of support. If your application runs on one of them, this is a good month to plan the move to Angular 22, the current major version.

Angular support dates

Each major Angular version gets six months of active support and then twelve months of long-term support (LTS), during which only critical and security fixes ship. The dates below come from the official Angular release schedule, checked on 23 November 2026.

Version Released Status Support ends
Angular 19 and older up to Nov 2024 Out of support Ended
Angular 20 28 May 2025 LTS 28 Nov 2026
Angular 21 19 Nov 2025 LTS June 2027
Angular 22 3 Jun 2026 Active June 2028

The latest release at the time of writing is Angular 22.3.0, published on 18 November 2026. Angular 23 is planned for around June 2027.

What changed between Angular 20 and Angular 22

Angular keeps moving towards signals instead of Zone.js. These are the changes that affect an upgrade:

  • OnPush is the default. In Angular 22, a component that doesn't set changeDetection uses OnPush (v22.0.0 release notes). Components that relied on the old behaviour, where Angular checked everything after every event, may stop updating when you mutate an object in place. I explain how OnPush and signals work together in Angular signals and OnPush: a practical guide.
  • Zoneless by default for new projects. Angular 21 made zoneless change detection the default for new applications. Existing applications keep Zone.js until you decide to remove it.
  • Signal Forms are public API. Angular 22 graduated the Signal Forms APIs from experimental. Reactive forms still work, so you can move form by form.
  • Newer TypeScript. Angular 22 dropped support for TypeScript 5.9, so plan the TypeScript upgrade as part of the same step.

Upgrade one major version at a time

Angular's update tooling is built to go one major version per step: 20 to 21, then 21 to 22. Each ng update runs migrations that rewrite your code for that version, and skipping a version skips its migrations. The Angular update guide lists the manual steps for each pair of versions.

  1. Check your dependencies first. Component libraries, chart packages and authentication libraries need versions that support the target Angular version. A library that never moved past Angular 19 is the most common reason an upgrade stalls.
  2. Run ng update @angular/core@21 @angular/cli@21, commit, build and run the tests. Then do the same with 22.
  3. Look for components that stopped updating. After the move to 22, click through the screens that show live data: lists after a save, counters, forms that enable a button. A component that relied on default change detection shows stale data rather than an error.
  4. Test server-side rendering separately if you use it. Hydration errors show up in the server logs and the browser console, not always on screen.
  5. Leave the optional changes for later. Removing Zone.js or moving to Signal Forms can each be its own release. An upgrade that changes one thing at a time is easier to roll back.

Why staying on an old version costs more each year

An unsupported framework still runs, but security fixes stop, libraries drop support for it, and every year you wait adds another set of migrations to run in one go. Moving from 20 to 22 now is two steps. Moving from 19 to 23 next summer is four.

I build and maintain Angular frontends on ASP.NET Core as part of custom web application development, including server-side rendering and the performance work that comes with it. If your Angular application is on version 20 or older, send me the version and the main libraries and I will tell you what the upgrade involves.

Sources

  • Angular versioning and releases (angular.dev)
  • Angular v22.0.0 release notes (GitHub)
  • Angular update guide (angular.dev)

title: What international patients expect from a medical tourism website
description:
A medical tourism website has a harder job than most healthcare sites. Its visitors are deciding whether to travel to another country for treatment, often in a language that isn't the site's first one, and usually without having spoken to anyone yet. Everything they need to make that decision has to be on the site and easy to find.

I built the patient, doctor and administrator sides of a platform for Shiraz University of Medical Sciences and its 11 medical centres, used by international patients. These are the expectations that shaped it.

1. Their own language, all the way through

A translated home page is not enough. Patients expect treatment descriptions, packages, forms, confirmation emails and their own patient panel in their language. Persian and Arabic also need right-to-left layouts, and the site should never redirect someone to another language because of where they are browsing from. Every language needs its own addresses and search engine titles, so patients searching in Arabic or German find the page written for them.

2. Clear treatments, packages and prices

Patients compare options across countries. A page per treatment that explains what is included, how long the stay is, what happens before and after, and what it costs, or at least how the cost is worked out, answers the questions they would otherwise email about. Packages that combine treatment, accommodation and transfers are easier to understand than separate price lists.

3. A way to ask before committing

Few people book surgery from a web page. They want to ask a doctor first. An online consultation request, with a secure way to upload existing reports and scans, is often the real first step of the patient journey. The site should say how quickly they will get an answer and in which language.

4. The practical side of the trip

Accommodation near the hospital, airport transfers, visa letters and interpreters are part of the decision. A medical tourism website that covers them, or clearly says who arranges them, removes a reason to hesitate.

5. Proof that the centre is real

Patients look for signs they can trust: named doctors with their specialities and qualifications, the hospital or university behind the centre, accreditations, real photos, and a physical address. Vague claims and stock photos do the opposite.

6. Their data treated with care

Medical documents are among the most sensitive data a person shares. Documents and results should be visible only to the people who need them, logins should be protected against password guessing, and changes should be traceable. Hosting and data location should follow the clinic's own rules and local law, and the privacy policy should say so in plain words.

7. A site that works on a phone with a weak connection

Many patients research on a phone, sometimes on slow mobile data. Fast, server-rendered pages with light images are not a technical nicety here; they decide whether the page loads before the patient gives up.

Behind the scenes: what the clinic needs

The patient sees the front. The clinic needs the back: reception screens for appointments, doctors' views of consultation requests, tariffs and packages per centre, and administrators who can update all of it without a developer. On Smart Med Tourism, one frontend serves 11 centre sites and more than 2,000 users, and each centre's own administrators manage its content.

A checklist for your medical tourism website

  1. Every page, form and email in each patient language, with right-to-left support where needed.
  2. A page per treatment with what is included, the timeline and the cost.
  3. Online consultation with secure document upload.
  4. Accommodation, transfers and visa help, or who arranges them.
  5. Named doctors, the institution behind the centre and a real address.
  6. Role-based access to patient documents and a protected login.
  7. Fast pages on a phone.

Next step

If you run a clinic, hospital or medical tourism company, see how I approach healthcare portal development, or tell me about your patients and the languages they speak.

title: Planning a multilingual website: 8 questions to answer before you build
description:
A multilingual website usually starts life as a single-language site with "we'll add Arabic later" written somewhere in the brief. Later arrives, and the team finds that menus are hard-coded, dates are stored as text, the layout only works left to right, and the CMS has one field for every title. Adding a language at that point means rebuilding parts of the site.

Planning for languages up front costs very little. Here are the eight questions I ask before building a multilingual site or platform. You don't need to be technical to answer them, and the answers shape the whole project.

1. Which languages, and which one comes first?

List every language you need now and every one you might need in the next two years. A site built for two languages can usually take a third without much work. A site built for one usually can't.

Also decide which language is the default. It affects what visitors see when their browser language isn't supported, which version search engines treat as the main one, and which language your team writes in first.

2. Will every page exist in every language?

This sounds simple, and it decides a lot. There are three common answers:

  • Full parity. Every page and every article exists in every language. Clean for visitors, but every new page needs a translation before it goes live.
  • Core pages only. Services, contact and key landing pages are translated, the blog is in one language. Often the right balance for a small team.
  • Different content per market. Each language has its own pages, offers or prices. Common for clinics or shops serving different countries.

Whichever you choose, the site has to handle missing translations properly. A visitor switching to German on an English-only article should land somewhere useful, not on an error page.

3. Who writes and maintains each language?

This is the question teams skip most often. A site with four languages and one person who speaks two of them will drift out of date within months.

Decide who translates (staff, an agency, a freelancer, or machine translation with human review), who approves, and how they know a page needs updating. A good admin dashboard shows which translations are missing or older than the original, so nothing is forgotten. I build this into the content model rather than leaving it to a spreadsheet.

4. Do you need a right-to-left language?

Persian, Arabic, Hebrew and Urdu are written right to left. Supporting them is more than flipping text alignment. The whole layout mirrors: navigation, icons with direction, progress steps, tables and form fields. Numbers, product codes and English brand names inside a right-to-left sentence still run left to right, and they need care so they don't jump around.

If any right-to-left language is on your list, even for later, the site should be built with logical layout rules from day one. I wrote about how that works in practice in RTL layouts with CSS logical properties. Retrofitting it into a finished site means touching almost every stylesheet.

5. What will the URLs look like?

Each language version needs its own address so people can share it and search engines can index it. The usual options are:

  • A folder per language: example.com/en/, example.com/fa/. Simple to run, and every language benefits from the main domain's reputation. This is what I recommend for most projects.
  • A subdomain per language: fa.example.com. Workable, but each subdomain tends to be treated more like a separate site.
  • A domain per country: example.de, example.ae. Strong local signal, but more domains to buy, renew and promote.

Also decide whether page addresses themselves are translated. /fa/services is easier to build; a translated slug reads better to local visitors. Both work, as long as you choose before launch. Changing URLs afterwards means redirects for every page.

6. How will search engines find each language?

A translated page that search engines don't connect to its siblings can compete with them or not appear at all. Multilingual SEO needs a few things in place:

  • hreflang tags on every page, listing each language version, so Google shows the right one to the right visitor.
  • Translated titles and descriptions, written for how people search in that language, not just translated word for word.
  • A sitemap that includes every language version.
  • No automatic redirects based on the visitor's location. Search engine crawlers mostly come from one country, so forced redirects can hide your other languages from them. Offer a language switcher instead.

Keyword research matters per language too. The term your Persian-speaking customers search for may not be the literal translation of your English keyword.

7. What else changes between languages?

Text is the obvious part. These are the parts that usually surface during testing, when they are more expensive to fix:

  • Dates and calendars. Iranian users may expect the Solar Hijri calendar; others the Gregorian one. Store dates in one standard form and format them per language.
  • Numbers and currency. Digit shapes, decimal separators and currency position all vary.
  • Forms. Name fields, phone formats, address layouts and validation messages differ by country.
  • Text length. German text often runs a third longer than English. Buttons and menus need room to grow.
  • Fonts. Not every font includes Persian or Arabic characters, and pages load slower if you ship fonts for every script to every visitor.
  • Emails and PDFs. Confirmation emails, invoices and notifications need the same languages as the site.

8. Who switches languages, and how?

Make the language switcher easy to find, show each language in its own name ("فارسی", not "Persian"), and keep the visitor on the same page when they switch. Remember the choice for next time.

For platforms with logged-in users, also decide whether each user has a preferred language for emails and notifications. Patients, staff and administrators may each work in a different one.

What this looks like on a real project

On Smart Med Tourism, eleven medical centres share one frontend, each with its own content, and international patients use the site in their own language. Answering these questions early is what made that manageable: the content model, the URLs and the admin screens were all built around more than one language from the start, so a new centre or a new language is configuration, not a rebuild.

A short checklist

  1. Languages now and within two years, and the default one.
  2. Which pages exist in which languages, and what happens when one is missing.
  3. Who translates, who approves, and how out-of-date pages are flagged.
  4. Whether any right-to-left language is on the list.
  5. URL structure and whether slugs are translated.
  6. hreflang, translated metadata, sitemap, no forced redirects.
  7. Dates, numbers, forms, fonts, emails and text length.
  8. The language switcher and per-user language preferences.

Planning a multilingual site?

If you are planning a site or platform in more than one language, especially one that includes Persian or Arabic, I can help you answer these questions and build it so adding the next language is easy. See how I approach multilingual website development or tell me about your project.

title: Measure web performance before you optimise
description:
"The site feels slow" is not something you can fix. "The largest image on the home page takes 3.1 seconds to appear on a mid-range phone" is. Before changing any code for performance, I measure, find the biggest cost, fix that, and measure again.

What to measure

For websites, Google's Core Web Vitals are a good starting set because they describe what a visitor actually experiences:

  • Largest Contentful Paint (LCP): when the main content appears. Aim for under 2.5 seconds.
  • Interaction to Next Paint (INP): how quickly the page responds to taps and clicks. Aim for under 200 milliseconds.
  • Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS): how much the layout jumps while loading. Aim for under 0.1.

For an API, measure latency percentiles (p50, p95, p99) per endpoint, not averages. One slow query hides easily in an average.

Lab data and field data

Lab data comes from a controlled run: Lighthouse, WebPageTest, or the Performance panel in Chrome DevTools. It is repeatable and shows you why something is slow.

Field data comes from real visitors: the Chrome User Experience Report, or the web-vitals library sending numbers to your own endpoint. It tells you whether the problem matters to real people on real devices.

Use field data to choose what to fix and lab data to work out how.

Common findings and fixes

When I audit a site, the same few problems account for most of the slowness:

  1. Unsized or oversized images. Serve modern formats (AVIF or WebP), use srcset so phones download smaller files, set width and height to prevent layout shift, and add fetchpriority="high" to the LCP image.
  2. Render-blocking fonts and CSS. Self-host fonts, subset them, use font-display: swap, and preload only the one or two files needed above the fold.
  3. Too much JavaScript at startup. Lazy-load routes and heavy components. In Angular, @defer blocks load a component only when it scrolls into view.
  4. No server rendering for content pages. SSR or prerendering puts the text in the first response, so LCP no longer waits for the JavaScript bundle.
  5. N+1 queries on the backend. One query per item in a list. EF Core's query logging or a profiler shows them quickly; Include or a projection usually fixes them.

Keep the numbers from slipping

A fix that is not guarded comes back. Two cheap guards:

  • A performance budget in the build, for example a maximum initial bundle size in angular.json, so the build fails when it is exceeded.
  • Lighthouse CI on pull requests for the most important pages.

Change one thing at a time

When several changes ship together and the numbers improve, you don't know which change helped. When they get worse, you don't know which to revert. Make one change, measure it, and keep a short log of what each change did. It is slower in the moment and much faster over the life of a project.

title: RTL layouts with CSS logical properties
description:
Most stylesheets are written as if every reader reads left to right. Then a Persian or Arabic version is needed, and someone writes a second stylesheet full of [dir="rtl"] overrides that flip margins, paddings and floats. It works until the next feature ships and nobody remembers to add its override.

There is a simpler way. CSS has had logical properties for years, and every current browser supports them.

Physical vs logical

A physical property names a side of the screen: margin-left, padding-right, border-left. A logical property names a side of the text flow:

  • margin-inline-start is the side where a line starts. Left in English, right in Persian.
  • margin-inline-end is where a line ends.
  • margin-block-start and margin-block-end are the top and bottom in horizontal writing.

Set dir="rtl" on the html element and every logical property flips by itself. No second stylesheet.

.card {
  padding-inline: 1.5rem;
  border-inline-start: 3px solid var(--accent);
  text-align: start;
}

That card has its accent bar on the left in English and on the right in Arabic, with one rule.

The shorthands worth learning

  • padding-inline and margin-inline set both inline sides.
  • inset-inline-start replaces left for positioned elements.
  • border-start-start-radius is the top corner on the starting side.
  • text-align: start and text-align: end replace left and right.

Flexbox and grid already follow the writing direction. justify-content: flex-start puts items on the right in a right-to-left page, so most layouts need no change at all.

What still needs a look

A few things do not flip by themselves:

  1. Icons that point somewhere. An arrow meaning "next" should point left in Persian. I flip those with transform: scaleX(-1) under :dir(rtl), and only those. A search icon or a logo must not flip.
  2. Transforms and animations. translateX(20px) is physical. If a drawer slides in from the start side, the sign has to change with the direction.
  3. Numbers and code. Phone numbers, prices and code samples stay left to right inside right-to-left text. Wrapping them in <bdi> or giving them dir="ltr" keeps them readable.
  4. Fonts. Persian and Arabic need a font with proper shaping, and usually a slightly larger size and line height than Latin text at the same visual weight.

A migration path

You do not have to rewrite a whole stylesheet at once. I usually do it in this order:

  1. Add a lint rule (stylelint has liberty/use-logical-spec and similar plugins) that warns on new physical properties.
  2. Convert components as you touch them.
  3. Test with dir="rtl" on a page that has no translations yet. Broken alignment shows up immediately, even with English text.

When a site has to support English, German, Persian and Arabic, this is the difference between maintaining one layout and maintaining two.

title: Stackin SDK Go: NF-e e NFS-e
description:
O SDK oficial da Stackin para Go simplifica a integração com a API fiscal. A struct Invoice reúne as operações para emitir e acompanhar NF-e e NFS-e, sem precisar montar manualmente cada chamada REST.

Instalação 

go get github.com/stackin-io/stackin-go-sdk

Requer Go 1.21 ou superior.

Operações disponíveis

Invoice inclui Issue(), Consult(), Cancel() e Reissue() para o ciclo da nota. Também oferece Correct() (carta de correção, somente NF-e), Invalidate() e Invalidations() (inutilização de numeração), além de métodos para PDF, histórico, envios, rejeições, estatísticas, documentos recebidos, manifestação, uso e prontidão.

Os itens usam br.Product, com campos fiscais brasileiros como NCM, CFOP e CEST. O pacote também inclui:

  • Clients para clientes salvos (ClientID);
  • Items para produtos e serviços do catálogo (ItemID);
  • Webhooks, Company, FiscalReference e Taxpayer para webhooks, empresa, referências fiscais e consulta de CNPJ/CPF.

Autenticação

Use a mesma API key Bearer da API REST. A chave identifica a empresa emitente e suas configurações fiscais.

  • Chave com contexto sdk: use sdk.stackin.io.
  • Chave com contexto api: use api.stackin.io.

A chave no host errado retorna 401. Se a credencial OAuth der acesso a várias empresas, selecione uma usando WithCompany ou ForCompany.

Erros e novas tentativas

O SDK separa erros da API (*APIError, com StatusCode e Detail), falhas de conexão (*ConnectionFailedError) e validações locais (*InvoiceError). Erros como PaymentRequiredError (402) e RateLimitedError (429) têm tipos específicos. Com errors.As, você também pode identificar o *APIError dentro deles.

O SDK não repete chamadas nem cria chaves de idempotência automaticamente. Se a resposta se perder, a nota pode já ter sido autorizada. Para repetir com segurança, passe IdempotencyKey no IssueRequest ou use stackin.WithIdempotencyKey em Reissue. A mesma chave e o mesmo conteúdo retornam a primeira resposta, sem gerar outro documento ou crédito.

Os SDKs de Python, Node e PHP seguem o mesmo contrato; mudam apenas algumas convenções de nomes.

title: Rustux: Rebuilding the Linux Kernel From Scratch in Rust — and Teaching It to Speak Windows Too
description:
Five days ago, Rustux was a UEFI stub that printed a banner and exited. Today it's a working kernel — written entirely in Rust, from scratch, with no Linux code — that boots into GNU bash, runs BusyBox and dynamically linked ELF binaries, executes native Windows .exe files without a single line of Wine, and speaks a brand-new internet protocol on a real e1000e NIC. This is why it exists, and why it matters.

The idea: port the kernel, not just enable Rust in it
The Linux kernel is ~30 million lines of C, grown over 34 years. Rust-in-Linux lets you write drivers in Rust, but the core stays C — the allocator, the scheduler, the page tables, the syscall table. Rustux asks a different question: what does the kernel actually do, specified by its ABI, and can we rebuild all of it in Rust from zero?
So we're doing exactly that. Survey what Linux requires subsystem by subsystem, implement it in Rust with matching semantics and errno values, and prove it with real userspace binaries — not toy shells. The result already includes:

  • Boot to userspace: UEFI boot, own GDT/IDT, page tables, buddy allocator + slab heap, ACPI/LAPIC/I-APIC interrupt routing, PCI.
  • The real Linux ABI: 120+ syscalls, ELF and static-PIE loading, dynamically linked binaries through PT_INTERP/ld.so, fork/execve/waitpid, signals, mmap/brk, pipes, sockets, epoll, eventfd, timerfd, signalfd, inotify, futexes, vfork, process groups, sessions, and terminal job control.
  • Real userspace: Debian dash, GNU bash 5.2 (job control, &, jobs, kill %1 all work), and BusyBox running unmodified.
  • A real VFS: flat filesystem, symlinks, /proc, getdents64 with d_type, inotify.
  • Real networking: an e1000e driver with DMA rings and MSI-X, UDP and TCP.
  • IPv8: the first kernel to speak the draft Thain IPv8 protocol on the wire — 32-bit route numbers, EtherType 0x8080. Experimental, not a replacement for IPv6, but it's a first.

The suite that gates every change is 62 compiled test tasks that must run back-to-back in QEMU with zero frame leaks and a clean exit — kernel memory accounting is verified after every boot, not assumed.

The second personality: native Windows .exe, no Wine
Here's the part that surprises people. Rustux doesn't just speak Linux. It also speaks NT — natively, in the kernel.

Wine works by translating every Windows API call through a giant userspace compatibility layer, because Linux only understands Linux syscalls. Rustux takes a different route: the kernel itself owns a Windows syscall table. When a PE binary runs, it gets a TEB and a PEB, NTSTATUS return codes, a real NT handle table, process and thread objects with Windows wait semantics — the actual NT execution model, not an emulation of it.

The Win32 API surface is then a thin marshalling layer: CreateProcessA, CreateThread, WaitForSingleObject, GetExitCodeProcess, VirtualAlloc, CreateFileMapping + MapViewOfFile, LoadLibrary with full DllMain attach/detach lifecycle, TLS callbacks, FLS slots, GetSystemInfo, QueryPerformanceCounter, and the file/directory APIs. A real MinGW-compiled .exe runs unmodified — our test fixtures are ordinary x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc output.

One kernel, two personalities, selected per binary. No Wine tower, no userspace shim — the kernel is the compatibility layer.

Why this is a good thing
Memory safety at the core, not the edges. The entire kernel is #![no_std] Rust. Use-after-free, buffer overflows, and whole classes of memory-corruption CVEs are structurally impossible in safe code — and where unsafe is required (page tables, port I/O, context switch), the boundary is explicit and auditable.

The ABI is the spec. Because we implement against documented behavior rather than porting code, every divergence is a deliberate, recorded decision — the repository keeps a running CVE matrix mapping each subsystem to the vulnerability classes it's hardened against (121 tracked entries and counting, audited every rung).

A kernel that can outgrow Linux's monoculture. Dual personality means the same safe core serves two ecosystems — and the architecture admits a third, a fourth. IPv8 shows the stack isn't locked to today's protocol decisions either.

It's honest. Every gap is documented — divergences are recorded, not hidden. This isn't a claim of feature-parity; it's a method for getting there one verified rung at a time.

Five days from banner to bash-and-.exe. The destination is a drop-in Linux replacement in memory-safe Rust — with Windows binaries as first-class citizens. The roadmap is public, every rung is tested, and the code is on GitHub.
