title: I open-sourced the front door to what I build: a zero-trust verification core in Rust, limits included
description:
I'm a solo developer, and I build local-first security tooling in Rust. This week I open-sourced the starter edition of the verification core I build on: mack-zerotrust-rust-starter — a default-deny token policy engine with a SHA-256 hash-chained audit log, written in safe Rust.

  • Repo: https://github.com/a95674127-beep/mack-zerotrust-rust-starter
  • 22 of 22 tests passing, CI and a full-history secret scan green on the public Actions page
  • MIT licensed

What it does

Tokens are verified against an explicit policy. Anything not allowed is denied by default — there is no implicit trust path. Every verification decision is appended to a hash-chained audit log, so a later edit to an earlier entry breaks the chain from that point on.

The two limits, stated plainly

Most launch posts hide the weaknesses. Mine are pinned as tests so they can't silently disappear:

  1. Tail truncation is invisible to verify_chain alone. Chop entries off the end and what's left is still a valid prefix. You only catch it by comparing the tip or length against a value recorded outside the chain.
    Test: limitation_tail_truncation_is_not_detected

  2. The chain is unkeyed. Anyone who knows the public hash construction can rewrite the whole history and recompute every link, and it verifies. It's tamper-evident against partial edits, not tamper-proof against a full rewrite — an externally anchored tip is the countermeasure, and that's out of scope for this kit.
    Test: limitation_whole_chain_rewrite_is_not_detected

A companion crate, aegis-seal, covers Ed25519 signing, the same style of hash-chained ledger, and secret/entropy scanning — 18 of 18 tests, MIT or Apache-2.0.

Why post the limits first?

Because the people I want using this are the people who check. A verification tool that oversells its own guarantees is worse than no tool. If you build in Rust and care about audit trails, I'd rather you start from what this doesn't do, and decide if the rest is still useful.

Issues and criticism welcome on the repos — the sharper the better.

title: Go PDF Parsing — Debug Empty Text in Scanned Versus Digital Contracts
description:
Consider this proposed page in a healthtech contract service: a contract is waiting for a server-side signature, the extraction step returned empty text, and the on-call sees a document reference with no record of whether the input had a text layer. The dashboard is green because the request completed. What page fired, and what decision can the responder make from it?

Short answer: when PDF parsing returns empty text, check whether the document is a scan without a text layer and route it to OCR; record the extraction path and its outcome before allowing the contract into the signing workflow. Digital PDFs can yield text directly, while scans need recognition, even though both look like ordinary documents to the person uploading them. An empty result should become a routing decision, not an assertion that the contract contains nothing.

The signing job raises the stakes. Recognizing words does not prove who signed, establish consent, or create a signature audit trail. Keep those responsibilities explicit.

How do you debug empty PDF text from scanned versus digital contracts?

Treat the opening as a design exercise, not a reported incident. Work backward from the responder's missing evidence: the signing prerequisite lacked usable text, but nobody could distinguish direct extraction from recognition, so the page described the consequence without identifying the next action.

A useful document record connects an internal contract reference, the attempted extraction path, whether that path produced usable text, and the decision that followed. Those are proposed application fields, not vendor response fields. Keep contract contents out of the alert. In a healthtech service, paging someone with extracted contract text would add exposure without improving the routing decision.

Check the input.

A root cause checklist should start with the document and the extraction decision, before investigating the signing queue. If a parse result is empty, don't assume the downstream service lost the contract.

First establish that the job references the intended document. Then inspect whether it has extractable text rather than assuming that a PDF extension means digital text is available. If direct extraction yields no usable text, attempt OCR and record that transition. If recognition still does not produce usable text, hold the signing handoff for review; a second empty result is not evidence that there is nothing to sign. This branch follows the usual scan-versus-digital distinction without pretending it explains every possible empty extraction.

Teams building this contract intake branch should try Infrai for PDF parsing and OCR because its plain REST API can be called from Go without installing a provider SDK. Its public, self-describing discovery surface supplies request and response schemas, which helps a small team inspect the integration contract before wiring the extraction decision into a signing service.

That recommendation concerns document processing. A PDF signing operation and a defensible record of signer identity, intent, and authorization are separate evaluation questions; the existence of an operation alone cannot settle the latter.

Instrument the decision instead of trusting the dashboard

The earliest actionable signal is the application reaching a state where the next step needs usable text and neither extraction path has supplied it. Counting every empty direct extraction as a page would turn ordinary scanned uploads into incidents, while counting only successful HTTP requests would miss the business state entirely.

The following runnable Go program models that decision with synthetic inputs. It makes no network calls and logs no document contents. Save it as main.go and run go run main.go; the counters describe this small example, not a production threshold or a measured workload.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "os"
    "strings"
)

type Document struct {
    Ref       string
    ParseText string
    OCRText   string
}

type Event struct {
    Ref         string `json:"document_ref"`
    Path        string `json:"extraction_path"`
    UsableText  bool   `json:"usable_text"`
    NextAction  string `json:"next_action"`
}

func usable(s string) bool {
    return strings.TrimSpace(s) != ""
}

func main() {
    docs := []Document{
        {Ref: "contract-demo-a", ParseText: "Service agreement"},
        {Ref: "contract-demo-b", OCRText: "Service agreement"},
        {Ref: "contract-demo-c"},
    }
    enc := json.NewEncoder(os.Stdout)
    held := 0
    for _, d := range docs {
        path, text := "direct", d.ParseText
        if !usable(text) {
            path, text = "ocr", d.OCRText
        }
        action := "review_before_signing"
        if usable(text) {
            action = "continue_contract_validation"
        } else {
            held++
        }
        if err := enc.Encode(Event{
            Ref: d.Ref, Path: path,
            UsableText: usable(text), NextAction: action,
        }); err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
    }
    if err := enc.Encode(map[string]int{
        "documents": len(docs), "held_for_review": held,
    }); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
}

Whitespace is only a minimal emptiness check. A contract-specific validation step still needs to decide whether the extracted material is usable for the intended operation; treating a single recognized character as permission to sign would defeat the point of the gate.

The short example intentionally separates routing from legal authorization. Its output gives an incident responder a reason for a hold, while the contract service must retain the evidence that belongs to signing itself. Correlate the original artifact and its processed version with the signing decision in your application record. Do not silently substitute OCR output for the original signed artifact.

Count the work that the empty result creates

Consider a planning workload of 1,000 contracts, with 800 yielding usable text directly and 200 needing OCR. These are hypothetical inputs for capacity planning. The branch requires 1,000 extraction attempts and 200 recognition attempts; sending everything through recognition would require 1,000 recognition attempts instead. There is no measured performance or savings claim in that arithmetic.

The real operating bill also includes reviewing unresolved documents, retaining the relevant evidence, reconciling usage, and answering the contract owner when the signing prerequisite is held. A parser's successful response can therefore be operationally expensive if it leaves the responder to reconstruct the document path by hand. Conversely, recording an outcome for each stage makes the scan mix visible without opening every contract.

The account-platform, content-processing, and email seam matters here because usage reporting becomes another document workflow. Metering, the PDF, and the email can share one API key in Infrai, rather than becoming a separate integration project after the signing service ships.

Here is the smallest honest handoff example without inventing request fields: retrieve the account usage response, then make that response available to a PDF request template that you author against the documented generation schema. Both calls use the same base URL and key. The template is configuration, just like the key; it is supplied through PDF_REQUEST_TEMPLATE, uses Go's text/template syntax, and receives the decoded usage object as .Usage. The json helper serializes a selected value for a JSON request body. Select actual response fields from the documented schema rather than guessing them.

This runnable adapter needs INFRAI_API_KEY and that schema-specific template in its environment. It prints the PDF operation's response without assuming a particular output field, so an email adapter can consume the documented result instead of guessing an attachment or URL shape.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "text/template"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    source := os.Getenv("PDF_REQUEST_TEMPLATE")
    if key == "" || source == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY and PDF_REQUEST_TEMPLATE")
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}
    base := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
    call := func(method, path string, body []byte, id string) ([]byte, error) {
        for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
            req, err := http.NewRequest(method, base+path, bytes.NewReader(body))
            if err != nil {
                return nil, err
            }
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
            if body != nil {
                req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
            }
            if id != "" {
                req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", id)
            }
            resp, err := client.Do(req)
            if err != nil {
                return nil, err
            }
            data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
            resp.Body.Close()
            if readErr != nil {
                return nil, readErr
            }
            if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
                wait := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
                header := strings.TrimSpace(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))
                if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(header); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                    delay := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                    if delay > wait {
                        wait = delay
                    }
                } else if when, err := http.ParseTime(header); err == nil {
                    if delay := time.Until(when); delay > wait {
                        wait = delay
                    }
                }
                time.Sleep(wait)
                continue
            }
            if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
                return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s %s: HTTP %d: %s",
                    method, path, resp.StatusCode, data)
            }
            return data, nil
        }
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry limit reached")
    }

    raw, err := call(http.MethodGet, "/account/usage", nil, "")
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    var usage any
    if err := json.Unmarshal(raw, &usage); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("decode usage: %w", err)
    }
    tmpl, err := template.New("pdf").
        Option("missingkey=error").
        Funcs(template.FuncMap{
            "json": func(v any) (string, error) {
                b, err := json.Marshal(v)
                return string(b), err
            },
        }).Parse(source)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    var body bytes.Buffer
    if err := tmpl.Execute(&body, map[string]any{"Usage": usage}); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if !json.Valid(body.Bytes()) {
        return fmt.Errorf("PDF_REQUEST_TEMPLATE must render valid JSON")
    }
    id := os.Getenv("STATEMENT_OPERATION_ID")
    if id == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set a stable STATEMENT_OPERATION_ID for this statement")
    }
    result, err := call(http.MethodPost, "/pdf/generate", body.Bytes(), id)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    _, err = os.Stdout.Write(result)
    return err
}

Use a stable operation ID across retries of the same logical statement and preserve the same request body. A production workflow should persist the usage snapshot and rendered request before issuing the write; rerunning the program after usage changes is a new calculation, not an identical retry. Template rendering checks JSON syntax, while schema validation remains an integration responsibility.

The email step follows the PDF result, with its own durable delivery decision and idempotency boundary. The adapter stops before it because an account statement and a signed contract are different artifacts: do not accidentally attach a contract when the intended email is a usage statement.

In the alternative stack, Stripe Metering plus Puppeteer plus Amazon SES means two hosted-service signups, Stripe and AWS, two service credential configurations, and a Puppeteer runtime to package and operate. Puppeteer itself does not require a vendor signup. You would write the usage-to-template mapping, browser rendering job, artifact handoff, email construction, and reconciliation glue. A shared API still needs those business decisions, but it reduces the number of provider interfaces the team maintains. Its trade-off is plain: one vendor to trust, one bill, one outage surface.

Compare the evidence boundary before choosing a provider

A fair comparison asks which part of this workflow a tool owns. Mixing text extraction, server-side PDF signing, and a full signing ceremony into one checkbox would make the purchasing decision look easier while handing the missing responsibilities to the on-call.

Option Role to evaluate Boundary that matters for this contract workflow
Apache PDFBox Direct PDF processing and text extraction under your control The team owns the recognition branch, service operation, and application audit record.
Tesseract OCR for image-based document processing Recognition is one stage; document preparation and the signing workflow need separate integration.
Gotenberg A self-hosted document-conversion option for the usage-statement branch Compare the runtime ownership with a hosted API; rendering a statement does not supply the contract's signing evidence.
WeasyPrint HTML/CSS rendering for a controlled statement template Useful to evaluate for the reporting artifact; it does not replace the scanned-contract recognition decision or signing workflow.
DocuSign eSignature A specialist signing workflow Evaluate signer participation and audit requirements here when the job extends beyond applying a server-side PDF signature.
Infrai Plain REST access to PDF parsing, OCR, generation, and signing operations, with account usage and email capabilities under one key Evaluate exact schemas and the signing evidence required by the application; a broad API surface alone does not establish compliance.

These are workflow distinctions, not benchmark results. Gotenberg and WeasyPrint belong in the usage-statement comparison because the combined workflow includes generating a report; neither should be mistaken for the answer to an empty text layer. PDFBox and Tesseract are reasonable candidates when controlling the processing runtime matters more than reducing integration ownership; a specialist signing product deserves priority when the dominant requirement is managing the signer journey and its evidence. Infrai fits the team that wants HTTP integrations for the document branch and neighboring backend tasks, provided the contract's signature and audit requirements survive evaluation.

Healthtech adds a procurement boundary the extraction test cannot answer. Verify the applicable contractual, data-handling, and evidence requirements for every provider before sending real contracts. No scan detector establishes those properties.

Close the incident with a threshold someone can defend

The proposed correction is small: record direct extraction versus OCR, distinguish a routine recognition handoff from an unresolved document, and page on the signing workflow's inability to make progress under an explicitly chosen service objective. A chart showing a larger OCR share can help explain workload changes. It cannot tell the responder whether a signature was authorized.

The threshold has a cost.

Page on every empty direct extraction in the hypothetical workload and the team creates 200 alert opportunities for documents that merely need recognition. Suppress every empty outcome and the unresolved contracts disappear into a green dashboard. Neither behavior helps the person carrying the pager; route the expected scans, retain the evidence, and reserve the interruption for a state with an owner and an action.

Further reading

References for evaluating the document format, processing tools, and signing boundary:

  • ISO 32000-2, Portable Document Format
  • Apache PDFBox documentation
  • Tesseract documentation
  • Gotenberg documentation
  • WeasyPrint documentation
  • DocuSign developer documentation
  • Stripe billing meters documentation
  • Puppeteer documentation
  • Amazon SES documentation

If this document-processing boundary fits your contract service, inspect the request schemas and examples in the Infrai documentation.

title: 78 faster: my Python dedupe, 5% rewritten in Rust
description:
78× faster: my Python dedupe, 5% rewritten in Rust

10.06 seconds became 129 milliseconds. I changed exactly one function — 48 lines of Rust, zero changes to the rest of the app — and the tool that did it was released yesterday. It found the hot function, recorded its real calls, generated the port task, and then proved the port gives identical results on 34 test cases before it would let me switch it on.

The tool is fast-anything. It was created on 2026-11-21, has 1,845 stars already, and its pitch is the one every Python developer has heard and ignored: don't rewrite it in Rust, rewrite the 5% that's slow. I ran it on my own code to see how much of that pitch survives contact with a real machine.

The app

A fuzzy dedupe: 700 names, some with typos, collapse near-duplicates within Levenshtein distance 2. Pure standard library, deliberately naive — the quadratic pairwise loop is the whole point, because that's what real "it's just a script" code looks like:

def levenshtein(a, b):
    if a == b:
        return 0
    la, lb = len(a), len(b)
    if la == 0:
        return lb
    if lb == 0:
        return la
    prev = list(range(lb + 1))
    for i in range(1, la + 1):
        cur = [i] + [0] * lb
        ca = a[i - 1]
        for j in range(1, lb + 1):
            cur[j] = min(prev[j] + 1, cur[j - 1] + 1, prev[j - 1] + (ca != b[j - 1]))
        prev = cur
    return prev[lb]

def dedupe(names, threshold=2):
    kept = []
    for name in names:
        dup = False
        for k in kept:
            if levenshtein(name, k) <= threshold:
                dup = True
                break
        if not dup:
            kept.append(name)
    return kept

Baseline, before touching anything:

700 names -> 478 unique in 10.066s

Scan: it found the 5% in one pass 

$ fast-anything scan -- python3 dedupe.py

   #  function                        time                  calls  verdict
   1  dedupe.py:dedupe                █████████  99.9%          1  ✓ port it
   2  dedupe.py:typo                              0.0%        226  · too small to matter
   3  dedupe.py:levenshtein           █████████  99.5%    151,315  ↳ ported inside dedupe
   4  dedupe.py:make_names                        0.0%          1  ✗ not deterministic: random.Random

Two things worth noting. First, the 5% claim undersells it here: dedupe is 99.9% of runtime, and it drags levenshtein along — 151,315 calls. Second, the profiler is honest about what it can't port: make_names uses random.Random, so it's flagged non-deterministic and left alone. A tool that tells you what it won't do is a tool I trust more.

Port: the tool writes the spec, I wrote the Rust

fast-anything port re-ran the app, recorded the one real call to dedupe, and generated a crate plus a TASK.md containing the original Python, the helper, the recorded call, and rules: same result on every input including edge cases, Python strings index by code point so use .chars(), floats within 1e-9, raise where Python raises.

Normally you'd hand TASK.md to Claude Code or Codex with --agent. This box has neither configured for the job (the doctor check found codex-cli but no Claude Code), so I wrote the Rust by hand — two-row DP, Vec<char> per string, same early exits as the original:

fn levenshtein(a: &[char], b: &[char]) -> usize {
    if a == b { return 0; }
    let (la, lb) = (a.len(), b.len());
    if la == 0 { return lb; }
    if lb == 0 { return la; }
    let mut prev: Vec<usize> = (0..=lb).collect();
    let mut cur: Vec<usize> = vec![0; lb + 1];
    for i in 1..=la {
        cur[0] = i;
        let ca = a[i - 1];
        for j in 1..=lb {
            let cost = if ca == b[j - 1] { 0 } else { 1 };
            cur[j] = (prev[j] + 1).min(cur[j - 1] + 1).min(prev[j - 1] + cost);
        }
        std::mem::swap(&mut prev, &mut cur);
    }
    prev[lb]
}

And here is the one genuine wart: the generated stub didn't compile. The template emits the function with &Bound<'_, PyAny> parameters and a signature default of threshold = 2 — and PyO3 can't turn the integer literal 2 into a &Bound. The fix was mine, not the tool's: change the parameters to concrete types (Vec<String>, i64) and let PyO3 do the conversion. One line of real friction in an otherwise smooth loop, and exactly the kind of thing that would have cost a first-time user half an hour of staring at a macro error. The tool's verify step can't catch a bug in its own template, because verify only runs after the crate compiles.

Verify: 34/34, then the real number 

$ fast-anything verify dedupe.py:dedupe
✓ 34/34 calls give the same result (1 recorded + 8 edge cases + 25 derived)
✓ dedupe.py:dedupe per call: 10069.1ms in Python, 81.8ms in Rust: 123× faster

34 cases: the 1 recorded call, 8 edge cases (empty input, non-ASCII, very long input, and the rest), and 25 derived cases the tool generates by shrinking and mutating the recorded input. That's the part of the pitch that matters most to me. A speedup you can't trust is a bug with good marketing, and the replay step is what separates this from "I rewrote it in Rust and it seemed fine."

Then the whole-app bench, 5 interleaved runs each:

  Python       ████████████████████████ 10.06s
  Rust         ▎                        129ms

✓ python3 dedupe.py is 78× faster end to end (median of 5, ±81ms)

Same output both ways — 700 names -> 478 unique — with only the timing line differing, which the tool itself flagged and correctly dismissed as run-to-run variation.

How it compares to the README's claims

The README reports its own runs on an i5-10500: Python fuzzy dedupe (700 names) 4.91s → 42ms, 116×. Mine: 10.06s → 129ms, 78×. My baseline is slower — this VM's Python is slower than their Windows box, and my Levenshtein is the naive textbook version — and my Rust result is slower too. The shape holds, the absolute numbers don't transfer, and that's the honest way to read any benchmark table: same workload class, different machine, different constant factors.

What I'd actually trust this with

The loop works: profile, port one function, prove equivalence on recorded plus derived calls, swap it in reversibly (FAST_ANYTHING_DISABLE=1 runs the original any time). The verification is only as strong as the recorded behavior — if your function has a branch the recorded calls never hit, the port can be wrong there and nothing in this loop will notice. That's the real limit, and it's a limit of the method, not this implementation.

But for the job it advertises — a hot, deterministic, plain-data function eating 99% of a script's runtime — it did the whole thing in about ten minutes, including the stub bug I had to fix by hand. The 5% rule works when the 5% is really 99.9% of the runtime. The profiler will tell you whether that's true before you write a line of Rust, which is the part I'd keep even if I threw the rest away.

Sources

  • fast-anything, https://github.com/EL4CTEO/fast-anything — created 2026-11-21, 1,845 stars, v0.7.0, MIT. README results table quoted from the repo.
  • All timings are my own runs on 2026-11-22: AMD EPYC VM, Python 3.12.3, rustc 1.100.0 (installed via rustup for this test), fast-anything 0.7.0 via npm. Baseline python3 dedupe.py: 10.066s; after fast-anything enable: 129ms median end to end.

title: I built the same multi-step MUI form twice: react-hook-form + Zod vs. SurveyJS
description:
Every MUI app seems to have one: the form that started as three fields and slowly became a four-step wizard. It has a section that appears only when a switch is on, a table where users add rows, fields that are required only in some cases, and a product manager who wants "just one more question" every sprint.

MUI gives you excellent inputs, but no form engine. So you assemble one: react-hook-form for state, Zod for validation, a Stepper for pages, and glue code to hold it all together. It works, and most of us have shipped forms exactly like that.

There is another way: describe the form as JSON and let a form library render it, while it still looks like the rest of your MUI app. That's what SurveyJS and its MUI theme adapter do.

To compare the two approaches honestly, I built the same multi-step form twice:

  • Version A: MUI + react-hook-form + Zod, written by hand.
  • Version B: SurveyJS Form Library + the MUI theme adapter.

Then I measured both, applied the same change request to each, and noted where each approach wins. Full disclosure: this post comes from the SurveyJS team. So every number below comes from a companion repo you can run and check yourself, and I'll point out where SurveyJS is the worse choice too.

SurveyJS in two minutes

If you've never used SurveyJS, three pieces matter for this post.

Form Library (survey-core + survey-react-ui, MIT-licensed). You give it a JSON schema; it renders the form at runtime and handles the behavior: pages, conditional visibility, validation, dynamic rows, input masks, localization. Your React code shrinks to "create a model, render it, handle the result". The answers come back as a plain JSON object that you send to your own API.

The MUI theme adapter. This is a stylesheet that ships with survey-core (survey-core/themes/adapters/mui.css). It also needs a one-line setup call, shown below. SurveyJS v3 styles everything through CSS variables called design tokens (--sjs2-*). The adapter points those tokens at the CSS variables MUI generates from your theme (--mui-*). So SurveyJS forms pick up your palette, typography, shape and light/dark mode, and they update live when your theme changes.

Does SurveyJS render MUI components? No, and it's worth knowing upfront. SurveyJS renders its own components; the adapter makes them look like MUI by reading your theme's variables. The upside: no coupling to MUI's component internals or version-specific APIs, and one styling system shared by everything SurveyJS renders. The trade-off: styling decisions that never reach MUI's CSS variables (an sx prop, a Grid layout) aren't picked up automatically. More on that later.

Survey Creator (optional). Because the form is JSON, it can also be edited visually. Survey Creator is a drag-and-drop builder that produces the same JSON, so non-developers can change forms without touching code. It reuses the same tokens, so it follows your MUI theme too. You don't need it for anything in this post; if you're curious, there's a free online demo you can try in the browser.

The test form: a patient intake wizard

A login form proves nothing, so I used a realistic one: the Patient Intake form from the official SurveyJS MUI adapter demo. It has four pages:

  1. Patient: name, date of birth, sex, a masked phone number, preferred contact method.
  2. Insurance: a primary insurance group, plus a switch that reveals a required "secondary insurance" section.
  3. History: a yes/no/unsure grid of conditions, an allergies table where users add and remove rows (each row needs an allergen), and a free-text medications field.
  4. Consent: two checkboxes that must be ticked, a signature and a date.

On top of that, a progress indicator shows the pages, "Next" validates only the current page, and errors appear under the fields that caused them. Both versions implement all of it, with the same labels and error messages.

The stack: Vite, React 19, MUI 7.3, survey-core 3.2.7, react-hook-form 7.92, Zod 4. Both versions run side by side in one app shell, using the same MUI theme, behind two tabs.

Version A: MUI + react-hook-form + Zod

This is the stack most MUI developers would reach for, so I tried to write it the way a careful team would: one Zod schema, a small set of reusable field components, and one form component.

The Zod schema

The schema holds the field rules. Conditional rules, like "secondary insurance is required only when the switch is on", go into a superRefine, because they depend on more than one field:

export const patientIntakeSchema = z
  .object({
    firstName: required("First name is required."),
    phone: z
      .string()
      .refine((v) => v === "" || /^\+1 \(\d{3}\) \d{3}-\d{4}$/.test(v), "Enter a complete phone number."),
    hasSecondary: z.boolean(),
    carrier2: z.string(),
    allergies: z.array(
      z.object({
        allergen: required("Allergen is required."),
        severity: z.enum(["Mild", "Moderate", "Severe", ""]),
        reaction: z.string(),
      }),
    ),
    consentTreatment: z.boolean().refine((v) => v, "Consent to treatment is required."),
    // ...15 more fields
  })
  .superRefine((v, ctx) => {
    if (!v.hasSecondary) return;
    if (!v.carrier2.trim())
      ctx.addIssue({ code: "custom", path: ["carrier2"], message: "Insurance carrier is required." });
    // ...same for memberId2
  });

Pages and per-page validation

MUI's Stepper is purely visual, so you decide which fields belong to each page and validate only those before moving on:

const PAGES = [
  { title: "Patient", fields: ["firstName", "lastName", "dob", "phone"] },
  { title: "Insurance", fields: ["carrier", "memberId", "carrier2", "memberId2"] },
  { title: "History", fields: ["allergies"] },
  { title: "Consent", fields: ["consentTreatment", "consentPrivacy"] },
];

async function next() {
  if (await trigger(PAGES[page].fields)) setPage((p) => p + 1);
}

This list has to stay in sync with the JSX: add a required field to a page and forget it here, and users can skip past it.

Conditional sections, dynamic rows and masks

The secondary insurance section uses useWatch, the allergies table uses useFieldArray, and the phone mask is a small formatting function passed to the input:

const hasSecondary = useWatch({ control, name: "hasSecondary" });
const allergies = useFieldArray({ control, name: "allergies" });

{hasSecondary && (
  <Stack direction={{ xs: "column", sm: "row" }} spacing={2}>
    <TextInput control={control} name="carrier2" label="Insurance carrier" required />
    <TextInput control={control} name="memberId2" label="Member ID" required />
  </Stack>
)}

One more detail: when the switch is turned off, the hidden values are still in the form state, so onSubmit clears them before sending anything to the server.

A bug I didn't see coming

My first version had a silent failure: on the last page, Complete did nothing. No error, no console message. The cause was the conditions grid. Each row is registered with Controller, so unanswered rows exist in the form state as undefined. My Zod schema expected "yes" | "no" | "unsure" for every row, so validation failed on fields that had no error message in the UI.

The fix was one .optional(). Tracking it down took far longer than the fix. It's a small example of the hidden coupling between schema, registered fields and UI that you maintain by hand in this approach.

The tally

Version A is 451 lines in 3 files (non-empty, non-comment lines):

File Lines Reusable?
patientIntakeSchema.ts (Zod) 65 no, one per form
RhfIntake.tsx (form component) 276 no, one per form
fields.tsx (Controller + MUI bindings) 110 yes, shared by all forms

It's good, readable code, and you get full TypeScript inference from the Zod schema. But every page, condition and rule lives in code.

Version B: SurveyJS + the MUI theme adapter

Setup

Install the Form Library:

npm install survey-core survey-react-ui

The adapter reads MUI's CSS variables, so your theme must generate them. That's the cssVariables option in createTheme. If you already use it, there's nothing to change:

export const theme = createTheme({
  cssVariables: { colorSchemeSelector: "class" }, // required by the adapter
  colorSchemes: {
    light: { palette: { primary: { main: "#1565c0" } } },
    dark: { palette: { primary: { main: "#90caf9" } } },
  },
  shape: { borderRadius: 10 },
});

cssVariables: true is enough for the adapter. The colorSchemeSelector: "class" form is what you want if you switch light and dark modes with useColorScheme.

The component

This is the React side of Version B (the repo version also shows a thank-you screen after submit):

import { useEffect, useState } from "react";
import { Model, setupThemeAdapter } from "survey-core";
import { Survey } from "survey-react-ui";
import "survey-core/survey-core.css";
import "survey-core/themes/adapters/mui.css";
import { patientIntakeJson } from "./patientIntakeSchema";

// Apply the adapter's MUI layout defaults. Run once at startup, before creating any model.
setupThemeAdapter("mui");

export default function SurveyJsIntake() {
  const [survey] = useState(() => new Model(patientIntakeJson));

  useEffect(() => {
    const onComplete = (sender: Model) => saveIntake(sender.data); // POST to your API
    survey.onComplete.add(onComplete);
    return () => survey.onComplete.remove(onComplete);
  }, [survey]);

  return <Survey model={survey} />;
}

Three details matter:

  • Order of the CSS imports. Load survey-core.css first and the adapter second, so the adapter's mappings win.
  • setupThemeAdapter("mui") applies the adapter's MUI layout defaults (and aligns Survey Creator, if you use it). The CSS file does the color and font mapping; this call handles the rest. Call it once at startup, before you create any survey model. Module level, as above, is the simplest place.
  • Create the model once. useState(() => new Model(json)) (or useMemo) keeps the model, and the user's answers, across re-renders.

Render it anywhere inside your existing ThemeProvider. No extra provider is needed.

The schema

Everything else is in the JSON. Here are the parts that matched the code in Version A:

// Masked phone input: the mask also validates that the number is complete
{
  type: "text",
  name: "phone",
  title: "Mobile phone",
  inputType: "tel",
  maskType: "pattern",
  maskSettings: { pattern: "+1 (999) 999-9999" },
},

// Conditional section with its own required fields
{
  type: "panel",
  name: "secondaryInsurance",
  title: "Secondary insurance",
  visibleIf: "{hasSecondary} = true",
  elements: [
    { type: "text", name: "carrier2", title: "Insurance carrier", isRequired: true },
    { type: "text", name: "memberId2", title: "Member ID", isRequired: true, startWithNewLine: false },
  ],
},

// Table where users add and remove rows
{
  type: "matrixdynamic",
  name: "allergies",
  title: "Allergies",
  addRowText: "Add allergy",
  rowCount: 0,
  columns: [
    { name: "allergen", title: "Allergen", cellType: "text", isRequired: true },
    { name: "severity", title: "Severity", cellType: "dropdown", choices: ["Mild", "Moderate", "Severe"] },
    { name: "reaction", title: "Reaction", cellType: "text" },
  ],
},

Note what isn't there: no list of fields per page, no trigger(), no useWatch, no useFieldArray, no mask function, no Stepper markup. Pages are just a pages array. "Next" validates the current page automatically. Answers to hidden questions are removed when the form is completed (the default clearInvisibleValues: "onComplete"). The phone mask both formats the input and rejects an incomplete number; by default it stores digits only, and saveMaskedValue: true keeps the formatted string.

Note on the progress indicator. The adapter styles SurveyJS's page progress bar in MUI colors, but its states don't look exactly like MUI's Stepper. The current page is an outlined circle (MUI fills it), and completed pages keep their number (MUI shows a check mark). The logic is also different. MUI marks every page before the current one as completed. SurveyJS marks a page as completed only if it was shown, has at least one answer, and has all its required questions answered. So an optional page the user skipped without answering anything stays grey. If you need an exact match, you can restyle the states with a few CSS rules; the "completed" logic itself is SurveyJS's.

The tally

Version B is 282 lines in 2 files:

File Lines Reusable?
patientIntakeSchema.ts (JSON schema, 4.6 KB minified) 253 no, one per form
SurveyJsIntake.tsx (renderer) 29 yes, renders any schema

Yes, the JSON is most of it. It's still code you review and version. But it's data: it can live in a database, come from an API, or be edited in a visual builder, which matters for the next sections.

Side by side

Here's how the two versions compare on the measures I'd care about in a real project. Line counts use the same rules on both sides; bundle sizes are gzip, for each version's lazy-loaded chunk in a production build.

MUI + react-hook-form + Zod SurveyJS + MUI adapter
Code for this form 451 lines, 3 files 282 lines, 2 files
Code for the next form a new Zod schema + a new component a new JSON schema
Where pages, conditions and rules live Zod + JSX + page config one JSON schema
Hidden-field cleanup, page validation, masks you write them built in
Who can change a form developers developers; non-developers via a visual builder
Look and feel native MUI follows your MUI theme, incl. dark mode
Layout control anything (sx, Grid, Stack) design tokens + your own CSS overrides
Type safety full inference from Zod runtime schema; typing the answers is extra work
JS added to the bundle ~74 KB (incl. the MUI components it uses) ~505 KB, plus ~61 KB of CSS

Three things stand out.

The line count gap is real but modest: about 1.6x. If you came for a "10 lines vs. 1,000 lines" headline, this isn't it. A well-factored react-hook-form version is not huge, and a complete JSON schema is not tiny. The gap grows with every additional form, because Version B's per-form cost is only the schema, but line count isn't the strongest argument either way.

The bigger difference is where the logic lives. In Version A, one rule like "secondary insurance is required when the switch is on" is spread across the Zod schema, the JSX, the page config and the submit handler. In Version B it's two properties in one place: visibleIf on the section and isRequired on its fields. The next section shows what that means when requirements change.

Bundle size is SurveyJS's weak spot. Half a megabyte of gzipped JavaScript is a lot, and you should weigh it. In practice, forms like this usually live on their own route, so load that route lazily (the companion app does, with React.lazy) and the cost is paid only by users who open the form. If your form sits on a performance-critical landing page, Version A is the better choice.

The change-request test

Forms rarely stay finished, so the most useful test is a realistic ticket:

If any allergy is marked Severe, the Reaction field becomes required, and the form asks a new question: "Do you carry an epinephrine auto-injector?" (required when shown).

I applied it to both versions. Each change is a separate commit in the repo, so you can see the full diffs.

Version A: 3 files, +29 / -3 lines

The Zod schema gets the new field and two cross-field rules:

+    carriesEpinephrine: z.enum(["yes", "no", ""]),
   ...
+    v.allergies.forEach((a, i) => {
+      if (a.severity === "Severe" && !a.reaction.trim())
+        ctx.addIssue({ code: "custom", path: ["allergies", i, "reaction"], message: "Describe the reaction for severe allergies." });
+    });
+    if (v.allergies.some((a) => a.severity === "Severe") && !v.carriesEpinephrine)
+      ctx.addIssue({ code: "custom", path: ["carriesEpinephrine"], message: "Response required." });

The component needs the question, a watcher to decide when to show it, an updated page config, and cleanup on submit:

-  { title: "History", fields: ["allergies"] },
+  { title: "History", fields: ["allergies", "carriesEpinephrine"] },
+  const watchedAllergies = useWatch({ control, name: "allergies" });
+  const hasSevereAllergy = watchedAllergies.some((a) => a.severity === "Severe");
   ...
+    if (!data.allergies.some((a) => a.severity === "Severe")) {
+      data = { ...data, carriesEpinephrine: "" };
+    }
   ...
+          {hasSevereAllergy && (
+            <RadioInput control={control} name="carriesEpinephrine" ... />
+          )}

And a surprise: my shared RadioInput had never needed to show a validation error, so it couldn't. A shared component had to change for a one-question ticket.

Notice that the condition "has a severe allergy" is now written three times: in the schema, in the visibility check and in the submit cleanup. They must agree forever.

Version B: 1 file, +16 / -1 lines 

-            { name: "reaction", title: "Reaction", cellType: "text", placeholder: "Reaction" },
+            {
+              name: "reaction",
+              title: "Reaction",
+              cellType: "text",
+              placeholder: "Reaction",
+              requiredIf: "{row.severity} = 'Severe'",
+              requiredErrorText: "Describe the reaction for severe allergies.",
+            },
           ],
         },
+        {
+          type: "boolean",
+          name: "carriesEpinephrine",
+          title: "Do you carry an epinephrine auto-injector?",
+          displayMode: "radio",
+          visibleIf: "countInArray({allergies}, 'severity', {severity} = 'Severe') > 0",
+          isRequired: true,
+        },

Each condition is written once, next to the thing it controls. Validation, visibility, the required marker and clearing the hidden answer all follow from those two expressions. No component changed. (displayMode: "radio" shows the yes/no question as radio buttons, like Version A. A boolean can also render as a segmented button, a checkbox or a switch.)

And because the change is pure data, it doesn't have to be a code change at all. If the schema is loaded from your backend, this ticket ships without a frontend deploy, and someone outside the dev team could make it in a visual builder. Whether you want that is a team decision, but it's an option Version A doesn't have.

Your theme, applied live

This is the part that makes SurveyJS usable in an MUI app at all. The adapter reads the variables MUI generates from your theme: the palette (primary, error, text, background, divider, action states), shape.borderRadius, the font family, spacing and shadows. Change any of them in createTheme, and the survey follows; there's no separate SurveyJS theme to keep in sync.

Light and dark mode work the same way. The companion app's header button is plain MUI:

const { mode, systemMode, setMode } = useColorScheme();
const isDark = (mode === "system" ? systemMode : mode) === "dark";

<Button color="inherit" onClick={() => setMode(isDark ? "light" : "dark")}>
  {isDark ? "Light mode" : "Dark mode"}
</Button>

There's no SurveyJS code involved: the survey switches together with the rest of the page, keeps the user's answers, and isn't re-created.

Version A gets this for free too, of course: it is MUI. The point is that Version B doesn't stand out as "the embedded third-party widget" next to the rest of your UI.

Where the adapter stops, and how to finish the job

The adapter can only follow what MUI puts into CSS variables. Decisions you make in components never reach it:

  • sx props and styled() rules
  • layout from Box, Stack and Grid (spacing, columns, responsive breakpoints)
  • custom component variants and theme components overrides
  • your own design system built on top of MUI

So expect the colors, fonts, corners and shadows to match right away, and the spacing and a few layout conventions to need a small nudge. In my test, the most visible difference was density: SurveyJS puts 40px between questions by default, while my hand-built form used <Stack spacing={3}> (24px).

An override file you own

The fix is a small stylesheet that you load after the adapter:

import "survey-core/survey-core.css";
import "survey-core/themes/adapters/mui.css";
import "./survey-overrides.css"; // yours, loaded last

Prefer design tokens over selectors. Tokens are a stable API; SurveyJS's internal class names are less so. Matching MUI's spacing={3} is one line:

.sjs-theme-overrides {
  --sjs2-layout-component-page-content-area-gap-vertical: 24px;
}

The design token reference lists the tokens for spacing, radius, typography and individual components. Use a class selector only when no token exists, and keep it narrow.

Example: error messages in a row

Here's one I hit while testing. When a short input (Date of birth) shares a row with a taller question (a radio group), SurveyJS stretches both to the same height and places the error message at the bottom of the row, well below the input. MUI developers expect helper text directly under the field. One rule fixes it:

/* Keep error messages directly under their inputs, like MUI helper text */
.sd-question__header-and-content-container {
  flex-grow: 0;
}

Practical gotchas

  • Mobile layout follows the container, not the screen. SurveyJS switches to its single-column mobile layout when its own container is narrower than 600px (--sd-mobile-width). In a two-column page or a narrow drawer, you can get the mobile layout on a desktop screen.
  • Next.js. Render the survey in a client component ("use client"). If you add Survey Creator, create it only on the client, after mount.
  • Heavily customized themes. If your app goes far beyond the standard MUI theme, the official MUI form builder page covers the limits, and the demo repo has a complete override file to start from.

So which one should you use?

After building both, here's my honest checklist.

Stay with react-hook-form + Zod when:

  • you have a few forms that rarely change
  • the form needs custom interactions or pixel-exact layouts that a schema-driven renderer would fight
  • end-to-end type safety from schema to API matters more than speed of change
  • the form sits on a page where every kilobyte of JavaScript counts

Consider SurveyJS + the MUI adapter when:

  • you maintain many forms, or forms whose questions change every few sprints
  • forms have real logic: conditional sections, dynamic rows, rules that depend on other answers
  • you want to store form definitions on the server, version them, or load them per customer
  • people outside the dev team should be able to adjust forms
  • you want all of that without the forms looking foreign in your MUI app

The two also mix well. Nothing stops you from keeping your login and settings forms in react-hook-form and moving the long, frequently changing ones to SurveyJS.

Try it yourself

  • Companion repo with both versions and the change-request commit: Try it yourself
  • Live demo of the MUI adapter, with a hand-coded form next to it: mui-theme-adapter.demos.surveyjs.io
  • Adapter setup guide: Theme adapters: Material UI
  • Free online form builder that generates the JSON: surveyjs.io/create-free-survey

title: Lessons from 3D scanning St John’s Co-Cathedral
description:
Seven nights, 99,000 photographs and 25 billion triangles showed us where photogrammetry works and where gold, marble and fabric still beat it, as we reported at SIGGRAPH 2026.

Summary

Over seven nights of evening-only access, we digitised St John’s Co-Cathedral in Valletta, Malta, a UNESCO World Heritage site holding two Caravaggio paintings. The result is a photogrammetric reconstruction of 25 to 30 billion triangles, built from 99,000 photographs and 43 laser scans, alongside an experimental Gaussian splatting reconstruction of one chapel.

I served as the external technical expert for St John’s Co-Cathedral Foundation, leading this project. Andre Grima, Peter Pullicino and Matthew Pullicino from Stargate Studios Malta carried out the digitisation and production. Matthew Kenely from SeyTravel and Mark Bugeja from the University of Malta handled the documentation. This project was part-financed by The Melita Foundation.

7 nights · 99,000 photographs · 43 LiDAR scans · 2.18 TB processed · 3 months of processing · 25 to 30 billion triangles

The complete technical methodology, including the equipment specifications, accuracy metrics and processing pipeline, is documented in the peer-reviewed paper, Large-Scale Photogrammetric Documentation of St John’s Co-Cathedral: A Workflow for Cultural Heritage Preservation, presented at ACM SIGGRAPH 2026 Art Papers and available on The ACM Digital Library as Open Access (free) here: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3816089.

Once-in-a-generation opportunity

The year 2023 sounds like just another year in the 400+-year-old history of a cathedral, but it did, in fact, open a once-in-a-generation opportunity. The last pieces of the Perellos Tapestries had just returned to Malta after an extensive 16-year restoration process of the entire set of 29. This is the largest set in the world and was designed and tailored for St John’s Co-Cathedral in Valletta.

In April 2023, the co-cathedral decided to display them in the church, probably for the last time, since they are destined for the new museum now under construction.. The last time they were displayed in the church was in 1990, during Pope Saint John Paul II's visit.

The tapestries were to be brought down in July of the same year, and we were responsible for creating a digital model of the cathedral with the tapestries set up. I was tasked with leading this process, and within weeks, the team was formed, and the work began. Stargate Studios were chosen to carry out the digitisation and production aspect of this project.

St John’s Co-Cathedral receives approximately 3,000 visitors every day, making it Malta’s most popular tourist attraction. At the same time, it is an active place of worship, and Mass is celebrated daily. In other words, this limits scanning to late evenings and nights.

When your access is limited to evenings, you cannot afford to waste a moment. We meticulously planned and started immediately.

The scanning stage

We could access the space for scanning only from 7 pm onward, which also provided controlled lighting. We completed the entire acquisition over seven nights.

Three instruments were used for the scanning:

  1. DSLR: Canon EOS R5 cameras with 24mm lenses captured at native 8K, including from scaffolding and lifts for ceiling coverage.
  2. Drone: A DJI Mavic 3 Pro Cine drone provided elevated 5K perspectives at altitudes of 3 to 15 metres, with manually planned flight paths.
  3. LiDAR Scanner: A Faro Focus M70 delivered geometric structure through 60-minute scans, each producing over 100 million points.

Traditional photogrammetry requires circling objects from every direction, but that is impossible within such a space. A modified approach was therefore developed, beginning with wide shots, then moving incrementally closer and shooting chapels from outside their entrances to maintain alignment with the nave.

Stargate Studios carefully chose the range of instruments to maximise the processing stage. The sharp focus mattered more than a clean ISO in a dark building because it revealed fine detail for the photogrammetry algorithm to detect and align. Noise, or digital grain, can be removed later, but features cannot be reconstructed. The drone was manually piloted in key strategic areas of the cathedral to capture visual features at altitudes that were difficult for a human operator to reach. Finally, the LiDAR scanning provided the geometry within which the texture features captured by photography could be anchored.

Why gold leaf and photogrammetry are not friends

Photogrammetry fails on shiny surfaces that look too good. It assumes a point on a surface looks the same from every angle. Gold leaf, bronze and dark marble break that assumption, because their highlights move with the camera, so the software matches reflections instead of surfaces.

This was addressed by reducing contrast to flatten the images, because textures respond better to manual lighting in final applications and photogrammetry algorithms interpret colour variation as geometric change. Flattening dark imagery captured at ISO 12800 to 25600 introduces significant digital grain, particularly across the cathedral’s bronze, wood, and metal.

Adobe’s AI denoiser performed excellently but struggled with batches larger than 2,000 photos, so denoising all 99,000 images took approximately one month of continuous processing. The result preserves fine detail in the gilt work while producing much cleaner dark areas.

Where software stopped, and people started

LiDAR software merges scans on its own but cannot distinguish a 400-year-old column from a stack of chairs left out overnight or a scaffolding pole. This meant that all 43 scans were manually cleaned after capture. Separately, denoising had smoothed away some of the fine detail that the aligner depended on, so 108 control points, landmarks marked by hand in several photos so the software could tie them together, were entered manually. That is what produced 98.6% of images in a single aligned component.

Point cloud to mesh

We combined the three capture methods into one detailed model in four stages. First, there is a sparse point cloud with visible gaps, such as the altar painting. Then, a denser cloud is created by merging the remaining photographs and LiDAR data. The third step is an aligned, cleaned point cloud (without texture and colour), and the blue patches you see are just the back faces of the cropped section. This shouldn’t be confused with missing data. The fourth and last image is the finished, textured mesh.

The figure below shows the visual result of the process.

For scale, this one chapel section alone results in around a billion triangles. The full cathedral reconstruction sits somewhere between 25 and 30 billion.

What still resists the process

Not every surface was reconstructed cleanly, and the paper documents the failures as openly as the successes.

The tapestries

The twenty-nine Flemish tapestries, woven on Rubens’ designs, were photographed in 8K while hanging in the nave. They came out worse than anything else in the building. These tapestries are made out of fine wool and silk, with the largest ones measuring approximately 6x6m.

Hanging fabric moves with the building’s air circulation, and any movement between frames reads as error. The size of the tapestries, coupled with the time required to capture the images, meant there were enough small movements to distort the tapestries’ visuals in the first iteration of the 3D model, as shown below.

This was eventually fixed by photographing them flat during conservation and reprojecting onto smoothed meshes.

The dark curved marble

The funerary monument of Grand Master Zondadari, extremely dark, highly reflective and geometrically complex, pushed the pipeline to its limits. Visible artefacts remain on its curved marble edges despite LiDAR support. This demonstrates the technique’s limits with specular materials in low light.

The 3D asset

We merged the LiDAR point cloud with the photographic dataset. Of 93,066 images imported after quality review, 91,721 were successfully registered into a single aligned component, a 98.6% success rate. This produced 137.2 million tie points, the matched features that hold the model together, with a mean reprojection error of 0.26 pixels. In other words, each point lands on average about a quarter of a pixel from where the photos say it should be. Where automatic alignment failed, 108 manually placed control points bridged the gap. Total alignment time was roughly 24 production hours.

We also tested Gaussian splatting on one chapel, the Chapel of Germany. It kept the reflections on the gilding that the mesh loses, but the surfaces dissolve at close range, so we treat it as a companion to the mesh and not a replacement.

The LiDAR data required extensive cleanup before integration, since reflective surfaces degrade laser scan accuracy, introducing noise and, in some cases, false points below ground level. Across all 43 scans, mean point error came to 1.3 millimetres, tightening to 0.9 millimetres across the 28 scans covering the core nave.

The dataset was too large to process as a single unit. Each chapel was reconstructed individually before being combined by side; the altar section’s 33,000 photographs were split into roughly five processing chunks, and the completed point cloud was divided by room for mesh generation, with the altar alone split into nine overlapping pieces. Each room section produced approximately one billion triangles, for a project total of 25 to 30 billion triangles.

What is the archive for?

This project focused on scanning and creating a high-fidelity, millimetric scan of the cathedral. The completed reconstruction supports several applications documented in the paper.

These include disaster recovery documentation, providing a precise geometric record in the event of damage. When fire tore through Notre-Dame in 2019, laser scans made years earlier by the art historian Andrew Tallon became a reference for the restoration.

Conservation planning, allowing structural analysis without repeated physical access. Virtual tourism, opening global access to a space most visitors will never enter. As a dataset, this project also aims to strengthen scholarly research by enabling detailed examination of architectural and artistic elements at a level ordinary site visits don’t allow.

From a graphics and scientific perspective, the paper is equally clear about the model’s limitations. It captures the cathedral at a single point in time, geometry and colour, but not physical material properties like hardness or composition, and movable elements such as furniture and liturgical items were removed or repositioned during processing, so the model does not reflect the building’s day-to-day “in use” state. That gap between how a space looks and how it behaves is also an open problem in physical AI, where a machine needs to know what a surface is made of before it touches it. Periodic rescanning, as the paper notes, would be needed to track ongoing conservation change over time, and that in itself opens the dataset to further research opportunities.

Frequently asked questions

I posted about this paper and project on social media, and I received direct messages with specific questions. To make it easier to follow, I put together these FAQs:

What is photogrammetry? Photogrammetry is a technique for reconstructing three-dimensional geometry from overlapping two-dimensional photographs. Software identifies matching points across many images taken from different positions and triangulates their location in 3D space.

What is Gaussian splatting and how does it compare to photogrammetric meshes? Gaussian splatting represents a scene as a cloud of translucent 3D primitives rather than solid triangle geometry. It preserves reflections and view-dependent lighting effects that meshes struggle with, but loses geometric solidity at close viewing range. The two are best used as complementary representations.

How much data was captured? The processed dataset totalled approximately 2.18 TB, or roughly 22 MB per image after grading and denoising. All images were downscaled to 4K before alignment to keep the computational load manageable.

What software was used? Photogrammetric reconstruction was carried out in RealityCapture v1.5.1 (now RealityScan), which handled the alignment of the photographic dataset and its integration with the LiDAR point cloud. LiDAR registration and cleanup were done in Faro SCENE. Grain introduced during grading was removed with Adobe’s AI denoiser. The final meshes were subdivided for real-time use in Unreal Engine. Custom scripting handled proxy generation and systematic file naming across the 55 SD cards, and an automated plugin was used to split the altar mesh into overlapping pieces.

Can the public access the 3D model? Not yet, but the Foundation and our team are already working on the next phase.

The full SIGGRAPH 2026 paper

This post summarises the workflow at a high level.

The paper itself contains the complete methodology, full equipment specifications, all accuracy metrics and processing tables, and a discussion section with practical recommendations for heritage professionals planning similar large-scale digitisation projects.

Citation: Matthew Kenely, Mark Bugeja, Andre Grima, Peter Pullicino, Matthew Pullicino, Dylan Seychell, Large-Scale Photogrammetric Documentation of St John’s Co-Cathedral: A Workflow for Cultural Heritage Preservation, ACM SIGGRAPH 2026 Art Papers, Los Angeles, 19 to 23 July 2026. Published in the Proceedings of the ACM on Computer Graphics and Interactive Techniques (PACMCGIT).

Dr Dylan Seychell is a resident academic in the Department of Artificial Intelligence at the University of Malta, where he founded and leads the Dawl AI Lab. His research applies computer vision and machine learning to the environment, through drones and geospatial AI, and to the information ecosystem, through news analysis and media transparency tools. The lab’s litter detection work won the Research and Innovation Award at the Sustainable Development Action Awards 2026. He is Principal Investigator of Malta’s National AI Literacy Programme, AI Għal Kulħadd, which has reached over 50,000 learners. Since 2019, he has advised the St John’s Co-Cathedral Foundation on technology, including the Caravaggio Wing. Face to Face with Caravaggio won the Best Use of Digital award at the 2026 Museums + Heritage Awards.

title: Introducing Dioptra: A Zero-Config, Pure-Go Interactive UI Engine for AI Agents
description:
Hey everyone! I'm Bryan, a software engineer. Over the past few months, I've been reflecting a lot on where our profession is heading and how our daily workflows are evolving alongside AI. Because I genuinely love software engineering and building for builders, I started creating open-source tools to give back to the community—and today, I'd love to share my latest contribution with you.

Meet Dioptra: a local-first, zero-config interactive reporting and UI engine built for developers and AI agents.

JbryanH187 / Dioptra

Tired of reading raw Markdown walls, ehh 😏? A fast single-binary Go MCP viewer that turns AI agent outputs into slick local UI reports & clickable approvals.

DioptraEngine (dioptra)

Tired of reading raw Markdown walls, ehh 😏? A fast single-binary Go MCP viewer that turns AI agent outputs into slick local UI reports & clickable approvals.

A fast, local, single-binary technical report viewer and MCP server for AI coding agents — written in pure Go, with zero API keys and near-zero token overhead.

AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, OpenCode, Antigravity, Gentle Shell, etc.) generate rich audits, architecture plans, code reviews, diffs, and postmortems that get buried in terminal scrollback. Dioptra moves those long deliverables out of the terminal into an interactive local web workspace (http://127.0.0.1:7474) backed by SQLite FTS5, live SSE updates, bidirectional human-in-the-loop checklists, a multi-role agent board, and an E2E test observer.

Why Dioptra?

  • Deterministic Markdown → Rich UI (Zero LLM calls by default): Plain GitHub Markdown converts in milliseconds (fast_goldmark, ~1% extra token overhead) into sortable…
View on GitHub

What is Dioptra?

When working with CLI coding agents or automated workflows, reading massive walls of terminal Markdown or managing human-in-the-loop approvals quickly gets messy. Dioptra solves this by turning standard Markdown into rich, interactive local dashboards in milliseconds—with zero external dependencies or API keys required.

Key Highlights

  • Pure Go single binary (CGO_ENABLED=0), MIT licensed: Zero Node.js or CDN runtime required. Features embedded Shadow DOM Web Components and pure-Go SQLite (WAL + FTS5/BM25). Cross-platform binaries are ready out of the box via GoReleaser (linux/darwin/windows on amd64/arm64).
  • Deterministic Markdown → UI (fast_goldmark, 0 API keys, ~1% token overhead): Converts standard GitHub-Flavored Markdown (## sections, sortable tables, kpi fences, mermaid → D2 SVG, syntax-highlighted diff, [!WARNING] callouts, and - [ ] checklists) into interactive views in milliseconds.
  • Bidirectional human-in-the-loop approvals: Check or uncheck action items directly in your browser at http://127.0.0.1:7474, and your MCP-connected agent reads the exact approval state back via get_report_state.
  • Idempotent updates + Live SSE: Republishing a report updates the UI in place seamlessly via Server-Sent Events instead of cluttering your workspace with duplicates.
  • Local-first security: Runs strictly on loopback (127.0.0.1) with a Host allowlist, Origin / Sec-Fetch-Site / Content-Type write guards, and a strict Content Security Policy (CSP).

Try it out & Share your thoughts!

Dioptra is completely open-source and MIT licensed. If you work with MCP agents, CLI tools, or local automation workflows, I'd love for you to give it a spin:

Repository: github.com/JbryanH187/Dioptra

Feedback, ideas, issues, and stars are hugely appreciated. Let me know in the comments what you think or what kind of workflows you'd plug this into!

title: React: reserva espacio para mensajes de email
description:
Un formulario de registro puede estar bien diseñado y aun así sentirse roto cuando llega el mensaje de validación. El campo crece, el botón baja y la persona pierde el lugar donde estaba leyendo. En móvil, ese salto es más molesto todavía.

La solución no es esconder el error ni mostrarlo en un toast que desaparece. Es reservar un espacio estable para el resultado, anunciar el cambio a tecnologías de asistencia y mantener la interacción predecible. En React, este patrón también hace más sencillas las pruebas de interfaz con email.

El problema: el mensaje llega y mueve toda la pantalla

Imagina un formulario que pide una dirección de correo temporal para crear una cuenta de prueba. Al enviar, la aplicación espera la respuesta del servidor y luego agrega un texto bajo el campo:

{error && <p className="field-error">{error}</p>}

Visualmente parece practico, pero el párrafo no existía durante el primer render. Cuando aparece, empuja los controles siguientes. Si la persona estaba a punto de pulsar el botón, puede terminar pulsando otra cosa.

Hay dos problemas distintos:

  • Estabilidad visual: el contenido nuevo cambia la posición de elementos existentes.
  • Comunicación: una persona que usa un lector de pantalla puede no enterarse de que la validación terminó.

El segundo problema no se arregla solo con color rojo. El estado debe tener nombre, relación con el campo y una forma clara de anunciarse.

Reserva el espacio antes de conocer el resultado

Una forma sencilla es mantener el contenedor del mensaje en el DOM y darle una altura mínima. El contenido puede estar vacío cuando no hay error, pero el campo conserva su geometría.

.field-message {
  min-height: 1.5rem;
  margin-block-start: 0.35rem;
  color: #8a1c1c;
  font-size: 0.9rem;
}

.field-message:empty {
  visibility: hidden;
}

visibility: hidden conserva el espacio sin dejar un mensaje invisible en el recorrido visual. No uses display: none para el estado vacío si esa decisión hace que el layout vuelva a saltar.

En diseños con mensajes de dos líneas, reserva la altura realista para el caso más largo. No hace falta dejar un bloque enorme: basta con que la interfaz no cambie de forma cada vez que una respuesta del servidor es un poco mas larga.

Un componente React con estados previsibles

El componente puede asociar el mensaje con el campo mediante aria-describedby. role="alert" es apropiado para un error que necesita atención inmediata, pero no conviene aplicarlo a cada pequeño cambio de ayuda mientras la persona escribe.

function EmailField({ value, error, onChange }) {
  const messageId = "email-message";

  return (
    <div className="field">
      <label htmlFor="email">Correo electrónico</label>
      <input
        id="email"
        name="email"
        type="email"
        value={value}
        onChange={onChange}
        aria-invalid={Boolean(error)}
        aria-describedby={messageId}
      />
      <p
        id={messageId}
        className="field-message"
        role={error ? "alert" : undefined}
      >
        {error || ""}
      </p>
    </div>
  );
}

Hay una frontera importante: el cliente no debe inventar que un email fue entregado. Puede mostrar “comprobando” mientras espera y “no pudimos validar todavía” cuando la respuesta falla. Los textos deben describir el estado real, no el estado que nos gustaria tener.

Para una explicación relacionada, vale la pena revisar estos estados de verificación que sí explican. El mismo principio funciona para errores de formato, códigos expirados y respuestas tardías.

CSS para accesibilidad y rendimiento

Reservar espacio evita cambios de layout, pero no convierte automáticamente el formulario en accesible. Revisa también el contraste, el foco visible y el orden de lectura. El mensaje debe aparecer cerca del campo que lo origina, no en una zona que la persona tiene que buscar.

Si prefieres animar el estado, anima opacity o transform con cuidado y respeta prefers-reduced-motion. No animes la altura de todo el formulario cada vez que llega una respuesta. Ese movimiento puede ser costoso y además dificulta leer el mensaje.

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  .field-message {
    transition: opacity 160ms ease;
  }
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .field-message {
    transition: none;
  }
}

El rendimiento percibido mejora cuando el botón no cambia de posición, aunque la petición tarde unos milisegundos más de lo esperado. Es un detalle pequeño que suele tener mas impacto que añadir otro indicador decorativo.

Cómo probarlo con mensajes de email

En una prueba de componente, comprueba primero la geometría conceptual: el mensaje existe aunque esté vacío, tiene una relación accesible con el input y cambia cuando llega el resultado. En una prueba de extremo a extremo, provoca tanto un email inválido como una respuesta retrasada.

Para una revisión manual puedes usar una bandeja aislada como tempmailso, pero no mezcles esa comprobación con cuentas personales ni con datos reales. También ayuda comparar las señales útiles en emails de trial con los estados que realmente enseña tu interfaz.

Si el equipo escribe tempail mail en una incidencia, trátalo como texto de búsqueda y no como nombre de una variable o un contrato de API. Los typos aparecen en el trabajo real; los identificadores del código deben permanecer estables.

Checklist y preguntas rápidas

Antes de cerrar el formulario, revisa:

  • ¿El mensaje tiene espacio reservado desde el primer render?
  • ¿El input usa aria-invalid cuando corresponde?
  • ¿aria-describedby apunta siempre a un nodo existente?
  • ¿El foco y el contraste siguen siendo visibles con error?
  • ¿La prueba cubre respuesta lenta, error y reintento?
  • ¿La interfaz respeta prefers-reduced-motion?

¿Debo reservar espacio para todos los mensajes? Para errores, ayuda contextual y estados que cambian la posición de los controles, normalmente sí. Si el mensaje aparece fuera del flujo, como una notificación global, usa otro patrón y asegúrate de anunciarlo.

¿Puedo validar solo al perder el foco? Sí, suele ser menos ruidoso que validar cada tecla. Para el envío final, muestra el error junto al campo y conserva el espacio para que el resultado no desplace el botón.

¿Qué pasa si el mensaje es muy largo? Define una longitud razonable, escribe el texto con claridad y deja que crezca cuando sea necesario. Un salto ocasional es preferible a cortar información importante, pero los casos normales deben quedar estables.

Un formulario React no tiene que elegir entre buen aspecto y buena accesibilidad. Si reserva espacio, comunica el estado y prueba la llegada real de los mensajes, la validación se siente tranquila incluso cuando el email tarda. Esa combinación de CSS sencillo y estados honestos suele ser el pulido que más se nota.
